Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
- Published
Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.
The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.
The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.
The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday.
In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.
The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.
White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.
It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.
This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.
The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".
Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.
Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.
In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.
A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.
In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.
White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.
In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

Dozens stranded at sea after Solomon Islands ferry engine fails
More than 70 passengers have been stranded aboard a drifting ferry in Solomon Islands waters since Friday, as an international operation scrambles to get supplies to the vessel.
The ferry was sailing between the remote islands of Anuta and Vanikoro in Temotu Province when its engine failed on Friday, leaving it adrift at sea.
A Panama-registered bulk carrier reached MV Awka on Sunday morning and began transferring water and food, passenger John Tua said.
Mr Tua, a nurse with the provincial government, said the engine was overheating when it broke down about 100 nautical miles from its destination.
"Everyone is OK, no-one panicked, passengers were calm … we're just waiting for the rescue ships to come,"
he said.
While the seas have been mostly calm, Mr Tua said the ship had also experienced rough swells.
A distress call was issued on Friday, with the Solomon Islands enlisting help from the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) and New Caledonian government.
An AMSA spokesperson said its Cairns-based rescue jet made several drops of critical items including food, water, medical supplies and communications equipment.
A French aircraft from New Caledonia was first on the scene on Saturday, dropping life rafts and desalination equipment.
"The urgent need was water. We've run out of water onboard … the ship's water supply was used to cool the engine down when it was heating up," Mr Tua said.
"We have lots of brown coconuts on board to drink, but our water is finished."
On Sunday morning, the Panama-registered bulk carrier Sunnine 3 reached the vessel early and began transferring water and food, which was lifestreamed online by Mr Tua.
Passengers have stayed in touch with families using the ship's Starlink internet, while Mr Tua has been the main source of news for worried relatives.
Temotu Premier Stanley Tehiahua said a police patrol boat was on its way from Honiara.
"To all relatives, families and friends anxiously awaiting news of their loved ones, we recognise the emotional distress and uncertainty you are experiencing," he said in a statement.
"We call on everyone to remain calm, united and prayerful during this difficult time,"
Mr Tehiahua said.
The ABC has requested comment from the Solomon Islands Maritime Safety Administration and the country's Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre.
The incident comes three weeks after the inter-island ferry MV Matui sank in rough seas in neighbouring Vanuatu with more than 50 people onboard. More than 30 people from the MV Matui are still missing.
There have been calls for Australia and New Zealand to invest more in maritime safety, including from Peter Nuttall, a sustainable researcher at the University of the South Pacific, who told the ABC after the Matui sinking that Australia could easily invest in better vessels for the Pacific.
"We could have built 40 to 60 safe, brand new, low-carbon ferries for the same budget as we've spent on 20-something patrol boats, several which have already been scrapped," Dr Nuttall said.

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

Why Elon Musk is taking on India's richest man over Starlink
- Published
Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure final approval to launch in the country.
The remark came a day after Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. He then singled out Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network operator.
India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory.
Ambani and Reliance Group have not responded to Musk's remarks. The BBC has reached out to them for comment
The row comes as competition grows in India's satellite internet market, with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel also preparing to launch services.
The rivalry is complicated by the fact that Starlink has also partnered with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel.
In March 2025, both companies signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment and services in India, subject to government approval. The companies also said they could explore sharing network infrastructure. The BBC has also reached out to Bharti Airtel for comment.
Musk first made the allegations on Wednesday, accusing "certain oligarchs" of maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers.
"You can guess who they are," he wrote on X, external, adding that blocking Starlink was "a crime against the people of India".
On Thursday, India's Ministry of Communications responded, saying that three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services.
"The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said, without naming Musk directly.
Musk continued to question the delay, saying Starlink was already licensed in more than 165 countries.
"Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?" he wrote on X on Thursday.
Starlink, owned by Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install.
The company has been trying to enter India since 2021 and has secured key licences. But it still needs final security clearances and spectrum allocation before it can begin commercial services.
Wednesday's row unfolded as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in Delhi, where all three companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services.
Speaking at the event, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and Mukesh Ambani's son, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards regulatory approvals.
Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment and only said, "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Bharti Airtel chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said his company's satellite venture was also awaiting government approvals.
SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer, who oversees Starlink's business operations, said the company had spent years working with Indian regulators and had built security controls into its network to meet the country's requirements.
Security has been a key concern surrounding Starlink's entry into India. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had recovered Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the remote Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army operation in the northeastern state of Manipur.
Musk said at that time that Starlink's service had never been active in India, arguing that the equipment recovered by authorities could not have been using its satellite network.
Questions also remain over how affordable the service would be for Indian consumers, particularly those in rural areas.
India is one of the world's largest internet markets but access remains uneven, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to build.
Musk has argued that Starlink could help bridge this gap. "Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all!" he wrote on X on Wednesday.
The company has yet to announce prices for India, but some experts say its plans elsewhere suggest the service could be beyond the reach of many Indian households.
In the US, Starlink's residential plans start at $55 a month, although prices and equipment costs vary by plan and location.

The most moving scene in “The First Taste of Loneliness” is not, in fact, its most tear-streaked. Gu You‘s heartfelt family portrait opens on an extended, anguished scene of three women — a mother, her daughter and her granddaughter — keeping vigil at the bedside of their beloved husband, father and grandfather as his longtime battle with pancreatic cancer comes to a close. Emotions run high and loud; the camera peers closely into their grief. But it’s a quieter, more composed moment a little later that really jabs at the heart. A short time after her father’s death, Yue (Zhou Xun) opens the final jar of his famous homemade pickles, tastes them, and with the bittersweet knowledge that she’ll never get to do so again, declares it a good batch.
“The First Taste of Loneliness” is best when focused on such small but important everyday details. Its portrayal of the immediate, intense pain of mourning can be overwrought, but the bulk of this admittedly overlong film is given over to a more patient, restrained and gracefully observed study of how life reshapes itself around an absence — as Yue, her mother Luna (Xi Meijuan) and her teenage daughter Moon (Wang Shengdi) deal with the sadness, the relief and the faint sense of betrayal that comes from carrying on, while keeping space for the dead man’s spirit in their respective lives.
Popular on Variety
Shot and structured with grand-scale elegance to counter the intimacy of the storytelling, this is a stirring final entry in Gu’s “Landscape” trilogy, which began with his Cannes-premiered 2019 debut “Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains” and continued with 2023’s “Dwelling by the West Lake” — the three films connected not directly by characters or narratives but a shared style of melancholic family portraiture. Premiering in the main competition at the Busan Film Festival, “Loneliness” again demonstrates the filmmaker’s formal prowess, with its preponderance of ambitiously floating pans and heavily populated setpieces. It has a broader, more populist streak than its predecessors, which could net it greater global distribution, but has its artistic downsides: An overreliance on stickily emotive ballads to unnecessarily articulate the characters’ feelings is a particular debit.
Somewhat heavily expository dialogue informs us that Yue, formerly a fashion director in Beijing, has recently returned with Moon to the family apartment in the city of Hangzhou in southeast China. Home to Luna and her late husband for decades, it’s a roomy, rambling space with spectacular views of the Qiantang River and, in Zhou Xingyu’s excellent production design, a storied buildup of clutter. Mikiya Takimoto’s camera lingers affectionately on stacked bookshelves — not even old cassette tapes have been thrown away — and desktops heavy with ornaments, notes and photographs that reveal in shorthand a life rich in love. Even in death, the man maintains a palpable presence in the home.
But it may be time for at least some remnants of the past to make way for the present. Luna implores Yue, recently divorced, not to get stuck in a holding pattern, either in her career or her relationships — but Luna, too, needs to make some changes. She tentatively accepts the romantic advances of another man, Xu (Xu Chaoying), opening herself to a kind of happiness she’d largely forgotten how to feel. Moon, meanwhile, is struggling at school but on the precipice of adulthood; as the young woman begins to make her own decisions in life, Yue must relinquish a degree of maternal responsibility.
Written by Gu with Yang Yikun, the screenplay, delicately braids these three arcs in such a way that each woman’s new freedoms complement the others’, while Takimoto’s bravura camerawork — painting in watercolor shades of misty gray and mossy green — often physically connects their stories in languid, widely swooping movements. And while the three leads’ performances are sensitively synched, Xi Meijuan is especially poignant as a widow trying to maintain a level of grieving decorum while embracing fresh experiences and sources of joy: A lovely scene of her and Xu dancing with other couples in a public square hits just the right note of romantic sentimentality tempered with elegiac sorrow. If “The First Taste of Loneliness” hits overly maudlin notes elsewhere — literally so, in the case of Sylvian Wang’s plaintive, piano-heavy score — it never feels cynical or manufactured in its emotions. Its moments of overstatement are entirely human, en route to a lighter, softer state of serenity.

Betsy Pleasants was studying one historic disruption to abortion access when a more seismic one emerged.
In spring 2022, as a graduate student at UC Berkeley School of Public Health, Pleasants was researching the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic on abortion services when a leaked draft opinion indicated that the U.S. Supreme Court would overturn Roe v. Wade. The court finalized its decision that June, ending the nearly 50-year-old constitutional right to abortion and ushering in an era of rapid change and increased state restrictions.
Working with her thesis committee, Pleasants, who is interested in expanding access to abortion and other reproductive health care, adapted her dissertation to study conversations on the social network Reddit. Her new focus was tracking emerging barriers to abortion access in real time and examining the role of online resources in connecting people with evidence-based health information and services.
“When it became clear that Roe v. Wade was going to be overturned, we all agreed that we had to shift the project,” said Pleasants, now a postdoctoral research associate at the Center for Women’s Health Research at the University of North Carolina. The Supreme Court decision “is something that required a response, and this project was positioned to offer timely insights into what this policy change means in people’s lives.”
Pleasants and her colleagues plumbed thousands of posts from the Reddit forum r/abortion using natural language processing (NLP) — a type of computational analysis used to identify patterns in human language — alongside a qualitative close reading of a subset of posts. Through this dual approach, grounded in safeguards for user privacy, Pleasants is defining a framework for using artificial intelligence tools without losing sight of the context, complexity, and people behind the data.
“We are in a complex policy moment for reproductive health,” said Pleasants, who was recently named a STAT Wunderkind. This type of research “is an act of documenting in an effort to work towards evidence-based policy change over time, and to advocate for the change that’s needed to promote access to reproductive health care.”
Findings by Pleasants and her colleagues reaffirmed well-established barriers to access, including high costs and limited appointment availability, while also revealing lesser-known challenges, such as delays in receiving abortion medications by mail, low credibility of online ordering platforms, and concerns about the legal risks of seeking abortion or related medical care.
“Embracing this opportunity and new methods was visionary,” said Ushma Upadhyay, professor in the Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Reproductive Sciences at the University of California San Francisco, who mentored Pleasants during her doctoral research. “At the time, I didn’t know of any other studies using NLP to study online discourse on abortion. Most researchers will just take a random sample of a manageable number that they can analyze, and so this approach was really great because Betsy was able to get a more complete picture.”
For scientists like Pleasants, the value of NLP goes beyond making large-scale research more efficient. It offers a broader view of how people communicate and behave at a scale that would otherwise be difficult to capture.
“Computational research is like a stepping stool over a tall fence that lets you look at the other side and see everything that’s around you,” said Danny Valdez, associate professor of public health at the Indiana School of Public Health-Bloomington, who has employed NLP to study vaccine misinformation, addiction and recovery, and cancer care. “NLP, machine learning, and, increasingly, AI methods give you a 1,000-foot overview of how people communicate when they need help. You can learn a lot about the pulse of the nation, which helps us understand and inform where future policy could be headed.”
A new model for studying online discourse
Growing up in North Carolina, Pleasants got her first window into how people access health information, sparking an interest that would eventually shape her career. Even in Durham, a liberal core city of North Carolina’s Research Triangle, she recalled receiving abstinence-only sex education from a gym teacher. The contrast between the information she received at school and at home made her aware of how unevenly health knowledge and resources could be distributed.
“I saw peers and other people in the community navigating not having good sex education, not having access to desired health services, and stigma,” said Pleasants. “All of these things really shaped the capacity they had to make decisions for themselves about their reproductive health.”
Those early observations would become a throughline in Pleasants’ career, from earning her undergraduate degree at the University of North Carolina to completing her master’s and doctorate at UC Berkeley, and ultimately returning to UNC for her postdoctoral research.
Pleasants entered college with an eye on becoming a physician, but was instead drawn to medical anthropology and broader discussions of how history, politics, and culture have shaped, and continue to shape, the U.S. health care system.
“A big question that came up for me was: ‘Do I want to work within that system or do I want to critically engage with it?’” said Pleasants. “So, I ended up on this trajectory of research with an interest in asking questions of how we offer health services, particularly for women, and seeking to understand how we can make that better for all people as much as possible.”
Analyzing r/abortion while at Berkeley allowed Pleasants to capture perspectives often overlooked by conventional research methods. The platform’s relative anonymity gave people space to speak candidly about personal experiences they might hesitate to share elsewhere. And because most community members had not interacted with the health care system, their experiences would often be missed by practice-based analysis.
“Following the reversal of Roe v. Wade, a lot of people were turning to Reddit for support,” said Upadhyay.
Pleasants and her collaborators used NLP to analyze more than 7,000 posts from the months before, during, and after the leak of the Supreme Court’s draft decision, identifying 55 distinct topics. Human oversight was integral throughout, both to validate the computational approach and to guide deeper qualitative analysis. The team closely examined posts within the identified topics to understand not only what people were discussing, but how they were navigating their experiences.
The research revealed a wide range of barriers to abortion care, from state bans, high costs, and long travel distances to stigma and lack of social support. It also surfaced emerging challenges, including delays receiving abortion medications by mail, uncertainty about the legitimacy of online services, and concerns about potential legal risks. The qualitative analysis provided further insight into the impacts of these barriers, including anxiety and isolation and, in some cases, the need to self-manage abortions.
The emphasis on human supervision also extended to protecting the privacy of Reddit users. As NLP and AI tools become more widely integrated into public health research, their use has fueled broader discussion, both within the research community and among the public, about the ethical use of online data. Pleasants said the stakes are particularly high in reproductive health research.
“We are studying issues that are, at minimum, sensitive and stigmatized, and in some cases even pose risks for prosecution,” she said. “This becomes even more complex when you’re working with publicly available data where people may not be aware that their posts could be used for research.”
To protect Reddit users, the team employed a “heavy disguise” process, replacing potentially identifiable posts with composite quotations that combined and rephrased similar experiences. The researchers then tested these composites using online searches and plagiarism-detection tools to help ensure they could not be traced back to their original sources.
Together, these practices have established a model for studying sensitive online discourse at scale.
“As this technology keeps getting faster and faster and faster, you do have very talented and forward-thinking researchers like Betsy, who are slowing things down and looking at how to make this as rigorous and concrete as possible through a very firm qualitative lens,” said Valdez, who was not involved in Pleasants’ research, though both have received funding from the Society of Family Planning. “We need work like Betsy’s that’s already acknowledged the difficulties of social media mining … and to show very high regard for the content that people are leaving on social media.”
Today, Pleasants said her research, which has now expanded to include contraception and misinformation online, has taken on greater urgency as shifting policies increasingly constrain access to reproductive health care. She noted that researchers, advocates, and clinicians in the field have long worked amid scrutiny and uncertainty.
“The importance of the research doesn’t lessen just because policies make the work harder. Rather, the opposite seems true right now,” she said.

During my 10+ years of clinical experience in various States and with numerous patient populations, I have seen that dental anxiety is a constant challenge. I have seen this phenomenon in children clutching their parents’ hands before their first cleaning and in accomplished professionals quietly cancelling appointment after appointment in the hope that the problem will somehow resolve itself.
It doesn’t.
In my experience, the longer you leave a fear unchecked, the greater the clinical and human cost becomes. Dental anxiety is not a moral failing. This is a well-documented psychological response—and one with important, measurable public health consequences.
How severe is it?
Roughly a third of people have significant dental anxiety, and roughly a tenth have a clinical phobia. That’s not a little footnote. That means a lot of the population is actively avoiding or delaying care that could prevent serious disease. The downstream consequences of this avoidance are visible daily in my clinical work: infections tolerated for months, decay advanced far beyond what early intervention would have required, and patients presenting with pain that could have been prevented years ago.
Knowing where it starts
Dental anxiety typically has a definite source. A painful or poorly done procedure in childhood can be a source of dental anxiety. A provider who was in a hurry or didn’t tell the patient what was happening. The specific sensory environment of a dental office—the sounds, the smells, and the physical vulnerability of lying back with your mouth open—can leave powerful imprints, especially in young patients. That memory is not just wiped out; it impacts behaviour for decades. For some, it’s not just one event but an accumulation. Years of avoidance layered on top of embarrassment about how their teeth look now, and a fear of judgment prevents them from asking for help. This cycle of shame avoidance is one of the hardest patterns I see clinically. When these patients do come in, they need much more intervention than if they had come in sooner, and this becomes an instance of the very fear that kept them away.
The health price of avoidance
Research literature teaches us, that oral health is not an island. Untreated dental disease is a chronic inflammatory load on the body. It has been linked to cardiovascular risk, dysregulated blood sugar, and impaired immune function. When a patient avoids dental care for years, it is not just their smile that is at risk; they are carrying a preventable health load that will rise elsewhere in time.
In addition to the system effects, the impact on quality of life is immediate and real. A toothache interferes with sleep. It impacts nutrition, concentration, and the ability to speak with confidence. These are not trivial consequences; they affect how people show up in their professional and personal lives every day.
What works in practice
The most significant change I’ve made in my practice is making communication a priority before any procedure begins. When patients feel informed and in control, it greatly reduces their dental anxiety. A stop signal—a raised hand that stops everything instantly—can alter the psychological dynamic in the room. It shifts the patient from passive recipient to active participant, and that shift matters enormously. I also allow extra time for anxious patients. The problem is not that procedures take longer, but that rushing them increases anxiety. I explain everything before it happens, check in frequently, and never minimise what a patient is feeling. These should not be luxury accommodations; they should be routine parts of effective care.
For patients with more severe anxiety, pharmacological support is appropriate. Nitrous oxide is safe, effective, and rapidly reversible. There are also oral sedation choices if needed. These are clinical tools, not last resorts, and patients should feel comfortable asking about them.
A message to patients
If fear has kept you from the dentist, remember you are not alone, and you are not too far gone to be helped. What I ask of patients in this situation is one small step—not a treatment plan, not a procedure, simply a conversation. Come in and tell us about your nervousness. A good provider is a good listener and will start there. There is no need to be afraid of the dental chair. With the right approach, it can be a place where you take difficult things and make them manageable—and where the relief on the other side is worth it.
(Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula is a U.S.-licensed dentist with international training who focuses on preventive and evidence-based oral healthcare and contributes to advancing community and public health dentistry. sowji.gunukula@gmail.com)

The Supreme Court on October 5 said it had not approved any modification to the contents of Form 6, directly contradicting the Election Commission’s (EC) recent claim that it alterations made in the form were upheld by the court. Form 6 is the document used by citizens to apply for inclusion of their names in the electoral roll.
The apex court was hearing a bunch of petitions challenging the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process and seeking the suspension of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar who has come under intense scrutiny following an Indian Express report published on September 25. It showed that Kumar had overruled written objections from election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi at least on 14 occasions in 10 months. One of the points of contention was modifications to Form 6.
On September 26, the ECI issued a press note saying that the “declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR” had been upheld by the Supreme Court.
On Monday, while arguing in front of a Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, senior advocates Menaka Guruswamy and Vikas Singh questioned the decision-making process followed by the three-member Election Commission. Guruswamy raised concerns over the use of a modified Form 6 during the SIR process.
“Let us see how the SIR was conducted in Delhi. Form 6 has two new conditions added. The modified Form 6 was circulated. The Schedule to the RPA contains Form 6. It cannot be modified in this manner,” she submitted.
In response, chief justice Surya Kant made the court’s position clear: “We have not approved Form 6. A modified Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let us be very clear.”

Guruswami also noted that the supposed ‘illegality’ of the SIR process had prevented the conduct of free and fair elections in India. “We have grown up with free and fair elections in this country. They do not exist today,” she said.
The court issued notices to the central election commission, the chief election commissioner and the two other commissioners, seeking their responses. The Bench further mentioned that if any decision taken by the Election Commission was found not to be in accordance with the law, it would be annulled.
The Controversy Regarding Form 6
Form 6 is a statutory form prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, framed under Section 28 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. This means the ECI cannot simply change the form or add new requirements whenever it wants. Any change to the statutory format has to be made through the parliament, rather than through an internal decision of the poll panel.
In states where the SIR is currently ongoing, such as Delhi and Karnataka, the online Form 6 available on the Election Commission’s website contains an additional declaration section between Sections J and K. In this section, an applicant has to state whether their name appears in the electoral roll from the previous SIR, whether their parents’ or grandparents’ names appear in that roll, or whether neither their name nor their parents’ names appear in the previous SIR electoral roll.
Although this declaration is not marked as mandatory, applicants cannot submit the online Form 6 without filling it in.
However, in states where the SIR has already been completed or has not yet started, such as West Bengal, the Form 6 link on the ECI website does not show this additional declaration.
Interestingly, if the Form 6 PDF is downloaded from the same ECI website for offline submission, there is no section asking for any SIR-related information. This means that the additional declaration appears to be present only in the online version of Form 6 being used in states where the SIR is underway.
SC’s May 2026 Bihar SIR Judgement
In a May 27, 2026 judgment on the Bihar SIR, the Supreme Court had said that the EC had some power to decide what documents it could ask voters to provide during an SIR.
On October 5, the ECI cited this to seemingly claim that the declarations added to Form 6 had been upheld by the Supreme Court. However, the SIR declarations in question added to Form 6 are different from what the Supreme Court had examined in the Bihar case. During the Bihar SIR, the ECI used a separate document called Annexure D.
The new declaration started appearing on the ECI’s online voter-registration system from July 2026.
Reacting to the controversy, Calcutta high court advocate Samim Ahammed said, “Despite being the holder of a constitutional post, the chief election commissioner’s conduct over the past few years has been arbitrary, with the Commission acting in violation of the Constitution and the laws of the land. The Commission does not have the power to legislate or make changes to a statute. The rules have to be laid before Parliament before they can be enforced. But the way in which the Commission has tried to bypass this process is extremely unfortunate for the health of our democracy.”

One of the regulations that make vehicles in the US different from those in Europe or Japan is our headlight rules. They’re laid out in the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), and changing them is—or used to be—a lengthy, laborious process, which is a major reason automotive lighting technology has lagged in the US. But the current administration says it’s time for “bolstering driver safety, slashing red tape, and embracing new technologies,” so it’s going to start a negotiated rulemaking process to rewrite the regulations to suit 2026.
“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Jonathan Morrison said. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.”
While it is fair to be skeptical of the government’s efforts to streamline bureaucracy, it is also fair to say US headlight regulations really could use an update.
When Ars started covering cars, automakers like Audi, BMW, Mercedes, Toyota, and Volvo were trying to import adaptive headlight technology. At the time, the FMVSS only allowed for “dumb” high- and low-beams, nothing else. Meanwhile, lighting technology evolved, adopting first lasers and then LEDs with addressable pixels that can block out those that would otherwise illuminate oncoming cars.

On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-income banlieue town in the suburbs north-east of Paris.
“There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.”
The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates.
“Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.”
The biggest youth protest movement in the country in decades brought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating against inequality in the French education system, decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned of alleged police brutality, with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand.
Mohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorest départements, Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking their grievances to the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns.
Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking.
“We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.”
The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainland France, one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income. Local high schools have a high turnover of young teachers.
Despite co-hosting the 2024 Paris Olympics, and numerous government plans to try to combat long-running problems of inequality and poverty, the area north-east of Paris is still disadvantaged compared with the capital.
In 2005, Seine-Saint-Denis was the starting point for weeks of unrest on housing estates across France, leading to a state of national emergency being declared, after the death of two young boys hiding from police in an electricity substation. This week’s protests have shown that inequality and discrimination has not been addressed in the Paris suburbs and the mistrust between young people and police persists.
Sevran’s Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, with more than 1,000 pupils, has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. In 2024, students and teachers made a viral video about the state of classrooms, toilets and equipment. The local Île de France region said it had put in place a major refurbishment project for high school buildings. But the teenagers said key issues had not been addressed.
“We’re starting at an unfair advantage because our parents aren’t as rich as others, they can’t buy us books, they can’t take us to films,” said Ilian, 17, whose family has Moroccan roots and whose father is a traffic warden. “We’re missing school during these protests, we risk falling behind in an exam year, we’re desperate to get back into class to study, but the conditions we’re facing are so bad we can’t stop until the government promises action.”
The education ministry this week promised 3,000 teachers to urgently fill gaps, but teachers’ unions expressed doubts and said longer-term plans and more funding was needed, even if the government argues there is little spare cash.
Children’s mental health is also an issue in Seine-Saint-Denis. Ilian has been waiting to see a child psychiatrist for months. At the high school, there was no school nurse and a lack of support staff for children with disabilities, he said.
“The police look down on us as if we’re animals”, Ilian said. “They talk to us with such cruelty.” He told local politicians that some teenagers alleged police had made racial insults against them during protests.
Stéphane Troussel, the Socialist head of the Seine-Saint-Denis département council who met the pupils this week, said: “It’s intolerable that policing is causing part of the difficulties.” He called for the police to stop using a type of rubber-bullet launcher, after they suspended use of stun grenades following injuries. The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has defended policing tactics.
Stéphane Blanchet, the mayor of Sevran, said he supported the school protesters’ demands. He said many in his town of 52,000 people, with a higher than average poverty rate, felt “relegated” and forgotten by the state.
Sarah, 17, who wanted to study at an elite Paris engineering faculty, and whose warehouse worker father was proud she was protesting and meeting the mayor, said teenagers in the banlieue “really feel abandoned”.
She said: “We’ve been surprised and so appreciative of other teenagers in better-off places in France marching in the streets to support us this week. We know we’re disadvantaged and that we have to work 10 times as hard as others to escape discrimination against our postcode. But we can’t learn properly in these conditions when we’re not even guaranteed a chair to sit on in school.”
Students’ names have been changed

US President Donald Trump has said he is still deciding whether to allow the planned execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan to be livestreamed, while Vice President JD Vance has expressed doubts about whether the broadcast will go ahead, saying he would not watch it if it does.
Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death in 2013 for killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009. His execution is scheduled for December 3 and is expected to be carried out by firing squad.
The Pentagon had indicated that the execution would be livestreamed after Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the public would be able to watch it. However, Trump's latest remarks have left the proposed broadcast uncertain, despite his support for the death penalty in Hasan's case.
“We’re making a determination about that, but he will be killed. He will be, through firing squad,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday, October 9.
Trump also referred to the number of people killed and wounded in the attack while expressing support for Hasan's execution.
Vance, who converted to Catholicism, questioned whether the Pentagon would proceed with the livestream, despite its earlier confirmation of the plan.
“I don't know that that's actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters on Friday when asked about the proposed broadcast.
He said Hasan had committed what he considered “the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11”, adding that the controversy over the execution method should not overshadow the crimes.
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said.
“Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it,” he added.
The Pentagon confirmed the livestream plan on Thursday after Hegseth said the military would ensure people could watch the execution.
“We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public,” Hegseth said.
In a video shared on official Pentagon accounts on X, he argued that the execution would underline the consequences of such attacks.
“People need to understand that... there's serious consequence for these types of things,” Hegseth said.
If carried out as planned, Hasan's execution would be the first US military firing squad execution since 1945, according to the information cited in reports on the case. The last US military execution took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.
The proposed livestream has drawn bipartisan opposition, including from some Republicans, as well as religious leaders and international observers.
The controversy has unfolded amid renewed debate over capital punishment in the United States, following a botched lethal injection involving a woman in Tennessee last week.
Pope Leo XIV also renewed his opposition to the death penalty on Saturday, saying it violated human dignity and deprived people of the opportunity for redemption.
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” Leo said in a social media post marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty.
“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” he added. The Pope did not directly refer to the Pentagon's livestream plan.
The Catholic Church has long opposed capital punishment, placing Vance's comments in the context of a wider debate over the morality of the death penalty and the public broadcasting of an execution.
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at Fort Hood, a US military installation in Texas, in November 2009. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were members of the military.
A civilian police officer who responded to the attack shot Hasan, leaving him paralysed from the waist down.
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, represented himself during his trial, called no witnesses and gave no testimony. He did not attempt to deny the charges and was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.
During the proceedings, the court heard that Hasan opposed the US military's wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and had communicated online with radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an alleged Al-Qaeda figure and US citizen who was later killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
Hasan's execution remains scheduled for December 3. However, while Trump has backed carrying out the death sentence by firing squad, whether the execution will be livestreamed remains uncertain, with the President saying a decision is still being made.

Allahabad HC quashes FIR order against Uttar Pradesh police personnel
The Allahabad High Court set aside a Maharajganj court order directing an FIR against police personnel. It said the special judge ignored mandatory BNSS procedure and basic criminal law principles.
The Allahabad High Court has quashed an order of a special court in Maharajganj that had directed the registration of an FIR against a sub-inspector, a constable and about 20 police personnel. The high court said the order had been passed in a "casual" manner and without following the statutory procedure under Section 173(4) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
Justice Santosh Rai said the way the Special Judge (SC/ST Act), Maharajganj, handled the matter was a serious concern. "The manner in which the learned Special Judge, SC/ST Act, Maharajganj, has dealt with the application under Section 173(4) of the BNSS is a matter of serious concern. The impugned order reflects a serious lack of appreciation and application of the statutory procedure under the BNSS and the binding principles laid down by the Supreme Court," he said. The judge also said, "The impugned order reflects a fundamental lack of understanding of the basic principles of criminal law and procedure on the part of the Special Judge, SC/ST Act, Maharajganj."
The case arose from an application filed under Section 173(4) of the BNSS by Sheela, 29, wife of Pramod, and Anju, 26, wife of Rajesh, both from Basantpur village in Maharajganj district. They said they belonged to the Chamar caste, which falls under the Scheduled Caste category. According to the application, there was a dispute over land and money between their families and the family of Ramasare.
The application said a clash took place on the night of June 6, in which Rajesh and a man named Pintoo were injured. It said that later that night, police took away Pintoo, Molai, Suresh and Rahul. It further alleged that sub-inspector Rakesh Kumar Yadav, constable Amit Kumar and about 20 policemen, with no female police officers present, entered the house of the opposite party without a search warrant and outraged their modesty while making caste-based remarks.
The high court noted that the special court had passed the order against the police personnel without examining their comments or the other material on record. It was argued before the high court that the allegations of physical search, indecent behaviour and intimidation were vague, omnibus, uncorroborated and motivated. It was also argued that since the alleged incident took place inside a private residential premises, the essential requirement of "public view" under the SC/ST Act was not prima facie satisfied. The appellants further said the lower court had failed to comply with the mandatory procedural safeguards under Sections 175(3) and 175(4) of the BNSS.
In its October 9 judgment, after considering the record and the arguments made on behalf of the police personnel, the high court said the special judge had not exercised jurisdiction in line with the mandatory provisions of the law. "In view of the foregoing discussion, this court is of the considered opinion that the learned Special Judge, SC/ST Act, Maharajganj, while passing the impugned order, has failed to exercise the jurisdiction vested in him in accordance with the mandatory statutory provisions contained in Sections 175(3) and 175(4) of the BNSS. The learned court neither undertook the requisite consideration as to whether an inquiry under Section 175(3) was necessary nor recorded \"cogent reasons\" for dispensing with such an inquiry." The high court thus set aside the order, saying the statutory procedure had not been properly followed.

Rights group says paramilitary drone strike in Sudan killed 41 near Ethiopian border
A drone strike blamed on Sudan's paramilitaries has killed 41 displaced people near the Ethiopian border
CAIRO -- A drone strike blamed on Sudan’s notorious paramilitaries hit a gathering of displaced people on the border with Ethiopia and killed 41, a rights group said.
Friday’s strike by the Rapid Support Forces took place in the Abu Shandi area in Sudan’s Blue Nile province, according to Emergency Lawyers, which tracks the war in the northeastern African nation.
Among the dead were eight children and many women, the group said.
A spokesperson for the RSF didn’t respond to a request for comment.
The U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said it was appalled by the reported strike that also wounded dozens.
“Condemning these senseless killings is essential, but there must also be accountability for this flagrant disregard for international humanitarian law,” said Denise Brown, the U.N. resident and humanitarian coordinator in Sudan in a statement. “As each day goes by in this war, the world continues to accept the suffering of the people of Sudan.”
Sudan’s war started in April 2023 when tensions between the military and the RSF exploded into open fighting in the capital, Khartoum, and spread across the country.
The conflict has killed at least 150,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the real number is likely higher.
It has forced more than 12.4 million to flee their homes, according to U.N. figures, creating what aid groups call the world’s largest humanitarian crisis. Across Sudan, 33.7 million people, including 17.3 million children, urgently need aid this year, and an estimated 825,000 children face severe acute malnutrition.

Stelco says Hamilton layoffs still happening despite Ottawa's threats of legal action
In a letter obtained by CBC News, Stelco Inc. says it is not violating employment commitments
Hamilton-based steelmaker Stelco says it will proceed with hundreds of layoffs, despite threats of legal action from the federal government.
In a letter obtained by CBC News, Stelco Inc., which is owned by Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs, says it rejects allegations from Ottawa that it is violating binding employment commitments under the Investment Canada Act (ICA).
"Your representation that Stelco's planned layoffs cause it to breach its undertakings is false," says a letter written to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly by Paul Simon, president and general counsel at Stelco Inc.
Citing the ICA's guidelines, Simon went on to write that "the undertakings do not stipulate a commitment to avoid layoffs, nor do they include a requirement that employment levels be above a certain amount on each day of the five years of the undertakings."
The letter comes after Joly issued an ultimatum last week to the company: share a plan to save the up to 500 jobs that could be impacted at the Hamilton plant or face potential legal action.
In a statement to CBC News, Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said he was "not surprised with Stelco's convoluted response."
"The bigger problem is that the union, which represents the affected workers, was not privy to the agreement in the first place," he said. "As the group with the most at risk, we weren't consulted or [given] a chance to review the undertakings."
Cleveland-Cliffs acquired Stelco in a $3.4-billion cash-and-stock deal that, according to a news release at the time, kept "national interests at the forefront" and recognized the "importance of the workforce."
According to Joly's letter, this includes "undertakings to continue to employ at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees as were employed when the transaction was announced."
In a statement to CBC News on Saturday, Joly's office said the federal government still expects Steclo to "meet its legally binding commitments to employees."
"These commitments were agreed upon as undertakings under the Investment Canada Act and do not cease to apply because of changing business strategy or market conditions," the statement said. "As our legal team reviews the Stelco letter, all options are on the table."
Prime Minister Mark Carney also said last week that Ottawa will "use all powers that we have" against Cleveland-Cliffs as it pursues the Ohio-based company to the "fullest extent of the law."
In 2009, Industry Canada sued Stelco's previous owner, U.S. Steel, over job protection. The matter was settled out of court in 2011.
Stelco alleges Ottawa knew of its intentions
In its letter to Joly, the company emphasized "Stelco’s situation is a result of factors beyond its control" — citing the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs and the ongoing trade war.
The federal government has said that Stelco refused offers of financial support before choosing to announce it was idling its Hamilton plant.
Stelco's letter alleges that "the government's offers of financial assistance were not responsive to the issues at hand and did not address the root cause for Stelco's decision to indefinitely idle its Hamilton Works finishing lines."
The company goes on to allege that the industry minister was "inaccurate and misleading to the Canadian public" when she said Ottawa only recently learned of Stelco's intentions.
Stelco alleges that it was in constant communication with the federal government about its financial concerns. "By failing to mention or acknowledge these regular communications, your letter created the false impression that we have not been co-operative and transparent."
Stelco did present a plan to comply with ICA job commitments in its letter, as requested by Joly.
The company reaffirmed that it will proceed with its Hamilton layoffs, again citing "exenstive external factors" that make it difficult to produce and profit off of those steel products.
It said laid off workers could be given the opportunity to fill open positions at its Lake Erie plant. Stelco said it would continue to engage with the federal government.
In terms of what the company wants to see from Ottawa, it wrote: "The most important step the government could take would be to impose further restrictions on imports of cold-rolled and coated steel products into Canada, limit import substitution, and eliminate remissions for steel products that Canadian producers, including Stelco, can supply."

A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows
- Published
A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have found.
The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The eye-catching monal - the male has distinctive green, blue and copper feathers - is the state bird of India's Uttarakhand state and the national bird of Nepal, reflecting its cultural significance across the Himalayas.
But studies show that infrastructure development and tourism are squeezing its habitat, while increasing noise is altering how it communicates with potential mates and rivals.
Researchers from Uttarakhand conducted two separate studies over five years which flagged key threats to the bird.
One study found that the birds are forced to move higher in the mountains as their natural habitat in the alpine meadows above the tree line get crowded. The other says the monal is changing its pitch to cut through human noise in a busy valley.
"These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" says Vishal Singh, an environmental practitioner working on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas.
Dr Rajeev Lochan, lead researcher of both studies, told the BBC that they chose to study the monal as the bird has a narrow habitat range - it moves seasonally between the lower montane zone - an ecological belt found on the lower slopes of the mountains - and high-elevation alpine zones. This, he says, makes it a key indicator of ecosystem health in the north-western Himalayas.
"If the species is facing issues on this particular landscape, there might be a chance that the ecological disturbances are affecting other birds too," said Lochan.
The monal, researchers say, can be seen as a stand-in for the health of a fragile Himalayan ecosystem pushed to a tipping point due to unregulated tourism and heavy urbanisation.
While the region has always drawn tourists, trekkers and researchers given its scenic landscape and biodiversity, rapid infrastructure expansion in the past decade has made more places accessible, increasing footfall and disrupting the wildlife. This, coupled with mounting human pressures, suggests that climate change is emerging as another major threat to the region's already vulnerable biodiversity.
"There are a lot of factors at play but at a broader level, the problem is that the economic development of the region is not aligned to its ecological integrity," Singh said.
According to the first study, climate change is projected to continue shrinking and destabilising the Himalayan monal's habitat across the Indian Himalayas through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios.
Currently, the birds are found in alpine meadows, located high in the mountains above the forests, which form some of the Himalayas' most important seasonal grazing and biodiversity-rich habitats.
The researchers modelled how climate change could shift the monal's suitable habitat across the Indian Himalayan region in the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It was based on the kind of global climate models and emissions scenarios used for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's climate science unit.
"These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said.
The model assumes that the bird needs the current climate set-up that exists in alpine meadows in the future too, a reasonable but not certain assumption.
The birds' seasonal migration may become increasingly difficult as changes in climate may force them to move to higher elevations on hills, to smaller and fragmented areas. Their population would be scattered in disconnected pockets, which reduces chances of breeding between groups and increases their risks of long-term decline or local extinction, which is already a threat, the study says.
The second study, also conducted by Lochan, Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, who work at the Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, focuses on the bird's behavioural changes. They conducted the study in two valleys in Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand - at Chopta, a tourist spot with busy traffic and visitors, and the largely quiet Madmaheshwar.
They recorded more than 700 monal calls across both sites using microphones and passive recording devices and then measured pitch, call length and background noise levels for a year from April 2023.
Birds in noisy environments consistently produced calls with significantly higher peak frequencies compared with those in quieter habitats, the study said.
The researchers found subtle changes in the monal's pitch that could be picked up by recording devices but might go unnoticed by the human ear.
"This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said.
Compared with the birds in Madmaheshwar valley, the monal in Chopta also produced shorter call durations likely to cut through low-frequency human noise from traffic and tourist footfall.
Bird calls are one of the most sophisticated forms of sound-based communication in the natural world, and significant changes can interfere with, among other things, their mating success.
"When a species must raise its pitch to be heard over tourist traffic, or climb higher as meadows turn crowded, it reveals how human pressure is rewriting the rules of life in the Himalaya," says Anjal Prakash, a public policy professor at FLAME University and contributor to IPCC reports.
Lochan says he and his team consider this a preliminary study and hope to expand the scope and depth of it.
The research comes with the caveat that it is not conclusive on ecological consequences, and more research is needed. But together, the two studies signal broader ecological stress across the Himalayas.
"In listening to the monal, we hear the Himalayas asking for space, silence and care," says Prakash.

Anyone from Massachusetts knows that during Halloween, Salem is packed tighter than a Candy Crush board.
I've visited Salem many times, but I like to avoid the area from September through the beginning of November because of the surge in tourism. Each year, the city welcomes roughly 1,000,000 visitors every October, with 96,000 people going on Halloween alone.
During the fall, crowds flood the streets on ghost tours, take selfies in front of the statue of Elizabeth Montgomery from "Bewitched," line up at the Salem Witch Museum, and try to snag a ticket to the Haunted Witch Village at the Salem Wax Museum.
It's always exciting to welcome new guests who are eager to learn about the city's twisted history. But during October, Salem's narrow streets and scarce parking make its charm hard to enjoy.
However, a recent three-day staycation in Beverly, Massachusetts —just three miles away from Salem's city center — gave my family and me the best of both worlds: easy access to Witch City, plus a quieter place to eat, explore, and sleep.
Until this year, I'd thought of it as mostly Salem's sleepier sister, but my time there made me realize I'd been overlooking it as a must-visit destination in its own right.
Beverly has Halloween spirit without Salem's October crowds
Downtown Beverly has the independent restaurants, family-owned boutiques, and historic architecture that I love about Salem, minus the holiday crowds.
I loved checking out the trails at Long Hill estate, which houses 114 acres of land and gardens. For most of October, the grounds' pathways feature thousands of hand-carved glowing jack-o'-lanterns, twinkling lights, decorations, and treats like cider as part of the Halloween on the Hill event.
I've attended the event twice and can't recommend it enough.
Our hotel was beautiful — and cheaper than many places in Salem
My family and I stayed at the recently renovated Wylie Inn in Beverly, which sits on Endicott College's leafy seaside campus and has direct beach access.
Not only is the hotel stunning, but most rates for a late-October night are cheaper compared to places I've stayed in Salem.
Plus, parking at the Wylie Inn is free, so you don't have to worry about competing for a spot at a public garage.
The food and sweet treats were incredible
During our time in Beverly, we dined at Flip the Bird, a fast-casual restaurant that had the most delicious, crispy chicken sandwiches and frothy frappes.
The desserts in Beverly also blew me away. On our last day, we hit up Prides Crossing Confections. This family-owned candy shop — housed inside a former train station — featured Halloween treats and tasty chocolate lollipops.
Like Salem, Beverly is rich in historic charm and cultural activities
Sure, Salem is full of incredible tales and features many cultural attractions, but the same is true for Beverly.
While visiting, we checked out Cabot House, an 18th-century Georgian-style mansion. Stepping inside this home, which was the first brick mansion built in the city, I instantly felt like I had traveled back in time to Beverly's founding.
Along with Cabot House, there are plenty of other activities to plan a getaway around — instead of just limiting yourself to Halloween-themed activities in Salem.
For example, the Montserrat College of Art offers five free galleries in Beverly, and the nonprofit Cabot Performing Arts Center hosts comedy and music acts.
Hiking through Witches' Woods was incredible
One of my favorite moments during the staycation was hiking at the Beverly Commons Conservation Area.
This 409-acre preserve was once a major thoroughfare during colonial times, and during the witchcraft hysteria of 1692, the forest became known as Witches' Woods after families sought refuge there.
Now, centuries later, as I walked beneath peaceful canopies of trees, I couldn't believe that Salem's busy streets were only a few miles away.
If you want to brave the Salem crowds, it's a short drive or train ride away
Beverly is incredible, but if you're still itching to check out the scene in Salem, luckily, it's conveniently located nearby.
Beverly has multiple rail stations, with direct trains to Salem that take about five minutes. Plus, during October, the Massachusetts Bay Transit Authority offers extra train cars, more departure times, and discounted fares.
But if you have a car, Salem is only about a 15-minute drive from Beverly, though holiday traffic can make the trip much longer. I'm a fan of Salem's free parking lot at Fort Avenue, which is about a 20-minute walk to the center of the action.
