The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) may introduce its proposed insurance commission caps as early as January 2027, amid opposition from brokers over potential revenue losses and job cuts. The regulator is considering January 1 and April 1, 2027 as possible implementation dates for its distribution reforms, Girija Subramanian, whole-time member (distribution) at IRDAI, told Bloomberg in an interview. The proposals seek to curb distribution costs through product-wise commission caps and tighter limits on insurers’ overall expenses. IRDAI has argued that commissions have risen faster than premiums since rules were relaxed in 2023, without a corresponding increase in insurance coverage. Subramanian said commission caps should take effect sooner, arguing that phased reductions could encourage distributors to rush sales and increase the risk of mis-selling. Separately, IRDAI’s consultation paper proposes a five-year transition to lower expense limits for insurers, with the first interim milestone in FY29. “There is an earlier-the-better case, but getting the reforms right is more important than getting them early,” she told Bloomberg. The proposals have implications for listed insurance distributors such as Policybazaar parent PB Fintech and Turtlemint, whose businesses depend on commissions from insurance sales. Shares of PB Fintech and Turtlemint have slumped over 47% each since IRDAI proposed the commission caps on September 23. However, the framework is still under consultation. Stakeholders have until October 25 to submit comments, after which IRDAI will review the feedback and publish draft regulations for another round of consultation before issuing the final rules. Brokers Flag Revenue, Employment Risks The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) has warned that the proposed norms could cut broking sector revenues by 60–70% and result in the loss of up to 10 Lakh jobs across insurance distribution. At a press briefing, the association’s representatives said the distribution sector employs more than 83 Lakh people. While supporting IRDAI’s objective of making insurance more affordable and accessible, they argued that the proposed changes threaten small businesses and MSMEs. The resulting job losses could affect insurance awareness, policy renewals, assistance to policyholders, and insurance penetration among underserved communities, they added. The association has sought an extension of the feedback deadline to December-end from October 25 and submitted letters to the Prime Minister’s Office and the finance ministry. The IBAI also disputed IRDAI’s interpretation of data showing that general insurance premiums sourced through brokers grew 37%, while commission payouts rose 173%. It argued that the increase in commissions since FY23 largely reflected the reclassification of previously off-book marketing expenses following regularisation, rather than inflationary pressures on insurance consumers. The association claimed that general insurers’ operating expenses averaged around 26.5% of gross premiums, below the mandated 30% limit. It also said policyholders received ₹84.4 in non-life insurance claim payouts for every ₹100 of premiums paid over five years, compared with a global average of 72–75%. The representatives said the association was ready to work with IRDAI to address specific market anomalies, including mis-selling and disproportionate remuneration. IRDAI Backs Wider Distribution IRDAI, meanwhile, has pointed to rising expenses at private insurers. Expenses at private life insurers increased to about 22% of total premiums from 16% in FY21, while those at private general insurers rose to roughly 32% from 25% in FY19. Additional rewards have also pushed distributor remuneration 30–60% above base commissions in some cases. Subramanian rejected concerns over large-scale job losses, arguing that the reforms would create employment by widening the distribution network and lowering entry barriers. To encourage expansion beyond major cities, IRDAI has proposed allowing distributors to earn an additional 10% of the applicable commission limit on business generated in towns with populations below 10 Lakh. This would rise to 20% for areas with fewer than 50,000 residents. Other proposals include allowing distributors to undertake financial and non-financial activities beyond insurance.

Cairo, Oct 10: The airport in the Saudi capital has been attacked again, two regional officials said Saturday, two days after three Saudi citizens including a pilot were killed there.
One official said the Riyadh airport had been evacuated, and the other said air traffic had stopped. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorised to speak to the media.
King Khalid International Airport has been targeted in an extraordinary series of attacks in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the earlier attacks, including another on Wednesday that killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight other people.
There was no immediate Houthi statement Saturday.
A Riyadh resident, Ahmed Sayed, told The Associated Press he heard at least two loud explosions that rocked the capital.
The airport issued a terse alert telling passengers to check their flight status with airlines before heading to the airport.
Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces in an attempt to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. (AP)

Afcon move to every four years under review by Caf

The Africa Cup of Nations could continue to be held every two years, with discussions under way to reverse its proposed switch to a four-year cycle.
Speaking on Friday at a Confederation of African Football (Caf) strategy conference in Cape Verde, president Patrice Motsepe said: "We've discussed it over the last few days.
"We are looking at everything, including having the Afcon coming back every two years. We are very clear, the matter is being reviewed."
The tournament has taken place every two years since 1968, bar a one-year gap between the 2012 and 2013 editions.
However, in December 2025 CAF announced it would shift to being staged every four years after the 2027 Afcon in East Africa and a 2028 edition.
That planned alteration to the schedule had received widespread criticism across the continent.
National associations had raised concerns about the visibility of their teams, the commercial implications and where Africa's biggest competition would sit in the international football calendar.

Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.
Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”
Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”
Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.
Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.
She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”
In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.
Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”
In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.
In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.
Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.
In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.
Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”
A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

America’s good hurricane luck is about to run out
Hurricane Isaias is almost here. Are we ready?
The first hurricane of the fall season is expected to strike the Gulf Coast overnight, marking the latest onset of hurricane season in living memory. As of early Friday afternoon, Hurricane Isaias had grown to a Category 3 storm, with sustained winds of 120 miles per hour. It will strike along the shores of the Florida Panhandle, Alabama, and Mississippi, posing a threat to life and property for millions of Americans. Weather forecasters anticipate between 8 and 12 inches of rain in the areas near where the storm makes landfall.
Isaias’s imminent arrival signals the end of a period of unusual good luck when it comes to hurricanes striking the United States. Last year, no hurricanes reached the US mainland at all. And this year, Isaias is breaking a more than 100-year-old record: October 9 is the latest date since 1905 for the first Atlantic hurricane of the season to take shape. August and September have historically been the busiest periods of hurricane season.
Not lately, though. It’s a strange recent phenomenon, and it’s been even more fortuitous than it would ordinarily be. That’s because the Trump administration has slashed weather forecasting and emergency relief funding over the past two years, leaving us less prepared for a disaster.
And now our luck seems to be running out — with even more rough weather on the way.
Hurricane season may be quieter than usual — but El Niño is on the way
Here’s the secret ingredient that’s pushed off hurricanes even as warming planetary temperatures raise concerns about more extreme weather events: El Niño. This notorious shift in global wind patterns, which occurs every two to seven years, moves warm water around the oceans, disrupting traditional weather patterns and leading to intense rain and sometimes disastrous flooding, as well as droughts. If there is an upside, however, it’s that this temporary change in ocean conditions prevents hurricanes from forming as frequently as they otherwise would.
The downside is, well, El Niño is still on its way. Forecasters expect this year’s version to be historically bad — using words like “super” or “Godzilla” to describe it. The worst of the bad weather is projected to arrive in December: The southern half of the continental US is expected to see unusually rainy and stormy weather, while areas of the Great Lakes and Pacific Northwest could see extreme dry spells.
It will also serve as a crucial test of our reduced capacity for predicting and responding to disasters. Trump’s “big beautiful bill” cut funding for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s weather forecasting and public alert programs by $200 million, and 17 percent of FEMA’s workforce left the agency in 2025 amid the administration’s DOGE purge.
For now, if you’re in the danger zone for Isaias, please pay attention to local and national weather alerts this weekend. If you’re not, count yourself lucky — but there are storm clouds on the horizon.

The unprecedented crackdown on protesters by Delhi Police and paramilitary forces prompted many youth organisations to shift their demonstrations on Saturday (October 10) to other areas, including the Safdarjung flyover, Dilli Haat, Raj Ghat and various makeshift detention centres in north-west Delhi.
The central part of the national capital was sealed with heavy police deployment and barricading while metro stations, schools, colleges and markets remained closed.
Announcements were made from loudspeakers across central Delhi that Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) was in place and citizens should follow the directions of the police and maintain law and order.
Curbs in place
Despite the restrictions, hundreds of protesters continued their attempts to reach the planned protest site – Jantar Mantar – but were stopped by the police, detained, bundled into buses and driven to the city’s outskirts.
While larger groups of 100-200 showed up under the banner of various youth organisations, several protesters, including women and children, made their way in smaller groups of four or five. The police, however, stopped the groups immediately and forced them to sit inside the buses.
Near Safdarjung flyover, several people tried to stop a bus full of detainees, including All India Students’ Association president Neha Bora.
While some stood in front of it, others sat on the road and lay down in front of the bus. The police pushed them away from the bus, and used batons to do so. Protesters noted the presence of a woman officer in civil clothes and several other police personnel without name tags.
“Police were very aggressive, pulling our hands and legs and brutally manhandling us. I was not expecting this kind of aggression... the way they are detaining people and the amount of restrictions put in place,” said a 15-year-old who came to the national capital from Goa along with her younger brother and father. Around 1 p.m., members of Disha Students’ Organisation, Naujawan Bharat Sabha and Revolutionary Workers’ Party of India (RWPI) organised a protest at Raj Ghat with over 150 people turning up. The protesters said many were detained, with the police using “excessive force and manhandling” them.
‘Pushed and pulled’
“There were five-seven police officers in civil clothes who picked me up and threw me on the pavement. There was another person named Aragya whose leg got twisted while the police picked him up. He is now admitted to a private hospital in Rohini. Another police officer punched several people inside the bus. The girls were pushed and pulled aggressively,” said Chiranshu, a member of RWPI.
They continued their protest inside the bus. They were taken to Rajiv Gandhi Stadium in Bawana – more than 30 km from Jantar Mantar – where they sang protest songs and talked about the alleged irregularities by the Election Commission of India with other protesters.
Members of the Students’ Federation of India (SFI) held a public lecture on ‘India under undeclared Emergency’ by R. Gopinath, a retired professor from Jamia Millia Islamia who was also detained along with students, at the Bawana detention centre.
At Nangloi, Rajya Sabha member A.A. Rahim announced the begining of‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ and sang the national anthem along with other protesters.
‘Hunger strike’
He also began a hunger strike and demanded action against and apology from Inspector Pawan Tomar for allegedly misbehaving with women students and for the return of all the phones and bags “snatched illegally” by Delhi Police.
Police officers claimed they too received injuries on their arms and legs while detaining protesters.
At least 12 people, including members of the Indian Youth Congress and two advocates, were detained from Raisina Road on Saturday morning and were not released until late at night.
Several others, including UPSC aspirants and an autorickshaw driver, all of whom said they were not even going to participate in the protest, were also detained from the area.

Women account for 43% of the workforce in India’s Ayush services sector, with their representation crossing 50% in several organised segments, including hospitals, day-care centres, educational institutions and wellness establishments, according to a new assessment of the sector released by the Central government on Thursday (October 8, 2026).
The Ayush Services Sector Report, prepared by the Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) and released on Ayurveda Day 2026, estimates that the sector supports 1.76 million livelihoods across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services.
Women’s representation is highest in spas and wellness resorts, where it exceeds 60%, followed by educational institutions at 58%, day-care centres at 57% and hospitals at 53%, says the report.
The findings come as the Ayush services economy expands beyond traditional clinical practice into wellness, education, preventive health and medical value travel.
16.91% growth
The sector, comprising Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy, was estimated at $36.92 billion in 2024-25. It has registered a compound annual growth rate of 16.91% since 2022-23.
Standalone clinics remain the largest segment, generating an estimated $16.21 billion, or 43.9% of the sector’s revenue. Day-care centres contribute another $10.13 billion. Together, the two segments account for more than 70% of the sector’s revenue.
“More than one million livelihoods are concentrated in local and standalone clinics, underlining the sector’s employment footprint across urban and rural areas,’’ says the report.
The wellness segment has recorded a 21.29% compound annual growth rate, while yoga centres registered about 75% growth in revenue over two years, according to the assessment.
Ayurveda remains the largest individual Ayush system, accounting for $17.73 billion, or about 48% of the total services revenue.
The sector is also gaining a foothold in medical value travel. Ayush-related medical value travel generated an estimated $1.77 billion in 2024-25. Although international patients account for only around 5% of patient volumes, they contribute an estimated 15-25% of hospital-segment revenue, with therapeutic programmes typically involving stays of five to 11 days.
The assessment projects that the Ayush services economy could expand to between $216 billion and $318 billion by 2047.
Job opportunities
Union Minister of State for Ayush Prataprao Jadhav said the sector’s expansion was creating employment opportunities across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services, while also opening avenues for entrepreneurship and women’s participation.
The report projects further employment opportunities in healthcare delivery, wellness, education, medical travel, research, digital health and allied services as the sector expands.

Delhi witnessed an extensive security operation on Saturday as police moved to prevent the CJP's proposed demonstration
NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has announced another march to Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on Sunday a day after an unprecedented security clampdown and mass detentions thwarted its planned demonstration demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The Delhi Traffic Police has issued an advisory warning commuters of possible disruptions across several key roads and intersections in the national capital.In a post on X, the CJP said the government feared the consequences of people uniting against it but asserted that the organisation would not back down.
The fresh call for mobilisation comes after more than 7,000 protesters were detained across Delhi on Saturday, according to police sources, cited by news agency PTI. Those detained included CJP leader Abhijit Dipke, former chief ministers, opposition leaders, student activists, lawyers and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee.Despite heavy security deployment, barricades and restrictions on movement across central Delhi, some groups of protesters attempted to reach the designated protest site. Incidents of stone-pelting and clashes with security personnel were also reported at multiple locations.
The developments have triggered a sharp political confrontation, with opposition leaders accusing the government of suppressing dissent and the BJP defending the police action. With the CJP announcing another march, authorities have warned that traffic movement could be affected across several parts of the capital on Sunday.
Delhi Traffic Police issues advisory
The Delhi Traffic Police said traffic could be affected on October 11 in view of the prevailing law-and-order situation. Diversions will be enforced from 6am, depending on the situation on the ground.Commuters have been advised to account for possible delays while travelling through central Delhi and other affected stretches. The advisory lists 30 intersections, flyovers and road junctions where movement could be disrupted.The affected locations include:
Jantar Mantar and central Delhi: Ashoka Road-Jantar Mantar Road roundabout, Jai Singh Road-Sansad Marg crossing, Outer Circle Connaught Place-Sansad Marg T-point, Tolstoy-Janpath crossing and Mandi House roundabout.
Connaught Place and adjoining areas: Outer Circle Connaught Place-Barakhamba Road T-point, Chemsford Road-Outer Circle Connaught Place T-point, Guru Nanak Chowk, Jhandewalan roundabout and Panchkuian roundabout.
Key road junctions and flyovers: Dhaula Kuan flyover, Lodhi Road flyover, Moti Bagh flyover, Bhikaji Cama Place underpass, Neela Gumbad roundabout and Sardar Patel Marg-Panchsheel Marg crossing.
The police said the diversions would depend on the prevailing circumstances. Motorists travelling through these areas should check official traffic updates and allow additional time for their journeys.
What happened in Delhi on Saturday?
Delhi witnessed an extensive security operation on Saturday as police moved to prevent the CJP's proposed demonstration. More than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed, barricades were erected across Lutyens' Delhi and security checks were intensified at several locations. Jantar Mantar remained largely deserted as protesters were prevented from reaching the site.CJP leaders Abhijit Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained inside an aircraft shortly after it landed in Delhi from Mumbai. Rathee was detained from his residence in Gurugram's Sector 56. In a pre-recorded video released after his detention, Dipke said CJP organiser Ajinkya Shinde would lead the protest.Several opposition leaders were also detained while attempting to join the demonstration. They included AAP convenor Arvind Kejriwal, Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan and former Tripura chief minister Manik Sarkar. Left leaders, student activists, lawyers and other protesters were picked up from multiple locations.
Tensions escalated in the afternoon when protesters allegedly hurled stones at security personnel near Akashwani Bhawan and Hanuman Temple in Connaught Place. Police personnel were injured in the incidents, while officers moved to disperse the crowds and detain those involved.Opposition leaders condemned the crackdown. Banerjee described the situation as a “Super Emergency”, while Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge accused the government of turning the “mother of democracy” into a “muzzled democracy”. Rahul Gandhi urged young people to continue protesting against what he alleged were attacks on democratic institutions.

UK government blocks Northern Ireland march after standoff fueled sectarian tensions
The British government has blocked a contentious march in Northern Ireland after a two-week standoff
LONDON -- The British government has blocked a contentious march from taking place in Northern Ireland after a two-week standoff between groups that support the region’s continued union with the United Kingdom and those who favor reunification with the Republic of Ireland.
Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant intervened Friday night to ban the procession along Garvaghy Road in Portadown, saying it wasn’t possible to find a compromise between the union-supporting Orange Order and residents of the traditionally republican area through which it wanted to march.
“I’ve decided that it’s not in the public interest for it to proceed, and I’ve therefore banned the procession,” Bryant said.
The standoff grew out of the traditional marches held by unionist groups during the summer months to celebrate their Protestant roots and historic ties to the U.K. The marches have long caused tensions with the largely Catholic republican community, which says they are intentionally provocative and fuel conflict.
Tensions flared again this year after a court ruling seemingly paved the way for the Orange Order to march down Garvaghy Road for the first time in almost 30 years. Garvaghy Road was a notorious flash point between the republican and unionist communities in the years before the 1998 Good Friday Agreement largely ended the bloodshed in Northern Ireland known as the Troubles.
When Orange Order members gathered for their planned march on Sept. 27, they were blocked by republican protesters, including First Minister Michelle O’Neill, the republican politician who leads Northern Ireland’s regional government.
The two sides have been locked in a stalemate ever since, raising concerns that the dispute could trigger a broader conflict in Northern Ireland.
Bryant said he held talks with both the Garvaghy Road residents and the Orange Order but had been unable to find a resolution.
“I heard the concerns of people on all sides and I only regret that we could not reach a compromise on a way forward and that many residents across Portadown have felt anxious and worried,” he said. “With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions.”

తెలంగాణ ముఖ్యమంత్రి రేవంత్ రెడ్డి, 2026 బతుకమ్మ కానుకగా ప్రతి మహిళకు Rs. 2500 నగదు, పెళ్లి చేసుకునే ప్రతి ఆడపిల్లకు 10 గ్రాముల బంగారం ఇస్తానని హామీ చేస్తున్న బిగ్ టీవీ ప్రచురించిన వీడియో ఒకటి సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. దీని వెనుక ఉన్న నిజాజిజాలేంటో ఈ కథనం ద్వారా తెలుసుకుందాం.
క్లెయిమ్: తెలంగాణ ముఖ్యమంత్రి రేవంత్ రెడ్డి, 2026 బతుకమ్మ కానుకగా ప్రతి మహిళకు Rs. 2500 నగదు, పెళ్లి చేసుకునే ప్రతి ఆడపిల్లకు 10 గ్రాముల బంగారం ఇస్తానని హామీ చేస్తున్న బిగ్ టీవీ ప్రచురించిన వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: 2023 అసెంబ్లీ ఎన్నికల సందర్భంగా కాంగ్రెస్ పార్టీ పేద కుటుంబాల ఆడపిల్లల వివాహానికి రూ.1 లక్ష ఆర్థిక సాయంతో పాటు 10 గ్రాముల బంగారం అందిస్తామని మేనిఫెస్టోలో తెలిపింది. ముఖ్యమంత్రి రేవంత్ రెడ్డి కూడా పలు సందర్భాల్లో దీని గురించి ప్రస్తావించారు. అయితే, వైరల్ వీడియోలో ముఖ్యమంత్రి మాట్లాడుతున్న దృశ్యాలు 2025 ఏప్రిల్లో రవీంద్రభారతిలో జరిగిన 892వ బసవ జయంతి వేడుకలకు సంబంధించినవి. ఈ వీడియోలో ఉన్న దాని ప్రకారం అక్కడ ఎటువంటి హామీలు ఇవ్వలేదు. ఈ వీడియోలోని ఆడియోని AI ద్వారా రూపొందించి, అసలు వీడియోకు జోడించి షేర్ చెయ్యబడుతోంది. 2026 బతుకమ్మ సందర్భంగా ఇటువంటి హామీలు తెలంగాణ ప్రభుత్వం చేసినట్టు ఎటువంటి ఆధారాలు లేవు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టు తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియో యొక్క కీ ఫ్రేములను ఉపయోగించి రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, V6 2025లో ప్రచురించిన వీడియోకి దారి తీసింది. ఈ వీడియో 2025 ఏప్రిల్లో రవీంద్రభారతిలో జరిగిన 892వ బసవ జయంతి వేడుకలకు సంబంధించింది. ఇందులో రేవంత్ రెడ్డి బతుకమ్మ గురించి కానీ, ఆడపిల్లల వివాహానికి రూ.1 లక్ష ఆర్థిక సాయంతో పాటు 10 గ్రాముల బంగారం అందిస్తామని గానీ చెప్పలేదు.
వైరల్ వీడియోను Hive AI మరియు Hiya AI డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్ ద్వారా పరిశీలించగా, ఇది AI ఆడియో ఉపయోగించి ఎడిట్ చెయ్యబడ్డ వీడియో అని స్పష్టం అయింది.
తెలంగాణ ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ విభాగం కూడా తెలంగాణ ముఖ్యమంత్రి రేవంత్ రెడ్డి బతుకమ్మ పండుగ నుంచి మహిళలకు నెలకు ₹2,500 ఆర్థిక సాయం, కల్యాణలక్ష్మి పథకం కింద రెండు తులాల బంగారం అందిస్తామని ప్రకటించినట్లు ప్రచారం అవుతున్న వీడియో మార్ఫింగ్ చేసిన వీడియో అని వివరణ ఇచ్చింది. అంతే కాకుండా, బిగ్ టీవీ కూడా ఇది ఫేక్ వీడియో అని నిర్ధారించింది.
అయితే, 2023 అసెంబ్లీ ఎన్నికలలో కాంగ్రెస్ మేనిఫెస్టో ప్రకారం పేద కుటుంబాల ఆడపిల్లల వివాహానికి రూ.1 లక్ష ఆర్థిక సాయంతో పాటు 10 గ్రాముల బంగారం అందిస్తామని మేనిఫెస్టోలో హామీ ఇచ్చింది. ప్రస్తుతం తెలంగాణలో కల్యాణలక్ష్మి, షాదీ ముబారక్ పథకాల కింద అర్హులైన వధువుల కుటుంబాలకు ఒకేసారి రూ.1,00,116 ఆర్థిక సహాయం అందుతోంది. CM రేవంత్ రెడ్డి కూడా 2023లో పలు సార్లు ఈ పథకాల గురుంచి మాట్లాడారు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). కానీ, తాజాగా 2026 బతుకమ్మ సందర్భంగా తెలంగాణ ప్రభుత్వం మహిళలకు రూ.1 లక్ష ఆర్థిక సాయంతో పాటు పెళ్లి చేసుకునే ఆడపిల్లలకు 10 గ్రాముల బంగారం అందిస్తామని హామీ ఇచ్చినట్టు ఎటువంటి ఆధారాలు లేవు.
చివరిగా, 2026 బతుకమ్మ సందర్భంగా CM రేవంత్ రెడ్డి మహిళలకు రూ. 2500, పెళ్లి చేసుకునే ఆడపిల్లలకు తులం బంగారం కానుకగా ప్రకటించలేదు.

The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination”.
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Samuel Sévigny, 32, the cofounder and marketing director at Chaletô, a short-term rental property management company based in Quebec, Canada. Sévigny started Chaletô in 2022 with four of his friends and has scaled to over 500 cabins and condos. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
It started as six friends fresh out of college. We all had other jobs. It was in 2016, and we wanted to invest in real estate, diversify, and get started in life.
One of our co-founders had condos in downtown Quebec City already, so he pitched us the idea of investing all together and building our own cabin, and to manage it ourselves. So that's what we did.
We launched our first cabin together in 2019, then our second in 2020, right in the middle of COVID.
Fast-forward to 2022, and we had four different units that we owned and managed, and we wanted to delegate the process of managing them. We couldn't find anyone who was professional enough for our standards, so it was just like most origin stories: it starts with a problem that we're trying to solve.
In the meantime, our neighbor started pressuring us, asking if we could manage his property because he could see that we were rented pretty much the whole year. We said no at first, but he kept asking. At some point, we decided to say yes. It started with our neighbor, then it was the neighbor's neighbor, and then the whole street.
Then we had 10 properties under management in 2022.
The six of us had to sit down and say, "Hey, what are we going to do with this? It's getting serious." Either we'll make this a serious, legitimate business, or we stop, because there's no in-between.
So in 2022, we decided to incorporate Chaletô. We grew from 10 to 500-plus units in four years. We decided to make it a real thing and to go all-in.
When we scaled our business, our gains scaled, too
The biggest difference between an individual host and a property management company is really the optimization at scale.
When you're a professional host, you're dealing with your own cleaner, your tech stack is under one roof, and you've got one or two listings. You're paying the higher-bracket price for all the tools you're using.
You probably decide to cut different tools because you maybe don't have the resources, or the time, or the training to be able to use them well. I'm thinking about dynamic pricing tools. I'm thinking about AI automation for operations. I'm thinking about a bunch of things like that, because that's not your day job.
I was working in advertising in Montreal and doing Airbnb hosting on the side. I was managing the guest messaging on nights and weekends, so I really lived the individual host dilemma of having a full-time job and then dealing with guests Friday and Saturday when you're off from your day job. I lived through that for several years, so I really, really understand how it feels.
When you make this a full-time gig and it becomes a full-time business, then you make gains at scale.
You get a little bit more leverage with relationships within the industry. For example, you can negotiate cleaners' contracts a little bit easier. That comes with professional management, and that's the main benefit of having it at scale.
Also, you can attract talent for specific things in your business that you couldn't if you were alone. If you're managing only one or two properties, there's no need to have a full-time dedicated revenue management person, someone who's trained for this, sophisticated, and educated about that. But when you manage 50 or 100 properties, it becomes interesting because you can optimize each function of your hosting business.
Our business works best when we're not distracted by the latest trends
When you scale, it's easy to get distracted. You see it in every industry possible: real estate, service, and tech. It's like when something starts clicking, and it works, and everything seems to be working for you, then the easiest shortcut for entrepreneurs, I think, is jumping on all the opportunities.
It would be easy for us to say, "We're going to keep investing in real estate because we're giving the service to support it," but it's a different beast. Investing is totally different than servicing the owners. Now you're distracted between two different businesses: you're scaling one, and then you're trying to scale the other.
Another problem we face is the speed at which AI is moving, not only for our industry but for everyone.
At what stage does it become mature enough to be implemented within our business, and where do you focus? Because it seems like there is a new tool and there's a new shiny object being created by the next engineer every other week.
One of our challenges is always, do you keep hiring people and training them and keep it very hospitality based, or do you optimize with AI, and is it mature enough to support that optimization, or is it just a super shiny object and a gamble?
So far, I'll say I don't think we have 100% the right answer to that. We prefer to hire and grow our team for now and really double down on service when everyone's running towards AI.
We also prefer to hire actual people from Quebec. They speak French first, English second, and they can support any type of customer service issue because they live here, they understand the market, they understand the region, and the experiences around it.
We use tech to support our business, but every couple of months, it feels like you have to re-challenge yourself. Is this still the right tech? Are you overpaying for it? Because AI is going at a speed that is so fast.

విద్యా వ్యవస్థలో సంస్కరణలు చేపట్టాలని, పాఠశాలలకు నిధులు పెంచాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ ఫ్రాన్స్లో హైస్కూల్, యూనివర్సిటీ విద్యార్థులు, ఉపాధ్యాయులు పెద్దఎత్తున దేశవ్యాప్త నిరసనలు చేపట్టారు. 2026 అక్టోబర్ మొదటి వారంలో ఈ నిరసనలు తీవ్ర స్థాయికి చేరి హింసాత్మకంగా మారాయి. నిరసనకారులు కార్లకు, పాఠశాల భవనాలకు నిప్పుపెట్టడం, పోలీసులపైకి తిరగబడటం వంటి చర్యలకు పాల్పడ్డారు. ఇప్పటివరకు దాదాపు 6,000 మందికి పైగా నిరసనకారులను పోలీసులు అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు. వీరిలో అత్యధికులు మైనర్ విద్యార్థులే ఉన్నారు. పరిస్థితి అదుపు తప్పడంతో ఫ్రెంచ్ ప్రభుత్వం దేశవ్యాప్తంగా ఉన్నత పాఠశాలలకు సెలవులు ప్రకటించి, తరగతులను ఆన్లైన్ విధానంలోకి మార్చింది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, పారిస్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ను నిరసనకారులు స్వాధీనం చేసుకున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: అక్టోబర్ 2026 ఫ్రాన్స్ నిరసనల్లో భాగంగా నిరసనకారులు పారిస్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ భవనాన్ని స్వాధీనం చేసుకుంటున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియో ఏప్రిల్ 2023లో పెన్షన్ సంస్కరణలకు వ్యతిరేకంగా జరిగిన నిరసనలకు సంబంధించినది. ఆ ఘటనలో ఆందోళనకారులు భవనం లాబీలోకి మాత్రమే ప్రవేశించారు తప్ప స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ను స్వాధీనం చేసుకోలేదు. అలాగే, ఈ వీడియోకు అక్టోబర్ 2026 విద్యార్థుల నిరసనలతో ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 20 ఏప్రిల్ 2023 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. పారిస్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ యూరోనెక్స్ట్ భవనాన్ని నిరసనకారులు ఆక్రమించినట్లు ఇందులో పేర్కొన్నారు.
ఈ ఘటనను రిపోర్ట్ చేసిన స్థానిక, అంతర్జాతీయ వార్తా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, 20 ఏప్రిల్ 2023న దాదాపు 200 నుంచి 300 మంది నిరసనకారులు పారిస్లోని బిజినెస్ డిస్ట్రిక్ట్లో ఉన్న యూరోనెక్స్ట్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ కార్యాలయ లాబీలోకి ఒక్కసారిగా దూసుకెళ్లారు. నిరసనకారులు తమ చేతుల్లో యూనియన్ జెండాలను పట్టుకుని, ఎరుపు రంగు పొగ గొట్టాలు వెలిగించడంతో ఆ ప్రాంతమంతా ఎర్రటి పొగతో నిండిపోయింది. అధ్యక్షుడు ఇమ్మాన్యుయేల్ మాక్రాన్ ప్రభుత్వం రిటైర్మెంట్ వయసును 62 ఏళ్ల నుంచి 64 ఏళ్లకు పెంచుతూ చట్టం చేయడాన్ని నిరసిస్తూ ఆ సమయంలో ఫ్రాన్స్ వ్యాప్తంగా కార్మిక సంఘాలు, రైల్వే కార్మికులు పెద్ద ఎత్తున ఆందోళనలు చేపట్టారు.
అయితే ఈ నిరసన కేవలం కార్యాలయ ప్రవేశ ద్వారం (లాబీ) వరకే పరిమితమైంది. లోపల ట్రేడింగ్కు ఎలాంటి నష్టం వాటిల్లలేదని, స్టాక్ మార్కెట్ లావాదేవీలకు అంతరాయం కలగలేదని మీడియా పేర్కొంది. ఇక, అక్టోబర్ 2026లో జరుగుతున్న నిరసనల్లో యూరోనెక్స్ట్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ కార్యాలయంపై దాడి జరిగినట్లు ఇప్పటివరకైతే ఎటువంటి విశ్వసనీయ సమాచారం లేదు.
చివరిగా, పారిస్ స్టాక్ ఎక్స్చేంజ్ భవనంలోకి నిరసనకారులు దూసుకెళ్లిన ఈ వీడియో ఏప్రిల్ 2023 నిరసనలు సంబంధించినది.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.

Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Cocos (Keeling) Islands left behind as Australian government raises Pacific profile before COP31
In short:
A delegation from the Cocos (Keeling) Islands has been denied the opportunity to attend COP31 after their application was not selected by the federal government.
A contingent of federal ministers, including the prime minister, has wrapped up pre-COP talks in Tuvalu.
What's next?
UWA's Oceans Institute says despite the setback, it remains committed to working alongside the Cocos (Keeling) Islands community.
Residents of Australia's remotest territory say they feel forgotten by the government's global climate change efforts ahead of the major COP31 forum in Türkiye.
The federal government hosted pre-COP meetings in Tuvalu and Fiji this week in a bid to raise the voices of Pacific Island nations.
But on the far opposite side of Australia's recognised territory, and 8,900km from this week's Pacific meetings, residents of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands (CKI) feel they have been left in the lurch.
Faced with coastal erosion, flooding and other climate-driven issues mirroring those of Pacific nations, the Cocos Islanders made a bid to be represented at COP31.
Their application was approved by the United Nations, but not selected for funding by the Australian government, with the delegation informed they had been unsuccessful just before this week's talks.
Their panel proposal, submitted by the University of Western Australia's Oceans Institute, would have featured the challenges faced by the Cocos (Keeling) Islands as a low-lying island community.
Residents rue missed opportunity
Home Island resident Luluk Sloan said COP31 presented an opportunity to bring global awareness to the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.
With a coastal hazard management plan suggesting retreat slammed by the islands' residents, they had hoped attendance would have allowed them to learn how other island communities were dealing with climate-driven challenges.
"A council delegation was actually looking at visiting the Pacific Islands just to see what sort of mitigation they've got planned in terms of not retreating," she said.
"I think it's a disappointment that we don't have that link; we can't really tell our story globally."
Ms Sloan said it felt like the islands were being left behind.
"We are an Australian territory, who's voicing for us? Who's vouching for us? No-one."
West Island resident Rose Cummins also would have attended the conference.
"I certainly applaud the Pacific Islands. I think they've done an incredible job in raising the profile of climate change and how it's directly impacting them," Ms Cummins said.
"I guess we would just like the same opportunity."
A spokesperson for the Department of Climate Change, Energy and Water acknowledged the impact climate change was having on the Islands.
But the department rejected suggestions that the focus on the Pacific came at the expense of Australian communities.
"Engagement with Pacific partners complements, rather than replaces, our support for Australian communities facing climate risks," the spokesperson said.
The Oceans Institute said it remained committed to working with the islands' community to help address the ongoing challenges posed by climate change.
Community not heard
Residents say there has been a lack of meaningful consultation on the plan to manage the islands' ongoing coastal risks.
"I think a lot of people felt that it's another consultation," Ms Sloan said.
"What are they going to do about it? Possibly, probably, nothing."
Ms Cummins said expressions of interest for a community reference group, promised since the start of the year, were only issued last month.
"There's no decision-making abilities; it won't affect any policy or anything like that," she said.
"That will still be done by experts who don't live here."
The Climate Change Department spokesperson said the Coastal Hazard Risk Management and Adaptation Plan (CHRMAP) was a key step in supporting CKI to respond and adapt to climate change.
"The [plan] gives us a clear picture of the coastal hazards facing the islands and will help guide the work we do together to strengthen preparedness and improve community safety," the spokesperson said.
But Ms Sloan remained sceptical.
"I think people are slowly realising that … the delivery of services is on the decline," she said.
"And that's probably because they're thinking: 'Oh yeah, 50 years from now, the islands are going to go under.'"

Premier who oversaw Canada's first assisted dying law says he worries it's gone too far
Quebec passed MAID bill 2 years before federal law was approved by Parliament
The former Quebec premier who oversaw passage of Canada's first-ever medically assisted dying law says he now feels conflicted after seeing how far the practice has progressed since then.
Quebec's National Assembly passed the law in 2014 outlining conditions under which terminally ill patients could formally request medical assistance in dying (MAID).
While the bill was initially introduced by the Parti Québécois, it gained multiparty support while Philippe Couillard's Liberals were in government.
The former premier told CBC's The House that he sometimes questions his 2014 decision after seeing how MAID has expanded in Quebec and Canada since that first law was passed.
"It was clearly reserved for terminal or pre-terminal conditions with a defined, unfortunate road to the end of life. And this is not the case anymore," he told host Catherine Cullen.
"I'm not sure that I would have again voted for that law with the extension that we have seen in the recent years."
Two years after Quebec passed its law, the federal government passed its own MAID legislation — prompted by a 2015 Supreme Court ruling that said a prohibition of medically assisted dying ran contrary to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Former prime minister Justin Trudeau consulted with Couillard before the 2016 federal MAID law was adopted.
That federal legislation was struck down by the Superior Court of Quebec in 2019 because it was limited to those whose deaths were "reasonably foreseeable." The federal government passed a subsequent law in 2021 to fall in line with the court's ruling.
Quebec took things a step further in 2024, allowing for people to submit advance requests for MAID before a person's condition, such as Alzheimer's, renders them incapable of giving consent.
Couillard, a former neurosurgeon, emphasized that the intention of Quebec's original law was to limit MAID to those solely suffering from a terminal illness.
"I was warned about this by people opposing the law that told me, 'We see your motivation is good, but you will see, once you open the door you will not close it and it will open wider.' And this is what happened," he said.
The federal government announced this week that, after deliberation in the wake of the 2019 court ruling, it wouldn't proceed with expanding MAID to people who are solely suffering from mental illness. (There are multiple cases before the courts arguing for further expansion to include people suffering from mental illness).
In addition, Justice Minister Sean Fraser said new coming legislation will "open the door" for people to give advance consent if provinces allow.
"We need to create space for people to be able to provide consent when they know they're going to lose capacity in order to live out their remaining years rather than being put in a position where they fear they have to take that decision prematurely," Fraser said earlier this week.
"We don't have the jurisdiction to create these services in the different provinces. We only have the jurisdiction to determine when a particular set of behaviours will be treated as criminal under Canada's criminal laws."

- This is why Quebec is the only province where you can pre-approve your death
Despite his current reservations, Couillard praised the passing of the original bill as "one of the best moments of democracy" during his premiership, noting that he allowed for a free vote within his Liberal caucus.
But when asked, he said he does sometimes have regrets about passing the law.
"In general, when this hits me, I think about specific patients that I've known in my medical career that were in such deep distress and pain that I think we did the right thing," he said.
"But I hope we didn't go too fast. I hope we didn't take this as a trivial matter, which is certainly not the case."

Sanjay Dutt appeared on Shekhar Suman’s Shekhar Tonite for a Gandhi Jayanti special episode, where he remarked that he could no longer feel “peace” in the country. His comments drew backlash, following which Dutt clarified that the conversation was scripted and intended to be light-hearted and humorous. Shekhar Suman also defended him, saying the remarks were taken out of context.
Following the controversy, a purported video of actor Sanjay Dutt is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows him speaking about protecting Muslims from discrimination, opposing the saffronisation of government institutions and the armed forces, and saying that the people of Kashmir should decide their own future.
In the video, he can be heard saying (translated from Hindi to English), “I will not let Muslims suffer in India the way my mother suffered as a Muslim. I do not need the saffronisation of government institutions, especially the armed forces. The Army belongs to the country, not to any one colour. The decision on Kashmir should be made by the people of Kashmir. Let them choose their side and remove the Army from there.” Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows actor Sanjay Dutt making controversial remarks about Muslims, saffronisation, and Kashmir.
Fact: The video is AI-manipulated. The original visuals are from Sanjay Dutt’s appearance on Shekhar Tonite, but the alleged remarks about Muslims, saffronisation, the armed forces, and Kashmir do not appear in the original episode. AI voice detection tools also indicate that the audio has likely been generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
We searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible reports confirming that Sanjay Dutt made the alleged remarks.
We then reviewed the entire ‘Shekhar Tonite’ episode shared on Shekhar Suman’s official YouTube channel on 02 October 2026. However, we found no instance of Sanjay Dutt making the alleged statement anywhere in the episode, indicating that the audio in the viral clip has been added or altered.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. This suggests that the original footage was paired with fabricated audio to make it appear that actor Sanjay Dutt was speaking about protecting Muslims from discrimination, opposing the saffronisation of government institutions and the armed forces, and calling for the people of Kashmir to decide their own future.
To sum up, this video of Sanjay Dutt allegedly making controversial remarks about Muslims, saffronisation, and Kashmir is AI-manipulated.

Volkswagen’s ID.4 is no more. The midsize crossover debuted in 2021, one of VW’s first new electric vehicles designed in the wake of dieselgate. A year later, the company began local production in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and a couple of years ago facelifted the model, adding a much-improved rear drive unit in the process. But Chattanooga turned its attention away from the ID.4 earlier this year. And, having sold almost a million ID.4s (and near-identical ID.5s) globally, the German automaker has decided it’s time for its replacement. Meet the ID. Tiguan.
Dropping the numerical and adopting the moniker of VW’s big seller is a statement. “The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars. The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together,” said Thomas Schäfer, CEO of the VW brand.
VW was an early pioneer of using flexible vehicle architectures to create a multitude of bodystyles and sizes with common parts, and its transition into building EVs hasn’t changed that. The ID. Tiguan uses an updated version of the company’s mass-market EV platform, now called MEB+, with either 58 kWh or 77 kWh battery packs. The smaller pack is only available with a 187 hp (140 kW) rear electric motor, but the 77 kWh battery can be had with either a 281 hp (210 kW) rear-wheel drive powertrain or as a 295 hp (220 kW) all-wheel drive version. Range is up to 373 miles (600 km), at least according to the European WLTP test.
Alongside the mainstream name, it has a more mainstream look, though it’s part of VW’s new design language. For those keeping track of the various interesting names car companies give their design languages—it can’t just be me—this one is called Pure Positive. The automaker says it wants the ID. Tiguan to feel like it belongs to the premium rather than mainstream segment, both inside and out.

Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out
- Published
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an incident-packed sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix after Mercedes driver George Russell crashed out of the lead.
Russell was leading in tricky conditions, with half the track dry and half wet, when he got a little too wide at the final corner at the end of the first lap.
He lost control of his Mercedes, which spun across the track into the inside wall, before bouncing back again to the outside, the rest of the field somehow avoiding him.
Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton took second having made a superb start from sixth on the grid with team-mate Charles Leclerc third.
A final-lap collision between the McLarens as Lando Norris tried to pass Oscar Piastri at Turn Five promoted Russell's team-mate Kimi Antonelli to fourth place.
In combination with Russell's retirement, that extends the Italian's championship lead to 89 points.
A chaotic race saw the start delayed by 30 minutes by a tropical downpour, and then Verstappen navigating a safety car period following Russell's accident, a restart, and initial pressure from Hamilton to eventually ease away into a comfortable lead.
It was the Dutchman's second Formula 1 win in seven days, after his maiden victory this season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and the first time he has won in Singapore.
The rain before the start hit only parts of the track. The second sector stayed dry while the first sector, particularly Turns Two and Three, were soaking wet with standing water.
Once the rain abated, the field did two laps behind a safety car to check conditions before racing began with a standing start.
Russell gave himself a golden opportunity to breathe some life into his almost-extinguished title hopes when he beat Verstappen off the line and took the lead into the first corner.
But after leading the first lap, he made a mistake at the final corner.
Russell said: "I just misjudged it, got more power than I was expecting from the battery, got a little wider than I expected and touched the white line. Rule number one in the wet is don't touch the white line. Very silly mistake."
That left Verstappen in front, with Hamilton behind. But after the seven-time champion pursued his erstwhile 2021 title rival for a few laps, the Red Bull began to ease away and was clearly in control, leading Hamilton, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris and Antonelli.
With overtaking difficult around Marina Bay, the field was static until the closing stages.
Leclerc was struggling, and he began to be caught by the McLarens and Antonelli.
Norris had been pressuring Piastri for some laps before the Australian also began to close in on Leclerc, and Antonelli, struggling with oversteer in the early laps, picked up the pace.
On the final lap, Norris made a better exit out of Turn Three and saw an opportunity to try to pass Piastri at Turn Five.
He got the car well enough alongside to make a legitimate passing attempt, but Piastri defended his position robustly, the cars touched, and spun in unison.
Piastri, who hit the barriers, was out on the spot, but Norris was able to keep going, although he fell down to eighth, behind Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson, Haas driver Oliver Bearman and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg.
The stewards will investigate the Norris-Piastri incident after the race.
The delayed start to the sprint means grand prix qualifying will begin 30 minutes later than originally scheduled, at 14:30 BST.

Burnout is not always easy to recognise, particularly when physical tiredness can be mistaken for mental exhaustion. Arjan Bajwa, who has been part of films such as Rustom, Fashion, Kabir Singh and Demon Hunters, an India-Taiwan official co-production, and will next be seen in Madhur Bhandarkar’s film The Wives, speaks about the difference between the two, the signs that tell him it is time to step back, and why mental health deserves equal attention.
World Mental Health Day: Arjan Bajwa says, “Mental health is just as important, if not more than physical health”
“I think one can always deal with physical exhaustion by sleeping or taking some time to rest. But mental exhaustion never ends. Even when you are resting or completely disconnected from your social and professional life, your mind doesn't stop working,” he said.
That is why he believes people need to pay attention to what is happening internally rather than simply relying on physical rest. “The main emphasis has to be on your mental well-being as well. When your mental peace is disturbed, when you can't stop thinking about certain issues, and when something is really bothering you, that is when one needs to take a step back,” he said.
For him, that is when burnout can begin to make itself clear. “That's when you know you are moving towards burnout. Mental health is just as important, if not more important, than physical health,” he said.
The pressures of professional life, particularly in a career where everything can be scrutinised, can make that balance even harder to maintain. “Personal and professional expectations are a part of the job that you have chosen, so you can't run away from them,” he said.
He believes anyone choosing such a career needs to understand the responsibility that comes with it. “You have to be mentally strong enough to take on these kinds of responsibilities, or not be in that space at all,” he said.
At the same time, he admits that being constantly measured and scrutinised can become overwhelming. “Once you have decided that you want to be in a profession where everything is being measured, scrutinised and noticed, it definitely can be overwhelming,” he said.
The key, he feels, is finding a way to manage that pressure without allowing it to take over personal life. “At the same time, one has to remind themselves that this is the path they have chosen and that they can't hide away from it,” he said.
“All you can do is maintain a balance, keep some kind of sanity and find peace in your personal space to neutralise the overwhelming effect you may have experienced through the day,” Arjan signed off.

What reception awaits Man City at Anfield?
- Published
It was December 2024 when Pep Guardiola's Manchester City side were 2-0 down at Liverpool and the Anfield crowd chanted "you're getting sacked in the morning" towards the opposition boss.
No-one truly believed he was going to be given his marching orders but his side were on their way to a remarkable fourth consecutive Premier League defeat.
Guardiola could not help but lift six fingers up to the Liverpool crowd in response - representing the six Premier League titles he won with City.
Now, some may question each of those successes after an independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 financial charges the Premier League brought against them.
On Friday, current City boss Enzo Maresca said the club's titles are "absolutely not" tainted. But come Sunday, he and his players will face up to their new normal.
Such is the script that a trip to what promises to be a ferocious Anfield - a place Guardiola always described as difficult - is next.
City have won five out of five in the Premier League this term and it would be huge if Maresca can maintain that 100 % start.
But for Andoni Iraola and Liverpool, this will be an opportunity to truly kickstart their own campaign, fuelled by a backstory like no other.
"It's an exciting game," said the Reds boss. "We are playing at home at Anfield against City that is top of the league, they have won all of their games.
"We will go for the game, they will go for it and it will be quite an open game and we have to be ready. I hope we will be at the level of the game, which will be high."
Asked if it was the kind of fixture he relished when taking the Liverpool job, Iraola added: "Yes, we are here to play this game. We know it's going to be challenging. They are very good but we also are very good."
It will be the first time since 2015 this clash will have neither Jurgen Klopp or Guardiola on the touchline, but nevertheless, a hostile atmosphere awaits and Tom Werner, the Liverpool chairman, will be in attendance.
Liverpool finished second in the Premier League to Man City in 2013-14 under Brendan Rodgers and again in 2018-19 and 2021-22 when Klopp's side put up 97 and 92 points respectively, but were one shy of Guardiola's City as they were pipped to the title.
A verdict on City's appeal awaits. City insist they are innocent but there will be sections of the Liverpool fanbase and former players and staff that feel aggrieved.
"You think about the memories and the successes that you were wrongly denied," John Achterberg, who was Liverpool's goalkeeping coach under Rodgers and Klopp, told The Athletic., external
"We won one Premier League title [in 2019-20], but it could have been four given that we missed out to City three times by such narrow margins."
Iraola added: "The worst thing probably is the uncertainty. No-one knows what's going to happen. We have to focus on Liverpool and being the best club we can be, the best team we can be. That's my challenge."

The Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, had to intervene on Saturday after a significant number of advocates were detained by the Delhi Police amid protests in New Delhi.
“Yes, on my verbal intervention, I believe they have been released. I am out of town,” the CJI told ANI.
This came after the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) sought the inteference of the CJI on an urgent basis over the detention of a number of advocates, which included senior lawyers and women advocates as well. The SCBA alleged that those detained had been subjected to excessive police force as they were peacefully protesting in the Supreme Court area.
Quick answers to key questions
The lawyers were detained amid protests in the Supreme Court area during the wider security measures for the CJP demonstration in Delhi. The SCBA said they had been peacefully protesting and alleged that police used excessive force.
The CJI intervened after the SCBA, SCAORA and Solicitor General Tushar Mehta brought the detentions to his attention. He said he spoke to the authorities, after which the lawyers were released.
CJI Surya Kant told ANI that the lawyers had been released following his verbal intervention. He also said he was out of town.
The SCBA urged the CJI to intervene with the authorities, establish the whereabouts and safety of every detained advocate, and ensure legal assistance. It also sought the release of those held without lawful grounds.
The SCBA, the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (SCAORA) and Solicitor General Tushar Mehta apprised the CJI of the situation, who then spoke to authorities, following which the lawyers were released.
SCBA Honorary Secretary Pragya Baghel wrote a letter to the CJI on Saturday, urging him to take up the matter with concerned authorities and ensure that the whereabouts and safety of all detained advoates be ascertained.
The Association has also called for swift legal assistance for those lawyers who have been detained and the release of those against whom there is no lawful ground for detention.
“The Supreme Court Bar Association resolves to request the Chief Justice of India to intervene urgently and take up the matter with the concerned authorities,” the resolution stated.
The resolution further emphasised the need to ascertain the whereabouts of every detained advocate, ensure their safety and provide them with legal assistance.
The incident comes amid protests in Delhi linked to the proposed demonstration by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, which had led to security measures and disruptions concerning public transport.
More than a thousand protestors have been detained today by the Delhi Police, including leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka, Sourav Das, and others.
Four former chief ministers - Pinarayi Vijayan, Manik Sarkar, Arvind Kejriwal, and Mamata Banerjee were also detained. AISA president Neha Bora was also detained.
Mamata Banerjee claimed she and her party leaders were "kidnapped" by police and "driven around in a prison van for two hours" before being brought to Dwarka North Police Station.
