Welcome to Kernel Panic!, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
Even as AI supercharges digital scamming and cybercrime, it’s also being recruited in the fight to protect potential victims. Governments around the world have consistently struggled to address the global crisis of online crime, grappling with the limitations of attempting to crack down on criminals beyond their borders. This has inspired alternative efforts, like using automation to attempt to go after scammers en masse—perhaps by spamming the spammers to squander their resources. Now, AI platforms are turning these types of experiments into real tools in the fight against cybercrime.
For the last two years, the Australian company Apate, named after the Greek goddess of deception, has been building a system that diverts phone scammers onto calls with AI bots that are trained to keep conversations going as long as possible without, of course, ever actually falling for the scam. The goal is to give scammers enough hope that they stay on the phone, while also collecting intelligence about the scams they’re running.
“What we really like to think is that we’re building the perfect victims for scammers,” Dali Kaafar, the founder and CEO of Apate, tells us. “A minute that a scammer is talking to a bot or an agent is a minute where you’re probably saving hundreds, if not thousands of possible people being reached out to by that exact same scammer,” he says, referencing the ability for scammers to use automated dialing tools.
Kaafar says Apate’s platform, which is used by banks and supported by telecom companies, has around 350,000 bots. They not only pick up calls, but also infiltrate scam chat groups online and respond to text messages with similar goals of frustrating scammers while collecting intelligence from them. He says the company has collected more than 250,000 pieces of information about fraudsters in real-time, from scam URLs to money mule accounts and bank details.
The bots have different personalities, language skills, and profiles, Kaafar says, so scammers hopefully don’t detect that they’re conversing with an AI. Like real people, “sometimes [the bots] do have WhatsApp, sometimes they don’t. Sometimes they pick up the phone, sometimes they just actually hang up on the scammer saying, ‘I'll come back to you later,’” he says.
But are they convincing? Kernel Panic tested the tool using a demo version where users play the role of the scammer and talk to one of Apate’s AI “victims.” The personas are designed to express a healthy amount of skepticism but leave enough openings for scammers to continue to try to win them over, a dynamic that we could immediately feel and found intensely frustrating.
Scammers are likely familiar with this type of skeptical interaction, and Kaafar says that Apate calls regularly go on for more than two hours. In our testing, the Apate system was engaged and responsive, and the timing of the conversation felt natural, even with both of us tag-teaming the AI as a friend, “Lucy,” and her financial adviser “Mickey.” We did not succeed at getting the Apate AI system to invest in our cryptocurrency opportunity even after six minutes of diligent effort. (The returns are truly incredible, though, we swear.)
For now, even with Apate’s massive swarm of bots on the case, it’s only a matter of time before you get your next scam call or text. Cybercriminals initiate billions of messages and calls each year, with the most sophisticated operations running physical, industrial scale scamming sites. And while professional scambaiters and initiatives to infiltrate scam operations have done critical deterrent work for years, law enforcement and research efforts haven’t been able to stop the expansion of digital scamming overall.
But AI could create a new era for anti-scam efforts, not just scammers themselves. Better intelligence sharing between cops, social media companies, banks, and other industries is desperately needed and could potentially be aided by AI-driven monitoring and data analysis. Increasingly, too, innovative efforts have been looking to disrupt cybercriminals by exploiting their “psychological vulnerabilities.” In some cases, these psyops have included directly trolling those behind ransomware attacks. As the focus on disrupting scammers and cybercriminals expands, the use of generative AI as a way to keep them preoccupied, wasting resources, and not launching other attacks appears to be increasingly effective.
Take honeypots, for instance. For years, companies and security researchers have deployed false virtual machines to attract hackers, waste their time, gather information, and understand their secret hacking techniques. Mark Vero, a doctoral researcher at the department of computer science at ETH Zurich, says open source honeypot providers have increasingly been incorporating LLMs into their systems to make them appear more realistic.
In recent research, Vero and colleagues found an LLM-powered honey pot would keep AI agents attacking their system “significantly longer” than a honey pot with more predictable behavior. “The agentic attackers are much more convinced by the LLM simulated honeypots and they also mark them as actual honeypots at a much lower rate,” he says. “If these systems are built well enough, then I think it’s quite advantageous for defenders.”
Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

Anthropic's Claude AI submits a false tip on a Philadelphia unsolved homicide case
Latest example of AI agents meddling with government websites amid growing calls for regulation
An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said.
It's the latest example of AI models acting on their own and manipulating government and other websites in ways testers did not intend. In a report Friday, Anthropic also disclosed a separate incident when its AI model submitted forms to an undisclosed government website instead of stopping before submission.
The incident in Philadelphia occurred on July 18 when the AI model Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said.
Claude filled out a form on police site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com indicating it might have information regarding an unsolved murder listed on the site.
- OpenAI says its bots have interacted with multiple U.S. government sites in unexpected AI activity
- AI agents tried to hack Library and Archives Canada website, research firm says
Philadelphia police said in a statement they were unaware of the incident until Anthropic notified them on Wednesday. Then they found the submission in the website's tip records and confirmed it was marked spam and never forwarded to police.
Latest incident of rogue agents
There are rising concerns about AI companies' unchecked AI agents meddling with everything from U.S. government websites to health-care data. Critics have been calling for more regulation.
In September, another AI company, OpenAI, disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behaviour in artificial-intelligence models.
"Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers," the Philadelphia Police Department said in a statement. "Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement."
Anthropic said in its report that most of the reported behaviours are forms of what it calls persistence "in which Claude, when it cannot complete a task as given, works around a restriction instead of stopping."
The company said it was modifying its training to "reduce the likelihood of further misbehaviour."
Anthropic said it briefed the White House on cases that involved U.S. government agencies at the federal, state and local levels, and notified each agency involved.

Spain's slow response to the crisis in Ceuta leaves teen migrants on the streets
Hundreds of teenage migrants lined up outside a church in Ceuta in early October, hoping for good news from Spain's youth minister
CEUTA, Spain -- Hundreds of teenage migrants lined up outside a church in Ceuta in early October, hoping Spain's visiting minister of youth would bring them some good news: passage to continental Europe or at least a spot in a shelter.
For two months, they had slept on cardboard sheets and ripped sofas in squalid tent camps, or on the streets of the Spanish city in North Africa that juts into the Mediterranean like a thumb. On clear days, southern Spain is visible on the horizon.
Among them was a 17-year-old aspiring model from northern Morocco. In late July, he crossed into Ceuta with around 80,000 others in what would become Spain’s deadliest border crisis.
“Pray for me!” he told an Associated Press reporter. But instead, the teens were led down a steep hill to a soccer field so as not to overwhelm the minister. Within hours, many were back on the streets and hillsides.
Another setback for the young migrants, the scene also illustrated the Spanish government’s slow, often improvised response to the migration crisis in the territory. Thousands of minors reached Ceuta alone and, under Spanish law, are entitled to shelter, healthcare and education. Experts acknowledge the difficulties authorities face, but say the government may simply be hoping that many of them give up and head home.
“I was expecting a really easy experience,” said the 17-year-old, who did not want his name used because he is alone in Ceuta and fears for his safety. “I was expecting two to three weeks of this.”
Open-air, makeshift camps with adults and children have festered on beaches, at warehouses and on hillsides since tens of thousands of people swam or climbed around a breakwater that separates Morocco from Ceuta in July. About 140 people died trying to cross. Most of those who made it left within days, but officials do not have an exact count of how many people stayed.
A few thousand people lived in one beachside camp where the air reeked of human waste. Children as young as 13 slept and showered among adult men who frequently broke into fights.
Elsewhere, minors hid in the steep, narrow streets of some of the city’s predominantly Muslim neighborhoods.
“Our streets are littered with kids,” said Ahmed Enfed-Dal, the president of a neighborhood association.
Spanish prosecutors are investigating reports of torture and mistreatment of migrants, including minors. In September, Amnesty International published a report detailing allegations of cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment by Spanish soldiers. The report also mentioned the unsafe conditions of underage migrants and allegations of sexual abuse of girls.
In early October, the 17-year-old said he was sleeping in a car with other teens from Morocco. When he first arrived, he slept in a garage with two other minors. A resident charged them each 15 euros ($17) per night. Unable to keep paying, he went back to the streets.
“People tried to rob me twice and hit me,” he said. As weeks became months, he has started questioning why he stayed, but feels he cannot return to Morocco.
Like many Moroccan teens, he told the AP his high school diploma afforded limited opportunities back home. In Tetouan, just 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Ceuta, he worked with his father as a butcher. He said his family has encouraged him to stay.
“Morocco is a good tourist place,” he said. “But it’s not a good place to be a citizen.”
Minors who reach Spanish soil alone are the responsibility of regional governments or, in Ceuta's case, the city. Under Spanish law, a child can be sent back to his or her home country only under specific circumstances.
Spain's national government has told Ceuta to process those below 18 on a case-by-case basis, approving more than 90 million euros ($101 million) in funding, but the city insists it does not have the resources. Spain's Youth Minister Sira Rego has said most minors in Ceuta wish to stay in Spain, and “they will do so,” she told Spanish radio station Cadena Ser.
But Ceuta's Mayor Juan Vivas has urged national authorities to find a way to send the minors from Morocco back home.
“It’s easy to judge from over there,” Vivas said in September. “But you’ve got to be here.”
The two sides also have disagreed over something even more fundamental: How many migrants are still in Ceuta.
After the initial border rush, Spain’s interior minister said all but 2,000 people had gone back to Morocco. Spain revised the figure to up to 10,000 migrants in September. But Ceuta’s mayor says up to 15,000 people remain, acknowledging “the figure changes from one day to the next.”
Estimates of the number of unaccompanied minors have also fluctuated. Authorities say thousands remain in the city, though it's unclear how many are unsheltered.
Rights groups have criticized Spain for still not knowing how many minors there are.
“We understand that the protection system is currently overwhelmed, but that does not change the fact that there should be an official registry of all individuals in the city who declare themselves to be minors,” said Jennifer Zuppiroli, a migration expert at Save the Children in Spain.
As more minors have entered shelters, those still waiting are growing weary.
For weeks, the aspiring model visited the beachside tent camp to collect food from the Red Cross. He and dozens of migrant boys staged small demonstrations, appealing to authorities for help.
“We just want one thing — that Spain protects minors. Long live Spain!” read a tattered sign that boys as young as 13 held up as traffic whizzed past.
In early October, Spanish police started bulldozing the camp and mountains of detritus. Groups of migrants were bused elsewhere. Rights groups and others said some minors were taken to the border.
Over WhatsApp, the 17-year-old said he knew some teenagers whom police had taken from the beach. Some ended up in shelters. He was disappointed it happened on the one day he didn’t visit the camp.
Fearful that the police will send him back to Morocco, he has stayed hidden.
“I’m feeling tired for the first time since I came,” he said. “It’s been two months and we’re still living in the streets.”

Time to rise? Ranking European football's sleeping giants
- Published
Deportivo, Parma, Hamburg. Not just a football hipster's holiday hit-list, but a sample of erstwhile headline acts who have returned to their respective top flights in recent years.
You can throw Leeds United, Nottingham Forest, Schalke and Malaga into the mix too.
But with such footballing royalty back in the big time, where can you find Europe's current sleeping giants? Which one-mighty sides are still snoozing?
We first need to establish some criteria - history, heritage, fanbase, stadium. Clubs with huge potential who currently exist outside the top flight.
Calling a big city home helps, but it is not a deal-maker - sorry to fans of Bristol City and second-tier Russian outfit FC Ufa, where the local population tops one million.
Likewise, some clubs with good-sized stadiums have not made the cut. Bari, whose Stadio San Nicola is the third-largest in Italy and was built for Italia '90, stands out, though some of their calcio colleagues outside Serie A also have grounds of more than 30,000 - Hellas Verona, Messina and Palermo among them.
There's a plethora of ex-Premier League teams with top-flight worthy arenas and storied pasts, while Germany is stacked full of historic clubs with huge homes who arguably deserve a spot - Fortuna Dusseldorf, Wolfsburg, Hannover 96 - but we can't include them all.
A sleeping giant must have experienced some element of former glory and Pro Vercelli are the obvious candidate there, winning seven Italian titles by 1922. But, despite being under new ownership, the third-tier side boast neither the ground nor local population to awaken that historic status any time soon.
The other nuance is, that success cannot have come too recently. West Ham, for example, won a European competition three years ago, Wolves are recent top-flight regulars; likewise Stade de Reims, twice European Cup runners-up, and eight-time French champions Nantes.
Leaving out Steaua Bucharest was another big call. European Cup winners 40 years ago and Romania's most dominant club, they now play in Liga II. But, following a deeply divisive split, many of the traditional fanbase follow top-flight FCSB. So who really owns that legacy?
And there was a case for Boavista, title winners in 2001 but whose existence now hangs by a thread. Facing financial ruin, despite fans' best efforts, they have been ejected from Portugal's professional leagues.
Anyway, let's get on with this. Piped through the matrix above, here are my top 10 European sleeping giants - you can have your say in the comments, too.
10. Bursaspor
League titles: One (2009-10). Domestic cups: One (1985-86). Division: 1.Lig, second tier. Stadium: Centennial Ataturk Stadium (43,361)
Historically dominated by Istanbul's elite teams, Bursaspor snapped that long-running streak by becoming only the second club from outside of the capital - and first since Trabzonspor almost three decades earlier - to clinch the Turkish title in 2010.
That meant Champions League nights against Manchester United and Rangers, but in 2024 the Green Crocodiles dropped into the fourth tier for the first time in their history.
Based in a city of about 2.5m people - Bursa sits in the north west, south of Istanbul, near Mount Uludag - and with a unique crocodile-shaped stadium that can house 43,361 fans, Bursaspor have soared up the pyramid since and are looking to return to the Super Lig for the first time since 2019.
9. Dynamo Dresden
League titles: Eight (most recent East German DDR-Oberliga 1989-90). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 89-90). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Rudolf-Harbig-Stadion (32,085).
Without wanting to turn this into a 2.Bundesliga table, this is the first of four German entries. But Dynamo Dresden, bearing a complex history and situated in the underrepresented east, feel a little different.
Initially enjoying the support of the security forces before their best players were relocated to Berlin, Dynamo became European regulars and lost to Liverpool in the Uefa Cup in 1976 and European Cup two seasons later.
One of East Germany's most dominant clubs, they won eight titles and seven cups and joined the Bundesliga in 1991 following reunification, but they dropped into the third tier four years later amid relegation and mounting debts.
Dynamo, with alumni including Matthias Sammer, have bounced around the regional and lower leagues for many years but now sit in 2.Bundesliga.
Based in a city of more than half a million people, their potential is underpinned by a large, passionate fanbase who averaged over 30,000 for home games in the second tier last term.
8. Kaiserslautern
League titles: Four (most recent 1997-98). Domestic cups: Two (most recent 95-96). Division: 2.Bundesliga. Stadium: Fritz-Walter-Stadion (49,327)
With their 1997-98 success, Kaiserslautern remain the only side to win the Bundesliga immediately after promotion, albeit following a surprise relegation having also been champions in 1991 and enjoyed cup triumphs in 1990 and 1996.
European regulars in the 1990s and early 2000s, it is now almost 15 years since they competed in the Bundesliga, spending four seasons in the third tier before a promotion in 2022.
Despite modest league finishes, the club continue to record average crowds of more than 46,000 and almost pulled off another shock in 2024 when they reached the German Cup final, losing to Xabi Alonso's Leverkusen.
7. Sheffield Wednesday
League titles: Four (most recent 1929-30). Domestic cups: Four (most recent 90-91). Division: League One, third tier. Stadium: Hillsborough (39,732)
Sheffield United fans may argue that they, not city rivals Sheffield Wednesday, should make this list. But the Owls edge it on history and heritage - even if the most recent of their four league titles came almost 100 years ago.
Wednesday were League Cup winners in 1991, and in living memory for many gave us magical moments from the likes of David Hirst, Chris Waddle and Paolo di Canio. Yet they now sit in the third tier after entering administration and enduring relegation last season, before a US consortium bought the club in May.
The Owls, boasting England's 12th biggest club stadium, were relegated from the top flight in 2000, but fans are fuelled with fresh optimism that a reawakening is possible.
6. Hertha BSC
Leagues: Two (most recent 1931). Domestic cups: Two (most recent 2002). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Olympiastadion (74,475).
I'm convinced Hertha have huge potential, if not the history to match some of their counterparts. Their only titles, for example, precede the Bundesliga era.
But the Old Lady once reached a Uefa Cup semi-final and beat Chelsea in the Champions League in 1999.
This season is their fourth consecutive campaign outside the top tier, but Hertha continue to play at Berlin's Olympiastadion and regularly attract more than 50,000 fans. A new ground on the Olympic Park site, housing up to 52,000, is being considered.
Currently top of 2.Bundesliga, Hertha can tap into a deep talent pool on their doorstep - highly rated youngsters Ibrahim Maza and Kennet Eichhorn have joined Leverkusen, goalkeeper Tjark Ernst went to Feyenoord - and look equipped to return to the Bundesliga in fine shape.
5. Bordeaux
Leagues: Six (most recent 2008-09). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 12-13). Division: Regional 1, sixth tier. Stadium: Stade Atlantique (42,115)
Bordeaux's recent troubles have been well documented. Relegated from Ligue 1 in 2022 before administration meant they tumbled into the fourth tier, this summer they were again demoted to the regional sixth tier because of financial issues.
Having seemingly hit the bottom, the 2009 French champions now at least have something to build on after being bought by US investment fund Park Bench for one euro.
Les Girondins are dripping in history. Once home to former greats Jean Tigana and Zinedine Zidane, as well as current France internationals Aurelien Tchouameni and Jules Kounde, their decade-old home hosted a Euro 2016 quarter-final - albeit Bordeaux are not playing there at present as they try to shape their future.
4. FC Nuremberg
League titles: Nine (most recent 1967-68). Domestic cups: Four (most recent 06-07). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Max-Morlock-Stadion (50,000).
Perhaps it's not overly imaginative to be opting for the current top two in Germany's second tier but FC Nuremberg meet all the selection criteria laid out above.
They have the history - nine titles, with the latest of four cup triumphs coming in 2007; a 50,000-seater home; large local fanbase in a one-club city - and the heritage.
They're nicknamed 'Der Club' because of their status in early German football.
Oh, and World Cup winner and Germany's all-time top goalscorer Miroslav Klose is their boss.
3. Real Zaragoza
Domestic cups: Six (most recent 2003-04). European: Cup Winners' Cup (1994-95). Division: Primera Federacion, third tier. Stadium: La Romareda (under reconstruction but projected 43,000).
David Seaman, look away now. Arsenal fans of a certain vintage will remember former Spurs boy Nayim's long, looping winner beating the moustachioed stopper in the final minute of extra time to give Real Zaragoza the Cup Winners' Cup.
There have been two Copa del Rey triumphs, European journeys and star names since - Pablo Aimar, Diego Milito and David Villa among them - but three decades later, Los Manos find themselves in Spain's third tier.
Ander Herrera, aged 37, is back at his boyhood club, who are in the process of developing a new 43,114-capacity stadium for the 2030 World Cup, in an attempt to help the fallen giants return to former glories.
"Real Zaragoza belong to Europe, they belong to compete for trophies, to be fighting with the biggest clubs in Spain and in Europe," said Herrera.
2. Saint-Etienne
League titles: 10 (most recent 1980–81). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 2012–13). Continental: European Cup runners-up (1975–76). Division: Ligue 2, second division. Stadium: Stade Geoffroy-Guichard (41,965)
Saint-Etienne were, until Paris St-Germain overtook them in the past decade, the most-decorated club in France with 10 league titles in 25 seasons from 1956-57 to 1980-81.
Les Verts reached the European Cup final in 1976, losing to a vintage Bayern Munich side, while their last silverware came in the now-defunct Coupe de la Ligue 13 years ago with a team spearheaded by Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang.
They are presently spending their fourth season in five in the second tier, but they continue to produce top prospects. Star defenders William Saliba and Wesley Fofana came off the production line, while 18-year-old attacking talent Djylian N'Guessan will join Liverpool in January.
Then there is their 41,965-capacity Stade Geoffroy-Guichard home, nicknamed the 'cauldron', which was a whisker from seeing Ligue 1 football again this term - Les Verts lost to Nice in the promotion/relegation play-off, meaning the wait to rejoin France's elite continues.
1. Sampdoria
League titles: 1990-91. Domestic cups: Four (most recent 93–94). Continental: Cup Winners' Cup (89–90), European Cup runners-up (91-92). Division: Serie B, second tier. Stadium: Stadio Luigi Ferraris (33,205)
Sampdoria were once continental big-hitters, not merely domestic champions during a golden era of Italian football.
Buoyed by Paolo Mantovani's investment, the Genoa outfit won the Coppa Italia four times between 1985 and 1994, clinched the Scudetto in 1991 and reached three European finals, winning the Cup Winners' Cup in 1990 a year after losing to Barcelona in the final.
In 1992, the team of Gianluca Vialli, Roberto Mancini and Gianluca Pagliuca were again beaten by Barcelona in extra time of the European Cup final at Wembley.
More big names followed in the period between Sven-Goran Eriksson's side winning the club's last major trophy in 1994 and a first relegation five years later - Clarence Seedorf, Juan Sebastian Veron and Ariel Ortega included.
Samp had spells back in Europe before finishing bottom of Serie A in 2023 amid serious financial problems and almost dropped into the third tier.
Under new ownership, though, fans hope the club's future is more stable - and the architecturally iconic Stadio Luigi Ferraris home they share with rivals Genoa is set to undergo an expensive redevelopment before Italy host Euro 2032.

Afcon final to play out in court - when will Morocco or Senegal be crowned champions?
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes but, in its own way, the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) has been playing out for nearly nine months.
Now, finally, one team or the other - either Morocco or Senegal - willl grab the winner. Only that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Thursday, Sport's highest legal authority - the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) - will hear Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they had won back in January against the hosts in Rabat.
But those hungry for a resolution have already been warned it will not arrive on the same day.
So how did we get here? And what happens next?
What happened in the Afcon final?
In front of 66,000 home fans creating an electric atmosphere inside Rabat's Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco appeared set for a date with destiny as they chased their first Afcon title since 1976.
Instead, the final descended into chaos deep into stoppage time.
With the match still goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had already blown for a Moroccan free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a VAR review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Real Madrid's Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the grateful arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
Or so they thought.

Why was the Afcon final result overturned?
Unsurprisingly the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled "Withdrawals", states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team… leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" they shall be "considered the loser and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March, a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, others, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.

  - Published13 May
- Denounce 'abject' Afcon decision - senior Caf member 
  - Published19 March
What is the Court of Arbitration for Sport?
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The appeal will be heard by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
In this instance, the panel will be led by 76-year-old Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
If the panel fails to come to a consensus, its president will make the final decision.

  - Published28 September
When will we get a verdict?
While the hearing, which will be heard in private at the request of the parties involved, is expected to end on Thursday afternoon, Cas have already warned that this is merely the starting point of the panel's deliberation.
In a statement, the court warned it "cannot state when a final decision will be rendered but it will not be on the day of the hearing".
Having already waited nearly nine months to get to this stage, the bad news is that the Cas code states that appeal verdicts should be delivered a maximum of four months after a hearing, though guidelines also say panels should aim for less than three months.
The good news is that it can be quicker.
In 2020, Manchester City appealed to Cas over Uefa's decision to ban them from European club competitions for breaching financial fair play regulations.
The hearing took place on 8 June with the verdict landing in City's favour on 13 July.
What could the long-term fallout be?
Even though Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has already been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said back in March that they will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Teranga Lions' walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, back in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw has already been given his marching orders by Senegal, having lost his job following the team's last-32 World Cup exit, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Moroccan dugout back in January, was dismissed in March.
Both men will no doubt still view success with Cas as a moral victory.
Whatever the outcome, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy were furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have, meanwhile, leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked them, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which eventually led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.
With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.
But while the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

NEW DELHI: Unprecedented security arrangements from central Delhi to the borders, phalanxes of 35,000 police and paramilitary personnel and a virtual choke on metro services and trains foiled Cockroach Janta Party's march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday. The city, however, remained on edge, with young protesters being detained on their way to the protest site and bundled into buses and vans, kicking and screaming, through the day.With CJP's Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das detained at the airport, the outfit's national organisation in-charge, Ajinkya Shinde, was named to lead the protests. The computer science grad, a former AAP worker, said protests would continue till Gyanesh Kumar resigned as CEC.With top CJP functionaries being kept away from Jantar Mantar, small groups dodged security personnel and staged flash protests at Safdarjung flyover, Dilli Haat and Gurdwara Bangla Sahib complex, among other places.
The impromptu gathering near Safdarjung flyover by AISA national president Neha Bora, lawyer Prashant Bhushan, political commentator Yogendra Yadav, and several others caught police off-guard momentarily around 1pm.
The protesters were eventually detained.It was obvious since Thursday that the call by CJP, supported by some political outfits, for a protest against the CEC and SIR at Jantar Mantar at 10am on Saturday would be met with stiff resistance. New Delhi was divided into 20 zones, with 1-2 companies of CAPF and Delhi Police deployed at every nook and corner. BSF was also present at the city's borders.
Security arrangements may not see let-up today
Water cannons and tear-gas vehicles were kept ready. Multiple layers of barricades were erected and police personnel closely questioned people heading towards the New Delhi area, particularly in the direction of Jantar Mantar. Police said there were only some isolated incidents of minor confrontations. While three or four personnel, including women, were injured in incidents of stone-pelting and other skirmishes, a DCP fractured his hand, they said.Police claimed they had detained 2,500 people in the city — 600-700 people on stretches leading to Jantar Mantar, and others from different parts of Delhi, including the borders. The police figures were, however, hotly contested, with sources saying around 7,000 people were detained, counting those who were not allowed to leave their homes and were put under preventive detention.CJP’s Ajinkya Shinde, who will lead the protests now, alleged more than 15,000 people, including students, civil society members and political functionaries, had been illegally detained across the country. An undeclared emergency had been imposed in Delhi, he said.Police said apart from the fact that permission had not been given for the protest, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) were in force, making the proposed gathering illegal.Four former chief ministers — Aam Aadmi Party convener Arvind Kejriwal, Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, Kerala’s Pinarayi Vijayan, and Manik Sarkar of Tripura — were detained. CPM veteran Brinda Karat, Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas, and TMC functionaries Derek O’Brien and Dola Sen were also detained.
Detained protesters were taken in buses to Chhatrasal Stadium, Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, Yamuna Sports Complex and Surajmal Stadium, all designated earlier for this purpose. Around 600 buses, including some from Third Battalion used to transport prisoners, were used to ferry those detained.Around 9pm, police claimed they had released everyone, but refused to respond when asked about Dipke, Ranka and Das. Multiple cases will be registered in connection with violation of prohibitory orders and assault, besides other sections, police said.With CJP sources saying they will continue their protests and Congress and other INDIA bloc parties planning a march in the city Monday, the security paraphernalia is likely to remain in place for the next few days.

South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
- Published
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.
But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.
In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
- Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
  - Published11 January 2025
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

Priya (name changed), 32, from Kerala, had been struggling with recurring episodes of depression that affected her ability to carry out everyday activities. Despite taking medication for several weeks, she continued to experience symptoms. With her symptoms persisting, she sought further medical advice and is now undergoing repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). This non-invasive procedure uses magnetic pulses to stimulate specific areas of the brain.
Priya’s experience reveals a challenge in managing depression, say experts. While antidepressants help many people, some continue to experience symptoms despite treatment, requiring doctors to reassess the diagnosis and consider other interventions.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Even in the 21st century and despite government efforts, child marriages are growing in Madhya Pradesh. The state witnessed an almost 46% jump in child marriages in 2025 compared to 2020. Nearly 20% of women in the state get married before turning 18.
According to the latest data from the Madhya Pradesh Women and Child Development Department, 538 child marriages were reported in the state in 2025, up from 366 incidents in 2020.
The growth in the numbers was steady. From 366 cases in 2020 to 436 in 2021, to 519 in 2022, to 528 in 2023. The numbers rose to 529 in 2024 and then to 528 last year.
According to the National Family Health Survey-6, 23.4% of women in rural areas and 9% in urban areas got married before 18. Damoh district topped in child marriages in 2025 with 115 cases.
It was followed by Rajgarh (44), Chhatarpur (35), Guna (28), Sagar (24), Dewas (24), and Narsinghpur (23).
However, child marriage was less prevalent in tribal regions. Jhabua, where nearly 87% of the population is tribal, recorded just 68 child marriages between 2020 and 2025. In comparison, Alirajpur recorded only seven such cases.
According to social activists, apathy towards the ill effects of early marriage and early pregnancy on the health and education of girls is one of the reasons for child marriages.
The cases
Case 1: Underage couple migrates to repay bride price
A Bhilala girl from Barwani district was married in 2025 at the age of 16. Her father was a labourer and she had six sisters and one brother. As is the custom among Bhilalas and some other tribes, the groom's family pay bride price to the bride's family.
The boy’s parents demanded a bride price paid by their son. To repay the bride price, the underage couple has now migrated to a city to work as labourers. The girl is pregnant and anaemic.
Case 2: Teen mother severely anaemic, child malnourished
A girl got married at the age of 14 in a Bhopal s neighbouring district. Social activists tried to stop the wedding but the whole village rose in support of the parents of the child couple.
The teen girl became a mother at the age of 15. Now, she is severely anaemic, with a haemoglobin level of 7. Her child is severely malnourished and unlikely to survive.
No one asks girls what they want
Patriarchal mindset of society doesn't allow parents to ask the girls what they want to do - whether they want to study further or whether they want to get married.
Parents, especially in rural areas, begin thinking about marrying off their daughters immediately after they attain menarche.
The fear of girls having an affair and thus bringing a bad name to the family is also one of the reasons for child marriages, said social activist Shalini Saxena.

Satya Nadella says that in the relationship between AI and a company, trust issues can be healthy.
In a lengthy X post on Saturday, the Microsoft CEO said companies don't always understand an AI model's decisions or behavior, so they need to build walls to protect themselves from the tech.
After all, it's very possible that AI is already exploring new connections.
"We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient," Nadella said. "Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system."
Nadella said that AI models aren't inherently malicious, but anything with access to vital systems can become compromised or make mistakes. He added that AI models shouldn't be able to operate the controls that determine what they can access or what actions they can take.
"Today this means separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work, as well as the action space that defines what it can do. It also means externalizing controls and safeguards," Nadella said.
He added, "The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least."
Box CEO Aaron Levie responded to Nadella's post and said AI will need to go through a "zero trust era."
"And all of this leads to needing various layers of protection and auditability of what agents are doing, what data they can work with, and controls for when things go wrong. And a huge opportunity right now for those building such systems across the enterprise," Levie said.
As the pace of AI development continues to pick up, everyone is clamoring for stricter guardrails, including the companies building the AI models themselves.
In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the industry needs to slow down AI development. His blog post drew support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk.
The Trump administration, which has supported rapid AI development, has resisted regulating the industry. This month, Senators Josh Hawley and Chris Murphy proposed bipartisan legislation to hold AI agent developers and operators liable for hacking incidents.
Nadella's remarks come after a series of cybersecurity incidents rocked the AI industry. Last month, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent breached a government website this summer. In July, Anthropic said it had identified three incidents in which a Claude model accessed the internet and breached unauthorized systems.
On X, Nadella shared a list of suggested principles that companies should follow, including the assumption that models are "compromised" and must be contained from the start.
"Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task," he said. "More advanced models will require more advanced containment technologies that we need to standardize on."
Nadella also said companies need to disclose when their AI systems fail or become compromised to the affected parties in a timely manner.

A large randomised controlled trial among heart failure patients in India led by the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) in Kerala, has found that hospitalisation episodes and all-cause mortality among heart failure patients can be significantly reduced if patients are systematically followed-up by a nurse, with the help of a mobile health application.
The two-year Telemonitoring and Integrated Multidisciplinary care for Heart Failure (TIME-HF) trial found that heart failure patients with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) who received nurse-led collaborative care had a 22% lower risk of death than those receiving usual care. They were also more likely to remain alive without hospitalisation during the two-year follow-up.
The trial results were published in the American Heart Association’s Journal, Circulation, on August 30, 2026.
What makes the trial relevant is that it addresses critical gaps in heart failure care: in Keralam, heart failure registries have reported high mortality post-discharge — 82.7% mortality over 10 years, alongside the fact fact that only 25.4% of the patients with heart failure receive guideline-based therapies. It also holds lessons for the rest of the country: with nearly 27% of all deaths in India being due to heart disease, and 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease occurring between the ages of 40 and 69 years, there is an urgent need for quality, post-discharge care.
What the trial did
The TIME-HF trial involved 1,507 adults at 22 government and private hospitals in Keralam and neighbouring States, with 755 patients assigned to the intervention and 752 to usual care. The mean age was 61.9 years; 77.6% were men, 57.3% lived in rural areas and 70% had relatively low educational attainment. Ischaemic heart disease was the predominant cause of heart failure, accounting for 77.4% of cases.
Results indicated that nurse-led intervention substantially improved prescription of the four major components of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure — renin-angiotensin system inhibition/ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.
“Our heart failure patients receive sub-optimal care, as most of them do not adhere to therapies or follow up with the doctor on time. There is also the issue of physician inertia. HF Registry evidence indicates that the median survival after diagnosis of heart failure is just 3.7 years. This collaborative care model is proof that survival and quality of life of these patients can be improved if we systematically address the gaps in care so that proven therapies for heart failure become part of routine care,” said lead researcher and additional professor at SCTIMST P. Jeemon.
Centring nursing care
The model put a trained nurse at the centre of the care pathway, who would closely monitor heart failure patients after discharge, educate the patient and family about heart-failure self-care, lifestyle modification and encourage medication adherence.
Nurses reviewed the patients’ medication regimen at discharge to ensure that there was no deviation from the guideline-mediated therapies. This was again reviewed at every follow-up visit with the help of a mobile-health app. The m-health app helped the nurses monitor all physical parameters of the patient real time and to identify warning signs of worsening disease, communicate and connect with patients and physicians so that timely hospitalisation was possible.
All participants underwent scheduled follow-up visits every three months for two years. Adherence to all four guideline-directed medical therapies was only 22.1% in the usual-care group, while it was 37.3% in the intervention group at two years.
“The health system engaging with the patient regularly was the key here. The m-health app gave the patient updates in real time to the nurse. Oxygen saturation levels, weight gain, weight loss, drop in blood pressure or respiratory rate comes as alerts, and then were escalated to the physician,” Dr. Jeemon points out.
The TIME-HF trial thus helped address one of the health system’s persistent weaknesses: that of proper follow-up care of patients with chronic diseases. The model is suited for strengthening chronic disease management and reducing the burden of hospitalisation and mortality in resource-limited settings across the country, experts said.

‘Build here, scale here’: IIT alumni body urges institution's diaspora to ‘come home’ to India amid US green card crackdown
Pan IIT Alumni India argued that India now offers opportunities in research, deep tech and innovation that previously drove many skilled professionals to leave.
Pan IIT Alumni India, the umbrella body representing alumni of all 23 Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), on Friday urged the global IIT diaspora to “come home” and “build here, scale here, contribute here”, amid the United States' decision to freeze Green Card filings by eight companies, including Indian IT majors Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) and Infosys.
The alumni body described its appeal as “not a rejection of the world” but “an invitation to come home to a nation that has arrived”, arguing that India now offers opportunities in research, deep tech, and innovation that had previously driven many skilled professionals to leave the country.
Pan IIT Alumni India is a registered society representing more than 500,000 IIT alumni worldwide. The organisation, operating from IIT Delhi, promotes India as a source of innovative technology solutions and serves as a platform for policy engagement, mentorship, and collaboration across the global IIT diaspora.
What the IIT alumni body said
Deep Dive
In a statement, the alumni body expressed concern over the US administration’s action against the permanent labour certification programme, known as Program Electronic Review Management (PERM), and the treatment of skilled Indian professionals on H-1B visas.
While acknowledging the sovereign right of countries to frame their immigration policies, it called for their implementation to be “fairly, transparently, and without stigmatising a community of professionals whose contributions to the American economy and society are well documented”.
“For over five decades, Indian engineers and technologists — a large number of them IIT alumni — have been among the most productive contributors to American innovation, research, and industry,” the statement said, adding that they had built products, filed patents, founded companies and created jobs in the US.
The alumni body also criticised the collective characterisation of Indian professionals as “indentured servants”, calling it “neither accurate nor fair”.
The statement comes amid a widening US crackdown on skilled-worker immigration. On Thursday, the US Labour Department suspended PERM filings involving eight companies — Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Microsoft, Adobe and Capgemini — and opened investigations into nine universities, citing concerns over fraud and American job losses.
PERM certification is required for most employment-based Green Card applications. Under the process, employers must demonstrate that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages, working conditions or job opportunities of American workers. The freeze does not appear to directly affect existing H-1B visa holders, but could disrupt a key route through which employers sponsor temporary foreign workers for permanent residency.
Against this backdrop, Pan IIT Alumni India said the developments should also prompt a reassessment within the Indian diaspora of career opportunities at home. It argued that the factors that once compelled many of India’s brightest engineers to seek opportunities abroad — including the lack of world-class research opportunities, deep-tech infrastructure and patient capital — had changed.
“India today offers the challenges and opportunities that were once only available abroad,” it said, renewing its appeal to IIT alumni overseas: “From Silicon Valley to the Indus Valley — build here, scale here, contribute here.”
Prabhat Kumar, an Indian Revenue Service (IRS) officer and chairman of Pan IIT Alumni India, said the latest developments highlighted the risks of building a career dependent on immigration status.
“For decades, we celebrated when our brightest minds left for American shores. It is time we asked what we lost in the process. A visa was never a stable foundation for a career, and this week's events prove it,” he said.
“The most exciting problems — and the greatest impact — now await our engineers at home. Build here. Scale here. Die here,” he added.

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

5 Samsung Galaxy features you should be using after updating to One UI 9
One of them is a pretty useful security feature.
With its latest crop of foldables in August came Samsung's One UI 9 update, the first version of the company's interface for Galaxy devices to be built atop Android 17. Along with a fresh new version of the operating system, One UI 9 brings some welcome updates and features. It's rolling out widely as of this writing to recent flagships prepped for the update.
By now, we've grown accustomed to a slew of sloppy AI features accompanying new smartphones, so it's a great relief to report that many of the new inclusions this time around seem like things real people might actually appreciate. Even some AI features are a bit more grounded than the gimmicky photo generation features from the past couple of years.
After installing One UI 9 on both a Galaxy S26 Ultra and S25 Ultra, we tested its most exciting new features to figure out which are the most useful. While some features seemed great on paper, like the Now Nudge feature that's supposed to serve up contextual information when you need it, they turned out to be lackluster in practice. Now Nudge still hasn't shown me anything useful, even with a scary amount of my data being fed into it. On the other hand, some of the more pedestrian additions to the software turned out to be quite handy. Here are the five Samsung Galaxy features you should be using after updating to One UI 9.
My FanCam lets you turn a wide video into a tracking shot
Samsung has spent a lot of effort on AI photo and video editing features you've probably never touched, but now it seems to be homing in on the things people will find useful. One of the marquee features in One UI 9 is My FanCam, which lets you turn a wide shot into a tight tracking shot of a single person. One marketing clip from Samsung shows a video of a rock band, and when My FanCam is invoked, each of the band's members is highlighted on screen. Once the user chooses the guitarist, the video crops around him in close-up.
Aside from concerts, the feature is perfect when shooting dance videos for social media. Rather than being forced to stay in the frame of a vertically shot video, you can dance in widescreen and then crop to the vertical framing afterward. It also seems like a promising way to get highlights of your kids' sports games. My FanCam will simply track a subject across an entire video, and you don't need to shoot video in a specialized mode to make it work. The magic happens when you open a video you've already recorded in Samsung Gallery and tap the Galaxy AI button, which is an icon that looks like sparkles.
AI-powered video editing apps like CapCut have offered similar functionality for years, so the fact that you can now produce the same thing natively in Samsung's Android software is a welcome addition. Accomplishing this kind of tracking shot in a manual editing program like Adobe Premiere Pro can require hours of tedious work, so it's remarkable to see this automatic capability run on a smartphone. Blessedly, the feature works on-device without sending data to the cloud. In Engadget's testing, My FanCam was available and worked while the phone was in airplane mode. You will, however, need a Samsung account login. Engadget tested the feature on a Galaxy S26 Ultra and S25 Ultra, but One UI 9 is still in the process of rolling out to older models. Outside reporting shows that Galaxy phones in the S24 series are the oldest models to have My FanCam in the beta version of One UI 9.
Even more Quick Panel customization
Customizing your phone is easier in One UI 9. With One UI 7 in 2024, Samsung visually overhauled One UI, and among the biggest changes was the decision to split quick settings and notifications into two different panels. One UI 8 and 8.5 went even further by allowing users to customize the Quick Panel, as it's called. Settings can be placed anywhere they fit, and they can even be resized. Now, in One UI 9, Samsung is giving users even more control.
The biggest change this time around is to the volume and brightness sliders. Yes, you could reorient them vertically before, but the volume slider always had the ringer mute shortcut glued to one end. The same was true of the brightness slider and dark mode toggle. Now, you can ditch those buttons and turn the sliders into solo operators. Sliders in general are now also more minimal, shimmying free of the large UI pads around their borders in previous software versions. Borders around tiles have also been nixed.
The most subtle change is to the music player widget that lives in the Quick Panel (though it also appears atop the notifications panel and in the live notification chip in the top left of the screen). The little waveform that appears on the scrubber bar during playback now matches the current album art.
Better document scanning helps flatten the curve
For many years, Samsung has offered a document-scanning feature inside its native One UI camera app. It's one of the most convenient ways to quickly scan paper documents, signage and more. But it does struggle with curved surfaces, making it difficult to scan book pages or anything else that doesn't lie completely flat.
In One UI 9, Samsung gave the document scanner a major upgrade that should help it to digitize books and other bound documents more accurately, as well as documents with folded corners. Previously, if a document appeared warped after scanning it with the camera, there were a few tweaks you could make after the fact to help smooth it out, but the odds of doing so successfully weren't great. Ditto for folded paper, in which case dog-ears and other folds showed up as harsh lines in the scanned photo. In One UI 9, the scanner will automatically compensate for both scenarios, meaning you can scan two pages of a book and it will look like a flat, digital render of the pages rather than like a reading packet handed out by your high school English teacher.
There are a few more goodies this update brought to the scanner. An updated finger eraser automatically removes your thumb from photos you took of documents while holding them. The tool can compensate for moire and glare, too, and there's even a new home screen shortcut so you can launch right into the scanning tool the moment you need it — no fiddling in the camera app required. In tests we performed (shown above) scanning book pages, the scanner did a decent job of removing my thumb and doing away with a dog-ear, though a full two-page book layout seemed to stymie it.
Generative Now Brief cards show information you actually want
First introduced in One UI 7 with the Galaxy S25 series, the Now Brief on the lock screen's Now Bar has never lived up to its promise. Samsung claimed it would use AI to show "real-time updates that matter most right on the lock screen," but it was mostly useless. "The day rolls on" is helpful information if you're unaccustomed to linear time, but otherwise? Not so much.
In One UI 9, Samsung has lightened up on figuring out what the Now Brief should tell you, and that's a good thing. Instead, you can create custom cards that will update at a set time with information of your choosing from a handful of apps, including Samsung Health, Samsung Weather and YouTube. For example, you might tell Samsung Health to update you at 9PM with your step count and calories burned for the day.
You build Now Brief cards with a Mad Libs-style generative prompt. Oddly, and perhaps to save on cloud processing costs, there is a daily cap on how many times you can generate or edit Now Brief cards. It's a bit reminiscent of the new generative Create My Widget feature Google showed off for Android 17, and which Samsung will reportedly ape for One UI 9.5.
There's no getting around the fact that this feature requires a lot of your personal data and processes off-device. For all the new capabilities in Now Brief, it will only serve up each generated card once per day. The rest of the time, it's doing things like telling me I've been ignoring my parents and should catch up with them — even though I spoke with both of them last night. Is this the "super intelligence" I've heard so much about?
Security Brief alerts in real time
Yet another Now Bar feature arrives in One UI 9, and many people will find it more useful than the ability to generate a weather or health widget. After switching on the "Security and privacy" toggle in the Now Brief settings, you'll get an alert on the Now Bar every time your phone detects an app that may be malware or is behaving strangely. Hopefully, you'll never see such an alert, but the more proactive your device can be at spotting threats, the easier it is to deal with them should they ever manifest. Samsung is calling the feature Security Brief.
Apps from the Play Store generally shouldn't trigger an alert from Security Brief unless they're abusing their permissions by requesting your location a lot in the background or otherwise acting suspiciously. If you determine the threat to be legitimate, you can follow the alert to take action.
If you're the type of person who installs software on your Android phone from outside the Play Store, Security Brief may bug you with false positives. App packages from the internet are often unsigned by their developers, especially if they're made by hobbyists, and SammyGuru reported that an app it routinely uses for Galaxy tutorials was flagged by Security Brief. In Engadget's testing, we could not get an alert to appear in the course of normal use, and I was reticent to install unsigned APKs in the hopes of triggering one. Samsung lists support for Security Brief as far back as the Galaxy S23 series.
When Now Bar launched in 2025, many saw it as a response to the iPhone's Dynamic Island for live information. But whereas that feature garnered robust support from third-party developers, Now Bar languished for years without a great deal of even first-party support. Very few apps work with it even now, and it would have made sense for Samsung to throw in the towel, so seeing new capabilities added multiple years later is encouraging.
