Odette’s longtime wine director Vincent Tan is leaving after 10 years to join Park90
Vincent Tan, who helped shape the three-Michelin-starred restaurant’s wine programme, is taking on a new group role at Park90 as it expands across Southeast Asia.
On paper, the headline is a change of address. Park90, the sommelier-led wine programme that spent its first eight years at Regent Singapore and, later, Conrad Singapore Orchard, has relocated to Pan Pacific Orchard’s Garden Terrace. It now operates as an independent brand in partnership with the hotel rather than as part of it. The programme brings more than 1,000 labels, including verticals of Domaine de la Romanee-Conti and allocations of Screaming Eagle, to what is billed as Singapore’s first luxury hotel with a fully integrated, sommelier-led wine programme.
The scale of that integration is worth spelling out. Across Pan Pacific Orchard’s four themed terraces, the programme extends from poolside pours to the hotel’s Claymore Ballroom on Level 18. A Neo-French menu developed with Michelin-starred Marguerite chef Michael Wilson sits alongside a wine-led cocktail programme created with Anthony Zhong of Shin Gi Tai. Hotel guests can also book the Park90 Stay Experience, a package running through December that includes lounge access, evening cocktails and a bottle of Chateau Lafite Rothschild on arrival.
That, however, isn’t really the headline. The headline is who’s arriving to run it.
From Oct 19, Park90’s wine direction passes to Vincent Tan, who is leaving his role as Odette’s wine director after 10 years – effectively since the three-Michelin-starred restaurant opened – to become Park90’s newly appointed group wine director. It is arguably the most consequential sommelier move Singapore’s hospitality scene has seen this year: A respected figure leaving one of the country’s most decorated dining rooms to lead a wine programme with ambitions beyond a single venue.
Ask him how he intends to run the team he’s inheriting, and he doesn’t reach for a leadership platitude. He reaches for penguins instead. “If I were to go in and dictate that everyone on the team behaves like me, I’m taking away a lot of what makes Park90 unique,” he said. “I’d rather not have a bunch of tuxedo-wearing penguins recommending the same wine.”
10 YEARS, ONE CONVERSATION
Leaving after a decade rarely comes without friction, and Tan admitted there was some. “I did say no, actually,” he said of an earlier approach from Park90. It wasn’t a cold approach. Tan has known Park90’s owners for years, but casual conversations about a role turned serious only after longtime wine director Mason Ng left the company at the start of 2026.
Even then, the timing didn’t feel right. Odette was mid-renovation and preparing to reopen, and Tan had already decided he would not leave before that was done. “It was something I felt I needed to complete before I could go,” he said.
Chef Julien Royer’s reaction, when the conversation finally happened, was brief – the kind of exchange two people rarely need to spell out after 10 years of working together. “He said to me: you’ve already given me 10 years. Whatever I’m going to do, he’s going to support,” Tan recalled.
What stings, he said, isn’t the handover itself. “Ten years is a long time to put a system in place, and to believe in that system, knowing I could disappear tomorrow and things wouldn’t change.”
The harder part has been telling regular clients and suppliers who assumed he would be there indefinitely that he is moving on. “Every conversation got a little more personal,” he said.
While his succession at Odette remains unresolved, Tan said the process is being handled with restraint. He has given Royer a shortlist but deliberately stayed out of the final decision. “I didn’t want to overly influence it,” he said. “I want to have a clean break, without people saying, this is what Vincent did, or this is what Vincent would have done.”
Tan isn’t in a hurry to put his own stamp on Park90’s programme before he has properly started, either. He has seen what the team has shared with him, but wants to taste through the list and experience the space himself before committing to specifics.
Some of the most eye-catching details already announced predate him, including a Screaming Eagle-by-the-glass offering and an upcoming Members’ Night lineup featuring wine figures such as William Kelley, Sylvain Cathiard and Kei Shiogai. “I won’t claim to say I’ve had much involvement in this,” he said of the lineup, “but I do agree with it.”
His belief that rare wines are meant to be tasted rather than kept as trophies is not merely theoretical. Park90 founder Soo Hoo Khoon Peng made headlines earlier this year after uncorking an 1899 Romanee-Conti at a private tasting in Burgundy. The 127-year-old bottle even predates the oldest wine in the domaine’s own stock, which dates to 1911.
If a bottle can be the reason someone falls in love with wine for life, as Tan said happened to him, that is reason enough to pour it.
It’s the same posture he takes toward his own title. Tan arrives to find a leadership structure already in place, with joint head sommeliers Terry Lim, who has been with Park90 since 2019, and Zhen Jie New in Singapore, and Justin Ho as regional head sommelier. The structure comes ahead of planned launches in Kuala Lumpur and Bangkok, part of a renewed ambition to grow Park90 into a wine hospitality platform across Southeast Asia. Tan’s own title suggests his remit will extend across that same footprint, though, true to form, he isn’t ready to define exactly how yet.
Tan’s group wine director title suggests his remit will extend across that same footprint, although, true to form, he is not ready to define exactly how.
NOT JUST FOR WINE PEOPLE
If there’s one thing Tan isn’t hedging on, it’s Park90’s image – and changing it is near the top of his list. Despite being open to the public since its early days as a wine bar, the brand has long been dogged by the misconception that it is members-only. “It’s perhaps one of the main challenges Park90 faces,” he said – less a gripe about the operation he is joining than a diagnosis of something he wants to fix.
Tan traces a deeper industry problem to a conversation with a hospitality group’s HR director about why the trade struggles to recruit junior sommeliers at all: Many graduates in their early 20s do not even know what the job entails.
His answer is not to lean further into wine media or wine-literate circles, but to go around them entirely – meeting people where they already gather for reasons that have nothing to do with wine, whether over a pickleball game or a round of golf. “We should stop talking to wine people,” he said, half-joking.
His approach to leadership starts from an equally blunt premise. “The type of wine is probably secondary. The pricing of the wine is very much secondary,” he said.
What matters more is the person recommending it. He points to Park90’s own history as proof – sommeliers who have passed through the programme over the years, each memorably different from the last.
“Whether it’s Mason Ng, Yeo Xi Yang, or Celine Jung, they’re all very different people,” he said of Park90’s past and present wine leadership. “The beauty is in that difference.”
It is the same instinct behind his line about tuxedo-wearing penguins, and why he would be genuinely disappointed to become the only person deciding what makes it onto the list. He wants sommeliers to feel comfortable pushing back when they think he is wrong, rather than deferring simply because of his title.
Any producer relationships he brings over from Odette, he added, will only make it onto Park90’s list if the team agrees they belong there. And with more than 1,000 labels already on the list, he said the goal is not to impress collectors with every bottle, but to ensure there is something worthwhile at every price point.
THE THRILL OF DISCOVERY
If one detail captures how much Tan still loves wine beyond the leadership talk, it is the story of a bottle he spent nearly a year chasing.
A friend in Singapore’s small sommelier circle told him about Domaine Guilbert-Gillet, a young estate in Savigny-les-Beaune founded in 2020 and run by winemaker Benjamin Guilbert and his wife, Caroline. The domaine farms just 3.6 hectares across Savigny and Chorey.
“The parcels are less impressive, generally speaking,” Tan said, “but they’ve bought high-quality old vineyards, and when you give good material to a talented producer, that’s where the excitement comes from.”
After being impressed by the wines at a tasting, he now plans to bring the producer into Park90. It offers perhaps the clearest preview of his approach to selection: Not simply chasing famous labels or prestigious regions, but paying attention to the people and philosophy behind a bottle, wherever it comes from.
“I want it to be a treasure box,” he said of the programme he is looking forward to building.
He wants both the enthusiastic newcomer and the serious oenophile to walk in and find something worth returning for, each chosen with the same conviction. And when someone asks what is good on the list, he wants his team to be stumped – not because nothing stands out, but because everything does.
“Every single bottle was selected either by themselves or by someone they trusted,” he said. “I never want a bottle there just because corporate said so.”

As Nandigram and Rejinagar constituencies in West Bengal go to the polls on October 6, several local journalists in Murshidabad district, where Rejinagar is located, have alleged that access to their news Facebook pages has been restricted in India. These outlets primarily covered Opposition parties and the limited campaigning they were able to carry out in the constituency.
The notices they received stated: “We repeatedly had to restrict access to content posted by you pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules… We have accordingly temporarily restricted access to your account for 7 days in India.”
Two Seats: Little in Terms of Electoral Contest
Byelections are being held in these constituencies because the elected representatives also won from other seats in the state elections earlier this year. The Nandigram assembly constituency has about 2.5 lakh people, with Muslims accounting for around 27% of the electorate. It is Suvendu Adhikari’s home constituency. In 2021, Adhikari defeated former chief minister Mamata Banerjee here by 1,956 votes. In the 2026 assembly polls, he won from Nandigram as well as Bhabanipur. He chose to retain the Bhabanipur seat where he defeated Banerjee, necessitating the byelection in Nandigram.
The Nandigram contest took an unexpected turn when the candidate of the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress faction, Sanchita Pradhan Dey, withdrew her nomination on September 18. Banerjee then decided to support Congress candidate Milan Pradhan. However, within hours of Banerjee announcing her support for Pradhan, he was arrested in connection with old cases related to the 2007 Nandigram violence. Congress and the TMC questioned the timing of the arrest, while the BJP said the police action was based on pending cases and involved no political intervention. He was later granted interim bail by the Calcutta high court.
Rejinagar presents a different electoral landscape, with Muslims accounting for around 69% of its electorate. The constituency was a closely watched seat in the 2026 assembly election. Aam Janata Unnyan Party (AJUP) leader Humayun Kabir won both Nowda and Rejinagar and subsequently vacated the latter, where his victory margin was more than 58,000 votes.
The Rejinagar by-election has seen little campaigning by the main Opposition candidates, who allege police intimidation and interference by the ruling party. The Banerjee-backed Trinamool Congress faction has fielded former three-term MLA Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, who had considered withdrawing from the contest before Banerjee persuaded him to stay. The Congress has fielded Abdullahil Kafi, while the Democratic TMC faction has nominated Safiuzzaman S K and the CPI(M) Saeed Asad Ali.
Kabir has alleged that police arrested 15 of his workers in what he calls false cases, while others have fled the area. He was also questioned twice over a viral audio clip. He says he has therefore halted major campaigning and is reaching voters primarily through Facebook, while his son continues to visit some areas. Independent candidate Saiful Islam, who is close to the AJUP leadership, was arrested on September 19.
With arrests, alleged intimidation, and lack of opposition campaigning, the elections in both the seats appear to offer little in the way of a competitive contest.
Facebook Pages Reporting Local News Restricted
With the Opposition campaign already muted in both constituencies, the election is also unfolding amid allegations of censorship in Rejinagar. Local journalists who reported on issues critical of the government or law enforcement, or covered Opposition campaigns, suddenly found their Facebook pages, which were their primary outlets for publishing their work, restricted in India.
Alt News identified at least 12 such pages: Murshidabad Global Times run by Asif Roni; Hariharpara Times Bangla run by Jabbar Sheikh; Murshidabad Today run by Swapan Karigar; Murshidabad Shironam run by Rinku; Murshidabad News Time run by Baktar Sk; Reporter Press run by Rajib Sheikh; M News TV run by Muhaimenul Haque; Bartabahi News run by Aminul Islam; Hi News run by Saidur Rahman; BNS News Bangla; AN Bangla News run by Abdus Samad; and News Front Digital run by Abdul Halim.
Swapan Karigar’s Murshidabad Today, which had a following of around 7.4 lakh, was among those worst affected. A practising journalist with more than 26 years of experience, he now has a restricted account, limiting his ability to report on politics ahead of the election.
Karigar said the page had been reporting allegations of intimidation by police made by residents who support Opposition parties, including AJUP and the Congress. “A lot of common people, who have aligned themselves with opposition parties like AJUP and Congress, people who have, say, walked in political rallies, have alleged that their family members, especially women and children, are being intimidated and tortured by police officials. They (the police) have visited these houses with 12-14 cars, even. A child was also pulled by her hair, and a woman was physically assaulted. They have totally created an atmosphere of fear and intimidation before the election. We were covering these incidents, upholding the truth. That is probably why our accounts have been withheld,” he told Alt News.
We spoke to Asif Roni, whose Facebook page, Murshidabad Global Times, had around 4.47 lakh followers before it was taken down on the night of October 1 — the same day chief minister Suvendu Adhikari visited Rejinagar. Roni said the page had recorded 39 million views in the preceding 28 days. Law enforcement officials told him that the page would be withheld for seven days.
“This happened once around April, right before the assembly election,” he said. “I used to run a different page called AN Bangla. It still hasn’t been reactivated. They shut quite a few pages then, and those haven’t been restored either. So I had to switch to Murshidabad GT, which used to be a backup page.”
Roni said that after the earlier restriction, a senior police official had told him that the page would be restored “after the election”.
Jabbar Sheikh, who runs Hariharpara Times Bangla, told us that his Facebook page, which had around 4.39 lakh followers, was taken down on September 30, after it published a report on Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury. “More than thirty pages have been restricted. The main reason is that we covered news about the Opposition parties, especially Humayun’s campaign. So there was possibly a political motive. It’s the Indian government that did it. The pages don’t show in India, although they would show in other countries,” Jabbar said.
This was the first time Jabbar had faced such a restriction. He, too, approached police, but said officials told him they had not ordered the restrictions. “They told us that Meta itself had found guideline violations and restricted the pages on that basis, and that cyber crime had no hand in it,” he said.
For a lot of local journalists, publishing news content on Facebook was their only source of livelihood.
It took Swapan Karigar six years to build Murshidabad Today. “This has never happened before. This was my only source of income. I know nothing apart from journalism. I have another small page with around 14,000 followers, and I am posting non-political content from there now. I can’t give up my profession, but I’m cutting down on political content for the time being,” he said. The page had around 24 million views before it was restricted.
Roni said around 25 to 30 such pages had been restricted across the district. When we asked why these pages had been targeted, he said he was told that they had published news that could be perceived as anti-government. “Mostly they’ve closed those who give a bit more coverage to the Opposition political parties’ news. For me, they restricted it after I posted my report on Adhir Chowdhury,” he said.
Roni now publishes from another page, MGT, which has around 15,000 followers. Jabbar is similarly posting content from a second page with barely 2,000 followers.
“All of our pages were monetised. Good money came from it, and a lot of us were getting by. Educated, unemployed youth started this trend alongside other things,” Roni said.
They are not Journalists, Says Murshidabad SP
We spoke to Sachin Makkar, superintendent of police, Murshidabad, who first asked us to “read the notice carefully”.
“Does the notice mention the police or the cyber crime wing? You should contact Meta about this. Does it say that the police restricted the pages?” he asked. When we pressed further, he said, “I do not have a lot to say on the matter. And they are not journalists; they are not accredited journalists. Whatever action has been taken, we have not done it. You can talk to Meta about the rest…”
It is worth noting that the notices received by the administrators say the pages were withheld pursuant to legal requirements. This indicates that the restrictions followed a legal request or complaint concerning the content on these pages, rather than being solely the result of Meta’s own content-moderation process.
We have written to Meta seeking details of the requests it received and the reasons for restricting the pages. This article will be updated if and when we receive a response.

Several photos are circulating online purportedly showing a gold-covered statue depicting a naked U.S. President Donald Trump on display at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, in early October.
For example, a popular Facebook page that shared one picture of the alleged sculpture wrote (archived):
NEWS: A 2.5-meter-tall statue depicting a naked, gold-covered Donald Trump has been unveiled inside the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
The satirical sculpture, titled "Orange Plague" and also called "King of Injustice," shows Trump sitting on the shoulders of another man while holding an enormous golf club. It is reportedly covered in 23-karat gold.
Other photographs of the artwork are also circulating on X (archived) and Instagram (archived).
In short, the photos are authentic and the statue is real. Danish sculptor Jens Galschiøt created the piece and named it "The Orange Plague." On Oct. 7, a spokesperson for the European Parliament's press service confirmed via email that, as of this writing, it is on display at the parliament's Winston Churchill building in Strasbourg, France. Galschiøt said via email that it is set be taken down on Oct. 8.
The sculpture in the pictures shared online matches the piece that can be seen in photos that Galschiøt and reputable news agency Reuters have published. The photographs spreading online also show no signs of being digitally edited or created. Therefore, those photos are authentic and do truly show a naked statue of Trump on display at the European Parliament.
Snopes contacted the White House for comment and for Trump's take on Galschiøt's work. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Why Galschiøt created the statue
On his website, Galschiøt describes "The Orange Plague" as "a satirical out-cry against Trump and the U.S. assault on the green transition and the rule-based world order."
The artwork is 2.6 meters (approximately 8 feet, 5 inches) tall, made of copper and covered in 23 carat leaf gold, according to the sculptor. Danish author Hans Christian Andersen's "The Emporer's New Clothes" tale — in which an emperor parades naked in front of his subjects because he believes he is wearing the finest clothes — inspired Galschiøt to depict Trump as naked.
"The illusion — sustained by fear and flattery — endures until a child cries out, 'He's not wearing any clothes' — and the emperor becomes a figure of ridicule," Galschiøt's website says. The page adds that the gold on the sculpture also plays on this illusion, "Like Andersen's emperor, he [Trump] believes the gold makes him great. It merely makes his nakedness shine brighter."
Speaking via email on Oct. 7, Galschiøt said he initially approached left-wing Danish politician and European legislator Per Clausen MEP about displaying "The Orange Plague" at the European Parliament. The sculptor added that he was "astonished" the exhibition actually happened.
Galschiøt said he thought the European Parliament was the right place to display the piece because "it fits right into the discussion about whether the superpowers should have the right to bully smaller nations, and here Europe is the key player in standing up to them."
When asked whether the artist had heard any reaction to the sculpture from Trump or the White House, Galschiøt said he had not heard from the U.S. president but also had not "had time to look" for reactions to his work.
On Oct. 7, a spokesperson for Clausen said via email that the pair had been discussing displaying the statue at the European Parliament for a couple of years. The politician reportedly said of the sculpture:
I know some people think we shouldn't provoke Trump and therefore shouldn't exhibit a sculpture like this. To them, I have to say two things: First, we cannot accept living in fear and self-censorship. Second, if someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot handle this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no business on the world stage.
A European Parliament press service spokesperson said the office could not comment on individual cases but that, in general, its lawmakers, known as MEPs (Members of the European Parliament), could sponsor "two cultural events or exhibitions per parliamentary term." The spokesperson said:
The rules in place foresee that cultural events and exhibitions shall under no circumstances be offensive or of an inflammatory nature or contradictory to the values on which the Union is founded or likely to give rise to disturbances in the designated exhibition areas.
The spokesperson said all sponsored events must be approved in advance by the College of Quaestors, a political body "responsible for administrative and financial matters directly concerning Members and their working conditions."
A spokesperson for Clausen said the politician sponsored "The Orange Plague" exhibition at the European Parliament.
Before visiting Strasbourg, the piece was previously on display at the United Nations COP30 climate conference in Brazil. According to Galschiøt's website, the artwork is also set to be on display at the COP31 climate conference in Turkey in November.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated other golden Trump sculptures, and statues the Trump administration coated in gold.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.
Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.
One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.
“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.
In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.
Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.
Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Journalists’ Syndicate, whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.
Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.
The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.
For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.
“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

The story so far: The Serum Institute of India’s indigenously developed quadrivalent human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, CERVAVAC, has received prequalification from the World Health Organization (WHO), allowing the vaccine to be procured by United Nations agencies and potentially supplied to countries running HPV immunisation programmes. The WHO lists its prequalification as effective from September 25, 2026.
The development is significant for India as well as the global effort to prevent cervical cancer. CERVAVAC is India’s first indigenously developed gender-neutral quadrivalent HPV vaccine and targets HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18. It is licensed in India for girls and boys aged 9 to 26 years.
CERVAVAC is the first Indian-made quadrivalent HPV vaccine to receive WHO prequalification. This prequalification means the vaccine has met WHO standards for quality, safety and efficacy, following evaluation of data, samples and manufacturing sites.
Globally, cervical cancer caused an estimated 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths in 2020. In India, where cervical cancer remains a public-health burden, the national HPV vaccination programme was launched on February 28, 2026, targeting about 1.2 crore 14-year-old girls with a free single dose; more than 80 lakh doses had been administered by September this year, according to the Union Health Ministry. India’s national HPV vaccination programme uses Merck’s Gardasil-4, a quadrivalent vaccine protecting against HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18.
India also has an indigenous quadrivalent vaccine, CERVAVAC (now WHO-prequalified) and access to other HPV vaccines, including Gardasil 9 and Cervarix, through the private market.
What exactly is WHO prequalification?
WHO prequalification’s biggest significance is access. A vaccine that has already been licensed in India can now potentially enter international procurement channels used to supply national immunisation programmes, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.
WHO prequalification is not a marketing authorisation or regulatory approval. For the prequalification, the vaccine undergoes assessment of its quality, safety and efficacy, including evaluation of data, testing of samples and inspection of manufacturing facilities. A vaccine that meets WHO standards is placed on the WHO List of Prequalified Vaccines, making it eligible for procurement by United Nations agencies and giving countries an internationally recognised assurance about the product and manufacturing standards.
What is HPV and why is this important for prevention?
HPV is an extremely common sexually transmitted infection. Most infections clear naturally, but persistent infection with high-risk HPV types can lead to cervical cancer. WHO estimates that persistent infection with high-risk HPV types causes more than 95% of cervical cancers. HPV can also cause anal, vulval, vaginal and some other cancers, as well as genital warts.
The vaccine is a cancer-prevention vaccine and not just a vaccine against an infection.
WHO’s priority target is girls aged 9–14 years, before exposure to HPV. The organisation recommends either a one- or two-dose schedule for this age group, depending on the vaccine and national programme.
The four HPV types targeted by CERVAVAC are important for different reasons. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types responsible for a large proportion of cervical cancers. Types 6 and 11 are responsible for most anogenital warts. The quadrivalent vaccine therefore provides protection against both cancer-associated HPV types and genital warts.
Its indication for both sexes also matters. Although cervical cancer is the largest component of the HPV disease burden, HPV can cause disease in men, including anal cancer and genital warts.
What could the WHO listing mean for India?
CERVAVAC’s WHO prequalification does not automatically mean that it will now be substituted into the Indian government programme. Vaccine selection for a national programme involves considerations including regulatory status, evidence, price, supply capacity, presentations, logistics and programme requirements.
But the new status gives India another WHO-prequalified HPV vaccine from a domestic manufacturer. It could also potentially strengthen competition and supply security if CERVAVAC is considered for future procurement.
How many other Indian vaccines have WHO prequalification?
India already has a substantial presence on the WHO prequalified-vaccine list.
Serum Institute is among the largest Indian participants. The company has WHO-prequalified vaccines covering a wide range of diseases, including BCG, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis combinations, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, measles, measles-rubella, measles-mumps-rubella, meningococcal disease, pneumococcal disease, polio, rabies, rotavirus, rubella and malaria, among others.
Other Indian manufacturers with WHO-prequalified vaccines include Bharat Biotech, Biological E, Zydus Lifesciences, GreenSignal Bio Pharma, Haffkine and Panacea Biotec, among others.
Bharat Biotech’s Typbar-TCV, for example, was the first typhoid conjugate vaccine to receive WHO prequalification; Zydus’s ZyVac TCV received WHO prequalification in September 2026.
What is different about CERVAVAC?
The HPV milestone is distinctive because, until now, WHO’s prequalified HPV portfolio consisted of vaccines manufactured outside India. WHO’s HPV product-choice document lists bivalent vaccines such as Cecolin, Cervarix and Walrinvax, quadrivalent Gardasil, and nonavalent Gardasil-9. CERVAVAC was previously nationally licensed but was not WHO-prequalified.
Its inclusion therefore adds an Indian-made HPV vaccine to the global WHO-prequalified pool.
For India, the larger significance is that a vaccine developed and manufactured domestically can now potentially contribute not only to India’s cervical-cancer prevention programme but also to HPV vaccination programmes elsewhere.
The WHO’s global target is to have 90% of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, alongside screening and treatment targets for women. By the end of 2025, HPV vaccination had been introduced in 165 countries, but global first-dose coverage among girls was only about 33%, well below the 90% target.

Haiti police say US missionary detained following sex abuse allegations at orphanage
Haitian police tells The Associated Press that a U.S. missionary accused of running an illegal orphanage in Haiti has been detained following child abuse allegations
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti -- A U.S. missionary accused of running an illegal orphanage in Haiti has been detained over allegations of child abuse, Haitian police told The Associated Press on Friday.
Arold Jean, a spokesperson for the Cap-Haitien police department, said U.S. authorities arrested Thomas Osbeck there on Wednesday. He did not identify the U.S. agency involved.
It wasn’t immediately clear if he had an attorney. An Associated Press journalist was barred from visiting Osbeck in jail on Friday.
Jean said Osbeck did not have the required paperwork to operate an orphanage in Cap-Haitien, where Haitian authorities found at least 12 minors. He said he expects Osbeck to be extradited to the United States.
Osbeck was detained nearly two weeks after U.S. authorities charged Maylon Foshee, 23, of Mansfield, Louisiana, with sexually abusing minors during mission trips to Haiti.
Authorities said Foshee traveled to Haiti numerous times between 2023 and 2026 while working with a ministry in the coastal city of Gonaives and allegedly sexually abused several minors under his care, including those who lived with him or received financial support from him.
Last year, a jury in Miami convicted Michael Geilenfeld of sexually abusing boys at an orphanage he founded in Port-au-Prince.
Geilenfeld had pleaded not guilty. The orphanage, founded in 1985, was one of several that he operated in Haiti and the Dominican Republic, was closed in 2014.

NASA on Friday released a much-anticipated “request” to the US commercial space industry to develop private space stations that, as early as 2030, will succeed the International Space Station as a place for astronauts to live in low-Earth orbit.
In a cover letter accompanying the 360-page “request for proposals,” NASA stated its plan: “This will ensure NASA has a sustained human presence in LEO for crew members to perform science and exploration.” Several private companies that have worked for years on designing and developing such stations have been keen to learn exactly what capabilities NASA is seeking. These new documents finally provide some answers.
NASA’s solicitation can be found here. Industry responses are due back to NASA on December 8. NASA said it plans to select “two or more” contractors in this phase of the competition, and intends to make a final decision in April.
In LEO to stay
“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement that accompanied the release of the new documents. “We will continue to need a place to conduct research, develop technologies, train crews, and prepare for missions to the Moon and Mars. Commercial space stations may provide that capability while creating new opportunities for American industry and allowing NASA to concentrate more of our resources on the near-impossible missions ahead.”
Bidders for this funding phase will certainly include Axiom Space, Voyager Space, and Vast Space. Blue Origin won an earlier round of funding from NASA, but questions remain about the company’s commitment to the program. SpaceX appears unlikely to bid, at least for now. Phase 1 winners will be guaranteed at least $100 million.

- The claim that an image of U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth standing in front of an eagle emblem with his arms raised closely resembles a real image of Nazi leader Adolf Hitler is unfounded.
- The image of Hitler has strong indications of artificial intelligence generation. The image of Hegseth also has signs pointing to AI editing, although real video footage from an Oct. 3 speech authentically shows that the changes were minor and that Hegseth did raise his arms in front of a stylized version of the Department of Defense's eagle seal.
- The eagle emblem in the image of Hitler matches the "Reichsadler" symbol Hitler's Nazi regime used — but it's worth noting that the emblem was a highly stylized version of an eagle symbol used in Germany both before and after the Nazi Party came to power. The DOD has since 1949 used a seal featuring an eagle holding arrows above an olive branch; the version on display during Hegseth's Oct. 3 speech omitted the olive branch and had a more stylized design.
- We've reached out to the DOD to ask about the reason for the redesign and whether any similarities to the Reichsadler were intentional. The DOD denied any similarities existed.
On Oct. 3, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth delivered a speech at the U.S. Air Force Academy. Images from the speech of Hegseth with his arms spread wide in front of the Department of Defense's eagle seal went viral, drawing comparisons to Nazi leader Adolf Hitler and an official Nazi symbol.
Snopes readers shared the images with us, asking to confirm whether such comparisons were accurate. One Facebook meme showed Hegseth in front of a simplified version of the DOD's eagle seal without its traditional olive branch. Next to him, in a similar pose with his arms outstretched is Hitler in front of the "Reichsadler," the eagle emblem of Nazi Germany. The accompanying caption stated: 
On Saturday, Hegseth traveled to the U.S. Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs to address the cadets.
As he walked on stage, the Department of War seal was visible behind him and on the podium in front of him.
Before he began, he raised both arms out to the side and told the cadets to take their seats.
That was all it took.
Within hours, critics were posting side-by-side images comparing the staging of the speech to old photos of Adolf Hitler speaking in front of an eagle emblem.
(Facebook user "Really American")
The image of Hegseth showed signs of artificial intelligence editing in the form of garbled letters in the seals behind and in front of him, but video footage of the Oct. 3 speech shows that the content was not meaningfully altered. The accompanying image of Hitler, however, carries signs of heavy manipulation and was likely entirely generated by AI.
That said, there are still other authentic photographs of Hitler that show him standing in front of a Nazi eagle emblem that in some ways resembles the new DOD one.
Given the heavy manipulation of the Hitler image, we found the claim that the image of Hegseth closely resembled a real image of Hitler unfounded.
We reached out to the DOD to ask about the reason for the redesign and whether any resemblance to the Reichsadler was intentional. Deputy Pentagon Press Secretary Joel Valdez said to us over email: "The American bald eagle is an icon of our country and used on many state and federal seals, including the seal of the Department of War. If for some reason you see imagery of a bald eagle and begin having delusions about Nazi Germany, then you may need to get your head checked for serious brain damage."
The moment where Hegseth raised his arms wide occurred in the very beginning of his speech at the 5-second mark on the official DOD YouTube video. We captured a screenshot below:
(YouTube user "Department of War")
The image of Hegseth in the Facebook post appears to have been edited or manipulated. The color is much brighter and the "M" behind Hegseth's right arm appears misshapen. Hegseth's face also appears different. The image itself is similar to its original YouTube video.
There are several indications of AI generation in the purported photograph of Hitler. Firstly, the individuals on either side of him on the bottom left and right of the frame all have incomplete facial features, with sections of their heads cut off or blurred. The flags behind him also have inconsistent patterns that show signs of heavy editing or cropping.
Real photographs of Hitler standing in front of flag poles show that, even on draped flags, the swastikas are recognizable. The two swastikas on either side of Hitler's head are almost perfectly round circles. Considering they are placed over what could either be rounded pillars or curtains, they are clearly overlaid or heavily edited.
We compared the image to real photographs of speeches Hitler made, and found none that resemble the room in the image from the meme. One authentic 1939 image on Getty Images shows Hitler speaking to the Reichstag, or German parliament, with a much larger eagle symbol and the Nazi symbols farther apart. Images of Hitler speaking at Nuremberg rallies do not align with the one in the above meme. Videos show that Hitler often spoke with his arms held wide, but there are no specific videos corresponding with the image in the above meme. 
Despite the above image of Hitler being heavily manipulated, Hegseth's backdrop still has loose similarities to other real photographs of Hitler speaking in front of an eagle emblem.
During Hegseth's speech, many online noted the simplified (archived) version of the DOD seal, which removed the traditional olive leaves below the eagle, made the eagle's design more angular and replaced the 13 stars above the eagle with five stars.
We should note that the eagle symbol was used in Germany before and after the Nazi Party came to power. The DOD has been using the eagle seal since 1949. The DOD website, which still showed the version of the seal containing the olive branch as of this writing, explains its meaning thus: "The American bald eagle, long associated with symbolism representing the United States of America and its military establishment, has been selected as an emblem of strength. In facing to the right, the field of honor is indicated."
Hegseth has also been in the news for his Sept. 30 "State of the Force" address, in which he announced he was creating an Office of Religious Affairs at the Pentagon and initiating "Project Meridian," which he described as "an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare."
Snopes has frequently reported on rumors about Hegseth and the Department of Defense.

Hi there, it’s Sarah. Last night, STAT scored an awards hat trick, taking home a Gerald Loeb — the most prestigious honor in business journalism — for the third year in a row! This year’s Loeb recognized Lizzy Lawrence for her exceptional beat reporting on the Food and Drug Administration. This is also STAT’s fourth Loeb overall in our 11-year history. Not too shabby, y’all.
Does MAHA still matter to voters?
The Make America Healthy Again movement has been credited with helping to propel Donald Trump to a second term at the White House. But as midterm elections draw near, MAHA is nearly invisible on the campaign trail.
In today’s story, Isa Cueto, Daniel Payne, and Chelsea Cirruzzo take stock of MAHA’s current political influence, and its struggles to translate popular support for some of its core issues (like the dangers of ultra-processed foods) into policy. “This whole election in November is a contrast election. Democrats are making it about Trump, Republicans are making it about communists,” said Republican strategist Joel White. Read more.
What motivates two young scientists focused on breast cancer and abortion access
Amid relentless and sometimes depressing news cycles, one of the best things about working for STAT is that with projects like STAT Wunderkinds, we get to celebrate scientific achievements and the extraordinary talents who make them possible.
Yesterday, Allessandra DiCorato profiled cancer biologist and first-year resident physician Neal Carleton, whose work is focused on improving treatment for older patients with breast cancer. The hope, Carleton says, is to turn breast cancer into “more of a chronic disease” that can be managed with a daily pill and regular (but not too frequent) monitoring. And in today’s profile, Justin Chen interviewed researcher Betsy Pleasants, who’s using artificial intelligence to offer a more complete picture of online discourse about issues like abortion access and contraception.
Asking questions before we know why
Fifty years ago, researcher Robert Gallo and his colleagues made the landmark discovery of the protein interleukin-2, or IL-2. He reflects in a new First Opinion piece on the various reasons why that finding was so important. Not only did IL-2 make possible the discovery of the first human retroviruses, including HIV as the cause of AIDS, and become widely used in cancer cell immunotherapy, he writes, “its larger lesson is about the nature of scientific discovery.”
Gallo didn’t know all the things that IL-2 would make possible — and scientists shouldn’t be expected to answer questions about direct applications of their research in order to secure funding, he says. “If scientists must know the practical outcome before asking the question,” he writes, “they’ll never ask some of the most important questions.” Read more.
The census changes threatening public health
The Trump administration wants to make three big changes to the U.S. Census: eliminating questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation; excluding anyone who is not a citizen or “lawful permanent resident”; and changing how it determines where people like college students or retiree “snowbirds” reside.
These changes, if passed, pose a big problem for both public health research and real-world federal assistance, social epidemiologist Nancy Krieger writes in a new First Opinion. That’s because things like race and ethnicity data are essential for how we track trends in U.S. morbidity and mortality and how federally funded programs determine who is eligible and where resources need to be allocated. This isn’t the first flaw to be highlighted in the census system, but Krieger suggests it’s what tennis fans might call an unforced error.
The future of mifepristone
Mifepristone, a pill used to terminate early pregnancies, has been caught in a tug-of-war throughout the second Trump administration as abortion opponents push for crackdowns on its use. Now the Food and Drug Administration say its safety review will continue into next year, with a report on findings expected by March 2027. Read more.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Friday that the planned consumption tax cut for food is expected to reduce household financial burdens by about ¥36,000 per citizen.
“The tax rate cut will basically be reflected in prices,” Takaichi said at a plenary meeting of the Senate, the upper chamber of parliament.
She explained that the ¥36,000 figure was calculated by dividing the total tax revenue loss to the central and local governments from the tax cut by the country’s population.
During the Upper House meeting, Yasue Funayama of the Democratic Party for the People asked the prime minister how her administration will make up for local government revenue losses.
Takaichi vowed to fully cover these revenue losses with state funds, saying, “We’ll properly secure necessary local tax grants.”
The prime minister also said the government is considering measures to support agricultural and fishery businesses, as well as food companies and restaurants whose operations could be affected by the tax cut. “It is necessary to assess circumstances on the ground and respond according to the impact on each sector,” she said.
Meanwhile, Komeito Secretary-General Makoto Nishida called on the government to clarify who would be eligible for a financial aid program for workers that will be introduced alongside the consumption tax cut.
Takaichi indicated that the government will explain the matter during parliamentary deliberations, based on discussions by the suprapartisan National Council on Social Security.
Sanseito leader Sohei Kamiya argued that the consumption tax reduction should apply across the board, not only to food.
Takaichi countered that such a move could affect public services, including pensions, medical care, nursing care and measures to address the declining birthrate.

India has rejected concerns raised by the United Nations Human Rights office over reported detentions during demonstrations in New Delhi, describing the remarks as “misplaced” and an “unwarranted interference” in the country's internal affairs. The protests were linked to demands by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and others for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
In a response issued by India's Permanent Mission to the UN in Geneva on Saturday (October 10) said the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by the Constitution and protected by the country's democratic institutions, independent judiciary and free media.
The response came after the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) expressed concern over reports of detentions involving demonstrators, leaders, civil society members, lawyers and journalists before and during the Delhi demonstrations.
India also urged the UN Human Rights office to devote comparable attention to large-scale protests in other parts of the world, citing the need for impartiality and non-selectivity in its work.
Quick answers to key questions
India described the concerns as “misplaced” and an “unwarranted interference” in its internal affairs. It said the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by the Constitution and protected by democratic institutions.
The office cited reports of detentions involving demonstrators, protest leaders, civil society members, lawyers and journalists before and during the Delhi demonstrations.
India said the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by the Constitution. It also pointed to the role of democratic institutions, the independent judiciary and free media in protecting that right.
India urged the office to give comparable attention to large-scale protests in other parts of the world. It said this was necessary to ensure impartiality and non-selectivity.
The office called on authorities to respect peaceful assembly, exercise restraint and immediately release people it said had been arbitrarily detained. It also urged meaningful dialogue to address demonstrators’ concerns.
In its response, India said peaceful assembly was a constitutional right, but noted that its exercise was subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order.
“India is the world’s largest democracy, where the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by our Constitution and safeguarded by robust institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media,” the Indian mission said.
It added that authorities acted in accordance with the law and that courts remained accessible to citizens seeking redressal of grievances.
“The OHCHR’s concerns are therefore misplaced and constitute an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India,” the statement said.
India also questioned what it described as the UN office's approach to protests across different countries.
“In this context, OHCHR would also do well to devote comparable attention to large-scale protests elsewhere, consistent with its mandate of impartiality and non-selectivity,” the mission added.
The UN Human Rights office had earlier expressed concern over reports of mass detentions linked to the protests in Delhi.
“We are concerned by reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, members of civil society organisations, lawyers and journalists, before and during today’s large-scale demonstrations in Delhi,” the OHCHR said.
The UN office called on Indian authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly was fully respected and upheld.
The office also called for the immediate and unconditional release of anyone arbitrarily detained.
“All those arbitrarily detained must be immediately and unconditionally released,” the statement said.
The UN Human Rights office further urged the authorities to engage in meaningful dialogue to address the concerns raised by protesters.
The exchange comes amid heightened tensions surrounding large-scale demonstrations in the national capital. The protests were linked to demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Over 7,000 protesters, including Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leader Abhijit Dipke, several opposition leaders, activists and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, were detained across Delhi on Saturday as authorities thwarted a planned mass mobilisation at Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The security deployment, involving more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel, left the designated protest site largely deserted. Multiple layers of barricades, restrictions on movement and the closure of 45 metro stations disrupted movement across parts of the national capital.
The protest was organised by the CJP amid controversy over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Opposition parties criticised the detentions, with Congress leader Rahul Gandhi urging young people to continue protesting and accusing the government of attacking the Constitution.
The scale of the detentions remained contested in initial police accounts. Delhi Police sources had earlier said around 1,000 protesters had been detained while attempting to march towards Jantar Mantar.
Barricades were erected across Lutyens' Delhi, while intensive checks were carried out at border points, railway stations, bus terminals, hotels and other sensitive locations.
Authorities also monitored social media platforms for attempts to mobilise protesters. More than 200 content creators were reportedly under scrutiny as police examined online posts and messages linked to the proposed gathering.
CJP convener Abhijit Dipke and party leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained at Delhi airport upon their arrival from Mumbai, according to the account provided.
In a video shared by the CJP, Dipke was heard telling police officers who entered the aircraft: “We are here to be arrested, come and arrest us.”
Before detaining the CJP leaders, police personnel told them that they did not have permission to hold the protest at Jantar Mantar.
Dipke accused the authorities of treating party leaders like criminals and described the action as dictatorial.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, who lives abroad and had travelled to India to join the demonstration, was detained from his residence in Gurugram's Sector 56 on Saturday.
Several opposition leaders were also detained at different locations across the capital, including former chief ministers Arvind Kejriwal of the Aam Aadmi Party, Mamata Banerjee of the Trinamool Congress, and Pinarayi Vijayan and Manik Sarkar, both associated with the CPI(M).
The detentions triggered sharp criticism from opposition leaders, who compared the government's response to the Emergency.
Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi expressed solidarity with the protesting youth and urged them to continue their demonstrations.
He challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to arrest all protesters, asserting that they would continue their fight to defend the Constitution and protect the voice of the Indian people.
“We are going to ensure that this regime and the people who have attacked the Constitution are defeated,” Gandhi said, urging young people to “keep protesting”.
The opposition has argued that the detentions undermine democratic freedoms and the right to peaceful protest. The authorities, meanwhile, cited the lack of permission for the proposed gathering and maintained a heavy security presence across the city.
A senior police officer said multiple first information reports (FIRs) were likely to be registered in connection with the alleged assault on police personnel.
Regular announcements were made at Jantar Mantar, instructing members of the public and mediapersons not to gather in one place.
The clashes came amid extensive security checks and restrictions on movement across the national capital, with commuters advised to follow official announcements and plan their journeys accordingly.
Activist Sonam said he would consider launching a peaceful protest, including a hunger strike or a march in Leh or Delhi, if the detained protesters were not released within 24 hours.
Wangchuk had participated in an earlier 36-day CJP agitation at Jantar Mantar over the NEET paper leak issue, which ended on July 25 following the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, according to the supplied account.
That agitation had also witnessed disruption during a march towards Parliament on July 20, when security personnel attempted to stop protesters.
Wangchuk's latest warning adds to the pressure on the authorities to address the detentions and the demands raised by demonstrators.
The demonstrations and detentions extended beyond Delhi, with police detaining around 400 people in Mumbai during protests held in solidarity with the CJP's proposed march.
Those detained reportedly included actor Imran Khan, activist Tushar Gandhi and CPI(M) workers.
The demonstrations took place at August Kranti Maidan, Hutatma Chowk and other locations across the city. Police detained participants on the grounds that the protests were being held without permission.
The immediate flashpoint remains the CJP's demand for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid concerns surrounding the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

Former Mayor V.K. Prasanth has alleged that the United Democratic Front (UDF) government is planning to relocate animals in the Thiruvananthapuram zoo to the Vantara zoological centre in Gujarat and the Puthur zoo in Thrissur. A team of senior officials has been sent to Vantara for this purpose, Mr. Prasanth, who had earlier slammed Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan’s proposal to relocate the Thiruvananthapuram zoo from the heart of the city to elsewhere, alleged on Saturday.
Mr. Prasanth said the remarks made by Minister for Museums and Zoos O.J. Janeesh at the valedictory of the Wildlife Week celebrations, organised by the Department of Museums and Zoos, regarding privatisation of the zoo and the possibility of seeking sponsorship, indicated the government’s intentions. The Minister said it took 16 years for the Thrissur Zoological Park to shift to Puthur. He ruled out such a long wait, saying the government was trying to shift the animals to forest areas through private partnership and sponsorship.
The Minister’s announcement clearly indicated that commercial interests are at play, the former Mayor alleged.
The city zoo is one of the oldest zoos in the country categorised as ‘large’. The nearly 170-year-old zoo was also part of the city’s heritage. The animals were the guardians of the green lung that made up the zoo and museum campus. There was no doubt that the moment the zoo animals were relocated, all the trees here would be cut down, he added.
A meeting will be held at Sathyan Memorial Hall in the city at 5 p.m. on Monday (October 12) to form a ‘Thiruvananthapuram zoo protection committee’ to strengthen the demand for retaining the zoo in its current location, Mr. Prasanth said.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Dubai – The co-pilot who attacked the captain of a flydubai jet last week had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv’s international airport, the United Arab Emirates’ top prosecutor said on Friday.
In the aftermath of the incident, people on board — the majority of whom were Israeli — described a sudden plunge in altitude and a fight for control of the aircraft, which was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The passengers were repatriated on a second flydubai flight hours later.
The unnamed Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda’s Sept. 11, 2001 suicide attacks on the United States, and carried out his attempt “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life,” according to the Emirati prosecutor’s findings published by state media.
