Inside the £1-an-hour official football shirt factories
- Published
Workers are being paid a basic wage of less than £1 an hour to make official football shirts for some of the world's biggest clubs, BBC Sport can reveal.
Our investigation traced authentic replica shirts to two factories in Cambodia, where conditions were described as "grim".
We followed the supply chain behind official shirts after fans told us they were frustrated by rising prices, with many turning to cheaper counterfeits instead.
Images obtained from inside Bowker Garment Factory and Trax Apparel show kits being made for clubs including Arsenal, Celtic, Liverpool and Real Madrid.
Employees there told us they struggled to make ends meet and worked on up to 700 items a day as part of a production line.
In rare interviews, supported by documentary evidence and published anonymously, workers also described:
- Factory temperatures above 35C.
- Verbal abuse when targets were missed.
- Safety concerns about electrical equipment.
The Clean Clothes Campaign, external - a global workers' rights network - said our findings painted a "very grim picture".
"These are issues that many garment workers around the world face every day," added spokesperson Emma Vogt.
Similar issues, such as low pay and high temperatures, have been reported across Cambodia's garment industry.
Research published last year suggested that, of a typical £85 shirt, £8.50 covers fabric, sewing and shipping, £37.45 goes to the retailer, £16.25 to the manufacturer, £9.50 on marketing and £13.60 in VAT.
Shirt prices have increased significantly over the past decade, though industry experts argue advances in technology and expensive kit deals with elite clubs have contributed to the rise.
Adidas does not own either factory, but both are primary suppliers subject to its workplace standards., external
The sportswear giant supplies eight of the 20 Premier League teams.
Adidas said: "We have taken a variety of measures to ensure fair and safe working conditions for workers across our supply chain for more than 25 years.
"Through around 1,200 factory audits per year, we review and evaluate supplier conduct, work with suppliers to address issues and make improvements where necessary."
Life on the production line
Six thousand miles from the club shops where these shirts will be sold, a meeting is taking place inside Bowker Garment Factory.
In a photograph obtained by BBC Sport, mannequins display Benfica, Aston Villa and Celtic kits beneath an Adidas logo on the wall.
About 3,400 people - most of them women - work here on the outskirts of Phnom Penh. Another 3,200 work 10 miles east at Trax Apparel.
Fabric is imported from Thailand and Vietnam before a specialist tailor makes a sample for other employees to follow.
Much of the shirt-making process then takes place at these factories, including sewing, ironing and packaging.
'These shirts contain the sweat of Cambodian workers'
Staff typically work six eight-hour shifts a week and, according to five payslips seen by the BBC, receive basic monthly salaries of $210-$220 (£158-£166).
The salaries comply with local minimum-wage laws, and three of the payslips indicate total monthly earnings of about $300 (£226) once overtime and allowances are included, albeit with significant extra hours worked.
"It's hard to live with this amount," said a Bowker worker, who explained she had little left after rent, food and utilities.
"I want international customers to hear that one shirt they buy costs more than two weeks' salary for a worker," said another worker at Trax.
"Every one of these shirts contains the sweat of Cambodian workers."
Trax told us its average monthly employee earnings range from $305-$342 (£230-£258) this year.
Adidas said average net wages across a sample of its Cambodian suppliers were 34% above the Anker Research Institute's living-wage benchmark,, external adding staff were "usually paid considerably higher than the local minimum wage".
Bowker did not respond to our request for comment.
'One shirt sells for $120. How much are they pulling in from 600 of them?'
In another photograph taken inside Bowker, a thermometer shows 35.2C and humidity of 57.6%.
"The heat stress is really taking a toll on our health," said an employee on the ironing line.
Workers at both factories described pressure to meet group production targets of between 300 and 700 items a day.
"Just think about that," they added. "If one shirt sells for $120 (£90) in the store, how much are they pulling in from 600 of them? They make a ton of money but give almost nothing to the workers."
Others described verbal abuse when targets were missed.
"When we can't complete the quota they scold and yell at us and tell us to resign," said a third worker at Bowker.
The same employee said they received two electric shocks from an exposed wire.
"I tried to report it multiple times, but they only took action after the second time I got shocked," they said.
Adidas told us both factories had "heat-management measures", that its standards "do not permit any form of harassment", and that "no electrical-related accidents" had been found in Bowker's records.
Trax acknowledged "periods of elevated temperature" but said cooling systems were in place and insisted its approach "is not based on enforcing output targets".
Such concerns are widespread across Cambodia's garment industry, with a 2024 International Labour Organization report, external finding 69% of factories had issues with heat and 84% with worker protection.
From Cambodia to the club shop
It's August Bank Holiday in England and two of the Premier League's top sides - Aston Villa and Arsenal - are about to meet.
Tens of thousands of people are at Villa Park - many wearing shirts made in Cambodia.
Arsenal's latest home design was released in May, but we were sent photographs showing it inside Trax months earlier.
Fans of both clubs told us official shirts have become overpriced.
One Villa supporter has just paid £95 for his, complete with a Champions League badge.
"You buy your season ticket. Three shirts, that's around £300 on top. It's ridiculous," he said.
An Arsenal fan is struggling with the outlay for his whole family.
"I've got young kids now and I've started getting them kits, so it's started getting expensive," he said. "They're not cheap if you get the official ones."
Various studies estimate the global market for official football teamwear is worth several billion pounds.
"The mark-up on football jerseys... it's hard to imagine a more lucrative brand market," said Dave Welsh from The Solidarity Center, external - a US-based workers' rights organisation.
But former Puma and Umbro kit designer Rob Warner told BBC Sport last year that the economics behind shirt prices are more complex.
"A lot of the profit margin is made by the retailer because they're so dependent on the success of the team... it's a risk," he said.
"Then you factor in the cost of the kit deals going up, and the brands having to try to recover some of the money they're paying to the elite clubs."
Adidas supplies eight of the 20 Premier League clubs, plus Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
Fellow sportswear giant Nike supplies three, as well as England. Its football shirts have been produced in Thailand and Vietnam, and more recently Georgia.
Nike does not publish salary data by country, but told us 71% of its key suppliers pay at or above living-wage benchmarks relevant to their location.
Hummel, which also provides kit to three Premier League sides, did not respond to our enquiry.
'Respect has got to be a baseline in sport'
The average price of an adult replica Premier League shirt has risen by 50.7% over the past decade, helping fuel demand for counterfeits sold for as little as £12.
Many of those counterfeit shirts originate from China.
Fans have been warned against buying fakes, with police saying, external they can be "manufactured without regard for safety standards or workers' rights" and Trading Standards warning that "counterfeiters have no morals and no standards".
The Premier League expects clubs to carry out appropriate due diligence on their kit manufacturers and supply chains.
None of the clubs named in this article responded to our request for comment.
"Respect has got to be a baseline in sport," said Anna Bryher, from UK campaign group Labour Behind the Label., external
"Clubs need to send a really strong message that they won't put their name on a shirt if workers are not treated with respect."

Cardiac rehabilitation, a multidisciplinary approach to recovery and risk-reduction, is an important addition to medications, interventional and surgical procedures in heart patients. A cardiac rehab programme usually includes medical assessments, supervised exercise, nutritional guidance, psychosocial counselling and health education tailored to the clinical, cultural and behavioural needs of the patient.
Cardiac rehab has been incorporated into the routine care of patients in developed countries, while it is just now gaining inroads in low- and middle- income countries like India. The primary benefits of attending a cardiac rehab programme are faster recovery from cardiac procedures, reduced risk of future complications, improvement in blood sugar, blood pressure and lipid levels, increased cardiorespiratory fitness, adherence to a heart healthy diet, better weight management, abstinence from tobacco and excessive alcohol consumption, better emotional health and health-related quality of life, and decreased mortality.
The scenario in India
There is now a growing prevalence of heart diseases in the young Indian population, both in urban and rural parts of the country. According to the Global Burden of Disease, 2021, heart disease is the most common cause of death in India, accounting for 28.6 lakh deaths. Estimates indicate that nearly 27% of all deaths in India are due to heart disease, while 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease in the country are premature, between the ages of 40 and 69 years. Among those who survive, the effects can linger for years, affecting productivity and quality of life. This has brought to the fore, the urgent need for more widespread and accessible cardiac rehab facilities. There is a wide gap in the number of heart patients requiring cardiac rehab and the actual numbers being referred for these services.
Barriers to rehab
Even among those who access and enrol in cardiac rehab programmes, not everyone completes the programme. The main barriers to completing the cardiac rehab program after enrolling include patients’ work commitments, family responsibilities, financial constraints, and medical complications. Programmes that can offer personalised solutions including flexible scheduling, return-to-work counselling, sliding scale payment options and close collaborations with the referring cardiologist to identify and treat complications early, could help decrease drop-outs. Programme facilitators must also be able to proactively identify cues for potential non-adherence and work with patients and their families to circumvent challenges and complete the programme.
What works
A ‘TRACK and CARE’ policy could help in improving patient engagement in cardiac rehab programmes. TRACK denotes establishing Trust, involving the patient’s Relatives, helping them set clear Aims for the programme, Checking on the progress made on a daily, weekly and monthly basis and finally remembering to say Kudos to every single positive behaviour change made by the patient. The CARE refers to multidisciplinary care, comorbidity care and holistic care, where various specialists work together to address the different medical and psychological needs of the patient.
Young people are increasingly contracting heart disease. Getting them back to be productive, healthy and happy members of society is vital. While prevention remains the most important goal, cardiac rehabilitation must become an important part of treatment, not just an add-on that is optional. And to do that, we have to proactively address the potential barriers to access, adherence and programme completion.
(Dr. Priya Chockalingam is the clinical director, Cardiac Wellness Institute, Chennai. drpriya@cardiacwellnessinstitute.com)

The Jan Swasthya Abhiyan (JSA) and the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatment have called for regulation of charges levied by private hospitals and ceilings on trade margins for medicines, medical devices and medical consumables, amid renewed scrutiny by the Supreme Court of pricing practices in hospital pharmacies.
The groups, in a statement issued on Monday (October 5, 2026), said patients continued to face high and arbitrary charges for treatment, medicines and consumables, with limited avenues to challenge hospital bills.
The Supreme Court has recently questioned steep markups on medicines sold through hospital pharmacies and practices that require patients to purchase medicines from hospital-linked pharmacies. The court has also asked the government to examine regulation of trade margins.
Pricing vs determining charge
“The problem extended beyond the pricing of individual medicines to the broader question of how private hospitals determine charges for procedures, services and consumables. Private healthcare has expanded enormously in India, but regulation has simply not kept pace,” said Abhay Shukla, co-convener, JSA. He added that patients often had little bargaining power at healthcare facilities.
The Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 provides a framework for registration and regulation of clinical establishments and envisages standardisation of services and charges. However, its implementation is not uniform across the country, and several States have their own legislation or regulatory arrangements.
The groups said the absence of a uniform mechanism to regulate hospital charges had left patients vulnerable to hefty bills, particularly for prolonged hospitalisation and procedures involving multiple medicines, devices and consumables.
They are now demanding that the Centre and States introduce ceilings on charges levied by private hospitals for procedures, services and treatment and establish accessible, time-bound mechanisms through which patients can challenge excessive or unjustified bills.
The groups have also called for regulation of trade margins on medicines, medical devices and other medical consumables.
K.M. Gopakumar, co-convener, Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatment, said that the maximum retail price (MRP) cannot become a licence to charge patients many times the procurement price.
The group has also cited earlier concerns raised by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) regarding margins in pharmaceutical sales and incentives created when hospitals or hospital pharmacies control the products patients are required to purchase.
Financial incentives for doctors
Raising concern over the effect of financial incentives on clinical decision-making, Gayatri Sharma, a community health physician and researcher, said revenue-linked incentives could put pressure on doctors to increase investigations or procedures.
“Doctors should be able to make treatment decisions solely on the basis of what is medically necessary for the patient,” she said, calling for the National Medical Commission (NMC) to examine incentive-linked remuneration practices for doctors.
The group, in its statement, has called for a stronger public healthcare system alongside regulation of private providers, including increased public health spending and strengthening of government hospitals to provide accessible care. The demands include immediate regulation of trade margins on medicines, medical devices and consumables; ceilings on private hospital charges; a competition-law review of potentially anti-competitive practices; and an independent and time-bound grievance redress mechanism for patients.

In Silicon Valley, AI founders cheer Trump’s calls for the industry to police itself on safety
At Tech Week in San Francisco, venture capitalists and AI founders have been ebullient about the White House's hands-off approach to AI regulation

Tech Week is in full bloom in San Francisco, packing the city’s restaurants this week with venture capitalists and AI founders ebullient about the White House’s stance on regulating artificial intelligence — namely, don’t do it.
And after months of debate about leading AI companies’ unchecked AI agents meddling with everything from U.S. government websites to healthcare data, the nation now finds itself further from governing AI systems than it was a few years ago.
President Donald Trump brought tech titans to Washington late last month for a luncheon and ceremonial signing of a voluntary safety pact he described as “almost a constitution” surrounding “Super Intelligence,” the administration’s new preferred term for AI.
The 308-word agreement lays out that advanced AI labs should follow safety protocols and set up internal teams to monitor their own progress, but the administration has yet to provide details on how, in OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s words, to keep “bad things” from happening.
Safety challenges were not top of mind inside a crowded event space in San Francisco on Wednesday, where founders and funders said the government’s hands-off approach would net higher profits for companies building AI-powered defense and security systems.
Panelists praised the government’s bullish industry support at one meeting aimed at “investing in the forefront,” part of the blitz of popup events organized by Andreessen Horowitz, a venture firm whose head is a Trump science and tech adviser.
“I want to start with one figure that I think really emphasizes the investment opportunity of defense, and that’s $1 trillion. The U.S. government, for the first time, is allocating $1 trillion to its defense spending. And $13.5 billion of that will go to autonomous systems and AI,” said Kyle Stanford, a venture capital research director at PitchBook, a market intelligence platform. “That has obviously brought a lot of capital into defense tech spending, more than we’ve ever seen.”
New concerns emerge on AI safety
A day later, three researchers at OpenAI's headquarters said the ChatGPT maker had fired them, posting that “fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work.” Separately, David Robinson, a leader on OpenAI’s safety team until he recently resigned, said he was worried about letting the advanced labs police themselves.
“This is no substitute for hard law, and it does give a lot of freedom to the companies,” Robinson said. “The time between model generations is measured in weeks … and I think we have some very serious safety challenges in front of us in the nearer term.”
Trump has staked his political capital on the AI industry’s success, saying its unbridled development is key to winning the AI race against China. On the first day of his second term, the Republican president repealed a Biden-era executive order aimed in part at guarding against the risks that AI systems pose to consumers, workers and national security.
His administration has since reoriented federal policy away from oversight and toward rapid growth, including by canceling previous requirements for AI developers to share safety test results with the federal government. In December, Trump signed an executive order aimed at blocking AI regulations at the state level, saying a patchwork of rules could stifle the industry.
Even as Silicon Valley companies have disclosed their models’ involvement in troubling cyberattacks throughout the year, the burgeoning tech sector has continued to drive economic growth.
Concerns about AI safety centered on existential risk, rather than current real-world harms, landed at the center of debates last month, when a relatively unknown Anthropic engineer quit and called for a pause on tech development to keep “superhuman” systems from eluding controls. Then, Anthropic and OpenAI CEOs echoed the call to slow AI development. To some critics, their public manifestos appeared aimed at currying favor with investors ahead of their public listings and the midterm elections, when the political tides could turn with many voters opposed to data centers.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump posted in response on Truth Social, warning voters not to “kill the Golden Goose,” a term he has used to refer to both AI and data centers.
White House pact preserves wide latitude for AI companies
As calls mounted for stricter control of AI, the administration brought tech executives to the White House for lunch, followed by a ceremonial signing of the agreement on AI safety.
“I'm seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters after the event.
The document was signed by representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, SpaceXAI and Nvidia.
OpenAI is committed to embedding external assessors and finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors, said a spokesperson, who referred AP to a company post stating that the researchers were fired for violating “clear policies on handling sensitive information.”
Google referred to CEO Sundar Pichai's post that the company does appropriate testing and evaluations and is collaborating “to establish norms and build public confidence.”
Meta recently updated its standards for training, evaluating and releasing its most capable AI models, and spokesman Andy Stone pointed to the company's efforts to refine its board of directors’ governance structure.
Nvidia and SpaceXAI did not respond to requests for comment.
Anthropic, which voluntarily disclosed Friday that its agents had meddled with U.S. government websites, is bringing in independent evaluators and discussing collaborations with industry groups, a spokesperson said.
In a statement, the White House reiterated Trump’s comments about working with industry to balance innovation and security and did not directly answer questions about how the administration plans to monitor the AI companies’ implementation.
Following the new Anthropic disclosure, it added that the Trump administration expected full transparency from the company, saying notification and remediation was “not optional. It is a critical national security obligation.”
Under Democratic President Joe Biden, leading AI companies also made voluntary commitments to promote “safe, secure, and transparent development” of their models that included specific guidelines for tests and transparency reports. The current accord lacks that, said Sarah Myers West, a former senior AI adviser to the Federal Trade Commission.
“Across the board, this self-regulatory approach has consistently done one thing, which is failed to work. It’s failed to in any meaningful way ensure that these companies are honestly even keeping their house in order, let alone ensuring that they are compliant with existing law,” said Myers West, now co-executive director of the New York-based nonprofit AI Now. “All that they’re getting is grace from this government.”
After last month's luncheon with Trump, the FTC said it had opened an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other companies over dangers their technology may pose to consumers. The FTC didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump recently appointed National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson to serve on his new “Super Intelligence Force,” which the president said would keep the U.S. dominant in AI development. He posted Thursday that the White House would consider anyone who does not refer to AI using his preferred term as “THE ENEMY!”
Members of Congress, as well as civil liberties and consumer rights groups, have pushed for more regulations on AI, saying there is not enough oversight.
Graham Steele, a former assistant secretary in the U.S. Treasury Department, said even if AI companies set up internal evaluation teams or hire outside evaluators, such a structure can make them vulnerable to undue pressure on their work.
“We live in a democratic society. Are they the right ones to have the power to be able to make decisions that have broad, structural, social, and political consequences?” Steele said.

Reusable water bottles are a matter of personal taste, and WIRED reviewers have strong opinions on which jug reigns supreme. We’ve spent years testing, sipping, and spilling our way through the best water bottles to round up our favorites.
A note to remember: You only need one reusable bottle (though I won’t judge if you rotate between two). More than that defeats the environmental purpose of purchasing a reusable bottle in the first place. Also, be aware that some insulated bottles use lead solder. We’ve removed those from our list. We have some standards, after all.
Does your water need to be even cleaner? Check out our guide to the Best Backpacking Water Filters. Then get one of our Best Travel Mugs or Best Tote Bags.
Updated October 2026: We’ve added the Owala FreeSip Sway and Path Water Bottle as picks and the Bentgo Lift Chug as an honorable mention. We also moved the Owala FreeSip Twist to honorable mentions and ensured up-to-date prices and information throughout.
Featured in this Article
A PSA on Lead
Some water bottle companies use lead soldering to manufacture their vacuum-sealed bottles. The Stanley Quencher tumbler is one of them. No amount of lead exposure is safe, but it poses particular risk for children and pregnant people. The company has confirmed that some pellets used to seal the bottom of the cup use lead, but unless you remove or damage the bottom of the cup, the lead will not come into contact with your beverage or skin.
The risk of exposure might be very low, but it should be zero. Given that many brands practice lead-free manufacturing, we think the proximity to exposure is unnecessary.
Best Overall
A longtime favorite of outdoorsy folks and anyone else who wants a water bottle that’s not easily damaged, Hydro Flask has staying power. That may be due in part to its customization capability: Pick your preferred type of bottle, cap, and color, and if you buy from Hydro Flask, you can also engrave many styles. You can choose one color for the bottle, another for the lid, and depending on those choices, yet another for the strap or straw. —Boutayna Chokrane
Best for Straw Lovers
Owala perfected its FreeSip design with the Sway, which includes familiar features of other bottles in the line, like fun colors, triple-layer insulation, and a multifunctional mouthpiece that lets you sip through its straw or tilt the bottle upward to swig through its spout. Details that lift the Sway above its FreeSip cousins include its convenient top-carry handle that’s easy to hold, contoured side edges that let you get a comfortable grip while you drink, and its attached push-button opening with a locking mechanism that both lets you drink one-handed and also saves you from unfortunate spills.
Its materials are durable, it comes in four sizes (the 30-ounce option is plenty big for me without being too cumbersome), and the lid is dishwasher-safe. Even so, because the lid has a lot of edges and ridges where gunk can get trapped, I like to clean it by hand, which is a bit of a pain.
The wider top lid screws off completely, letting you add ice or easily pour in any other beverage, but it’s important to close it tightly before throwing it in your bag. The same warning applies to ensuring you’ve toggled on the mouthpiece lock. While the Sway is indeed leakproof when used as directed, the bottle is ripe for user-error spills, as I’ve learned the hard way. But if you look over to your passenger seat while you’re driving and see water pooling around your bottle because you forgot to close it correctly, at least you can snatch it up easily and plop it into a cup holder—a win that some other FreeSip models don’t offer. —Alexis Berger
Best BPA-Free Plastic
Today’s youths love their wide-leg jeans and Nirvana T-shirts, but ask any ’90s kid, and they’ll tell you that the look is incomplete without the water bottle of our times: the classic Nalgene. Originally made of bulletproof (and BPA-rich) Lexan, the Nalgene was the original name-brand water bottle, a symbol of good taste and outdoorsy vibes to be toted between Planet Hollywood and Blockbuster. The Nalgene had a complete chokehold on the premillennial culture, propping up water at a time when Surge and Josta were at such ready supply that human beings may well have stopped consuming plain water entirely were it not for the Nalgene. The brand has since replaced the chemical plastic with modern materials like Tritan, which is BPA-free and made of half-recycled plastic, but it otherwise remains the same: a perfect bottle, carrying a reasonable supply of fluid for the day with a secure screw-top lid, handy measurement lines, and a wide mouth for ice cubes and easy cleaning—unlike the bacteria-teeming straws on those adult sippy cups. —Martin Cizmar

The Larq bottle eases all my germaphobic concerns with reusable water bottles. It uses a nontoxic UV-C LED light in the lid to sterilize the water every two hours (or more often, if prompted), which reduces funky odors and bacterial buildup. Frequently Asked Questions
How Much Water Do I Need?
The eight-glasses rule isn’t exactly accurate, but it’s a solid starting point. Since water intake is highly individualized (kind of like the bottle itself), it’s best to consult your doctor about the right amount for you. Several lifestyle factors can influence your hydration needs. If you’re active or sweat a lot, for example, you generally should increase your intake to make up for losses. Remember that while warmer temperatures can make us thirstier, drinking too much water can cause overhydration and sodium levels to drop to dangerous levels in a condition called hyponatremia.
Certain medications can lead to water retention, which is another reason why it can’t hurt to ask your physician about your personal ideal water intake during your next check-up. In the meantime, if you’re not thirsty and your urine is colorless or light yellow, you’re likely doing great, sweetie.
How Do Insulated Water Bottles Work?
An insulated water bottle consists of a double-wall construction with insulating materials that prevent heat transfer. Insulated bottles are heavier and can typically hold less water compared to their uninsulated counterparts, given similar exterior dimensions. However, the advantage is that insulated models are typically vacuum-sealed, allowing them to better maintain the temperature of the liquid inside for far longer periods.
Condensation is typical in non-insulated water bottles, where beads of water form on the exterior of the bottle. In this case, you may end up avoiding packing the bottle inside your bag to protect your personal items from your sweating water bottle.
Insulated bottles are made of stainless steel and other similar durable, damage-resistant materials. While they’re typically more expensive because of the higher-quality materials, advanced technology, and complex manufacturing process, insulated water bottles may also have a longer lifespan than their noninsulated counterparts. This can minimize waste and also save you money in the long run as a result of needing to buy fewer replacement water bottles over time.
For hiking and outdoor climbing trips, you may prefer uninsulated bottles because they are lighter weight, and your concern is likely having enough water rather than cold water. For most other purposes, insulated options work just fine.
How Should I Wash My Water Bottle?
Even if they never hold anything but water, bottles get gross. Mold can grow quickly, especially if you leave the cap on. Straws and mouthpieces accumulate bacteria, oils, and grime from your mouth, and any dirt and dust they pick up in your backpack.
Some bottles can go right in the dishwasher, but be sure to take everything fully apart first, like any silicone pieces that can trap bacteria. For lids that have more nooks and crannies, I recommend hand-washing by soaking them in soapy water and then scrubbing.
Get yourself a bottle brush and straw brush—many kits are available that include both. Even if you don’t use straws, the smaller brush is a helpful tool for getting into any crevices. There are special bottle-cleaning tablets around, but cleaning with regular dish soap works perfectly fine.
Plastic bottles tend to trap odors over time. You can fix this by putting a teaspoon of bleach and a teaspoon of baking soda in the bottle, filling it up with water, and letting it sit overnight. Rinse it out well the next day.
How We Test Reusable Water Bottles
We test every new water bottle for at least two weeks; however, most top picks are ones that members of the WIRED team have loved and carried for months or years. Here’s what we look for:
- Design: First and foremost, we note which materials are used and evaluate whether they feel safe, sustainable, and durable. Because taste can also make or break a bottle, we evaluate whether materials retain odors or leave water tasting metallic or plasticky. We also consider how simple it is to replace parts like lids and straws.
- Portability: We consider the size, weight, cup holder compatibility, and whether it’s designed with ergonomic features like a carry loop.
- Durability: We drop bottles, toss them in totes, and use them daily to see if they dent, crack, or leak. We’ll also twist lids aggressively and test whether the hinges hold up after dozens of openings.
- Ease of use and cleaning: Overall, we’ll judge how intuitive the bottle is to drink from and refill. Each bottle also goes through several rounds of hand-washing and dishwasher cycles (when safe) to evaluate how easy it is to clean and whether odors or stains linger.
- Insulation: For insulated bottles, we’ll fill them with hot and ice-cold water for the advertised time to track how well they maintain temperature.

Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine as “thanks” for a deal cut by Donald Trump with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, accusing Washington of helping fund Moscow’s war.
The Ukrainian president has expressed repeated outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November midterm elections where the cost of fuel is a key voter issue.
The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.
He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.
That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 15 people, including three children.
“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday.
“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.
There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.
In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian news agency Interfax quoting an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.
“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump.
The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.
Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationship with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.
The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.
Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four civilians and wounded five, the region’s Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said on Saturday.
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.
Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The Financial Times reported that during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes.

9 killed in separate incidents in communal clash across 3 districts in Manipur
As tensions escalated, unidentified persons set several houses ablaze. At least 14 homes belonging to members of the Kuki and Naga communities were burnt
Violence in Manipur escalated on Saturday, with nine people, including a woman and a Nepali citizen, killed in clashes between Kuki and Naga groups in three districts of the state over the past 24 hours. At least 14 homes were set ablaze, police officials said.
As a precautionary measure, the district magistrate of Kamjong district imposed prohibitory orders within a 400-metre radius of Chassad police station.
The violence followed the death of a 42-year-old Kuki woman who was shot during crossfire between armed groups and security forces in Manipur’s Kamjong district on Friday night, when security forces arrested some village volunteers.

Police said that, after receiving information about the construction of illegal bunkers near Chassad police station, teams from the civil police, Indian Reserve Battalion (IRB) and Border Security Force (BSF) launched a drive to demolish them.
During the drive, women from the area tried to disrupt the operation. Police claimed that unknown assailants opened fire at security forces, who retaliated. The woman sustained a bullet injury to her upper left chest, near the neck, and died on the spot.
According to the police, the victim was identified as Domkhonei Touthang (42), a mother of five children — three boys and two girls.

As tensions escalated, unidentified persons set several houses ablaze. At least 14 homes belonging to members of the Kuki and Naga communities were burnt. In an attempt to stop those involved, police opened fire, leading to an exchange of fire that continued until early Saturday morning. Officials confirmed that an attempt was also made to set fire to Chassad police station.
Amid the escalating tension and violence, two Naga village guards were killed in a separate incident in the district at around 9.30am on Saturday in Ningchou Chingdong village, around 17 km southeast of Chassad police station.
A senior police officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, said, “Armed groups from across the Indo-Myanmar border might be involved in the attack. However, there is no official confirmation, and an investigation is underway.”
Police identified the two deceased as Ngachanso Ningshen (30) and Leishishan Hungyo (50), both from Ningchou village in Kamjong district.
Imphal-Tamenglong road incident:
One Naga village volunteer was killed and two others sustained bullet injuries in an ambush allegedly carried out by suspected armed Kuki militants in Tapon village, Kangpokpi district, on Saturday.
According to police, the incident occurred at around 6am between Makui and Tapok villages along the Imphal-Tamenglong road in Kangpokpi district, around 15 km northeast of Chalwa police station.
Police identified the deceased as Machungwangbou (35), a resident of Thalon village under Tamei subdivision. The two injured were identified as Nahason (29), from L Pabram village, and Mathangambou (30), from Kadi village.

Litan incident:
Meanwhile, a commuter travelling along NH 202 (Imphal-Nagaland via Ukhrul) was killed in an ambush by unidentified armed miscreants on Saturday at Konjang village, around 12 km northwest of Litan police station in Ukhrul district.
Police said the incident occurred at around 5.30am on Saturday. Those responsible for the attack and their motive are yet to be ascertained.
Police identified the deceased as Sandeep Rai (30), who was residing in Taphou Senapati Nepali village in Senapati district.

Civil body reaction:
The Committee on Tribal Unity (COTU), a Kuki organisation, announced a 24-hour total shutdown across Kangpokpi district, effective from 6pm on Saturday.
A statement issued by COTU’s information and publicity wing said the shutdown was announced “in view of the grave and escalating security situation arising from the reported coordinated attacks in Chassad village Kamjong district, Yaolen Ukhrul district and along the IT Road in Kangpokpi district, involving Tangkhul and Luangmei elements associated with NSCN-IM.”
COTU strongly condemned all acts of violence and intimidation directed against civilians.
The statement added, “This shutdown is a precautionary measure in response to the serious security threat facing civilians. CoTU appeals to all concerned to remain vigilant, maintain peace and refrain from actions that could further aggravate the situation.”

I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.
The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.
The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.
The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.
It has a nearly cab-over design, meaning that front-seat passengers sit almost directly over the front axle. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights or roll silently past.
The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.
Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.
People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights
Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.
“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. “I mean, they’re fun to be up super high and look out and feel like you’re dominating the world, but they’re killing an extra, roughly, 5,000 people per year, so do we want to just give them a pass for that?”
How Telo was born
Marks and North both live and work in the San Francisco Bay Area with their families, and both own pickup trucks: Marks because he has a 150lb three-legged dog he shuttles back and forth to the office every day, and North because he has a passion for the outdoors. Large pickup trucks can be useful, but they’re far from suitable for city life. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.
Marks previously worked on automotive safety and validation at National Instruments, while North is a former battery engineer at Tesla, founder of Mission Motors (one of the first electric motorcycle companies to break the land speed record for an electric motorcycle), and cofounder of Recargo, which developed EV charging app PlugShare. Behar is the founder of fuseproject, an industrial design and brand development firm. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.
“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”
— Telo cofounder Forrest North
Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.
“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. “The only thing they can do now is be big.” Telo aims to change the conversation about what electric transportation in urban centers can look like.
Battery, range, and layout
For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco.
Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. Each cell is individually fused so that a single failure won’t trigger a cascade across the pack. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. The passive thermal management system operates while the vehicle is parked, maintaining cooler temperatures even in direct sunlight, while active liquid cooling engages only when the vehicle is running. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago.
For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range
I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed.
To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. It’s accessible from either side and is large enough for a pair of roll-aboard carry-on suitcases to slide in endwise. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects.
The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. The steering wheel also has small scroll wheels, but most features will be controlled through the screen interface.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks
Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. But making that actually happen is far more complicated because kei vehicles don’t meet US crash safety regulations.
Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify. In the Telo, the redesigned hinge pillar does the structural job of a conventional one while also carrying the strut mount, the cross-car beam, and the dash — consolidating several separate parts into one. This allowed the company to cut the front-end part count roughly in half, Marks said.
“We pretty much threw all [the conventional crash architecture] away and had to start from scratch,” Marks said. The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety, brought on to help tackle the new front end and completely reengineer it.
“We have effectively six crash [paths], two bumper beams and two shock structures, a completely different architecture of a hinge pillar, a completely different architecture of a torque box to distribute the energy appropriately to the various parts of the car and save that occupant compartment as much as possible,” he said, comparing the crash innovations to those in a Smartcar. “Would any other automaker say we’re going to bet the world on being able to rethink crash?”
The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety
AI tools have made the virtual crash-testing process much more affordable for startups, and Telo recently locked in its body in white, the sheet metal shell made up of the major structural pieces of the truck (think of it like a skeleton of a vehicle). It’s currently being built by US supplier Schwab Industries in Michigan.
Marks said Telo uses AI to run virtual crash tests around the clock, averaging roughly one test per hour. The next phase of crash testing will include cutting the body in white apart for what Marks called a “quasi-static validation,” and full crash testing (slamming the vehicle and its various parts into a wall to validate the virtual testing the company has done) will start next year before Telo starts customer deliveries.
“I think it’s one of the most exciting times to start a hardware company,” North said. “It’s always been like, hardware is hard. That’s always been the cliché, and I wouldn’t say hardware is easy, but I would say it’s gotten so much easier because of software and AI.”
Pricing, delivery, and other features
The Telo MT1 will come in single-motor (rear-wheel drive) and dual-motor (all-wheel drive) layouts and offer add-ons like a solar-capable tonneau cover or camping shell. Reservations are open now for a refundable $152, and the base vehicle starts at $41,520. Marks said the company isn’t really worried about larger competitors like Ford’s upcoming midsized electric truck or Slate’s bare-bones EV because he sees their market entry as proof that a viable market exists for small electric pickup trucks.
North argued that Telo is also in a better position than either Slate or Ford right now because the company has fewer parts moving in and out of the country; it’s assembling its own battery packs and building the body in white stateside, making it largely exempt from the Trump administration’s tariffs. “The pack is the most expensive part of the vehicle build and the heart and soul of the vehicle,” Marks said, “so we had to keep it in-house.”
Marks said he’s been surprised by the volume of reservations: just over 14,000, with 70 percent of reservation-holders configuring AWD versions with the longer-range battery pack. He also noted that around 20 percent are first-time car buyers.
Telo is aiming for profitability at around 5,000 vehicles within roughly 24 months of deliveries. The company plans to get vehicles into customers’ hands sometime in 2027, depending on the validation timelines, but the MT1 still has to go through EPA and California air quality certification. Most reservations have come from places like LA, New York, the Bay Area, Seattle, Dallas, Washington, DC, Miami, and Denver, with almost everyone opting for the larger battery pack, regardless of drive configuration.
Marks pointed to Tesla as the trailblazer of EVs’ first real wave, proving electric cars could be fast, fun, and sporty. However, he believes the industry ultimately missed the chance to fully exploit their potential. Telo is tackling the problem by rethinking vehicle architecture from the ground up, returning to a “one-box” design made possible by eliminating wasted space.
Ultimately, Telo’s focus comes down to purpose, according to Marks: “What does electric enable for the experience of the user, and what value does that bring?”
While history has shown that the market isn’t kind to EV startups, in a world where giant American trucks increasingly barely fit in an average parking spot, the Telo MT1 and its creators are aiming to offer a capable electric pickup built for today’s cramped cities in the hope that Americans can get behind smaller and more capable electric vehicles.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

For at least several months, people have attributed a quote to Oscar-winning actor Denzel Washington in which he allegedly praised and pledged support for U.S. President Donald Trump.
Snopes received website searches from readers looking for more information about the quote, which read as follows:
I've worked with a lot of people in my life, and I've never met anyone braver, smarter, or who cares more about America than Donald Trump. He's a great friend and an even better president. I'm proud to be a steadfast supporter, and I'll never apologize for it. God Bless America and our president.
Searches for Washington and Trump located users posting the rumor in quote memes, for example on Facebook, Threads (archived) and X (archived).
(Redline News via Facebook)
Some users' comments indicated they believed Washington truly spoke out in favor of Trump, while others expressed skepticism that the actor would say such a thing.
In sum, an extensive search for credible evidence turned up nothing at all, indicating Washington never said this. Also, we previously reported as similarly untrue that fellow Oscar winner Matthew McConaughey and musician Mick Jagger uttered the words after people reposted memes attributing the exact same quote to them.
As such, we rate this claim as an incorrect attribution.
Snopes emailed a representative for Washington for confirmation and will update this article if we receive further information.
Digging into the rumor
We performed an initial search for Washington and Trump on Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo. Those searches failed to locate any credible sources reporting that Washington praised Trump, either in the words displayed in the meme or in any similar manner.
Likewise, searches of the news media outlets ABC News, CBS News, CNN, Fox News, MS NOW, NBC News, Newsmax and NewsNation found no reporting that Washington spoke favorably of Trump.
If any actor of Washington's prominence who had never publicly expressed such support in the past were to say the words attributed to them in the meme, national and international outlets covering entertainment and politics would have widely reported it. We found no such reporting.
We reported in 2016 that, despite another rumor, Washington did not publicly announce his support for Trump. We also fact-checked a false rumor alleging the actor said that electing Trump saved the U.S. from becoming an "Orwellian police state."
People who create and repost misinformation often exploit the names of actors known for portraying tough, "he tells it like it is" leading men in movies, for example Clint Eastwood, Tom Selleck, Sam Elliott, Washington and others, to boost the credibility of their fabricated claims.

One year on from the Gaza ‘ceasefire’, Trump’s promise of peace is a distant dream as Israeli attacks continue
The glimmer of hope when Israel and Hamas signed a ceasefire one year ago has been buried under the rubble of ongoing Israeli attacks on Gaza - and the humanitarian situation is becoming increasingly desperate. Alex Croft reports

Three-hundred-and-sixty-five days have passed since a long-awaited ceasefire was signed in Gaza, designed to bring peace and safety for Palestinians after two years of devastating Israeli invasion.
The reality of the past 12 months, however, is a far cry from Donald Trump’s promise of “peace for all eternity” last autumn.
Nearly 1,400 Palestinians have died in Israeli strikes since the ceasefire came into place and more than 74,000, according to the Palestinian authorities, since the bloody October 7 attacks three years ago in which 1,200 Israelis were killed and 251 taken hostage.
The Israeli military has continued creeping forward in Gaza, squeezing Palestinians into increasingly smaller territory, and has not allowed a free flow of humanitarian and medical aid into the strip. Hamas is still armed, and five Israeli soldiers have been killed in combat.
“Everybody is living in fear,” Musallam Abukhalil, a 32-year-old doctor from Nuseirat in central Gaza, tells The Independent. “There are still people living in torn tents with no proper sewage, looking for opportunities to have a livelihood.
“Everybody in Gaza is asking: what happens if I go to a place where the Israeli army targets for some reason? We have heard so many stories about people being at the wrong place at the wrong time, being killed or injured with irreversible or disabling injuries, because there were no warnings.”
Dr Abukhalil, founder of the United for Dignity Alliance who also does clinical work in Nasser Hospital, paints a bleak picture of the humanitarian situation. The medical sector, he says, is suffering the consequences of three years of Israeli bombardment, with just 19 of the 36 hospitals partially functioning while many Palestinians are unable to access drinking water or sufficient food.
The October 2025 ceasefire was met with much fanfare. Trump said his newly-created Board of Peace - complete with himself as chairman-for-life and former UK prime minister Tony Blair as an executive board member - possessed “unlimited potential”.
The board, which contains several heads of state accused of presiding over human rights abuses, would, the president said, kick off an “age of faith and hope and of God" in Gaza.
Phase one of the truce saw Hamas release the remaining living hostages and the bodies of those that had been killed, while Israel partially withdrew within the strip and released hundreds of Palestinian prisoners.
But during the initial months of the truce Israel continued its attacks, failed to allow the free flow of aid into the strip, and encroached beyond the so-called ‘Yellow Line’, behind which it was supposed to position its forces. The government media office in Gaza said Israel has carried out more than 5,100 ceasefire violations since 10 October.
Israel refutes the allegations, and says it has abided by the terms of the ceasefire, describing victims of its attacks as suspected terrorists.
“Claims that Israel is violating the ceasefire agreement disregard the continued military activity and military buildup of terror organizations in the Gaza Strip, their plans to carry out attacks against Israel, as well as Hamas’s refusal to disarm, which are contrary to the agreement,” the IDF said in a statement.
“The IDF remains committed to the ceasefire agreement and continues to operate in a focused manner, solely to remove threats and protect Israeli civilians and IDF troops, in accordance with the agreement.”
But Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East programme, says Israeli incursions are damaging the peace process.
“The constant violations of the ceasefire and the fact that so many hundreds of Palestinians have been killed, and at the same time Israel is extending its occupation in Gaza, and the slow progress on the humanitarian issue, makes the situation always worse as a result,” he says.
The question of what comes next lingers. The second phase of the truce, supposed to involve Hamas’ disarmament and Israel’s full withdrawal from the Gaza Strip, is yet to kick into action, with the Board of Peace so-far failing failed to force progress in negotiations.
It comes amid the backdrop of spiralling violence in the West Bank, where more than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli settlers or troops since 7 October, according to local authorities.
Settler attacks, more common than ever, are carried out largely with impunity, prompting several of Israel’s allies in Europe and beyond - including the UK - to impose unprecedented trade sanctions on the settlements.
International pressure on Israel has been mounting in recent months. In June, a UN commission of inquiry found that Israeli authorities and security forces have committed genocide and war crimes by intentionally targeting Palestinian children.
The pressure on Netanyahu’s hard-right government also comes from within Israel, with elections later this month that could see him ousted from the role for the third time - and have a direct knock-on effect on Gaza.
“The election is crucial, and the internal dynamics within the Palestinian society, almost equally crucial,” says Mr Mekelberg. “And the [actions of the] international community. The UK and EU have started showing - and rightly so - impatience with certain behaviours. The question is will they keep doing that.”
But as diplomatic wrangling stalls and high-level talks trudge on, the humanitarian picture on the ground is becoming increasingly bleak.
A joint call to action from Australia, Denmark, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UK last month said Israel’s aid restrictions were the “biggest barrier to a functioning health service”, and called on the government to “allow and facilitate rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza”.
Around 94 per cent of Gaza’s population need shelter assistance, the UN says. Around 1.4 million people, which is two thirds of the population, are expected to suffer food insecurity between July and December this year, up from 1.2 million people between April and June, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC).
Nine in 10 people face high levels of water insecurity, and more than half of households have drinking water access which is below the daily minimum of 6 litres-per-person, according to Swiss non-profit WASH Cluster.
But Israel nonetheless insists that it imposes no limits on the quantity of humanitarian aid entering Gaza. The IDF says the accusations are “biased and recycled claims that are echoed and disseminated by Hamas”.
It adds: “Throughout the ceasefire, humanitarian aid has entered the Gaza Strip in quantities significantly exceeding international humanitarian requirements, contributing to significant improvements in food security, the medical response, and WASH infrastructure.”
Doctors on the ground share a very different picture. Healthcare in particular has suffered catastrophically, and there has been no meaningful rebuild of Gaza’s health system. In fact, it remains under attack, with the World Health Organisation recording 56 attacks on healthcare this year, killing 10 people and injuring 49.
Neonatal care has faced the brunt of the desperate medical situation, with the number of newborns and babies who require intensive care having “significantly increased” in recent months, a doctor working in neonatal care said in a testimony to Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP).
“During the worst periods of the war, our immediate problem was just huge numbers of trauma patients arriving at hospitals,” says Dr Abukhalil.
“But now, we are dealing with the consequences of the three years of destruction.”
The rebuild of the strip is yet to begin in earnest. Across the strip, around 82 per cent of all structures have been destroyed or damaged, UN figures show. The scale of the destruction was recently aid bare when Google Earth updated its satellite images, showing a barren land reduced to rubble.
Trump’s promise to rebuild Gaza is only just kicking into action, after the Board of Peace proposed a six-month, $2.45 billion plan to start restoring basic services across 66 projects during a meeting at the UN General Assembly.
But given forecasts by the UN, EU and World Bank that the full rebuilt will cost an estimated $71.4 billion over the next 10 ten years, the pace appears slow.
For Palestinians in Gaza, the word ‘ceasefire’ is only synonymous with death, poverty and insecurity. Peace and safety remain little more than a distant dream.

NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.
The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.
In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.
Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.
For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.
For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.
Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.
The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.
