Medical debt is crushing hospital patients in LA. Health officials may have a fix
LOS ANGELES — Every Tuesday, Naman Shah sees tuberculosis patients at a small public clinic in Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley. Shah, a physician and epidemiologist at the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, pores over images of battered lungs, listens to labored breathing and checks medications.
It's part of an initiative dating to the early 20th century to control infections so tuberculosis doesn't spread. "We like doing things upstream," Shah said, "meaning before they happen, not after the damage is done."
Today, Shah and his colleagues are applying the same principle to medical debt. A key part of that effort is a new system to allow every hospital in LA County to easily screen patients for financial aid. The goal: to stop low-income families from getting a bill that buries them in debt.
Shah estimates this system could prevent several hundred million dollars of medical debt every year.
Vicious cycle
In the U.S., an estimated 100 million adults have some form of healthcare debt. In LA County, the nation's most populous, public health officials calculate that about 800,000 residents have medical bills they can't pay.
"The impacts of medical debt were staggering," said Shah, who used to staff a rural health clinic in India and, since 2023, has led a county initiative in LA to tackle the debt problem.
"People end up with credit card debt and then a vicious cycle of high interest rates and poverty," he said. "People forgo their prescriptions. People forgo appointments. And then you get into worse health."
Hospitals typically offer financial aid to patients with low incomes. But information about assistance is often hard for patients to get. Applying can be cumbersome. And many eligible patients never seek aid, research shows.
"Most people walk into the hospital and walk out without any knowledge of financial assistance," said Jared Walker, founder of Dollar For, a nonprofit that helps patients nationwide apply for aid, often called charity care.
That's fueling debt. It's also driving costly collection efforts that even hospital officials acknowledge pointlessly target low-income patients who are unlikely to be able to pay.
"They're turning their wheels trying to collect on debt that isn't collectable," said Adena Tessler, regional vice president for the Hospital Association of Southern California.
Presumptive eligibility
One potential solution is a system that automatically screens and qualifies low-income patients for financial aid without requiring an application. This is called presumptive eligibility.
Some hospitals already use such systems, which rely on software that checks patient eligibility based on publicly available information such as credit history.
The strategy can be very effective. Shah said hospitals that have deployed presumptive eligibility systems have reported as much as a 50% increase in the amount of financial aid they give patients.
Under a state law passed last year, all California hospitals will have to start doing presumptive eligibility screening by next July.
But the systems can be expensive and difficult for smaller hospitals to implement. Only about 1 in 5 hospitals in LA County currently use them, Shah said.
Public health officials wondered whether they could help more hospitals set up the systems.
The county, which, like many local governments, faces major fiscal challenges, couldn't pay for this, Shah said. But the public health department could bring together healthcare and hospital officials in the county to figure out another solution.
"The beauty of government is not when it always has to do the work," Shah said. "We have the ability to make sure that people cooperate."
The Hospital Association of Southern California, initially wary of the county initiative, came to see improving hospital financial aid programs as beneficial to hospitals, many of which were wasting money on collections. "The billing process is cumbersome and costly," said Paul Young, a senior vice president with the association.
The association agreed to procure a digital presumptive eligibility system and make it available to its members. This bulk-purchasing approach, which Young compared to "a Costco model," would lower the cost for individual hospitals, he said.
At the same time, L.A. Care, a nonprofit health plan that administers Medicaid coverage for more than 2.5 million low-income county residents, committed $2 million to set up the system.
The investment reflected the safety net insurer's mission to make medical care accessible to more people, said Melanie Fontes Rainer, who leads strategic planning for L.A. Care. "It's going to make Los Angeles County better," she said.
Making it work
Getting the new system up and running by January, as the partners hope, faces challenges.
Hospital officials are figuring out how the system will be funded in the long term. And it's unclear how many of the county's 88 acute care hospitals will ultimately use it, even if it's cheaper and easier to access.
The partners are also working to improve the data that the system relies on to screen patients. One goal is to link the system to tax records maintained by the state of California. This would provide hospitals with more accurate information on patients' income than current systems, which often rely on estimated income.
Walker, the patient advocate at Dollar For, said he's heartened by the county's effort. "I'm optimistic that we can make a better charity care system," he said. "And the fact that hospitals in LA County are willing to be innovative and creative about ways we can do that is super encouraging."
For his part, Shah said county public health officials recognize that a better screening system at hospitals won't by itself eliminate medical debt. But he said the public health department couldn't ignore a problem that affects more county residents than asthma or tobacco use.
"Prevention is our bread and butter," he said.
This article is part of Hidden Help, an investigative series from Tradeoffs and KFF Health News about how hospitals can protect their patients from the life-altering harms of medical debt.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling and journalism.

The Trump administration announced Thursday that it is investigating nine universities for alleged fraud related to visas commonly used by postdoctoral researchers, a core part of the nation’s biomedical workforce.
Vice President JD Vance announced during a press briefing that Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the California Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the University of Pittsburgh, and UC Davis are under investigation by the Department of Labor. During the briefing, Vance asserted that these schools are improperly using J-1 visas, the main class of visa used by international postdocs, to bring in cheap labor rather than relying on domestic researchers.
“They’re using these visas way too much,” he said. “They’re using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop.”
Vance asserted that these schools employ researchers on J-1 visas for work connected to federal grants at a rate of 61% compared to a national average of 38%. STAT contacted the White House and the Vice President’s office for clarification on where these figures came from but did not receive immediate replies. National Science Foundation data show that nearly 60% of postdocs in science, engineering, and health are temporary visa holders; most of these researchers would be on J-1 visas.
The labor department’s inspector general, Anthony D’Esposito, said during the briefing that his office has already issued subpoenas to the schools under scrutiny. He added that he will investigate whether “foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research.”
“If an American university is breaking the law to save a dollar while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It’s institutional betrayal,” he said. “I don’t care how prestigious a university thinks it is. Break the law and screw the American people, and I will personally cuff you in the university square.”
Kimberly Allen, an MIT spokesperson, confirmed in an email to STAT that the university received a “very broad subpoena” on Thursday morning that it is now reviewing. She did not elaborate on the details of the subpoena or what kinds of information had been requested.
“Each J-1 visa holder at MIT has been vetted and authorized to come here by the U.S. government, and we take seriously our obligations to follow U.S. law,” Allen wrote.
Spokespersons for Stanford, Yale, and Harvard did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
It’s unclear how much evidence the administration has to support its visa fraud concerns, and D’Esposito’s office didn’t immediately respond to questions about the investigation’s scope or expected timeline. But Thursday’s announcement fits into a series of moves by the Trump administration to more tightly restrict the entry of international students and scholars into the U.S.
The Department of Homeland Security has attempted to place a four-year cap on how long foreign graduate students and postdocs can stay in the country, alleging that the current system allows these scholars to remain indefinitely and incentivizes fraud. On Wednesday, the Trump administration announced a proposed $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program used by international students seeking professional experience. And DHS is attempting to revive plans to institute a $100,000 fee for H1-B visas, which are used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as engineering and biotech.
These proposed restrictions have yet to take effect and have in some cases been temporarily blocked by lawsuits. But Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney in Boston, warned that these efforts send a clear sign to international scientists that their contributions are no longer valued, a message she worries could compromise U.S. scientific leadership.
“This is an incredible series of self-owns,” she said. “The government also knows that none of this will stand up in court. They just want to send a message: Don’t come here. But we will lose [out] on so much. It’s going to take decades for us to repair the damage when this is over.”

Pretorius breaks Gayle's T20 record score
- Published
CSA T20 Challenge, Bloemfontein
Titans 267-3 (20 overs): Pretorius 188* (79); Boast 1-46
Knights 143 (17.2 overs): Cloete 39 (25); Ferreira 3-16
Titans won by 124 runs
Lhuan-dre Pretorius has broken Chris Gayle's record for the highest score in a men's T20 match with an unbeaten 188 in a domestic fixture in South Africa.
The 20-year-old South African's knock off 79 deliveries, including 13 sixes and 15 fours, helped Titans post 267-3 against Knights in the CSA T20 Challenge.
It eclipsed the 175 made by Gayle for Royal Challengers Bangalore (now Bengaluru) against Pune Warriors in the 2013 Indian Premier League.
Pretorius, who has played 17 T20s, three one-dayers and two Tests for South Africa, finished with a strike rate of 237.97.
He made his half-century off 24 balls but only required 16 more balls to get to three figures and then got to 150 off just 58 deliveries.
Titans then bowled out Knights for 143 to wrap up an emphatic 124-run victory at the Mangaung Oval in Bloemfontein.

New Delhi, Oct 10: Anti-terror agency NIA has registered a case to probe and unearth the larger conspiracy behind last month's mid-air attack on Captain Smit Machchhar inside the cockpit of an Israel-bound flydubai flight, officials said on Saturday.
It was reported that on September 30, 2026, the Omani first officer of flydubai flight no 1073 stabbed the Indian pilot, Captain Machchhar, mid-air "in an apparent attempt to hijack or cause it to crash", according to the First Information Report (FIR) filed by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) on October 9.
The FIR mentions the "Omani first officer" as the accused.
The NIA has invoked Section 3 (hijacking) of the Anti Hijacking Act, 2016 and Section 16 read with Section 15(1)(a) of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, officials said.
Section 16 of UAPA entails punishment for terrorist act.
The Section 15(1)(a) details punishment for terrorist activities for "whoever does any act with intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, security, (economic security) or sovereignty of India or with intent to strike terror or likely to strike terror in the people or any section of the people in India or in any foreign country, (a) by using bombs, dynamite or other explosive substances or inflammable substances or firearms or other lethal weapons or poisonous or noxious gases or other chemicals or by any other substances (whether biological radioactive, nuclear or otherwise) of a hazardous nature or by any other means of whatever nature..."
Captain Machchhar sustained critical injuries after he was stabbed by the Omani co-pilot inside the cockpit of the flydubai flight heading from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The incident occurred in the "Saudi airspace while flying near the Jordan-Saudi Arabia border".
The case was filed on the direction of the Home Ministry, considering the gravity of the offence and the need to unearth the larger conspiracy, the officials said.
"The Central government has received information that flydubai flight no 1073, which was being piloted by Indian national pilot Captain Smit Machchhar and an Omani first officer, departed from Dubai on September 30, 2026 at 7.05 am (GST) with 174 passengers and six crew members and dived rapidly and turned back into Saudi airspace while flying near the Jordan-Saudi Arabia border at around 9.21 am (GST)," the FIR states.
"And whereas passengers reported that the first officer stabbed Captain Smit Machchhar during the flight in an apparent attempt to hijack or crash the plane but was overwhelmed and restrained by passengers and crew. However, Captain Smit Machchhar sustained deep cuts to the head and hands as a result of the attack," it said.
The other flydubai pilots on board then landed the plane safely at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz Airport in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia at 10.45 am (GST), leading to the arrest of the first officer by Saudi authorities, the FIR reads.
The Central government is of the opinion that a scheduled offence under the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008, has been committed and the case is related to an attack on an Indian national pilot with an apparent attempt to hijack or crash the plane, and "having regard to the gravity of the offence, its grave national and international ramifications, and the need to unearth the larger conspiracy, the matter requires thorough investigation by the National Investigation Agency," it said.

How to use the parental controls on iOS 27
Extra layers of protection keep Apple devices age-appropriate for your kids.
The iOS 27 update in September was headlined by Siri AI, but there are also a lot of little feature enhancements throughout the new OS. One that you might have missed is an overhaul of parental controls. For these changes, Apple worked alongside the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) to bring new safety tools. They also created a Building Healthy Digital Habits companion guide to aid parents in creating healthy digital habits for their kids, balancing screen usage with essentials like sleep, exercise, schoolwork and family time.
Among the new parental control features introduced are Time Allowances, Ask to Browse, Ask to Add Contacts, a Pause Device feature and expanded Communication Safety. The setup process has also been simplified, offering age-appropriate app recommendations for new child accounts, rather than dumping every default app onto a kid's home screen.
However, these features don't activate automatically when a device updates. Every device in a Family Sharing group (whether it's an iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch or Apple TV) needs to be running iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, or tvOS 27 before the new Screen Time system will function. Devices that can't be updated will continue using the older iOS 26 controls, which creates a gap for families with older hardware. If you haven't updated your devices yet, walk through the preparation steps for a major software update and install them all.
What's new in iOS 27's parental controls?
The most notable shift is the replacement of App Limits with Time Allowances, which gives you more granular control over how your kids spend their screen time. For instance, if you allow your kids to spend three hours daily on their phones, you can decide how much of that time can go to social media, entertainment and gaming. There are also custom categories parents can create themselves, setting one allowance per category instead of managing dozens of individual app limits.
Ask to Browse gives parents oversight over Safari activity by requiring approval before a child visits an unapproved website. Approval requests arrive in Messages, so parents can review and approve links without digging through a separate app. The Communication Safety feature, which flags nudity in messages, AirDrop and FaceTime, now also detects and blurs graphic violence and gore. Ask to Add Contacts is also a new feature, making kids get parental approval before they can call or text a new phone number.
Finally, Pause Devices makes it easy for parents to instantly lock a child's device with a single tap — great for when your kid won't stop fiddling with their phone at dinner or during homework time. All together, these tweaks make setting up your child's iPad (or any other Apple device) an easier task.
How to set up and adjust parental controls
Getting started requires a Child Account for each kid, if you don't have them created already. First, make sure you have a Family Sharing group set up, then head to Settings > Family on your iPhone. If any devices aren't updated yet, you'll see information about what needs the latest version here. To manage an existing child, tap their name to access their settings. Review iOS 27's additions to confirm they're set up as you like.
If you need to add a new child, you'll be able to take advantage of the new setup process: tap the Add button at the top-right, then follow the steps. The default settings vary by age. For instance, Ask to Browse, Limit Adult Websites and contact management features are on by default for kids under 13. Communication Safety is also enabled for everyone under 18. Most other restrictions fall to a parental decision once a child turns 13, as Ask to Browse and contact management no longer switch on automatically.
From there, parents can build separate weekday and weekend schedules, layer category-specific caps within an overall daily limit, and enable Ask to Buy for app purchases. The redesigned Screen Time dashboard gives you a quick overview of usage, so you spend less time fumbling through menus. Apple recommends revisiting settings periodically with the AAP's age-group guidance as children grow.

A man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo in Yorkshire, police have said.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park was evacuated shortly after the incident and the site will remain closed on Sunday.
South Yorkshire police said that at 1.35pm it received reports of an individual entering the enclosure at the zoo near Doncaster.
The force said the attack “resulted in serious injury”.
The statement added: “Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.
“The man’s family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time.
“Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.”
The force earlier said: “We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this distressing footage.”
Yorkshire Wildlife Park said a “serious incident” occurred inside the enclosure.
It said in a statement: “Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated, and emergency services are currently attending the scene.
“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened.” It added that the “safety and wellbeing of visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”.
Footage shared on social media appeared to show a man wearing a black jumper sitting on the ground of the enclosure and being attacked by a tiger.
A Yorkshire ambulance service spokesperson said it sent a number of resources to the scene including two ambulances, Yorkshire air ambulance and a doctor.

Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.
In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.
“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote.
“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”
He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”
Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach.
Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.
The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.
“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” the Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Failure to follow the law and the bipartisan will of Congress that only weeks ago passed legislation aimed at cutting off revenue for Russia’s war machine and curbing purchases of Russian oil and gas.”
Some Republicans were also critical of the agreement.
“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”
Perhaps the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.
In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.
“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.
Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.
“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.
Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.
The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”
But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.
Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.

Attack on Riyadh airport leaves 12 dead, more than 300 injured
At least 12 people were killed and 309 others injured in an attack on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International airport in Riyadh as Iran-backed Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom.
The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement on Sunday that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack on late Saturday.
The authority said some of the injured were in critical condition and that all were receiving medical care at several hospitals. Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter told Reuters.
Jordan's foreign ministry said in a statement on Saturday that two injured Jordanians were discharged from hospital while two others were still receiving treatment.
One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport.

An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.
Saturday's attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, occurred without warning, with no alert issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system.
This week's two previous attacks on the airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.
All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The Iran-backed group, which is yet to claim responsibility for the latest attack, has aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there – except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina – is a target.
The attack on the airport comes amid escalating fighting between Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces and Houthis. Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, spokesman for the government forces, said more than 1,900 operations carried out in the past 24 hours targeted weapons and ammunition depots, camps and military positions, reinforcements and other “military objectives deep within areas controlled” by the Houthis.
The coalition called the attack a 'war crime' and said it will respond firmly to the attack on the airport, Reuters reported.
Riyadh due to hold major summits
Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.
Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences, including the World Petroleum Conference.
Organisers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, according to Reuters.
Advisories issued
In an advisory issued earlier on Saturday, King Khalid airport urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and check their flight status before heading to the airport amid reports of disruptions to air traffic, without specifying the cause of the disruptions.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also instructed Saudi citizens travelling to the kingdom to contact local embassies if their travel itineraries have been disrupted following the attack.
At the same time, foreign embassies in Riyadh, including those of the US, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Canada, issued advisories on social media to their citizens in Saudi Arabia.
The US mission said it was “aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh” and “strongly recommends” all US citizens avoid the airport and surrounding areas.
The UK and Irish embassies advised their nationals about “a serious incident” at the airport. Canada’s embassy advised citizens in Riyadh to avoid all travel to the airport, noting “ongoing military activity”.
US may join Saudi strikes on Houthis, Trump says
Following reports of the latest attack, United States President Donald Trump was asked by reporters outside the White House whether Washington planned to join the Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
“We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said.
The attack was widely condemned, with Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs calling it “a direct threat to the security of the region”.
Qatar’s former prime minister says today’s attack on King Khalid airport shows that it is “more urgent than ever” to stand with Saudi Arabia in a “practical and decisive” manner.
“It has now become clear that Iran is our primary adversary”, Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani said in a post on X, adding that the Gulf Cooperation Council today confronts “several hostile plots and conspiracies” that require “unity and profound foresight”.
He said it has become “more urgent and evident” that Qatar stands with Saudi Arabia against the “threat from within Yemen” that is being “plotted and directed from outside [Yemen]”.
The situation “necessitates setting aside all peripheral disputes” among Gulf Cooperation Council members and “demonstrating unity” instead, he said.
Japan’s embassy also “strongly” condemned Houthi attacks on airports and other Saudi civilian facilities.
Kuwait Airways said it was cancelling flights because the airport had closed due to a “security situation”.
Egypt's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Egypt expressed its “profound denunciation of these blatant attacks”, their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail.
Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces.
The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.
That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

The State informed the Kerala High Court that in-principle approval had not been granted to Keralam for establishing an All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS).
The Division Bench of Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice V.M. Syam Kumar enquired into the reason why Keralam was not prioritised for building an AIIMS, even though the matter had been pending for almost 10 years. The Bench was considering a petition seeking establishment of an AIIMS under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY).
The court observed that the matter was presently at the stage of inter-ministerial consultation and any decision for setting up an AIIMS could be taken only after the continuation of the PMSSY scheme for the next five financial years, FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, was approved.
In a previous order, the court noted that the idea of having an AIIMS in Keralam was raised in June 2016 and four locations were identified for this purpose. The court opined that Keralam should be considered on a priority basis considering the density of population, and asked the Union government to take a conscious decision concerning the proposal for the institute.
Prioritising other States
The Deputy Solicitor General of India, O.M. Shalina, informed the court that since Keralam had better health-care conditions than other States, the Union government was prioritising those States with a weaker health sector. At this point the court enquired whether the Union government’s stand was that Keralam did not require an AIIMS. The court orally asked whether the hospitals in the State were a disqualification or a ‘handicap’ to consider the establishment of the institute. The court orally remarked that Keralam had the highest density of population in the country, and that the existing hospitals would not be sufficient to provide medical facilities to the needy and poor.
The Union government responded that while considering all other States and Union Territories, Keralam’s status was much better, and that was the reason for the delay in approval. The court then enquired why there was an AIIMS in Delhi and two or three institutes in some other States, if the criteria was availability of medical facilities.

In late September, two images circulated online purportedly showing ancient Egyptian sculptures depicting cats walking and resting on their owners.
One of the images shows a sculpture, possibly a wood carving, of a cat in a museum display as either standing or walking on a person at rest. The other image features a cat sitting right up against the chin of a person whose eyes appear to be open.
For example, on Sept. 29, a Facebook user posted a graphic (archived) featuring the two images, with text reading, "4,000-year-old statues prove cats have always ignored personal space." The post's caption adds, "Cats Have Been Sitting on Their Humans for 4,000 Years." The pair of images also spread on Threads and X (archived, archived).
(Nathanistic via Facebook)
Reverse image searches uncovered examples of the standing cat image on Facebook, Instagram and Threads, as well as the resting cat image on Instagram, Threads and X.
Cats prominently feature in ancient Egyptian artifacts, including in mummification. That may be one reason why some commenters under posts have posted remarks indicating they believe the images are authentic. Others mention artificial intelligence, saying they are skeptical about whether the images show actual artifacts that truly exist.
In sum, the images are fake and appear to be AI-generated — as do other images of Egyptian sculptures depicting cats interacting with people.
The aforementioned reverse image searches indicate that the earliest posts featuring the image of the cat standing or walking on top of the person first appeared on Soft Cat Memes (@softcatmemes) accounts on Facebook, Instagram and Threads on Sept. 25, as well as on the possibly-affiliated @hardcatmemes X account. The image contains overlaid text, reading, "Cats have been bothering their humans since the dawn of time."
(@softcatmemes via Facebook)
The image of the cat sitting on a person also first appeared on the same accounts on Sept. 26, receiving more engagement. That second image also features overlaid text, reading, "Evidence suggests cats have never understood personal space."
(@softcatmemes via Facebook)
Snopes contacted the manager of the accounts to confirm the user created the images with an AI tool. We also asked for the name of the tool and the exact text prompts submitted to create the content. We will update this article if we receive further information.
How we know images are fake
Reverse image searches failed to locate any posts or websites containing the same two images prior to late September. With the ongoing popularity of internet cat content, the idea that no one, until recently, would share supposedly real photos of ancient Egyptian sculptures depicting cats acting silly is unlikely.
As one Reddit user has noted, scans of the images with OpenAI's free tool, that verifies content generated using the company's chatbot, display the results, "This content was generated using OpenAI tools," and, "We found a SynthID watermark that originated from OpenAI." For example, a scan of the image of the cat sitting displays the information shown below.
(via OpenAI)
There is also an inconsistency with one of the shadows in that image. The faint shadow nearest where the photographer is meant to be standing (running from left to right along the long edge of the bed) indicates there is a light source on the other side of the display. However, only a shadow of the bed is cast. If the image were authentic, the angle of the shadow suggests the viewer would also be able to see a faint shadow of the human and cat sculptures. That is not the case in this image.
A scan of the other image of the cat standing or walking displays the same result using OpenAI's tool. The absence of a shadow of the cat's tail also further suggests this image is fake.
For further reading, we previously reported about another feline rumor that wild cheetahs have never killed humans.

Hong Kong-based Cappu Films has taken on sales beyond Australia and New Zealand for “Her Last Laugh,” Joy Hopwood’s Australian dramedy featuring Peter Thurnwald (“XO, Kitty”) and Ana Thu Nguyen (“Mortal Kombat II”).
The finished film is being introduced to buyers at the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market.
Hopwood wrote, directed and produced the film. Tiana Hogben, Kya Stewart, Lyanna Kea, Tony Goh and Australia’s John Waters round out the cast.
The story centers on Willow and Annika Lim, Chinese Australian sisters who are left their late mother’s casting agency with a catch attached. Unless the business turns a profit inside 12 months, it passes to their estranged uncle. With clients walking out and a competitor putting the agency’s standing at risk, the siblings scramble to save both their income and what their mother built.
Popular on Variety
Willow, a one-time teen star now employed as a casting assistant, carries most of the strain. Annika parks her own plans to pitch in. A budding romance, along with a set of family diaries the sisters uncover, pushes the pair to rethink their inheritance and what is worth holding onto.
Produced by Joy House Productions, the film extends Hopwood’s run of stories about relationships and Chinese Australian life. Her earlier features include “It’s Our Time,” “The Gift That Gives,” “Get a Life Alright,” “Rhapsody of Love” and “The Script of Life.”
“We are delighted to be represented by Cappu Films and excited about the opportunity to bring ‘Her Last Laugh’ to international audiences through mainstream streaming platforms, following our Australian theatrical release in November,” said Hopwood.
“As an independent Australian filmmaker, I believe it is important to share culturally diverse stories that resonate across borders. Our cast and crew have poured their hearts into this film, and we hope audiences around the world will connect with its humor, heart and celebration of cultural diversity. We are proud to be bringing our 6th Asian Australian story to the global screen,” she added.
Janice Woo of Cappu Films said: “Joy brings humor and warmth to a story about two sisters finding their own way while preserving their mother’s legacy. We look forward to introducing the film to buyers in Busan and working with Joy to reach audiences internationally.”
Cappu is using the market to meet distributors and other possible partners on the title, with available rights to be confirmed on a per-territory basis.
The company’s Busan lineup also includes “Fox Hunt,” toplined by Tony Leung Chiu-wai; Shan Jiang’s Tribeca title “Ephemera”; “Operation Doolittle,” a WWII spy series running nine hourlong episodes; Erica Xia-Hou’s Slamdance selection “Banr”; martial arts film “Lion Fist”; and “Zombie Plane,” an action comedy with Vanilla Ice, Sophie Monk and Chuck Norris.

Delhi Police seeks cancellation of Sharjeel Imam's interim bail, cites ‘violation’ of conditions
In its plea, the police cited a video allegedly circulating in the media in which Imam “could be clearly seen” interacting with media persons.
The Delhi Police on Friday sought cancellation of the interim bail granted to student leader Sharjeel Imam in the 2020 Delhi riots larger conspiracy case, alleging that he violated bail conditions by interacting with media persons during his temporary release.
The plea, moved through Special Public Prosecutor Madhukar Pandey, will be heard by Additional Sessions Judge Sameer Bajpai of Karkardooma courts on Saturday.
On September 22, the court granted Imam seven days of interim bail, from October 4 to October 10, to attend his cousin’s wedding, subject to conditions barring him from using social media and interacting with the media.
In its plea, the police cited a video allegedly circulating in the media in which Imam “could be clearly seen” interacting with media persons.
“Therefore, the accused grossly violated the aforesaid condition that he shall not come in contact of any media person,” the plea said, describing his conduct as “wilful and deliberate”.
The police argued that Imam had misused the liberty granted by the court and sought cancellation of his interim bail.
Imam was arrested on January 28, 2020, and booked under the stringent Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA). The police have alleged that he was a key intellectual architect of the conspiracy behind the February 2020 communal riots in northeast Delhi, which left 53 people dead and hundreds injured.
In a related development, ASJ Bajpai on July 5 rejected fresh bail pleas filed by Imam and co-accused Umar Khalid, citing a January 5 Supreme Court order denying them bail and laying down conditions for reviving their applications.
The two had relied on a May 18 Supreme Court judgment granting bail to Syed Iftikhar Andrabi in a narco-terror case investigated by the National Investigation Agency. In that ruling, a bench of justices BV Nagarathna and Ujjal Bhuyan expressed “serious reservations” about the reasoning adopted in the January 5 order.
However, the trial court noted that the apparent divergence between the two Supreme Court rulings had been referred to a larger bench. It said the fresh bail pleas could not be considered until the issue was resolved.

In pink jackets over their uniforms, women police personnel manned barricades, negotiated with protesters and carried out detentions across central Delhi on Saturday (October 10) as demonstrators were prevented from marching towards Jantar Mantar.
Around 3,500 women personnel, including those from the Haryana and Uttar Pradesh police, were deployed, according to Delhi Police data. They were stationed along Ashoka Road, Jantar Mantar Road, Janpath, Connaught Place and Kharak Singh Marg. Buses carrying women personnel moved between locations.
The deployment was evident in the morning when women officers approached Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders aboard a flight from Mumbai before their detention. On the streets, women personnel took the lead in engaging with demonstrators, including young men, while male officers largely remained in the background. They also directed citizens and intercepted groups attempting to reach the protest site.
Near the Connaught Place entrance to Jantar Mantar, an officer said, “We have been asked to ensure that no protesters or journalists enter. We have been assigned to speak to them, ensure they do not crowd the area and prevent them from entering the premises.”
At Bangla Sahib Gurdwara, where protesters repeatedly sought shelter to evade detention, women officers negotiated with demonstrators and the gurdwara management during a standoff lasting hours. Protesters emerged with banners and slogans before being chased by the police. Women protesters were escorted away by women personnel.
An officer near gate number 4 of gurdwara said women personnel had been instructed to remain firm but calm and persuade protesters to comply with restrictions.
The deployment followed allegations of misconduct during earlier protests. A woman journalist had accused Assistant Commissioner of Police Vivek Bhagat of sexual harassment and manhandling, while videos circulating online purportedly showed male police personnel assaulting women protesters.

The Justice Department has launched an investigation of the five major networks that make up the White House TV pool, a probe focused on whether they violated antitrust laws by suspending participation in protest of Donald Trump‘s ban on CNN.
Emily Covington, a spokesperson for the Justice Department, said in a statement, “Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.” The New York Times first reported on the investigation.
After Trump announced his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds on Sept. 18, CNN also was restricted from the TV pool. As part of a long-running arrangement, CNN, CBS News, ABC News, NBC News and Fox News rotate assignments, providing technical, video and reporting coverage of the president that then is distributed to other networks.
Watch on Deadline
After the CNN freeze out, the other members of the TV pool jointly announced on Sept. 21 that they would suspend their participation.
“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” the five networks said in a statement at the time.
The suspension lasted for about four days, but it came during the White House visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping. That meant that there was a paucity of video coverage of major ceremonies and other events.
ABC confirmed that it has not received any notification of the investigation but it expects to. Other networks in the pool did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The White House has continued to restrict CNN from certain assignments, including flying on Air Force One on presidential trip.
After Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from White House grounds, those three media outlets sued on First Amendment and due process grounds. A federal judge imposed a temporary restraining order, which last until Tuesday, that has forced the White House to renew access to dozens of reporters. The judge, Timothy Kelly, is expected to rule by then on whether to grant the news outlets a preliminary injunction, something that would prevent the White House from denying access on a longer term.
The issue of access to the White House grounds is separate, yet related, to the issue of whether the administration can also freeze out members of the pool because the president does not approve of their editorial decisions. A different case, involving the Associated Press, is on appeal in the D.C. Circuit. The AP was barred from the White House pool because its style guidance did not adhere to Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

Three Saudi citizens have been killed and several other people were wounded in attacks targeting Riyadh airport for which Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility, Saudi officials have said.
The attack late on Thursday was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since the kingdom and allied forces in neighbouring Yemen launched a major military offensive last weekend against the Iran-backed Houthis.
It was also a significant escalation in the latest front in the Iran war, which has kept oil prices and markets jumpy.
The first attack on Thursday afternoon targeted airport facilities, while the second struck aircraft, the Saudi statement said. It did not identify those responsible, though the Houthis claimed to have targeted the airport with a ballistic missile.
Among the dead was Capt Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, the Saudia Group said in a statement. It appeared to be the first confirmed attack on the Saudi national carrier since the new offensive began. A separate Saudia Group statement said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers onboard.
The aviation statement said the injuries to citizens and people of other nationalities “ranged from minor to serious”. The Saudia Group statement said operational activities at the airport returned to normal at 6pm on Thursday, hours after the attack.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had destroyed three rocket launch platforms used by the rebels to threaten regional security.
The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen’s reignited civil war. Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised government to take back territory from the Houthis.
The Houthis have made a lightning advance across Yemen’s coastal plain over the last month, appearing to gain ground in the south-west on Wednesday as the group approached the city of Taiz.
Independent observers said earlier this week there was danger the group was on course to capture Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the government were pulling back to secure the major port city of Aden.
Riyadh is due to host a meeting of energy policymakers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week.

Police in New Delhi detained scores of protesters on Saturday as thousands of officers and paramilitaries patrolled India’s capital, metro stations were shut and mobile internet suspended to guard against a youth protest demanding India’s chief election officer quit.
The protest, called by the “Cockroach” youth movement, hopes to draw thousands of demonstrators who want the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to quit over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party.
Television images showed police in the city’s central business district chasing down a few dozen young protesters, before they were loaded into vehicles and taken away.
About 200 protesters were detained in the area, a police source told Reuters. Those detained outside Delhi included protest supporter Dhruv Rathee, a popular figure on YouTube, a police spokesperson said.
Touted by organisers as a protest to “save democracy”, it aims to be the biggest of the demonstrations that were launched last week after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s deputies had questioned and disagreed with him over the revision process that saw about 130 million voter names removed.
Opposition parties have long alleged the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage.
Kumar has not commented. The election commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.
The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some of the reasons for its electoral dominance and that opposition parties are misleading the country because they are unable to win elections.
Near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks.
It also comes months before a series of important state elections starting in early 2027, including in the BJP-ruled most populous state of Uttar Pradesh.
The protesters, led by the self-named Cockroach Janta party, that began as an online satire, said they would gather at Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning – a site designated for protests by authorities in the heart of New Delhi.
Delhi police said on Friday they had not given permission for the protest because the request did not come on time, adding that CJP had violated undertakings given during previous protests, and that authorities had to enforce the law and maintain peace.
Police said protesters would face the force of the law if they violated the ban.
Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest.
Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the supreme court on Friday said some trains must still run and there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” the CJP chief, Abhijeet Dipke, said on X.
“Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.”
Mobile internet services in a radius of 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area were ordered suspended from Friday night to Saturday night, ANI news agency reported citing a government order.
The CJP has said “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.
Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions.

Kimi Antonelli said Mercedes had identified the problems affecting his upgraded car after he qualified fourth for the Singapore Grand Prix on Saturday. George Russell, meanwhile, felt his performance had gone backwards following his sprint-race crash.
The championship leader, who holds an 89-point advantage over Russell, will start behind Red Bull’s Max Verstappen and Ferrari pair Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.
Antonelli said the team had made progress in understanding the upgrade package first introduced in Sepang, where he finished second. Russell returned to an older setup, the configuration that helped him win in Baku last month.

“It definitely felt in a better place today, even though the window is very small where the car operates,” Antonelli said after Saturday’s qualifying session.
“The team did a really good job because, first of all, we found the issues. Now we’re able to understand more of the package and now it’s more about trying to find the right window with the setup to make sure that the package works at its best.
“Let’s see what we can do from P4 but a podium will be very good.”
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff had described the back-to-back evaluation of the upgrades as a challenge, saying the team was effectively using “two test pilots” in Singapore to assess the changes.
“On Kimi’s side the updates seem to have worked now,” Wolff said.
“He and his engineers have dialled out the problems and we got closer and closer. We’re missing a tenth and a half or two-tenths, and that is, at least for qualifying, positive.
“It will take some more proof of concept until I’m feeling warm and fuzzy. But we will have more data tomorrow, in the race, whether we can have less degradation.”
Wolff said Russell’s sprint crash was an unusual error, recalling the Briton’s last-lap accident in Singapore in 2023, which ended his chance of winning.
Russell was sixth quickest in Q3 but is due to start Sunday’s race from the back because of an engine penalty. He said he used qualifying partly to check the car after retiring from the sprint.

Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
- Published
What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?
That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.
The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.
The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.
The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.
Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.
With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.
"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.
The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".
Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.
"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.
Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".
Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.
"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.
"But I did wrong."
It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).
Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.
"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.
"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.
"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."
The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.
In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".
"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".
In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.
That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.
Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.
"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.
"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."
The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.
When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.
But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.
"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."
As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.
"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.
"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.
"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."
The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.
In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.
At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.
Kim says that began to change as they filmed.
"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."
Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.
She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.
On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.
"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.
"And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."
Kim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule.
"But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.
The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted.
"It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim.
"I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."
In the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised.
"Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says.
"She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power.
"That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'.
"So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."

CJP renews protest call as Abhijeet Dipke, Dhruv Rathee remain detained; Delhi Police cite ‘broken promises’ amid crackdown
Delhi Police reportedly released all the detainees from the detention centers except CJP leaders. This comes amid a widespread crackdown in national capital.
Delhi on Saturday witnessed a major crackdown on a planned protest and the detention of thousands, including four former chief ministers, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijit Dipke, and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee. The action came amid CJP's call for protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, who faces allegations of carrying out irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
While the police released all the protesters after day-long detention, CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das, and Youtuber Dhruv Rathee remained in custody. The Cockroach Janta Party has given a fresh call for protest, urging people to begin march to Jantar Mantar at 10 am on Sunday.
Why Delhi Police stalled protests
The Delhi Police shared a video on X, explaining the reason for denying permission to hold the protest at Jantar Mantar. In the caption, the police wrote, "Broken promises, shattered trust."
Deep Dive
In the video, Delhi Police highlighted that the CJP failed to abide by its signed undertaking while protesting in June-July to demand the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged examination irregularities.

Key developments from protests against CEC
From the closure of 45 metro stations in the national capital to the detention of actor Imran Khan in Mumbai, Saturday saw escalating developments as protests erupted in various parts of the country.
4 ex-CMs detained: Several opposition leaders, including former chief ministers Arvind Kejriwal (AAP), Mamata Banerjee (TMC), Pinarayi Vijayan (CPI-M) and Manik Sarkar (CPI-M), were detained from multiple locations across Delhi as they attempted to join the protest.

CJP's Ajinkya Shinde calls fresh protest: Following the detentions, CJP's Ajinkya Shinde has renewed the call for demonstrations on Sunday, October 11.

Tushar Gandhi, actor Imran Khan detained: Police detained actor Imran Khan, activist Tushar Gandhi and CPI (M) workers from various locations in Mumbai for protesting without permission, news agency PTI reported.
Sonam Wangchuk's warning: Activist Sonam Wangchuk, in a post shared on his X handle, wrote, "Yesterday when I posted a message appealing for unity & peace in today's protest I had never imagined that the biggest democracy in the world would be under an undeclared EMERGENCY."
"I was happy there were so many leaders to lead the movement, but I now learn that they have all been arrested. I hope those arrested will be released soon. I will be compelled to consider an Anshan Fast or Padyatra March if they are not released by tomorrow," he warned.
BJP vs Opposition amid crackdown

Addressing a press conference, Patra criticised the remarks made by Gandhi outside Rashtrapati Bhavan on Friday.
"Yesterday a few politicians visited the Rashtrapati Bhavan. The statement of Rahul Gandhi after coming out of the Rashtrapati Bhavan was like that of a 'nalayak neta'... A dead pensioner, a snap election and protesters camping in tents: Inside Spain’s housing crisis
Some 20,000 people turned out across Spain following the death of a woman evicted from her flat after an investment firm tried to increase her rent 230%. Critics say the time has come for serious reform, writes Maira Butt

When 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal received an eviction notice from the apartment she’d lived in for more than 70 years, she could not have imagined that the letter would send thousands onto the streets.
The pensioner died on Wednesday, days after being forcibly carried away on a stretcher, having refused to leave her home after an investment firm snapped up the property with a view to increasing her rent by 230 per cent. In the days before her death, she had been admitted to hospital for severe anxiety and exhaustion.
The case has mobilised tens of thousands of people across the country, calling on the state to take action against greedy investors hiking rents to unaffordable highs. Many young people turned out on Thursday to mourn Maricarmen and decry the speculators standing between them and the hope of home ownership.
Protests have even prompted the beleaguered socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election for 29 November after parliament rejected his government’s proposals to address a mounting housing crisis. The crisis has seen parties on the left attack the right for shooting down legislation aimed at curbing soaring rental prices; the right says the left has had eight years in government to act.
News of Maricarmen’s death this week enraged protesters camped on squares in Spain’s main cities, who chanted that she had been “murdered” because of the greed of her landlords.
After an investment fund, Urbagestion, purchased the building where she had lived for more than 70 years, Ms Abascal lost a lengthy legal battle against rent increases far beyond her pension income, leading to her eviction on 23 September.
At first, her rent had been increased from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020), which was later reduced to €1,650 (£1,414; $1870). However, she was still unable to pay this, with her monthly pension of €1,350 (£1,157; $1,530). Three previous attempts to evict her had been blocked by Spanish courts.
“I’ve lived here for 71 years and I don’t want to leave,” Ms Abascal told reporters on the eve of the eviction.
While in hospital, she reached a deal to regain her home, but she died before she could return.
Outside her building on Thursday, mourners left flowers, candles, handwritten notes and children’s drawings. Protesters marched with placards, calling for action and demanding “not one more Maricarmen”.
“Maricarmen was the straw that broke the camel’s back... (she was) a symbol of resistance and unity,” said Alex Marinero, a 21-year-old protester.
The case has been called a “turning point in the history of this country” by the Madrid Tenants Union in a statement announcing her death on Wednesday.
In her final days, Maricarmen is said to have sent messages of support to protesters across the country, who have been spurred on by her story to take part in demonstrations on Spain’s housing crisis.
In the capital, lawmakers accused each other of cynically exploiting her case after her death.
The conservative People’s Party (PP), which has absolute majorities in the Madrid regional and local assemblies, refused to hold a minute of silence honouring Maricarmen, prompting hard-left deputies to stage one outside City Hall.
Madrid leader Isabel Diaz Ayuso, of the PP, blamed Prime Minister Sanchez, pointing out that the eviction had occurred under his government.
Opposition leader Manuela Bergerot of the leftist Mas Madrid party said Maricarmen had died because of “miserable people who put gain above a person’s life ... those responsible will carry that with them for their remaining days”.
She added that the last thing Ms Ayuso had done while Maricarmen was alive was “laugh at her” –a reference to when she quipped on 28 September: “At what age do I get to stop paying my landlords? Let me know.”
On Thursday, a survey by state pollster CIS conducted back in June, found that 76.3 per cent of Spaniards supported intervention in the market to guarantee access to housing, while 79 per cent believe the right to housing should take precedence over treating homes as a market commodity.
Anger has been mounting amid rising costs, with one student, 19-year-old Jorge Moreno, telling the BBC that “vulture funds and investment funds” have been “making a business of housing for a long time”.
“But it’s an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home,” he said.
Mr Sanchez attempted to make changes in response to the protests by proposing a limit to rent increases, protecting vulnerable tenants from evictions and several other policies aimed at curbing price increases. But this week they were struck down by Spain’s parliament.

Russell Crowe’s latest Netflix thriller, Unabomber, has emerged as one of the streaming platform’s biggest hits of 2026, attracting approximately 40 million views within its first two weeks of release. The film, which explores the life of notorious American domestic terrorist Ted Kaczynski, has found a sizeable audience despite receiving largely unfavourable reviews from critics. According to a report by Collider published on 10 October, the crime drama has continued to draw viewers since its release on 25 September. Its performance highlights the continuing appetite for true-crime stories, particularly those that revisit notorious criminal cases and examine the circumstances surrounding them The film is directed by Janus Metz Pedersen and features Crowe alongside Jacob Tremblay, Shailene Woodley and Annabelle Wallis. Unabomber reportedly attracted around 16 million views in its first week before reaching approximately 40 million views across its first two weeks, according to Collider. The figures place it among Netflix’s notable original releases this year. Its popularity has come even as the film struggles to win over critics. Collider reported that Unabomber held a 25% score on Rotten Tomatoes, with reviewers questioning its central argument despite acknowledging the performances. The contrast between its critical reception and streaming numbers is notable. While unfavourable reviews can affect a film’s reputation, they do not always prevent audiences from watching a story built around a widely recognised real-life criminal case. Released on Netflix on 25 September 2026, Unabomber dramatises the life of Kaczynski, a Harvard-educated mathematician who carried out a mail-bombing campaign across the United States over nearly two decades. The attacks killed three people and injured 23 others, prompting an extensive FBI investigation that ultimately led to his capture. The film follows two interconnected timelines, exploring Kaczynski’s formative years and the investigation that eventually brought his bombing campaign to an end. It examines how his experiences as a young academic intersected with the events that preceded his crimes, without removing the consequences of his actions from the story. Tremblay plays Kaczynski, while Crowe portrays Harvard psychologist Henry Murray, whose controversial experiments involving the young student form an important part of the film’s narrative. Woodley appears as FBI agent Joanne Miller, who is involved in the investigation, while Wallis plays Christiana Morgan, Murray’s academic collaborator and love interest. Written by Sam Chalsen and Nelson Greaves, the film draws inspiration from real events. Its approach combines psychological drama with the investigative elements of a crime thriller. The performance of Unabomber adds to Netflix’s run of successful mid-budget genre films. Collider noted that other releases, including The Rip, Thrash and Apex, have also crossed the 100-million-view mark.
