Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked out two of five data centers belonging to the Russian tech giant Yandex. The damage has left Yandex, known as “Russia’s Google” because it operates the country’s most popular search engine, struggling to maintain its AI chatbot and other online services.
The Ukrainian drones struck Yandex data centers in the Sasovo and Kaluga regions of Russia on October 8 and October 9, according to Reuters. Those actions came as a direct response to a Russian drone strike campaign targeting Ukraine’s data centers, which has disrupted mobile phone and Internet services for thousands of Ukrainians since late September.
“We continue to respond to Russia’s attacks on Ukraine, and we’re doing so with high precision,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a post on X. “Another data center was hit as well—our symmetrical response.”
The Ukrainian company Firepoint said its FP-1 one-way attack drones were involved in the latest strike on the Kaluga data center that is Yandex’s largest such facility, Reuters reported. The first Ukrainian attack targeted Yandex’s Sasovo data center that houses two of the company’s three supercomputers used for training the company’s YandexGPT AI model.
Yandex said no employees were hurt but acknowledged disruptions to some services. Russian users reported problems accessing media websites and popular apps for the Ivi video streaming platform, the digital banking service T-Bank and the state-owned Russian Railways, according to the independent Russian news publication Meduza.

Paytm began as a digital wallet, became a payments behemoth on the back of that and then built up the momentum with UPI. But two years ago it had to slow it all down and become a lending company. turn to profitability and the revival of topline after the Paytm Payments Bank bruising was down to this transition from payments to loans and distribution of credit products. But now, the company finds itself at another crossroads as the MDR rules for UPI could once again turn Paytm towards payments as a growth engine. How will that change the fintech platform’s revenue structure and how does the major focus on artificial intelligence (AI) play a role in this? Five years ago, Paytm was almost entirely a payments company. Payment services brought in ₹1,981 Cr of its ₹2,802 Cr operating revenue in FY21, about 71%. Financial services distribution contributed just ₹128 Cr, under 5%. That mix has since been turned on its head. According to the company’s FY26 annual report, financial services distribution, mostly loan distribution, grew at an 83% CAGR to ₹2,594 Cr, more than 20X its FY21 base. It now makes up 31% of the ₹8,437 Cr topline. Payment services is still the largest piece at 58%, but grew at a much slower 19% CAGR over the same period. More importantly, in FY26, the company reported a net profit of ₹552 Cr against a ₹663 Cr loss in FY25. In Q1 FY27, operating revenue rose 28% to ₹2,448 Cr YoY, so the company is on pace to stretch its profitability in FY27 too. Along the way, Paytm throttled its super app ambitions to a certain extent. It has exited businesses such as entertainment ticketing, scaled back its ecommerce ambitions and sharpened its focus on payments and financial services. But look closely, and Paytm’s super app playbook is still very much alive, but it is a focussed effort around its active payments users and merchants, not for just about every consumer out there. The fintech giant is increasingly looking to make more money from the financial relationships it already owns. Merchants Drive Paytm’s Payments Business One may see shades of PhonePe’s revenue model in Paytm’s payments business. The stakeholders are the same and the rules of the business are also the same. But Paytm had a different GTM strategy compared to PhonePe. The latter went for a user acquisition blitz on the UPI consumer side, which is reflected in its lead among consumers, while Paytm looked for deeper penetration on the merchants side. Paytm’s biggest contribution in that regard is the Soundbox, which was then emulated by every other player in the market. That itself makes it clear how Paytm approaches the payments business. It’s a merchants-first approach that set the company apart from other players, save for the likes of BharatPe, which also adopted a similar approach. But as with any other UPI app — in the zero MDR regime — a customer scanning a merchant’s UPI QR code does not generate any meaningful fee for Paytm. The zero-MDR framework has historically prevented direct merchant charges on UPI and Rupay. Paytm banked on its merchants base to monetise even as UPI monetisation remained a problem. This included merchant loans, insurance, point-of-sales device subscriptions and more. A similar playbook was adopted on the consumer side. UPI became the top of the funnel and other services down the funnel monetised this base. Even today, the MDR problem has not been solved as the government’s plans to implement a 0.4% MDR fee on certain high value transactions has now been deferred, as per reports. But merchant GMV rose 31% year on year to ₹7.1 Lakh Cr in Q1 FY27. Subscription merchant deployments reached 1.57 Cr storefronts, while payment processing margins remained above four basis points. Payment Services revenue grew 33% to ₹1,384 Cr in the quarter. The merchants-centric stack generated ₹4,891 Cr in FY26, 58% of Paytm’s operating revenue. The business grew by 21% from ₹4,039 Cr in FY25, when regulatory disruption disrupted parts of Paytm's payments ecosystem. While this is still 27.4% below Paytm’s peak ₹6,236 Cr payments revenue in FY24, this middle ground proves that Paytm has recovered to a large extent after the RBI crackdown in January 2024. Similarly, consumer activity also matters, even when individual UPI transactions are hard to monetise directly. In Q1 FY27, Paytm reported consumer UPI transaction value growth of 45% to ₹5.9 Lakh Cr, compared with industry growth of roughly 20%, and monthly transacting users of 8 Cr. Paytm's management describes the recovery as broader than a single payment product. It spans offline small merchants, large merchants, online checkout and consumer payments. That breadth matters because the company can use the same acquiring infrastructure to sell devices and, eventually, distribute financial products. “GMV growth is accelerating not just because MTUs (monthly transacting users) grew, but because usage per customer did. We focus on customer quality, product quality, and engagement, not just volume,” CEO and founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma said in the Q4 FY26 earnings call. However, in Paytm’s filings, one key disclosure is missing. The company does not separately report how much Payment Services revenue comes from Soundbox and POS subscriptions versus transaction processing. Without that split, investors cannot isolate how much of the recovery is recurring subscription income, or whether the incremental revenue is being generated more efficiently. This will also enable investors to track the expenses trajectory. Paytm incurred ₹2,573 Cr in payment processing charges in FY26, compared with ₹2,125 Cr a year earlier. Plus sales workforce reached 40,512 in Q4 FY26, up from 36,724. This is a particularly important figure because the company hinted in early 2024 that it would have to shrink its workforce to recover from the revenue drop as described above. Plus, quarterly sales employee costs increased 30% year-on-year to ₹317 Cr. So is the payments business still not seeing operating leverage? The next three to four quarters will be critical to understand this. Why Financial Services Could Change The Equation? That’s the payments side of things. On the other side sits the distribution of financial services. This is another way of saying Paytm is a channel for insurance providers, lenders such as banks and NBFCs as well as digital gold investments. But in the post-payments bank world, this is the fastest-growing part of Paytm’s business. Revenue climbed 52% in FY26 to approximately ₹2,594 Cr. and in Q1 FY27, financial services grew another 45% to ₹814 Cr. According to the company’s FY26 annual report, financial services distribution, mostly loan distribution, grew at an 83% CAGR to ₹2,594 Cr, more than 20X its FY21 base. It now makes up 31% of the ₹8,437 Cr topline. Payment services is still the largest piece at 58%, but grew at a much slower 19% CAGR over the same period. On the lending side, instead of disbursing loans from its own books, Paytm helps banks and NBFCs reach customers, distribute credit and support servicing. The partner lenders provide capital and bear the principal lending exposure, while Paytm earns distribution-related fees and commissions under its partner arrangements. The economics depend not only on disbursement volumes but also on repeat borrowing, credit performance and the terms offered by partners. In Q1 FY27, Paytm said more than half of merchant loan disbursements went to repeat borrowers, so it is increasingly capitalising on its existing base. But the lending business only covers about 7% of its subscription merchant base in Q4 FY26, compared with roughly 6% a year earlier. This needs to grow significantly for Paytm’s thesis to hold. After Q1, Sharma suggested that capital capacity with lending partners is not a constraint, but getting the right kind of demand for profitable credit growth is important. Interest rate movements, because of RBI riskweight changes or repo rates add another layer of dependence, but Paytm is hoping that by being a distributor only, it is able to distance itself from the higher costs here. After all, the company is just a channel now, and as such it shouldn’t bear a significant amount of the higher cost of capital under a higher repo rate as announced by RBI recently. But high costs can make NBFCs more selective about new loans. This is also why Paytm needs to focus on monetising its more active merchants which are not covered under its lending distribution business. Incidentally, while distribution of financial services goes beyond lending, the focus is always on loan distribution rather than insurance or digital gold investments, both of which follow the same model of distribution commission. Can AI Make A Difference? The competitive reality for Paytm is exactly the same as it is for PhonePe or CRED or any other UPI app that looks to scale into other areas. While the nature of revenue differs, the operating segments are all overlapping. And Paytm has to compete on multiple fronts like any other payments plus lending app. In consumer UPI, Paytm is well behind PhonePe and Google Pay. In August 2026, Paytm had a volume share of 8.03% compared to 45.64% for PhonePe and 32.26% for Google Pay PhonePe, Google Pay, BharatPe, CRED, Pine Labs, Razorpay are all competing with Paytm when it comes to merchants services, and investments is the core focus for Groww, Zerodha and Angel One, where Paytm Money is not a major player any more. These are different competitive battles, but they converge on the question of how much of a merchant’s or consumer’s financial activity can Paytm capture profitably? That’s where Sharma’s biggest new bet comes in. Software and AI-led services is the new focus. Paytm envisions the Soundbox evolving from a payment confirmation device to a small business engagement and management platform, which brings commerce tools, customer notifications and support in Indian languages. At its September 2026 AGM, it discussed the idea of Paytm Intelligence, or PI, as a potential offering. The company disclosed then that AI is already deployed in product, engineering and merchant sales, as well as loan collections and consumer acquisition and retention. On the software side, the company is looking to make software that can help enterprises create an “agentic workforce” for running workflows and business processes. Importantly, Sharma added that by FY28, Paytm shareholders will see AI revenue reflected in disclosures under the commerce and cloud verticals. Whether this helps reduce Paytm’s dependency on cross-selling to its consumers and merchants is not clear. How the AI business might connect to this vast user base is also not clear. And with the UPI MDR debate far from settled, Paytm is likely to find itself waiting at the current crossroads for some time. In fact, one could argue that given Paytm’s profitability right now, it can afford to wait for the transition to MDR. This allows Paytm to build up more profitability in the next 12-15 months by continuing its current approach, and by then, if Vijay Shekhar Sharma’s words hold true, it may well be a fintech and an AI company.

Rajinikanth has revealed what he believes is missing from Jailer 2, and his answer involves Tamannaah Bhatia. At a recent event for the upcoming film, the superstar said he had personally asked director Nelson Dilipkumar to include a song sequence featuring the actress, who appeared in the first instalment of the franchise.
Rajinikanth says Tamannaah is the missing element in Jailer 2; reveals he asked Nelson Dilipkumar for a song
“The only missing element in Jailer 2 is Tamannaah,” Rajinikanth said, explaining his suggestion to Nelson. When the director reportedly responded, “I can't keep it just because you like it, sir,” the actor clarified that his request was rooted in his understanding of audience preferences rather than a personal choice. “I didn't say I like it. If I had done whatever I liked, I would have become irrelevant and gone to Bengaluru. I'm still in the field because I'm doing what audiences are loving,” Rajinikanth said.
The exchange offered a glimpse into how the veteran actor approaches commercial cinema and the decisions that go into making a film connect with viewers. Rather than presenting the proposed song as a matter of personal preference, Rajinikanth linked his suggestion to what he believes audiences enjoy watching. His remarks also put the spotlight on Tamannaah’s association with the Jailer franchise, with the possibility of her featuring in a song in the sequel now becoming a talking point.
Tamannaah appeared in the 2023 film Jailer, directed by Nelson Dilipkumar and headlined by Rajinikanth. Her presence in the original film made her a familiar part of the franchise, and Rajinikanth’s latest comments have brought renewed attention to her possible involvement in the sequel. However, his statement about wanting a song sequence does not, by itself, confirm that one will feature in the final film.
Jailer 2 is written and directed by Nelson Dilipkumar, with Rajinikanth returning as retired jailer Tiger Muthuvel Pandian. Produced by Kalanithi Maran under the Sun Pictures banner, the Tamil action comedy also features S. J. Suryah, Vidya Balan, Mithun Chakraborty and Suraj Venjaramoodu, alongside returning cast members Ramya Krishnan and Yogi Babu. Mohanlal and Shiva Rajkumar are also set to make extended cameo appearances. The music is composed by Anirudh Ravichander.
The sequel will expand the world introduced in the first film, following Muthuvel Pandian as he goes undercover to investigate a cross-border criminal syndicate while facing new threats to his family and allies. Jailer 2 is scheduled for a worldwide theatrical release on October 15, 2026.
For now, Rajinikanth’s remarks have placed the question of a Tamannaah song in the spotlight, even as audiences await further details about the film. Whether the suggestion makes it to the final cut remains to be seen, but the superstar has made his preference clear: he believes Tamannaah is an element the sequel could use.

Imran Khan’s supporters have begun a march to Islamabad to demand his release from jail after efforts by the government to halt the protest failed.
The march began in the former prime minister’s stronghold province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in north-west Pakistan on Sunday, according to leaders of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
Concerns have grown over the health of the 74-year-old former Pakistan cricket captain who has been in prison since 2023. Party colleagues and family claim he is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied visits by his doctor or relatives despite having a serious eye condition and high blood pressure.
The government had gone to extreme lengths to try to stop PTI holding the long march, including shutting down Islamabad and barricading the capital’s entrances with shipping containers and sandbags. Khan’s three sisters were among those detained last week on grounds of national security.
Two rounds of negotiations between the government and PTI leaders took place over the weekend but broke down when Khan’s allies insisted that he be part of political talks.
Attaullah Tarar, the information minister, accused the PTI of “double standards and hypocrisy”.
Thousands of supporters had joined the protest by Monday afternoon and the crowds are expected to grow on the way to Peshawar, the main city in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which the marchers should reach by Wednesday.
The march is being led by the province’s chief minister, Sohail Afridi, who described those taking part as “Imran Khan’s soldiers”.
“I call upon you all to come out, the youngsters to come out for the sake of your leader who is sitting in jail,” he said.
Khan was prime minister from 2018 to 2022, when he was toppled by a parliamentary vote of no confidence. Since then, he and the PTI have faced mounting government pressure, which culminated in his arrest in 2023. The harassment and detention of other PTI leaders continues.
Khan is widely considered the country’s most popular politician, while the ruling coalition government, which is backed by the military, is facing discontent over an economic crisis and a surge in terrorism.
Ministers say the march is illegal and all measures will be taken to ensure it does not break through the capital’s boundaries.
Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed to Islamabad and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa last week, raising fears that Khan’s supporters will be met with state violence. Government politicians falsely claimed that the PTI was allowing militants from the Pakistan Taliban to take part in the march.
Opposition leaders fear the prime minister will impose emergency rule on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to stop the march.

A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Panama on Friday (October 9), collapsing buildings and roads, damaging historic structures and injuring at least 27 people. Authorities reported no deaths, although President José Raúl Mulino cautioned that the toll could change as rescue and damage assessments continued.
The shallow earthquake triggered panic across the Central American country, with residents evacuating buildings in the capital, Panama City. Authorities also issued a tsunami warning for parts of the eastern Pacific before lifting it later in the day.
The earthquake was followed by dozens of aftershocks, including one measuring above magnitude 6.0, according to local geosciences authorities.
Here's what we know so far about the earthquake, the tsunami warning, the aftershocks and the damage.
No. The tsunami warning issued after the earthquake was later lifted, according to reports.
The warning had covered the Pacific coasts of Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua and Guatemala. Alerts issued by El Salvador and Chile for Easter Island were also lifted.
Néstor Luque, director of the Geosciences Institute at the University of Panama, said waves measuring between 3 and 10 feet (1 to 3 metres) were expected around Isla Cañas and the southern coast of Los Santos province. He said major waves were not expected beyond those areas.
Seawater had already reached some homes near the coast on Isla Cañas, according to Luque.
Yes. More than 80 aftershocks were recorded by Panama's local geosciences institute, including one measuring above magnitude 6.0.
Several aftershocks measured magnitudes of 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2, according to reports.
The tremors prompted some residents to evacuate buildings more than once.
The US Geological Survey (USGS) said the earthquake struck at 12:56 pm local time on Friday (1756 GMT), with its epicentre around 10 kilometres (six miles) from Pitaloza Arriba, a small community in central Herrera province.
The tremor occurred at a shallow depth of approximately 10 kilometres, increasing the potential for strong shaking near the epicentre.
The USGS initially estimated the earthquake's magnitude at 8.0 before revising it to 7.6 and subsequently to 7.7.
The shaking was felt across Panama, including in the capital, which is about 200 kilometres (120 miles) from the epicentre. Residents reported objects falling inside homes and buildings, while people rushed outdoors as a precaution.
Damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Herrera, Coclé, Los Santos and Veraguas, according to officials. At least 27 people suffered minor injuries, the National Civil Protection System said.
President Mulino described the situation as a major disaster and said some roads had completely collapsed.
Among the reported damage:
- Collapsed buildings and roads: Sections of roads developed large fissures, while some structures were partially or completely damaged in affected provinces.
- Historic church damaged: The Church of San Atanasio, a colonial-style Catholic church in Los Santos province, was reported to have collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.
- Damage in Penonomé: The cathedral in the town suffered a partial collapse and cracks. Damage was also reported at the governor's office and the Dos Continentes hotel.
- Town cut off: Health Minister Fernando Boyd said Tonosí, in Los Santos province, had been cut off because of road damage. Authorities were exploring whether access could be restored by air.
- Damage to homes: Former president Ricardo Martinelli shared photographs showing his house in the town of Soná, in Veraguas province, had collapsed.

Sally Schultz thought she had struck gold when she purchased land in Rio Rancho Estates, an unincorporated, census-designated community just outside the city of Rio Rancho, New Mexico. A single mother of four, Schultz came there following a divorce to build a homestead of her own and finally gain some stability in her life.
For $3,500, she was able to purchase half an acre for her trailer in a rural area located close to numerous elementary schools and parks. In a relatively short time, she was able to coax crops like corn, squash, and green chile from the ground. This cheap land became Schultz’s haven, giving her a second chance at life.
Then a missile company showed up next door.
“We’ve already been through so much,” she says, “and now we have to leave. It is the unknowing that is scariest.”
Castelion, a startup founded in November 2022 by three former SpaceX executives, is building Project Ranger, which it claims will be America’s “largest dedicated hypersonic manufacturing production facility.” Construction is set to be complete by the end of the year.
The company’s chosen site for its mega-campus is, in some cases, it appears, a little more than 1,000 yards away from roughly 450 properties in Rio Rancho Estates, including Schultz’s. That puts the homes squarely within a danger zone should any explosive chemicals stored onsite catch fire.
A year into Castelion’s relationship with the state of New Mexico, the company—which declined to speak with WIRED for this story—still hasn’t answered basic safety questions, even as an official hazard assessment found buildings would simply be left to burn in the case of fire, releasing hydrochloric acid gas into the air. Emails between the company and Rio Rancho officials reviewed by WIRED also show Castelion was negotiating fire safety standards even after construction was well underway.
“I live next door to where World War III will be manufactured,” says local resident Laura Lundberg.
Big Plans
Castelion has become a bit of a darling among the new wave of defense tech startups. The company has recently hit a valuation of $13 billion—more than four times its Series B valuation of $2.8 billion from last year.
It has received over $500 million in US military contracts in just 18 months, swiftly securing its spot as one of the “Arsenal of Freedom” suppliers.
The firm touts its ability to make hypersonic missiles—a label for any missile flying at five times the speed of sound or higher—at a lower cost than its competitors. The US Army’s Dark Eagle is the most mature domestic hypersonic weapon, and it costs an estimated $41 million per missile, according to a 2023 Congressional Budget Office study. Castelion’s main product, Blackbeard, is a solid-rocket-powered missile that was set to sell for $384,000 per unit.
In reality, the missiles are looking as if they will turn out pricier than initially advertised.
Castelion kicked off the year with a nearly $50 million Navy contract to build full-scale prototypes of its Blackbeard missile. By June, the Navy expanded the effort, adding another $23.4 million to supply the first 50 operational Blackbeard prototypes. Then, in August, the Navy doubled down with another $90 million contract to cover manufacturing services for the same 50 Blackbeards—pushing the total to $163.4 million for 50 missiles, or $3.3 million per unit.
And most recently, in September, the Navy awarded Castelion the company’s largest contract yet—up to $200 million.
Recently, Castelion released the first photo of its Blackbeard hypersonic strike missile, but concrete performance figures for Blackbeard remain hidden. Castelion has not publicly released any test data to verify its weapon’s efficacy.
Project Ranger will become Castelion’s biggest manufacturing and testing hub. The company broke ground on the 1,000-acre facility on January 21, and it’s targeting mass production as early as next year.
The facility wasn’t always supposed to be in New Mexico, though.
Unredacted
In August 2023, the company applied to build a rocket factory in Churchill County, Nevada, under a different name—Pallas Industrials. Chief financial officer Andrew Kreitz signed a special use application, which disclosed the company’s plans to build rocket motors and ground-test them up to eight days a month at the site.
In response to the application, Churchill County officials provided eight pages of staff analysis and required the company to provide testing conditions and safety protocols. Not long afterward, Pallas Industrials pulled out of Nevada under the new name: Castelion. A few months later, the company began testing the soil in western Rio Rancho.
Rio Rancho Estates residents say that by the time they started noticing soil-probing trucks in the spring of 2025, Castelion was already in a conversation with New Mexico officials about using the land for the missile factory.
In June 2025, Sandia National Labs delivered a hazard report as part of the New Mexico Small Business Assistance Program, originally intended to help local small businesses access the expertise of Los Alamos and Sandia National Laboratories at absolutely no cost.
Under the Freedom of Information Act, Sandia later released a heavily redacted version of the report. Instead of scrubbing the underlying data layer of the file, the lab simply put black ink highlight over black text, leaving the full unredacted report accessible via copying and pasting.
The report alleges Castelion’s plans to build and operate the missile factory present significant risks.
It identifies a massive “storage facility fire” as the worst-case scenario. Castelion is set to store colossal stockpiles of propellants on Project Ranger’s site. The company has publicly stated its plans of working with at least one heat-sensitive chemical oxidizer—ammonium perchlorate—and storing up to 250,000 pounds inside covered magazines and bunkers, according to the Sandia report. But outside those bunkers, the report notes, Castelion is allowed to keep up to 81,000 pounds of active explosive material at a time inside the hazardous integration facilities during the assembly process.
A detonation of the facility’s largest allowed stockpile of explosive material would require a buffer from the nearest inhabited building of almost nine football fields in length. Sandia calculated that a worst-case explosion could shatter large windows as far as almost four miles away and have a 3.2 percent chance of causing minor eardrum damage to people 400 yards from the detonation.
Sandia declined to provide comment for WIRED. One of the hazard reports authors, Meg Davidson, has since left Sandia Labs and is now a senior manager of strategic partnerships at Castelion. She did not respond to requests for comment.
The report identifies a fire at the test stand as “the most probable foreseeable hazardous event.” A chemical fire would release a toxic haze containing byproducts like hydrogen chloride and chlorine. In gas form, both are highly corrosive and can cause severe eye, skin, and respiratory tract burns. Even short-term inhalation at high concentrations can cause chemical lung damage and asphyxiation.
Emails obtained through public records requests reveal that the Rio Rancho Fire Department determined 17 of the 26 buildings at the Project Ranger site would be left to burn if a fire ignited, due to the risks a chemical blaze would pose first responders. Firefighters would be barred from even entering the high-risk facilities.
Such events are hardly unheard of. WIRED reported on a June incident at Anduril’s Mississippi facility where a test run of an ammonium perchlorate–based rocket motor ended in an explosion. The blast—which didn’t cause any casualties—underscored the technical risks of scaling solid propellant production.
In May, a storage tank holding approximately 7,000 gallons of methyl methacrylate, a flammable liquid used to manufacture acrylic plastics and resins for military and commercial aircraft, began to overheat at a GKN Aerospace plant in Garden Grove, California, leading local authorities to evacuate more than 40,000 residents.
Despite these warnings, internal emails obtained through public records requests reveal that Castelion was still negotiating critical fire-response requirements between March and May—even as construction had already started.
Castelion’s site developer, Bryce Barlow, wrote to the city on March 23 that the company had not yet finalized the fire-flow response, offering to discuss the question by phone or in person instead.
After a few weeks, the requirements were replaced by city manager Matt Geisel with a statement that hard numbers would appear in the plans later on. Castelion only needed a signed memorandum of understanding to proceed—backed by the governing body’s resolution and a serviceability letter.
“Great news! Saves all of us both legal bills and headaches,” Kreitz wrote in response.
‘A Done Deal’
In August 2025, prior to Castelion’s formal announcement that it had selected New Mexico, Republican state senator Jay Block appeared before the Sandoval County Commission to speak in support of financing Project Ranger. Before becoming state senator, Block was a county commissioner.
The county had approved $125 million in industrial revenue bonds and had passed a resolution giving itself control over the state land picked for the site. The commissioners granted an astounding 95 percent discount on what Castelion would normally owe in property taxes. Finally, the county agreed to abate compensating taxes on out-of-state equipment, lowering the upfront costs for the incoming missile manufacturer to relocate to New Mexico.
Block’s district includes Rio Rancho as of January.
“I strongly supported Project Ranger as it moved through the local approval process, because I believed Rio Rancho and Sandoval County had the workforce, infrastructure, and defense heritage to help Castelion succeed,” Block tells WIRED.
Castelion held its first public information meeting on Project Ranger in October 2025.
“All of this happened behind the scenes. By the time it was public, it was already a done deal,” says Zachary Darden, a Rio Rancho resident who ran an unsuccessful bid for mayor on a platform opposing the development.
In November, emails show Alberto Solís, Rio Rancho’s economic development manager, coordinated Castelion CFO Kreitz’s four-day trip to New Mexico—part of the outreach process required by the state. The CFO asked to attend a Chamber of Commerce “Jingle Mingle” mixer and an event with the Sandoval Economic Alliance, a local nonprofit tasked with recruiting new business to the county.
More than a month after Kreitz’s networking trip, Castelion held its groundbreaking ceremony. Local residents weren’t invited, but many of the state’s most prominent political and business figures were. Block was there as well as US senator Martin Heinrich. So were Gregg Hull, Rio Rancho’s then mayor and Republican candidate for governor, as well as Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. County and state economic development officials were also in attendance.
“Castelion's Project Ranger shows what a strong public-private partnership can deliver for a local community,” Rob Black, New Mexico’s secretary of economic development, tells WIRED.
Residents living next to the site, though, are contemplating whether the risks are too high to stay. But for most living in Rio Rancho Estates—a low-income neighborhood—the costs of relocation might be too high.
“This land is affordable for people who need it,” says community member Jason Clifford. “We were sold out by our local officials.”

The gifts and payments that doctors receive from drugmakers increased inappropriate prescribing and the number of prescriptions written, likely leading to rising health care costs, according to a Cochrane review of dozens of previous studies that have explored the influence the pharmaceutical industry has on medical practice.
In addition, pharmaceutical advertising or education aimed at doctors may also increase inappropriate prescribing, probably increases the number of prescriptions written, and may increase the costs of prescriptions. But conflict-of-interest policies that restrict or manage interactions between companies and doctors probably improved prescribing practices, the analysis found.
However, there was not enough evidence to draw clear conclusions on whether free drug samples and other promotions affect decisions to place specific drugs on hospital formularies. These are the list of medicines approved for use and routinely stocked in a hospital or health system.

If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.
Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International.
In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed.
In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows.
Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities.
Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror.
Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority.
Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones.
In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook.
The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades.
In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City.
Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December. Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did.
Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years.
In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran, its highest number of executions in decades.
Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”.
“This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.

This Android Auto problem is affecting calls on foldable phones
It seems like Gemini is to blame.
Owners of foldable phones are reportedly running into issues when trying to place outgoing calls using Android Auto. Posts on Reddit, as well as Google and Motorola forums, describe various foldable phones losing their ability to make calls when they're closed, as first reported by Android Authority. And Gemini might play a role in the calling quandary.
Users say that when their phones are closed and they instruct them to call someone, the call doesn't connect. One poster on Reddit said they get a message to "flip open to continue." Incoming calls seem to come through just fine. Several of the posters report the issue only started after they began using Gemini.
While there's no confirmation yet on what may be causing the bug, both Google and Motorola appear to be investigating. Responses in forums show company representatives collecting information about the incidents.
Which foldable phones are affected?
So far, most of the posts mention the Motorola Razr Ultra (specifically the 60 and 70 models) with Android 16 installed. A post from April mentioned issues with a Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 7 and also noted that there were no calling issues until the poster started using Gemini. Android 16 started rolling out in June 2025 with updates like live notification updates, camera improvements and scam detection features.
In that same Reddit post from about three months ago, one user said they had to switch back from Gemini to Google Assistant. After doing so, they were once again able to place outgoing calls while the foldable was closed. While that might seem like an easy enough fix, as of last month, Google pulled Google Assistant from phones, tablets and other devices. The transition began September 4, 2026 but only for phones that have the minimum requirements to run the AI service.
Is there a workaround?
Google and Motorola haven't issued any official fixes yet, and although foldable phone owners have detailed the lengths they've gone to in order to solve the problem, there doesn't seem to be a solution yet aside from making calls with the phones open.
The increased presence of Gemini across the Google ecosystem mirrors the broader push to integrate AI tools into everyday life. While some embrace the myriad AI tools popping up at every turn, others are less convinced, particularly in these early days when bugs may run amok. For some, like a few in these forum threads, the answer is turning to apps and products that don't use AI — or at least offer a way to turn it off.

Cheap ways to impress a crowd never fall out of fashion, and describing a dish as containing “caviar” is a particularly cost-effective way — whether it’s really caviar we’re talking about or not.
Of course, real-deal caviar is salt-cured roe farmed exclusively from sturgeon. But there are plenty of other gourmet aquatic ova, especially in Japan: ever-popular ikura (salmon roe), tarako (cod roe) and even tobiko (flying fish roe).
Beyond the realm of fish eggs, “caviar” is also a term used in molecular gastronomy to describe the products of spherification, a technique that encapsulates oils and other liquids into miniature balls. This method is mainly aesthetic, with flavor profiles that usually veer away from anything approaching authentic caviar’s salty and creamy characteristics.

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.
A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Police authorities didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.
The CJP said that among those detained was a group of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being taken away in a bus to an unknown location.
The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.
The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.
The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.
The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.
The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.
“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture student who attended the Bengaluru protest.
There were also protests over police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.
On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of using “brute force” to briefly detain party leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, and other lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.
Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.
BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.
Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

Middlesbrough-born Renshaw's epic 190 lifts Australia
- Published
First Test, Durban (day two of five)
Australia 390: Renshaw 190, Cummins 43; Mulder 4-68
South Africa: Yet to bat
Matt Renshaw scored an epic first Test century in more than nine years to put Australia in control of the first Test in their highly anticipated series against South Africa.
After much talk about the issues among their ageing top order on day one, Renshaw ground out a majestic career-best 190 from 397 balls in Durban, emphatically pushing his case to be part of Australia's future.
The 30-year-old was born in Middlesbrough and a childhood friend of England captain Joe Root - their fathers played together in English club cricket - before his parents left the UK for New Zealand and then Australia when he was seven.
As well as potentially match-defining innings, having dragged Australia from 124-6 to 390 all out, it was a statement knock from Renshaw who has had an in-out international career.
"I like him as a player," former Australia batter Simon Katich said on SEN Radio.
"When he first came in, I liked him as a player, even though others thought he was too defensive.
"I think that is what this team has needed and been crying out for."
Renshaw scored 184 in his fourth Test against Pakistan in January 2017 after being handed a debut aged 20, but averaged 19.41 across 10 Tests before being recalled earlier this year.
Against South Africa, the left-hander hit only three boundaries on day one - he attacked only 14.2% of deliveries in making his first 50 runs, the lowest figure of the Australia's top order. A throwback innings continued as he left well throughout day two, largely scoring square or behind the wicket.
He extended his partnership with captain Pat Cummins in the morning session to 86 and then expertly controlled a stand of 134 with number 10 Nathan Lyon to frustrate and tire South Africa's bowlers.
Renshaw took the strike when needed, protecting Lyon from the pace of Anrich Nortje, but became increasingly aggressive to add boundaries and inflict further pain as the partnership grew.
He added a further 21 alongside number 11 Josh Hazlewood before falling in the first over after tea, leaving South Africa 22 overs to bat and losing opener Ryan Rickelton for a three-ball duck.
Australia's top-order dilemma
Renshaw's superb innings has left Australia well placed to push for victory on a pitch that flattened out on day two, but is expected to take turn later in the Test.
This series has been eagerly anticipated, given it is a repeat of last year's World Test Championship final, which was won by the Proteas.
It is also the third in a possible 21 Tests for Australia before the end of the Ashes next summer and, while Renshaw has surely secured his immediate future at least, his knock does not alleviate all questions over the make-up of their side.
When he was recalled in August it was in place of Jake Weatherald as opener, but he was moved down to number five for this Test when Cameron Green was ruled out.
Nic Maddinson came in at the top of the order alongside Travis Head, giving Australia an 11th different opening partnership since the retirement of David Warner.
With Green, the regular number five, expected to return and Maddinson making a 33-ball duck on day one, a solution to their top-order struggles would be to move Renshaw up again.
That would reunite him with Head, who made the surprise move to opener to impressive effect in the Ashes - he flogged England for centuries in Perth, Adelaide and Sydney - but has also shown vulnerability in failing to pass 22 in his four innings since.

More than 726,000 people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle have been left without power on Saturday after Hurricane Isaias crashed into the US Gulf Coast.
The storm made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply, weakening to a post-tropical cyclone, the US National Hurricane Center said in its latest advisory.
But residents are bracing for flooding and gusty winds in Isaias’ aftermath as authorities warned of the potential for tornadoes.
The storm is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland as the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still looms for parts of the Florida Panhandle.
It will travel northwards across Alabama and over the Tennessee Valley later on Saturday, according to the National Weather Service.
Forecasters also warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida governor Ron DeSantis said Friday.
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.
Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.
More than 726,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
Despite weakening, heavy rain is forecast as Isaias moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia.
Isaias, the first hurricane to hit the eastern US since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, is also expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.
The storm also grounded most Friday flights at several panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it approached Mexico’s coast.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

Evangelizing to his 512,000 TikTok followers occasionally requires that dating coach Chad Franklin post the private communications of his clients, who pay upwards of $5,000 for his services.
In September, Franklin shared a DM conversation in which a woman implied she couldn’t afford an Uber with the text overlay “Don’t date POOR women!!!” That same month, he uploaded a video of a client’s successful text exchange on Hinge where they talked about the need to “flirt over some margaritas.” In the clip, Franklin can barely contain himself, noting that it was the type of tête-à-tête that gets his “dick hard”: “This is what men are looking for. We lead, you follow.”
Franklin posts under the alias @DefundSimping, and has made it his mission to help straight, career-driven guys in their “post-breakup, post-divorce” era undo their “simp” behavior, which he defines as putting women on a pedestal or giving them too much attention.
I reached out to the 30-year-old content creator because I wanted to talk about Hinge’s decision to start testing screenshot protection in India. The announcement set off a firestorm of reaction across social media last week, rekindling a debate around digital etiquette, privacy, and shame.
“Everyone who’s downloaded the app has seen the debauchery and the drama,” Franklin says, explaining that being online in 2026 simply means there is a chance you will become the day’s main character whether you intended to or not. “People are aware that they could be the next haha moment, but that doesn't mean they deserve it.”
TikTokers, X accounts like @hingestrange, and other online creators have built entire brands out of screenshotting and sharing bizarre dating profile prompts, cringe pickup lines, or red flags found while swiping. But critics of the trend argue it’s a form of public humiliation that should end.
In response to news of Hinge revoking profile screenshotting ability in India, some responded with relief.
“People on here kinda turned being on a dating app into both an extension of the panopticon and a window into their own personal penchant for cruelty,” writer Tres Dean noted on X. “I actually think this might be the first ethical development in online dating in years if not ever.”
X user @randy_mossad added, “Better for a million cheaters to go unpunished than for one regular person looking for love to get humiliated by leaked chats.”
In a TikTok video, Florida-based creator Kiara said she understands the change despite having posted screenshots to shame men who were hypersexual or “super disrespectful” in their profiles. “But I’ve noticed now that we’re in an ‘I hate men’ apocalypse ... women are posting men’s profiles simply because they’re not just not attracted to them,” she continued, describing the latter as being “wrong” and “mean.”
At a moment when the apps feel broken for so many people, there seems to be a desire for more private, less performative forms of dating and communication.
While apps like Raya and Grindr already include screenshot protection, the India pilot is the first iteration of it for Hinge, which will block screenshots on surfaces containing personally identifiable profile information, including Discover, Likes You, and Standouts.
The company confirms to WIRED that testing in India is part of an initiative to help singles build trust among other users and with the platform. The insights will determine whether and how Hinge introduces the feature in additional markets, but there are no current plans to greenlight screenshot protection in US or other regions.
A 2025 study in the Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication suggested that screenshots create “privacy turbulence” by allowing a recipient to permanently store and redistribute private conversations without the original sender's knowledge or consent, noting that the screenshot feature eliminates a shared boundary of control and strips away context.
But for some women in particular, screenshotting profiles has become a necessary precaution when vetting potential suitors. “Privacy’s in tension with safety. Screenshots can document inappropriate behavior or allow someone to check in with a friend before meeting a stranger,” says Lizzie Li, a communications researcher, who adds that communities like Are We Dating the Same Guy? grew partly out of women sharing screenshots to address safety concerns.
Asked whether the company has an obligation to prevent users from having their profiles turned into public content—30 million people currently use the app—a Hinge spokesperson tells WIRED that screenshot protection, along with Comment Filter and Did This Bother You?, is “another way we’re exploring how to help daters control how and where personal details are shared.” Singles will still be able to screenshot their messages with other matches if they want to report an account for potential safety concerns, affording women an extra layer of defense on dating apps where they disproportionately experience harassment and privacy violations. According to Hinge’s community guidelines, harassment, bullying, and intimidation are prohibited.
“When you are a bystander, it is fairly obvious that a privacy violation is occurring and most people would not want it to happen to them. At the same time, discomfort has not stopped the behavior,” says Alexis Ingber, an assistant professor at Syracuse University whose research focuses on privacy and emerging tech. “Dating-profile dunking reflects a broader sense of entitlement to others’ data.”
But Franklin, who has a knack for speaking in clip-ready one-liners, doesn’t believe dating apps have a duty to protect users from becoming a punch line on social media. “If you enter the dragon’s den, you may get bit by the dragon,” he tells me.
Still, with 20 clients on his roster, he says he does his best to block “every name, lip, face, and eye, trying to keep people private” when posting screenshots, because he understands that people are “scared of getting hit-pieced.” Before ending our Zoom call to meet with another client, he tells me there is actually one way to completely sidestep the problem. “If you don’t want to be potentially doxed, just don’t get on a dating app. Go talk to a girl at a dog park. Go to a farmer's market. Do it the old-fashioned way.”

Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief
- Published
Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility as it prepares to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, according to Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), .
Banka was speaking at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi where he held talks with President William Ruto, government and sports officials, the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (Adak), athletes and representatives of law enforcement.
Wada said the visit was intended to build on recent progress in Kenya's anti-doping programme at a critical time following Nairobi's selection to host the 2029 World Championships.
"Kenya calls itself probably 'home of champions', but every home has to have a good host and has to be clean to be credible," Banka told the BBC.
"We absolutely need to instill the culture of clean sport."
Kenya was awarded the 2029 championships in September, making it the first African country selected to host the event.
The decision has increased scrutiny of its efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem.
More than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017.
The Polish former sports minister said he had received a clear commitment from Ruto's government to a policy of zero tolerance towards doping, but warned promises would have to be matched by results.
"Wada will monitor this situation and observe the dynamic. Action speaks louder than words," he said.
Banka said his discussions with Ruto also focused on strengthening an independent Adak, and ensuring it has sufficient government support.
- How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships 
  - Published15 September
2029 will be the real test
Nairobi 2029 could provide a global test of Kenya's ability to protect its sporting legacy.
For a country whose distance runners have helped define global athletics for generations, the stakes extend beyond staging a successful championship.
"The problem with anti-doping is not with rules and standards," Banka said. "The problem is with implementation."
Another challenge is testing infrastructure.
Africa currently has no Wada-accredited doping control laboratory following the loss of accreditation of the facility in Bloemfontein, South Africa.
Wada initially suspended the laboratory in March 2024 because of multiple failures to comply with its International Standard for Laboratories.
Its accreditation was formally revoked in May 2025 after those problems were not satisfactorily resolved.
Banka said Kenya has shown political interest in establishing its own facility, but cautioned against expecting a laboratory to be accredited in time for the 2029 championships.
The process, he said, takes years because the consequences of laboratory error can be enormous for an athlete.
That leaves Kenya facing a more immediate priority: strengthening the system around testing rather than relying on a new laboratory as a solution.
'Doping has no colours and flags'
Banka also rejected the idea that doping should be viewed as an exclusively Kenyan, or African, problem.
"Doping has no colours and flags," he said, pointing to cases across established sporting nations including the United States, Germany and his native Poland.
"The problem would be to ignore this issue, not to tackle, or to pretend that there is no doping here."
Wada, he added, can investigate sport but cannot dismantle the criminal networks supplying prohibited substances.
"We are not a superpower. We are not law enforcement," he said.
"They have tools to really go after those who are destroying the credibility of the sport and the country."
He said intelligence indicated performance-enhancing drugs were being produced in Kenya and described Africa as a significant market.
According to him, athletes are often the "weakest points in the ecosystem", arguing that anti-doping authorities need to pursue not only competitors who break the rules but also the coaches, doctors, managers and suppliers who enable doping.
Some athletes, he suggested, are being exploited by people "who have money, who have power" and see them as a route to profit.

“for some reason, I woke up at 5:30, and the first thing I did was go to the New York Times website to check the headlines,” Juan Carlos Díaz Vélez recalls of the previous morning. “To my great surprise, there was a breaking news story: Francis Halzen had just been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. I immediately started sending messages, only to discover that my colleagues in Europe had found out long before I did.”
Juan Carlos Díaz Vélez works at the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. The new Nobel laureate is his boss.
“When I arrived at the WIPAC offices, everyone was smiling and congratulating one another,” Díaz Vélez says. “We gathered in the conference room to watch the press conference with Francis Halzen, who was in Italy at the time attending a conference. We’ll wait for his return to celebrate, and in the meantime, we’ll keep working on the neutrino study, because this work never ends.”
That work is detecting an elusive particle using detectors inside a big block of ice.
“Neutrinos are subatomic particles that participate in reactions within the nuclei of atoms,” Díaz Vélez explains. “They are produced by radioactivity on Earth—and even in watermelons and bananas, due to their potassium-40 content—as well as in our own bodies.”
Not that any of us notice. These particles do not interact easily with matter. As their name suggests, neutrinos have no electric charge, so they can travel through space in a straight line without being affected by magnetic fields, and they constantly pass through the entire Earth without interacting with a single atom. “Neutrinos from the sun are so abundant that 1 billion of them pass through the nail of a thumb every second,” Díaz Vélez says.
The neutrinos studied by Halzen’s team are not the run-of-the-mill particles we’re encountering constantly—if unknowingly. They are interested in very high-energy neutrinos that come from deep space. These cosmic particles may originate from supernova remnants or even black holes. The intense magnetic fields of such phenomena can accelerate particles like protons to very high energies.
“When these particles collide with the interstellar medium—which consists of gas and plasma—they produce gamma rays and neutrinos,” Díaz Vélez says. “That is why neutrinos are perfect messengers from high-energy cosmic-ray sources. The highest-energy neutrino sources we have detected come from active galactic nuclei, which contain supermassive black holes.”
And the team Díaz Vélez is part of has detected such neutrinos at a facility located at the geographic South Pole known as the IceCube Neutrino Observatory—no relation to the famous rapper. The observatory contains an array of 5,160 optical sensors buried deep underground, covering 1 cubic kilometer of ice.
“The South Pole ice sheet is very transparent at a depth of 1.5 kilometers, so the sensors can detect the light produced by subatomic particles called muons, which are generated as a result of rare interactions between neutrinos and ice atoms,” says Díaz Vélez, who also participated in the construction of IceCube in 2010. The observatory began operations the following year.
The project’s first major discovery was the detection of neutrinos from astrophysical sources outside our solar system. One of the most notable sources was TXS 0506+056, located in collaboration with other observatories that collected various gamma-ray, optical, and radio signals. TXS 0506+056 is a high-energy blazar, a galaxy that appears extremely bright and revolves around a supermassive black hole. The researchers looked for other objects with similar characteristics and confirmed that this class of sources is capable of producing high-energy neutrinos. More recently, they have been able to observe the Milky Way as a diffuse source of neutrinos.
In addition to astronomy, IceCube has made significant contributions to our understanding of the nature and behavior of these particles. For example, there are three known types of neutrinos, and last year’s Nobel laureates in physics discovered that these particles can transform from one type to another as they travel. IceCube has enabled increasingly precise measurements of this phenomenon.
“Another area of research is cosmic rays, which is what I focus on,” says Díaz Vélez. “We have discovered that they do not come uniformly from all directions but rather from preferred directions, and this tells us about the distribution of their sources in the galaxy.”
Cosmic rays consist of protons and nuclei of heavier atoms, and they constitute a very high portion of the project’s data. “Detecting a neutrino is like looking for a needle in a haystack,” the researcher says. “For every neutrino IceCube detects, more than a million muons produced by cosmic rays are detected.”
Díaz Vélez serves as the product coordinator for the IceCube collaboration, overseeing the processing of experimental data and the production of simulations. “This involves calculating the direction of arrival, the energy, and the type of particle detected every two milliseconds,” he says. “We also need to simulate cosmic rays and neutrinos at comparable rates. Both tasks require high-performance computing networks distributed around the world, totaling approximately 10,000 CPU cores and 1,000 GPUs.”
The researcher notes that while the IceCube project is based in Antarctica and headquartered in Wisconsin, it’s an international collaboration of 450 people at 58 institutions across 14 countries. Many of those involved in the work are masters and doctoral students, and although the award bears only one scientist’s name, behind that name lies the work of dozens of colleagues.
“It’s worth mentioning that Francis is a great figure and a leader but also a very friendly and generous person,” says Díaz Vélez. “In general, we see him more as a colleague than as a boss. In fact, if it weren’t for his passion and dedication, this experiment would never have been successful.”
