Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Following a complaint regarding food poisoning among students at Hostel No. 10 (CD Block) on the MANIT Bhopal campus, the Food Safety and Drug Administration (FDA), Bhopal, conducted an on-site inspection on Saturday.
The team conducted a detailed inspection of the food preparation arrangements, food storage facilities and food safety protocols in the hostel mess.
A total of seven food samples were collected to assess food quality.
Collected samples include urad dal (split black gram), groundnut kernels, thick vermicelli (sevaiyya), chana dal (split Bengal gram), chickpeas (chlole), rice and arhar dal (split pigeon pea).
During the inspection, documents related to the food business licence, staff medical fitness certificates, pest control programmes and FoSTaC training records were not found to be available on-site.
Officials discovered unsanitary kitchen conditions, poor food storage and sanitation failures in the mess areas.

How does a backup camera actually work?
Aftermarket backup cameras might not work as well as integrated ones, but they're still a useful upgrade to an older car.
Most cars today come with backup cameras pre-installed, which makes parallel parking much less of a chore, and allows drivers to reverse more safely in crowded environments. But what if you have an older car and still want a better view for maneuvering your vehicle?
There are several ways to outfit an older vehicle with a backup camera, including wiring one into the car, which requires a complex installation process, more hours of labor and can cost upwards of $600. For a less invasive, easier fix, you can use a wireless, vehicle-mounted backup camera system. These devices can often be installed yourself, and like the wired cameras they transmit real-time video from the rear of your vehicle to a monitor on the dashboard. But how do these add-on cameras actually work? Here's what you need to know about the technology, its quirks, and how you can put one in your car.
How do add-on wireless cameras really work?
Wireless backup cameras can be purchased online for prices ranging from $40 to more than $400, and don't require a professional for installation. They typically turn on automatically when your car is switched to reverse, but some that are used more for accident monitoring automatically record video footage when any movement appears behind your vehicle. Backup cameras use different technology to stream video to your dashboard depending on the age and model. Most of them use Wi-Fi or dedicated digital radio frequencies, though some older systems use Bluetooth. Typically these cameras work offline, meaning you don't need to use mobile data for them to work.
The power source for the dashboard monitor typically comes from a USB port or a cigarette lighter, depending on the age of your vehicle. The camera installed on the back of the vehicle gets power by fusing to a light circuit in the car itself, or through a built-in solar-powered battery. When the camera's wires are spliced directly into your vehicle's tail lights, shifting your car into reverse will activate the camera automatically. If it is not connected to the car's wiring and works solely on battery or solar power, it typically requires opening an app on your smart phone to activate.
The system automatically flips the video footage horizontally to match the image that you would see from your rearview mirror. It also uses a camera with a wide or fish-eye lens to offer the most comprehensive viewpoint possible for maneuvering the vehicle.
What are the downsides of wireless cameras?
An aftermarket, wireless camera will inevitably be missing some of the in-depth features included in those pre-installed on new vehicles: don't expect a full back-up system with these cameras. New vehicles typically come with multiple back-up tools: a camera that gives you a visual feed of backing up as well as parking sensors to measure physical distance. While some models do include additional sensor or computer vision features don't expect a wireless camera system to measure physical distance or detect objects unless it's explicitly marketed. You'll be relying entirely on visuals and won't hear a "beep" as you approach potential obstacles.
Wireless backup cameras may have a slight delay compared to wired devices, though experts say it is hardly noticeable for most drivers. Still, connecting to an app to look at backup footage if your device is battery-powered is certainly less convenient than an automatic camera. Signal stability can also be prone to outside interference since it relies on wireless connectivity. Additionally, because footage is being sent over Wi-Fi rather than directly streamed through the vehicle, video can be more compressed and thus lower resolution.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Taiwanese leader welcomes talks between Washington and Beijing ‘to reduce risk of war’
William Lai’s Double Tenth speech this year avoided some of the rhetoric that has prompted a furious response from Beijing in previous years
Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te has welcomed talks between Washington and Beijing aimed at reducing the risk of conflict.
Lai’s annual Double Tenth address, marking the anniversary of the foundation of the Republic of China, Taiwan’s official name, also called for democracies to work together to safeguard regional peace and for the Taiwanese people’s right to exist to be respected.

The annual Conservative Political Action Conference billed itself as a chance for the leaders of the three main conservative parties – Liberals, Nationals and One Nation – to make their pitch and compete for rightwing voters.
The reception they received in Brisbane on Saturday suggests Pauline Hanson is effectively the preferred opposition leader, with Angus Taylor relegated to leading a minor party.
But how would they work together, if the opportunity arose? While Hanson repeatedly criticised the Coalition, to laughter from the audience, the One Nation leader is keeping the door open to some kind of arrangement to defeat Labor.
Discussion of how to “unite the right” echoed around the Brisbane convention centre.
It was always a risk for Taylor, still leader of the second-largest bloc in parliament, to agree to equal billing on the conference lineup with Hanson, who leads a party room of five others. The Liberal leader was the first guest speaker, with his office calling his opening address a “keynote”, but CPAC had effectively advertised all three leaders – Taylor, Hanson and Matt Canavan – as co-headliners.
This framing would be remarkable in itself, if Hanson hadn’t already been operating as de facto opposition leader through 2026, while filling a void left by Taylor who has struggled for mainstream cut-through and political oxygen. Hanson followed Taylor on the schedule, but it’s the first time in a while – Taylor has been following her lead all year.
That Hanson literally took a seat Taylor had just vacated as they conducted back-to-back interviews with Karl Stefanovic, the One Nation leader nestling herself into a spot Taylor had just warmed up for her, was a moment that felt symbolic.
Taylor was always up against it, in front of a CPAC crowd which leans more conservative than the centre-right. Beginning with a mea culpa for Liberal governments past – apologising for his role in immigration increases, pandemic spending and net zero – Taylor admitted his side “made mistakes” but were now “unashamedly on the right”. His speech favoured conservative talking points, including “big government”, “climate bureaucracy”, “NDIS fraud”, and no less than six mocking references to “socialism”.
While CPAC usually finds speaking slots for half the Coalition frontbench each year, Taylor is the first sitting Liberal leader to feature. It’s interesting that he felt the need to, or wanted to, front a convention where the demographic is somewhat outside the voters the Coalition must win back – those in the centre.
This audience represents a very activated, politically engaged conservative base. But with the Coalition vote still cratering eight months from Sussan Ley’s dumping, and One Nation’s rise carving off voters on the right, trying to win back some of that base makes sense for the Liberal leader.
It was a valiant effort to reclaim the Coalition’s mantle as “the most credible alternative government”, but not even Taylor’s newly announced immigration crackdown – confirmed, coincidentally or otherwise, just days before CPAC – could save him from heckles from those more partial to Hanson. A handful booed as he said net overseas migration would rise from 100,000 to 160,000 under the Coalition plan; more booed when he dodged questions from Stefanovic about why he wasn’t trying harder to work with Hanson.
This is where the problem lies for Taylor, presenting a vexed conundrum with no easy solution. While the Liberal leader’s speech ran through a list of relatively well explained Coalition policies – cutting taxes, indexing tax brackets, instant asset write-offs – and philosophical markers for how the Coalition would intellectually approach government, it was clear that much of the crowd wasn’t really buying what he was selling. The biggest claps Taylor got were when he railed against socialism and big government, not for talking up fiscal discipline.
Hanson, by contrast, got a standing ovation from most of the room before even walking on stage, with a hype video – set to Vanessa Amorosi’s Amazing – playing her on. More scripted than usual, Hanson’s speech went to economic pain, anger at climate policies and “mass migration”, and criticism of “elitists”. Nearly every line received enthusiastic applause.
Despite claiming Australians don’t want a “smarmy management consultant” replacing Anthony Albanese, and questioning how conservatives could “trust” the Coalition, Hanson repeatedly signalled her keenness for rightwing parties to cooperate in some way.
In a press conference, she wouldn’t say exactly how that would work. Hanson said she didn’t want ministry positions for One Nation in a Coalition government, nor would she accept Coalition ministers in a One Nation government, appearing to rule out a formal agreement.
But asked if One Nation would continue playing hardball and beating up the Liberals, or if cooperation might emerge, she said it was “up to Angus Taylor”.
After seeing how his message went across to the Brisbane convention room, compared to Hanson’s, Taylor may have a lot to think about.
- Josh Butler is a Guardian Australia political reporter and chief of staff in Canberra

SpaceX has a deal to purchase nationwide low-band spectrum licenses for a planned terrestrial mobile network that would complement the space-based Starlink cellular service.
SpaceX will buy up to 14 megahertz of spectrum in the 800 MHz band from investment firm Grain Management, which bought the spectrum rights from T-Mobile earlier this year. T-Mobile had obtained the spectrum when it bought Sprint in 2020 and was required to sell the licenses under a merger condition imposed by the US government.
“This prime low-band spectrum addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US,” SpaceX said yesterday. SpaceX this week also received US approval to launch 15,000 satellites for an upgraded version of its mobile service that it says will be far more powerful than the current offering.
The 800 MHz spectrum licenses cover “approximately 100 percent of the US population,” the Federal Communications Commission said in a July 2026 order approving Grain’s purchase of the T-Mobile licenses. While the licenses are nationwide, it’s not a huge amount of spectrum. It ranges from 4.85 megahertz to 14 megahertz depending on the county. The FCC said the 800 MHz spectrum can be used for terrestrial service, satellite-to-mobile service, or both.
SpaceX’s low-band purchase is in addition to 65 MHz of nationwide mid-band spectrum licenses it is buying from EchoStar. The FCC approved that $17 billion purchase in May 2026.
“While Starlink Mobile’s global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity in the United States, this new low-band spectrum will provide a coverage layer that ensures Starlink Mobile’s signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers’ devices even when they are in buildings. Critically, most existing mobile devices already support this underused band,” SpaceX said.
SpaceX’s big mobile plans
SpaceX’s spectrum deal is likely to be approved by the FCC, but it could face opposition from small carriers. The Rural Wireless Association opposed EchoStar’s spectrum sales to AT&T and SpaceX, saying the deals “continue the troubling pattern of spectrum aggregation that disadvantages rural wireless providers.” Across all carriers in the US, there is about 1.1 GHz of licensed spectrum allocated to mobile operators, with the big three holding dominant spectrum portfolios.

Cheetahs to play European games in Swansea

South African side Cheetahs will play their European Challenge Cup home matches this season at St Helen's in Swansea, the home of Welsh side Ospreys.
Cheetahs host Dragons on Sunday, 13 December and Perpignan on Sunday, 17 January with both games a day after Ospreys' home matches in the same competition.

The Ospreys' first game at the redeveloped St Helen's is scheduled to be the United Rugby Championship (URC) Welsh derby against Dragons on Saturday, 24 October.

Quick Answer
Meta Muse is a powerful AI agent that can handle emails, purchases, bookings, and more. But its need for deep access to personal data, combined with Meta’s privacy record and early reports of Muse ignoring user permissions, makes trust its biggest problem.
A few days ago, Meta hosted its annual hardware/software event, Meta Connect, at Menlo Park, California. The event was dominated by new hardware launches, such as the new Meta Ray-Ban glasses, new VR glasses, and camera-free Ray-Ban glasses (audio only), but swimming beneath the surface of all these was something that was actually introduced earlier. Meta had introduced Meta Muse in early September, but announced the rollout of the Muse AI agent on its Meta wearables and Meta Muse Charm at the event, and for us, that was easily the real highlight of Meta Connect.
After investing heavily in recruiting AI talent, Meta finally had something to show: an AI agent, which will basically make your dreams of having a robot butler come true. Not surprisingly, it has been making massive tech waves ever since. Since Meta Connect and its rollout, Muse has been topping app store charts, and its early numbers are being compared with ChatGPT, with many pointing out that it is far ahead of OpenAI’s chatbot’s numbers.
While this may paint a very rosy picture for Meta Muse, the reality may be a trifle thorny.
What those numbers do not tell – the “Threads” deception
These numbers, impressive as they are, do not necessarily mean Muse is a runaway success. There are a few reasons for this. Topping app store charts is more of a temporary phenomenon, often influenced by what is trending in a particular week, and does not represent real industry trends. Also, Meta has billions of users across different social media and messaging platforms, which makes it easy for the tech giant to get a few million users quickly without too much trouble. But the adoption rate might not match the number of downloads or sign-ups.
We have seen this happen with Meta’s X rival app, Threads, as well. It has more “active users” as per the numbers than X, which means it must be more used and popular than X, but that is mostly because of Threads’ integration with Instagram and Facebook, which gets the app most of its “active users.” However, the time spent on the app is not nearly the same as its other two sibling social media apps. Similarly, early ChatGPT comparisons with Meta Muse signups may not be fair, because ChatGPT was not launched or advertised as a tool for the masses when it was first launched. It did not have the sort of subscriber base and reach that Meta has, and back then, AI chatbots were not too common either.
Definitely a big deal
That does not mean Muse does not represent a big tech leap. So far, AI chatbots have generally been used for queries, information, help with work, and even personal advice, but that’s mostly about it. All of these chatbots are more about helping you with your queries, with no bar to the nature of the query. While useful in this regard, many are not able to perform actions that have an impact on your day-to-day life. That is where Meta Muse differs.
As we said earlier, Muse is actually the robot butler that the future always promised us. It can get tasks done and help you with managing your digital and even real life. Once you give it access, the AI agent can go through your mail, find messages, draft new messages, reply to emails, all without too much intervention. That might not sound too impressive, as most AI agents and virtual assistants can do the same with a simple command. But Muse goes a step further – it can even make purchases, make reservations, book appointments, and more, across different devices and platforms. In fact, if allowed, Muse can basically make deals on Facebook Marketplace or book you a table at your favorite restaurant or even call you a cab, all without needing any major intervention. Proper butling!
Muse has power and potential, but does Meta have our trust?
As impressive and life-altering as it may sound– some are calling it the biggest tech innovation since the iPhone – Meta still has a massive hurdle that it would have to cross to make Muse the AI butler it wants it to be. And that is the lack of trust in Meta.
For all its innovation and massive subscriber base, Meta has been in a number of controversial situations when it comes to security and privacy. Zuckerberg’s brand has been accused of and even found guilty in cases that range from rigging elections, pushing agendas and ads, to exposing young children to adult content and potential groomers, to monopolizing social media and personal messaging space and using unfair means and practices to kill competition. Its recent hardware “hit” the Meta glasses have also got into a privacy mess, and have been (in)famously christened pervert glasses, following reports of their being used to record people without their consent.
Now, Muse requires even more data and access to private information to actually deliver on its promises. For instance, to be able to draft emails, it needs access to your email account. To be allowed to send messages, it needs permission to read, understand, store, and reply to messages, and needs access to your contact list. To make a reservation, it needs to know your location; to order things online, it needs to have your bank details and also your address. Basically, it needs to have complete access to all your information to act like the magic help that Meta is claiming it can be.
Why I am not A-Muse-D
And that is where my beef with Muse really comes in. Had this been any other company– if Apple had managed to deliver on its intelligent Siri promises or Google had delivered Gemini with such prowess, I personally would have felt less apprehensive in handing over the keys to my digital life, but to give Meta even more access to my data than it already has just feels scary.
Even though I have come to terms with the fact that we are all under passive surveillance from brands at all times, it will take some time for me to give complete control of my data over to Meta without any struggle.
Some of the recent headlines Muse has made do not help its cause. Recently, the AI agent not only made a deal for its user on Facebook Marketplace but even shared his address with the buyer. All without consent. The user, a tech YouTuber, Matt Robb, mentioned how the AI agent accepted low offers and even pretended to be the user while chatting with the buyer, calling the buyer to his address when he was not home at all. Once Matt realized what was happening, he specifically instructed Muse to not share his address. He then asked his friends to send him messages on Facebook Marketplace to see if the agent shares the address. Rather disturbingly, it did: multiple times, and even accepted low offers, all without consent. In another report by Apple Insider, alleged that Muse accessed and uploaded past and present Apple Messages even though the user said he had not granted it permission to do so. All this despite Meta’s claims that Muse has strong privacy and security protections.
All of this does not take away from the fact that Meta has created something really powerful with Muse. It has managed to deliver a finished, capable AI agent which can manage your digital lives, if you let it. Unfortunately, it may also steal your data, force specific ads, and make conversations on your behalf by pretending to be you. And therein lies the problem. The AI Agent is not just about technology, but also about trust. Meta has delivered on the first front with Muse, but until it delivers on the second, I refuse to be A-Muse-D by it. Pun intended.

Sunmi is an undeniable force in K-pop. She first made her debut as a member of the Wonder Girls back in 2007, one of the first K-pop acts to really break through in the West. The English version of their single “Nobody” was the first K-pop song to hit the Billboard Hot 100 in October 2009.
K-pop star Sunmi loves Notion and ear cleaning videos
Nearly 20 years into her music career Wonder Girls’ Sunmi is staying humble, but persistent.
K-pop star Sunmi loves Notion and ear cleaning videos
Nearly 20 years into her music career Wonder Girls’ Sunmi is staying humble, but persistent.
In 2010 Sunmi left the group to go back to school, but the siren call of a music career pulled her back in. She released her debut solo EP Full Moon in 2014. That began a run of award-winning releases for the pop star, including Song of the Year for “Gashina” at the Gaon Chart Music Awards.
Despite her near-constant presence in the K-pop world as a solo artist and as a member of the Wonder Girls, whom she rejoined in 2015, Sumni only just released her first solo LP, Heart Maid, in 2025. This year she released the single “Forever July,” which blends ’90s R&B synths with rubbery bass and UK garage-inspired drums. Sunmi has called it one of her most personal songs. And she wasn’t afraid to get personal in our Q&A either, revealing details about her writing process, her greatest disappointment as an artist, and her love of ear cleaning videos.
What is your most indispensable tool?
My phone. I use the Notes app and Voice Memos a lot when I’m writing lyrics or making music. Whenever I have a good idea, I can immediately pull it out and write it down, so I really can’t live without it.
Which is the most underappreciated?
The Samsung Galaxy series. It has made my work environment so much easier.
Team Galaxyyyyyy!
What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?
These days, you can transfer all the apps and data from your previous device, so I don’t really have to install anything separately. But if that process didn’t exist, I’d probably install KakaoTalk, a messaging app, first.
What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?
I have so many unnecessary photos and screenshots in my gallery. I wish there were a feature that could recognize similar or duplicate photos and group them together, so I could delete them all at once.
What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?
Notion. I use it a lot because I work on many group projects. It’s convenient, but it takes quite a long time to get used to. I think the UI could use some improvement.
How many tabs do you have open right now?
Four: Notion, Google Drive, YouTube, and Claude.
Which social media platform do you use the most?
I don’t really use social media that much, but I think I use Instagram and X the most.
What is your happy place online?
Videos of people getting their ears cleaned on YouTube.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
I’m not really good with technology, but I think the Samsung Z Fold 8 that I’m using right now is probably my favorite device. I often need to work on documents or edit videos while I’m on the go, and it’s incredibly convenient. I can work with both hands on a wide screen, and it’s surprisingly light. It’s exactly the kind of device I’ve always needed.
What game do you have the fondest memories of?
MapleStory by Nexon. I played it when I was in elementary school, and even after becoming an adult, I would sometimes play the mobile version. The graphics really bring back memories of my childhood.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
Deepfakes. Ew.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
Stranger Things 5 and Game of Thrones 8.
What creation are you most proud of?
“Tail.” It’s a song that still gets me excited every time I perform it live. When I hold my breath, the audience holds their breath too, and when I explode, they explode with me. It creates this really unique experience.
Which are you least proud of?
“You Can’t Sit with Us.” It was the first song where I ever tried rapping. But the lyrics and even my voice were terrible.
What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?
Always stay humble. You should never let yourself become arrogant.
What is your current obsession?
I really love ice cream. Korean summers are shockingly hot, so it’s hard to survive without ice cream. I absolutely love Salt & Straw’s Salted Caramel Waffle Cone, but there’s nothing quite like it in Korea.
What do you do when you need to focus?
I find a small space to organize my thoughts.
What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?
I say “No?” out loud. For example, if I start thinking to myself, “I can’t do this,” I immediately say “No?” out loud.
When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?
When I’m shooting, I leave my phone with my manager. Even during short breaks, I barely look at my phone. But I’ve never actually gone somewhere without my phone.
What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?
The Senses of an Everydayist, a new essay collection by lyricist Kim Eana. She sent me a copy as a gift when it was published, but I believe there’s something meaningful about personally buying and reading someone’s creative work, so I bought a copy online.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
A meal with the people I love.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Dancing on the Borderline.
What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

The United Nations Human Rights office on Saturday (October 10), expressed concern over reports of mass detentions of demonstrators, protest leaders, civil society members, lawyers and journalists in Delhi ahead of and during large-scale demonstrations.
The UN body called on Indian authorities to respect the right to peaceful assembly, exercise restraint in dealing with protesters and immediately release those who had been arbitrarily detained.
“We are concerned by reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, members of civil society organisations, lawyers and journalists, before and during today’s large-scale demonstrations in Delhi,” UN Human Rights said in a statement.
Quick answers to key questions
The Cockroach Janta Party called for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls during the Special Intensive Revision. The planned demonstration was at Jantar Mantar.
It expressed concern over reports of mass detentions and called on Indian authorities to respect peaceful assembly, use restraint and immediately release people arbitrarily detained. It also urged meaningful dialogue with demonstrators.
Reports said more than 7,000 people were detained across Delhi. Around 400 people were detained at different locations in Mumbai.
Preventive detention is confinement based on a reasonable apprehension that someone may threaten public order or security. An ordinary arrest is generally linked to an alleged offence and the legal process that follows.
A warrant is not always required, but police must have a lawful basis to detain someone. Under Section 170 of the BNSS, detention under that power is limited to 24 hours unless further detention is authorised under another applicable law.
“Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality,” it added, urging the authorities to engage in meaningful dialogue to address the concerns raised by demonstrators.
The UN Human Rights office urged Indian authorities to ensure that law enforcement personnel exercised “utmost restraint” in responding to peaceful protesters, in keeping with India's democratic traditions and human rights obligations.
It also called for meaningful dialogue to address the demonstrators' concerns.
The statement came as an extensive security operation across the national capital thwarted a planned mobilisation at Jantar Mantar by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which had called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid a controversy over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
More than 7,000 protesters were detained across Delhi, according to reports, as police and paramilitary personnel were deployed at key locations to prevent demonstrators from reaching Jantar Mantar.
The security operation involved more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel, according to the supplied reports. Barricades were erected across Lutyens' Delhi, while authorities carried out checks at border points, railway stations, bus terminals, hotels and other sensitive locations.
Several metro stations were also closed, disrupting movement across parts of the capital. Police made repeated announcements at Jantar Mantar, instructing people and mediapersons not to gather in groups.
Despite the heavy deployment, some protesters attempted to breach barricades. Around 1 pm, a group allegedly hurled stones at security personnel near Akashwani Bhawan on Imtiaz Ali Marg, injuring two police personnel. The protesters were detained, and police were likely to register multiple FIRs in connection with the incident, a senior officer said.
Police also detained people at several locations, including Hanuman Temple, Safdarjung Flyover and Kerala House, as well as some protesters who managed to reach Jantar Mantar.
CJP convener Abhijit Dipke and party members Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained at Delhi airport after arriving from Mumbai, according to the reports.
In a video shared by the CJP, Dipke could be heard telling police officers who entered the aircraft: “We are here to be arrested, come and arrest us.”
Before the detentions, police personnel told CJP leaders that they did not have permission to hold the protest at Jantar Mantar.
Dipke criticised the action, saying party leaders were being treated like criminals. He also alleged that the detentions reflected authoritarianism.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, who lives abroad and had travelled to India to join the demonstration, was detained by police from his residence in Gurugram's Sector 56, the reports said.
Authorities also monitored social media platforms for attempts to mobilise people for the protest. More than 200 content creators were reportedly under scrutiny as police examined online posts and messages linked to the proposed gathering.
Several opposition leaders were among those detained as they attempted to join the demonstration from different parts of the capital.
They included former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal of the Aam Aadmi Party, West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee of the Trinamool Congress, Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan of the CPI(M), and former Tripura chief minister Manik Sarkar of the CPI(M).
The detentions triggered sharp criticism from opposition parties, which accused the government of suppressing dissent.
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge accused the Modi government of turning the “mother of democracy” into a “muzzled democracy”, alleging that the BJP and RSS were displaying cowardice through the crackdown.
Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi expressed solidarity with the protesting youth and urged them to continue their demonstrations.
Gandhi also challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to arrest all the protesters, asserting that they would continue their fight to defend the Constitution and protect the voice of the Indian people.
Activist Sonam Wangchuk said he would consider launching a peaceful protest, including a hunger strike or a march in Leh or Delhi, if those detained were not released within 24 hours.
Wangchuk had previously joined a 36-day CJP agitation at Jantar Mantar over the NEET paper leak issue. That protest ended on July 25 following the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, according to the supplied account.
The earlier agitation had also witnessed unrest during a march towards Parliament on July 20, when security personnel attempted to stop protesters.
The demonstrations also triggered detentions in Mumbai, where police detained around 400 people at different locations for allegedly protesting without permission in solidarity with the Delhi mobilisation.
Those detained reportedly included actor Imran Khan, activist Tushar Gandhi and CPI(M) workers. Demonstrations took place at August Kranti Maidan, Hutatma Chowk and other locations.
Across Delhi, the authorities maintained heightened security, including the deployment of more than 120 companies of Central Armed Police Forces to assist the police. Mock drills were conducted at several locations to assess preparedness, while liquor shops across the capital were closed as a precautionary measure.

D2C personal care brand Nat Habit has raised ₹142 Cr (around $14.7 Mn) in an all-primary Series C funding round led by Trident Growth Partners to expand its distribution, product portfolio, and manufacturing capabilities. Existing investors Bertelsmann India Investments, Mirabilis Investment Trust, and Sharrp Ventures participated in the round, while Physis Capital and Hero Family Office joined the cap table. The startup plans to expand its offline presence from about 20,000 stores to 2 Lakh over the next three years. Alongside growing its general trade presence, Nat Habit will enter modern trade and expand its team to support the rollout. The expansion also involves reaching a broader consumer base. Having primarily targeted consumers with higher income and education levels, Nat Habit is now looking to reach what it calls the “Bharat consumer”, with changes to pack sizes and communication. Beyond offline retail, Nat Habit will use the fresh capital to strengthen its quick commerce presence and expand its product portfolio. It plans to enter categories such as sunscreens and serums, which it does not currently offer, with investments in R&D, formulation, and manufacturing facilities. “Our ambition now is to make our products accessible to many more households across India,” said cofounder Swagatika Das. Founded in 2019 by Das and Gaurav Agarwal, Nat Habit sells personal care products, including hair oils, masks, scrubs, and face creams. It says it combines traditional ayurvedic principles with modern science to develop plant-based formulations across haircare, skincare, body care, and baby care. The startup claims to have served more than 60 Lakh households across India and its annualised gross revenue reaching ₹330 Cr. Prior to this, Nat Habit raised $10.2 Mn in its Series B funding round in 2023. Back then, the startup said it would use the capital for product diversification, brand building, offline expansion and hiring talent. The fundraise adds to investments in India’s ayurvedic and herbal wellness segment. In September 2025, Kapiva raised $60 Mn in a Series D round, comprising $28 Mn in primary funding and $32 Mn in secondary transactions. It planned to deploy the fresh capital towards R&D, manufacturing, marketing, and international expansion. In January this year, Kapiva also launched a ₹50 Cr innovation fund to support ayurvedic research, product development, and the use of AI in Ayurveda. However, expansion has proved difficult for some brands. Last month, The Ayurveda Co cofounder Param Bhargava announced the startup’s closure, after it ceased operations in July 2025.

Trump’s new diesel deal with Russia is ‘shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic’, experts say
Trump has announced a deal with Putin to increase Russian diesel supplies to the US

Donald Trump’s new deal with Russia to boost diesel supply over the next few months is unlikely to make a dent in high prices, experts have said.
The US president said he had made an agreement with Vladimir Putin to increase fuel supplies to the US and global markets, saying the move would help bring down costs for businesses and consumers.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by further shipments in November and beyond. His administration also temporarily eased sanctions on Russian fuel, reversing a policy intended to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war against Ukraine.
The US president also announced a decision to unilaterally lift fuel sanctions on Moscow so that it could supply the US and the global market with diesel. Trump has been keen to bring down the price of diesel, which has risen in recent months due to Russian and Ukrainian tit-for-tat strikes on energy infrastructure and the US war with Iran.
The national average for a gallon of diesel in the US hit a record high of $6.53 on 22 September. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky, responding to the reported diesel deal between Russia and the US, told Axios the agreement is “not fair and not honest”.
“You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible,” Zelensky said, referring to the Russian president’s birthday on Wednesday.
n Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation.
“Trump has once again shown his true face,” said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. “He didn’t care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he’s interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay.”
“Knowing Trump, he tries to manipulate the markets. He’s got an election coming up soon,” Petrenko said. “So he needs to emphasize to his voters that gasoline will be cheap. But it won’t be effective.”
Senior policy experts have suggested the move from Trump is unlikely to have a significant impact on oil prices in the US or globally.
Michael Lynch, a fellow at the Energy Policy Research Foundation, said: “It’s kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic.
“If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they’ll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now.”
Mr Lynch said: “The best you could hope for is a tiny dip in prices locally in places like the New York-New Jersey area, Philadelphia maybe.”
Meanwhile, Gregory Brew, an analyst with Eurasia Group’s Energy, Climate & Resources team, said in an email quoted in CNN that the deal would be “a band-aid, nothing more.”

As the Trump administration has carried out a nonstop effort to undermine the midterm elections this year, the Department of Homeland Security appears to have looked into whether it could use a Palantir-supported tool to track people it believes have voted illegally.
The revelation is found in a tranche of documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request and published this week by Democracy Forward, a legal advocacy group. As well as revealing that DHS officials have investigated over 150 nonprofit groups in search of evidence they’re helping noncitizens register to vote, the documents show how Immigration and Customs Enforcement is now central to federal voter fraud investigations.
More specifically, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)—one of ICE’s two major components—is spearheading the effort to uncover voter fraud, with its Innovation Lab (known internally as iLab) developing tools for agents.
ICE, it seems, wants to build “a system that is going to get good at determining how to find people to investigate and potentially bring action against,” Chinmayi Sharma, an associate professor at Fordham Law School who has closely tracked the Palantir-supported tool called ELITE, tells WIRED.
“You would want to build off of what already exists, what might already have the infrastructure and data sources that you would want,” says Sharma.
“iLab’s processing focuses on DOJ voting rolls and [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] data; criminal histories are currently excluded, with efforts underway to address this,” a worker in HSI’s Countering Transnational Organized Crime unit wrote on May 26 in an email with “Voter Fraud” in the subject line. (Like other workers, their name was redacted in the records released to Democracy Forward.)
“Coordination with iLab continues,” they wrote, “particularly on ingesting processed voter roll data into the ELITE enforcement system to enhance lead management, analytical review, and investigative tracking.”
The existence of ELITE, which stands for Enhanced Leads Identification & Targeting for Enforcement, was first reported in January by 404 Media, which revealed that ICE agents using the tool can create maps featuring potential deportation targets, pull up files on each target, and see a “confidence score” on the person’s current address.
“Voter roll data has never been integrated into ELITE,” a Palantir spokesman tells WIRED.
ELITE was again mentioned in a July 7 email with an attachment named “Fraud WAR”—WAR typically refers to a weekly activity report—from a DHS worker who shared an update on the agency’s “election integrity investigations,” including the news that Connecticut, Georgia, Kentucky, Missouri, Michigan, and New Mexico had “been enriched by the iLab and are pending Palantir entry into ELITE.”
What specifically was enriched and pending Palantir entry is unclear from the records, but in another email in the same chain, a DHS official said that someone from the agency would send the update to the White House.
“ICE does not disclose the existence of investigative methods and techniques,” an agency spokesperson tells WIRED.
“While ICE Homeland Security Investigations is not able to comment on any active investigations, HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED.
The White House did not comment on ICE’s possible use of ELITE to track noncitizen voters in a statement provided to WIRED.

The claim that noncitizens are voting in numbers sufficient to sway the outcomes of US elections has been a central narrative pushed by the Trump administration in the run-up to next month’s midterms. All available evidence shows that noncitizen voting is vanishingly rare.
DHS, under secretary Markwayne Mullin, has led the charge on identifying noncitizen voters but has so far only found a handful of possible cases. Earlier this week, the Justice Department announced it had brought charges in 16 cases involving foreign nationals allegedly committing voting-related crimes. (All were lawful permanent residents.) Last month, a whistleblower alleged that federal employees directed by DHS leadership may have broken the law when they searched state websites for illegally registered voters.
While Mullin and the Trump administration have been vocal with their claims about noncitizen voting and short-term victories ahead of the midterms, in the background, ICE appears to have been working on tools that will work in the long term.
The May 26 email sent under a “Voter Fraud” subject line characterizes a weekly report as emphasizing “a network-based investigative approach, prioritizing organization and facilitation analysis over individual leads, now stated as a strategic direction.”
The language used in the documents related to the agency’s new approach to identifying voter fraud suggests this system was not live or even in pre-deployment at the time, but rather being built for the future, Sharma believes.
“I could be wrong,” says Sharma, “but there's a reason you choose to build voter fraud [investigations] within DHS when it does not intuitively fall within what you would think of as DHS's purview, and I think it's because of the authorities, the infrastructure, the vendor relationships, the contract vehicles, and privileges. There's just a lot of synergies you can take advantage of.”

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

Afrobeats singer Ayra Starr on making history at her NFL half-time show
- Published
Afrobeats singer Ayra Starr has already broken numerous records, and her NFL half-time performance this weekend is set to level up her list again.
The Nigerian star will become the first African artist to headline one of the American football league's international games when the Philadelphia Eagles take on the Jacksonville Jaguars in London on Sunday.
Ahead of the performance at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Starr told BBC Newsbeat her history-making performance "itself is a message".
Earlier this year, Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny used his Super Bowl half-time show to celebrate Latin American culture.
The 32-year-old also made history by becoming the first musician to perform entirely in Spanish at the sporting event, normally the most-watched each year on US TV.
Starr said it's "very important" for singers to seize opportunities like this.
"At the end of the day, as artists, we speak for the culture and we speak for the people that listen to us," she added.
"And we have to represent any way that seems fit, that they need."
She didn't want to give away too much about her performance, but confirmed it would feature tracks from her new studio album, Starrgirl, which was released in August.
"Sunday is gonna be amazing," she said.
"I'm still in rehearsals. It's a lot of work we're putting in so I'm really excited."
The 24-year-old has been making waves in recent years, becoming the first African woman to win best international act at the Mobo Awards and the first Nigerian woman to surpass one billion video views on YouTube.
But before she became a superstar, the singer studied for a degree in political sciences and international relations - and said this has influenced her work.
"When it comes to matters of women and equality and the girl child and even just children - I'm very outspoken on any platform that sees fit.
"Even with my music, my music is very much like 'I will do what I want' and freedom."
The Afrobeats genre, which originates from West Africa, has massively grown in recent years - dominating playlists and seeing artists, including Starr, featuring at major festivals such as Glastonbury.
She said the rest of the world is just "catching up" to a style that's been "popping in Africa for the longest time".
The singer added that becoming one of the dominant faces of the music she grew up listening to, alongside artists such as Wizkid and Burna Boy, is "crazy".
Starr acknowledged it's a male-dominated field and would like female artists to have more "space in the genre" and be "allowed the same privileges".
But she also feels this is just the beginning.
"Afrobeats just keeps evolving, it keeps growing and it just keeps getting better... I want it to be one of the top genres in the world."

The Center for Humane Technology, the online safety group cofounded by former Google product manager Tristan Harris and featured in the hit documentary The Social Dilemma, is laying off about half of its 16 non-founder employees, ex-staffers tell WIRED. The organization is ending its policy research and litigation work to focus instead on what it calls “founder-led” projects.
The nine departures, which include executive director Julie Guirado and senior director of strategy Camille Carlton, arrive shortly after the center scored a series of major courtroom victories against social media companies. The lawsuits drew on its research alleging that the platforms were deliberately designed to keep kids glued to their screens.
But amid that success, internal debates had been brewing for years over the organization’s direction, according to 16 former workers, most of whom spoke with WIRED earlier this year on the condition of anonymity because they feared professional repercussions.
CHT’s board ultimately determined that trying to operate both as an advocacy group fronted by Harris and a think tank producing policy papers had stretched it too thin. Moving forward, the organization will focus on initiatives with its founders at the forefront, including “public education, targeted briefings, and private coordination,” building upon their success “reaching broad audiences and engaging influential decisionmakers,” the board announced last week.
Functions such as assisting in litigation and evaluating AI tools would be eliminated, the board added, without specifying an exact number of layoffs.
“This moment of accelerated AI risk demands we focus on one strategy, and we have chosen to focus on what we have always done best so that we can meet the moment,” board chair Premal Shah said in a statement to WIRED.
In recent years, Harris has joined a growing chorus of voices sounding the alarm about the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence, warning of a potential “AI takeover” if the software evades control. “We have to act right now before it’s too late,” he told NBC News last month.
The center encouraged people to sign a major petition to pause AI development and helped organize a hearing in Congress about the dangers of chatbots. It also advised on lawsuits and investigations probing AI labs for their design choices, including an ongoing case filed against OpenAI by parents of a teenager who died by suicide after interacting with ChatGPT. Harris also starred in a documentary released on Netflix last month, The AI Doc, which urges viewers to demand that Congress intervene to protect the public from the technology’s risks.
Founded in 2017, the Center for Humane Technology competes with well-established nonprofits and numerous newer entrants for funding and attention to shape AI policy. Cyberattacks by AI agents from OpenAI and other labs have renewed calls to hold tech developers liable for design and engineering failures.
With an annual budget of roughly $6 million and a similar amount in reserves, the center has been funded by wealthy families and foundations. But as it doubles down on Harris, former employees fear resources might be diverted away from addressing what they believe are more pressing concerns about AI’s impact on democracy and civil liberties.
Gail Barnes, who advised the center on social media strategy in its early days, says the board is dropping work that was supposed to convert Harris’ fame “into durable pressure” that could help facilitate real change inside companies.
“Whether that is wisdom or a retreat depends on whether you think the binding constraint on AI right now is still ‘people haven’t heard the argument’ or ‘the argument has no institutional teeth.’ CHT is picking the first,” Barnes says.
Big Star
Harris excels at producing compelling sound bites, and he has long been a fixture in the media, at conferences, and on Capitol Hill. “He’s brilliant. He’s articulate,” a former CHT colleague says. “He could have easily spent his entire career on the dark side. For whatever reason, he came to appreciate that this was messed up.”
Harris cofounded the center with Aza Raskin, the self-proclaimed inventor of the infinite scroll, and Randy Fernando, who once worked in developer education at Nvidia. The goal was to push tech companies to take more responsibility for the social consequences of their products, which in the early days meant examining issues like whether they were fomenting political radicalization or harming the mental health of teenagers. The language Harris used to describe these problems was quickly adopted across Silicon Valley.
Internal documents from Meta released in court this year show company researchers discussed reaching out to Harris as early as 2018, when his warnings that apps were intentionally designed to be addictive entered the mainstream. His national profile grew further with the release of The Social Dilemma on Netflix in 2020.
“It’s hard to understate how helpful The Social Dilemma was for launching tech accountability” as an advocacy field, says a leader at another nonprofit, who also sought anonymity to protect their relationship with CHT.
But inside the organization, Harris sometimes clashed with his team about whether to focus their efforts on consumers, tech companies, or lawmakers, former staffers say. Some colleagues grew frustrated with Harris’ frequently shifting whims, describing the organization’s culture as needlessly “frenetic” and “insanity-inducing.” Shah disputed the characterization, but acknowledged the center’s culture is fast-paced given the urgency of its mission.
The center developed an online course at one point for tech workers who wanted to learn how to build humane systems, and while it drew thousands of participants, CHT decided to retire it as Harris’ focus shifted to concerns about AI, according to people familiar with the project. Another initiative to create resources for educators to make sense of issues around screen time fell by the wayside, the people say. Harris kept coming back to the center being “a vehicle for him to speak to the world,” according to one ex-employee.
The center’s podcasts and videos featuring Harris and Raskin have attracted large audiences, former workers say. Harris also landed private meetings with US lawmakers and executives at top tech companies. Former employees describe the group’s strategy as putting more emphasis on “grasstops” activism over the more familiar “grassroots,” which some viewed as misguided.
Shah says CHT believes “mass communications creates grassroots pressure, which unlocks action from the grasstops” and that Harris “is one of the very few people in the world who is invited and can communicate effectively to mass media audiences across the political spectrum.”
Some former employees allege that CHT’s founders were eager to remain Silicon Valley insiders, and thus were more reluctant to criticize companies where they previously worked or where close personal contacts have worked. (Shah disputes the characterizations and says CHT “has always been tough on companies.”)
Some ex-employees described Harris’ management style as taxing, which they allege led to high turnover. In 2023, employees returned from a staff retreat feeling upset after being asked to participate in trust-building exercises they felt were overly personal, according to several former workers. CHT’s independent board members got involved, and Harris later stepped down as executive director to become the organization’s president, according to the former employees.
Shah says that employee turnover "stemmed from differences in problem analysis and approaches to achieving the organization’s core mission.” He also denied that Harris’ role change was related to what happened at the retreat.
Whatever turmoil may have been happening inside CHT, the broader strategy Harris used to go after tech companies was paying off. In 2021, state attorneys general across the US opened investigations into Meta and later sued the company for allegedly misleading teens and parents. This year, Meta agreed to settle some of the lawsuits for billions of dollars. Juries, including one that heard testimony from Raskin, put the company on the hook for additional penalties in separate cases. Other social media platforms agreed to settle similar litigation this year.
In an interview with WIRED earlier this year, the leader of the other tech nonprofit praised CHT’s less flashy work in statehouses and courtrooms. The shift away from it is “disappointing,” the person says now. “Change comes from movements and democracy, not celebrities and backrooms.”
Some former employees say they expect that CHT will increasingly resemble what they jokingly refer to as the “Center of Helping Tristan.” Shah says the organization’s sole goal is ensuring “today’s most consequential technologies serve humanity.”

The Keralam government’s announcement that it will make private health care more “affordable” through consultations with the private health sector, and that a Bill in this regard was in the offing, should be seen against the State’s seven-year legal battle before the Kerala High Court upheld the Kerala Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulations) Act 2018, throwing out all objections raised by private hospitals.
The KCE Act was the first ever attempt made in the State to bring the entire health sector, public and private, under a regulatory framework.
But the Act was systematically opposed and its implementation stalled at every turn by the private health sector in the State.
It was in November last year that the Kerala High Court threw out all objections raised by the Kerala Private Hospitals’ Association (KPHA) and the Indian Medical Association (IMA) and upheld the validity of the Act.
Contentious area
Unlike the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 (Central Act 23 of 2010), which attempted to cap the treatment/procedure/diagnostic rates charged by the private health sector by fixing a price range, the KCE Act had not touched this contentious area at all.
The KCE Act just insisted on mandatory registration of all clinical establishments under all systems of medicines (including hospitals, clinics and laboratories) and that every establishment maintain certain minimum standards based on the category in which they fall. It also said that hospitals display their rates for various procedures openly so that there is transparency.
However, the private health sector argued that it violated rights under Article 14 and Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Appeal in SC
Even after the High Court specifically held that KCE Act’s Section 16 (mandatory registration of clinical establishments), Section 39 (display of fee rates and package rates for services) and Section 47 (obligations concerning life-saving treatment/emergency care and safe transfer of patients) were constitutionally valid and gave directives to the government to implement the Act without delay, KPHA went in appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court has not stayed the KCE Act, but granted members of the petitioning associations interim protection against coercive action by the government.
Yet to register
Kerala Clinical Establishments Council, which is responsible for the implementation of the Act, maintains that the registration process is continuing and that even now, many clinical establishments are yet to register themselves under the council.
Small hospitals with up to 15 beds have been given some concessions by the council, trimming down the checklist for assessment to just basic and essential points, so that at least the basic registration brings these establishments too within the regulatory framework.
The government’s efforts to draft a new Bill to bring in a regulatory framework that “protects patients’ interests while taking into account the operating costs and practical difficulties of private hospitals” is well-intentioned, but the fact remains that the private health sector is still holding out against the KCE Act at the Supreme Court.
Questions are also being raised whether a new legislation is in order or if the costing regulations can be incorporated into the KCE Act itself.
‘Entirely welcome’
Meanwhile, public health activists like B. Ekbal have stated that any attempt by the government to regulate the treatment expenditure in the private sector and save people from catastrophic health expenditure is entirely welcome.
Dr. Ekbal said that though private hospitals are an essential component of the health system, health care cannot be left entirely to market logic. It is the government’s responsibility to regulate the sector adequately so that patients are not exploited.
In a statement here, Dr. Ekbal said that the Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) should be insisted on and that the government initiate a scientific cost evaluation of various medical and diagnostic procedures and treatments so that a rational and transparent rate list suited to the State can be evolved.

Christa Pike discharged from hospital after surviving execution attempt, attorney says
Pike, 50, moved back to Tennessee prison
Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison, according to a statement released by her attorneys.
Pike, 50, was discharged from the hospital and is back at the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women's prison where she was housed for 30 years, her attorneys said in a statement.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery," her attorneys said in a statement released Saturday.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her by lethal injection on Sept. 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike had been in a hospital since the failed execution.
On Wednesday, a Tennessee judge ordered the state to preserve evidence related to the botched execution, including needles, drug lot numbers and gurney restraints.
Lawyers asking governor to commute sentence
Following the court hearing on Wednesday, her lawyers Luke Ihnen and Randy Spivey said she was awake and speaking after being unconscious and on a ventilator following the failed execution attempt. Her attorneys said her prognosis remains unclear and that she faces a long recovery.
Spivey also said Pike was "very aware" that the state tried to execute her and failed, and that she is both "angry and confused."
Ihnen and Spivey said Wednesday's hearing was the first of many of their attempts to gain answers and transparency from the state of Tennessee about what went wrong on Sept. 30 when Pike survived her lethal injection — as well as to have Pike's constitutional rights enforced.
Pike's attorneys said they were continuing to urge Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Lee halted further executions statewide following Pike's hospitalization and ordered a "comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred."
The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.

Srinagar, Oct 10: Encash Automotive Pvt. Ltd., an authorised dealership of Mahindra & Mahindra, unveiled the Thar OG at its Athwajan showroom in Srinagar on Saturday.
The vehicle was unveiled by Qazi Irfan, Regional Transport Officer (RTO), Kashmir, and Arshad Qadri, Divisional Head, J&K Bank, in the presence of Maham Rouf, CEO of Encash Automotive, senior officials from financial institutions, customers and SUV enthusiasts.
Speaking at the launch, Maham Rouf said the Thar OG succeeds the three-door Thar introduced in 2020 and carries forward the iconic SUV’s appeal while enhancing its design, capability and everyday usability.
She said the new model represents another chapter in the evolution of the Thar, retaining the features and character appreciated by enthusiasts while incorporating improvements aimed at a new generation of customers.
Addressing the gathering, Qazi Irfan commended the additions introduced in the Thar OG, including the M_Glyde 4G platform, advanced PENTALINK suspension, DAVINCI damping technology, electronic locking differential and terrain modes.
He also emphasised the importance of adhering to traffic regulations and practising safe driving.
Arshad Qadri said Mahindra had evolved the Thar for a new generation while preserving its distinctive boxy design, authentic character and strong road presence.
Congratulating Encash Automotive on the unveiling, Qadri highlighted the hassle-free vehicle financing facilities offered by J&K Bank to customers seeking to purchase their preferred vehicles. The Thar OG is priced at Rs 10.32 lakh onwards, ex-showroom. The model retains the appeal of the Thar brand while introducing changes aimed at enhancing its design, capability and suitability for everyday use.
Established in 2023, Encash Automotive currently operates at four locations across the Kashmir Valley: Athwajan and Lawaypora in Srinagar, Wanpoh in Anantnag district, and Gangoo in Pulwama district.

Taipei – A Chinese militia boat was spotted along with two other vessels off Taiwan’s Pacific coast in August, according to a surveillance report reviewed by reporters, the first known sighting of such a craft in the sensitive area.
The report by Taiwan’s Apex Aviation identifies the Minfudingyu 07902 as a fishing boat that doubles as a Chinese militia vessel, which was seen operating with a Chinese coast guard cutter and a research vessel one day in mid-August.
China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Officials in Taiwan, which rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims, say they believe China is practicing for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.

The Trump administration plans to blast famed cliffs in eastern Utah that contain historic inscriptions to make way for an oil-transporting highway, and are now being sued over the project.
Conservation groups filed a lawsuit last week against the Bureau of Land Management and its parent agency, the Interior Department, in a Utah federal court, claiming that its decision to allow Duchesne County officials to destroy the cliff walls of Gate Canyon violated several environmental and cultural preservation laws.
Gate Canyon is home to 47 historic sites and a “broad range” of wildlife, including the threatened Mexican spotted owls, according to the lawsuit.
In the 19th century, Black soldiers carved their names in the walls of Gate Canyon and European pioneers used axle grease to make their mark.
“This lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s disgraceful plan to transform a quiet backcountry road into a highway clogged with speeding oil tanker trucks,” Deeda Seed, senior Utah campaigner at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a press release.
The Center for Biological Diversity, the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, and the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance have joined forces to sue the administration, months after the Bureau of Land Management gave the green light to pave Gate Canyon.
The plan to blast Gate Canyon to make an alternative truck route to the Uinta Basin oil fields was approved by the Bureau of Land Management in April. The conservation groups claimed it was a “rushed” decision and hidden from the public.
“In the words of Joni Mitchell, the BLM has approved the 'paving of paradise.' But instead of putting in a parking lot, the BLM has given its OK to the building of a highway to carry crude oil from the Uinta Basin to Carbon County,” J. Michael Hansen, president of the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, said in the press release.
“It's like constructing a highway through the Louvre Museum."
The lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of violating laws such as the National Historic Preservation Act, the Endangered Species Act and the Federal Land Policy and Management Act.
The Bureau of Land Management has declined to comment on the lawsuit, citing “pending litigation.”
President Donald Trump, who campaigned on a “Drill, baby, drill” promise, has expanded domestic oil and gas production by reversing regulations, unleashing millions of acres of federal land and approving more than 6,000 drilling permits.
Trump said in a recent proclamation, “This month, we pledge to continue to chart a bold new course for American energy — harnessing the extraordinary abundance beneath our soil and securing a future of strength, prosperity, and independence.
“Our Nation’s energy renaissance is only just beginning, and the best is still yet to come.”
