The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that there are approximately 19 million visually impaired children in the world, and 1.4 million are blind. In India, about 3 lakh children are said to be blind. Yet, nearly half of these cases are entirely preventable or treatable if caught in time.
This month, global campaigns will urge the world to protect child eye health. There will be calls for governments around the world to unlock funding and prioritise eye care so everyone, everywhere can access the care they need along with community screening camps, eye care in schools and global pledges. And while these are vital calls, as a clinician standing on the frontlines of an outpatient department (OPD), I am forced to confront a quiet, uncomfortable truth: threats to a child’s vision are not always due to a lack of access to healthcare; they are sometimes also due to a missed opportunity to identify visual problems within healthcare systems that the child has already accessed.
What happens in the system
Consider a recent encounter in my clinic. A couple walked in with their five-year-old daughter; I will call her Anu. I could immediately see that she was visually impaired. She was one of a twin. Her parents felt that her sibling was developing normally, while she seemed to have delays in reaching developmental milestones. Gradually they started to notice that Anu could not see clearly. On examination, I found that Anu had dense bilateral cataracts with nystagmus (involuntary movement of the eyes). The presence of nystagmus says that the visual impairment had been present since infancy. When I asked why they had waited five years to seek help, they explained that they were simply overwhelmed by the weight of raising twins and assumed it was best to wait until she was older so she could ‘cooperate’ during a standard eye examination. Now they had arrived, but a bit too late.
Childhood eye diseases that cause profound visual impairment need to be detected and treated early. A baby is born with an immature visual system, and the development of vision happens through the interaction between the eye and the developing brain. When clear images do not reach the brain during this critical period, amblyopia, or lazy eye, can develop. Once this period of visual development has passed, treatment cannot fully restore the lost visual potential. Anu had lost the chance of getting back her vision fully, even if she was operated upon now.
What doesn’t get seen
Anu had not been completely outside the health system; her vaccinations were perfectly up-to-date, and she had documented encounters with health personnel seven distinct times from birth to age five. Yet, across all these visits her profound visual impairment went entirely unnoticed. Why did this happen?
One of the reasons is the poor integration of vision screening with the vaccination schedule and general paediatric screening.
India has an extensive network of frontline health workers and child health programmes. The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), for example, is designed to identify and manage health conditions in children from birth to 18 years. Screening programmes, notably have demonstrated that large numbers of school-aged children with vision problems can be screened. The tools placed in the hands of mobile health teams to detect developmental delays are proven to be highly capable of detecting developmental delays at the community level. What then is going wrong?
Let’s take the example of Karnataka. There is no published standalone government data of the number of children screened, ocular morbidity detected and treated, for the 0–6 age category. However, according to the Karnataka Health & Family Welfare Department’s Annual Report 2023–24, the State screened 62,45,424 children (6 to 16 yrs) in government and government-aided schools. But only 1.2 lakh children received spectacles, representing a distribution rate of just 1.9%. This is in sharp contrast to localised epidemiological studies in Karnataka’s southern districts, which place the actual prevalence of paediatric refractive errors as high as 8%. This pronounced gap could be due to operational challenges such as drop-outs in the multi-tier referral system and supply chain delays. A study assessing the coverage gaps in child health screening under RBSK found that only 47.4% of children detected to have health problems received further care, indicating a significant treatment gap.
Even if the system successfully flags a child, the path from detection to actual restoration of sight remains riddled with problems. Independent field evaluations in Tumkur highlight that the system has some problems when dealing with younger children and follow-up care. The management process faces significant on-the-ground challenges, including parental non-cooperation for follow-up, logistical barriers, and potential training gaps among screening teams. In my own experience, when talking to the ASHAs in Tumkur district, they said they did not have the training required to detect eye diseases in children. If the parents or caregiver of the children specifically complained about any vision related issues, the ASHAs referred them to the paediatrician who visited the taluk hospital once a week. This exposes a significant gap in training frontline workers.
Bridging gaps
There is no need for an entirely new system. We need to make better use of the system that already exists.
The red reflex test: A simple red reflex examination using the direct ophthalmoscope is one example. The test takes less than 30 seconds, does not require a child to cooperate verbally, and can identify major, sight and life-threatening abnormalities such as cataract, retinoblastoma (eye cancer) and high refractive errors. RBSK mobile health teams, primary health centre nurses, and paediatric residents must be trained to perform this test. This simple check must become as routine as measuring a child’s weight and must get incorporated in the immunisation schedule, so it is never missed.
Improving frontline training for pre-verbal visual milestones: We also need to train ASHAs in simple ways of assessing visual behaviour in infants and young children who cannot read a chart or respond reliably to conventional visual-acuity testing. Can the infant fix and follow light and objects? Is there visual engagement? Is there an abnormal or asymmetric corneal light reflex suggesting a squint? These are not sophisticated examinations. They are observations that, with appropriate training and referral protocols, can help identify children who need an eye examination.
Strengthening referral pathways from the periphery to tertiary care centre: Detection, however, is only the first step. A child identified with a possible eye problem must reach the appropriate facility where treatment is available. Referral pathways need to be clear, practical and monitored. Where possible, digital systems could link frontline screening with appointments at district or tertiary eye-care facilities. Tele-ophthalmology could also help connect peripheral health workers with specialists and reduce some of the logistical barriers that cause families to drop out of care.
Anu’s story is not simply about a child who reached an eye hospital too late. It is about a child who was already within the health system, but whose eyes were never looked at. Young children cannot be expected to understand there is a problem; parents may not recognise signs or may believe problems will resolve with age. A child should not have to reach the age of five, with dense cataracts and established nystagmus, before a visual problem that could have been detected in infancy comes to attention.
India already has an extensive network of frontline health workers, immunisation services, RBSK teams, school health programmes and primary and tertiary healthcare facilities. The challenge now is to connect these pieces. The goal should, therefore, not be merely to increase the number of children screened. It should be to build a system in which every contact with a child is an opportunity to protect vision, every abnormal finding triggers a clear referral, and every referral is followed through to care.
As we mark World Sight Day, the question we should ask is not only how do we reach more children. It is also how many children are already within our health system whom we are failing to see. For children like Anu, finding the problem a few years earlier can mean the difference between having sight and living a life with visual disability, because preventing blindness in a child is not merely about saving sight. It is about protecting education, independence and the opportunity to reach their full potential.
(Dr. Vasudha Kemmanu is a paediatric ophthalmologist and a public eye health specialist at Narayana Nethralaya, Rajaji Nagar, Bengaluru. vasudhakemmanu@gmail.com)

The image is a doctored version of a real Truth Social post from Trump’s account. The sentence about Musk did not appear in Trump's original post.
In October 2026, a screenshot of an alleged post from U.S. President Donald Trump's Truth Social account spread online, showing Trump seemingly thanking billionaire Elon Musk for artificially increasing Republican votes ahead of the November 2026 midterms.
The purported post (archived) stated:
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool—Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dummods with massive turnout! THANKS TO THE GREAT ELON MUSK EVERY REPUBLICAN VOTE COUNTS AS 3 VOTES! SO IMPORTANT - PLEASE GET OUT AND VOTE, AND MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President Donald J. Trump
(@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The above post is a doctored version of a real Truth Social post from Trump's account. The yellow highlighted line about Musk was edited into the post. As such, we rate this image as fake.
On Oct. 3, 2026, Trump wrote (archived) the following post on Truth Social. The fake highlighted line about Musk was added after "we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout!":
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool — Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout! SO IMPORTANT — PLEASE GET OUT AND VOTE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP
swampthevoteusa.com/
(@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The post in the screenshot is clearly edited, based on the nonsense phrase "Dummods" which appears to be a garbled version of "Dumocrats."
Snopes also looked up variations of the phrase on Trump's Truth, a website that archives his posts "every few minutes" and makes it easier to find them — including deleted posts. There was no evidence of Trump thanking Musk on Truth Social for making "every Republican vote" count as three votes.
Trump has been speaking at campaign rallies nationwide, trying to drum up support for Republican candidates ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections.
For further reading, Snopes has debunked numerous posts falsely attributed to Trump over the years.

I've got my own questions on Man City case - Carrick
- Published
Manchester United boss Michael Carrick still has his "own questions" over the Manchester City case which he says "affected me personally".
There is a clamour among some for Manchester City to be stripped of their silverware and also be relegated after they were found guilty of multiple Premier League financial rule breaches.
The 45-year-old was on the pitch at Sunderland when he learned City had won their first Premier League title in 2012 thanks to Sergio Aguero's legendary injury time match winner.
He was still part of Jose Mourinho's squad when United finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City side in 2018 and was part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching staff when it happened again in 2020-21.
However, Carrick says getting a title winners' medal years after the event would not make up for missing out at the time.
"In football, the strive to win, the emotion and the feeling about winning, a lot of it is in the moment," he said.
"You can't take that back. It's the moment you strive for. That's essentially what we're all in it for. That's the feeling we all crave.
"The beauty of trying to win trophies is a little bit the journey towards it and then the finale. Does it go for you, does it go against you? Once that's done, there's no getting that back in any direction.
"I'm not getting blasé about it, but regardless of anything, in any sport in history, if later on you get the medal, it doesn't bring the feeling of when you initially win or you don't."
An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
Manchester City have appealed against the decision. City boss Enzo Maresca has said he "trusts" his own club.
If the appeal adheres to strict Premier League guidelines, it should be concluded by Christmas Day, with a verdict to follow in the early part of 2027.
Carrick does not know how the situation will play out. However, as a very close bystander to the event, he feels there has to be a speedy resolution.
"It's thrown up a lot of questions," he said. "Some had answers, some haven't.
"Certainly, I've got my own questions about it. It's affected me personally in different ways over a period of time.
"As it's still not finalised, I think I'll hold that one (whether titles should be reassigned) until later on.
"What I will say is that the sooner it gets sorted, for everyone's benefit, is essential.
"It's unprecedented, a unique situation to be in at this level, with such a huge impact in so many ways. We all need to know what's going to happen."
Meanwhile, United's fans have delivered their own verdict by getting a 'ticker' banner showing the years since Manchester City last won a trophy rehung from the Stretford End.
The banner was initially displayed in 2000, at which point it was 24 years since City's last silverware - the 1976 League Cup.
It was increased by one each year until 2011 when City finally ended their trophy drought by beating Stoke City in the FA Cup final.
However, fans have a new version to display for this weekend's visit of Tottenham to Old Trafford, with the number 50 - signalling the years since their 1976 League Cup triumph, their final silverware before Sheikh Mansour bought the club.

For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”
In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.
An uninterrupted trip
Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.
Volunteers went through the same four-part sequence twice, once sober and once on psilocybin. The sequence included putting participants in four different settings or contexts: eight minutes of lying at rest, a guided meditation, an 11-minute curated music playlist, and finally six minutes of eyes-open video of clouds moving across a sky. Each participant did all four inside an MRI scanner about 80 minutes after dosing, and again on EEG about 150 minutes after.
There were no cognitive tasks researchers routinely go for in brain studies, but there was a purpose behind this omission.
“We wanted ecological validity,” Stoliker says. “We wanted to know what the brain was like when somebody was having an authentic, uninterrupted psychedelic experience. If somebody took a psychedelic in a therapeutic setting, you wouldn’t have them completing tasks.” Stoliker also points out that there’s evidence that giving someone a task mid-trip pulls them out of the state—a phenomenon researchers sometimes call grounding. “Once you introduce these sorts of tasks, you’re actually interrupting the very phenomena you are seeking to measure.” And it worked.

Margaret Hamilton, who coined the term “software engineering” and led the development of onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo program in the 1960s, died last week at the age of 90. A recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, Hamilton was also immortalized as a LEGO minifig the following year—part of the “Women of NASA” set that also included astronauts Mae Jemison and Sally Ride.
“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer—to say she was ahead of her time—would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” said Olivier de Weck, interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success.”
Born in 1936 in Paoli, Indiana, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a degree in mathematics and a minor in philosophy—the latter a nod to her father (a poet) and grandfather (a headmaster). She married her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, that same year. The plan was for her to work until he finished his law degree, after which he would support her through graduate school to earn a PhD in mathematics.
She ended up working for Edward Lorenz, the MIT mathematician who set out to construct a mathematical model of the weather using a set of differential equations representing changes in temperature, pressure, wind velocity, and the like. You’ve probably heard the famous story of how Lorenz kept a continuous simulation running on his LGP-30 computer, and of that fateful 1961 day when he realized that even small differences in starting values could lead to very different outcomes—a sensitivity to initial conditions that is a hallmark of chaos theory, along with strange attractors. You might not have known that it was Hamilton who was responsible for programming the LGP-30.

Keralam Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan’s statement at a recent function about avoiding unnecessary angioplasty seems to have stirred a hornets’ nest with many doctors objecting to the “generalised statement,” while some lone voices pointed out that Mr. Satheesan was 100% right and that unnecessary procedures had become the norm.
In a Facebook post, Rajesh Gopalan Nair, Professor and Head of Cardiology at the Government Medical College Hospital, Kozhikode, had appreciated Mr. Satheesan “for pointing out a truth.” But it set off an avalanche of comments from the doctors and public, with the latter narrating their harrowing experiences in hospitals and appreciating Dr. Rajesh for calling a spade a spade, while many doctors expressed disappointment at Dr. Rajesh’s stand.
Dr. Rajesh, however, made it clear in his post that a person coming into the emergency with a suspected heart attack should in no way distrust the doctor, for the situation may call for an immediate angioplasty.
Second opinion
He also explained clearly the situations when one could afford to wait and seek a second opinion, if angioplasty was suggested to a patient. He also cautioned the public against looking at every doctor or hospital with suspicion. Angioplasty should definitely be done when it is clinically indicated and these situations are clearly documented, he said.
Even though much of the medical fraternity expressed their displeasure at the “unsubstantiated” statement of the Chief Minister and the support that unexpectedly seemed to have come from one of their own, Dr. Rajesh refused to be cowed down. He maintained that he stood by his position that some of the angioplasty procedures done in hospitals were indeed not warranted.
On Monday, the Interventional Cardiology Council of Kerala (ICCK) said in a statement here that public’s apprehension over “unnecessary” medical procedures should not delay life-saving treatment during a heart attack emergency.
Responding to the Chief Minister’s remarks on avoiding unnecessary investigations and angioplasty, the council said it supported evidence-based and ethical medical practice and the principle that every intervention must have a clear clinical indication.
ICCK president Rajesh T. said that public discussion on angioplasty should clearly differentiate between elective intervention in stable patients and primary angioplasty during an acute heart attack, where treatment is highly time-sensitive.
What the data show
According to Statewide ICCK registry data presented at the council’s last annual conference, more than 70% of angioplasties performed in Kerala involved acute and emergency clinical situations.
He said the council welcomed any discussion aimed at strengthening evidence-based care, transparency and public confidence in the health-care system. “In stable patients, there is usually greater scope for detailed evaluation and for deciding whether medicines, further assessment or intervention would offer the greatest benefit. In an acute heart attack, however, delay can have serious consequences,” ICCK said.
However, the council cautioned that a general atmosphere of mistrust surrounding cardiac procedures could have unintended consequences, particularly when a patient develops severe chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of a heart attack.

Isaias kills four, about 670,000 without power after landfall
PENSACOLA, Florida: Four people died after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday (Oct 10), and about 670,000 residents in Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi were still without power as the storm weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, according to local authorities and electricity monitoring services.
Two of the deaths resulted from trees falling on homes, according to local media and authorities.
Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said. But hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast were expected, the National Hurricane Center said.
The tornado threat is expected to continue on Saturday across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said.
In Florida, power restoration was marked as a priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage.
"They're going to make assessments this morning, and I think that'll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration," DeSantis told a press conference in Tallahassee. Some 16,000 utility linemen had prepared to respond to the storm, he said.
About 420,000 customers in Florida, 190,000 in Alabama, 43,000 in Georgia and 17,000 in Mississippi had no power as of midday Saturday, according to tracking firm PowerOutage.us.
A separate storm on the Pacific Ocean, Rachel, was moving toward the coast of northern Baja California on Saturday, bringing wind gusts and increased tides, which left another 7,000 people without power in California.
Alabama's emergency management agency said the downed trees and power lines made travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning.
"Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X.
A category 2 hurricane when it hit Florida's coast and the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, Isaias is expected to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said.
On Saturday, oil and gas producer Shell said it was beginning to redeploy personnel to its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets in the Gulf, whileChevron was advancing efforts to redeploy staff to its platforms and seeking to restore full production. "Remobilization of crews will continue through Sunday," it said.
Despite the progress, about 69 per cent of oil output and 57 per cent of natural gas production in the US Gulf of Mexico remained shut on Saturday, slightly down from Friday numbers, the Marine Minerals Administration said.
Some 113 production platforms representing 30 per cent of the total remained evacuated, according to the agency.

The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay for her work as a judge and human rights lawyer, at a time when the committee said international law faces “tremendous pressure” and its institutions are “under attack.”
Pillay, 85, has “held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict,” the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in a statement on Friday, calling her “one of the great defenders of international legal principles.”
Pillay is currently serving as a judge at the International Court of Justice, in The Hague, in the case in which Myanmar stands accused of genocide. Last year, she chaired the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which investigated Israel’s retaliatory war in Gaza and concluded that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration had committed genocide against Palestinians, a finding that the Israeli government firmly denounced.

More Japanese companies have revealed that they have experienced major customer data breaches due to cyberattacks.
JR East said that about 6.09 million customer accounts may have been compromised, while JR Kyushu said about 1.3 million customer accounts may have been compromised. Both were a result of a ransomware attack on IDC Frontier, a cloud services subsidiary of SoftBank, they said Friday.
Bookoff Group Holdings, a secondhand goods retailer, reported that its subsidiary responsible for managing membership data had suffered unauthorized access, possibly resulting in a data breach affecting up to 6.43 million customers.
Daiichikosho, the operator of the Big Echo karaoke chain, also said personal information on about 8.72 million customers may have been compromised due to unauthorized access to a system managed by an external contractor.
Adventure Inc., the operator of the Skyticket travel booking website, reported a potential breach involving about 14.64 million sets of personal information, following a cyberattack on its servers and the business management system for its booking website.
The potentially affected information includes email addresses at JR East and customer names, dates of birth and telephone numbers at the other three companies. Adventure said it had confirmed that credit card and passport numbers had not leaked.
The companies respectively said that they had found no evidence of unauthorized use of the affected information by third parties. They are urging customers to watch out for suspicious emails and phone calls.

University leaders warn they’re struggling to fill international student places due to visa uncertainty and heated political debate on immigration, with regional areas hit the hardest amid concern that financial deficits could affect domestic students.
The latest numbers from the Department of Education in October show on average universities are filling just two-thirds of their allocated places, and just five public universities have reached more than 80% capacity, all in capital cities.
Mike Ferguson, pro vice-chancellor of international students at Charles Sturt University, which has campuses across regional New South Wales, said his institution has filled just 40% of its cap this year.
“At the moment, we’re around 35% down on where we were last year, and we had expected to grow from last year,” Ferguson said. “Currently we only have 20% of the international student volume we had prior to the pandemic.”
Charles Sturt has estimated the gap between international student recruitments pre-Covid and now is costing $35m, and the university has announced job cuts and restructuring in response.
Ferguson attributed the fall to government policy, including hiking visa applications to $2,500, high refusal rates, and growing uncertainty from announcements by the Coalition and One Nation targeting international students.
He said regional universities primarily recruited students from south Asian countries, which were experiencing higher visa refusal rates of about 53%.
“It’s not only resulting in us losing what we believe to be largely genuine students … but it’s also creating a large deterrent from new students to come in and apply, knowing they’re having to pay world record visa fees with only a one in two chance of actually getting a visa,” Ferguson said.
But he said the university did support Labor’s decision to crack down on onshore student transfers and visa hopping to improve integrity in the system.
Prof Andrew Norton, an expert in higher education, said the declining numbers were affecting all public universities because they cross-subsidise their teaching and research with international student fees.
“It creates massive problems because international students are basically the only profitable aspect of university operations,” he said.
Duncan Bentley, vice-chancellor of Federation University in regional Victoria, said he too supported those measures but that his university was also facing significant pressures with far fewer international students enrolling this year.
The university has pushed the government for a special regional skills student visa that would prioritise international students wanting to do courses in critical areas such as allied health or teaching.
“We endorse, and have been asking for a long time for, the 12-month ban on course hopping, apart from exceptional and genuine circumstances,” Bentley said.
“The criteria for this regional visa would be any overseas student who wants to come and study in a regional university can have access to a special visa … the course should be on a regional skills shortage list, based on the premise that domestic regional graduates can’t meet the demand.”
Western Sydney University vice-chancellor, George Williams, said his university had also experienced significant declines in overseas students and warned the financial deficits could have an impact on domestic students.
“It has an enormous impact on our budget and it means universities across the sector are asking where they can save money, where they can pull back,” Williams said.
“In our case, international students heavily subsidise domestic students, and it puts real pressure on the services we can offer to domestic students.”
Williams also said international students were being deterred by the heated political debate, “which would lead people to wonder whether they would be welcome in Australia”.
Adelaide University told the ABC in September it had only reached 60% of its international student capacity, after its merger with the University of South Australia, creating a potential $90m revenue shortfall.
The government’s 2026 planning level for international students was set at 295,000, and so far it’s tracking towards 250,000, which is just above the Coalition’s proposed level of 240,000.
Labor will also reduce the number of international students eligible to bring family to Australia while they study, while the Coalition has promised to abolish temporary graduate visas.
Phil Honeywood, chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia, said diminishing international student numbers in regional areas could also lead to critical skills shortages.
“The high non-refundable visa cost makes the system more like a lottery ticket,” Honeywood said.
“There’s not enough nurses, childcare workers, aged care workers or engineers in regional communities … so basically if you have diminishing numbers of international students in these regional areas and they’re not able to stay past their degrees, that creates a cascading skill shortage.”

Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 147, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, I missed you all, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
The techlash has gone Hollywood
Plus, in this week’s Installer: Amazon’s new tablet, a new book on the AI industry, Star Wars racing, and more.
I’m back from parental leave! Part time, anyway. Thanks to everyone who sent well wishes and tips for managing three kids. I need ’em all. This week, I’ve been reading about McMansions and data centers and sports cardsand ICANN, trying to run my life on the Dell XPS Googlebook, testing a new and very purple Kindle, reinventing my whole note-taking system now that Google Docs can handle Markdown files, listening to episode after episode of No Such Thing as a Fish,and watching all of Shrinkingbetween the hours of 1 and 5AM while feeding a baby.
I also have for you the new Facebook movie, a tech-related procedural, a couple of great new gadgets, the Star Wars game that is going to destroy my productivity, a terrific book about the AI industry, and much more. Let’s do this.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What have you been watching / reading / playing / listening to / putting in the air fryer this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The Social Reckoning. My hopes were not super high for this movie, and the reaction so far suggests it’s good but a far cry from The Social Network. (Which I just watched recently, and absolutely still rips.) Still, Aaron Sorkin and Jeremy Strong will end up in the annals of Big Tech Movies, and I will not be missing this one.
- The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. For the first time ever, Amazon decided — and I know this might sound far-fetched — to just build an awesome tablet. And it seems it may have! There’s lots of testing to do, and I’m particularly curious about this high-end model with the fancy screen, but I’m hopeful this is the “iPad but cheaper” we’ve been waiting for. For years.
- The AGI Chronicles. However bizarre you think the AI industry is, I promise Kevin Roose’s book will convince you it’s even more so. Roose has been deep inside the AI labs for the last few years, and I think came out with the most important story in AI: how a few executives, and the relationships between them, somehow came to determine the future of everything.
- Star Wars: Galactic Racer. It’s a super high-fidelity Star Wars racing game in which you (eventually) get to pilot a podracer. That’s all I needed to hear! Oh, and if you’re a Prime subscriber, you can play it for free on Amazon’s Luna service.
- Cupertino. The folks who made The Good Wife made a show about technology, and it is exactly what you think it is. I kind of love it! What I’ve seen so far is pretty thoughtful about some complicated real-life legal stuff in tech and AI, and the procedural setup is frankly a nice break from all these miniseries and four-hour docs.
- The Surface Laptop Ultra. Microsoft revealed all the details of its most impressive laptop, and while it’s expensive ($2,600!), it also looks and sounds fantastic. Microsoft is pushing the device’s AI capabilities, but this also looks like the uncompromising MacBook Pro competition a lot of Windows users might want.
- Gears of War: E-Day. When it comes to raw, brutal combat, Gears doesn’t miss very often. This one also seems to deliver on story and exploration, which aren’t always the series’ strong points; a lot of people have been waiting for the origin-story title, and I’m thrilled the game pulls it off.
- Blockers. Michael Lewis tells the story of Elon Musk and DOGE, and in particular of the government employees who tried to stop them from running roughshod over the federal government. I really enjoyed The Fifth Risk, Lewis’ last book about the government, and I expect to like this one too.
One thing about parental leave is that it involves a lot of time with one hand free. Over the last seven weeks I’ve spent dozens, maybe hundreds of hours on the couch while a tiny potato of a baby sleeps or cries or farts on top of me. So what did I do with all that time? Goofed around on my phone, mostly. Too much Reddit, too much TikTok, mercifully at least a little reading and crosswording.
I also redid my entire homescreen, because of course I did, and I figured I’d share. Here’s my current setup:
The phone: iPhone 17. I have no desire to upgrade to the 18… but I find myself hopelessly lusting after a Duo. I must not give in.
The wallpaper: Black. I am on an endless quest to make my phone less interesting to look at, and this helps. It also helps make my phone a little less blaring when I’m looking at it in the dark, which I do a lot these days.
The apps: Unread, Instapaper, Google Maps, Capacities, Daygame, Flora, Phone, Pocket Casts, Spotify, Camera, Prism, Mimestream, Arc.
A few things I want to mention here:
- The widgets at the top are Calendars and Acme Weather. Acme is a fabulous weather app, and I love the hourly widget; Calendars is, like, fine. I switch between it and Fantastical all the time. I don’t think I like any calendar app.
- The only truly new things on my homescreen are Flora and Prism. Flora is a journaling app currently in TestFlight for Apple devices, and it is fabulous. It’s simple and straightforward, but also pulls in workout data, photos, and more to give a really cool snapshot of your day. Prism is a note-taking app that is as fast as texting yourself but with many more organizational powers. I have spent forever looking for a quick, transient way to jot stuff down and organize it later; Prism might be it.
- In case you’re following my endless search for notes apps: I’m back on Capacities, which finally clicked for me. It is a project to get the app fully customized, but it turns out to work exactly like my brain does.
- I switched from Readwise Reader to Instapaper because I recently bought a Kobo, and Instapaper is so nicely integrated into the device. I like the whole setup, but also the Boox Palma 3 is coming, so my reading universe might be in for yet another overhaul soon.
- Daygame, in the middle there, is a thing I built for myself to manage all the daily games I play — it’s just a page full of links to games, which open in various apps and tabs. I might try and spruce it up and share it more widely. Send games I should include!
Before I forget, a few more recommendations from my parental leave:
- Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die. Maybe the strangest movie I watched over the last couple of months, and certainly the one that made me think the most about tech and AI and the future we’re heading toward.
- Tuner. A movie about a piano tuner who falls into a world of safecracking. Nothing I say about this movie will make it sound compelling, but I promise: It’s great.
- Furious. One of the most intense, propulsive crime shows I’ve seen in forever. Could barely put it down.
- Footnotes. A really cool (Apple-only) journaling and notes app, with emphasis on taking pictures and video right next to your notes. One of the most uniquely designed mobile apps I’ve ever used.
- Podcast Shuffle. I had no idea I needed this app until I tried it. You just press a button, and it randomly plays an episode from whatever podcast or podcasts you’ve selected. I use it for falling asleep, I use it for long drives, I love not having to scroll just to get something playing.

Lok Bhavan, the office and residence of West Bengal Governor R N Ravi, formerly known as Raj Bhavan, has declared a state-level essay writing competition for students from schools, colleges, and universities. The circular published on October 3 mentions two topics: Calcutta Massacre, 1946 – Causes and Consequences for students of Classes X to XII, and Direct Action Day by All India Muslim League – A Fatal Assault on Civilisational Bharat for college and university goers.
The competition carries handsome monetary awards going up to Rs 1,00,000.
Both the topics relate to the Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946) also known as the ‘1946 Calcutta Riots’ and ‘Great Calcutta Killings’ which marked the beginning of a period of communal violence in Bengal that preceded and followed Partition.
However, the choice of topics raises questions because they do not seem to be framed neutrally. The term ‘Civilisational Bharat’ is ideologically loaded and is not standard historical terminology, and it gives the topic a distinctly Hindu nationalist framing.
Secondly, while the Calcutta killings of 1946 and Direct Action Day are important subjects for understanding the events leading up to Partition, the phrase ‘a fatal assault on civilisational Bharat’ embeds a particular ideological interpretation into the topic, rather than inviting students to examine the political circumstances, the causes and consequences of the violence and the competing narratives around it.
The wording is also problematic because it turns a complex period of history into a communal binary, with the Muslim League positioned as an assailant and ‘Bharat’ as the entity under attack. It is not just the inclusion of a controversial historical event that is concerning, but also the communal framing through which students are being asked to approach it.
Anwesha Sengupta, author and assistant professor of history at the Institute of Development Studies, Kolkata (ISDK), views the initiation of this competition in schools and colleges as an attempt to push a certain narrative and memory of the Direct Action Day and 1946 Calcutta riots.
“The history of the 1946 riots is very complicated. The government has, in recent times, tried to turn this event into an opportune moment for a particular brand of history-writing. The chief minister himself has routinely referred to it, in his speeches and on social media, helping create the figure of the ‘other’, in the demography of Bengali Muslims,” she said.
Sengupta also pointed out that one needed to have a certain degree of academic maturity to teach or write about riots. “How can school and college students be incentivised to turn out well-researched essays on this topic?” she questioned.
The essay competition notification comes close on the heels of another student-centric initiative by the West Bengal government that drew scrutiny for its political content. Alt News recently reported on the ‘Namo Seva: Untold Stories’ play, part of a month-long programme marking Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and 25 years in public service. The play, which was staged by students at schools and colleges, eulogised PM Modi on his achievements.
The play script sent out by West Bengal government to schools and colleges makes actors (which means students) shout ‘Jai Sri Ram’ and ‘Modi hai to Mumkin hai’ or wonder how ‘Modiji has been working tirelessly day and night for the last 25 years.’

India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India's youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Police intercepted demonstrators before they could reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.
The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators.
Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.
Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.
The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July.
Police detain leaders and tighten grip around protest site
Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.
"The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement.
Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas.
Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.
"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights," said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?"
The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.
"Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press.
India's voter list dispute raises election fairness concerns
The protests center on India's Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Saturday's planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.
Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi's party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists.
The commission and the government deny the allegations.
India's youth movement broadens campaign against Modi
For the "Cockroach" movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.
The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.
For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi's home state, will test the party's standing.

Top management officials of some of the four major beer makers suspected of a price cartel are believed to have been informed of details of shipping price hikes negotiated among the companies, informed sources have said.
The Japan Fair Trade Commission is investigating whether these top officials recognized that the information was a result of negotiations, the sources said Friday.
According to the sources, some officials of the companies — Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Sapporo Breweries and Suntory Holdings — have admitted to the cartel during the commission’s investigation.
Officials from the companies are believed to have held unofficial talks after industry group meetings to exchange information on the timing and scale of shipping price increases and compile price tables.
On Wednesday, the commission conducted compulsory inspections of the headquarters of the four companies on suspicion of violating the Antimonopoly Act.
Under the act, companies found to have engaged in illegal price fixing can face penalties, including financial surcharges and orders to prevent further violations. Unlike routine administrative inspections, compulsory investigations allow authorities to search premises and seize evidence under court warrants, typically in cases considered particularly serious or damaging to consumers.
The four companies, which collectively control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market, are suspected of coordinating the timing and scale of price increases for beer, low-malt beer and other beer-like beverages over several years.

Four-time World Champion Max Verstappen crossed the finish line to take pole position for Redbull Racing at the Marina Bay circuit in Singapore on October 10.
This pole position follows an earlier victory in the afternoon sprint race at the same venue and marks fifty pole positions for Max Verstappen. Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and teammate Lewis Hamilton qualified second and third respectively.
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli meanwhile had to settle for fourth place, while his teammate George Russell will have to start from the back of the grid during the main race, following a power unit penalty.
Russell wasn’t the only driver to be caught out in the wet conditions. He was one of eight non-finishers after a spate of collisions and technical problems, with Red Bull Racing’s Isack Hadjar stopped by car trouble.
Verstappen said Red Bull will need to work on its “horrendous” starts after he lost the sprint lead off the line, just as he did in Malaysia last week.
“We don’t accelerate off the line,” he said. “Up until now we always have terrible starts so we need to understand what’s going on there.”
The qualifying and the sprint race start was delayed because of heavy rain, making it the second week running that an F1 race has started late. Last week’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at Sepang was first held up by a downpour, then because several cars’ software failed to cope with the wet conditions.

Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.
Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.
Meanwhile, heavy rainfall in Nepal last week resulted in 542 disaster incidents and left 27 people dead between 24 and 27 September, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Of the recorded incidents, 304 were related to landslides while 87 were linked to flooding.
During this extremely wet period, 186 meteorological sites recorded more than 100mm of rainfall, with Dedhgaun, in Lumbini province, recording 544.2mm. Nearly a million people received SMS flood warnings, and 2,000 people living in high-risk areas were relocated.
This heavy rainfall also affected the Gandak River in Bihar, north-east India, which reached a record water level of 91.25 metres on Tuesday, 0.35m metres above the previous record, set only in 2024, according to the water resources department. So far, 169 seepage points along the embankments have been repaired, with teams deployed across several sites along the river as the embankments continue to face heavy water pressure.
Strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal flooding have hit the north-east US as a very deep area of low pressure developed into a nor’easter on Saturday. Such storms are named due to the north-easterly winds typically affecting coastal areas. This was the first nor’easter of the autumn and winter season, bringing gusts of up to 74mph (119km/h) and waves rising to 3 metres.
The storm left approximately 200,000 people without power, inundated the streets of New York City and killed one person when a tree fell in Brooklyn. However, the storm also uncovered a piece of history as the wreckage from the Warren Sawyer, a three-masted ship destroyed in 1884, washed ashore on Nantucket, off Cape Cod in Massachusetts.

NABVENTURES, the venture capital arm of the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has announced the first close of its second fund at ₹450 Cr. The firm, which invests in early to growth stage agritech startups, is targeting a corpus of ₹1,500 Cr for the fund. This also includes a greenshoe option. India's apex agriculture focused financial institution NABARD is the anchor investor in the fund The investment arm intends to double down on early and growth stage startups using tech to address challenges across the agricultural value chain and rural markets. A company called Steakholder Foods has launched a line of products under the brand name Perfecta. While the meat is 3D-printed, it is made from a formulation of plant material like other plant-based meats are. It is not made from cultured animal cells, which is often what people refer to when they mention "lab-grown meat." It is not clear which grocery stores or retailers are selling Perfecta-branded food, though the company has said its products have reached shelves in certain Northeastern U.S retail locations.
Between September and October, social media users claimed that 3D-printed, lab-grown meat had started being sold in U.S. stores from early September.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claims the 3D-printed meat "has federal clearance" but will not have a "lab-grown meat" label on its packaging. The post reads, in part:
The first 3D printed 'meat' has federal clearance and is about to be sold in the United States.
Packaging will not say 'lab-grown meat' because there is not a law that requires the packaging to say it was printed.
3D-printed plant-based food is already on shelves in the U.S.
Federal labels for cell-grown chicken and pork fat must be pre-approved and have used the words "cell-cultivated."
The printed food was in stores on September 3 of this year.
The company Steakholder Foods put its Perfecta line into Northeast supermarkets.
The rumor has appeared elsewhere on Facebook (archived) and on Instagram (archived). Numerous Snopes readers also emailed us to ask if the story is true.
In short, on Sept. 3, Israeli company Steakholder Foods, which specializes in making 3D-printing technology for plant-based meats, announced the launch of its 3D-printed, plant-based meat products in Northeastern U.S. retailers under the brand name Perfecta. Therefore, the claim is true.
Steakholder Foods' news release says its "Premium Plant-Based Meat" products were launched at retail locations in the Northeastern United States on Sept. 3, "marking the brand's first commercial placement on U.S. store shelves."
According to the webpage, the launch "focuses on building awareness and consumer trial throughout the Northeast U.S. market while establishing a foundation for broader expansion across additional regions."
It is not clear which grocery stores or retailers have started selling or stocking the products.
Snopes reached out to the company via a contact form on its website for more information. We will update this article if we hear back.
According to Steakholder Foods, the company uses plant-based ingredients and cultivates cells to create what ultimately becomes the 3D-printed meat.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service do regulate "lab-grown" meat and require a label for such products. However, this regulation is specifically for food made with cultured animal cells, not for food made with other kinds of cells, which is what Perfecta products consist of.
Snopes reached out to both the FDA via contact form and the FSIS via email to confirm that there are not similar kinds of regulations for food made with other cultured cells, such as plant cells. Additionally, we asked both agencies to confirm if Perfecta products had received federal approval, as the above Facebook post states. We will update this story if we receive responses.
Based on how the product boxes appear on the website, there does not appear to be any text identifying the food as 3D-printed or made with cultured cells. The boxes do clearly identify the meat as "premium plant meat" and "plant-based."
Manufacturers of plant-based meat products usually have to process their ingredient mixes in a way that allows them to mimic the texture of conventional meat. According to the Good Food Institute's Asia-Pacific website, the most common processing method requires putting shear stress on the ingredients to align them into a meat-like texture. There are several other methods of processing plant-based meats, including 3D-printing.
For further reading, Snopes previously fact-checked a claim that a plant-based meat manufacturer was 3D-printing meat products in the Netherlands in 2024.

As Amitabh Bachchan prepares to celebrate his 84th birthday on October 11, producer Anand Pandit has announced an initiative to honour the legendary actor through educational support for young people. Anand Pandit to offer scholarships to 1,000 students as part of celebrating the 84th birthday of Amitabh Bachchan

Opinion: Can I keep the baseball I caught?
Opinion: Can I keep the baseball I caught?
This week, an ethical question, of all things, intruded into the baseball playoffs.
Tuesday night, Dodgers versus Braves, in Atlanta. A young man in a Dodger jersey caught a foul ball in the stands. As so often happens these days, someone seated nearby captured it on video, and then felt compelled to instruct the man, "Give it to the kid! Give it to the kid!"
And indeed there was a small boy, maybe preschool-aged, a few rows back in a Braves jersey.
But the Dodgers fan looked into the man's camera and told what turned out to be millions of viewers on social media, "I'm sorry, I can't! I'm not giving it to the kid! I feel bad, but I'm not giving it to the kid!"
Some commenters denounced the man for keeping the ball. Some others have inveighed against the little boy for looking disappointed.
Before we criticize anyone's ethics, we ought to ask ourselves: what would we do if a baseball fell into our hands at a playoff game? Keep it, or give it to the nearest child?
Because I am a father, I'm pretty certain I would give it to a child. But also because I'm a father, I know that within a few days, the ball so tenderly bequeathed might have rolled, abandoned, under a bed, surrounded by lost socks and forgotten Labubus.
Also, a foul ball hit by almost any player would be a nice souvenir. But what if it had been a home run struck by, say, Shohei Ohtani? That ball could be as much of an investment as a Picasso!
We sought ethical advice from Nancy Sherman, a Professor of Philosophy at Georgetown University, who told us, "Manners are not morals."
The professor said she was mostly alarmed by the public shaming of both man and boy, who, after all, were not aware that their instinctive, personal reactions would soon be turned into some kind of moral exercise for the digital age.
"The young guy who caught the ball says, 'I'm sorry…I feel bad, but I'm not giving it to the kid'"… says Professor Sherman. "I think that's a healthy, honest response."
So the next time you go to a game - if a fly ball seems to be arcing your way, you might pause before you reach for it to ask yourself, "Do I really want this ethical dilemma?"

The Museo de Historia de la Computación in Spain has unveiled a 1:1 scale visual replica of the famous Cray-1 supercomputer from 1976. Instead of sourcing expensive, cutting-edge tech to run the system, the creative team powered the project with 30 2012-era Mac Minis. Developed over 18 months, the project serves as a 50th-anniversary tribute to the Cray-1 and Apple’s founding.
Mac Minis from over a decade ago might not seem like the obvious first choice for building a cluster supercomputer, but when networked together, the developers can orchestrate the 64 active processing cores into a combined 1.3 teraflops of performance in their most recent tests. The museum reportedly achieved 1.5 teraflops previously using all 70 available cores, prior to one node going offline. Benchmarks were obtained using a custom matrix-multiplication Python script. Five PCs are quad-core i7s, and the remaining 25 are dual-core i5 models. Except for two units from 2014, the rest of the array dates to 2012.
The replica is a valuable tool for museum-goers to understand the shifts in computer architecture since 1976. The original Cray-1 used vector processing, applying a single instruction to multiple data elements simultaneously, whereas the replica distributes work across independent processors in a parallel cluster. The peak theoretical performance of the original Cray-1 was approximately 160 megaflops. What was originally a purpose-built research machine has been re-created with consumer hardware that’s vastly more capable than the machine that inspired it.
Rather than opting for a more standard Linux distribution, the team found that macOS Mojave (10.14) met their project needs by harnessing macOS’s built-in support for MPI (Message Passing Interface), the software layer that allows all the nodes in the cluster to pass tasks to one another.
Guests at the Museo de Historia de la Computación can watch in real time as the system runs matrix algorithms, mapping the scale of system performance from a single core to the full suite running in parallel.
Stealth supercomputing
Combining 30 consumer PCs into an operational cluster wasn’t the only engineering challenge the team faced. If you’ve ever stepped inside a server room, or, like me, foolishly installed one in your own basement, you know that fan cooling can be loud. The museum team used passive convection cooling via a steel rack chassis and aluminum tray mounts for each Mac Mini. Compared to the roaring thunder of a modern data center, this cluster is nearly inaudible.

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.
Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy revenues, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.
Trump's announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.
Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.
Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."
Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal
The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.
Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel futures prices dipped on Friday's news, the national average price per gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.
A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."
Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."
The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement.
Trump and Putin's deal draws immediate backlash
Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.
"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.
Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."
"This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels."
The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Treasury Department moves to ease diesel sanctions for six months
Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.
This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war.
The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year.
The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine.
Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine's repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told state news agency Tass that Russia is "immediately starting to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule." He said that Moscow could start supplies to the U.S. already in October, and that Russia's domestic market will be "fully supplied" with diesel, as well.

The increased instances of indigenous and imported cases of malaria over the past five years have left the health authorities a worried lot.
Imported malaria is acquired outside Keralam, while indigenous malaria is acquired through local transmission, when a local mosquito picks up the parasite from an infected person and transmits it to another person.
Going by the Health department statistics, as of October 5, four confirmed indigenous cases were reported in 2026, and 974 imported cases.
One death due to indigenous malaria and six deaths due to imported cases have been reported this year. Last year, no deaths due to indigenous cases were reported, while two deaths occurred due to imported cases.
The number of cases began to rise after 2021, when 252 imported and one indigenous death case were reported. The highest number of indigenous cases was reported from Malappuram, Kozhikode, and Kannur. Kollam, which earlier showed a high incidence of these cases, is in a recovery phase.
Health officials attribute the abundance of mosquitoes and the frequent influx of travellers to the increase in the number of infections.
“Over the past several years, the number of imported malaria cases has increased substantially. We need to strengthen surveillance measures, screening of migrants for the disease and ensuring intensive screening and testing for the disease in asymptomatic fever cases,” said the official.
The Health department plans to introduce insecticide-treated bed nets, which will kill mosquitoes on contact, in houses in regions where indigenous cases are reported. Steps are being taken to intensify malaria prevention activities to prevent the development of malaria-endemic regions in the State,” said the official.
“The increasing number of malaria cases in the past few years is a concern,” said. T.S. Anish, associate professor, School of Public Health, Kerala University of Health Sciences, Thiruvananthapuram.
“The consistent efforts by the Health department back in the 1960s succeeded in freeing the State from malaria. However, with increased travel and the influx of the migrant population from disease-endemic regions, malaria cases are getting reported. The delay in timely detection and intervention measures will contribute to the rise of indigenous cases. The local conditions are ideal to facilitate the spread of the disease,” Dr. Anish warned.
Climate change
He further added that climate change can also emerge as a key concern.
He warned that malaria could spread to hitherto unreported regions due to climate change-induced developments. “The climate in Keralam and the frequent movement of domestic workers are favourable to the spread of the disease,” he said.
