The mobile internet shutdown, from 10 p.m. on Friday (October 9, 2026) through Saturday evening, compounded the disruption caused by the massive crackdown on attempts to protest in the capital. Digital payments all but ground to a halt — except in restaurants, shops and facilities equipped with WiFi — while protesters scrambled to call friends and family in other parts of the city, unable to send pictures or video.
The shutdown was ordered for a 4-kilometre radius centred on the intersection of Janpath and Kartavya Path, normally two of the busiest thoroughfares in the administrative heart of the city. It was geographically the largest curb in Delhi since the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, over half a decade ago.
The shutdown crippled gig workers’ operations in the capital, as many needed mobile data to take orders or even to resume work after finishing a delivery or a ride in the affected area. Google Maps was affected too: it had no up-to-date information on traffic restrictions or even traffic flow, as its real-time updates rely on crowdsourced data from users.
Through the afternoon, turn-by-turn navigation showed extremely long routes snaking around Lutyens’ Delhi, since removed restrictions could not be updated quickly, even in spots the police had cleared. The curbs also appeared to be enforced inconsistently, with some users of one telecom operator reporting that they had access until late in the afternoon.
The shutdown also appeared to be paired with a measure of censorship online, though its scale was difficult to establish immediately. The Congress party’s Seva Dal had its account on X, formerly Twitter, withheld. B.V. Srinivas, the Seva Dal’s chief organiser, had his Instagram handle blocked in India by Meta. Mr. Srinivas said he would move the Delhi High Court to challenge the blocking.
The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemned the shutdown, noting that the order had not been published despite a legal mandate. “The communication shared by [newswire agency] ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked ‘Top Secret’, the highest security classification used by the Government of India,” the IFF said.
“The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer,” the IFF said. “The available research is to the contrary, as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford’s Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns ‘much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization’.”
As of Saturday evening, curbs had been lifted at least partially, with data access restored in some parts of central Delhi.

Jonathan Hale was ready to lay down his paint rollers. Hale, a law student turned viral road safety advocate, had run into legal trouble for painting his own DIY crosswalks across some of Los Angeles’s most dangerous intersections. In a meeting with LA Mayor Karen Bass earlier this year, he told her that if the city could commit to making its own streets safer for pedestrians, then he would stop his own vigilante activism.
What if making your neighborhood safer means breaking the rules?
Neighborhood vigilantes are making their own crosswalks, bus stop benches, and DIY bike lanes. Not everyone’s happy about it.
“Dude, you’re the mayor. Do something about this. It’s you, dude,” he recalls insisting to Bass — in so many words — after she apologized for his arrest on vandalism charges for a paint job last December. For months, Hale upheld his end of the bargain and stopped painting, believing in her office’s emailed assurances that a new executive order was coming soon.
But, eventually, after weeks of unresponsiveness, Hale grew tired of waiting, just as he had the first time he picked up a stencil and a bucket of white paint. “We’re so focused on looking for reasons why we can’t do stuff instead of ways that we can,” he said, “and it’s just paralyzed our institutions.”
Across the country, such civic paralysis has compelled a legion of guerrilla urbanists to take their city’s matters into their own hands. In Boston, a group of cyclists used strips of green and white duct tape to build a bike lane at an intersection where a truck struck and killed 36-year-old Louisa Gag in July. In Nashville, Kansas City, and across the Bay Area, volunteers have built and installed their own public benches at bus stops where city officials had slowly removed places to sit, after years spent curating increasingly hostile public spaces.
Every time one of these friendly neighborhood vigilantes paints a crosswalk, fills a pothole, or builds a bench, they remind us that it is not actually that hard — or even that expensive — to do many of the simple things that can make our cities safer and more pleasant places to live. Though our local governments may seem incapable of getting these basic tasks done, they are probably less constrained by money than they are by a sluggish status quo. And in some cases, they’re so afraid of being sued that they’d rather build nothing at all.
“We see the fear of litigation and liability” so thoroughly sabotaging mundane municipal projects that “a crosswalk takes half-a-million dollars in five years to do when it’s really a bucket of paint in an afternoon,” said Anthony Garcia, a Miami-based urban planner who, with his longtime collaborator Mike Lydon, pioneered the study of tactical urbanism, or low-cost, quick-fix interventions often led by ordinary citizens themselves. Both Garcia and Lydon now advise cities nationally on how to integrate the practices of guerrilla urbanists into the ways they govern and pilot their own new policies. “You don’t have to hold a crosswalk to the same standard that you hold a bridge,” Garcia said.
It can be inspiring when a random citizen feels compelled to pick up a paintbrush and finish what their city can’t seem to start, but it is also an infuriating embodiment of just how stunted some of our most basic systems of governance have become. These industrious urban vigilantes show that making our cities more livable can be an easy, and even joyous practice. But if their work is going to serve as more than mere symbolism, cities themselves will need to learn from their example — or, as some municipalities have recently demonstrated, find new ways to collaborate.
“The point of the crosswalks is the protest. It’s to draw awareness to the issue,” not to create a permanent class of illicit crosswalk painters, Hale told me. “We need to hold the government to a higher standard.”
The quasi-legal case for taking your street into your own hands
While there are some reasons that a municipality would take longer to install a bench or paint a crosswalk than a crew of local residents — compliance with regulations and the installation of proper signage comes to mind — they rarely need to take as long as they often do now.
Take Los Angeles, where even the most basic road safety projects can take years to build, racking up eye-popping bills along the way. Some of these delays have proved deadly. For over a decade, the city sat on funds to improve a perilous intersection in Koreatown, according to Streetsblog, an intersection where, last summer, a drunk driver hit and killed 9-year-old Nadir Gavarrete.
As the city twiddled its thumbs in the days that followed, the Crosswalk Collective LA — a DIY group that gave Hale his start — started painting. It wasn’t until three months after Gavarrete was killed that the city scrubbed the guerrilla crosswalks, replacing them with “official” crosswalks and a tiny, temporary traffic circle. A permanent solution is supposedly on its way this year.
It shouldn’t take this long, and though cities like LA have the resources and expertise to pull off more permanent and often more effective solutions than a group of vigilantes could, it also shouldn’t take a profound tragedy to convince them to finally act. And just as importantly, they should be capable of also making the sort of small, low-cost, even temporary interventions in the interim, ones that don’t require bespoke planning and a prolonged procurement process.
As much as Hale has come to enjoy painting crosswalks along with the group he founded, People’s Vision Zero, he does so not as a hobby, but as an expression of discontent with a government that rarely seems to take the safety of his streets as seriously as he’d like them to. Painting a rogue bike lane or giving bus riders a place to sit might not do all that much to fix what’s wrong with our cities directly, but every single DIY urbanist I’ve spoken to has told me that their efforts have helped them reclaim a sense of collective agency over how their cities function, after years of frustration with seemingly impenetrable civic institutions.
“It’s very easy to feel small, and that nothing that you do matters,” said Carter Lavin, co-founder of the TransBay Coalition, a transit advocacy group with ties to the San Francisco Bay Area Bench Collective, but “one thing about building benches is that every screw you drive, every board you sand makes your neighbor’s life better, and it does it for hundreds of people.”
Unfortunately, getting a city to formalize these often quasi-legal urban interventions is no easy feat, as Pastor Robin Owen, a local nonprofit leader in Nashville who writes a Substack called Jesus Urbanist, knows all too well.
For the past year, Owen has been embroiled in a cat-and-mouse game with the city of Nashville in which she and her growing bunch of bench-building acolytes install a DIY bench that the city later removes, after which they replace it with another bench, which the city will inevitably remove again. For many municipalities, getting rid of useful changes proves far easier than simply implementing them in the first place.
As ill-fated as that dance might seem, it can still feel more meaningful to locals, Owen told me, than the even more hapless task of prodding the government to get something done itself.
“When you care about a place and want to make it better, you’ve very likely spent hours in meetings or emailing elected officials, and progress is just really complicated and slow,” she told me, “and building a bench and then putting it on a street corner, you actually do something that impacts someone’s life.”
How cities can learn to build the simple stuff quickly
Advocates tell me that in almost every case they would much prefer to work with their city governments than against them. And sometimes they do: For well over a decade, the local transit advocacy group Reconnect Rochester has partnered with Rochester, New York to lay out boxy, brightly colored “bus stop cubes” at transit corridors around the city. Critically, these boxes were permitted.
“If we were to have just kind of gone out there and done this in the dark of night without following any sort of process,” Mary Staropoli, co-executive director of Reconnect Rochester, told me, “I think those bus stop cubes would have been quickly removed.”
Owen has tried for months to convince her city to issue a similar permit for her benches. Nashville happens to boast one of the nation’s only programs dedicated explicitly to facilitating tactical urbanism, which should have made this an unusually straightforward process. And yet, because of a new requirement compelling such projects to pay for liability insurance, she says that she cannot obtain a permit without paying thousands of dollars to protect benches that cost just $35 a pop to build.
With the exception of some disability protections, cities are indeed far likelier to get sued over the infrastructure they build than over the infrastructure they never bothered to build at all. A crosswalk that never gets painted is one less crosswalk to worry about. A bench that never gets built can’t lead to a lawsuit. But if they never get built at all, then they also have no chance of protecting a pedestrian from a speeding car, or giving an elderly commuter a place to sit.
“There is this massive moral disconnection where cities are not concerned about liability when it comes to people dying in traffic violence, but are concerned about liability when citizens take action ourselves,” Owen said. “We should be more concerned about our moral liability of people having to suffer as they navigate our cities.”
Nevertheless, when a citizen paints a crosswalk or builds a bench, whether as a stopgap as an act of protest, it can also exert a sort of “productive tension” on a city, said Lydon, one that can compel a static government to act much more quickly than it would otherwise, even if such changes takes time to materialize.
It wasn’t until a group of local wheelchair users took sledgehammers to sidewalks and began pouring their own cement ramps in the 1970s that Berkeley, California became one of the first cities in the nation to mandate curb cuts, now a hallmark of nationally mandated accessible design that benefit almost everyone at some point: parents pushing strollers, travelers pulling roller bags, and the rest of us in one way or another.
And in another famous example, a graduate student named Matt Tomasulo zip tied a few dozen wayfinding signs to street poles around Raleigh, North Carolina in 2012, telling passerby how far away various destinations were by walking. While the city initially tore down the signs, they proved popular enough that Raleigh changed course, eventually integrating them into its own planning.
“We’ve documented this over and over,” Lydon said, noting the shift that comes when a city stops fighting a guerrilla intervention and opts to embrace or iterate upon it instead. “You can do these small things, and it can very much lead to transformational change.”

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine defend itself after a Russian bomb attack on two passenger buses killed at least 35 people.
The attack, which struck public buses in the embattled city of Kramatorsk, came amid a wave of Russian strikes across Ukraine that killed 78 people and injured 215 over two days, according to Zelensky.
Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader criticised Washington for pursuing economic ties with Moscow while attempting to broker an end to the war, now in its fifth year.
He urged the US to expand Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite service to help its forces target Russian ballistic missile launchers.
“Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly – give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table,” he said.
It comes as Ukrainian negotiators will travel to the US on Friday and Saturday for talks, Zelensky added, urging Donald Trump to increase sanction pressure on Russia.
Russian air strike kills one, injures two in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia, official says
A Russian air strike has killed one person and injured two others in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, acting governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Telegram on Friday.
Ed Miliband says UK 'will not relent in its support for Ukraine'
UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband visited the site of the Russian strike in Pryluky along with Volodymyr Zelensky, where he condemned Vladimir Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".
He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war".
“My message to Putin is clear – you cannot wait us out. Until you choose the path of peace, the UK will not relent in its support for Ukraine, our values, or our national security. You will remain a pariah,” he said.
They visited a site where 22 people, including five children, were killed in a single strike on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky on Wednesday.
The sanctions package, which includes around 40 targets across Russia’s financial, oil and technology sectors, is designed to disrupt Russia’s supply chain and cut off financing streams.
Zelensky calls for US to expand Starlink access after deadly bus strikes
Volodymyr Zelensky urged the US to accede to his request to expand Ukraine’s access to its Starlink satellite service in order to better target Russian ballistic missile launchers, after Moscow launched one of the deadliest single aerial attacks of the war so far.
Speaking to reporters in Pryluky in the east of Kyiv, he said: “Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly – give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table.”
At least 30 people were killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials said.
Three others were killed in the nearby village of Bilenke, while 18 people were wounded, according to Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin, who accused Russia of deliberately targeting passenger buses to maximise civilian casualties.
Two dead in drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region, officials say
Two people were killed in Ukrainian drone strikes on Thursday in Russia's border region of Belgorod, regional officials said.
The regional operational headquarters reported one person died when a drone struck a car.
A later evening strike killed one person and injured three.
Reuters could not independently verify the reports.
Belgorod region has been a frequent target of Ukraine's forces.
Indian imports of Russian oil sink to lowest level since 2022
Indian imports of Russian oil have their lowest level since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, according to a report.
In the four weeks up to 4 October, shipments of Russian rude averaged just 310,000 barrels a day, Bloomberg data showed. This is the lowest level since March 2022.
India has gradually reduced its dependence on Russian oil since the US threatened punitive sanctions earlier this year.
Zelensky says Ukraine expects Europeans to join talks with US
Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine expected Kyiv's European partners to join talks with the US in coming days.
Zelenskiy earlier said that Ukraine's negotiators would hold talks in the United States on Friday and Saturday as part of efforts led by the United States to seek a settlement of the war with Russia.
The president, speaking to reporters in Kyiv, said Ukrainian negotiators would raise the issue of air defences in light of near-constant Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities. More than 70 have been killed in strikes over the past two days.
Zelenskiy also said Ukraine had "mirrored" Russian attacks on data centres, referring to a strike on a centre operated by Russian technology company Yandex.
"We always respond in mirror-like fashion," Zelenskiy said. "You all know, they have been hitting and continue to hit our data centres. We are responding. I can't share all the details."
Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Thursday it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data centre hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored.
Russian drone strike on Kramatorsk kills two, local authorities say
A new evening drone strike on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed two people on Thursday, local authorities said.
The Kramatorsk city council, in a post on Telegram, said the drone struck a car, killing two people inside. It said a total of 35 people had been killed in the city after a bomb attack tore through two buses.
Russia agrees with Rubio that Ukraine conflict is in a stalemate
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying on Thursday that Russia agreed with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the Ukraine conflict was in a stalemate.
"Yes, we agree with him," Russian news agencies quoted Peskov as saying on the sidelines of a meeting of leaders of ex-Soviet states in Turkmenistan.
State news agency RIA quoted Peskov as saying it was up to diplomats to find ways of moving towards peace.
"The art of diplomacy precisely involves finding some way out that would allow moving onto a peaceful track," Peskov was quoted as saying.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet Ukrainian representatives on Friday in Miami to discuss new ideas and try to produce a unified proposal for resolving the war, an American source familiar with the plan said on Thursday.
Peskov was quoted as saying he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Putin, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump.
He restated the Kremlin's position that Russia wanted an overall solution to the conflict and was not interested in temporary measures, like a limited ceasefire.
"We are not for a fragmented solution, we are for a comprehensive solution that will allow for sustainable settlement for many, many years, for decades," the agencies quoted him as saying.

Two of the world’s largest exporters of grain, locked in war for more than four years, have seen exports plunge even further over the last year. Prolonged conflict around the Black Sea threatens both economies - and those most in need, writes James C. Reynolds.

"We'd love to see a negotiated settlement to this war that is permanent, enduring, and fair," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Portugal.

Hundreds of thousands march worldwide against Israel’s genocide in Gaza
Hundreds of thousands of people joined coordinated pro-Palestine marches worldwide on Saturday to condemn Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza and stand with Palestinians living under Israeli apartheid in the occupied West Bank.
The Global Alliance for Palestine said the mobilisation involved at least 325 events worldwide, including 176 in Europe alone.
Organisers estimated that around 250,000 people joined the London march. Demonstrators carried signs demanding the “end” of Israel’s genocide and declaring “Free Palestine” as they marched towards the British parliament.
Marchers observed a two-minute silence for the more than 74,370 Palestinians Israel has killed in Gaza since October 2023. Its attacks have wounded at least 175,371 others.
Protesters demanded that the UK government stop supplying weapons Israel uses to bomb Palestinians.

“We are here today to mark three years of the ongoing genocide in Gaza,” Aimee Shalan, director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, told AFP.

Speaking at the demonstration, IPSC chair Zoe Lawlor called the Gaza ceasefire "an absolute fiction" and condemned Israel’s continuing restrictions on aid, fuel and food, in comments carried by Ireland’s public broadcaster RTE.

The marches followed a joint statement on Friday from more than 100 humanitarian, human rights and civil society organisations, which said the Gaza ceasefire “exists in name only with Israeli forces continuing to kill and injure Palestinians daily, and restrictions on aid, equipment and rebuilding materials preventing families from recovering.”
“It is utterly shameful that a full year after the ceasefire was signed, so little has improved for Palestinians in Gaza,” Jan Egeland, secretary-general of the Norwegian Refugee Council, said in the joint statement.
“A ceasefire is meaningless if children are still being killed and families are still unable to rebuild their lives,” said Inger Ashing, chief executive of Save the Children.
“Nearly one child has been killed every day,” Ashing added.

'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the US diesel deal with Russia.
The Ukrainian president warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against his nation, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday that Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries.
"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".
Global fuel supplies, including diesel, have been severely limited by the war against Iran launched by the US and Israel, which led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil products usually flows.
Russia - a major producer - and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes on each other's energy infrastructure and transport facilities, further straining energy markets.
"We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump continued.
"He could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does."
Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev described Trump's intervention as "iconic and historic", saying that Ukraine "needs leadership actually focused on peace".
The US president confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.
Zelensky reacted by saying it would allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.
He also accused Moscow of taking the deal "to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities" following deadly new strikes on Zaporizhzhia.

The Ukrainian president spoke to several allies on Saturday to discuss the latest developments, calling for "real decisions to protect lives in Ukraine" and to protect European security.
A Downing Street spokesperson said UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Zelensky and offered his "complete solidarity".
The pair had agreed Russia should acquiesce to "an immediate energy ceasefire" and end its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea, the spokesperson said, as "this would immediately release more energy and food supplies into the global market".
News of the US-Russia diesel deal was also met with criticism by EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas, who echoed Zelensky in saying that suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
The deal with Russia is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
The average price of diesel is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA – up from last month's $5.94 average, and $3.68 last year.
Under the deal, Russia would release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace" followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November.
A further million would follow, Trump wrote on Truth Social, and then another 3m tonnes "within a short period of time" – but he noted that this delivery will be "based on the condition of their diesel refineries".
In the past 10 months, Russia experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country due to Ukrainian drones strikes on its oil refineries.
Diesel production in Russia dropped by an estimated 30%, according to the International Energy Agency.
Trump had already called for new elections in Ukraine last December, external, saying Ukrainian voters should have the choice to replace Zelensky.
Since the war broke out in 2022 Ukraine has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.

Christa Pike discharged from hospital and returned to prison, her lawyers say
- Published
US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.
The 50-year-old murderer has been returned to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.
She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.
Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition in hospital.
Earlier this week, she regained consciousness and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," her lawyers said in their statement.
Pike's case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he does not know whether the state intends to reschedule Pike's execution.
The judge also ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
After Pike survived two lethal injections, she lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital.
She eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyers said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"

India’s cleantech startups attracted substantially more capital in Q3 2026, with large electric mobility rounds driving funding growth alongside an increase in deal activity. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026, cleantech startups raised $433 Mn across 23 deals, compared with $118 Mn across 16 deals in the year-ago quarter. The report tracks funding announced up to September 24. The increase stood out against a subdued funding environment. Overall startup funding rose just 5% YoY to $2.2 Bn, while funding for fintech and ecommerce startups declined 11% and 31%, respectively. However, the cleantech funding surge was heavily concentrated in electric mobility. River raised $120 Mn, Yulu secured $93 Mn, and Ultraviolette attracted $85 Mn. Together, the three startups accounted for $298 Mn, or nearly 69% of the sector’s funding. Adding to this, Simple Energy raised a mega $180 Mn round at the end of the month of September, further adding to this trend. The numbers raise two questions: what is drawing investors towards these businesses and how far does the momentum extend beyond a handful of large EV rounds? Commercial Viability Shapes Investor Bets For investors, the appeal is increasingly tied to whether technology can solve a tangible problem and support a commercially viable business. “What's different this cycle is that capital is backing businesses and not just the energy transition,” Elev8 Venture Partners managing partner Navin Honagudi told Inc42. The VC firm led River’s $120 Mn Series C in August. The round alone accounted for nearly 28% of the quarter’s cleantech funding. Shubham Jhuria, CFO and partner at Aeravti Ventures, also pointed to a shift in how investors assess the sector. “The biggest change we are seeing is that the cleantech conversation is moving beyond the climate-impact narrative towards businesses solving very specific economic and infrastructure problems,” he told Inc42. Funding activity extended beyond the three largest EV rounds, with Omega Seiki Mobility, Electric.AI, Simple Energy, and Yuma also raising capital during the quarter. Cleantech deal count increased about 44%, while the average cheque size rose to approximately $19 Mn from $7 Mn in the year-ago quarter. EVs accounted for 57% of deals, according to the report. This suggests that the increase was not solely the result of larger cheques, although electric mobility remained central to both funding value and deal activity. EV Adoption Supports The Investment Case Rising EV adoption is giving investors a more tangible basis to assess demand and business models. JMK Research estimates that 15.41 Lakh EVs were registered in H1 2026, up 43% YoY. According to Vahan, total EV registrations rose 64.6% YoY to 3.15 Lakh units in September. E2W registrations increased 12.2% to 2.07 Lakh units from 1.84 Lakh in August. Honagudi said electric mobility has matured into a demand-led market. He pointed to River’s position among India’s top seven electric two-wheeler brands by registrations, despite having far fewer retail outlets than established players, as evidence of product-led demand. Over the next 3-5 years, Elev8 expects deeper localisation of motors and electronics to improve margins and supply-chain resilience. Honagudi cited last year’s rare earth magnet shortage as an example of the vulnerabilities that localisation could address. He also expects consolidation to leave “a handful of scaled independents” alongside established incumbents. Can The Momentum Broaden? Stronger adoption does not automatically translate into attractive investor returns. Jhuria cautioned that investment appetite could moderate if businesses struggle to convert technological capabilities into scalable solutions or continue to require substantial capital without improving their unit economics. The quarter’s numbers reflect both wider deal activity and substantial concentration. More cleantech startups attracted funding than a year earlier, but three EV businesses still captured more than two-thirds of the capital. For the momentum to broaden, investor conviction will need to extend beyond large electric mobility bets. Within EVs, the test will be whether rising demand and deeper localisation translate into stronger margins and businesses that can scale without repeatedly requiring outsized capital infusions.

‘If a sibling uses a skin-lightening product, you may be more likely to use one too’. This was among the findings from behavioural research cited by the World Health Organisation (WHO) during a discussion on colourism in Hyderabad on Wednesday (October 7, 2026).
The discussion was part of ‘Complexion of Change: Challenging Colorism Through Policy, Art, and Science’, held at Goethe-Zentrum in Hyderabad. A documentary exploring global skin colour bias and the deep-rooted societal association of fair skin with higher status, beauty and success was also screened as part of the programme.
“Skin-lightening product use was not a single behaviour but was influenced by psychological, cultural and environmental factors,” said Ammaarah Martinus, Behavioural Insights consultant at the WHO.
The psychological dimension includes motivations such as wanting to appear fairer, younger or to fit into society. The cultural dimension includes the influence of families, communities and social networks. Mr. Martinus said research had found that people were more likely to use a skin-lightening product if a sibling used one. She also spoke about access to such products . In India, skin-lightening products could be easily purchased in local markets and supermarkets. “Interventions to address skin-lightening therefore need to work across all three levels rather than focus on only one aspect of the behaviour,” she added.
Psychologist and researcher Bharti Upparu said children begin receiving messages about skin colour at a very young age, often without anyone explicitly telling them that one skin tone is preferable to another. They observe who is complimented, who is bullied and who is teased, and gradually learn which physical characteristics society values. “A person perceived as fair and attractive may unconsciously be associated with other positive characteristics such as competence, goodness and trustworthiness. Such biases can compound into an overall perception of a person’s character and affect how others interact with them,” she said.
The discussion also highlighted that colourism is not restricted to women. Arpit Bhutani, co-founder of Circular Innovation Lab and moderator of the session, pointed to products marketed specifically towards men and noted that the pressure to conform to lighter-skin beauty standards also affects men.
Former Miss America Nina Davuluri recalled an incident involving a friend’s baby, when an older family member cautioned against taking the child into the sun because the child could become darker. “Such comments are not necessarily made with malicious intent but can come from a desire to see children succeed in a society where lighter skin is perceived to offer advantages,” she added.
Mercury in skin-lightening products
In remarks before the documentary screening, Monika Stankiewicz, executive secretary of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, said mercury was among the chemicals of highest public concern according to the WHO and that cosmetics were one pathway through which people could be exposed. “Mercury-containing skin-lightening products can damage the skin and may also contaminate households, potentially exposing other family members,” she added.
Ms. Stankiewicz stressed that the issue was not solely a chemical problem but also a social one linked to beauty standards and the pressure to conform to them. She said meaningful change could not come through regulations alone and that activism, art, culture and storytelling also had important roles to play.

- The claim that Matthew Ingalls, one of seven Cornell University students accused of rape in a September lawsuit, fled to Dubai is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from an article in the Daily Mail, a British tabloid, which cited an anonymous neighbor of Ingalls' uncle, who said they believed the accused man is in Dubai.
- Using old yearbook photographs and searches of public records, Snopes was able to determine Matthew Ingalls also was known as Umar Matthew Ingalls, an alumnus of Dubai International Academy. While we know Ingalls lived in Dubai at some point, we cannot confirm his current whereabouts.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Ingalls, the Dubai International Academy, Ingalls' former school in Washington state and the person tabloids identify as Ingalls' father in Dubai and are waiting for responses.
In October, several weeks after a lawsuit was filed accusing seven male students at Cornell University of drugging and raping a female student in 2024, a rumor spread about the whereabouts of one of the accused men. According to the claim, Matthew Ingalls — who reportedly initiated the encounter with the accuser, named in court documents only as Jane Doe — fled to Dubai, where he previously lived.
Posts on Facebook (archived) and Instagram claimed Ingalls, who the posts said also goes by Umar Matthew Ingalls, was in Dubai with his family:
Umar Matthew Ingalls, one of the "Cornell 7" accused in the alleged 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi house, is now reportedly in Dubai, where he grew up. Neighbors of his relatives in Connecticut told the Daily Mail they believe he's back in the Middle East with his dad. How convenient.
Quick refresher on Mr. Ingalls. He's the one Jane Doe says invited her to the house that night. He's also the one who, according to messages filed in her lawsuit, shared a photo of her in the frat's Snapchat group chat and wrote "Like you can walk in and whip it out." The New York Post reports he added "Boys come whip it out." Truly the words of a gentleman.
(Facebook user Feminist News)
The rumor originated from a report in the Daily Mail, a British tabliod, that relied on anonymous sources. Snopes is unable to verify Ingalls' whereabouts as of this writing, so we have left this claim unrated. We have, however, found records of an Umar Ingalls who studied at the Dubai International Academy in Emirates Hills, Dubai, whose appearance matches that of Matthew Ingalls.
We have reached out to Ingalls — whom The New York Times reported had been expelled from Cornell — via his old college email address, to a person believed to be his father, to the Dubai International Academy and also to the Annie Wright School in Tacoma, Washington, where Ingalls reportedly studied as a child. We will update this story as we learn more.
The Daily Mail identified Ingalls as Umar Matthew Ingalls and spoke to an anonymous neighbor of Ingalls' uncle in Connecticut, where Ingalls' address was listed in court records. That neighbor reportedly told the tabloid Ingalls hadn't been seen at the home in some time and that they thought he was in Dubai.
Our public records search for Umar Matthew Ingalls found his name appeared connected to an address in South Dartmouth, Massachusetts, that also was linked to the name Matthew B. Ingalls.
The Daily Mail identified Ingalls' father as a Yale-educated professor at the American University in Dubai. We found a Matthew B. Ingalls listed as an associate professor of Middle Eastern studies at the American University in Dubai. Snopes reached out to him to verify his identity and relationship to Ingalls and will update this story as we get more information.
Several purported photographs of Matthew Ingalls have circulated, including one showing him wearing a Cornell rugby T-shirt and another from what appears to be his now-deleted LinkedIn account. According to the university's student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, the school's rugby club confirmed Ingalls was previously a part of its roster.
We found that Ingalls' image from his deleted LinkedIn account had SynthID markers — which are inserted into images created with some generative artificial intelligence platforms — and was thus likely edited with AI. However, the photograph of Ingalls in his rugby shirt did not. We then compared that photograph to other images we found of him and found several matches.
Dubai International Academy's 2022-23 yearbook identifies Umar Ingalls as a member of the class of 2023 and part of the athletics team. The person in the yearbook photo appears to be the same person wearing the Cornell rugby shirt.
(Dubai International Academy)
Umar Ingalls also was mentioned in a 2022 story in the Khaleej Times, a Dubai newspaper. The article reported on a group of students who created their own version of a lunar rover. The accompanying photograph is blurry, but the student in the back right has a strong resemblance to Ingalls.
A 2020 blog post on the website for Annie Wright Schools, an elite private school in Tacoma, Washington, identified Umar Ingalls as half-American. He appeared to have studied at the Lower School until 2016 and lived in Dubai at the time the article was written. He commented on how Americans were perceived in Dubai after the election victory of U.S. President Donald Trump.
For further reading, we have previously reported on numerous rumors about the Cornell rape case.

South Africa hope to host first African Olympics
- Published
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed South Africa have shown an interest in becoming the first African host of the summer Olympics in 2036.
Hungary, India, Qatar and Turkey are also working towards becoming first-time hosts, while Germany and South Korea are in discussions with the IOC having held previous summer Games.
The IOC stated that the seven countries are engaged in "continuous dialogue" with the governing body and have set a deadline of 31 October for submissions of stated interest.
Virtual presentations will be given by interested parties to the body's future host commission in November, with IOC feasibility assessments to be carried out by March 2027.
After that, the national Olympic committees, all of whom have previously announced an intention to explore hosting bids, will enter strategic dialogue with the IOC.
The South Africa proposal involves hosting between three cities - Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg.
Durban had been set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2022, but withdrew in 2017.
Ahmedabad, which will welcome the Commonwealth Games in 2030 and has bid for the 2038 Asian Games, will be the host city in India's bid.
The city has also staged four of the last five finals in cricket's Indian Premier League at its Narendra Modi stadium, which is reported to have a capacity of 132,000 and is named after the current prime minister of India, who hails from the city.
Budapest and Doha, the capital cities of Hungary and Qatar respectively, are the hosts in their country's bids.
Qatar hosted football's 2022 World Cup, with multiple stadia in the capital, while Budapest has staged the 2022 World Aquatics Championships and 2023 World Athletics Championships.
Istanbul is the nominated city in Turkey's bid, having previously bid unsuccessfully for the 2000, 2008 and 2020 Games.
The largest city in Turkey will host the 2027 European Games.
Germany has hosted the Olympics in 1936 and 1972, in Berlin and Munich respectively, while the latter city is bidding again for 2036.
Meanwhile South Korea capital Seoul, which hosted the Games in 1988, is part of a bid that also involves the province of North Jeolla.
The IOC also confirmed that a number of national Olympic committees are taking part in non-committal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036.
The UK government said in May that it is in "discussions about supporting potential bids" for the Olympics and Paralympics in the 2040s.
The 2028 Games will be held in Los Angeles, while Australia will host the Olympics for the first time in 32 years when Brisbane stages the event in 2032.

Last month we covered the winner of Nikon’s Small World in Motion video: Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with a rare respiratory disorder. But allegations surfaced about Xu’s use of AI while making the video. Nikon launched an investigation and concluded that Xu’s entry did not comply with competition rules. The new winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam with a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism (above).
According to a BBC report, some researchers expressed concern that Xu’s video had structural abnormalities and that cell features appeared and disappeared in a way one would not see in actual cellular biology. Others spotted what looked like AI watermarks embedded within the source files. Xu said he used AI “to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images”; however, he denied that AI was used “to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.”
Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.
The other winners also moved up a notch with Xu’s disqualification. Benedikt Pleyer of Bavaria, Germany, placed second with a video of jellyfish larvae suspended in water droplets; Andrew Moore of Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the US placed third with a video of synchronized cell division in neighboring cells; Patrick Hickey of Hypha Research Ltd. in Edinburgh, Scotland, placed fourth with a video of the dynamics of mitochondria and chloroplasts in Turtle Vine leaf cells; and Igor Adameyko placed fifth with a video of a tiny, colorful sea slug (Cyerce kikutarobabai) on the move.

The Ranji Trophy 2026-27, India’s premier domestic cricket competition, will begin with the first round of fixtures between October 11 and 14.
Jammu Kashmir is the defending champion, while eight-time winner Karnataka is the runner-up. Eighteen teams have won the coveted title, while Mumbai is the most succesful team with 42 titles.
The tournament, which will enter its 92nd edition, will see 38 teams play 138 matches over the course of five months.
The 38 teams have been split into five groups- Group A, Group B, Group C, Group D, and the Plate group. The elite division comprises the first four groups and 32 teams, while the plate group consists of lower-ranked teams.
The winner of the plate group will earn promotion to the elite division for the following season, while the team with the fewest points in the elite division will get relegated.
Last season, Bihar was promoted after winning the plate final against Manipur, while Nagaland got relegated.
Bihar will contest in Group A along with J&K, Baroda, Goa, Madhya Pradesh Puducherry, Uttar Pradesh, and Vidarbha. Karnataka is in Group B, while Mumbai is in Group D.
In the opening round, J&K will take on Madhya Pradesh in Srinagar, while Karnataka will begin against Andhra. Heavyweights Mumbai and Tamil Nadu start their campaigns against Chandigarh and Rajasthan respectively.

Trade analyst Taran Adarsh does not give standing ovations easily. In an exclusive conversation with Bollywood Hungama, he revealed that he rose from his seat and applauded during a preview screening of Drishyam The Conclusion, the third instalment of Ajay Devgn's hit franchise. He also explained what moved him, and his praise goes beyond the film to a specific choice by its lead actor: Devgn's willingness to say very little.
EXCLUSIVE: Taran Adarsh gave Drishyam The Conclusion a standing ovation, calls Ajay Devgn a “secure actor” for letting Jaideep Ahlawat own the scene
A standing ovation, only the second this year
Adarsh said the latest film stands out in a series he has followed closely. "I really liked the first part of Drishyam. I loved the second part. And when I watched the third part, I actually— I have given two films a standing ovation this year. One was Dhurandhar, and the other was Drishyam. Especially the sequence after the interval. I just got up from my chair."
He added that he shared his reaction with the actor himself. "I was in the preview theatre, and I gave it a standing ovation. I told Ajay that I had given his film a standing ovation. I enjoyed that scene so much, and I loved the film overall as well. But if you look at it, this is a very, very good franchise. It is the kind of film you can watch with your family because it is a family story.
"What is surprising is the tremendous business this film is doing despite having no songs. There is no action in the film, and there is no elaborate dialogue-baazi either. Ajay Devgn has very few dialogues in the film. He conveys so much through his eyes and facial expressions. And that is the film's victory. He could have chosen to," he stated.
The 15-minute sequence that won him over
Adarsh pointed to a pre-interval sequence in which Jaideep Ahlawat's character visits Devgn's home and speaks at length. "If you have watched the film, before the interval, there is a sequence of about 15 minutes when Jaideep Ahlawat arrives at Ajay's house. They are discussing his daughter's marriage proposal, and Jaideep keeps talking and talking. I was thinking about it, and I even told Ajay— I said, "You haven't said anything." Then, at the interval point, when you finally respond to him, that is the film's victory."
"A secure actor"
For Adarsh, the restraint says something about Devgn as a performer. "It shows how secure an actor Ajay Devgn is. He could have told Abhishek Pathak, the director, to add one or two dialogues for him. He could even have told Kumar Mangat ji, "I should have some good dialogues. You aren't making me say anything!" But he lets Jaideep Ahlawat do all the talking, and when he delivers that one dialogue at the end, it is remarkable. Hello to Ajay Devgn."
He summed it up simply: "It's a secure actor. Absolutely. I mean, hats off to Ajay Devgn." Adarsh believes the confidence came from the actor's trust in his own craft. "He had so much confidence in his talent. He did not think that the other actor would eat up the scene or that something might happen that would make people call the other person a scene-stealer. Or he did not worry that people would say Ajay Devgn had been completely sidelined."
The casting of Jaideep Ahlawat and Prakash Raj
Adarsh also appreciated the addition of Jaideep Ahlawat. He said, "When the controversy around Akshaye Khanna happened, Kumar ji had explained the details to me. But anyway, that is beside the point. At the time, he told me that Jaideep and Prakash Raj would both be part of the film."
He explained why the casting matters to the franchise. "Jaideep is a very fine actor. I have said this before as well. I think that when you cast someone opposite Ajay Devgn, especially when you are replacing Akshaye Khanna, the audience also expects a worthy contest. There should be two equally formidable actors. Otherwise, the audience does not enjoy the confrontation. In this franchise, the responsibility largely rests on how these characters face off against each other."
Praise for the ensemble
Adarsh closed with a nod to the wider cast. "Tabu is an excellent actress, and this time too, the film begins with her. Every actor has contributed. Prakash Raj appears after the interval, and that scene outside the courtroom, when he takes a selfie— Oh my God! Just think about it - every scene has been carefully put together. What a brilliant film! What a brilliant film!"

The Union Health Ministry has proposed extending restrictions on advertisements of prescription medicines to drug retailers, wholesalers and distributors, seeking to close a regulatory gap in the Drugs Rules, 1945.
A draft amendment notified through Gazette notification G.S.R. 861(E) on September 28 proposes inserting a new sub-rule under Rule 65 to prohibit holders of licences to sell, stock, exhibit, offer for sale or distribute drugs listed under Schedules H, H1 and X from advertising these medicines without prior sanction of the Central government.
Under the existing framework, pharmaceutical manufacturers are prohibited from advertising drugs covered under these schedules without prior government approval. However, the corresponding restriction does not explicitly cover entities involved in the retail and wholesale sale and distribution of medicines.
The proposed amendment seeks to extend the requirement across the drug supply chain, strengthening oversight of the promotion of prescription medicines and reducing the risk of inappropriate self-medication.
Misuse of prescription drugs
The medicines covered by these schedules include drugs that require medical supervision, including certain antibiotics and psychotropic medicines. Unauthorised promotion of such medicines can encourage their use without appropriate medical advice, raising concerns over patient safety and the misuse of prescription drugs.
The proposal follows recommendations made at the 93rd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) on February 16, 2026, which examined the need for provisions regulating advertisements by holders of drug sale and distribution licences.
The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days of the date on which copies of the Gazette notification containing the draft rules are made available to the public.
The submissions received within the prescribed period will be considered by the Central government before the amendment is finalised.

Nine people, including a male suspect, have been killed after a shooting at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania.
Officers were alerted to the incident via a controversial gunshot detection system that relies on artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify gunshots.
What's next?
District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz urged the public to refrain from speculation as the investigation continued.
A pregnant woman, children and other relatives are among eight victims gunned down by a man at a home in Pennsylvania.
Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said the 45-year-old man was related to seven of the victims, while the eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman.
Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two "distressed" women arrived and began pounding on the door shortly before 5pm on Friday, local time, Mr Lorah said.
The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside.
Police arrived to find the two women dead outside.
After deploying a drone and robot, police went inside the home and found the bodies of a five-year-old boy; a one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.
"Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home," Mr Lorah said at a news conference.
"But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole."
Mr Lorah declined to discuss motive but said investigators would talk to other relatives and examine the mobile phones of the women who were killed outside the home.
"They knew something was going on at that house,"
he said.
"We have to figure out what that is."
Mr Lorah said officers arrived within minutes of receiving an alert via ShotSpotter, a controversial gunshot detection system that relies on artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify gunshots.
No additional shots were fired after that.
"Sounds that may have been mistaken for gunfire came from flashbang devices, chemical munitions, used by SWAT officers," he said.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said he offered his administration's "full support" to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin, who spoke directly to the victims' families during the news conference.
"I am so deeply sorry. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier," she said.
"But you do need to know that our entire community is with you, we're grieving with you. And we are here to support you."
District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz urged the public to refrain from speculation as the investigation continued.
"Please do not allow rumours, speculation or unverified information to add to the pain that these families are already experiencing,"
she said.
Erie is about 190 kilometres north of Pittsburgh.
Speaking at a campaign rally outside Philadelphia, Mr Shapiro mentioned both the Erie killings and the shooting of two Philadelphia police officers early Saturday.
"Today has been a dark day across this commonwealth," he said.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has announced a protest march to Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on 10 October 2026, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The party’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced the protest after demonstrations in Mumbai on 02 October and in Delhi in the days that followed. CJP leaders have said they will continue the protest even if the police stop them from reaching Jantar Mantar. As of 09 October 2026, Delhi Police had not granted permission for the proposed gathering and had tightened security ahead of the demonstration. CJP has also alleged that authorities were detaining its members and volunteers across the country to prevent them from participating in the protest, with party leaders vowing to continue the agitation (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows women police personnel assaulting students during the CJP protest in Delhi on 04 October 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows women police personnel assaulting students during the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi on 04 October 2026.
Fact: The video predates the October 2026 Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest and shows a confrontation between the family of a man found dead under suspicious circumstances and the police in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, in July 2026. Although clashes between protesters and police were reported in Delhi during the first week of October amid demonstrations demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, the viral video is unrelated to those protests. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several social media posts (here, here, and here) dated 01 August 2026 featuring the same video, confirming that it predates the October 2026 CJP protest. According to these posts, the video shows an incident in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, where a young man named Ganesh was found dead in a rented apartment. Following the incident, his family staged a protest by blocking the road and making serious allegations against the landlord. The posts also describe a clash between women and police personnel during the protest.
We also found news reports (here, here) published around the same time covering the incident. According to these reports, tensions erupted in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, after the body of a 30-year-old man named Ganesh was found under suspicious circumstances at his rented house on 31 July 2026. His family accused the landlord of murder and staged a roadblock, during which they alleged that the police assaulted them. The reports also state that a woman dressed in black, identified as the deceased’s aunt, alleged that a police officer had snatched her mangalsutra and pulled her hair. These findings confirm that the viral video shows a confrontation between the family and police in July 2026, unrelated to the CJP protest in October 2026.
Meanwhile, during the first week of October 2026, clashes broke out between protesters and police in Delhi during demonstrations demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Police detained several protesters and stopped groups from reaching protest sites, while some demonstrators alleged that police personnel pushed, dragged, and assaulted them (here, here, and here). However, the viral video predates these demonstrations and shows an unrelated incident in Budh Vihar, Rohini, in July 2026.
To sum up, an unrelated video is shared as showing women police personnel assaulting students during the CJP protest in Delhi.

AI emerged as the defining theme in the Indian startup ecosystem in the July-September quarter, with startups in the segment raising their highest-ever-recorded quarterly funding. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding surged 265% year-on-year to $438 Mn. The number of deals rose 35% to 35 from 26 in Q3 2025. The momentum builds on a strong first half of the year. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, more than four times the $162 Mn raised in the corresponding period last year. With another $438 Mn raised in Q3, the sector’s funding for the first nine months of 2026 stood at $1.1 Bn+. The surge stands out against a relatively subdued funding environment. Indian startups collectively raised $2.2 Bn across 210 deals in Q3, up just 5% YoY, even as the deal count fell 13%. Quarterly funding also remained below the $3.4 Bn raised in Q3 2024 and the eight-quarter average of about $2.7 Bn. AI was not the only segment to record a significant increase in investor interest during Q3. Cleantech startups raised $433 Mn, up 267% YoY, while funding for advanced hardware and technology startups, including robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% to $290 Mn. Meanwhile, fintech funding fell 11% YoY to $249 Mn, while ecommerce funding declined 31% to $245 Mn. The divergence suggests that AI is attracting a growing share of investor capital even as funding across the wider startup ecosystem remains under pressure. But with valuations under scrutiny and large funding rounds driving the headline numbers, the question is whether AI can sustain its momentum in the coming quarters. Investors Want More Than AI Exposure Inc42’s Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that about 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. About half of the investors who see valuation froth expect a correction within the next 18 months. Another 31% see mild froth but believe valuations are supported by real revenue. Pranav Obhrai, founding and managing partner at Atrium Ventures, said the rise in AI valuations is part of a global trend, particularly in the US. At the pre-seed stage, he said, valuations are often shaped more by capital requirements, future potential and acceptable founder dilution than by revenue or profitability multiples. For instance, a startup raising $3 Mn at 20% dilution would imply a $15 Mn post-money valuation, assuming the investor agrees to that price. Beyond valuations, investors are also becoming more selective about the AI applications they expect to create the most value. Vertical AI applications across sectors such as BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the top choice in Inc42’s survey, with 39% of investors expecting this segment to capture the most value over the next five years. AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%. Indian-language and sovereign foundation models received 14% of investor votes. Data, tooling and evaluation, and AI infrastructure and compute received 3% each. Obhrai said foundation models and AI infrastructure typically have longer gestation periods than venture investors prefer. Vertical AI, by contrast, offers a clearer path towards building a defensible business through distribution. “Distribution becomes the moat, especially in India, where technology alone offers limited protection against global competition,” he said. An investor who requested anonymity made a similar distinction, pointing to the capital required to scale foundation models and model-routing infrastructure. Such businesses may have to operate at nil or negative gross margins for extended periods, a commitment that Indian venture capital firms find difficult to sustain given their smaller asset bases compared with their US counterparts. The investor added that application-layer businesses could offer more durable revenue opportunities than model-routing or foundation-model companies. While some investors are backing small language models and task-specific model developers, the capital required to build and scale the underlying technology remains a constraint. The findings suggest that rising AI funding is not translating into an indiscriminate appetite for the sector. Investors are increasingly distinguishing between businesses that can use AI to solve specific problems and those that need substantial capital to develop the underlying technology. Can AI Sustain The Funding Momentum? The scale of the funding increase raises questions about how much of the momentum reflects a broad-based expansion in investor activity and how much is attributable to large growth-stage rounds. The investor who requested anonymity said funding figures need to be assessed after accounting for sizable Series B and Series C transactions, including rounds raised by companies such as Emergent. “One would have to normalise by excluding large Series B or Series C cheques,” the investor said, adding that, in their assessment, absolute AI funding had not moved significantly after accounting for these larger rounds. This distinction matters because a small number of large transactions can lift aggregate funding without necessarily signalling that more investors are deploying capital across the sector. Obhrai expects AI to retain a strong share of startup funding, even if capital flows fluctuate between quarters. However, he warned that a broader global AI bubble bursting could trigger a correction, given what he described as arguably inflated valuations of companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Several structural factors could continue to support investment in Indian AI startups. In its H1 report, Inc42 highlighted the transition of enterprise AI adoption from pilots to production, global hyperscalers’ investments in Indian AI infrastructure, and efforts to build sovereign AI infrastructure and foundation models as drivers of the sector. However, India's AI funding pool remains much smaller than the capital being deployed globally. The H1 report noted that Indian AI startup funding was still a fraction of global investment, even as companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic raised multi-billion-dollar rounds during the same period. For Indian startups, this gap presents both an opportunity and a constraint. Growing enterprise adoption and demand for specialised applications could support further investment, but businesses requiring substantial capital to develop foundational technology may find it harder to compete with better-funded global peers. The Q3 numbers establish AI as one of the biggest drivers of Indian startup funding in 2026. Whether that momentum continues will depend on more than the size of the next funding round: investors will be watching for sustainable revenue, defensible applications and valuations that can withstand a potential correction in the global AI market.
