Thieves pull off Italy's biggest-ever wine heist, stealing 30,000 bottles worth 5 million euros
Thieves have stolen about 30,000 bottles of premium wine worth an estimated 5 million euros from a Marchesi Antinori winery in Tuscany in what the company says is the largest wine theft in Italy’s history
ROME -- Thieves stole about 30,000 bottles of some of Italy’s most prized wines worth an estimated 5 million euros ($5.8 million) from a winery in Tuscany, in what the producer described Friday as the country's largest wine theft on record.
The theft targeted Marchesi Antinori’s facility near Cortona, in the province of Arezzo, where a group of at least seven thieves on Saturday night made off with bottles of some of Italy's most sought-after wines, including Solaia, Tignanello and Guado al Tasso. The theft was discovered Monday, but the company made it public on Friday to avoid interfering with the investigation.
Chief Executive Renzo Cotarella said the thieves disabled the winery’s alarm system and surveillance cameras before entering with two large trucks. Using the company’s forklifts, they loaded the vehicles with wine and fled during the night.
“It is certainly a very well-prepared gang,” Cotarella said, adding that it may be the same group that has targeted other Italian wineries in recent months. “A theft of this size and value has never occurred in Italy.”
The stolen bottles were all from the 2023 vintage and are typically sold at a retail price of between 150 euros and 500 euros each. They included about 10,000 bottles of Solaia, one of Antinori’s flagship wines, from what Cotarella described as an exceptional year.
The company, founded in 1385 and run by the Antinori family for 26 generations, said it was alerting customers worldwide to be wary of offers outside official sales channels.
“We are informing our clients around the world and asking them to pay attention to any offers outside the official channels,” Cotarella said.
Authorities are investigating how the stolen wine may be sold. Police and Carabinieri officers are examining surveillance footage and other evidence. Cotarella said he remained confident investigators could trace the shipment, noting that two truckloads of wine would be difficult to move without attracting attention.
The theft eclipses previous high-profile wine robberies in Italy. In 2017, thieves stole about 2,000 bottles of rare wines valued at 750,000 euros from a warehouse near the Adriatic resort town of Cervia.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Two days after a major fire at New Market exposed difficulties in accessing the blaze site, Bhopal Municipal Corporation (BMC) launched a major anti-encroachment drive on Saturday, October 10, clearing footpaths and market lanes and confiscating four truckloads of goods.
The operation began at 10.30 am with public announcements urging shopkeepers and street vendors to remove encroachments voluntarily. Two teams resumed action at 3.30 pm, removing stalls, counters, hanging displays and other materials kept outside shops.
Tarpaulins and plastic sheets installed above shops were also cut down and seized. The drive continued until 8.30 pm, leaving market lanes clear of encroachments.
Fire triggers safety checks
The action followed a massive fire at Balaji Chhole-Bhature on October 8, which engulfed five nearby shops and more than 12 street-vendor stalls, causing losses worth crores of rupees.
Encroachments and roadside stalls had hampered access for fire tenders, raising concerns about emergency preparedness in the crowded market.
During Saturday's drive, municipal officials also inspected fire-fighting equipment at two chhole-bhature shops and a namkeen shop, having the systems operated in their presence.
Officials expressed concern over nearby eateries and snack shops where cooking furnaces remain operational for extended hours.
Rs. 13,000 fine imposed
The corporation imposed fines totalling Rs 13,000 during the drive. Heera Namkeen was fined Rs 10,000 for operating a furnace and littering, while a Chowmein Fast Food stall was penalised Rs 2,000. The remaining Rs 1,000 was imposed on other defaulters.

It was my lifelong dream to live in New York City. Wild, given that I was born in a small rural town in Australia, where I grew up riding dirt bikes, not reading fashion magazines.
The Land Down Under was a big, beautiful place offering an idyllic, laid-back beach life, but I always felt a pull toward The Big Apple.
That lust further ignited in the '90s as I watched the city depicted in shows like "Friends" and "Sex and the City." So in 2014, on the cusp of turning 40, I dragged my husband, our Bengal cat, and our two sons — then 2 and 9 — to New York.
We told ourselves we'd come for a year, for an adventure. Twelve years later, I'm still here. It's certainly been one hell of a (ridiculously expensive) ride.
The rent we've paid feels astronomical, and we've moved so many times
In New York City, rental costs are no joke.
We traded our beautiful 1890s cottage — three-bedroom, two-bath, front porch, huge yard, tree-lined street, 10 minutes from Bondi Beach — for a two-bedroom loft apartment in Tribeca that cost us $8,000 a month. (This is not unusual for a two-bed in this neighborhood.)
By comparison, the monthly mortgage on our cottage in Sydney was, after conversion, less than half of that price.
Still, we knew we were choosing to live in a more expensive neighborhood in Lower Manhattan, and we did so because it felt like a great place to raise our kids. We loved the community, the quiet cobblestone streets, and the access to Hudson River Park.
Our loft was essentially a large box, with windows only at the front. It was also a fifth-floor walk-up, and between the angry downstairs neighbors who complained constantly about the sound of kids moving around and the fact that I had to carry a toddler and a stroller up five brutal flights of stairs, we left in under a year.
We moved around the corner to another loft, this one even more expensive, and lasted a little over a year until the building was condemned and we had to move — again.
At one point, my husband and I had considered buying a property in NYC with our nest egg, but we didn't have a clue how to navigate the competitive real-estate market, and it seemed clear we'd only get a teeny apartment for our budget.
The math didn't add up, and the risk of owning freaked us out. So we kept rolling the dice on renting.
Between my husband and me separating, the kids outgrowing smaller apartments, and landlords unexpectedly hiking up the rent, I've moved about 10 times since coming to the US.
My kids got a solid free education, but college costs felt tough to swallow
A financial reprieve in NYC is that public education is free, though school admissions can be complicated, with factors like zoning and lottery systems shaping where kids end up.
Thankfully, both of my boys got into a highly regarded public school in Manhattan, and I was impressed with their education.
I was also glad we (mostly) dodged expensive private schools — except when my youngest attended a language-immersion school for about $30,000 a year. He came out knowing basic Mandarin, which would have been worth the investment — only he's since forgotten all of it.
Then comes the killer: college. After graduating from high school, my oldest was accepted into a prestigious university in the Midwest to study engineering.
Sure, he could've attended a more affordable or in-state school, but a lot of "New York rats" (that's what my boys proudly call themselves) want to leave the city they grew up in — and their parents — to go to college somewhere else. Getting into a respected college also felt like a major flex, and we all felt the pressure for him to attend, no matter the cost.
So, his dad and I haggled over merit and financial aid and took out student loans to cover his first year. Add kitting out his dorm room, him blowing up our Seamless account (despite having a paid meal plan), and the costs of us flying out to visit and flying him home … year one probably cost around $70,000.
He didn't end up staying after his first year, which meant our student loans were due far sooner than we planned. The silver lining of not completing his degree is that, unlike many college graduates in the US, he's not saddled with four years' worth of debt.
Going home feels like an expensive, uphill battle — and it's tough being far from family
Our rent, as established, doesn't leave much in the budget for vacations — or for airfare back to Australia to see family and friends.
As Aussies, our ideal time to go home is around Christmas, when it's summer there, and many people are off work and school. However, that privilege can set us back upward of $4,000 in round-trip airfare alone for the four of us. On top of that, each way, we'd have to take two flights, totaling over 22 hours in the air.
In my opinion, we need three weeks for a proper trip Down Under, especially as I have to visit my loved ones in two cities.
Considering our sons' public schools only granted about a week off around that time of year, it rarely seemed worth the money or jet lag. This also explains why we typically only make it home every other year.
Some costs are even harder to reconcile with when living on a separate continent and in a different time zone from so many loved ones. From afar, I'm watching my mum age from 10,000 miles away (she just turned 80), and how my sister must carry the load of caring for our father as he faces health issues.
There are so many milestone birthdays, weddings, funerals, and family events I've missed and can never get back.
Still, I'd choose moving to New York City every time
To be clear, a lot of these costs were tied to choices we made as we sought to give our family a certain kind of life in NYC.
Despite the emotional and financial pain, do I regret moving? Not for a New York minute. This city has an incredible, lively vibe. We've forged deep friendships, created new traditions, and lapped up the electrifying culture on tap.
I also feel connected to the world in a way I never did in Australia; I can be in the Caribbean in about four hours, Europe in seven — and I've met people from all walks of life.
There's an energy and diversity here you won't find anywhere else in the world, along with a feeling that you can do anything.
Regardless of any financial regrets and mistakes from the past 12 years, New York City is home.

The Snack Wrap has officially landed overseas.
McDonald's brought the fan-favorite item back to UK menus on October 6, marking its first appearance there since it was discontinued in 2016. Much like in the US, British fans spent years calling for its return — and McDonald's finally answered.
However, shortly after the launch, The Sun reported that a few British McDonald's customers were disappointed by the "downgraded" menu item, lamenting the removal of cheese from the wraps and calling it "a bit plain" on social media.
We decided to put each version to the test.
Our London-based reporter, Roya Shahidi, thought the UK's version of the Snack Wrap, while light and crispy, was disappointing overall and needed cheese.
On the other hand, our US-based reporter Erin McDowell was impressed by the flavorful sauces and crispy chicken tenders included in each of her wraps.
Here's how McDonald's Snack Wraps in the US and the UK compare in terms of taste and value.
UK-based reporter Roya went to a McDonald's in Islington, London.
There were no ads inside the McDonald's about the Snack Wrap's return.
McDonald's in the UK has only one version of the Snack Wrap.
Unlike in the US, where you can choose between a spicy or ranch version of the wrap, the UK only has one option.
The UK version contains 282 calories and costs £1.99, equivalent to about $2.62.
When ordering in the app, you can upgrade the Snack Wrap to a medium meal deal for £5.59 ($7.38), which includes a drink and fries.
The UK Snack Wrap was neatly packaged.
Roya took the Snack Wrap to the office to eat.
The UK Snack Wrap comes with a chicken tender, black pepper mayo, and shredded lettuce.
Roya found it disappointing that there was no shredded cheese inside, unlike in the US, especially since the previous UK iteration did contain cheese.
At this McDonald's, adding a cheese slice would cost 50 pence — equivalent to about 66 cents.
There was a generous amount of mayo and shredded lettuce in the wrap. However, while she is a fan of the UK McDonald's Chicken Selects, Roya felt the portion was too small for the price.
The chicken breast was tender and crispy, but the wrap overall was quite bland.
Roya thought the mayo serving was generous, though as someone who prefers other sauces, she would have liked the option for something else.
The black pepper mayo had a mild kick, and the lettuce added a nice crunch, but overall, it was missing something extra, like cheese.
The UK-based reporter thought the ingredient distribution wasn't great, with one side containing no lettuce.
As its name suggests, the Snack Wrap makes a good snack because it's light; however, it's not filling enough as a meal in its own right.
Business Insider reached out to McDonald's for comment, but did not immediately hear back.
Snack Wraps have been back on menus in the US since July 2025.
McDonald's brought back its Snack Wraps nationwide last summer, marking one of the year's most anticipated fast-food launches. The $2.99 wraps come in ranch and spicy-pepper varieties, with chicken tenders, lettuce, and shredded cheese.
The wraps began disappearing from menus in 2016 and were officially discontinued in 2020. A petition calling for their return later drew more than 18,000 signatures.
The US Snack Wraps contain 390 calories for the ranch version and 380 for the spicy version, and cost $2.99 each.
When ordering in the app, you can upgrade the Snack Wrap to a medium meal deal for $11.09, which includes a drink and fries.
In the US, they come in two varieties — spicy and ranch.
This is arguably the biggest difference compared to the new UK version, along with the addition of shredded cheese.
Our US-based reporter Erin tried both wraps and was impressed by the amount of sauce in each.
Both wraps are made with McDonald's new chicken tenders, which launched in the US in May 2025.
The spicy Snack Wrap packed more heat than Erin expected.
The lettuce tasted fresh, and Erin was impressed by how substantial the wraps were. Though billed as snack-sized, one was filling enough for a quick lunch.
The spicy sauce had a noticeable kick without being overwhelming — enough heat to earn its name.
She also enjoyed the ranch version of the Snack Wrap.
The ranch version tasted lighter but still packed plenty of flavor. Its creamy sauce balanced the fresh lettuce and crispy chicken tender, while the shredded cheese added a mild savory note and a little extra texture to each bite.
The tortilla wrap itself also seemed lighter and less doughy in the US.
We can see why McDonald's fans across the pond are disappointed by this new release.
While both reporters were excited to try the Snack Wraps, we felt a little let down by the UK version.
The key differences between the US and UK versions of the snack wrap are the absence of cheese in the UK version and fewer flavor options, which ended up greatly affecting our final takeaways.
While Erin would — and has — order these snack wraps again after their first launch, Roya wasn't so sure, given the bland flavor profile, less-than-satisfactory presentation, and mediocre distribution of ingredients.
When it comes to Snack Wraps, McDonald's fans might have to head to the US to get the tastiest version possible.

Air France enforces Israeli ban affecting pilots from Muslim countries
Air France has agreed to enforce an Israeli order barring pilots and cabin crew of certain nationalities from flights to Israel, including those from Muslim-majority countries, according to a Mediapart investigation.
The restrictions cover 31 nationalities, including Algerian, Tunisian, Iranian and Pakistani citizens. They also affect French citizens who hold one of the listed nationalities.
The directive targets nationality rather than explicitly naming religion, but effectively excludes Muslim pilots from those countries, alongside other affected crew members.
Mediapart reported that Air France had informed affected employees that they could no longer operate flights to Israel under the Israeli instructions. The airline also warned staff to declare a second nationality and said failure to comply could lead to disciplinary sanctions.
Air France’s enforcement of the restrictions could expose it to a legal challenge in France. The airline has not publicly commented on Mediapart’s findings.

According to Israeli broadcaster N12, Israel’s Ministry of Transport issued the directive on 1 October. It requires airlines to ensure that pilots and flight attendants entering Israeli airspace do not hold the nationality or dual nationality of a country without diplomatic relations with Israel.
The order followed an alleged attempt by an Omani flydubai co-pilot to seize control of a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight on 30 September and crash it into a terminal at Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport.
The co-pilot told UAE investigators that he had acted alone. Neither the Israeli nor the UAE account has undergone independent verification, and little is known about the pilot beyond the information they have released.
The suspect previously worked for several airlines, including Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, before joining flydubai in January 2026.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 13 reported that at least one unnamed Israeli airline was conducting background checks on about 2,500 pilots and cabin crew working in the country’s aviation sector.
Middle East Eye contacted Air France for a response to Mediapart’s findings but received no reply by publication.

Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was attacked again on Saturday (October 10)prompting an evacuation and widespread flight disruptions, as the kingdom faces an escalating campaign of strikes linked to Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels.
A missile struck a passenger terminal and several people were wounded, one of two regional officials told The Associated Press. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.
The airport had already been targeted earlier in the week.
There was no immediate statement from the Houthis claiming responsibility for Saturday’s incident.
The US Embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed it was aware of attacks on the airport and urged American citizens to stay away from the facility and surrounding areas.
“The U.S. Mission is aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on October 10 and strongly recommends all U.S. citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas,” the embassy said in a statement posted online.
The Canadian, German and Spanish embassies also warned their citizens against travelling to the airport.
Spain’s embassy described the incident as a “new attack” by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis in a message on X. A diplomatic source separately told AFP that a missile had struck the airport at around 1200 GMT.
Canada’s embassy cited “ongoing military activity” affecting the airport, while Germany’s mission referred to the prevailing situation without providing further details.
France’s embassy had urged its citizens on Friday to exercise “utmost care” in Saudi Arabia following Houthi strikes in recent days. It also warned French nationals against recording images of affected areas or sharing them online.
Saudi Arabia’s government-run Centre for International Communication, which oversees foreign media in the kingdom, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The reported attack triggered major disruptions to air travel, with flights heading to Riyadh diverted to other airports, according to flight-tracking service Flightradar24.
The airport also issued an alert asking passengers to check their flight status with airlines before leaving for the facility.
The latest incident comes amid an escalation in attacks attributed to the Houthis, who have opened a new front in the wider Middle East conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran.
King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times over the past week, following the launch of a major military offensive by a Saudi-led coalition against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. The Houthis claimed responsibility for earlier attacks, including one on Wednesday that killed a Sudanese national.
Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government and has provided military support in its fight against the Houthis. Fighting between Houthi forces and Saudi-backed Yemeni government troops has intensified, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support to help government forces reverse recent rebel gains along the Red Sea.
The Houthis’ advances have also increased their ability to monitor shipping along the Red Sea corridor, an important alternative route for maritime traffic amid disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
However, responsibility for the latest attack had not been officially confirmed by the Houthis at the time of reporting.
(With AP, AFP inputs)

A student hated reading for years. Her podcast explores finding the right diagnosis
LONG ISLAND, N.Y. — Cora Walsh walks home from middle school every day. It's only a few tree-lined blocks in Rockville Centre on Long Island, but the movement helps clear her head of the school day. She probably thinks about how the brain works more than most seventh-graders.
"I want to be a doctor," she says. "And I want to go to Princeton and major in neuroscience."
Her fascination started a few years ago when she was struggling to figure out what was happening in her own head.
"It's kind of confusing what it is like in my brain," she says. All she knew back then was that reading was hard. Even when she spent more time working on it than her friends, she could never reach their level.
Like millions of Americans, Cora has dyslexia, but it took her almost five years to get the correct diagnosis.
Her podcast about the journey to understanding her own mind is the grand prize winner for middle school in this year's NPR Student Podcast Challenge. "Dyslexia and MEE" was chosen from nearly 1,500 submissions from 42 states and the District of Columbia.
"I feel really excited," Cora says about her victory. Her parents, who spent the whole journey right by her side, are thrilled too.
"This is a kid that works so hard and has such a good attitude," says her mom, Emily Johnson. "I'm so proud of her."
Finding the right learning style
Cora has come a long way. She has received tutoring for her dyslexia for two years now.
Her podcast takes the listener along to one of her lessons. She sounds out words over Zoom, and her tutor gives her feedback and tips. They don't move too fast, making sure Cora really understands something before moving on.
It can be tedious, but her hard work outside the classroom is starting to pay off.
"I think I'm a better reader now, and I enjoy it a lot more," she says. "I feel more comfortable reading bigger books, but not too big!"
Her mom says that this summer marked a turning point: She saw her daughter reading the first book in the Hunger Games series.
"She would pick it up for fun, and she would go read to [her pet] rabbit. Or we were traveling this summer, and she read on the train," Johnson says. "I mean, it's the first time that's ever happened."
It was a winding road to get to this point, but Cora and her parents are excited to see where it goes. Winning NPR's national competition is another bright spot.
"I'm kind of just proud of myself that I overcame this hard, annoying thing," she says. "And proud of myself that I created something really cool and interesting that everyone can listen to."
Cora hopes that her podcast might help dyslexia feel a little less scary for listeners and maybe even reach younger students who are still trying to figure out their own learning styles.
"I would say: Always try your hardest, and don't sell yourself short," she says. "I think trying is … the best thing you can do."
Cora Walsh is still trying: She just checked out that second Hunger Games book from the library.

The visuals in the footage have an authentic origin, but the audio has been edited to significantly change the meaning of the prayer.
On Oct. 4, a social media user posted a video purportedly depicting a man leading a group of Arkansas farmers in prayer, asking "baby Jesus" for "more Mexicans" to replace the "Mexicans we had deported" to save their farms.
The user posted the footage to Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived). The audio seemingly shows the man leading the prayer saying:
Dear Baby Jesus, please help us. We're losing our farms. We know we sent all the Mexicans away. Dear Lord, please send us some more Mexicans to replace the Mexicans we had deported. We're going to lose our farms; please, Baby Jesus and all things holy. Amen.
The clip spread amid numerous reports of rising prices and trade wars impacting U.S. farmers.
In short, the visuals in the video have an authentic origin, but the audio has been edited to significantly change the meaning of the prayer. Therefore, we rate the audio as fake.
The authentic footage originates from a broadcast by KATV 7, a TV news station in Little Rock, Arkansas. The channel posted the segment to YouTube on Sept. 2, 2025 (archived), more than a year earlier than when the edited clip was circulating. It shows hundreds of Arkansas farmers in a school gymnasium seeking the federal government's help regarding their financial struggles.
At about 2:24, the video cuts to a man leading the farmers in prayer. He can be heard saying:
Farmers, in my opinion, dear Lord, and it's only my opinion, are closer to you than anyone else on this Earth because we deal with your Earth every day. Dear Lord, we're hurting, dear Lord. We can't help what's happened to us.
According to KATV 7's article about the event, also published on Sept. 2, 2025, the farmer then said, "We need help, dear Lord."
Another piece of evidence that the "more Mexicans" iteration of the clip is edited is the quality of its audio. The prayer in the edited version is sharp, clear and lacking an echo. Inside a school gymnasium, the audio of the farmers praying should, in reality, feature an echo, like the man's voice does in the original footage.
Both Facebook and Instagram identified the audio as original to Aaron Beltrán, the person who appeared to first post the edited clip on both platforms.
Snopes reached out to Beltrán to ask whether he originally edited and posted the manipulated video, if the voice is his own and if the content was meant to be satirical. We will update this story if we receive a reply.

‘Incompetent leader tried to drag President into political street fight’: BJP fumes at Rahul Gandhi
Patra questioned why Rahul and the Opposition delegation did not submit evidence of alleged electoral irregularities to the President during Friday’s meeting.
Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) spokesperson Sambit Patra on Saturday criticised Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over his remarks following a meeting with President Droupadi Murmu over the ongoing CEC row, accusing him of trying to drag the President into a “political street fight” amid the Opposition’s allegations of “vote chori”.
Patra questioned why Rahul and the Opposition delegation did not present evidence of alleged electoral irregularities to the President during their meeting on Friday.
He also accused the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha of making misleading statements about the interaction.
Deep Dive
“An incompetent leader tried to drag the President into a political street fight. Rahul Gandhi does not even understand basic protocol. It is basic protocol that the President accepts a memorandum, but he turned it into a drama,” Patra said.
Questioning the Opposition's claims, the BJP spokesperson asked why the leaders had not submitted evidence to the President if they had been alleging electoral irregularities for nearly a year.
“If you are going to submit the evidence later, why did you go there in the first place without it?” Patra said.
He further alleged that Gandhi had misrepresented the President's response to the Opposition's claims.
“After coming out, this incompetent leader says that the President agreed with him,” Patra said, adding that Gandhi was not responsible enough to occupy a high position in the country.
The BJP spokesperson's remarks came a day after a 10-member INDIA bloc delegation, led by Congress and Gandhi, met President Murmu at Rashtrapati Bhavan and submitted a memorandum outlining four demands, including the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
After the meeting, Rahul said he was “shocked” that the President did not deny the Opposition's allegations of “vote chori”. He claimed that the President had sought proof of the alleged electoral irregularities.
“I just sat in quite an unbelievable meeting with the President of India. We presented our memorandum to her outlining PM Modi and HM Amit Shah’s gross subversion of India’s electoral system and seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. I was shocked that the President did not deny Vote Chori,” Rahul wrote on X.
Rahul also said he had told the President that evidence of alleged electoral manipulation was known to the country, claiming that elections had been “stolen” in state after state.

Nearly 45 years later, a new Blade Runner is back to make the Ridley Scott franchise “more human than human” once again.
On Saturday at New York Comic-Con, Prime Video released key art and a new trailer for the eight-episode limited series created by Silka Luisa with Amazon MGM Studios and Alcon Television Group, premiering in full Nov. 25 on the streamer.
Set 50 years after the events of Blade Runner 2049, Los Angeles has been reborn, just not by humanity. Cora (Hunter Schafer), a fugitive in a final bid to stop running, takes on one last identity: a Blade Runner. Forced to partner with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant days from dying, she hunts down a runaway hiding a truth that could collapse a fragile city.
Luisa, Yeoh and Schafer took the stage at Prime Video’s NYCC panel on Sunday, along with cast members Dimitri Abold, Lewis Gribben and Matthew Needham, as well as executive producers Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson.
Watch on Deadline
The series also stars Katelyn Rose Downey, Daniel Rigby, Johnny Harris, Amy Lennox, Sheila Atim, Tom Burke and Maurizio Lombardi.
Luisa serves as showrunner, creator and executive producer. Additional EPs include Ridley Scott, Alcon Entertainment co-founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, Alcon’s President of Television Ben Roberts, Steven Johnson, David W. Zucker and Clayton Krueger from Scott Free Productions, Richard Sharkey, Tom Spezialy, Michael Green, Cynthia Yorkin, Frank Giustra, Tim Gable, Isa Dick Hackett and Jonathan van Tulleken, who directed the first two episodes.
Directed by Scott, the original Blade Runner premiered in 1982, starring Harrison Ford and Sean Young. In 2017, Ford reprised his role as Rick Deckard in Denis Villeneuve’s Blade Runner 2049, starring alongside Ryan Gosling.

Catherine Zeta-Jones wants to see less AI “actors” onscreen and more undiscovered human talents.
The Oscar winner recently commented on actors that have “given themselves over” to artificial intelligence companies, explaining that she prefers “not knowing anything” about the actors she watches in movies and television.
“There’s so many actors already, who have given themselves over to an AI company, and that’s everyone’s choice,” she told the Associated Press. “But I like going to the theater and seeing real people talk.”
Zeta-Jones continued, “I like going to movies and not knowing anything about the actors. I don’t wanna know who they’re sleeping with, what they wore, what they drink in the morning, how they keep their figure. I wanna be taken away and see a character, and that has happened for years.”
Watch on Deadline
The Kill Jackie star’s comments come amid ongoing concerns around AI’s plagiarism of copyrighted materials and the threat it poses to jobs in Hollywood and beyond, as well as recent warnings from those working in AI that continued progress could “cause a billion deaths.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order last month to fast-track stringent oversight and control of AI. Convening “a group of world-leading experts” within the next 60 days, the order lays out a discussion of “safety plans” and “an emergency shutoff, or ‘kill switch,’ for frontier models.”
On a federal level, Trump has brushed off concerns about AI as “a hoax,” insisting the U.S. government “already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power” over AI companies.

Crafting in Anime Zero lets you turn collected materials into accessories that improve your character’s stats. You can also buy materials with Coins or convert items you have into rarer materials, making crafting useful when you are missing a few ingredients. This guide covers all confirmed crafting recipes, how to craft items, where to buy materials, and how to convert materials in Anime Zero.
All Crafting Recipes in Anime Zero
There are 14 craftable accessories in Anime Zero, each providing different bonuses to help you deal damage, survive longer, or collect resources faster. Before crafting, compare their stats and material requirements to decide which accessory fits your build.

How to Craft in Anime Zero
Once you collect the required materials through quests, story, or Anime Zero codes, follow these steps to craft accessories:
- Open the Areas menu from the left side of the screen.
- Select Crafting to teleport to the crafting area.
- Find Yugi, the Forger NPC, and open the crafting menu.
- Select the Craft tab.
- Choose an accessory from the list and select Quick Craft to create the accessory.
Anime Zero Crafting Material Shop
The Material Shop lets you purchase crafting materials with Coins instead of relying entirely on drops. Its inventory has a daily stock limit and restocks on a timer, so check back regularly if you need more of a particular item.
Here are the materials, prices, and stock limits visible in the Material Shop:

To buy materials in Anime Zero, you will need a lot of coins. Farm them by using the best Anime Zero build. Once done, you can purchase the materials from the shop tab of the crafting menu.
How to Convert Materials in Anime Zero
Material Conversion lets you exchange materials you already own for other materials. This is useful when you have extra lower-rarity items but need a specific ingredient for an accessory. Given that your Anime Zero weapons work better with accessories, you will need this trick quite often.
To convert items in Anime Zero, select the convert tab from the crafting menu. Set the conversion amount and check whether you have enough items. Confirm the conversion when the button becomes available.

‘System can’t be honest when you win and rigged when you lose’: 124 ex-bureaucrats defend Election Commission, SIR exercise
Defending SIR, the ex-civil servants described it as a necessary process to maintain accurate electoral rolls by identifying deceased voters, duplicate entries
After 42 former judges raised concerns over what they described as a sustained campaign against the Election Commission of India (ECI), 124 former bureaucrats have written an open letter defending the poll body amid allegations of irregularities in the electoral process.
In their letter to the citizens of India, the 124 former IAS, IFS and allied services officers said the country’s electoral system had undergone a significant transformation from the era of booth capturing, ballot box stuffing and election-related violence. They highlighted safeguards such as polling agents, the sealing of electronic voting machines (EVMs), strong-room security and Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) verification.
Also Read | Delhi protest: Right-wing groups assault protesters, journalists amid heavy security deployment
The letter comes amid protests in Delhi and Mumbai against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of electoral irregularities.
“A system cannot be honest when you win and rigged when you lose,” the letter stated, according to ANI, noting that the party ruling at the Centre had lost several state elections under the same Election Commission. The officers also referred to the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, in which the ruling party failed to secure an outright majority on its own.
Defending the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise, the former civil servants described it as a necessary process to maintain accurate electoral rolls by identifying deceased voters, duplicate entries and individuals who had permanently shifted residence.
They also maintained that the SIR process included safeguards to address concerns over wrongful exclusion, including the publication of draft electoral rolls, opportunities to file claims and objections, hearings and provisions for appeals.
“Questioning is every citizen’s right. Proving is the accuser’s duty,” the officers said, adding that unsubstantiated allegations could weaken public confidence in democratic institutions and the electoral process.

Meanwhile, in a separate open letter, 42 former judges and retired constitutional officeholders said they had no political brief and were speaking out because “silence is no longer a neutral choice”. They alleged that constitutional bodies were facing attacks driven by political interests and warned of the consequences of undermining public trust in the country’s democratic institutions.
“Our concern is grave. India's constitutional bodies are under sustained attack. The Election Commission of India stands at the centre of this assault,” the letter read.

Discord is simmering between some Congress legislators and Ministers over Cabinet expansion, fund allocation and alleged interference in constituencies, posing a fresh challenge to Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar’s efforts to keep the flock united.
The growing discord has also brought Mr. Shivakumar’s relationship with Karnataka Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC) president B.K. Hariprasad under scrutiny, with the two reportedly differing on several organisational issues.
While the first half of the Congress government’s five-year term was marked by differences between former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah and Mr. Shivakumar, the second half appears to be witnessing public confrontations between some Ministers and legislators. The discord has surfaced in Shivamogga, Vijayapura, Mysuru, Kolar-Chickballapur and Belagavi districts.
‘Political dynasties’
In Shivamogga, tensions have surfaced between School Education Minister and the district in-charge Madhu Bangarappa and Belur Gopalakrishna, Sagar MLA, who was denied a Cabinet berth. Mr. Gopalakrishna has criticised what he described as “favouritism towards political dynasties”.
The KPCC has also issued a notice to H.S. Sundaresh, former chairman of the Shivamogga-Bhadravathi Urban Development Authority and a former District Congress Committee (DCC) president, over his remarks against party leaders. Mr. Sundaresh had alleged corruption involving people close to Mr. Bangarappa and questioned the appointment of H.C. Yogesh as DCC president. Following this, C.G. Madhusudan replaced Mr. Sundaresh as the authority chief.
In Vijayapura, differences between Minister M.B. Patil and Congress MLAs C.S. Nadagouda and Yashvantharayagouda Patil have escalated. The legislators have accused Mr. Patil of conspiring to prevent them from securing ministerial berths.
An ‘open war’
Yashvantharayagouda Patil had threatened to resign as MLA over the failure to declare his Indi constituency drought-hit. He has also declared an “open war” against the Minister, saying the 2028 Assembly election would become a direct contest between the two.
In Mysuru, former Minister H.C. Mahadevappa’s absence from the swearing-in ceremony of Beerihundi Basavanna as DCC (Rural) president has fuelled speculation about his dissatisfaction with the party leadership. Former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah attended the programme. Mr. Mahadevappa is reportedly unhappy over being denied a Cabinet berth.
Former Minister Tanveer Sait is also believed to be dissatisfied with the elevation of Yathindra Siddaramaiah, MLC, to the Cabinet and Minister in-charge of Mysuru district.
In Kolar
Kolar and Chickballapur have emerged as another source of concern for the Chief Minister. Several legislators, including M.C. Sudhakar, K.Y. Nanjegowda, Bangarapet Narayanaswamy, Bagepalli Subbareddy and Kothanur Manjunath reportedly met Mr. Shivakumar to air their grievances against Minister K.H. Muniyappa.
The legislators are said to have sought a probe into alleged financial irregularities at the Kolar-Chickballapur DCC Bank during the tenure of its former chairman, Govinda Gowda. Differences involving Roopakala M. Shashidhar, KGF MLA, have further aggravated the tensions.
In Chickballapur, MLA Pradeep Eshwar’s social media post targeting Mr. Sudhakar’s constituency reportedly triggered resentment. The legislators are believed to have raised their differences with the Chief Minister and urged the party leadership to intervene.
No women Ministers yet
Meanwhile, women legislators have been sulking about the denial of Cabinet berths to them and the appointment of all men as chiefs of DCCs.
The reported differences between Mr. Shivakumar and Mr. Hariprasad over the proposed Political Affairs Committee (PAC), intended to improve coordination between the party organisation and the government, have added another dimension to the internal discord. The KPCC chief’s plan to launch the second leg of the Bharat Jodo Yatra in 84 constituencies defeated by Congress in 2023 has also believed to have emerged as a point of contention. Now, following the directions of the party high command, the name of Bharat Jodo Yatra has been changed to Jana Jagruthi Yatra.

Taiwan’s 23 million people live under the constant threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex it.

The era of Amazon's Fire tablets—cheap slate computers ranging from $60 to $280—is over.
All of the Fire tablets are being replaced by the all-aluminum Amazon Alexa Tablet. These tablets will, in a first for Amazon, run official Android and have full access to the Google Play Store. The lack of proper app support was always a sticking point for the Fire tablets, which ran a custom version of Android and had a much more limited app library.
The new Alexa Tablet series comes in three models: the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro ($500), Alexa Tablet 11 ($330), and Alexa Tablet 8 ($230), with the numbers corresponding to the display size. Amazon is also offering kids' editions of the latter two devices at the same prices. These include bumper cases for extra protection, a one-year, worry-free guarantee to replace the device if it breaks, and a year of Amazon Kids+ service to fill the tablet with age-appropriate content.
As for Fire tablets, Amazon says it will stop shipping the devices in the next month or two. It will support them for four years from the last ship date. Amazon is committing to at least four years of software updates for the new Alexa tablets, which will launch with Android 16 and will receive Android 17 early in 2027. Preorders for the new Alexa Tablets are open now, and they'll begin shipping on October 14.
Premium Tablets
The experience is largely the same on all three tablets, with aluminum builds designed to mimic the new aluminum Kindles. The MediaTek Dimensity 8189 chip powers the two smaller tablets, whereas the 12-inch device gets a little more power from the MediaTek Dimensity 8400.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is the outlier of the trio, as it's the only one with two display variants: a standard 12-inch LCD screen or a 12-inch Nanomatte display with anti-glare and anti-reflective properties. Upgrade to the Nanomatte—starting at $550—for a matte, paperlike look and feel. With a peak brightness of 500 nits, it should still be bright enough to view in sunlight.

Amazon says it developed this screen in partnership with Corning (the company that makes most of the glass that protects smartphone displays). It's similar to the matte displays found on devices like TCL's Nxtpaper series, though Amazon's vice president of devices, Kevin Keith, says the hexagon-shaped imprint on the Nanomatte display can push out vivid colors and crisp blacks while still retaining those matte properties.
The screen also offers a “really good” writing experience, according to Keith. He says the same engineers who worked on the Kindle Scribe worked with Corning to get that paperlike feel. The screen works with Amazon's new Alexa Tablet Pro Pen ($90), which has 4,096 levels of pressure sensitivity, plus tilt detection. The pen can magnetically dock to the top of the slate for charging and pairing. Amazon also sells a Pro Keyboard ($150) for the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which attaches to the device via the pogo pins on the bottom edge—no Bluetooth needed.
Now that Android has recently gained multiwindowing features, attaching the keyboard turns the largest Alexa tablet into a productivity machine: split apps across the screen, resize them into various windows, and “save” several desktop arrangements so you can pick up where you left off.
For the kids’ versions of the Alexa Tablet 11 and Alexa Tablet 8, Amazon says the software is still Android with a heavily customized interface for kid-friendly content and built-in parental controls. Keith says one in five kids in the US has an Amazon tablet, so it'll be interesting to see how that changes now that these devices start at a higher price.
Alexa Front and Center
It may look and feel like Android, but Amazon has tweaked the interface to make these Alexa Tablets feel like Amazon hardware.
The top-left corner of the home screen features a persistent widget called the Dynamic Tab. This scrollable widget lets you dive into Amazon content you may have been consuming on another device—say, if you were reading on your Kindle, watching a movie on Prime Video on your iPhone, or snapped some photos and you want to view them on Amazon Photos.
Swipe right, and instead of Google's Discover feed, you're instead greeted with Amazon's For You experience. Amazon's Fire tablets were a vehicle to put Amazon content in front of your eyeballs, and that hasn't changed with the Alexa Tablets. Again, you can continue consuming content here, with tabs for movies and TV, games, and Kindle. There's also a news feed, and you can tap Alexa prompts for more information on a story.
Uniquely, opening the Kindle app triggers “Kindle mode,” which disables all notifications, turns on the blue light filter, and extends battery life to 20 hours (less on the smaller tablets). You can also choose one of three display treatments in this mode: subtle warmth with natural color, a softened paper tone, or monochrome. There's even a fun page-turn effect that mimics turning a page in a book. As soon as you exit the app, notifications turn back on, and the screen returns to normal. Annotations you make with the stylus will sync with Kindle apps on pen-supported devices, like the Kindle Scribe.
As the tablets’ names suggests, Alexa+ is front and center. So far, Amazon has restricted Alexa+ access to paid subscribers or Amazon Prime customers, but Keith says you don't need to subscribe to anything to use Alexa+ on these devices.
In the bottom-right corner, a persistent “Ask Alexa” chat box lets you call up the virtual assistant immediately. You can also trigger it by saying, “Alexa,” just like an Echo device. It can control your smart home devices, but the marquee addition is Alexa's On-Screen Intelligence. It's opt-in—with an on-screen indicator whenever it's active—allowing the assistant to see what you're looking at and answer contextual questions.
For example, if you're traveling to a new city and are looking at a guide filled with restaurant recommendations, you can ask Alexa, “Which of these is closest to my hotel?” and it can filter the list. Got a schedule for your kid's soccer games? Bring up Alexa and ask it to add all the events to your calendar.
Alexa+ also supports live sessions—much like Google's Gemini Live or ChatGPT's Voice Mode, you can have a real-time back-and-forth conversation with the assistant without speaking the wake word at every turn. Watching a TikTok and wondering whether a product in the video is available on Amazon? Naturally, you can ask Alexa, and the assistant can even add it to your shopping cart.
The hardware may finally have the look and feel of other premium Android tablets, but these slates are still built to keep you hooked on Amazon's retail empire.

Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops cross border
- Published
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.
In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", following reported strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.
Fighting broke out between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), two weeks ago.
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended its civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea backs the TPLF, which it denies.
During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF.
But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.
Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.
Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.
US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.
One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.
Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.
Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."
But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.
On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".
In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.
This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.
Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.

"Affordability is only part of the story. What matters as much is whether affordable homes are actually for sale in the places where buyers want and need to live," Realtor senior economist Hannah Jones said. "For first-time buyers, the search is increasingly shaped by the geography of opportunity, not simply a metro's headline price. Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
- Published
A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report.
Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok.
Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him, and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities.
The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police.
Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault
Catching My Teacher
Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia
Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube, external.
The student detectives
Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar.
They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school.
By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta.
Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school.
Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school.
Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations.
In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation.
"Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said.
Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC.
In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent.
Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions.
Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name".
The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases.
More students come forward
The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands.
One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter.
"I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school."
Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married, were overwhelmed by the response from former students.
"It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'."
Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse.
"They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said.
Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously.
"It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC.
Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process.
The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time.
NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals.
In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward.

MacBooks have taken most of the spotlight away from Mac desktops in recent years. Now that mobile performance and battery life have improved so much, there's less of a reason to buy a desktop that chains you to your office.
But Mac desktops are getting a resurgence. The Mac Mini and Mac Studio were finally refreshed with brand-new chips and a newfound focus on running local AI. But which one should you buy? And where does the iMac land these days? I've been testing Macs for over a decade and have tested all these Mac desktops, so I can recommend what's right for you.
Also check out our complete guide to the Best MacBooks, Best Desktops, and Best All-In-One Desktops.
The Best for Everyone: Mac Mini
Apple's lovable mini PC was just upgraded with the M6 chip, and it's a big deal on a couple of fronts. Before the refresh, these little computers were sold out for months, and it has AI to thank.
The Mac Mini isn't the ultra-cheap mini PC it used to be. It's $300 more than in the past, but the base model now has higher specs and a focus on running local AI. If you want a truly affordable little desktop PC for occasional use, you'll have to opt for a Windows machine. The good news is that the Mac Mini remains a compelling offer across its configurations. You can choose between two new models: one with the M6 and one with the M5 Pro. The M6 model is the one most people should buy, especially if you're looking for a fast, reliable Mac desktop.
The new M6 chip is especially fast in terms of GPU performance, an area Apple continues to make strides. If you're a fledgling video editor or designer, the base configuration packs plenty of performance for creative applications. Unfortunately, it's only a couple hundred bucks cheaper than a similarly configured MacBook Air, which makes the buying decision frustrating given how much more versatile a laptop is. But for the first time, the Mac Mini's form factor is a benefit over a laptop. AI enthusiasts get excited about the prospect of an always-on, agentic AI box that sits on their desk and can then be controlled remotely from a MacBook or iPhone. That's exactly what the Mac Mini can do (just be sure to upgrade the memory). And given memory prices across the industry, you won't find many comparable options on Windows or Linux—at least not with this much performance and RAM.
I haven't tested the M5 Pro model yet, but the main difference is in the enhanced graphics. Despite the improvements I mentioned on the M6, you can configure the M5 Pro up to 20 GPU cores, which really come in handy for tasks like gaming, 3D modeling, and video rendering. As the name suggests, I wouldn't consider the pricier M5 Pro config unless you're a professional who sits in front of Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve all day. If you're more of a hobbyist or dabbler, the M6 will likely do you just fine.
Shipping times on the M6 Mac Mini have improved to the point where you can buy one and pick it up today from an Apple Store. The M5 Pro models, however, may take up to four weeks to ship.
Only for Pros: Mac Studio
Like with the Mac Mini, there are really two distinct versions of the Mac Studio. The base configuration comes with an M5 Max (the same chip in the MacBook Pro), sporting some really impressive GPU performance in particular. And that's the main thing to consider when deciding between the M5 Pro Mac Mini and the M5 Max Mac Studio. Like choosing between those two chips in a MacBook Pro, the main upgrade is in graphics performance. Going with the M5 Max also lets you configure it with up to 128 GB of unified memory, which matters if you plan to run heavy local AI models. On the other hand, this puts you over the $5,000 price point rather quickly.
And then, there's the M5 Ultra. This massive chip is literally two M5 Max dies stitched together, and to my surprise while testing, it sometimes resulted in double the performance, such as in GPU performance. But look, don't even bother considering this unless you know exactly what you intend to use it for. Just so you know what you're getting into, the model I tested had 256 GB of memory and cost over $11,000. You read that right. It's definitely the most expensive computer I've ever had on my desk.
But I downloaded and started running on the M5 Ultra some of the largest and most powerful AI models I could find, and soon enough I had a foundation-tier LLM running completely on-device—no cloud needed. That means direct access to your computer for a powerful agentic AI to run wild with, all without the privacy and security concerns. Some simple agentic tests I ran on the M5 Ultra took minutes, whereas it took five times as long on my M5 Max MacBook Pro.
And while this thing is clearly not intended for gaming, I was pretty blown away by how fast games like Cyberpunk 2077 ran. I've definitely never seen games play this smoothly on a Mac before.
Unfortunately, shipping times on the Mac Studio are still dicey. If you want anything with 128 GB or more of memory, you'll be waiting up to a month and a half for the M5 Max models. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio, meanwhile, will take up to four months to ship at this point.
Don't Buy the iMac Right Now
The iMac has been downplayed in recent years. The once-iconic all-in-one computer, which comes with the display, stand, and accessories, used to be an affordable go-to choice for students, families, businesses, and even content creators. But as Apple has shifted focus, the iMac seems less and less of a focus, with sporadic updates over the years. It hasn't been updated since 2024 and still uses the M4 chip.
It's not a bad computer, though. The screen is brilliant, and the performance is solid, even by today's standards. Its age, however, isn't reflected in the price you'd pay right now: $1,499 gets you 16 GB of RAM, 256 GB of storage, the M4 chip with an eight-core GPU, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, and a 4.5K IPS display. A second M4 model with a 10-core GPU and four Thunderbolt 4 ports starts at $1,699. (Like nearly all Apple products, the iMac got a price increase.)
The main issue for me is that there's currently only a 23.5-inch model, which is smaller than what most people will probably want. Until Apple releases a 27-inch model (as it has in the past), perhaps with an option for a “Pro” M-series chip, I can't see the iMac as a good choice for most people. The simplicity will be a draw, especially if researching and buying a separate monitor and peripherals sounds daunting.
Interestingly, it is also the only desktop-size Mac monitor that isn't at least 5K (it's 4.5K). So, while it's cheaper than buying a Studio Display paired with a new Mac Mini, the iMac also locks you into a one-time purchase you can't upgrade later. And as the focus on local AI only grows, I can't imagine the iMac regaining the relevance or attention it once had. On the plus side, it's the only Mac desktop available in seven colors.
At the very least, I hope it gets a refresh to the M6 in the next couple of months. It'll have been long overdue! Either way, now's not a good time to buy an iMac.
Why Is Everyone Buying a Mac Mini?
Before the launch of the M6 model, Mac Minis had been sold out for most of this year. Orders for Mac Studios were similarly backlogged for months before you could get one. The reason? Well, according to Apple on an earnings call, both computers are “amazing platforms for AI and agentic tools,” and that “customer adoption of that is happening faster than we expected.” In other words, they were caught off guard. AI frameworks released in 2026, such as OpenClaw, run best on a dedicated machine that never turns off and has lots of available RAM—such as a Mac Mini.
What Happened to the Mac Pro?
The last incarnation of the Mac Pro was one of Apple's most short-lived Macs. The most recent design was relaunched in 2019, alongside the Pro Display XDR. When it was unveiled, it was an exciting re-entrance for the Mac, focusing not only on Pro-level performance but also on upgradability. Unlike the current Mac Studio, the Mac Pro had modular components you could swap in and out—or upgrade. The design was much more akin to a traditional tower PC. For a company that had been moving in the opposite direction for so long, it was a breath of fresh air.
But it wasn't meant to last, and it survived only a few upgrade cycles. With the advent of Apple silicon and the rapid scaling of these system-on-a-chip (SoC) designs, the Mac Pro's focus on modularity made less and less sense. Apple didn't officially discontinue the Mac Pro until March 2026, but by then it had been almost three years since the Mac Pro was last updated. The Mac Studio with the “Ultra” chips has since fully replaced the Mac Pro.
M6, M5 Pro, M5 Max, or M5 Ultra?
Both the Mac Mini and Mac Studio have two configurations to choose from, which gives a clean delineation between the two in terms of performance. When you move from the base chip to the Pro and Max chips, the main differences are GPU cores and, in some cases, the maximum amount of RAM you can upgrade to. Certain applications and tasks benefit greatly from stronger GPU performance, speeding up things like video rendering, 3D modeling, gaming, and AI inferencing. These are the same chips that are available in the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro.
The jump between the Max and Ultra chips, however, is much more significant. This is where you enter performance territory not possible on a MacBook. It has twice the CPU and GPU cores of the standard Max chips, delivers far stronger performance, and lets you configure it with up to 512 GB of unified memory.
The iMac is still holding onto the M4. For most people, the chip is more than capable, but considering the age and the price of the iMac today, it's outdated for a new machine.

Following a deadly train crash, Indonesia steps up safety reforms as experts push for long-term improvements
Authorities have begun addressing communication, signalling and other safety gaps exposed by the deadly April train crash, but experts say Indonesia needs broader reforms to prevent similar accidents elsewhere.
JAKARTA: The unpaved alleyway of the neighbourhood of Gang Delima in the Indonesian city of Bekasi - which is 17km east of the capital Jakarta - has become noticeably dimmer since April.
A spotlight illuminating a local scrapyard has been removed, while street lights that once spilled onto the nearby railway tracks have either been redirected or fitted with shades. Residents and businesses in the working-class neighbourhood have also been barred from putting up red, green or orange lights that could be mistaken for railway signals.
“They plan to raise the height of that wall over there too,” Rahmat, a 55-year-old local resident, told CNA, referring to the authorities while pointing to the barrier separating the railway tracks from a traditional market, where brightly lit stalls stay open late into the night.
The changes are among a series of safety measures introduced around East Bekasi Station following a deadly train crash on Apr 27 that killed 16 people - all of whom were women, seated inside the women-only carriage at the rear.
The chain of events began when an electric taxi stalled at an unmanned level crossing near the station and was struck by a commuter train travelling west. As word of the collision spread, crowds gathered along the tracks, while another commuter train heading in the opposite direction was instructed to remain at East Bekasi Station.
A third train – an express service travelling from Jakarta to Surabaya in East Java – then slammed into the stationary commuter train at East Bekasi Station, crushing passengers inside the packed women-only carriage at the rear.
This fatal sequence of events – from the ramming of the stalled taxi and the fatal train collision - took just three minutes and 48 seconds.
An investigation by Indonesia’s National Transportation Safety Committee (KNKT), whose 141-page findings were released on Sep 29, highlighted communication problems, timetable management and the lack of standard operating procedures (SOP) to report and respond to emergency situations as contributing factors to the crash.
In the immediate aftermath, officials also took note of the intense lighting around Gang Delima and the traditional market beside the tracks. The KNKT report also confirmed that the surrounding lights had made railway signals more difficult to distinguish – a problem compounded by scratches and cracks on the express train’s windscreen.
The safety committee also issued 17 recommendations to train operators and the Ministry of Transportation, calling for tighter SOPs, more training and improvements of various infrastructures, systems and facilities.
But experts said limiting some recommendations to railway lines and areas directly affected by the April crash leaves a wider safety gap.
“Similar problems also exist across Indonesia,” Yusa Permana, a transportation planning and policy expert, told CNA. “There needs to be efforts to address the issues highlighted by the KNKT on a national level.”
POOR COMMUNICATION
According to the KNKT report, the first incident was communicated so poorly by the driver of the commuter train involved, it took the southern railway traffic controller, or PPKP Selatan, three minutes and 20 seconds to fully understand what had happened and activate an emergency response. This left the driver of the express train less than 30 seconds to react.
All train movements in the area were then suspended, including the second commuter train, which was instructed to remain at East Bekasi Station.
By then, however, the express train travelling from Jakarta was only one station away, travelling at more than 100kmh.
According to the KNKT report, the express train driver saw a red signal instructing him to stop when he was about 500m from East Bekasi Station, where the commuter train was stationary.
But the signal was located near a curve. The driver slowed the train to 78kmh before applying the emergency brake about 275m from the station, after the train had cleared the bend.
“Even on a straight track, suddenly applying the brakes could cause the train body to lift,” transportation policy analyst Azas Tigor Nainggolan told CNA.
“If the train driver had applied the emergency brake at the bend, the train could have overturned. That would have been even more dangerous and could have caused many casualties among the passengers.”
The KNKT report highlighted that there is currently no SOP on how emergency braking should be safely performed on a curved section of a track.
Despite the driver’s best efforts to avoid a crash, the express train was still travelling at 40kmh when it ploughed into the stationary commuter train. The safety committee concluded that it would have needed another 500m to 550m to come to a complete stop.
A CONTROVERSIAL DECISION
Jakarta police have since named the driver of the long-distance express train - identified only as 37-year-old AN - a suspect in the crash.
“Investigators concluded that the emergency braking could have been applied from farther away,” Jakarta police official I Dewa Putu Gede Anom Danujaya told a press conference on Sep 29.
AN faces up to 12 years in prison if convicted, Dewa said. He has not been detained.
The decision has drawn criticism from transportation experts, who argue that KNKT’s investigation identified broader failures beyond the actions of the driver.
“Don’t place all the blame on the driver. They operate according to instructions from the control centre. Fix the system,” Djoko Setijowarno, a transportation expert from Central Java’s Soegijapranata Catholic University, told CNA.
Members of parliament have also questioned the police’s decision.
“We believe KNKT’s findings show that this accident was not simply the result of an individual mistake, or human error, but involved systemic failures,” said Syaiful Huda, deputy chairman of the House of Representatives’ Commission V which oversees transportation and a lawmaker from the National Awakening Party (PKB).
“We believe it is unfair if the blame is placed solely on the Argo Bromo Anggrek train driver.”
Police, however, have stood by their decision, saying the case against AN was based on KNKT’s findings and reached after consulting transportation experts.
State-owned train operator Indonesian Railway Company (KAI) said that the company will be providing AN with a lawyer.
KAI is in charge of all express trains in Indonesia while its subsidiary Kereta Commuter Indonesia is responsible for local train networks in a number of Indonesian cities including Greater Jakarta.
“We want to make sure that our employee does not go through this (legal) process alone,” KAI spokeswoman Anne Purba said in a statement on Sep 30.
“KAI respects and supports the processes being carried out by both KNKT and the Jakarta Metropolitan Police. We will continue to cooperate fully to ensure that each process is conducted professionally.”
Police had previously named the taxi driver, identified as RRP, a suspect for alleged negligence in the initial collision with the first commuter train. He faces a maximum sentence of six months in prison.
A NATIONWIDE PROBLEM
In its report, the KNKT issued six recommendations to train operator KAI, three to Kereta Commuter Indonesia and eight to the Ministry of Transportation. They include reviewing existing communication guidelines, providing additional training for train controllers and railway crews, and assessing signalling systems and infrastructure along the affected railway line.
“Our focus is on implementing KNKT’s recommendations quickly and appropriately,” KAI president director Bobby Rasyidin said in a statement on Oct 3.
“We are carrying out those which can be implemented immediately. We are expediting those that require further study and refinement.”
Minister of Transportation Dudy Purwagandhi said he will make sure all of KNKT’s recommendations are implemented.
“We as the regulator will certainly encourage operators to continuously improve the quality of their personnel, as well as other facilities and infrastructure,” he told reporters on Sep 30, as quoted by local news website Kumparan.
But some changes on the ground had begun well before KNKT released its recommendations.
Rahmat, the Gang Delima resident, said government officials visited the neighbourhood not long after the crash and persuaded residents and businesses to redirect lights that could interfere with the visibility of signals.
“Everyone agreed that safety must come first,” he said.
About 700m from Gang Delima, the once-unmanned level crossing where the taxi was struck is now equipped with proper barriers, warning lights and bells to alert motorists and pedestrians of incoming trains.
But experts said reforms should go beyond KNKT’s recommendations and the railway lines directly affected by the Bekasi crash.
Among the measures they are calling for is the closure of Indonesia’s roughly 3,800 level crossings, which several local studies have linked to around 300 accidents each year.
Experts also want trains to be equipped with automatic emergency braking systems and authorities to work towards unifying the patchwork of signalling systems used across the country, which rely on different technologies from various manufacturers and countries.
“Having multiple different signalling systems will, sooner or later, create a risk of operational problems that could potentially develop into safety issues,” transportation planning expert Yusa said.
Djoko of Soegijapranata Catholic University said the government should also conduct a nationwide railway safety audit to determine how far the problems uncovered in Bekasi exist elsewhere in Indonesia.
“Accidents keep happening in Indonesia because whenever there is an accident and KNKT issues recommendations, they are often only partially implemented or limited to the affected area. The improvements tend to be one-offs and are not sustained. That’s why we see the same problems recurring again and again,” he said.
“There needs to be a safety audit so that improvements can be made continuously … Don’t wait for another accident before making improvements.”

How to Enchant Weapons in Anime Zero
Enchanting weapons lets you reroll their traits to obtain different stat bonuses. Traits are attached to weapons, so choose the weapon you want to improve before spending your Trait Rerolls.
Here are the steps you need to follow to reroll traits or enchant weapons in Anime Zero:
- Open the Areas menu.
- Select the Traits area and travel to the Enchanter NPC, Matilda.

Trait Rerolls are required to enchant weapons and obtain better traits. Here are some of the best ways to farm Trait Tokens in Anime Zero:
