Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code. But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code, meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output.
A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”
Cut once, measure twice
To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish, which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.
To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.
In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction).

Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.
But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month.
Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.
Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations.
Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific.
But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.
On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.
In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.
Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”.
Tabuya said: “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight. Our responsibility does not.”
The governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating would reach at least 1.8C, well beyond the 1.5C ceiling of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses.
Throughout the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for poor and vulnerable communities who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised.
Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority of Cop31.”
Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk.
Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.”
“The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.”
Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehicles coming from electricity by 2035. Now it is about 21%.
But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed.
Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global community at Cop28 in Dubai three years ago. But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing to back new coal and gas developments and being largely silent before the pre-Cop on the need to phase out fossil fuels.
Bowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants.
Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states, strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30 in Brazil.
Dozens of countries frustrated with what they see as a UN stalemate on the issue met separately in Colombia this year to discuss a path away from fossil fuels. They are due to meet again next July in Tuvalu, and want the issue to be in an agreement in Antalya.
Tzeporah Berman, the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, said Pacific leaders had been clear in Nadi that there should be an urgent fossil fuel phaseout.
“This means no new projects,” she said. “You can’t phase something out by building more of it.”

Bayern Munich twice came from behind to draw 2-2 at Augsburg on Saturday after a mistake from Manuel Neuer led to the fastest goal in Bundesliga history.
Neuer handed Augsburg the lead after 8.4 seconds with an error that Robin Fellhauer capitalised on, before two assists from Harry Kane helped rescue a point in the second half.
Bayern missed the chance to knock Borussia Dortmund off the top spot after the draw and remains two points behind the league leader in second.
“It feels more like a defeat. On another day we would have won this game, but that’s football. We gave away two sloppy goals, and they punished us for it,” Kane told DAZN.
Augsburg could not believe its luck after 40-year-old Neuer’s howler handed the side the lead after just eight seconds. Having received the ball straight from kick-off, Neuer chipped it directly into the path of Fellhauer, who ran it into the empty net.
“We would have preferred a better start, but Manu has played football long enough. He can’t change what happened; he just needs to do what he’s always done in his career and keep on showing how good he is,” Bayern coach Vincent Kompany told DAZN.
The Bundesliga later confirmed the goal had beaten the previous record of nine seconds held jointly by Kevin Volland and Karim Bellarabi. “Those guys must have been really slow,” Fellhauer told Sky with a laugh after the game.
“In all seriousness, it’s an unbelievable feeling because a record like this means you’re part of something really big,” he added.
Bayern remained shell-shocked for much of the first half and was lucky not to go 2-0 down when Juma Bah missed a sitter in the 36th minute.
The visitor found the net shortly after the break when Augsburg goalkeeper Finn Dahmen fumbled a brilliant volley from Luis Diaz, but the goal was ruled out for an offside in the build-up.

After Augsburg unlocked the defence with a long ball forward, Neuer parried Calvin Brackelmann’s shot straight at Rodrigo Ribeiro, who smashed the ball under the bar to restore the lead.
Both Diaz and Serge Gnabry had goals ruled out for offside before Kane set up Nathaniel Brown for Bayern’s second equaliser ten minutes from time.

Why is everyone screaming 5 Seconds of Summer lyrics during Harry Styles concerts?
What started as a fan remix on TikTok has become a feature on Styles’ massive world tour
Picture this: You've managed to score seats to Harry Styles' Together, Together tour, and you're jamming along in the stands when suddenly, everyone around you starts screaming the lyrics to not only a different song, but one by an entirely different artist.
Styles is 20 shows into a 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York City as part of his tour.
But while fans singing along to his songs is par for the course, a new viral trend is seeing fans chanting the lyrics to Australian band 5 Seconds of Summer's Telephone Busy during the instrumental break of Styles' song Ready, Steady, Go — and they're getting louder and louder every night as the trend picks up steam.
So how did we get here?
It started with a fan remix on TikTok. User @millsberry75 posted a video in March mashing up the two songs, with 5 Seconds of Summer's drummer Ashton Irwin talk-singing the intro of Telephone Busy, over top of Ready, Steady, Go.
The band took notice. In August, 5 Seconds of Summer incorporated the remix into a popular DJ set they performed at Salt Shed Chicago during the Lollapalooza festival.
Now, fans are bringing it to the physical stage of Styles' tour.
A flood of videos on social media show fans jumping in on the trend. In earlier Madison Square Garden sets in September, the 5 Seconds of Summer lyrics being chanted by the audience is barely audible. But in newer videos from shows this week, it's become a veritable roar.
"Nothing makes me happier than knowing the harry x 5sos propaganda is spreading," TikTok user @tehedorothytehe wrote earlier this week in her concert video.
Part of the excitement behind it comes from the history between One Direction, the English-Irish band where Styles first found fame, and 5 Seconds of Summer (affectionately known as 5SOS by fans).
In 2012, when One Direction was just starting to take over the world, 5SOS was still four teenage boys making YouTube videos in Sydney, Australia, with only one EP to their name. Then, One Direction member Louis Tomlinson shared one of their songs online, opening them up to a whole new audience.
From left to right, Michael Clifford, Luke Hemmings, Calum Hood and Ashton Irwin of 5 Seconds of Summer in California in 2022. (Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images)
The band was tapped to serve as opener for One Direction's worldwide Take Me Home tour in 2013, and later joined the boyband as a supporting act on their 2014 Where We Are tour. More than a decade later, there's still a lot of crossover between fans.
In the age of manufactured trends, it's exciting to see a "natural" trend evolve from fans just celebrating a catchy tune, user @mariamontour said in an Oct. 6 TikTok.
"This fan chant that just started happening and progressively started getting louder is proof that the internet really can translate things into real-life trends, especially within fandoms" she said.

5SOS responds
5 Seconds of Summer is well aware of the excitement around the two songs.
"I appreciate yall lol," Irwin commented in September on one fan's TikTok sharing her screaming the Telephone Busy lyrics at a Styles set. The band has also reposted multiple fan videos of Styles' crowds chanting the song in the last week.
Styles himself hasn't directly acknowledged the trend yet, but if the volume keeps climbing, the odds get higher.
Harry Styles performs Aperture on stage during The BRIT Awards 2026 on Feb. 28 in Manchester, England. (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images)
As for how loud it could get? Well, there's still 10 more shows at Madison Square Garden alone, and more than 50 shows in the rest of the tour. Styles will be performing four shows in May at Rogers Stadium, so if the trend continues, we could see those bleachers shaking.
"Everyone pls memorize this for toronto n2," user @bethanyannne wrote in a TikTok lipsyncing to the remix.

My friend and I felt like we were overdue for a trip without our kids. Between the two of us, we have seven children, ranging in age from 6 to 10, including three pairs of twins.
We knew we wanted it to be a warm-weather destination to extend the feeling of summer, as the leaves are already turning red in Maine, where we both live.
The one destination we kept coming back to was Florida. And because we are both huge Disney fans, I threw the crazy idea of going to the parks without our kids.
Getting to feel like a kid again alongside my friend was one of the most uplifting experiences in my years as a mom.
We got Park Hopper tickets
Because we still wanted to lounge by the pool and drink frozen drinks, we figured we'd dedicate one day and one day only to Disney World. So we got Park Hopper tickets that allowed us to move between parks.
The way we used them was absolutely key, and was very different from the trips I've taken with my kids. Whenever I've gotten Park Hopper tickets at the parks with my kids, I've felt like I wasted my money because they just wanted to do one park at a time, or we would take forever with meals, snacks, potty breaks, and all the things little kids require.
With just the two of us, we were able to do three parks: Hollywood Studios, Magic Kingdom, and Epcot. Our initial plan was just to do two and skip Magic Kingdom, but we did so much of Hollywood Studios by 1 p.m. that we decided to add one more stop.
We rode 12 rides
Sure, our approach was not to do absolutely everything in every single park. We were just going with the flow, especially considering that we didn't splurge on Lightning Lanes since we didn't have a firm plan and didn't want time slots to deter our adventure. On the Sunday we were there, Lightning Lanes ranged from $24 to $27, depending on the park.
We started our day at Hollywood Studios because we are both big Star Wars fans and hadn't done that area yet. We were able to get on rides super quickly without waiting in line. After we made our way to Toy Story, I finally rode the highly coveted Slinky Dog Dash, which had by far our longest wait at 45 minutes.
Both my friend and I grew up going to the parks, and we knew we had to ride the Tower of Terror because it's just a classic. I hadn't done that ride in 15 years (my kids are not enthused about thrill rides), and it was even better than I remembered.
When we entered Magic Kingdom, our first reaction was how empty it was — especially for a weekend day. I looked at the map, and wait times were surprisingly low. I think that going during a day when Mickey's Not So Scary Halloween Party was happening played in our favor. Those attending the ticketed event can enter after 4 p.m., so while we didn't have the park to ourselves, our longest line was at Tiana's Bayou, at 30 minutes.
To end the night, we moved on to Epcot to experience the International Food and Wine festival, another thing we had never been able to do because kids have little patience to walk from booth to booth to try new things. At one point, while we were eating, it started drizzling, so we made our way into the Frozen Ever After ride to wait it out, because after all, October is hurricane season in Florida, and some weather is to be expected.
We tried 6 different foods
We actually didn't know the food festival was happening, but we knew we wanted to end the night at Epcot because we wanted a full meal there, since we had only been snacking at the other parks.
As soon as we entered the festival section, we grabbed a frozen mango margarita (we had earned it) and started our dinner with samosas and chicken tikka masala at the India stand, then followed up with a spiked mango lassi. We then moved to Greece, where we had a spanakopita that was out of this world.
After that, we went to Brazil, where we had a moqueca de camarão and a frozen caipirinha — the latter had nothing on the margarita and mango lassi we had just finished. We finished the food portion of our tour around the world with some escargot in France. But the last thing we had was a Mexican paleta, which was, hands down, my favorite thing of the entire day. 
We then walked around the park, rode rides with no lines, danced to live bands, and kept reminding ourselves that we wouldn't have been able to do all of this if our kids had been there with us. 
After over 27,000 steps and hours of laughter, we headed out of the most magical place on earth and collapsed in our beds. For one day, I wasn't anyone's mom. I was just a girl at Disney with her best friend, and I didn't realize how much I'd missed myself.

Ethiopia tells UN it is acting in self-defense against Eritrea
Ethiopia has told the United Nations Security Council it is taking self-defense measures against Eritrea
NAIROBI, Kenya -- NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Ethiopia told the U.N. Security Council on Friday it is taking measures in self-defense against Eritrea, accusing its neighbor of sending troops across the border and occupying parts of northern Ethiopia.
The declaration adds to fears of a wider conflict as government-allied forces report advances in Tigray, a region devastated by a previous war.
In a letter dated Friday, Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos invoked Ethiopia’s right to self-defense under Article 51 of the U.N. Charter. He did not specify what measures the country was taking.
The letter, obtained by The Associated Press, accused Eritrea of deploying infantry and mechanized units in recent weeks and supporting, financing, arming and directing insurgent groups. It did not identify the occupied areas or provide evidence supporting its allegations.
Ethiopia had repeatedly urged Eritrea to withdraw its forces, Gedion wrote. The AP could not independently verify the allegations.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accused Ethiopia on Friday of pursuing aggression against Eritrea through its demands for sovereign access to the Red Sea. Writing on X, he did not explicitly confirm or deny the reported troop crossings.
Eritrea announced last week it was severing diplomatic ties after Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said it remained committed to dialogue with its neighbors.
The accusations deepen a rift between countries whose armies fought together against the Tigray People’s Liberation Front from 2020 to 2022.
Researchers at Ghent University in Belgium estimated the previous war caused about 500,000 civilian deaths in Tigray from violence, famine and the collapse of health services.
Government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force.
Residents also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi.
It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting.
Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel.
The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data monitoring group, known as ACLED, separately said Eritrean troops crossed at Zelambesa on Wednesday and came under drone attack while traveling toward Idaga Hamus. It attributed the strikes to Ethiopia’s military. The AP could not independently verify either account.
The TPLF joined six other opposition groups last month in an alliance seeking to oust Abiy. Fighting escalated late in September, undermining the 2022 peace agreement, and rebels seized Tigray's capital Mekelle and its airport.
The rebels announced their withdrawal Oct. 3 and government-allied fighters entered the city.
In Mekelle, federal police on Friday called over loudspeakers for residents to help establish a new administration. Government offices remained shut, and no administration had taken office by that morning. The Tigray Peace Force imposed an overnight curfew Wednesday.
The U.S. Embassy said Thursday that telecommunications had resumed in Mekelle and much of Tigray, while mobile banking and electricity had partially resumed. All remained subject to interruption.
During the previous war, the AP documented accounts accusing Eritrean soldiers of killings, rape and looting. Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki dismissed allegations of abuses by his forces as “a fantasy” in 2023.

The Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP), an umbrella forum representing Christians from different denominations in West Bengal, on October 5 formally submitted complaints to the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the West Bengal Human Rights Commission (WBHRC) and the National Commission for Minorities, alleging a pattern of targeted violence against the Christian community, including attacks, vandalism and desecration of small house churches and prayer gatherings across the state.
A public hearing was also held on the same day at Christ the King Hall on Syed Amir Ali Avenue in Park Circus, Kolkata, where pastors, victims and eyewitnesses recounted alleged incidents of attacks and intimidation before representatives of prominent human rights and civil rights organisations, including the Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR) and Banglar Manabadhikar Suraksha Mancha (MASUM). Civil society figures, including retired IAS officer Jawhar Sircar, were also present to hear the testimonies.
The gathering was held amid a series of reported attacks on Christian communities, mostly in the hinterlands of Bengal. Alt News has previously documented at least 35 such incidents of violence and intimidation between July 1 and September 20, 2026.
Based on the testimonies of victims, the BCP, which is the eastern chapter of the All India Christian Council, formally submitted its complaints to the rights bodies alleging recurring patterns of targeted violence and intimidation, as well as institutional and governmental negligence in responding to the incidents.
The BCP identified four key concerns:
1. Systematic attacks on peaceful prayer gatherings – According to the BCP, small house churches and local Christian congregations conducting prayer services have repeatedly been targeted over the past three months. The organisation alleged that the intruders had assaulted worshippers, vandalised places of worship and desecrated religious symbols and objects. The BCP also criticised the efforts to downplay the attacks, saying, “Regrettably, some public figures and local leaders have characterised these lawless disruptions as “public protests” while remaining silent on vigilante groups taking the law into their own hands.”
2. Disinformation and manufactured narratives – The BCP alleged that several incidents followed similar “scripted patterns”, in which aggressors forcibly entered private prayer gatherings to disrupt services, “engineer chaos” and “record selective footage”, which was subsequently circulated on social media in edited form. According to the organisation, the videos were then used to make allegations of “forced conversion through inducement”, allegedly fuelling communal tension. BCP founder Herod Mullick said, “These edited videos are subsequently circulated online after false allegations of forced conversion to mislead local authorities and justify vigilante actions”. The organisation further alleged that such videos were presented to local district magistrates (DMs) and sub-divisional officers (SDOs) as evidence, and used to promote what it described as false narratives. The BCP rejected the allegations of forced conversion as “unfounded”, saying that “peaceful believers gathered for routine prayer are being falsely framed as perpetrators.”
3. Discriminatory police action and non-registration of complaints – The BCP further alleged that police responses to the incidents had been inconsistent. It said alleged aggressors were often allowed to leave the scene without immediate action, while injured believers and pastors who reported being victimised were taken to local police stations, “subjected to late-night questioning” and allegedly intimidated. Of the dozens of reported incidents, the BCP said FIRs have been registered in only 13 cases, and only “after extraordinary effort and legal intervention”. “In all other instances, local police authorities have displayed severe reluctance to accept formal written complaints from the victims,” the BCP added.
4. Institutional apathy and unaddressed concerns –The BCP also alleged that repeated appeals to local administrative authorities had failed, with officials “consistently declined to engage in dialogue with state church leaders or representatives of our organisation”, the organisation said. It further alleged that “no independent or impartial inquiries have been instituted to verify the authenticity of these viral video clips”. According to the BCP, “this persistent administrative apathy creates a climate of impunity for vigilante groups and deprives minority worshippers of equal protection under the law.”
Citing violations of Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Article 14 (Equality before Law), Article 19 (Freedom of Speech and Assembly), Article 21 (Protection of Life and Personal Liberty), and Article 25 (Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice, and Propagation of Religion) of the Constitution of India— the BCP urged the NHRC, WBHRC and NCM to direct the West Bengal Government and the director general of police (DGP) to conduct a high-level independent investigation of all the recent incidents of violence targeting the churches and prayer gatherings.
The organisation also sought an investigation into alleged cyber disinformation and circulation of edited videos allegedly intended to portray worshippers as perpetrators of violence. Additionally, the council pleaded for clear directions to the police and administration to immediately register FIRs in all pending cases and ensure prompt legal action against those responsible.
The BCP further requested the commissions to direct district administrations to provide police protection to vulnerable house churches and congregations during weekly prayer services, and to ensure that victims are not harassed, intimidated or pressured by law-enforcement authorities under alleged influence from vigilante or extremist groups.
After attending the public hearing, former Union culture secretary Jawhar Sircar shared a post on Facebook describing the recent attacks on Christian churches and communities in West Bengal as “tragic and unprecedented” and condemned the attacks as “dastardly”. Sircar expressed his support for the Christian community and their right to practice their faith peacefully.

JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he will not watch it
- Published
US Vice-President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter.
Talking with reporters, Vance expressed doubt that the December execution would go forward as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen". He added, that "if it's through live stream, I'm not going to be watching it".
Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved the live stream plans but said the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.
Hasan killed 13 unarmed US soldiers at a base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. The firing squad execution would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute former US Army major Nidal Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad in the attack on the Fort Hood base.
Then on Thursday US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be livestreamed for the public. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth explained.
Trump, as he left the White House on Friday, was asked about the possibility that visuals of Hasan's execution could be used as propaganda for terrorists.
"He killed 13, 14 people, badly wounded 20-some-odd people, and he's totally nuts," Trump said. "So I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."
The BBC has contacted the Pentagon for more information about the livestream determination.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Vance condemned Hasan's attack on the base as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11". Asked about how his Catholic faith impacted his stance on plans to stream a public execution, Vance cast doubt on whether they would happen.
But he noted that Hasan, who was a US Army psychiatrist, was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems and "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived".
The announcement of the livestream plans has been met with criticism from both political parties.
Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched them, warning that public executions erode civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment".
Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider.
"The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent," he said.
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group.
Georgia lawmaker Austin Scott, a Republican, said that he "absolutely" supports the death sentence, but that live-streaming executions "is what jihadists do. America is better than that".
The US Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow" in a statement.
The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture".
Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
Military law requires that military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward.
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.

When Hegseth told reporters on Thursday about plans to ensure the public can watch the execution, he did not specify where or how live video of the execution would be shown.
A Pentagon spokesperson on Friday reiterated to the BBC that Hasan's execution "will be livestreamed," but said the government had no further details "to provide at this time".
The White House did not respond to an inquiry about whether it expected to show Hasan's planned execution on its social media channels.
The White House maintains official accounts and channels on the most notable and widely used online platforms that are capable of streaming live video, namely Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X.
All of the platforms have prohibitions in place on violent images and videos, as well as those that show death or glorify or make a spectacle of violence.
Meta, owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads, explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment.
YouTube bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers".
TikTok has a similar rule that bars "extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content—especially when it could cause viewers emotional distress." That includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual".
Both YouTube and TikTok make exceptions in instances of "public interest".
Asked if a live-stream of an execution qualifies for the exception if it is government-sanctioned , a TikTok spokeswoman said: "Regardless, I'd point you back to the not allowed section which reflects our approach."
The policy at X, which has loosened content moderation since billionaire Elon Musk took over the platform, prohibits content "glorifying" of violence. It will remove content depicting when a person dies will be removed if requested by certain parties.
Meta, YouTube and X did not respond to multiple BBC requests for comment on whether they would uphold their current policies in the event Hasan's execution is broadcast.

Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
- Published
An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.
The Philadelphia Police Department said the tip, sent on 18 July, was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation, but it criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.
In a statement police said that the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had written that it may have information on a case, and claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".
It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.
Citing Anthropic, the police department said the AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent the fake tip.
Anthropic discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said.
But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October.
"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media, external.
"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."
The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems, and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.
But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide," the police statement said.
Anthropic this week published a report, external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.
Organisations that have been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.
The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.
President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will coordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers, and religious groups.
Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, Open AI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.
In another instance, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents went rogue and started unexpectedly communicating, leading to a large group banding together to hack into AI platform Hugging Face.

A new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show.
Earlier this year, Guardian Australia revealed catastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024.
The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president.
But new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use at Melbourne immigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator.
The documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”.
On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects.
The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”. That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said.
“I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed.
“While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.”
Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres.
A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May.
That’s despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised.
The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations.
“The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said.
The Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them.
Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”.
The union has continually raised concerns about understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line.
“The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said.
A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said:
“In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.”
The Australian Border Force was contacted for comment.

The story so far: India is working towards eliminating dog-mediated human rabies by 2030. Yet the country does not have a single, comprehensive national count of human rabies deaths. While the Health Ministry’s disease surveillance system recorded 54 deaths in 2024, an ICMR-led study estimates that 5,726 people die of rabies in India every year.
Is rabies a notifiable disease in India?
Rabies is not a notifiable disease nationwide. Unlike diseases for which there is a clearly established national notification mechanism covering every State and Union Territory, rabies notification has historically depended on State-level notification requirements and the disease surveillance system.
The National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) has been working to make human rabies a notifiable disease across the country. Communications have been sent to States to notify the disease under the relevant State legislation.
However, a disease being under surveillance does not necessarily mean that every case or death occurring in the country is automatically captured in one central database.
Rabies is a particularly difficult disease to count because a large proportion of deaths can occur outside the formal health system. Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is almost invariably fatal, but patients may die at home or in facilities that do not routinely report the death through disease-surveillance channels.
How is a disease chosen for notification in India?
Disease notification is largely a public-health surveillance and State-level regulatory function, while the Union government maintains national surveillance systems such as the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP).
A disease is generally prioritised for notification or surveillance when it has significant public-health importance — for example, high mortality or morbidity, epidemic potential, rapid spread, risk of international transmission, emergence of a new pathogen, or where early detection can trigger effective control measures. India’s disease-prioritisation exercises have considered epidemiological, clinical, economic and public-health factors, with expert consultation.
Once a disease/condition is designated for surveillance, health facilities, laboratories and health workers report cases through the surveillance system. Under IDSP, reporting includes suspected (S), presumptive (P) and laboratory-confirmed (L) cases. Data move from reporting units to District and State Surveillance Units and ultimately to the Central Surveillance Unit at the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC).
A rising or unusual cluster triggers investigation by Rapid Response Teams, which can lead to laboratory confirmation, containment measures and further reporting.
The exact legal notification requirement can depend on the State/UT and the particular disease. Leprosy, for instance, was declared a notifiable disease nationally in 2025.
So, how many people die of rabies in India?
There are different answers, depending on what is being measured. The Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme/Integrated Health Information Platform (IDSP–IHIP) recorded 21 human rabies deaths in 2022, 50 in 2023 and 54 in 2024.
The Registrar General of India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) system, meanwhile, recorded 66 medically certified rabies deaths in 2022 and 271 in 2023.
But neither set of numbers represents all rabies deaths in India. The MCCD figures are based on medically certified causes of death. The system does not cover every registered death in the country. At the national level, medically certified deaths accounted for only about 22% of registered deaths in both 2022 and 2023.
The IDSP–IHIP figures serve a different purpose. They are generated through disease surveillance and are intended to identify and track cases and deaths reported through the surveillance network.
This is why the figures cannot simply be added together or compared as if they were measuring the same thing. Then where does the figure of 5,726 deaths come from?
An ICMR-led study published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases estimated that India has about 5,726 human rabies deaths every year.
The researchers did not arrive at this number by counting death certificates or hospital records.
They conducted a large community-based survey involving 337,808 people in 78,807 households across 60 districts in 15 States. The study estimated that India sees about 9.1 million animal bites every year, including around 5.6 million dog bites.
The researchers then combined information from the community survey and laboratory data with a probability decision-tree model to estimate how many people bitten by animals would develop rabies and subsequently die.
The 5,726 figure is therefore a modelled estimate of annual mortality, rather than a tally of deaths reported to the government.
Why is the difference so large?
This is because each system is designed to capture its own unique data.
IDSP–IHIP is primarily a disease-surveillance system. It depends on cases and deaths being detected and reported through the health system and surveillance network.
MCCD records medically certified causes of death. It provides valuable information on the causes of deaths that are medically certified, but it does not cover every death.
The ICMR-led study, on the other hand, attempts to estimate the actual burden in the population, including deaths that may never enter either surveillance or medical-certification systems.
This means that a low number in a surveillance database does not necessarily mean that the disease burden is low.
In rabies, the problem is compounded by the nature of the disease itself. Patients may not reach a hospital after symptoms begin; some deaths occur at home; and the animal bite that initiated infection may have happened weeks or months earlier.
There is also a critical point between the animal bite and a possible rabies death: post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). If a person receives appropriate wound care, rabies vaccine and, where indicated, rabies immunoglobulin promptly after exposure, death can be prevented.
What happens to a case of a notifiable disease?
India’s disease surveillance system works through multiple levels.
At the frontline are healthcare facilities, laboratories and other reporting units. When a suspected, probable or confirmed case of a disease covered by surveillance is detected, information is reported through the appropriate surveillance mechanism.
The information moves through district and State surveillance structures and is consolidated nationally through the IDSP/IHIP platform. The purpose is not simply to count cases. Surveillance is intended to detect unusual increases, identify outbreaks, understand geographical patterns and enable public-health authorities to respond.
But notification depends on detection, diagnosis and reporting. A person who never reaches a reporting facility, a death that occurs outside a medical setting, or a case that is not recognised as rabies may not enter the surveillance database.
This is why notification should not be confused with a census of every person who has the disease.
Does that mean the 5,726 figure is the “real” number?
The 54 deaths recorded by IDSP–IHIP in 2024 tell us how many deaths were reported through that surveillance system.
The 5,726 estimate attempts to answer a different question: how many people may actually be dying of rabies each year, including deaths that are missed by routine systems.
The study itself is therefore important not because it replaces surveillance data, but because it draws attention to what routine surveillance may be missing.
A senior Health Ministry official has also pointed out that the two figures are generated through different methods and should not be treated as directly equivalent. Together, however, they point to a substantial gap between reported surveillance deaths and estimated mortality.
Why does this matter when India wants to eliminate rabies by 2030?
Reliable surveillance is essential to rabies elimination. India cannot determine whether it is moving towards elimination if it cannot accurately establish where human rabies deaths are occurring, where dog-mediated transmission continues and which populations are not receiving timely post-exposure care.
The ICMR-led study also found important gaps after animal bites. About one in five dog-bite victims had not received anti-rabies vaccine, while only 66.2% had received at least three doses. Among those who received only one dose, nearly half did not complete the vaccination course. Only about one in 10 eligible victims received passive immunisation.
The gaps are therefore not confined to counting deaths. They extend across the entire rabies-control chain — from preventing dog bites and vaccinating dogs to recognising exposures, completing human post-exposure prophylaxis and recording outcomes.
As medical scientist and former ICMR Director-General Nirmal Kumar Ganguly puts it, the absence of consolidated data remains a challenge for rabies elimination. Cases and deaths can occur in places where they are difficult to measure, making stronger surveillance, dog vaccination and timely human post-exposure treatment critical.
Rabies is almost entirely preventable, but once symptoms appear, it is almost invariably fatal. That makes every missed exposure, incomplete vaccination course and unrecorded death significant.
For India, therefore, the question is not simply why one database reports 54 deaths while a study estimates 5,726.
The larger question is how many deaths the health system is failing to see — and whether India can close that surveillance gap before it attempts to declare dog-mediated human rabies eliminated by 2030.

An Internet shutdown amid heightened security restrictions in central Delhi on Saturday (October 10) left commuters struggling to access navigation apps and make digital payments, autorickshaw drivers without bookings and tourists unable to reach their hotels.
Along Janpath, passengers struggled to find their way to their destinations, while tourists carrying suitcases searched for accommodation in Connaught Place. Several people heading to the protest against the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls said they were dropped off kilometres short of their destinations as drivers struggled to access navigation apps and passengers could not complete digital payments.
“Idhar location, paisa kuch nahi pata chal raha (I cannot figure out the route or fare here),” an autorickshaw driver told a passenger on Janpath.
The passenger, who had travelled to participate in the protest, said he was stranded and unsure how to reach Jantar Mantar. “I don’t know the way to Jantar Mantar from here. It was showing three kilometres when I last checked maps before the Internet shut down. Now I don’t know how to pay him or navigate my way,” he said, requesting anonymity.
Vikas, another protester who had booked a Rapido bike taxi, said his driver had offered to let him pay later.
“I took a Rapido bike to come to the protest, and we realised after reaching here that the Internet was not working. He dropped me off at the nearest location and told me I could pay him later in the night, after I had internet connectivity. I will pay him extra for the kind gesture,” he said.
Business takes a hit
For autorickshaw drivers, the disruption meant losing app-based bookings and potential passengers on the streets. Jagjit, an autorickshaw driver operating in Connaught Place, said business had come to a near standstill, with road restrictions further limiting his ability to pick up and drop off passengers.
“I have lost a significant amount of business. Usually, I take at least 30–40 trips within Connaught Place, but today no bookings have come in. With the routes blocked, we are unable to take passengers through the area either,” he said.
Tourists left stranded
The shutdown also caused difficulties for visitors unfamiliar with the area, particularly those trying to reach hotels in the restricted zone. Near Shivaji Stadium metro station, a tourist couple with a booking at a private hotel in Connaught Place said police personnel were not allowing them to proceed without proof of their reservation. Unable to access their booking details online, they struggled to establish that they had a reason to enter the area.
“Our hotel is right in this street,” the man said, pointing towards a road near the metro station. “But the police are not letting us in. They are asking for proof of our booking, but the Internet is shut here and I am unable to access my tickets in my e-mail or even through the app. Now we are stranded. We are trying to find a place with internet to at least get a sense of things here,” said the couple.
Elsewhere in Connaught Place, families who had arrived in the Capital were seen pulling suitcases along pavements as they searched for accommodation. With transport difficult to arrange and online booking platforms inaccessible, some were unsure where they would spend the night.
Madhav, a tourist who had arrived from Jhansi that morning, said his family had struggled to find an autorickshaw to Connaught Place. Once there, they were unable to arrange accommodation.
“We came to Delhi this morning from Jhansi, and at first, we could not get an auto to Connaught Place. When we finally got one, we were unable to book a hotel and are now trying to find a place to stay,” he said.

Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army
- Published
You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.
But Zaw Min has no choice.
"I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time.
"People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."
Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.
According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.
Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.
Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.
The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.
Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions.
"Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.
The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.
They said they had no comment on the matter.
With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.
The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.
International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.
In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025.
Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law.
"In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.
Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.
"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."
Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time.
"We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."
Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.
The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.
In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.
U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities.
When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.
But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription.
"[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls.
"If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward.
"I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."
In the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.
The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.
She does not know where her husband is now.
Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.
Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says.
"Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."
In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.
The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison.
BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful.
"Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says.
"They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."
While conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.
So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.
Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".
But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.
It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.
The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".
In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.
Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.
As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
- Published
"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."
