A claim that retired professional U.S. soccer star Megan Rapinoe called for Super Bowl champion and ESPN analyst Jason Kelce's firing began circulating online this week.
Snopes readers searched for references to Rapinoe and Kelce on this website, which led us to consult search engines DuckDuckGo and Google for basic details about why the two names were making the rounds together. We located a popular Facebook post (archived) that appeared on the Empire Sports Facebook page on Oct. 5, reading in part:
MEGAN RAPINOE: Calls for Jason Kelce to be FIRED..
Megan Rapinoe criticized Jason Kelce after he used Washington's former team name during a live broadcast.
"I know Jason Kelce said that racist name on purpose to create division. He should be fired immediately."
— Megan Rapinoe
The comments under Empire Sports' post indicated some people believed Rapinoe truly called for Kelce's firing.
Other users shared the rumor on Facebook (archived) and Threads (archived), though the original Empire Sports Facebook post earned far more likes, comments and shares than other examples.
In sum, while it's true Kelce mentioned the old Washington Redskins' team name during a TV broadcast, Rapinoe did not call for his firing.
The Empire Sports page displays a disclaimer acknowledging it publishes fabricated content of a parodical and satirical nature, reading, "Delivering the Finest of Sports Parodies / Satire / Updates / Insider News & much MORE." In other words, Empire Sports does not publish authentic news reports.
The aforementioned searches of DuckDuckGo and Google located no news media outlets credibly reporting Rapinoe said any such things about Kelce. Rapinoe's active Instagram page also did not feature any content about him.
Snopes emailed representatives for Rapinoe and Kelce to ask if either wished to address the popular made-up story. The Empire Sports page didn't display a Messenger button or any other contact methods.
Purveyors of misinformation and fabricated stories — whether labeled as parody and satire or not — have long wielded Rapinoe's name and image as politically-fueled engagement bait, whether for social media posts or website traffic, sometimes thinly disguised as satire. Part of the reason for the firestorm of controversy in this instance stems from U.S. President Donald Trump's comments about Rapinoe, and vice versa.
What Kelce said
On Oct. 4, Kelce served as an analyst during the ESPN-owned NFL Network TV broadcast of the Indianapolis Colts' 30-13 victory over the Washington Commanders, which took place in London.
A video from that broadcast shows Kelce apologizing to the Washington Commanders after he used the team's former name. In the clip, Kelce breaks down the Commanders' defensive coverage, saying, "The Redskins right now are doing a great job of not only staying tight but making the play when the ball is in the receiver's hand and keeping it short of the sticks."
Announcer Dave Pasch laughs, telling Kelce he accidentally said Redskins, to which Kelce responds, "Oh my gosh! I almost made it out." Pasch then says he, Kelce and former Super Bowl MVP Kurt Warner, also working as an analyst, all had a "gentleman's bet" regarding who would slip up first. Kelce replies, "Well, sorry Washington."
Snopes has debunked similar pieces of media before, including past satire-labeled rumors suggesting Rapinoe was leaving the U.S. due to a "massive red wave," going bankrupt and was banned from the Olympic sports.

WASHINGTON — The Food and Drug Administration says its ongoing safety review of the nation’s main abortion pill will continue into next year, a timeline that was quickly condemned by abortion opponents hoping to see the drug’s use curtailed.
The FDA gave a court-ordered update on its progress in a legal filing late Wednesday, providing the first substantive information about the controversial reevaluation ordered by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Mifepristone was first approved by the FDA in 2000. The agency has repeatedly reaffirmed the pill’s safety and effectiveness over the years, in addition to easing a number of restrictions on the drug, including dropping a requirement that it be dispensed in person.
But since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, anti-abortion groups and their allies in Congress have pushed the administration to revisit the pill, in the hopes of restricting its use.
The FDA said in its filing that it expects to complete a safety study of the pill by mid-December this year. A report on the findings is expected “no later than March 2027,” after which the agency will decide whether to impose new restrictions or other changes on the drug’s use.
Gavin Oxley of Americans United for Life, an anti-abortion group, criticized the move as a lack of “true leadership” by Trump administration officials.
“The administration continues to find itself on the wrong side of women’s health, clearly uninterested in mitigating the ongoing harms caused by the abortion pill,” Oxley said.
The two-drug regimen of mifepristone, combined with a second drug misoprostol, is the most common form of abortion in the U.S.
The FDA was directed to provide the latest update by a federal judge in a case brought by the state of Louisiana alleging that mail-delivery of mifepristone undermines the state’s abortion ban. It’s one of several state lawsuits related to mifepristone winding their way through the courts.
Last month a three-judge panel for the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals questioned the merits of Louisiana’s case, including whether the state had the legal standing to challenge FDA’s oversight of mifepristone.
Any ruling from the 5th Circuit on the Louisiana case would not immediately change the landscape because the Supreme Court has blocked changes to the drug until it sees the case again.
The FDA said Wednesday it is using a “statistical data mining method” to discover “unknown safety concerns,” that may exist with the drug. The data comes from an electronic database that collects reports of medical injuries and drug side effects from major health networks and insurers.
In addition to the safety study, the agency said it is considering a number of petitions proposing changes to how mifepristone is prescribed and distributed.
Abortion opponents have focused most of their efforts on a 2021 decision allowing doctors to prescribe the drug online and send it through the mail during COVID-19. That decision, made permanent under President Joe Biden in 2023, had the effect of undermining a number of state abortion bans, since women can receive the drug through the mail.
— Matthew Perrone

Winning a Nobel Prize is a matter of great prestige. Winning a Nobel Prize also means the award going to a small number of people while a large number are left out, even if they really deserved to win.
This is partly because of the prizes’ rules. Alfred Nobel’s will said nothing about the number of people that can be awarded at one time but the Nobel Foundation’s statutes limit each prize to at most three people at a time, and no one that has died by the time a prize is announced. Also, scientists need to have been nominated by nominators who have their own eligibility criteria.
A big-picture view of the science Nobel Prizes through history brings another pattern into view: a preference for singular breakthroughs rather than lifetime achievements.
Boyden, Bamberg, and beyond
Start with the Nobel Prize this year for physiology/medicine, to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel, for their work on optogenetics. In 2002, Austrian scientist Gero Miessenböck & co. had first sensitised to light some neurons that were not naturally light-sensitive. Miessenböck is now at the University of Oxford, where his profile page describes him as an ‘inventor’ of optogenetics.
Hegemann and Nagel have been feted for identifying and characterising the protein channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2). The next step was to show that it could control neurons. The first author of the paper that did was Edward Boyden, who helped pioneer the application of ChR2 to neuroscience. Boyden is now a professor of neurotechnology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the Broad Institute.
Another author of this paper, Ernst Bamberg, had supervised Nagel’s PhD and was part of the team that established the importance of ChR2. A page on the website of the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics, Germany, where Bamberg is now an emeritus professor, says he was instrumental in translating the ChR2 finding into practical applications.
Yet another author, Feng Zhang, is also at MIT now, and in 2007, he was a member of one of two teams that adapted another protein, called halorhodopsin, to silence neurons with light instead of activating them. The other team, consisting of Xue Han and Boyden, had demonstrated the same capability.
These contributions together — rather than only those that the laureates led — turned the ability to control neurons with light into a tool of neuroscience with real-world applications, including in medicine.
No lone wolf
Next, the physics prize — which this year demonstrated the brokenness of the Nobel Prizes on a whole other level. Francis Halzen won the prize all by himself “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. But IceCube is an international collaboration involving around 450 experts from 58 institutions in 14 countries.
Crucially, the prize-giving committee was not constrained to give the prize to one person here. The Nobel Foundation statutes allow the committee to decide whether its prizes can be awarded to associations or organisations. But the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the physics, chemistry, and economics prizes, does not seem to have adopted this option. If it had, the physics prize could have recognised the IceCube collaboration as a whole.
But even if this rule did not exist, it is hard to say why the committee picked Halzen alone. In 1988, Halzen and (today) University of Hawai’i physics and astronomy professor John G. Learned reported the idea of using Antarctica’s ice mass as the target in which neutrinos from outer space could interact with atoms together. Learned then focused on an underwater neutrino experiment called DUMAND while Halzen pursued a project that eventually became IceCube.
Also, in 2012, while searching IceCube data for neutrinos coming from outer space with very high energies, scientists found two candidate events. The data quickly snowballed into evidence proving that neutrinos could be energised significantly by natural phenomena in space — and the prize citation credits this feat to Halzen alone.
But in real-life (as opposed to Nobel-life), the IceCube collaboration had credited Japanese physicist Aya Ishihara with finding those two candidate events, and for which she received an International Union of Pure and Applied Physics award in 2013. This particular oversight is oddly reminiscent of the infamous Jocelyn Bell Burnell story. Ishihara is currently a professor at Chiba University, where she continues to study high-energy neutrinos and develop the next generation of neutrino detectors.
Furthermore, the 2013 Science paper that reported the high-energy neutrinos also named three scientists named Claudio Kopper, Naoko Kurahashi, and Nathan Whitehorn as its corresponding authors.
The physics prize for Halzen is not misplaced. Halzen was very good — but the point is so were very many others. Aside from the scientists named here, it also required engineers and technicians who could build it in one of the most hostile locations on our planet. And all these people had to work together to make the project and its subsequent achievements possible. Halzen alone could never have done it.
Drawing difficult lines
Finally, the chemistry Nobel Prize this year illustrates the problem with the rule that it cannot be given to people who have died by the time the prize is announced. In 1953, the British physicist Frederick Charles Frank came up with a mathematical way to explain how a small chemical imbalance in a specific kind of reaction could force the reaction to make that imbalance the norm. This way required the reaction to have three properties, called autocatalysis, enantioselective catalysis, and mutual inhibition.
Between 1986 and 1995, Henri Kagan in France and Kenso Soai in Japan had reported evidence of all the conditions of Frank’s model, providing experimental evidence that it could work in the real world. However, Frank died in 1998, aged 87.
That said, the 1995 paper by Soai et al. included Takanori Shibata, who made essential contributions to this branch of chemistry (and was second author on the paper). And whereas Kagan and Soai had demonstrated different aspects of Frank’s model, Shibata was the first author of a 1999 paper that extended the work of Soai et al. to demonstrate the reaction Frank had tried to model. Shibata is currently at Waseda University. And again, it is not easy to rationalise the prize-giving committee’s decision to not include him among this year’s chemistry laureates.
On the other hand, the committee’s decision to exclude U.S. chemical engineer Donna Blackmond throws light on one possible line of reasoning. A technical statement accompanying the chemistry prize credited her with extending Kagan’s attempts to use mathematics to understand non-linear effects in chemical reactions. Blackmond and her team later also took big strides in making sense of the mechanism of the so-called Soai reaction.
And yet, the committee elected to reward the discovery of the validity of Frank’s model rather than work that explained and further extended it.
The S.N. Bose example
In the final analysis, the citations for the Nobel Prizes should not be mistaken for the history of science. Scientists build on the work of others and science advances in these slow but steady increments. When Peter Higgs and François Englert were awarded the Nobel Prize for physics in 2013 for predicting the Higgs boson, there was some clamour in India for not recognising the work of Satyendra Nath Bose. The objection was fair to the extent that you can’t have a fruit without the whole tree and yet petty because it is not reasonable to expect one prize to laud the entire history of a field.
This is why each Nobel Prize award can be a chance to reflect on its limitations, and remember that it is not an ultimate recognition. No prize is.
In that vein, we should also not confuse the number of winners every year with the number of people it takes to do excellent science — from grad students who perform simple experiments to senior colleagues to discuss complicated ideas with. In fact, depending on where in the world you are and your socio-economic standing, your ability to be a good scientist may turn on something as deceptively simple as having someone to help with household chores.
Perhaps most of all, while the Nobel Prizes recognise good science, not all good science wins Nobel Prizes.

The Union Health Ministry is engaging with youth volunteers to find people with tuberculosis (TB) who may be missing from the health system. JOSH teams of the National Cadet Corps (NCC) and MY Bharat volunteers are deploying for household-level outreach in 55 districts across 11 States and Union Territories.
Health Minister J.P. Nadda launched the JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) teams under the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan on Thursday. The teams will work at block and ward levels to identify people with symptoms, encourage testing, and support patients so they can complete treatment.
Each team will comprise five NCC cadets and five MY Bharat volunteers and will function under a designated Class-I officer. The initiative is being implemented jointly by the Ministries of Health and Family Welfare, Youth Affairs and Sports and Defence.
The government’s emphasis is on active case finding, with the Health Minister stating that people could be living with TB without recognising their symptoms and therefore remain outside the formal healthcare system. “Awareness is important, screening is important, but our responsibility does not end there,” he said, stressing the need to ensure diagnosis and completion of treatment.
The Centre also felicitated 67,933 Panchayats across 697 districts that were declared TB Mukt in 2026. The JOSH initiative is expected to be expanded to other districts after orientation and mobilisation of volunteers.

How some separatists are responding to Smith’s pledge against 2nd referendum if remain vote wins
Smith made the comment during interview with CBC News
Premier Danielle Smith’s pledge that she won’t hold another referendum on separation if the remain vote wins this month — at least as long as she is premier — is getting pushback from some prominent Alberta separatists.
“Well, I guess it depends on how long she plans to be premier,” said Cory Morgan, who heads the third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence.
“I'm not saying that as a threat sort of thing, you know, they’d kick her out if she didn't support it,” Morgan told CBC News Saturday.
“I'm just saying, you're quite a crystal ball if you would say that it would never be in the cards. I mean, what if she were premier six years still from now, and the winds had changed?”
Smith made the comment during a one-on-one interview with CBC News’ chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault Friday.
On Oct. 19, Albertans will choose either Option 1, to remain in Canada, or Option 2, to begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation.
Morgan said he sees Smith's statement as the premier “trying to make what appears to be a stronger stance during the tail end of this campaign.”
“To set it out saying that there would never be one as long as she's premier, well that means that she doesn't respect the principles of direct democracy she said she does,” Morgan said.
“If there were another referendum within a few years and Albertans said they wanted it, I believe that's her obligation to allow that to happen.”
Cory Morgan speaks to supporters during an Alberta independence rally in Taber, Alta., on Sunday, June 28, 2026. (Matthew Bruce/The Canadian Press)
Morgan says if Option 2 is unsuccessful, he understands another referendum is unlikely for at least a couple of years. But the movement is not going to go away, he said.
Alberta Prosperity Project CEO Mitch Sylvestre has agreed on that point.
He told CBC News Saturday that he does not think Smith’s stance on a second referendum “could go very well for her,” given the number of people in her party in favour of Alberta independence.
A recent Janet Brown Opinion Research Poll for CBC News suggested 53 per cent of respondents who would vote for the United Conservative Party would also vote in favour of the separation option in the upcoming referendum.
Party members could have a chance to voice their opinions on the matter next month, when the UCP holds its annual general meeting.
With just over a week of campaigning left until the referendum, Sylvestre described himself as “cautiously optimistic” about his side’s chances.
“A lot of people I talk to are basically closet separatists. And hopefully they’re gonna come out and vote, and if that's the case, then there's a chance that we can win.” he said.
Morgan says he’s seeing more people “flirt with” the idea of voting Option 2, but says those in favour of independence still have their work cut out to win a majority vote.
Advance polling runs from Oct. 13 to 17, with polling stations on referendum day Oct. 19 open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.
With files from CBC's Adrienne Arsenault and Joel Dryden

Wildfires threaten Indonesia's orangutans as rescuers find injured animals
Wildfires sweeping across Indonesia’s Borneo island have left endangered orangutans struggling to survive
JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Wildfires sweeping across parts of Indonesia’s Borneo island have left endangered orangutans struggling to survive, prompting rescuers to evacuate animals found injured, stranded and surrounded by thick haze.
A female Bornean orangutan nicknamed Novita was among dozens of apes rescued from wildfires in parts of Sumatra and Borneo in recent months. She was found clinging to a nearly leafless tree as dense smoke billowed across the scorched landscape in the Katune forest in Central Kalimantan province, said Jamartin Sihite, the chairman of the Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation.
“The palms of her hands and the soles of her feet suffered burns that were likely sustained when Novita crossed a burned area while trying to reach a tree,” Sihite told The Associated Press in an interview. He said that Novita, estimated to be 3 to 4 years old, was tranquilized, given oxygen and intravenous fluids and taken to the rehabilitation center in Nyaru Menteng.
Once her burns have healed, Novita will be evaluated to see if she can climb and survive in her natural environment, Sihite said. “We have previously released orangutans missing several fingers and they were still able to survive in the forest, so we remain hopeful that Novita can eventually return to the wild.”
Forest and land fires in Indonesia have worsened this year as El Niño intensifies a prolonged dry season, not only in the Indonesian part of Borneo but also in some regions on Sumatra island. Water shortages in the areas have hampered firefighting, while Japan has provided firefighting assistance to the island.
A male orangutan named Sampurna, believed to be around 20 years old, was found struggling to breathe by residents early last month on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan’s Ketapang district, an area affected by wildfires. He died hours after being rescued, Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry said.
It said more than 270 wild animals in Kalimantan had been rescued, rehabilitated or guided to safer habitats as of Saturday.
Government data showed more than 202,000 hectares (499,000 acres) of land burned between January and July. The independent Nusantara Atlas project, which monitors fires using satellite imagery, estimated that nearly 896,000 hectares (2.2 million acres) had burned by the end of August.
Toxic haze and smoke have caused a health crisis in neighboring countries as well. The smoke has drifted as far as the Philippines, more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) away. In Malaysia, authorities declared an emergency last week in Sarawak on Malaysia’s part of Borneo.
Novita’s case highlights the impact of forest and peatland fires on wildlife as well as people, said Andi Muhammad Kadhafi, head of the Central Kalimantan's Natural Resources Conservation Agency, a government body.
“Wildfires do not only affect humans but can also threaten wildlife and their habitats,” he said. “Fire prevention, habitat protection, monitoring and rapid response need to go hand in hand.”
____
Associated Press writers Edna Tarigan in Jakarta, Indonesia, and Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, contributed to this report.

The Trump administration will no longer allow Microsoft and other tech companies to participate in a program that allows H-1B visa holders to apply for green cards, one of the most common pathways for skilled foreign workers seeking permanent residency in the United States.
In addition to Microsoft, administration officials said on Thursday that software giant Adobe and IT companies including Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata will be suspended from the PERM program, the Labor Department's permanent labor certification program. PERM is a key step for H-1B visa holders to gain permanent residency, requiring employers to prove that there are no American workers who would be suitable for the applicant's permanent job opportunity.
Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said that the agency is investigating whether these companies committed fraud, undercutting American workers by hiring foreign employees.
Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, singled out Microsoft. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said during a press conference.
In a statement provided by Microsoft representative Kaitlin Haskins, the company said it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," adding that it develops its workforce by "strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world."
Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.
The suspension marks a victory for tech workers who have complained about unfairly losing out on jobs to immigrant workers.
Jobs Now, an advocacy group composed of US citizens working in big tech, celebrated Vance’s announcement on its X account with a video of dancing crabs. The group publicizes otherwise difficult-to-find PERM job postings and says it helped Americans apply to nearly 500,000 jobs across 7,000 employers between last January and this past July.
The organization and its members have also filed complaints against tech companies about alleged abuse of the PERM system, and have called for a number of changes to the employment immigration system. “Every job in America should be offered to an American first, no exceptions,” the group told WIRED in an unsigned statement.
This isn't the first time tech companies have been targeted over PERM. Earlier this year, OpenAI and a company it acquired agreed to settle accusations from the Trump administration about violating rules for the program. Apple reached a similar deal in 2023.
The administration's disparagement of H-1B visas—one of the most common work visas in the US—has sent waves of panic through Silicon Valley since Trump's reelection. Tech companies are some of the H1-B program's biggest users: So far in the fiscal year 2026, the top three employers with the most visas approved are Amazon, Tata, and Infosys.
Microsoft is No. 5, with 3,688 visas approved in 2026; in 2025, 6,258 visas were approved. According to the company, 80 percent of last year's visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees, not to hire new people.
"The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our US workforce," Microsoft’s statement said.
It's unclear if Thursday’s announcement would affect the ability of employees at these companies to apply for H1-B visas themselves. The Office of the Vice President and the Department of Labor did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for clarity on if the suspension would impact those seeking H-1B visas.
"It's one thing if you want to bring in someone like Elon Musk" who aims to "build something great in America," Vance said on Thursday. He equated the current state of the H-1B program to bringing "indentured servants" into the US, taking jobs away from American workers. (Musk, who was born in South Africa, came to the US via Canada to pursue a bachelor's degree at the University of Pennsylvania.)
The announcement came shortly before Trump was set to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. When asked about the upcoming event, Vance said, "We’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.”
Vance also said that the administration is investigating nine universities to see if they might be committing fraud with the J-1 visa program, which allows international candidates to study and conduct research in the US.
“I don’t care how prestigious a university thinks it is, break the law and screw the American people, and I will personally cuff you in the university square," Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said.
Paresh Dave contributed reporting.

Like many freshly minted adults, when I graduated from college, I wasn't sure exactly what to do next. I had dreams and goals; as a writer, I wanted to pursue an MFA, but the timing didn't feel right. My future was obscure to me — except for one thing. '
Whatever I did, I wanted to do it with my girlfriend of a year. And I did know for certain what my girlfriend wanted to do next: to get her master's at a university closer to her family in Kentucky than our New England undergraduate school. She was admitted to Vanderbilt in Nashville, and suddenly, moving there seemed like my most likely destination.
My friends and family advised against the move
Without exception, my friends and family urged me not to make a major life decision based on a relationship that might not last. They thought I would feel alienated in Nashville, and not without reason, since I grew up in Seattle and was living in Massachusetts, and had never spent any meaningful amount of time anywhere that fell between the West Coast and the Northeast.
I found ways to rationalize my decision to follow my girlfriend — getting recommendations on what Nashville might have to offer writers, securing an entry-level position at a book review magazine — but secretly, I felt ridiculous whenever I said I had my own reasons for moving. My reason was that I wanted to be with her.
The move was fraught from the start, both practically and emotionally. We fought while packing. On the harrowing drive down, my girlfriend's car was so full that she couldn't see her blind spot, and I had to lean out the window to check for oncoming traffic every time she changed lanes.
At first, I questioned whether I had made the right decision
Once in Nashville, I picked up a second job to afford my half of our rent, working late into the night scooping ice cream after days at the magazine's office. On the weekends, we went to tailgates with my girlfriend's graduate school cohort or drove to visit her family. I didn't know anyone in the city, and I didn't have a car of my own. I was entirely dependent on her, and it was suffocating.
Exhausted and terrified that the advice I'd ignored had been absolutely right, I sought out something, anything that might lead to making a friend. I started showing up alone to writing events, forcing myself to chat with strangers. And I decided to join a choir, though I had no idea how I would get to and from the rehearsals.
At the first meeting, I asked if anyone might be interested in carpooling, trying not to seem as desperate as I felt. I had no idea that the two people who offered to give me rides would become part of my life for many years to come.
I made friends, and they have been there for me
It was those two friends who cheered me on when my temporary position at the magazine became permanent, which allowed me to quit my second job. They came to support me when a new friend I'd met at an open mic night invited me to lead a writing workshop. They celebrated me when I was promoted to an editor at the magazine. And they were the ones to comfort me when my relationship finally fell apart.
So, yes, the relationship didn't last. But, as I reflected afterward, though I was sad things hadn't worked out the way I wanted them to, I was surprised to realize that I couldn't regret the path I'd chosen.
We can never know what the future holds, and however we try to justify our choices, they're rarely perfectly rational. But perhaps the more reasonable thing to expect of ourselves is not that we choose perfectly, but that we work to make whatever we choose worthwhile. I moved to Nashville for love, but once I was in Nashville, I found an incredible job, a creative community, and two lifelong friends (one of whom is now my romantic partner). If I could do it all over again, I wouldn't change a thing.

BJP chief Nitin Nabin accuses INDIA bloc, CJP of trying to destabilise country
The remarks came as the CJP and other groups planned protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on Saturday demanding the resignation of CEC
Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national president Nitin Nabin on Saturday termed the Rahul Gandhi-led ‘INDIA’ bloc and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)—whom he described as associates of Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leader Arvind Kejriwal—as “anarchist” groups attempting to destabilise the country, accusing them of seeking to create unrest after being rejected by voters.
“Today, an attempt is being made to create an extremely dangerous and serious situation in the country,” Nabin said, adding, “And who is doing this? These are two anarchist groups, one led by Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the ‘INDI alliance,’ and the other led by CJP, an associate of Arvind Kejriwal.”
The remarks came as the CJP and other groups planned protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on Saturday demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Deep Dive
Delhi police on Friday denied the CJP permission to protest, setting off a security operation that by Friday night reached well beyond the Capital. Authorities imposed curbs without precedent in Delhi, ordering the gates of 45 metro stations shut, cutting mobile internet across central Delhi, cancelling trains into the city and bringing in paramilitary reinforcements by special train.

Describing the two groups as “anarchist,” Nabin alleged that they were seeking to create instability after facing electoral defeats. “When the people rejected them and democracy punished them, instead of digesting that punishment and learning from it, they hatched a plan to destabilise the country,” he claimed.
Nabin further alleged that the protests were not driven solely by domestic political considerations, claiming that foreign powers were also attempting to undermine India because of its economic growth and development. “The country is fully advancing on the path of development and, despite ongoing global crises, is steadily progressing towards continuous growth today. But this fact is stinging all of you,” he said.
He also accused the Opposition of challenging the constitutional framework while invoking the Constitution. “Challenging democracy in the name of the Constitution with the support of lies is an insult to the people’s mandate,” he said, adding that the country’s youth were watching the language used by Opposition leaders and would reject what he described as attacks on constitutional institutions and holders of high office.
Nabin said the government would deal firmly with forces seeking to create tension. “The way attempts are being made today to create a tense situation, the Government of India will deal with it strictly, and at the same time, BJP workers will also stay among the people and thwart your schemes,” he said, reiterating the party’s commitment to building a “developed India”.
“We will deal firmly with all such forces active outside or inside the country,” Nabin added.

In a bid to make cancer treatment more affordable and reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure, the Union government has decided to cap trade margins at 30% of the maximum retail price (MRP) for all non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs.
Also read | Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
The measure will cover branded and generic drugs, domestically manufactured and imported medicines, and patented and non-patented products. An expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) will finalise the list of medicines to be brought under the measure.
Current mark-ups up to 700%
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), which analysed market data, found that the average trade mark-up on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was around 170%, with mark-ups reaching up to 700% in some cases. It also found substantial differences between prices charged through retail, hospital, and online pharmacies.
The government said the decision was prompted by the high financial burden of cancer treatment. Around 75% of cancer treatment expenditure is estimated to be borne out of pocket.
The anti-cancer medicines market comprises around 225 drugs and 500 formulations, with an annual turnover of approximately ₹12,500 crore. Scheduled cancer medicines account for about ₹2,250 crore.
Massive savings
A senior official said that the government is drawing on the experience of a similar intervention in 2019, when the NPPA capped trade margins on 42 selected non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs by invoking its extraordinary powers under Paragraph 19 of the Drug Price Control Order, 2013. The exercise had reportedly resulted in price reductions of up to 91%, with annual savings of ₹984 crore across 526 brands.
The latest intervention is expected to result in price reductions of up to 70% of MRP and annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore, the government said.
‘Production must be maintained’
Under the new framework, the trade margin will be capped at 30% of MRP, equivalent to 42.86% of the price to stockist.
“To ensure availability, manufacturers will be required to maintain their existing production level,” said the official.
The government said the measure would regulate trade margins rather than manufacturers’ selling prices or revenue, with the intervention aimed at reducing the margins retained across the distribution chain.

Telangana ACB arrests civil supplies manager over ₹9.41 crore disproportionate assets
Telangana ACB arrested civil supplies manager Vasamsetti Narasimha Rao over alleged disproportionate assets of ₹9.41 crore, with market value estimated above ₹40 crore.
The Telangana Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) on Saturday arrested a state civil supplies department assistant manager for allegedly amassing assets worth ₹9.41 crore disproportionate to his known sources of income, with their market value estimated at over ₹40 crore, officials said.
An official statement from ACB director general Charu Sinha said that ACB teams on Friday conducted searches at seven places linked to Vasamsetti Narasimha Rao, who is working as an assistant manager (technical) in the state civil supplies department and currently serving as district manager in Mahabubabad district.
“The searches went on till late in the evening. Searches are also being conducted in the properties belonging to the suspected benamis of Narasimha Rao. As per the market value, the assets belonging to him and that of his benamis together are worth nearly ₹100 crore,” a senior official of the ACB privy to the information said.
The case was registered under relevant sections of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Investigators identified several residential buildings, agricultural lands, open plots, vehicles, gold and silver ornaments, and other valuables during the searches.
According to ACB officials, five open plots measuring a total of 1,230.16 square yards were identified at Ballepalli, Raghunathapalem and Velugumatla in Khammam district. The properties, registered in the names of Narasimha Rao and his wife, have a combined registration value of ₹30.72 lakh.
The bureau also identified agricultural lands in Suryapet district, including approximately 1.08 acres at Kalmala Chervu, 21.3 acres at Sirikonda and two parcels measuring 5.31 acres each at Namavaram in Mothe mandal.
While the combined registration value of these agricultural properties was recorded at approximately ₹1.17 crore, the ACB found that the agreement values of certain properties were substantially higher.
In particular, the 21.3-acre agricultural property at Sirikonda had a registered value of ₹76 lakh, whereas its agreement value was ₹6.54 crore. Similarly, each of the two agricultural properties at Namavaram had a registered value of ₹19.25 lakh against an agreement value of ₹1.92 crore.
Investigators also identified three residential properties, including a ground-plus-two-storey RCC building and a ground-plus-four-storey RCC building at Kaviraj Nagar in Khammam, besides a three-storey residential property at Sagar Enclave in Bairamalguda, LB Nagar, Hyderabad.
These buildings, standing in the names of the official, his wife and his father-in-law, have a combined documented value of ₹1.58 crore.
Among the movable assets identified were a Hyundai Creta car valued at ₹18.49 lakh, a TVS Jupiter scooter worth ₹1.05 lakh and a Honda Activa scooter valued at ₹50,000.
The ACB also identified household articles valued at ₹33.48 lakh, besides approximately 360.97 grams of gold and 331.58 grams of silver ornaments with a combined estimated value of ₹9.39 lakh. Cash amounting to ₹15,600 was seized from the official’s residence.
The bureau stated that the total value of assets identified so far was approximately ₹9.41 crore, based on its property statement. It said the prevailing market value of the immovable properties could be substantially higher than their recorded registration values.
The ACB is also investigating allegations that Rao acquired a rice mill in the name of another person as benami property. “We are verifying the ownership of the suspected benami asset, the source of investment and the financial transactions involved in its acquisition,” Charu Sinha said.
Officials are also examining his bank accounts and lockers to determine whether he holds additional assets. Transactions linked to certain businesses have also come under scrutiny.
The agency is expected to establish the extent of the alleged disproportionate assets after completing the searches and examining the financial records and property documents.
The ACB director general said further investigation was underway to establish the actual ownership of the identified properties, their sources of acquisition and the funds used to purchase them.
Rao joined the civil supplies department as a technical assistant in 2011 and subsequently worked in Khammam and Nirmal before taking up his present responsibilities in Mahabubabad.
The ACB said its preliminary findings indicated that he had allegedly accumulated assets disproportionate to his known sources of income during his 15 years in service.

Two tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of people, damaging buildings including a school, and overturning cars.
A series of videos began to circulate on Friday morning showing two waterspouts approaching the Sicilian town from the sea as people braced for their arrival.
Dozens of people were reported injured, with at least 11 taken to hospital after being struck by flying debris and shattered glass. Among the most seriously injured was a 70-year-old man admitted to Mazara del Vallo hospital in a critical condition with several fractures.
A school was also hit by the powerful winds, leaving six children with minor cuts and abrasions. At the time the tornado struck, 273 pupils were inside the building, all of whom were safely evacuated. Drone footage showing the aftermath revealed extensive damage to the school, with windows shattered and desks and chairs overturned.
In recent years, people in southern Italy have been bracing for the arrival of a “medicane” – a rare Mediterranean storm with hurricane-like characteristics, capable of producing winds exceeding 60 miles an hour and waves reaching five metres in height.
The weather system developed amid intense heat over north Africa and unusually warm Mediterranean waters. Scientists have warned that rising sea temperatures, driven by the climate emergency, can provide additional energy for powerful storms in the region.
According to experts, record temperatures in the Mediterranean contributed to the freak storm that sank the Bayesian, a super yacht off the coast of Sicily, in August 2024, killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter.

Forget the spendy flagship smartphone. Every year, we test a dozen or more devices to find the best cheap phones that perform where it counts and aren’t annoyingly slow. Wireless carriers in the US go out of their way to make expensive smartphones seem affordable. AT&T will advertise a Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra for just $36 a month, but don’t let that fool you. With over 36 monthly installments, you spend more than a thousand bucks on a phone. Your pricey device may also keep you locked into the network, unable to switch wireless carriers until the phone is paid off.
Get a seriously great, affordable smartphone instead. Our top pick, the Google Pixel 10a, costs $499 and is as good as almost any flagship device. Our other recommendations strike a great balance between price and luxury. There’s even a folding phone in this guide! But it’s currently very tough to find phones worth considering under $400, since manufacturers slapped an extra $100 on most of their phones in response to the memory shortage.

Best Cheap Phone Overall
The Pixel 10a disappointingly may not change much from its predecessor, the Pixel 9a, but it remains the best smartphone on the market, especially for anyone trying to curb their spending.
It’s not the cheapest phone, but it has the best suite of features for the price, from an excellent dual-camera system to a sharp, 120-Hz screen, and performance that can run most apps and games perfectly fine thanks to the Tensor G4 chip. It’ll even get software updates for seven years, and Google says the battery is slightly easier to replace than the older model.
The biggest changes from the Pixel 9a are a brighter screen, faster wired and wireless charging (still no Pixelsnap magnets for Qi2 charging), and a tougher glass protecting the display. The plastic ring on the camera module is also gone, so the back of the Pixel 10a is even flatter than before—great for anyone who hates bulky camera bumps. These updates are still fairly minor, so if you happen to catch the Pixel 9a on sale, it’s still worthwhile if it means saving $100 or $150 bucks. However, the Pixel 10a will almost definitely also go on sale during major sale events like Prime Day and Black Friday, if you can be patient.
It’s nice to have faster charging speeds, but battery life overall is OK. It adequately lasts a full day with average use and then some, but folks who spend a lot of time on their smartphone during the day—whether it’s for navigating, music streaming, or reading fanfic—will likely find themselves hunting for an outlet in the afternoon.
The dual-camera system is versatile. The main 48-MP camera can snap pleasing photos, in low light and daytime, whereas the 13-MP ultrawide lets you capture sweeping scenes or group photos. Even the 13-MP selfie camera is pretty reliable. Naturally, with all the smart software features that Google is known for on its Pixel phones, there are some new AI perks here. Camera Coach lets you ask Google’s AI to give you suggestions on how to take a better photo, and Auto Best Take for group photos will automatically snap multiple pictures when you tap the shutter button and choose the best of each person, like fixing someone’s blinking eyes.
Speaking of, software is the top reason why I heartily recommend Pixel phones. I’ve detailed many of them here, but you can use Add Me to make sure everyone is in the group photo, including the photographer. Audio Magic Eraser lets you strip out unwanted sounds from your videos, like sirens. And Google’s Call Screen technology nips spam calls in the bud. I used the Hold for Me function to not have to listen to Delta’s terrible hold music for four hours after my flight was canceled.
Other perks include secure face unlock and fingerprint unlock—both work with sensitive apps that require biometric authentication, so you have multiple unlocking options. Secure face unlock is virtually nonexistent for every other Android phone at this price. There’s also NFC for contactless payments and an IP68 rating that protects it from the elements.

Best Cheap iPhone
Apple’s cheapest iPhone—the iPhone 17e—is a better value than its predecessor, the iPhone 16e. MagSafe is the biggest addition here (one of the strangest omissions last year), so now you can take advantage of the large accessory ecosystem, whether you want to use a magnetic wallet that sticks to the back of your iPhone or a magnetic tripod to snap selfies on your travels.
Like the rest of the iPhone 17 lineup, the iPhone 17e also uses the same Ceramic Shield 2 glass mixture to protect the display, which is more durable and scratch-resistant and matches what’s on the pricier iPhones—always a plus. It’s no iPhone Mini, but this is Apple’s smallest phone in the lineup, which is nice for anyone who hates big-screen handsets, though you’re stuck with the old-school notch design instead of the Dynamic Island found on the rest of the iPhones. (There’s still Face ID!)
It’s powered by the latest-generation A19 chip, like the iPhone 17, though there’s one less graphics core, so there’s a minor hit to performance. I still had no trouble running all my usual apps and games, even Genshin Impact at its max graphical settings. Battery life is also solid, comfortably lasting me a full day, though extreme users will likely need a top-up before bed. I suspect the improved and energy-efficient C1X 5G modem is what helps extend battery life despite the small size of the phone.
Where this iPhone doesn’t quite feel like its $599 price is the camera. You can snap perfectly good photos with the 48-MP sensor, but that’s it; that’s the only camera on the back. Now compare it to the Pixel 10a and its dual-camera system, or the Samsung Galaxy S25 FE and its triple-camera module (often on sale for under $500). Apple should really have added an extra camera here for versatility, as the lone camera is too limiting.
Generally, camera performance is also a little lackluster in low light, especially if you’re trying to capture a moving subject like a pet. It may sound like it has the same 48-MP camera as the iPhone 17, but the sensor is smaller, so you’re not getting the same image quality. The selfie camera is also OK, but it can struggle with high-contrast scenes.
There’s no ultrawideband chip on the iPhone 17e, so you can’t precisely track AirTags—this iPhone will only give you the general vicinity of the tag’s location. And the screen is still stuck on a 60-Hz refresh rate when nearly every phone that costs this much has moved on to 120 Hz.
These concessions make the iPhone 17e feel a little overpriced, but it’s sure as heck better value than the iPhone 16e. If you don’t find the flaws off-putting and don’t care much for the camera experience, this smartphone will satisfy anyone looking for a good, reliable, and price-friendly iPhone. Apple also sells the iPhone 16 for $100 more, but I don’t think it’s worth paying more for less storage and slightly lesser performance, even if it has perks like a dual-camera system.

Best Design
Midrange and budget phones usually don’t experiment too much with design, so they’re rarely exciting, but London-based Nothing has been trying to fix that for a few years with its attractive, stylish, and unique handsets. The latest iteration is the Nothing Phone (4a) and Phone (4a) Pro, though only the latter is available in the US.
It looks nothing like its peers. The Pro has a fresh camera module with a unique camera layout and the Glyph Matrix that the company debuted last year on the Phone (3). The triple-camera system boasts a 50-MP main camera, an 8-MP ultrawide, and a 50-MP telephoto zoom offering 3.5X zoom. What Phones Should You Avoid?
If you’re eyeing a cheap phone, try to stick to name brands. There are several smartphones you’ll find for dirt cheap on Amazon, but you’re about to load up whatever you buy with your personal information and photos—it’s important to make sure it’s a reputable brand with good security practices (or at least some kind of record that it does issue security patches).
Outside of that, we generally recommend avoiding the previous generation (unless otherwise mentioned above). It may not get updates for much longer (if any), and prices aren’t usually that different. That’s why I don’t recommend Motorola’s Moto G series phones from 2024 or older—you may want to skip some of the 2025 models too, like the Moto G 2025, since its successor is already here.
We also don’t recommend you buy any HMD devices anymore. Sadly, the company has ceased its operations in the US market.
Should You Buy Now?
For the most part, yes. Cheap phones typically launch in the first half of the year. Google’s Pixel 11a, Apple’s more affordable iPhones, and releases from Nothing and others likely won’t land until the spring of 2027.
Consider Last Year’s Flagship Phones (or Used)
If none of these phones have the features you want or they aren’t as powerful as you’d like, your best option is to look for a previous generation flagship smartphone, which might be steeply discounted. Sometimes they’re easy to find, but manufacturers may stop selling them. Keep in mind that you’ll lose a year of software support, but that’s often still better than the software support available on cheap phones anyway. Prices fluctuate, so purchase accordingly.
Alternatively, consider buying a used smartphone. (We have some tips here.) You’ll need to research, but sites like Swappa, Gazelle, and Back Market have a good reputation and are solid places to buy a used or refurbished device. Look for the current top models on Android and iPhone from the past year or two, and see what they're going for in mint or good condition.
5G Smartphones, Explained
5G is the current cellular network generation, and it’s widespread enough that you should try to stick to phones that support it. It’s not replacing 4G LTE entirely, so you’ll see 4G in your status bar as you roam the country. You can read more about it here, but in short, 5G comes in two major types: sub-6 and millimeter wave (mmWave). The latter is usually only available in flagship phones and allows you to access superfast speeds, but you’ll rarely encounter mmWave (think select areas in major cities and certain venues, like stadiums and airports). Sub-6 isn’t much faster than 4G LTE, but it has a broader range and is more widely accessible. Most of the smartphones we recommend here support sub-6 5G, even those as low as $180.
Check Network Compatibility
If you buy an unlocked phone on this list and try to take it to one of your wireless carrier’s retail stores, they may tell you it isn’t compatible with the network. It likely is. Just use a paper clip or SIM ejection tool to pop the SIM card out of your current phone, then slide that SIM into your new phone. If it doesn’t work at first, reboot the phone. (Most cheap phones support eSIM technology, too.)
If you need a new SIM, try ordering one online from your carrier or see if they’ll give you one when you activate a line in the store (if you’re starting coverage). Tell them you have a phone. Often, reps will want to sell you a phone; that’s one reason they might hassle you into buying a different device in the store. Having said that, please make sure whatever phone you buy will work on your wireless network. Listings on retailers like Amazon should state clearly which networks a device will be compatible with. Also, make sure the listing says the phone is being sold “unlocked.”
In this guide, we’ve listed whether a phone works with a major US carrier. But what if you’re not on AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon? If we note that a phone works on T-Mobile, for example, that means it’ll likely work on smaller carriers like Metro by T-Mobile and Mint Mobile, both of which utilize T-Mobile’s cellular network. If you’re nervous about compatibility, look up the specifications of the exact model you’re considering. Make sure it has the LTE or 5G bands it needs to run on your carrier.
Warning for Verizon users: There’s a higher chance an unlocked phone will not work on your network. Make sure it is labeled to work on Verizon, or that it says the phone is CDMA-capable. If something strange is going on, like you don’t get any texts, you may also need to contact customer service and ask them to enable CDMA-less roaming. AT&T and T-Mobile are GSM carriers, which is the standard for most of the world; most unlocked phones are compatible with them.

Srinagar, Oct 10: The Kashmir Electric Equipment Manufacturers Association (KEEMA) has expressed deep dismay over the objections raised by a group of retired bureaucrats operating under the banner of the Group of Concerned Citizens (GCC).
In a statement issued on Saturday, KEEMA President Raja Nayeem Ahmad Khan said the apprehensions expressed over the legislation risked undermining progressive economic reforms and discouraging investment in Jammu and Kashmir.

Vague warnings about regulatory changes, without identifying specific provisions or demonstrating actual adverse consequences, would only discourage local enterprise and fresh investment, he said.

Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election
'Complete hoax,' says Israeli PM as calls grow for an inquiry
With just weeks before Benjamin Netanyahu is set to face a potentially pivotal election, the Israeli prime minister is defending against new allegations that he ignored high-level warnings from Arab allies that might have prevented the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.
In a new book excerpted in Israel's Haaretz newspaper, journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval contend that the United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed telephoned Netanyahu 10 days prior to the attack to warn of a potential significant move by the militant group against Israel.
"The [worst thing] was that Netanyahu heard his warning and didn't deliver it to the security echelon," Eldar told CBC News at his home near Tel Aviv.
"Not the chief of staff, not the head of the Shin Bet, not the head of the Mossad," he said, referring to the country's internal security and spy agencies, respectively. "And also not the defence minister."
The Oct. 7 attacks would prove to be the deadliest in Israel's history. Some 1,200 people were killed, including more than 800 civilians, with 251 people taken back into Gaza as hostages.
Israel's subsequent war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 people, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Eldar says, according to his sources, the U.A.E.'s warning was not specific about a date, only that Hamas's leader in Gaza at the time, Yahiya Sinwar, was planning something "very big."
A new book co-authored by Israeli journalist Shlomi Eldar contends that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed called Netanyahu more than a week before attacks to warn of a potential significant move by Hamas. (CBC)
Shortly after Haaretz published the allegations, other media outlets including the Wall Street Journal and The Atlantic reported that Egypt's intelligence head, Abbas Kamel, had delivered similar warnings in the days just prior to Oct. 7.
Netanyahu has dismissed the allegations as fabrication by political opponents and regional actors he accuses of trying to scupper his chances of winning another term in office when Israelis go to the polls on Oct. 27.
"I didn't ignore any warnings because I didn't receive any warnings, I mean that's a complete hoax," Netanyahu told CBS News. "It's politically propagated by certain countries or certain elements abroad, but they're completely false."
The U.A.E. has not confirmed or denied the allegations contained in Eldar's and Yuval's book Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment.
But they've added fuel to the fire for Israelis who have been demanding a state commission of inquiry into Israeli security failings for three years now.
A protester dressed as Netanyahu kneels on a sheet covered with red paint with a sign in Hebrew announcing the 'untimely death of responsibility' on the third anniversary of the attacks, in Tel Aviv, on Monday. (Avi Ohayon/Reuters)
This year's memorial ceremonies for the victims of Oct. 7 were accompanied by protests in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv demanding accountability from Netanyahu.
Some demonstrators held signs reading: "No forgiveness for failure, no forgiveness for abandonment."
Others read: "The people will remember Oct. 7 on Oct. 27," referring to the election.
The face of Eyal Eshel's 19-year-old daughter Roni now graces a memorial stone along the Israeli/Gaza boundary, close to the Nahal Oz base where she and 14 other young women performing their Israeli military service were killed on Oct. 7.
"I don't know what to say. I don't know how to think. I don't know what to recognize," Eshel said.
"I just know that it's three years and it's become harder. We have a big hole, a black hole, at home."
Eyal Eshel stands beside a poster of his 19-year-old daughter Roni, who was killed in the attacks. She was part of a military unit that also warned of unusual activity by Hamas. (CBC)
The women were part of a surveillance unit at the base, each monitoring a section of Israel's fortified fence with Gaza in shifts.
That their repeated warnings of unusual activity by Hamas were dismissed by senior officers is already well documented.
Eshel remembers his daughter coming home from the base one morning, 72 hours before the attacks.
"She stood at home and she told me: 'It's hot there — not the weather, the situation.'
"I put my hand on her shoulder, and I told her, 'Ronnie … we have a good army. Everything will be OK.'"
Eshel has since become a leading member of the October Council, made up of bereaved family members and victims, campaigning for a state inquiry.
He spoke to CBC News sitting in a small garden next to his home in Tzur Yitzhak, north of Tel Aviv where he has re-created a memorial that includes replicas of the women's monitoring stations in the Nahal Oz command centre.
Neighbours still light candles and leave messages of condolence there, where he has also planted the fruit trees and foliage, which he says Roni loved.
He can barely bring himself to say Netanyahu's name out loud.
"Today, because of him and the IDF chiefs, I'm a grieving father. Because of these people. They need to be in jail. I lost Roni with her big smile just because of them," he said.
Eshel is not surprised by the latest allegations against Netanyahu.
"He knew everything. He knew everything."
'A big mistake'
If Netanyahu did ignore or dismiss credible warnings, delivered by regional allies, reportedly repeatedly in Egypt's case, the obvious question is why.
Some analysts suggest Netanyahu was worried that any action in Gaza had the potential to derail what he hoped at the time would be an agreement to establish formal relations with Saudi Arabia.
Others connect it to Netanyahu's policy of propping up Hamas in Gaza over the years as a tactic designed to undermine the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, and thus undermine the prospect of a Palestinian state.
Eldar says the initial warning from the U.A.E. came via a Palestinian mediator negotiating between Israel and Hamas on a potential easing of Israel’s blockade of the Strip.
Netanyahu continued to allow funding from Qatar to reach Hamas even though he knew it went directly to the Hamas military wing, according to Eldar.
Making it easier for Sinwar, the Hamas leader, to mislead Israel, says Danny Yatom, who served as the Mossad chief in the late '90s, during Netanyahu's first term.
Former Israeli spy chief Danny Yatom says the misperception, among Netanyahu and others, that Hamas leader Yahiya Sinwar didn't want war was a 'big mistake.' (CBC)
"The misconception that was shared by the heads of the intelligence and Netanyahu and almost everybody … was that Sinwar did not want war, and he is going to do his utmost in order to avoid a war. Of course, it was a big mistake."
Yatom, who also served as military secretary to Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and later as chief of staff to Prime Minister Ehud Barak, says Netanyahu's refusal to convene an independently appointed state inquiry is telling.
"The fact that Netanyahu … did not take responsibility on himself I think says a lot about his behaviour," Yatom told CBC News.
In a recent poll by the Israel Democracy Institute, 68 per cent of Jewish Israelis said the Oct. 7 attacks would be central to the way they vote in upcoming elections.
But political analysts are not writing off Israel's longest serving leader — often dubbed the "Teflon Prime Minister" for his staying power despite numerous political scandals over the years.
"The government has shown that it is completely and utterly inept at everything other than staying in power, which means that the opposition should have had this election handed to it on a silver platter," said Hebrew University political scientist Reuven Hazan.

"The fact that it's even a race is mind-boggling."
Eldar says that in the absence of a state inquiry, the vote has taken on the feel of a referendum on Netanyahu's conduct before, during and after Oct. 7.
"[Many times we] had chance to release the hostages and stop the war and bloodshed in Gaza Strip," he said. "We could stop the war before, but Netanyahu refused [for] his political survival."
Netanyahu has threatened to sue Eldar and other Israeli journalists who have published the allegations against him.
"He tried to say that we're just recruited by the opposition," said Eldar, denying it and insisting that the timing of the book's publication coincides with the time it took to verify the allegations contained within it.

Srinagar, Oct 10: A delegation of the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA), Jammu and Kashmir, led by its chairperson Sanjay Aggarwal, met Transport Minister Satish Sharma to discuss issues affecting the ease of doing business in the automobile sector across the Union Territory.
The delegation highlighted procedural difficulties faced by automobile dealerships in obtaining Trade Certificates and called for simplified documentation, uniform implementation of rules and a transparent, time-bound compliance mechanism.
During the meeting, Aggarwal said the automobile sector had emerged as an important pillar of Jammu and Kashmir’s economy, generating employment for around 20,000 people while contributing to government revenue, consumer services and the growth of the automotive ecosystem.
He said further improvements in the Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) framework were essential to unlock the sector’s potential and encourage fresh investment in the Union Territory.
Raising concerns over the Trade Certificate application process, Aggarwal said automobile dealers in J&K were currently required to submit approximately 16 documents to obtain the certificate. He pointed out that the extensive documentation requirements were creating difficulties for dealers and delaying the completion of applications.
He also referred to the three-month, one-time relaxation recently provided by the government to eligible automobile dealers who had already initiated the statutory process for obtaining Trade Certificates. However, he said the existing documentation requirements continued to pose significant challenges despite the temporary facilitation.
Aggarwal further highlighted the recent closure of some automobile dealerships in J&K, citing the cumbersome documentation process for obtaining Trade Certificates. He stressed the need to rationalise the requirements to ensure that regulatory compliance did not become an unnecessary obstacle to business operations.
Referring to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules (CMVR), the FADA chairperson said the documentation requirements prescribed under the applicable rules were considerably fewer than those currently required in Jammu and Kashmir. He urged the government to review the process in line with the relevant provisions of the CMVR.
Drawing a comparison with neighbouring Punjab, Aggarwal said the documentation requirement there was understood to be around six documents. He maintained that reducing unnecessary procedural requirements would make compliance easier without compromising statutory obligations.
The delegation also called for the implementation of the ‘One UT, One Trade Certificate’ system in Jammu and Kashmir. Aggarwal said dealerships operating across multiple districts were currently required to obtain separate Trade Certificates for different districts, increasing the compliance burden and restricting operational flexibility.
He proposed that a single Trade Certificate should enable a dealer to conduct business anywhere in the Union Territory, describing the arrangement as consistent with the principles of Ease of Doing Business. He cited the GST registration framework, under which branches can be endorsed, as a model for consideration.
Aggarwal requested the Transport Minister to issue suitable directions to the concerned authorities for simplifying and rationalising Trade Certificate applications across J&K in accordance with the applicable CMVR provisions. He said such measures would support the government’s objectives of improving the business environment, transparency and digital governance.
Transport Minister Satish Sharma gave a patient hearing to the delegation, appreciated the concerns and suggestions put forward by FADA J&K, and assured the members that the issues discussed would be addressed on priority.

A woman in the remote Siberian region of Irkutsk has died of plague, a regional official said Friday, as a Russian media outlet reported dozens were under quarantine.
Local media named her as 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova.

As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the outlet added, without elaborating.

Four dead and thousands without power after Hurricane Isaias lashes US
- Published
Four people have died and hundreds of thousands are without power after Hurricane Isaias battered parts of the southern US with powerful winds and heavy rain.
Officials reported two deaths each in the states of Alabama and Florida, which included people who were killed when trees fell on their houses.
At least 600,000 people were without power in several states as of Saturday afternoon, according to tracker PowerOutage.
Isaias made landfall in Florida late on Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105mph (168km/h) before being downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone.
The storm felled trees and ripped the roofs off buildings. Alabama, Florida and Georgia all declared states of emergency ahead of its arrival, while both Florida and Alabama issued mandatory evacuation orders to thousands of people.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon is bearing down on Mexico's Pacific coast and has strengthened to category four. It is expected to make landfall sometime overnight.
And Tropical Storm Rachel, also in the Pacific Ocean, is edging towards land and is expected to hit southern California later on Saturday.
Two deaths related to Isaias were reported in Florida's Escambia County. A woman was killed when a tree fell on her house, local Sheriff Chip Simmons said.
Joey Williams told NewsNation his wife had died in the storm. He said they went outside to snap pictures of the damage but, when they went back into their home, a tree fell through the roof and trapped them.
"I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn't make it," Williams told the outlet.
Simmons later reported that a man had died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a garage that was not properly ventilated. Four other people who were in the same house were taken to hospital.
Officials had to rescue people in vehicles that became submerged by floodwaters. The Florida National Guard shared pictures of a truck stuck in a flood ditch, saying soldiers "stopped, swam to the vehicle and pulled its occupants to safety".
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said flooding was a continued risk and warned of a "very hazardous situation".
In neighbouring Alabama, a sheriff was injured when a tree fell on him as he was responding to a car crash.
"Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives," Governor Kay Ivey said in a post on X, without giving further details on the circumstances of the deaths.
She also said officials were concerned about "spinoff tornadoes" in the state from the strong winds and heavy rain.
"As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop," she said.
In Charleston, South Carolina, officials asked people to stay home on Saturday night as high tide is expected to reach 7.5ft (2.3m).
"After dark, floodwater is much harder to see and it's impossible to judge how deep it is from behind the wheel," the city said.
The storm is expected to continue to weaken as it travels to the north-east, but the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) warned that the Carolinas and Georgia could see floods from up to 10 inches (25cm) of rainfall.
Hurricane Isaias was the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.
