The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

The MRP debate, which has been recently triggered where a hospital purchased a product for ₹11 and billed it for ₹325, is misplaced and lacks the context we need to understand the issue properly.
Hospitals rightly point out that the gap between procurement and billing is not all profit: storing supplies, maintaining sterility and ensuring availability carry costs. But patients are entitled to ask a more basic question. How did ‘maximum’ become the price they routinely pay?
Understanding maximum retail price
MRP was designed as a ceiling to protect consumers. In healthcare, it can, however, also conceal how a price is built. The printed figure tells a family little about the manufacturer’s returns, the margins taken along the supply chain, or whether the product offers any advantage over a cheaper alternative. A patient in an emergency cannot shop around. When choice disappears, a ceiling risks becoming the default charge.
This is a serious problem, and price controls can help. In 2019, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority applied trade-margin rationalisation to 42 non-scheduled cancer medicines. The government estimated that this could save patients 200 crore annually. But the wider lesson is not that every medicine and device should have the same permitted margin. It is that India needs to decide what each margin is paying for.
Different products, therapies
A standard syringe sold by multiple suppliers does not justify the same return as a therapy developed for a rare disease after years of research and clinical trials. Nor should a familiar medicine acquire an innovation premium simply because it has a new brand name and a large marketing budget.
India needs a differential profit and margin strategy. Routine, high-volume products should have modest, transparent distribution and hospital margins, informed by comparable procurement prices. Bulk purchasing should benefit patients, insurers and public programmes. Genuine costs of stocking, safe handling, wastage and round-the-clock availability should be recognised openly, rather than recovered through an inflated price for the item itself.
Companies that take substantial scientific risks deserve a different approach. Those investing in original research, rare and neglected diseases, or products that demonstrably improve outcomes while reducing hospitalisations and total care costs should be able to earn higher profits. Fair returns give investors a reason to fund difficult work. But the premium should go to the organisation creating the clinical value, not automatically to every intermediary between the factory and the patient.
Science must earn
‘Novel’ must not be a label a company awards itself. A claim for a higher return should be tested against existing treatments: Does the product help patients live longer or better? Does it prevent complications? Is it safer or easier to use? Does it lower the total cost of treatment, even if its purchase price is higher? A product that costs more upfront but prevents repeated admissions may be better value than the cheapest item on the shelf.
Societal impact should count too. Research into diseases affecting small or neglected patient groups, reliable supply in underserved areas, and meaningful differential pricing for vulnerable patients merit consideration. These commitments must be specific and measurable. A patient-assistance scheme that reaches a handful of people cannot excuse a price that excludes everyone else.
India has an institution on which to build: Health Technology Assessment already evaluates clinical effectiveness, costs and equity to inform public decisions. Its evidence could help distinguish genuine advances from claims designed to justify a higher price.
Margins under microscopes
The government should establish an independent Healthcare Pricing and Value Panel with clinicians, scientists, health economists, patient representatives and pricing regulators. It should assess products against published criteria: clinical benefit, research risk, development investment, disease burden, total health-system cost and access for those least able to pay. Its members should disclose conflicts of interest, explain decisions and provide an appeal process.
A higher return would come with obligations. Companies seeking one should submit evidence and relevant costs for independent review. Premiums should be reconsidered as products mature or competitors enter the market. Where promised benefits remain uncertain, agreements could link part of the payment to observed outcomes. Concessional access for eligible patients and public programmes should be enforceable, rather than left to goodwill.
The panel must also separate manufacturer profits from trade and hospital margins. Otherwise, a policy intended to reward research could simply enlarge the amount captured downstream. Regulators need visibility into invoice prices, rebates and patient charges. Patients need itemised bills showing the product charge and any separate handling fee. Small and rural pharmacies, meanwhile, need viable returns to keep essential products available. A pricing policy that closes the last-mile supplier has failed its patients.
Profit, but not profiteering
MRP should remain a shield against overcharging, but it cannot be our entire definition of fair price. Companies should be able to make a profit, but not profiteer. India can protect a family buying an IV set and reward a company developing a breakthrough for a child with a rare disease. To do both, we must ask what the price rewards, what benefit the patient receives, and who can actually afford it. In healthcare, margin should follow proven value and access, and not bargaining power over a captive patient.
(Dr. Rajendra Pratap Gupta is the chairman of Health Parliament, a global executive think tank on healthcare, and former advisor to the Health Minister, government of India. founder@parliament.health)

Raphinha's brilliant Barcelona start interrupted by injury concerns
- Published
Raphinha has made a phenomenal start to the season for Barcelona, cementing his status as one of Europe's most formidable attackers.
The 29-year-old has scored 14 times and provided three assists as the Spanish champions have racked up eight successive wins in all competitions.
His performances have been so impressive that his omission from the 30-man Ballon d'Or shortlist prompted debate, with some arguing his form warranted greater recognition among the game's elite.
Yet, just as Raphinha appeared ready to take his game to another level, injury concerns have interrupted his momentum and he looks set to miss Barcelona's next two fixtures.
Facing a demanding run of fixtures, including meetings with Paris St-Germain and Real Madrid this month in the Champions League and La Liga, keeping the Brazilian fit could prove just as important as making the most of his remarkable goalscoring form.
'Was it necessary for him to play in Australia?'
Raphinha withdrew from international duty with a right thigh injury after he was substituted at half-time in Brazil's match against Australia.
"The tests show something," Barcelona boss Hansi Flick told the media.
"It's not a serious injury, but we have to be careful because he had three injuries last year, and we have to take care of him."
Flick defended Raphinha's decision to want to play for Brazil.
"It's the national team and everyone wants to play for their national team," he said. "That's Raphinha's mentality. Always give 100%."
Although the setback does not appear to be major, the timing has not been ideal.
"We must reflect on whether it was necessary for him to play in Australia, travelling so many thousands of kilometres," added Flick. "It's incredible. They have to choose friendly matches and in Europe it is not possible because of the Nations League."
With tough tests to come, Flick will want all his leading attackers available and hope even a short spell on the sidelines won't disrupt Raphinha's rhythm.
The situation has also presented Flick with a familiar dilemma. At the start of the season, there were concerns Barcelona had no established number nine after veteran Poland striker Robert Lewandowski left the club.
Raphinha has mainly been playing as a false nine this season, rather than his usual role on the wing and the team have looked unstoppable.
They sit top of La Liga, five points clear of Atletico Madrid and Real Betis, with Real Madrid a point further back in fourth place, and thrashed Feyenoord 5-1 in their Champions League opener. With 36 goals scored and eight conceded, they've been dominant at both ends of the pitch.
For now, fellow Brazilian Gabriel Jesus - a deadline-day arrival from Arsenal in September - is likely to cover Raphinha's absence for the next two matches against Getafe on Saturday and then the European trip to Galatasaray.
Flick, though, has huge depth in his Barcelona squad, and Anthony Gordon, Dani Olmo and Karim Adeyemi could all play as a false nine if necessary.
Huge impact as Barca close in on record
Raphinha's numbers tell an impressive story, but his contribution to Barcelona extends beyond the stats.
He is the team captain and has become a central figure in their aggressive, high-intensity approach, combining direct attacking play with relentless pressing and a willingness to work for the team.
His finishing has become a defining feature of his game. Rather than relying on creating chances for others, Raphinha has developed into a consistent source of goals himself and Barcelona's performances so far have reflected that influence.
The former Leeds United player has been a key factor in why Flick's side have looked so threatening in the final third and could equal the 2013-14 record for the best start to a La Liga season if they beat Getafe for an eighth straight league win.
Avoiding repeats of last season
Raphinha, though, will be determined to avoid a repeat of last season, which demonstrated how quickly fitness problems can complicate the club's plans and ambition.
He was restricted to 33 appearances, with recurring fitness issues and a hamstring injury contributing to his absences.
Raphinha played seven times in the Champions League but, crucially, was missing as his side went out in the quarter-finals with defeat by Atletico Madrid.
His tally of 21 goals helped deliver the league title and he scored twice in a standout performance in the Spanish Super Cup final against Real Madrid.
Given his importance, the temptation for Flick to rush Raphinha back will be understandable and Barca will hope this is a brief interruption rather than the beginning of another frustrating injury cycle.

NAMSCON 2026, the 66th annual conference and convocation of the National Academy of Medical Sciences (India), will bring together medical professionals, researchers and academicians from across the country in Chennai from October 8 to 11.
Hosted by SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankulathur, the conference will focus on the theme ‘Synergy of Science and Technology in Healthcare for a Healthier Tomorrow’.

The four-day programme will include pre-conference workshops, symposia, keynote addresses, National CME sessions, and oral and poster presentations.
The scientific sessions will cover antimicrobial resistance, CAR-T cell therapy, biosimilars and biologics, senolytic therapies, rare genetic disorders, emerging infections, pandemic preparedness and the Indian diabetes phenotype. Discussions will also focus on medical education, robotics in surgery, organ donation and transplantation, and evolving approaches to tuberculosis management.
Eight workshops on October 8 will cover trauma care, neonatal resuscitation, AI in clinical research, spine surgery, endoscopic gastroenterology, palliative care, diagnostic reasoning, and physician entrepreneurship.

The conference is being organised under the leadership of R. Jayanthi, Organising Chairperson and Dean, SRM MCH&RC, and Melvin George, Organising Secretary and Head, Centre for Clinical Pharmacology and Clinical Trials Research, with Rajarajan Swaminathan as State Convenor.

In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.
Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.
Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.
So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.
Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.
Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.
Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.
Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.
Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.
Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?

Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.
The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”

Bay Area lettering artist Jesscia Hische knew that when she took a freelance gig to design the M logo for Meta’s new AI assistant Muse, it was bound to make some people angry. “AI is such a third rail, and Meta is such a third rail,” she tells me.
Still, as a small business owner who relies on client work to keep her two brick-and-mortar art and stationary shops in Oakland afloat, she says she needed the money. “New Work! (Don’t be mad at me),” Hische wrote in her newsletter last month. “I worked with Meta on an icon and logotype for their latest release: Muse, which just launched! It’s Meta’s foray into the AI agent / personal assistant world. I know folks have big feelings about both AI and Meta, but this has been a really fun project for so many reasons.”
The news quickly went viral on Threads, where dozens of fellow designers criticized Hische for selling out. She responded to the haters by trying to explain the decision:
“For the past year, I pretty much have 2-4 payrolls in my account at any given time, which if you own a small business, you know is pretty precarious,” she wrote. She added that she had also invested $100,000 in Studioworks, an admin platform she runs for creatives, and $30,000 in Drawling, her art shop for kids in Oakland, where she hosts classes and workshops. “I have 4 people on payroll including myself, my mom, and two shop employees,” she added. Nothing she said seemed to help.
“Disgusted,” wrote one user. “It’s not about money, it’s about ethics.”
Another person responded saying, “Doing this job is like doing a hit for the mob, and being surprised later when the mob takes you out too.” Other users posted photos of Hische’s house and speculated about her wealth and finances.
Hische had expected some pushback from the artist community, but the level of vitriol caught her off guard. Even if people didn’t like Meta, she felt the company should be commended for hiring an independent artist rather than using generative AI. But the backlash made it clear just how unpopular generative AI has become in some circles, to the point that working for one in any capacity is seen as a betrayal.
We spoke on the phone last week about the backlash, her design process, and whether she was instructed to not make the Muse logo look like a butthole.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Zoë Schiffer: In your newsletter, you acknowledge that people have complicated feelings about Meta and about AI. Did that make it hard for you to take this job?
Jesscia Hische: The last year or two, my client work has been really slow, and my client work is what supports the other things I do, because the brick-and-mortar businesses are not hugely profitable. My margins are razor thin. I think between the two shops, I had like $10,000 in profit last year. I can't sustain myself on $10,000 a year.
So when the Meta project came around, it was like, alright! Let's get some money in the account so I can pay my staff and I don't have to feel so stressed out every time I have to run a pay cycle.
What were you hired to do, specifically?
I specialize in logo refreshes. I did the redesign of Squier from Fender, I redesigned Jeni’s Ice Cream a few years ago and did Southern Living magazine. When I work on logos, I want them to look like they went to the spa for a weekend—not that they went and got a ton of plastic surgery, you know? Just fresh and new, where you're like, “Oh, something's different. I can't tell what, but I like it.”
The [Meta] team had done an exploration of the M internally. They knew it wasn't quite right. It’s just a bunch of product designers and engineers designing type. Some of them are very skilled at typography, but it's just such a super unique thing to be able to draw letterforms. They wanted to refine what they had already done in terms of the M.
It was a huge sprint for that M. I did the work in two days. There were 32 different versions. The logotype took another two weeks.
What did the team tell you they wanted to change?
They had drawn the M as a single stroke, a vector stroke. It was the same width all the way around. When something is just a mono-weight stroke with no adjustments, there's not a lot of subtlety around the shape. This is where the fun happens with type design. As strokes touch each other and join, it creates this heavier pocket, visually. You get these little inky moments. And what type designers often do is sort of play with subtracting and adding bits of weight.
Their big ask was, “We want this thing to feel inspiring and creative and to get people thinking that Muse is a fun thing you can play with, not that it's like this very rigid, engineered, cold thing.”
How much do you get paid for a project like this?
I charged what I thought was an amazing fee for a two-day sprint for a big company, which was like $12,500. That’s an amazing amount of money to make in two days, but it’s not life-changing.
Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang has been talking about the logo recently, noting he’s happy it doesn’t look like a butthole, unlike some of Meta’s competitors.
I do think the “don't make it a butthole logo” thing was probably something they had top of mind internally. But for me, the discussions were more about looking at the Meta infinity loop logo and wanting the Muse logo to look like it was part of the same universe.
How did you decide to start talking about the work publicly?
I wanted to share it because I like sharing about my work. Within my newsletter group, everybody knows that my husband worked for Meta for ages, so they know that I have an association with the company.
I also wanted to acknowledge that AI is a very sensitive topic for people, but acknowledge it to an audience that understands my relationship to both Meta and AI.
I noticed that you responded to a bunch of the people criticizing you. Why?
Generally, if something happens online where there's a misunderstanding, I've been able to just come at [whoever is posting about me] and say “Hey, I hear you,” in an open and conversational way. I’m not trying to persuade them, I’m trying to say, “I agree with this part, but have you considered this?” That's always kind of worked for me in the past to help de-escalate stuff.
But with this, I made a comment about how hopefully, because of this job, I won't have to carry $50,000 in credit card debt through the holidays for my shop, because I have to do a bunch of inventory purchasing. Then that got taken out of context by someone being like, “This rich girl spends $50,000 on Christmas.” And I was just like, OK, wait, someone will see that and not the original post, and then all of a sudden it spins into this story about me being like a kajillionaire sitting on like a pile of emeralds, yelling at poor suffering artists, which is the opposite of my whole vibe.
How did it feel to you, when all this was happening?
The first day when I was like replying to people, I was not torn up about it at all, because I was like, “Oh, these people just don't understand that I'm a small-business owner, that I want to pay my employees. This helps me offer a health plan to like one of my employees. This is good!” And also, this company isn’t hiring me to use AI, I didn’t use AI at all in the process. Isn't this ultimately the future that we want? Large companies hiring independent artists to do things?
But then, as it started to escalate, it just blew up way bigger than I could have ever anticipated. It wasn't just a handful of people talking about it online. It felt like the entirety of Threads, you know? One of the things I have the hardest time with is feeling really misunderstood. I love teaching, but I'm not a guru that's making a predatory $1,500 course or whatever. I tend to charge $35 for a five-hour workshop.
I’m very intentional about things, and I don't just flippantly say yes to things that I obviously feel conflicted about, but I'm also like, this didn't feel like one of those conflicts just because they were paying me as an artist, and I wasn't using AI at all, you know?
So I felt deeply sad. I felt like I had been hit by a truck. For the two days following it, I sat in my bed and sobbed. It just made me feel so awful, like everything I have done up to this point, all the good decisions I tried to make, the free resources I've put out, have been for nothing.
Did it make you regret taking the job?
Not exactly. There was one camp of people who were like, “Of course, do the work if you need to, but just don't talk about it.” But I felt like I was doing a good thing for artists by commending a company that is hiring artists instead of making generative work.
Where do you think the reaction comes from, for designers in particular? Is it fear?
I mean, the fear is real. There’s real fears about AI's impact on commercial art. My husband and I really got into it at one point, because he was working on AI and really excited about it, and I was vehemently anti-AI. Eventually I started seeing the infrastructure, low-level data-processing side of it and how useful it is for things outside of creativity. Then I was like, OK, well, there are silver linings to using this thing. I think that softened the edges for me. My husband also came around to AI’s impact on commercial art, which helped.
Most of the folks in AI are like, “AI helps creativity because it makes human-made things more valuable!” Maybe in fine art, but that's not how commercial art works. Of course, there’s anti-AI purists, and their whole thing is that AI is built on theft, which is true. I think I’m going to benefit from the Anthropic settlement, because they've definitely scraped my books.
I don't use AI for generative art or anything like that. I just use it for admin and for help with coding and web building. But anytime that AI takes the place of a person or does the heavy lifting on stuff that requires human creativity, that's when it becomes problematic.

The American Hospital Association is once again suing the Trump administration over its plan to test revamping a federal drug discount program into one that provides after-the-fact rebates instead of upfront discounts for certain drugs.
It’s the second time the powerful hospital lobbying group has sued over such a plan. The first time, in 2025, a judge agreed to temporarily halt a more limited version from taking effect, and the Health and Human Services Department voluntarily withdrew the plan after losing on appeal. In February, the agency announced an expanded version, set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027, that would target 25 of the costliest, most widely used drugs covered under Medicare. The original plan included 10 drugs.
The AHA’s argument is largely the same as in the first case: the government failed to accurately account for the costs hospitals would incur by having to pay market prices for drugs and then apply for rebates. The lawsuit says that the Health Resources and Services Administration, the HHS division that administers 340B, received more than 2,400 comments on the rebate model’s second iteration, including hospitals describing in “granular detail the catastrophic impact” it would have.

AdBlock360 is a system-wide ad blocker for Windows 10 and 11 that blocks ads in browsers, YouTube, Spotify, and other apps. It also blocks trackers and supports custom filters and whitelisting. A free version is available, but app-level blocking requires premium. It does not support ARM-based Windows devices.
Ads are very common across apps and websites. Most apps and websites use a freemium business model, which has ads in the free version. This model is proven and benefits both the creator and the consumer. But a few apps cross the line and make the whole experience cluttered by aggressively pushing ads.
This is where an ad blocker can come in handy. It blocks intrusive ads on any web page or app, making the whole experience a lot cleaner and clutter-free.
Ad blockers come in many forms. The most popular ones are ad-block extensions used in browsers, but because of the changes in Google Chrome Manifest Version 3, which restrict access to some browser features for ad-blocker extensions.
Another common way of blocking ads is using an ad-blocker DNS. I personally use it on my mobile devices.
Finally, if you want to get rid of ads throughout the system, the easiest way is by installing an app.
If you use Windows, AdBlock360 for Windows can come in handy. It offers a complete solution to block all types of ads on your Windows device, whether they are in a browser or system-level apps, even ads on YouTube and Spotify, without requiring premium subscriptions. AdBlock360 blocks most ads on your Windows device. I have been using AdBlock360 for the past few days, and here are the five features that stood out during my usage.
Table of Contents
AdBlock360 for Windows: 5 Features That Make It Worth Using
Block Ads Across Browsers and Windows Apps
One of the biggest advantages of using AdBlock360 is that it runs natively on Windows and blocks ads at the system level. It eliminates the need to install ad blockers for your browser separately. It uses a kernel-mode Windows Filtering Platform driver for system-wide network filtering. Because of this, it won’t have any restrictions, unlike the ones recently raised due to Chromium changes. So it works even if your browser is updated to the latest Manifest V3.
You also don’t need to install separate ad-block extensions for your browser. One ad blocker is enough for blocking all system-level ads on your Windows laptop, including ads from browsers and even on YouTube, Spotify, or any third-party or native apps that consist of ads.
Block YouTube and Spotify Ads Using AdBlock360
Not just the browser, AdBlock360 also blocks ads on YouTube, including the watch page and pre-roll ads that appear before the video. If you upgrade to the AdBlock360 premium version, it also skips the sponsor segments in a video. Not just that, this ad blocker also works for other popular platforms, including Spotify, where ads in the free version can be annoying. AdBlock360 works natively on Windows, so it can work on any app that’s installed on your Windows device.
Protect Your Privacy From Trackers and Fingerprinting
Some websites and apps aggressively track your background to serve you relevant ads. This is why, when you search on any e-commerce platform, you immediately see ads related to the product you searched for.
AdBlock360 says it blocks ad trackers at the network level; ad providers inside browsers or platforms won’t be able to fetch your ad profile data from advertising and other analytics or tracking servers to serve you ads.
This way, not only the ads but also the tracking and the data collected by these trackers will be blocked.
Choose What to Block With Custom Filters
While AdBlock360 is a convenient way to block ads across Windows, sometimes it may not block certain ads that use a different architecture or newer techniques to bypass Ad blockers, or ads on your own websites or the sites you want to support and whitelist.
AdBlock360 also offers you the option to set custom filters, so you will have complete control over which types of ads to block. We can also whitelist certain apps and websites to show you ads.
Works on Low-End PCs and Offers a Free Version
Apps like ad blocker applications generally don’t require advanced PC configurations, so it is the same for AdBlock360.
It works on both Windows 10 and Windows 11. It requires just 2 GB of RAM (although 4 GB is recommended) and only 200 MB of free space.
Low-spec Windows devices are most affected because of the ads. Sometimes they can make constant requests to the backend, which can bring a laggy experience if you have installed any apps that display ads on your Windows PC. AdBlock360 works in the background and requires a minimum amount of processing power, which can be an advantage if you want to block ads completely on your low-end Windows devices.
Not everything about AdBlock360 is bells and whistles; there are a few notable limitations to the app. First, the app is limited to Windows. If you bought a premium version, you can only use it on Windows. If you use other devices like a mobile phone, you won’t benefit from the premium subscription you bought for your Windows device.
Moreover, the AdBlock360 app is not available for ARM-based Windows laptops.
I tried to install the app on my Snapdragon X2 Elite-powered ASUS ProArt PZ14, but it showed an error stating “ARM64 devices are not compatible,” which you can see in the image below.
So, although the app is exclusive to Windows, it still requires an x86-compatible device to run this ad blocker on your Windows device.
The HTTPS filtering requires installing a root certificate. Although the process is easy, it can be limited if you have advanced security settings enabled on your Windows device.
You also require a premium version to block ads inside apps and to skip sponsored content on YouTube.
Finally, the app can also be overkill if you just want to block ads on your web browser.
A Simple Way to Block Ads Across Windows
Running ad blockers natively is extremely important today, especially at a time when popular browsers are limiting ad-blocking extensions and websites, and apps are aggressively putting more ads on their sites.
AdBlock360 is a nice solution to block different types of ads. It blocks ads in your browsers, as well as ads from native apps in the premium version, including YouTube ads and ads on third-party apps like Spotify.
With just one subscription, you get a clutter-free experience. AdBlock360 also comes with a free version, so you can try AdBlock360 out right now on your Windows device and check if it works for you.

Veteran actress Saira Banu paid tribute to Nana Patekar following his demise, sharing a heartwarming anecdote about the late actor and her husband, the legendary Dilip Kumar. In a social media post, she recalled an incident from the time Patekar received the Best Actor award for Krantiveer, highlighting a thoughtful gesture by Dilip Kumar that left a lasting impression on the actor.
Saira Banu remembers Nana Patekar with heartwarming anecdote about Dilip Kumar after his best actor win for Krantiveer
Recounting the memory, Saira Banu wrote, "Today, my thoughts go back to an incident that Nana ji once shared about Dilip Sahib, a memory that has stayed with me for the profound humanity it holds. After Nana ji received the Best Actor award for Krantiveer, Dilip Sahib invited him to our home in Pali Hill. As fate would have it, it began to rain heavily on his way to meet Sahib, and by the time he arrived, he was completely drenched.”
She went on to describe how Dilip Kumar responded when Patekar arrived at their home soaked in the rain. Rather than making a fuss, the veteran actor brought him a towel and a fresh shirt so he could dry himself and change.
“When Dilip Sahib saw him standing there, soaking wet, he did not make a fuss or utter a word. He simply went inside, brought a towel, gently dried Nana ji’s head, and then brought him a fresh shirt to change into. Just imagine that moment. Here was Dilip Sahib, an institution in himself, a legend whose very presence was an honour, expressing his affection not through grand words or gestures, but through the simplest, most beautiful act of kindness. Nana ji later said something that touched my heart deeply: “Isse bada kya award chahiye ek insaan ko?” And truly, what greater award can life give you than the love, warmth, and respect of someone you have admired so deeply? May he be remembered not only for the extraordinary characters he brought to life, but also for the memories, emotions, and impressions he leaves behind. Rest in peace, Nana ji. You will be deeply missed."
The anecdote offers a glimpse into Patekar’s admiration for Dilip Kumar and the personal memories that stayed with him beyond his professional achievements. Saira Banu’s tribute also reflected on the late actor’s legacy, remembering him for both his performances and the impressions he left on those who knew him.
View this post on Instagram
Nana Patekar, a recipient of the Padma Shri, passed away on October 8, 2026, at the age of 75. According to the details shared about his demise, the veteran actor suffered a cardiac arrest at his residence in Dona Paula, Goa, and was taken to Manipal Hospital, where attempts to revive him were unsuccessful. His son, Malhar Patekar, confirmed the news.
Known for his acclaimed work across Hindi and Marathi cinema, Patekar earned widespread recognition for performances in films including Krantiveer. His contribution to Indian cinema spanned decades, with roles that showcased his range across intense dramas and mainstream films.
Saira Banu, one of Hindi cinema’s prominent actresses of the 1960s and 1970s, is known for films such as Junglee, Padosan and Victoria No. 203. Through her tribute, she remembered Patekar with affection, sharing a story that underscored the enduring value of kindness and respect among artistes.

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

She turned her kids’ old clothes into keepsakes – now it’s a thriving home business
Siti Nur’ain Awari turned them into bears and quilts her children could keep. That idea grew into Patchwork Handmade Keepsakes, where the mum of four has transformed other kids' clothes, from baby onesies to school uniforms, into treasured mementos.
Siti Nur’ain Awari is that mum who keeps everything – her baby’s first onesie, the pyjamas her children wore as she cuddled them to sleep, their preschool uniforms.
“I know I will never throw these clothes away,” said the stay-at-home mum of four children aged 4, 8, 10 and 12.
But rather than leaving them forgotten and collecting dust in her storeroom, the 37-year-old sat down one day and cut these beloved pieces up. Her children were right beside her when she did so.
“I told them: This is your baju (Malay for clothing) when you came back from the hospital, these were your favourite army-print clothes that grandma bought, this is your K2 graduation outfit,” she told CNA Women.
For her first three children, she transformed the fabric pieces into stuffed bears. For her youngest, she made a quilt. These became her kids’ most treasured possessions.
One thing she did not expect was for it to grow into a thriving home business. At Patchwork Handmade Keepsakes, Nur’ain has since transformed thousands of pre-loved baby and children’s clothes into stuffed animals and quilts for other families. Prices start from S$85 for a bear and from $120 for a quilt.
A PATCHWORK OF MEMORIES
The idea actually came from Nur’ain’s cousin.
In early 2024, inspired by something she saw online, this cousin sent Nur’ain a bag containing 30 pieces of her daughter’s baby and toddler clothes, featuring the prettiest floral prints and cutest cartoons. She asked Nur’ain to sew a quilt with them.
Nur’ain, who has been sewing and altering her own clothes since she was a teenager, spent months researching and practising before she felt confident enough to cut up her niece’s preloved baby onesies.
Each piece of clothing is a precious and irreplaceable memento. “You cannot mess it up,” Nur’ain told CNA Women.
Making a quilt is more technically complex than most imagine, she added.
“A quilt has three layers – the top layer, middle layer and backing fabric. It is quite thick. You need to know what type of thread to use, and how to adjust the sewing machine so it turns out well,” she explained.
Since her quilts are made up of square pieces of fabric, Nur’ain has to make precise measurements and align the squares properly. This becomes more complex if some fabrics are stretchier and others stiffer, she said.
It also requires some skill to piece the different fabrics in such a way that they complement one another, she added.
In May 2024, Nur’ain completed her first quilt for her cousin, and posted a picture of it on Instagram, generating some interest from friends. She decided to polish her skills by making two more trial quilts – one with her father’s and brother’s preloved clothes, and one with her youngest son’s baby clothes.
She posted pictures of these on Instagram and an Etsy shop, which she has since closed. A month later, she received her first order of two baby quilts.
WHEN A TOY BECOMES A KEEPSAKE
After quilts came turning pre-loved clothing into stuffed bears. After watching YouTube videos, she made a bear with her eldest son’s clothes that same month and posted a picture of it online. A few weeks later, four bear orders followed.
Encouraged, Nur’ain continued learning how to make different stuffed animals. She now offers eight, including rabbits, lions, horses and rhinoceroses.
These caught the eye of her own kids and they asked for their own. The doting mother happily obliged. Since her three older children graduated from the same preschool, she decided to make a bear with their old school uniforms.
“Preschool days are special. It is their first time going to school, their first time wearing a school uniform, and they have their first teacher… There are so many firsts,” she reflected.
Cutting up the uniforms was definitely bittersweet, she said. “I was the one who buttoned up these uniforms for them every day, you know?”
These school bears unexpectedly became her best-sellers, especially for graduation ceremonies and PSLE results day. With their popularity, Nur’ain now frequently receives more orders than she can fulfil and caps her monthly workload at 25 orders, working around her mummy duties and when her kids are asleep.
Nur’ain, who worked in an administrative role until she got laid off in 2020 during the pandemic, said that her home business now earns her almost as much as her former job.
MAKING NEW MEMORIES WITH OLD CLOTHES
One of her most difficult jobs arrived in three big bags two years ago. In them were more than 200 pieces of baby, toddler and children’s clothes tracing the life of someone’s beloved child.
The child’s mother requested for three large quilts – one for her, one for the father and one for the child, who was around seven then and unwell, Nur’ain said.
“I didn’t ask a lot because I wanted to respect their privacy, but it felt like it might be a serious illness,” she shared.
“When I first received the clothes, I couldn’t touch them for a week. It was quite hard for me to start cutting up the clothes. As a mother myself, I could imagine how painful it would be for the parents,” she said.
“When I first started this keepsake business, I thought I’d just be making things with cute baby clothes. I did not expect to feel these kinds of emotions,” Nur’ain added.
The parent returned a second time in December 2025 to make another quilt with the remaining clothes as a Christmas gift for the child’s grandmother in the United Kingdom, she said.
Nur’ain also recalled another job where a parent requested a quilt made from the clothes of 22 preschoolers. It was for a beloved teacher who was unwell, and the class hoped that she could use the quilt while undergoing treatment and feel comforted by their love and support.
“Clothes carry not just memories, but emotions,” Nur’ain said. They belong to someone’s special son or daughter – a beloved child who is deeply cherished, she reflected.
This understanding has given the mumpreneur a deeper appreciation for upcycling these treasured pieces.
“Instead of throwing them away or letting them get dirty in the cupboard, why not make them into a new memory?” she said.

To strengthen campus mental health support and facilitate timely referrals for students in distress, NIMHANS-Bengaluru will launch an online certificate course for Student Wellbeing Ambassadors in higher education institutions.
To be launched on the occasion of World Mental Health Day on October 10, the self-paced course will be offered through the NIMHANS Digital Academy by the institute’s Department of Clinical Psychology. The first batch will accommodate up to 350 participants, with applications open until October 30. Classes are scheduled to begin in November.
To be nominated by institutions
The course is open to faculty members from any discipline, wardens, deans, and student welfare officers who have at least three years of service remaining, and are nominated by their institutions.
Participants will learn to recognise signs of student distress, respond supportively, reduce stigma around mental health, and encourage students to seek appropriate help. The programme is also intended to strengthen suicide-risk reduction efforts.
The three-month course will involve 12 to 15 hours of learning through videos, quizzes, assignments, reflective exercises, and reading materials.
NIMHANS clarified that the course is not professional training in counselling, psychology, or psychotherapy. Instead, it will help faculty understand the role and limits of a well-being ambassador, and work within existing student support and crisis-response systems.
The initiative is among the steps towards implementing Karnataka’s student mental health policy for higher education. NIMHANS is also developing a follow-up programme to help trained faculty apply the learning in their institutions.
Course details and online application forms are available on the NIMHANS website and the NIMHANS Digital Academy website under Course Announcements.

How to reset your Samsung TV
If your Frame or other Samsung TV is acting up, give these resets a try,
Resetting devices is, oddly enough, an essential skill in the modern tech landscape. Aside from the fact that selling or trading devices like smartphones and laptops is incredibly common, it's an effective troubleshooting technique. Factory resets force a device to revert to its out-of-the-box state, including options, processes and installed apps. It can be a royal pain to get things back the way you like — but it's better than dealing with crashes or broken features.
There are few reasons to reset a smart TV, including Samsung models, yet things do sometimes go haywire. A favorite streaming app might repeatedly freeze no matter how many times you reinstall it, or the OS might develop problems like video glitches. There's no guarantee that a reset will come to the rescue, but it's a good troubleshooting step.
There's not much to performing one on a Samsung TV. Just be sure to try simpler tactics first, some of which we'll go over later. Remember, once you've triggered a factory reset, there's no going back. On top of reconfiguring picture and sound preferences, you'll be redownloading apps and OS updates.
All you need to know about factory resetting your Samsung TV
Before initiating a factory reset, be sure you have any PIN codes and passwords written down somewhere, including the logins for streaming apps and your Wi-Fi router. Once the reset is complete, you'll need these to get back to watching anything. Unless, perhaps, you're content with over-the-air TV, Blu-ray or a connected game console or PC. Even then, you may want to get back online briefly to install updates for Tizen, Samsung's OS.
Once you're sure you want to go ahead, follow these steps:
1. From the home screen, select Settings.
2. Click All Settings.
3. Choose General & Privacy.
4. At the very bottom of the menu, click Reset.
5. You'll need to enter a PIN, even if you haven't created one. If you haven't chosen a custom PIN, enter 0000.
6. Select OK. Your TV should begin the reset process a moment later.
Periodically, Samsung updates Tizen in a way that relabels certain buttons and menus. As a rule, though, the process shouldn't vary much from generation to generation. Just look for similar-sounding labels, and explore a bit if you have to.
If you're apprehensive about going nuclear, there are some soft resets you can try first. For minor or one-off glitches, these may be all you need. Some are specific to particular problems, though, as you'll see.
The soft reset options for Samsung TVs
To simply reboot your TV, unplug it for 30 seconds or hold the power button on the remote for five seconds. Your TV will briefly turn off, then pop back on with the Samsung logo. A reboot might not seem very dramatic, but this does clear out your TV's RAM and system cache. It also restarts background processes, which can sometimes glitch out.
You might, in rare cases, benefit from resetting the Smart Hub without performing a full factory reset. This reverts the Hub's options to defaults and wipes associated apps and account info. You'll have to redownload apps and log in again. To reset the Hub, follow these steps:
1. Go to Settings > All Settings.
2. Click Support.
3. Choose Device Care, then Self Diagnosis.
4. Click Reset Smart Hub.
5. Enter your PIN. If you didn't choose one, enter 0000.
Lastly, you might try resetting network settings if you're specifically dealing with connection issues. Chances are the problem lies with your router or service provider, so troubleshoot those first. It can't hurt to reconnect with a fresh start, however, as long as you have your router's login info handy. Here's the process:
1. Head to Settings > All Settings.
2. Click Connections, then Network.
3. Choose Reset Network. To confirm, click Reset.
4. Return to Network Settings to enter your router's SSID and password.
You might understand now why you'd want to jump straight to a factory reset if a reboot doesn't work. If an issue is hard to diagnose, a total reset can save you the hassle of resetting components one by one. There's also nothing to be lost unless you simply can't remember a critical login.

An Oct. 2 video shows Trump fielding reporters' questions outside the White House. Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy asked, "What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?" (James, New York's attorney general, previously led a civil fraud case against Trump.) Trump thrice called James corrupt, saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes and alleged that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
A rumor circulated online in early October that U.S. President Donald Trump said he feels "badly" for the seven current or former male Cornell University students whom a female former student accused of rape.
Trump purportedly made the remarks while answering a question about New York Attorney General Letitia James' appointment as a special prosecutor to investigate the case.
Snopes readers asked about this claim via email, with one person inquiring, "I saw something that says Donald Trump said he feels bad for the 'Cornell 7,' but can't find reputable sources. True??"
In sum, people correctly attributed this statement to Trump. A C-SPAN video shows Trump standing outside the White House on Oct. 2 and responding directly to a reporter's question about the Cornell case, thrice calling James corrupt and saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes, alleging that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
James previously sued Trump and his associates in a civil fraud case beginning in 2022, leading to Trump repeatedly targeting her on social media.
In an emailed response, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis referred us to Trump's own comments, adding that the White House believes James has weaponized the justice system to unjustly target the president.
Digging into the rumor
The Cornell accuser, identified in court documents only as Jane Doe, claims the seven men sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. She filed a lawsuit against the seven men, the university, the fraternity and others, in mid-September.
On Sept. 28, Tompkins County, New York, prosecutors announced they were reopening the criminal investigation, citing a "discrepancy" between Doe's original statement and the allegations in the lawsuit.
Prior to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case on Oct. 1, James posted a statement of compassion for Doe on her official social media accounts, writing, "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."
In an example of the claim from Oct. 2, a Facebook post (archived) displayed a meme reading, "This is disgusting: Trump just said he 'feels badly' for the people accused in the Cornell rape case because Letitia James is now overseeing the investigation. Not one word for the victim."
(Really American via Facebook)
Other users shared the rumor about Trump's remarks on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Some posts didn't mention James but did include a video showing a reporter's question about James and Trump's answer. Examples of those posts appeared on Bluesky (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
The remarks occurred when Trump spoke to a group of reporters outside the White House. Videos show Fox News' Peter Doocy asking Trump about Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor:
DOOCY: What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?
TRUMP: Letitia James is a corrupt person. She's totally corrupt and I can't imagine it. And, I feel badly for whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake. But Letitia James is a corrupt person.
C-SPAN posted remarks on social media. (Readers can also watch the full press gaggle on YouTube, with the pertinent moment beginning at 6:24.)
Trump has made other remarks about the Cornell case. During a similar gathering of reporters on Oct. 1, a video shows an unidentified reporter asking Trump, "Mr. President, do you think that Cornell University has done enough to investigate the alleged rape on campus?" Trump answered, "Well, I don't know that much about it but Cornell is a fine school, and I'm sure they'll do what's right." (Readers can watch that full gaggle on YouTube, with the Cornell question occurring at 11:43.)
Trump has also posted about the case on Truth Social (archived), labeling it "the highly controversial Cornell University rape case" and questioning why Hochul would appoint James.
For further reading, we previously reported Trump authentically expressed well wishes to Ghislaine Maxwell, the close associate of deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, prior to her conviction on federal sex-trafficking charges.

- Reports spread in early October 2026 that a Russian lab worker may have died of the pneumonic plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
- The pneumonic plague "has a nearly 100% case-fatality rate when untreated," according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The illness requires antibiotic treatment that should start as soon as the plague is suspected, before test results, per the CDC.
- The rumor stems from news media reports saying Russia announced that a 28-year-old lab worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia had died of an "unknown" infection, and that nearly 200 people have been isolated as a result. The reports cite Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian public agency responsible for "federal state sanitary and epidemiological supervision," according to the Russian government.
- Snopes could not reach the website of Rospotrebnadzor and does not have access to primary sources, therefore we cannot confirm the details of the lab worker's death. Russian news agency Interfax reported the Russian government as saying she had died of a pneumonia pathogen of "unknown etiology," meaning its origin is not clear.
- On Oct. 4, Interfax also reported Rospotrebnadzor as saying, "based on the results of extensive testing, no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities were detected in the patient's sample." If true, this would suggest the lab worker did not die of pneumonic plague.
- 
A U.S. Department of State spokesperson said via email that the department is aware of the reports and is "monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners."
- 
Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have also reached out to the CDC and the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety of the European Union Commission. We are waiting for responses.
In early October 2026, a rumor spread that a worker at a Russian lab that studies Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes the plague, had died of the pneumonic plague.
Some social media users said the lab worker's death resulted from an accident at the lab. One X post reads, in part, "A lab worker in Russia has died from pneumonic plague."
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers emailed us asking for details about the story.
The claim stems from various news reports about a 28-year-old woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia. Around 200 people have reportedly been isolated as a precautionary measure. The articles cited Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian public agency responsible for "federal state sanitary and epidemiological supervision," according to the Russian government.
In short, it has not been possible to independently verify the rumor without access to primary sources or confirmation from Russian authorities. Therefore, this claim is unrated. We will update this article if we learn more.
Russian authorities reportedly implement containment measures
Snopes could not reach the website of Rospotrebnadzor, therefore we could not confirm the details of the lab worker's death. On Oct. 4, Russian news agency Interfax reported that the Russian government said she had died of a pneumonia pathogen of "unknown etiology," meaning its origin is not clear.
The same report adds that Rospotrebnadzor said no microorganisms associated with the individual's professional work were detected in that person's samples following "extensive testing." If true, it would suggest the lab worker did not die of pneumonic plague.
Local authorities have reportedly implemented preventative measures. Interfax cites the Rospotrebnadzor health agency as saying:
Due to the patient's professional activities, upon receiving information, a comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures was immediately and fully implemented in accordance with sanitary legislation. This included identifying the widest possible circle of people who had been in contact with the patient, inpatient medical observation, and daily laboratory testing. The results revealed two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection. No other infectious agents were detected.
View from U.S. Department of State
"We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia," a U.S. Department of State spokesperson said via email. "We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners."
We contacted the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety of the European Union Commission requesting updates on the situation. We will update this report if we receive responses.
There are three main types of plague: bubonic plague, which infects lymph nodes; septicemic plague, which infects the blood; and pneumonic plague, which infects the lungs. The bubonic and septicemic plagues are most commonly transmitted via flea bites and handling infected animals, while the pneumonic plague spreads through the air via infected droplets.
The pneumonic plague "has a nearly 100% case-fatality rate when untreated," according to the CDC. The illness requires antibiotic treatment that should start as soon as the plague is suspected, even before test results, per the U.S. health agency.
"Plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early," the State Department spokesperson said via email. "Cases occur naturally in many parts of the world."
