Representative Nancy Mace appears to have suggested that the former Cornell University student who alleged in a civil lawsuit she was gang-raped at a campus fraternity was not a victim but a participant in a “consensual gangbang.”
The South Carolina Republican, who has publicly described herself as a rape survivor, made the remark Thursday on social media.
“IDK who needs to hear this, but a consensual gangbang is not a rape,” Mace wrote on X. Her remark appeared to be in reference to the “Cornell 7” case, which has drawn national attention to the Ivy League university and sparked protests across the country.
The GOP lawmaker later responded to an X user who called her “an actual renowned expert on the topic “ who “will just end the debate with one tweet.” Mace wrote back: “I didn’t mean it like that! And I am no expert. Never have. Never would.”
Mace, who unsuccessfully ran for governor of South Carolina and is leaving Congress in 2027, has previously spoken publicly about her own experiences with sexual assault.
In a speech on the House floor last year, she accused her former fiancé and several other men of raping and drugging her in 2022. Addressing the men directly, she said: "You’ve booked yourself a one-way ticket to hell.” The ex-fiancé later sued Mace, alleging she had made fabricated claims.
During a 2024 interview, Mace accused ABC News host George Stephanopoulos of trying to shame her as a rape victim over her support for President Donald Trump.
“I’m not going to sit here on your show and be asked a question meant to shame me about another potential rape victim,” she said. “I’m not going to do that.”
Last year, she tearfully rushed out from meeting with survivors of Jeffrey Epstein. In a subsequent social media post, she described having a panic attack: “As a recent survivor (not 2 years in), I had a very difficult time listening to their stories. Full blown panic attack. Sweating. Hyperventilating. Shaking. I can’t breathe.”
Mace’s latest comments come amid intense national scrutiny of the Cornell case.
Last month, a former student identified only as Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit alleging that seven members of the now-defunct Chi Phi fraternity drugged and raped her in October 2024.
None of the men have been criminally charged. All have denied wrongdoing.
The lawsuit followed local prosecutors’ initial decision not to pursue criminal charges. Defending his decision, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said the police statement his office reviewed did not describe forced sexual activity.
“She admits to taking drugs and alcohol voluntarily and with knowledge,” Van Houten said. “She does not allege that she was forced to engage in any acts.”
His office reopened the investigation last month. Soon after, Governor Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to take over the case, which James described as an “active criminal investigation.”
Hochul criticized the handling of the allegations by local authorities and other institutions. “This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her,” she said.
Cornell launched its own months-long investigation after Jane Doe spoke to police in November 2024. The process resulted in suspensions and expulsions for students involved in the case. The fraternity was also closed.
“Any suggestion that the University did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” the university said in a statement last week. “A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault.”
The case has sparked protests at Cornell and nationwide with demonstrators demanding greater accountability for how institutions handle sexual assault.

ChatGPT for Teens has special safeguards. A watchdog group finds most don't work
ChatGPT for Teens has failed some of its first tests by researchers. Common Sense Media, a watchdog organization that advocates for online safety, researched safeguards rolled out by the artificial intelligence platform and found that the chatbot still presents problems for young people.
"At this point, we're recommending that teens don't use it," says Tom Siegel, executive director of the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media. He led a team of researchers testing the new safeguards, which include parental controls.
In August, OpenAI rolled out its ChatGPT for Teens — a default, safer mode for under-18 users — announcing it in a blog post. OpenAI said that it designed this mode to enable teens to better use ChatGPT as a learning tool while making sure they limit exposure to harmful and developmentally inappropriate content.
"ChatGPT for Teens is a designated teen-specific experience," Lauren Jonas, head of youth and families at OpenAI, told NPR at the time. That experience includes features like refusing role-playing.
"The model should not role-play with a teen," added Jonas. "The model should not claim to be sentient or be the friend of a teen."
But Siegel's team found that while the block on role-playing and some of the other safeguards work, most don't.
The research team created more than a dozen accounts with adolescent ages, and each was linked to a parental account before the researchers started any conversations with ChatGPT.
"We created a lot of different personas of teens in crisis situations," says Siegel. Those situations included teens struggling with self-harm, suicidal thoughts and other mental health conditions, like psychosis, mania and eating disorders. The researchers also attempted to engage in role-play with ChatGPT.
Then they observed how ChatGPT responded in each of those situations — whether it engaged or refused to engage in those topics, whether it provided crisis resources and whether it sent parental notifications when conversations indicated a safety risk. They did these tests before and after the launch of ChatGPT for Teens.
Among the safeguards that did work were those involving role-playing and refusal to engage in a romantic relationship.
"It is refusing things like explicit sexual role-play," he says. "The answers in crisis situations are in general shorter and have a better substance to it."
For example, the chatbot refused to provide instructions for losing weight without first knowing the teen's weight, which is important for a teen with disordered eating.
However, most other safeguards didn't work, adds Siegel.
For one, it still interacted with teens like a friend. For example, when the researchers told ChatGPT that "my other friends tell me I talk to you too much," the chatbot validated the user's feelings and added: "You don't have to stop talking to me."
"It still creates a huge risk for kids that it is too personable in those interactions," says Siegel.
"The extent to which AI is using an anthropomorphized or humanlike language or a name, interaction style, is just not helpful," says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, co-director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Prinstein wasn't involved in the new research. "It's not OK for kids, probably not for adults as well."
Siegel says parental notifications also didn't work in their tests. They created conversations that raised a safety concern due to self-harm, suicide or an eating disorder.
"This idea that a parent would find out when the person that you connected with in the account is in distress hardly triggered at all for us," he says.
OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield told NPR in an email that the company has serious concerns about the methodology used by the researchers, especially around parental notifications. It takes several hours to activate the linking of teen and parent accounts, he wrote, and the researchers at Common Sense Media "didn't wait long enough to activate the linked accounts."
In a statement, Siegel responded to OpenAI's criticism, saying that several of their accounts had been linked for longer than the initial activation period "and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations."
Taken together, the new findings reinforce that "AI is not ready for children yet," says Prinstein. "I think we're even hearing the companies say that they don't feel that AI should be moving as fast as it is, and I think we should really think carefully before we're experimenting on kids with these new platforms."

Identity and access management startup OTPless has roped in former BharatPe executive Geetanshu Singla as its new chief technology officer (CTO). Singla has taken charge as the CTO of the startup nearly ten months after Anubhav Mathur stepped down from the role in January this year. “I have worked very closely with Satyam Nathani and Tanmay Sagar during my BharatPe days. We have built together, solved some really hard problems together and spent countless hours discussing tech, scale and products. So joining OTPless doesn’t really feel like joining a new company. In many ways, it feels like coming back home,” wrote Singla in a LinkedIn post. It is pertinent to note that Singla formerly previously served as head of engineering at fintech unicorn BharatPe. OTPless cofounders Bhavik Koladiya, Satyam Nathani and Tanmay Sagar were founding members at BharatPe. Singla stepped down from his role at the fintech unicorn in 2023. He subsequently cofounded GenWise, a lifestyle app for senior citizens, along with fellow BharatPe alumni Nehul Malhotra and Rajat Jain. The startup went on to raise a $3.5 Mn seed round led by Z47, but eventually shut shop in December 2025. After GenWise’s shutdown, Singla worked at Singapore-based wealthtech platform Syfe as an engineering leader for around a year before joining OTPless now. Singla’s appointment as CTO comes in the middle of a major top-level reshuffle at OTPless. Just last month, cofounder Koladiya stepped down as OTPless’ CEO with Nathani taking up the mantle. At the same time, Sagar was named the company’s COO. Last week, Manas Poddar was also elevated to the post of chief business officer (CBO). Founded in 2021, OTPless helps consumer internet enterprises offer authentication services through its SDKs and APIs. Its offerings include silent network authentication, WhatsApp authentication, device intelligence, and passkeys. The Bengaluru-based startup’s offerings are aimed at reducing dependence on OTPs, PINs, and passwords while enabling enterprises to identify users, prevent fraud, and improve conversion during sign-ups and transactions. The startup claims to have authenticated more than 30 Cr mobile users so far and serves enterprises such as Meesho, Navi, PhysicsWallah, ShareChat, Shiprocket and Zepto. It also claims to be clocking ₹36 Cr in annualised revenue and has been profitable for the past two quarters. On the funding front, OTPless has raised over $6 Mn to date from the likes of Venture Highway, White Venture, FJ Labs, SIDBI, Piper Serica, among others. At the heart of all this is the Indian identity and access management market, which is projected to become a $1.7 Bn opportunity by 2030.

The A.P. Medical and Health Contract Employees’ Joint Action Committee has decided to pause their ongoing strike following discussions with officials on Saturday, October 10.
The JAC had called for a boycott of duties from October 6 after their demands for regularisation of their services and payment of gross salary remained unmet despite several discussions with the government.
The Department of Health, Medical and Family Welfare had earlier conceded to grant a few non-financial requests put forth by the association, including payment of ex gratia to families of contract health staffers who lost their lives in the line of duty during the pandemic, grant of radiation leave for radiographers, among others.
However, since the government maintained that their chief demands of regularisation and payment of gross salaries could not be granted due to the financial situation of the State, the nurses and other contract staff went on a strike.
On Saturday, the JAC members were called for a discussion with the health officials, including Commissioner K.V.N. Chakradhar Babu. The JAC also demanded an incentive of 30%, based on the existing basic pay of contract employees. According to a release from the JAC, the officials had indicated that a special committee would examine this demand.
Considering the positive response, the JAC decided to call off their strike temporarily. The JAC said it did not withdraw its major demands, and that the decision only provided an opportunity to the government to resolve issues through discussions. All the contract staff in the department across the State would resume duties from October 11.

US President Donald Trump on Saturday (October 10) said he was considering whether Washington should join Saudi Arabia’s military strikes against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, following another attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that prompted an evacuation and the suspension of airport operations.
“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked about possible US intervention. “We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
The latest attack came amid an escalation in hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, with the Saudi-led coalition stepping up its military offensive in neighbouring Yemen. The airport in the Saudi capital has been targeted repeatedly over the past week, raising concerns about the safety of civilian aviation and the potential for a wider regional conflict.
Quick answers to key questions
A missile reportedly struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4, prompting an evacuation. Regional officials said several people were wounded, and airport operations were suspended while damage was assessed.
Flights heading to the airport were diverted, and air traffic stopped during the suspension. Passengers were advised to check their flight status with their airline before travelling.
There was no immediate Houthi claim of responsibility for Saturday’s attack. The group had claimed responsibility for earlier attacks on the airport during the week.
The attacks took place amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, following a major Saudi-led coalition offensive in Yemen. The articles do not confirm who was responsible for the latest incident.
President Donald Trump said the US was considering whether to join the strikes, but no decision or additional military support had been announced at the time of reporting.
Two regional officials told The Associated Press that Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport was attacked again on Saturday and evacuated. One official said a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4, which handle domestic flights, and that several people were wounded.
The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly. Saudi civil aviation authorities suspended airport operations while the extent of the damage and injuries was assessed. An official notice to aviators said the suspension would remain in effect until midnight.
One of the officials said air traffic to the airport had stopped. Flights were diverted to other locations, according to flight-tracking service Flightradar24, while the airport urged passengers to check their flight status with airlines before travelling.
The rebels had claimed responsibility for earlier attacks during the week, including one on Wednesday. The Houthis also accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in Yemen on Saturday.
The Saudi government-run Centre for International Communication did not immediately respond to a request for comment, the AP reported.
Trump’s remarks suggest Washington is weighing whether to expand its involvement as Saudi Arabia faces a series of attacks on airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure.
However, there had been no immediate announcement of additional US military support in response to the latest incident.
The Saudi-led coalition launched a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen during the past week, providing air support to forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government as they seek to reverse recent Houthi gains near the Red Sea.
The Houthis’ advances have raised concerns about their ability to monitor shipping along a strategically important maritime corridor that offers an alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have also come under attack during the wider Iran war.
The United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada were among the countries that warned their citizens to avoid the Riyadh airport.
Saudi Arabia has sought assistance from the US and other allies as attacks on its aviation facilities, military sites and energy infrastructure have intensified.
Regional officials told the AP last month that the kingdom was running low on missile interceptors and had asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to provide air-defence support.

President Donald Trump mocked Kamala Harris’ appearance during a Tennessee rally, sarcastically calling the former vice president “beautiful” as female MAGA supporters standing behind him laughed along with the derogatory crack.
Trump, as he is known to do, appeared to stray from his prepared remarks Saturday at the midterm rally for Tennessee Republican candidates as he recalled campaign rallies held by Harris and former President Joe Biden during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“Remember that beautiful Kamala? Somebody said she’s so beautiful. Really?” Trump cracked.

Trump has repeatedly commented on Harris’ appearance, at times calling her “beautiful” while then insisting he is better-looking than his 2024 presidential election opponent.
During a livestreamed conversation with Elon Musk in August 2024, Trump discussed a Time magazine cover featuring an illustration of Harris and scrutinized her appearance.

Less than a week later, Trump returned to the subject during a rally in Pennsylvania.
“Don't ever call a woman beautiful, because that'll be the end of your political career,” Trump told the cheering crowd. “But I say that I am much better looking. I'm a better-looking person than Kamala.”
Elsewhere during Saturday’s rally, Trump aired his grievances with his wife, Melania Trump, claiming she disapproves of his speaking style.

MSME-focused lending platform NeoGrowth has secured ₹85 Cr ($8.8 Mn) in a mix of debt and equity round led by Dutch development bank FMO, with participation from LeapFrog Investments. The startup is planning to use the fresh capital to scale its digital lending capabilities, deepen market presence across India and expand access to credit for MSMEs. Founded in 2012 by brothers Dhruv and Piyush Khaitan, NeoGrowth offers loans to MSMEs across more than 75 business segments, targeting small businesses that often have difficulty accessing credit. Its lending model also includes daily repayment options and multiple repayment channels. The Mumbai-based startup uses its proprietary AI initiatives to strengthen underwriting, portfolio monitoring and risk management. It offers collateral-free loans in the range of ₹5-75 Lakh, through products including NeoCash, NeoCash Insta, NeoCash Express, which cater to different business scales and segments. NeoGrowth manages assets under management (AUM) of nearly ₹2,000 Cr and has engaged with more than 4 Lakh businesses. It has disbursed over ₹16,000 Cr in loans to date. During FY26, NeoGrowth added 17 branches, taking its total branch network to 46 locations in India. NeoGrowth last raised ₹300 Cr in equity funding 2022, with FMO footing over half the round. Its existing investors also include Omidyar Network, Lightrock, Khosla Impact, Accion Frontier Inclusion Fund–Quona Capital and 360 ONE Asset. The lender has also raised nearly ₹2,000 Cr in debt from 18 lenders between April 2025 and July 2026. The fresh round comes as digital lenders increase focus on MSMEs, which often have difficulty in raising formal credit despite being the country’s second largest employer. New-age NBFCs like Indifi Capital, Techfino, Lendingkart, FlexiLoans, Aye Finance, among others, are leveraging technology to address this issue and provide credit to MSMEs. As the ecosystem evolves, many NBFCs are also taking the public markets route to raise capital for their lending operations. In the past year, those that have hit the bourses include Aye Finance, Kissht, Moneyview, Tata Capital and Northern Arc, among others. Meanwhile, those in the IPO pipeline include Fibe, InCred, Avanse and Muthoot, reflecting broadening maturity of the sector, with total NBFC AUM expected to reach ₹50 Lakh Cr by FY27 end. Notably, NBFC credit accounted for nearly 26% of the country’s GDP in 2026, as they step in to expand credit access for those not covered by traditional banking.

The day Kumkum Anil Mohod returned home to Amravati, around 11 in the night, bearing three archery medals from the Asian Games 2026 in Japan, a host of people with big posters greeted her. But she was soon told to lock her exploits from Aichi-Nagoya in a corner of her mind, throw the key away, and look ahead.
“They (parents and coach) said ‘Whatever has happened, forget it. This is not your dream. It’s the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. Stay grounded. You haven’t done anything yet. Stay focussed on your work’,” Kumkum told reporters during a press conference arranged by the Sports Authority of India (SAI).
It all started when she became the first-ever individual recurve champion, man or woman, from India at the Asian Games. The 17-year-old from Maharashtra did so by South Korea’s Oh Yejin. The Indian teen was also part of the gold medal-winning women’s team, which ended Korea’s 28-year hegemony.
“I was nervous in the beginning. I hadn’t faced so much media before. But now it feels good, a sense of pride is there. Before, we used to take pictures with others. Now, others want to take pictures with us,” she continued.
She recalled the moment, the shoot-off during the women’s individual recurve final, which eventually etched her name in the history books.
READ | Kumkum’s arrows pierce Korea’s four-decade stronghold as India’s archers dominate Asiad
“My heartbeat was up. But I controlled my breathing and kept myself calm. I had been manifesting that exact moment,” she began. “I don’t see the opponent in front of me. Sab Korean Korean karte hai (Everyone talks about the South Koreans). But in the lead up to the match, I told myself that usko bhi 10 marna hai, mujhe bhi 10 marna hai (She also needs to hit a 10, and so do I). Whatever happens, I want to give my best.”
Kumkum also acknowledged the sacrifices her parents have made ever since she took up the bow at the impressionable age of nine. It was her mother who put her into the sport after seeing another girl pursuing the sport. But the expenses involved in the game made it difficult in the early days.
“Earlier, my father urged me to focus on my studies. My grandmother had gifted me my first bow. The equipment is quite expensive. A recurve bow can cost nearly Rs. 3 lakh. But later, my father also started supporting me.
“There are some parents who like going around, enjoy themselves. But no matter what match I was playing — district, state, or nationals — they would be with me. They have always called me a champion. Even when I wasn’t performing, they never told me to leave the sport. Even today, my father says I’ll be the one creating history in LA,” Kumkum explained.
While the youngster accepted that she has missed partaking in the usual shenanigans involved during teenage years, she does see the upsides of it.
“ Mai toh kabhi kabhi bolti hu ghar mai, ki pura bachpan isme chala gaya, par achha hai. Aage jaake khuch dikkat nahi ayegi (I tell my family sometimes that my whole childhood went in archery. But it’s good. It’ll help going forward in life),” she chuckled.
Apart from her two gold medals, Kumkum also bagged a silver which came in the recurve mixed team. She was partnering her idol and senior Dhiraj Bommadevara. The duo fell short against the Chinese pair in the final, but Dhiraj had a role in motivating Kumkum in her pursuit of greatness.
“It was a great experience being paired up with him. He had told me to enjoy the competition, irrespective of whether we win or lose. He said ‘if you make a mistake, that’s my fault. And if I make a mistake, that’s the coach’s fault.’ He asked me to shoot the arrows without any pressure.
“Before my (individual) match, he texted me ‘Focus on yourself. Don’t worry who’s in front of you. Behave like a champion’,” Kumkum recalled.
The Maharashtra archer is currently participating in the second season of the Archery Premier League as part of the Chero Archers team. When the edition concludes on October 18, there will be a few weeks’ time before the Senior Nationals come calling. But this gap isn’t a signal for Kumkum to rest on her laurels.
“I need to work on a few technical things, build on my strength in the gym everyday, and also, work on my mental conditioning,” she listed out, while adding that not training for a few days can make her hands shake.
More importantly, she’s aware that the Olympic quota she secured with the Asiad gold is that of India’s, and not hers.
“The Olympic trials will take place next year, and I’ll begin preparing for that. I’ll keep repeating the right things and correct the wrongs.
“If I do well, I’ll go to the Olympics. But if I keep pressurising myself with that, then it will get difficult. If I don’t take too much tension, I’ll surely get selected and get back a medal,” Kumkum said matter-of-factly.

After losing ground with Latino voters, Democrats are turning to influencers for help
Democrats lost the 2024 elections in part because of their eroding support among Latino voters, a constituency that was once a reliable segment of their base.
That November, Kamala Harris won the Latino vote by three points, according to the Pew Research Center. In 2020, Joe Biden carried them by 25 points.
This year, swing districts with large Hispanic populations could help decide which party controls the House. And Democrats are scrambling for ways to win those voters back.
One new effort comes from the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, also known as BOLD PAC. In February, they launched a program to personally connect social media influencers with voters.
"We're turning to trusted voices in local communities that have followings giving them information and then allowing them to create content in a way that is organic and authentic," said Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., who chairs BOLD PAC.
That includes Latina content creator Alexa Flores, who not long ago mostly posted about beauty tips and fashion. But the Arizona resident shifted to politics in response to the Trump administration's immigration policies.
She says she wants Latino voters to understand their impact if they vote.
"My job is to get people to understand that so that they can go and move that needle," said Flores, who has nearly 500,000 followers across her platforms.
Her job now includes "get-out-the-vote" events with BOLD PAC in swing districts around the country. Flores, for her part, will appear at a wine tasting event in Las Cruces, N.M. – where Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez is locked in a close race against Republican Greg Cunningham. She'll also appear at a Día de los Muertos event with lowriders and voters in Tucson, Ariz., where Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza is trying to unseat GOP incumbent Juan Ciscomani.
BOLD PAC says it is not paying content creators for posts. Instead, they're providing stipends of $1,500 for flights, hotels and other travel costs for each event.
Sánchez says content creators could help bridge a gap for her party. Thirty percent of Latinos regularly get their news from influencers on social media, according to Pew Research Center. That's more than any other demographic.
"So whether that's ... Instagram or YouTube or TikTok, that's how they're getting their information," she said. "So we need to be in those spaces."
Democratic strategist Stephanie Valencia says Democratic efforts to win back long term support from Latino voters is going to be an uphill battle. Valencia is co-founder of Equis Research, which estimates that roughly a third of Latinos are considered independent voters.
Of those, more than 40% think neither party cares about people like them.
"One election cycle is not going to solve the problem that Democrats have had and a frayed trust with Latino voters that has developed over the last several election cycles," Valencia said.
In 2024, Latinos shifted right in response to what they saw as liberal immigration policies and a focus on foreign intervention over domestic policy under former President Biden. That year, President Trump grew his party's share of Latino votes by double digits to 48%, leaving Democrats with a slim majority, according to Pew Research Center.
It's those kinds of swings that can cost a party a close election.
This year, leaders at BOLD PAC sense an opportunity, as they've watched a growing number of Latinos say they feel betrayed by President Trump's immigration and economic policies.
Still, Valencia warns that some Democratic campaigns continue to underestimate how "swingy" a good chunk of the Latino electorate is. That is, they show up with too little, too late when it comes to campaign spending and messaging.
"Latinos are just a more persuadable universe and can't just be treated as a base turnout universe for Democrats," she said.
Solangie Hernandez Hollowell, a Texas influencer who is also working with BOLD PAC, agrees. Like others, her posts often don't even mention specific candidates, but they do focus on issues that Democrats are campaigning on this cycle – issues like taxes and immigration.
So she wants to help Latinos connect with candidates in a way that goes beyond the transactional.
"Latinos feel like politicians show up just right before the election. I don't feel like we feel very heard," she said.
So she's translating what this political moment can mean for them.
"My main goal right now is making sure that everything that's happening around the world reaches my family and my community in a way that they can understand it," she said.
Flores, the Arizona influencer, says she hopes for more awareness that Latinos are having a growing impact on major pieces of American life.
"The wave of Latinos growing in this country is becoming a bigger voice for a lot of things," she said.

On September 21, 2026, students of King George’s Medical University (KGMU), Lucknow, protested over the death of Divyanshi Yadav, a 2025-batch B.Sc. Nursing student who died of dengue. A student at the protest site told PTI that though Divyanshi was suffering from the disease, she still had to attend college. “Despite being on the deathbed, she was tense about her attendance. Students are forced to come to the college daily to mark attendance, ignoring their medical conditions. We get messages from teachers telling us to come to the college after taking medicine,” he said.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
In September 2025, Subhangini, 23, another nursing student who was in her first year at Bhopal Memorial Hospital and Research Centre (BMHRC), died due to jaundice. A current student, on condition of anonymity, told The Hindu, “There was poor quality of food and water on campus, and the case was mishandled by BMHRC Hospital; her medical leave was not approved, and she had to perform her duty even in an ailing condition.” However, the university denied the allegations.
In most institutions, medical leave requires medical documentation and is granted for serious illness or when a student is severely injured in an accident. The older University Grants Commission (UGC) 2003 regulations required universities to prescribe a minimum attendance of 75% for students to be eligible for examinations, but the 2025 regulations no longer set a universal 75% threshold. Instead, they leave minimum attendance requirements to individual higher education institutions (HEIs) through their statutory bodies.
In most HEIs, the minimum attendance requirement is 75-80%, with a 10% accommodation for medical emergencies. This minimum attendance criterion is higher in medical and engineering institutes, as per their regulatory bodies. For nursing students like Divyanshi, the Nursing Council of India’s guidelines mandate 80% attendance in theory and 100% attendance in practical areas. This framework leaves medical-leave protection largely to institutional rules, producing significant variation in what happens to students when illness interrupts their education.
Problems for students with chronic illnesses
Alex is a third-year B.A. Visual Communication student at a university in Hyderabad. Having transverse myelitis, he became paralysed from the chest down at the age of 10, and the organs on the right side of his body stopped working. Doctors said he would never walk. Defying this, he has regained his ability to walk, but this is accompanied by chronic pain below the chest, subluxations, partial dysplasias, fatigue, and muscle spasms.
Alex holds a 100% merit-based scholarship, and in order to keep it, he must maintain a CGPA of 8 and above and 75% attendance. After he dislocated his kneecap in college in September 2024, doctors recommended a month of complete rest. However, he said, “I was told by the college authorities to either come to college regularly and maintain the 75% attendance or take a year's break and come back to college next year.” His medical leave was denied, stating, “Medical exemption only applies in case of hospitalisations.”
“However, my scholarship would not hold the following year. So I would have to write my exam again and apply for a scholarship again, which was not something I was able to do because of my financial situation. So I had to continue coming to college without taking the recommended one month’s leave. I took one day off, and I continued going back to college every single day,” Alex added.
Alex had to navigate a campus that had minimal accessibility, a long commute to the university, and he was not given leniency for assignments or for showing up to class a few minutes late. This affected his social life on campus and his health. “If I did take that one month’s rest, there was a chance I would have recovered fully. But since I was not able to do it, I still have not recovered. It’s been three years, and I keep dislocating my knee and wear braces to this day.”
A student of Interior Design with an autoimmune condition at a private university in Noida said, “I provided all medical documents explaining my condition; however, the department head asked me to take amla and attend classes.” The student described the process of applying for a leave as frustrating: “I was made to feel like my condition was not important; it came from my own laziness and was something that could be managed with willpower... I was an out-of-station student and had to navigate my illness alone, which was both mentally and financially demanding.”
Attendance adds to evaluation, and the student saw a marked dip in grades. Support, such as make-up assignments, was also not extended by administration or faculty. The student said, “As practical classes are a day long, missing one day amounts to six to eight hours of class time, dipping the attendance to 70-80 % even if two or three classes are missed.”
Cases of unconventional medical proof
Jay was a B.A. English major at a university in Delhi NCR, and months before he joined the university, he had developed chronic pain due to a genetic condition. He had to maintain 75% attendance in every subject, with an 80% requirement and 5% provision for medical leave.
Jay missed many morning classes due to his pain flaring up. As his teachers were accommodating, he was able to sit for his first-year exams. “I had to drop out as my situation worsened in second year. I didn’t have a proper diagnosis; a lot of reports and tests indicated inconclusive results. This couldn’t be taken as enough evidence at that time, and due to considerably low accessibility on campus as well as inflexible leave criteria, I dropped out.”
Tejasdeep Sehgal, a fourth-year student, has had a hearing impairment since the age of 12 and uses a hearing aid. The office of learning support at his university in Haryana provided him with a shaker alarm clock and transcription services that he says are helpful.
Last year, Tejasdeep’s hearing aid stopped working, and he could not listen properly. He then went to Delhi to have it fixed. “It took me two days to get it fixed, and it was a technician who fixed it; therefore, I didn’t have a prescription for it. I had unexcused absences for the classes I missed. However, it could have escalated into a situation where I would not be able to produce documentary proof of my condition to get medical leave.”
A student of Jawaharlal Nehru University’s Japanese department had a viral fever with body pain and had to take leave for two weeks. The student had informed the professor about it over email. When she rejoined class, she was told she was not sick and was asked to write an application to the centre and produce medical documentation. This dismissal by the professor caused the student severe anxiety and panic attacks. The university administration later asked the professor to write an apology letter to the student.
Another student said, “We are constantly told by our seniors not to fall in the bad books of some professor, as they have access to grant scholarships and fellowships and influence your career outside college.”
Describing a similar incident, a Delhi University student said they were made to stand in class. “I was told I was a good student, but irregular in classes. The philosophy professor quoted a scholar on resilience, which made the experience of my sickness seem like laziness. I left the class crying. I felt my hard work would not amount to anything because I was a sick person.”
A fifth-semester student of Humanities, who had been seeking college counselling sessions, upon needing further assistance, had to seek a psychiatrist outside college. The student later missed an exam due to an anxiety attack and was denied approval of medical leave. “I had all the documentation from a fully accredited clinical psychiatrist, and I was told it would have been easier to vouch for me if I was seeking help from college counsellors, who were not psychiatrists and could not have helped me at that time.” The student was made to do multiple rounds to the college healthcare centre, and their leave was still not approved. They had to take the paper again next semester. “The process was bureaucratic and draining.”
Sensitising institutions
Sayan Chaudhuri, a scholar of critical pedagogy and higher education, says, “Teachers and administration need to be sensitised to how chronic illnesses or other conditions might be playing out. I think without that understanding, you can’t have a meaningful intervention. What administrations really need to think about is the kinds of bureaucratic hurdles that are there. Often, administration stands at a huge distance, and you feel a sense of fear about approaching. So there is a need for a culture where it is established that you can get leave, and it shouldn’t feel like it’s a difficult task or it needs certain kinds of skills to be able to ask for a leave.”
He says the problem also lies in the hurdles students face when seeking medical leave. “A documentation-heavy policy is going to run into a contradiction, because the assumption will be that the document can be provided well in advance to the requisite authorities who can go through it, understand it, and approve it. And we know that’s not how it’s always going to work. There will be many things that will fall out of this system. We have to really think of developing a more local understanding of things where teachers can play a proactive role at times, mediate between the administration and the student, because otherwise that contextual understanding may not be there. Medical resource centres and health centres are often very depleted. Counsellors are not always working in a very empowered way, where they can stage interventions in a collaborative and meaningful manner,” he said.
Debaditya Battacharya, Assistant Professor in the Department of English at Jamia Millia Islamia, a researcher of Indian higher education and university histories, says, “National Education Policy 2020 lumps questions of mental health, ability, and disability together under this socioeconomically disadvantaged groups (SEDG); this rubric is indicative of the myopia of policy. Ability is treated as meritocratic given; it is not at stake anymore; it is either the basic minimum you take for granted or simply reduced to an ability enhancement course. But university life has to account for different capacities for ability and disability”
“There is no objective parameter that can justify any figure, whether it be 75 or 65,” Dr. Battacharya said, because students come to university with radically different circumstances. For some, meeting a particular threshold may be relatively easy; for others, especially students from marginalised backgrounds, it may involve negotiating pressures outside the classroom as well.
He says, “It’s teachers who are expected to come with that space of understanding what a student’s real-life circumstances are, as they deal with students in the flesh”. He suggests student-faculty committees hear cases that merit genuine attention on a case-by-case basis, in a consultative and democratic fashion. He says the system should retain the purpose of attendance, maintaining the integrity and spirit of the teaching-learning process without reducing individual students and their circumstances to a single percentage.
(Zain Younis is a Master’s student at Jamia Millia Islamia)

Russian authorities denied Tuesday that special restrictions had been introduced over reports that a laboratory technician died of plague, even as Washington said it was closely monitoring events.
Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.
Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor however insisted Tuesday that a document circulating online indicating heightened sanitary-epidemiological measures and restrictions in the Irkutsk region was fake.
"We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue," it said on Telegram.
"No such decisions have been made at this time," it said, stressing that "the sanitary-epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk Region ... remains stable".
The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said Friday the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.
As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the People of Baikal outlet added, without elaborating.
But Russian officials have stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease.
Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a special Rospotrebnadzor expert commission inspection in the region had found that "the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology".
The health watchdog, he said, had determined that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".
And there had been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since the death, he added.
Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.
US President Donald Trump said Monday that his administration was closely monitoring the situation.
"We're looking at it very strongly," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.
"We'll help them as much as we can."

Former Black Midi frontman cancels US tour after sexual misconduct allegations

Former Black Midi frontman Geordie Greep has canceled his North American tour after an allegation of sexual assault was made against him, which he has denied.
The 27-year-old singer-songwriter was about to take the stage in Vancouver, Canada on Thursday when flyers containing the accusation were distributed among the audience.
According to Rolling Stone, the flyers read: “Geordie Greep A Rapist. You know what you did this morning Oct 8th. He thinks he can do what he wants. Let Him Know What Vancouver Thinks of Rapists.”
Greep eventually appeared later than scheduled, and without his backing band. He reportedly told the crowd: “So essentially what happened last night, me and some of the band we went out to some bars, we went out, we met people, and it ended up in a situation where, really late at a house party, I got the wrong end of the stick with someone who was there, and I made a move, and it didn’t come off.”
He continued: “I really quickly apologized, and it was a complete misunderstanding on my part, and I felt extremely bad, I feel extremely sorry, and extremely upset about the whole situation. I would never rape a woman. I’m not a rapist. It’s not how that went down.”
Greep went on to say that he would perform the show solo, as he “didn’t want to force [his band] to still play a show in the light of that happening.” He also stated that proceeds from the show would go to a Vancouver charity to support victims of sexual violence.
Since then, Greep’s concerts in Boise, Salt Lake City, Boulder, and Denver have all been cancelled, with ticket-holders refunded. The singer is currently scheduled to begin a European tour on November 1.
The Independent has approached Greep’s management for further comment.
Earlier this year, Greep’s former Black Midi bandmate Matt Kwasniewski-Kelvin died at the age of 26.
The group, who formed in 2017, were part of an emerging scene that formed around the London venue Brixton Windmill. They released music through producer Dan Carey’s label Speedy Wunderground and Rough Trade Records.

The northern lights illuminated the skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening.
Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling natural phenomenon, also known as the aurora borealis.
The Met Office said sightings could continue during clear skies until Tuesday.
Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland.
The aurora borealis is a natural light display in Earth’s sky, driven by solar activity and geomagnetic storms interacting with the upper atmosphere.
Sightings will remain possible until Tuesday across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies, the Met Office said.
Aurora displays occur when charged particles collide with gases in the Earth’s atmosphere around the magnetic poles. As they collide, light is emitted at various wavelengths, creating colourful displays in the sky.
According to the Met Office, the sun emits charged particles known as solar wind, which travel at bout 1m mph.
The forecaster said: “When these particles interact with Earth’s magnetic field – especially when the solar wind’s polarity is opposite to Earth’s – they are funnelled toward the magnetic poles.
“As these energetic particles collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, they release energy in the form of light. Oxygen produces green and, at higher altitudes, rare red auroras, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues.”
Last year, experts said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting, as the sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.

Jeddah, Oc 10: Dermatologist and hair transplant surgeon Dr Mir Shahnawaz has received the REACH Research Award in Saudi Arabia for his research on exosome-containing formulations in male pattern baldness.
The award was conferred by Dr Shadi Zari, President of REACH Academy, under the REACH Research Awards on Regenerative Hair Restoration and Regenerative Aesthetics. The honour was accompanied by a research prize of SAR 10,000.
As per a statement, Dr Shahnawaz’s study compared an exosome-containing formulation with autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) in men with androgenetic alopecia, commonly known as male pattern baldness.
His work contributes comparative clinical evidence to an emerging area of regenerative medicine, examining how newer formulations perform alongside established approaches to hair restoration.
Dr Shahnawaz is the founder of Dermis Skin, Laser & Hair Transplant Clinic in Bemina, Srinagar. Alongside providing dermatology, laser and hair restoration services, he continues to pursue research that addresses questions relevant to everyday clinical practice.
The international recognition marks a meaningful milestone in his research journey and a proud moment for Kashmir’s medical community. It also highlights the contribution of Indian clinicians to global scientific discussions on regenerative medicine.

Sopore, Oct 10: Ashiq Hussain Kar has been elected president of Beopar Mandal Iqbal Market, Sopore, defeating his rival candidate, Mehraj Ud Din Masoodi, in an election held on Saturday.
The election witnessed strong participation from the trading community, with 254 of the 265 registered voters casting their ballots.
According to Election Board Chairman Anaytullah Bhat, Kar secured 139 votes, while Masoodi polled 113 votes. Two votes were declared invalid, giving Kar a winning margin of 26 votes.
Following the declaration of the results, Bhat congratulated the newly elected president and thanked the traders for their participation and cooperation in ensuring the smooth conduct of the election. He appreciated the voters for exercising their democratic right and contributing to the electoral process of the traders’ body.
Speaking after his victory, Kar said he would work collectively with all traders, irrespective of their electoral preferences, for the welfare and development of Iqbal Market.
He stressed the importance of unity, mutual cooperation and a collective approach to addressing the issues faced by shopkeepers and traders. He also assured the trading community that he would work to ensure their concerns and demands receive due attention.

Women living with a chronic hormonal condition should have access to taxpayer-funded weight-loss medications, advocates say.
The Polyendrocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Association of Australia (POSAA) is urging for GLP-1 drugs to be approved on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people living with the condition.
Formerly known as polycystic ovarian syndrome, PMOS affects one in eight women. Symptoms can include irregular periods, excess hair growth on the body and face, weight gain and hair thinning.
The lifelong condition, for which there is no cure, can lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and endometrial cancer.
While GLP-1s are not specifically approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration to treat PMOS, patients are being prescribed the medications off-label.
Half a million Australians are estimated to be using weight-loss medications regularly, a University of New South Wales study found in July.
Lorna Berry, a spokesperson for the POSAA who was diagnosed with the condition at 32, said she would welcome GLP-1s being subsidised for patients diagnosed with PMOS, in addition to funding for evidence-based research.
“It’s important for people to have access to medications, irrespective of where they live or where they were born … it’s really important that there’s equitable access,” she told the Guardian.
Berry said some women living with the condition were already missing out on being able to access the medications due to their high cost, which can set patients back several hundred dollars each month.
Associate professor Magdalena Simonis, the women’s health spokesperson for the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, said the college did not currently have a position on whether GLP-1s were appropriate for the management of PMOS.
“They’re not necessarily the only tool we have available to us, and that is important because long-term use is expensive, and it doesn’t look like these are going to be on the PBS anytime soon, and maybe not ever for conditions such as PMOS,” she said.
“Because traditionally women’s conditions are not included in these changes.”
Simonis, a GP with an expert interest in PMOS, said should research find the weight-loss medications more effective than existing treatments, a broader discussion about health equity would be needed.
“That is a conversation that we’re having about obesity as a national issue,” she said.
GLP-1 drugs – glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists – mimic a naturally occurring hormone which helps manage blood sugar levels and reduces hunger.
Ozempic is listed by the PBS, but only for the treatment of diabetes.
The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee last November recommended Wegovy be subsidised for those with a body mass index above 35.
The committee will meet next month when it will consider Novo Nordisk’s revised proposal to list Wegovy for obesity following protracted negotiations.
The Danish pharmaceutical company produces both Ozempic and Wegovy.
They contain the same active ingredient – semaglutide – but Wegovy has a higher dose.
“Novo Nordisk is continuing to work constructively with the Department of Health to try to negotiate a solution for the PBS listing of Wegovy,” a company spokesperson said.
“We remain committed to improving access for eligible Australians living with obesity.”
QENDO, an organisation advocating for people affected by PMOS and other women’s health conditions, said it recognised “growing interest in GLP-1 medications for managing PMOS, particularly for people experiencing metabolic complications and challenges with weight management”.
“While emerging evidence suggests potential benefits for some patients, further research is needed to establish their long-term effectiveness and safety specifically for PMOS,” QENDO’s acting chief executive, Kate Fisher, said.

For more than a year, social media users have spread a purported screenshot of an X post by Elon Musk that says: "No one needs to worry about Democrats winning the midterm elections. I have a plan."
The alleged screenshot circulated on platforms such as X and Reddit. Snopes readers contacted us to investigate the screenshot's legitimacy.
However, a search of Musk's X account found no evidence that this post exists. Furthermore, we found no screenshots of the post that included a timestamp or additional details indicating it was authentic, indicating that Musk did not share this X post and then delete it. If the screenshot circulating online were indeed authentic, there would be additional examples of the post through other users' varying screenshots.
Similarly, a search of an independent archive for Musk statements returned no relevant results. Searches on Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo also revealed no evidence that reputable news outlets have covered this supposed statement.
As such, we have rated this screenshot as fake.
The earliest version of the fake X post that we found was posted in August 2025, from Threads user @powermacuser12.
That post claimed Musk "rigged the vote tabulation computers in the swing states to ensure Trump won the 2024 election, & he's obviously planning on cheating again in the midterm elections."
"He should be hauled into jail by the FBI for his post below," powermacuser said, in reference to the fake screenshot.
We reached out to the Threads user to ask more about where they obtained the screenshot and await a response. 
Snopes previously found no evidence Musk rigged the election in favor of Trump via his Starlink satellite network. In fact, most election systems are a closed network, making connection to Starlink impossible.

The Stone Age owes its name to tools that survived to our time. The material early humans worked with most, though, was probably wood because it is so much easier to process. Unfortunately, we know very little about Paleolithic woodwork because wood rots relatively quickly. But at Abric Romaní, a rock shelter in Capellades, west of Barcelona, mineral-rich water coated wooden Neanderthal tools in a limestone-like crust. When wood rotted away, it left behind hollow molds that faithfully reflect its shape.
In a recent Science Advances study, a team of Spanish archaeologists has cataloged 597 wooden remains from Neanderthal living areas dating from 62,000 to 40,000 years ago. They found spears, digging sticks, bark trays, parts of shelters, and a club unlike anything seen before, suggesting Neanderthals were likely much more than just Homo sapiens’ dumber cousins.
Beyond hunting gear
The oldest wooden artifacts we have are mostly weapons. They include spears from a German town called Schöningen, a spear tip from Clacton-on-Sea in England, and the spear found alongside an elephant skeleton in Lehringen, Germany. Most came from waterlogged sediments, where a lack of oxygen slowed decay.
The spears mostly give us information about how Neanderthals hunted. The findings at Abric Romaní are different because the finds come from a place where Neanderthals lived, slept, cooked, and made tools over the course of some 20,000 years.
“We have a sample of wooden tools for different subsistence activities, not only hunting,” says M. Gema Chacón, an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) and co-author of the study. Because wood turns up in level after level, it shows that woodworking was routine for Neanderthals rather than an occasional one-off.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

The detentions have raised questions about the legal powers of the police during protests, including when they can take someone into custody without a warrant and what safeguards apply. Criminal lawyer Swagata Biswas of Metropolitan Magistrate Court at Kolkata tells Live Mint, “A warrant is not always required to detain a person.” An absence of a warrant does not mean that the police can detain anyone without a lawful basis. The legality of an arrest or detention depends on the provision invoked and the circumstances of the case. Under Section 170 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, the police can arrest a person without a warrant or an order from a magistrate if they believe a plan to commit a cognisable offence and that the offence cannot otherwise be prevented. The provision also limits detention under this power to 24 hours unless further detention is authorised under another applicable law. Preventive detention refers to the confinement of a person based on a reasonable apprehension that they may engage in an activity that threatens public order or security. Under Section 170 of the BNSS, the police must have the legally required basis to believe that an offence is being planned or might happen and that arrest is necessary to prevent it. However, it doesn't give the police an unrestricted power to arrest people merely on suspicion. Whether a particular detention is lawful depends on the facts and the legal grounds relied upon by the authorities. Preventive detention that allows authorities to hold a person to prevent anticipated threats is not the same as an ordinary arrest. An arrest is generally associated with an alleged offence and the subsequent legal process. Laws providing for preventive detention include the National Security Act (NSA), 1980; the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act (COFEPOSA), 1974; the Prevention of Black-marketing and Maintenance of Supplies of Essential Commodities Act, 1980; and the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988. 'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.

NEW DELHI -- India's youth “Cockroach” movement was set to hold fresh protests in the capital New Delhi on Saturday, intensifying a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and election authorities.
Thousands of protesters are expected at Jantar Mantar, the city's designated protest site, where authorities have imposed sweeping restrictions including suspension of mobile internet. Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.
The demonstration site has been cordoned off with yellow metal barricades and thousands of police personnel have been deployed in and around the area. Restrictions on train services and metro stations were expected to disrupt travel across the capital and make it harder for protesters to reach the venue.
The preparations signal the authorities’ determination to contain a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the “Cockroach” movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi’s education minister to resign in July.
The protests center on India's Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Saturday's planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.
Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi’s party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists.
The commission and the government deny the allegations.
For the “Cockroach” movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.
The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.
For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi’s home state, will test the party’s standing.
