Donald Trump’s administration has temporarily banned Microsoft, Adobe, and several other tech companies from sponsoring workers for permanent US residency, claiming they abused immigration programs at the expense of American citizens.
Vice-president JD Vance said on Thursday that the H-1B visa programme for highly skilled foreign workers had “become rife with fraud” and that over-reliance on such schemes was “a fundamental insult to the American worker.”
He added that “no company in the US” had “abused this system” more than Microsoft.
Vance’s message to Microsoft that it could not “lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants” triggered an angry reaction from the Indian government.
“Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive,” the foreign ministry in New Delhi said in a statement on Friday.
Referring to Vance’s remarks, it said “such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem.”
Six other IT outsourcing companies—Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini—were also suspended from the Permanent Labor Certification, or Perm, program, which allows US employers to hire foreign workers on a permanent basis.
“Subpoenas have been served, investigations are under way and nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” said Labor Department Inspector-General Anthony D’Esposito.
Microsoft said the “vast majority” of its employees in the US were American, while Tata Consultancy Services, India’s largest outsourcing company, said its strategy was centred on hiring locally in the US and that Perm applications were in “single digits in the last two years.”
Adobe and Tata as well as Cognizant, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini did not respond to requests for comment.
The announcement marks the latest move in the Trump administration’s broad crackdown on immigration. It has previously taken aim at H-1B visas widely used by tech companies and specialist industries.
Last year, the White House attempted to impose a $100,000 fee on new applications, but, in June, a federal judge ruled the fee amounted to an unauthorized tax and infringed on Congress’ authority to raise funds. The Trump administration has appealed against the ruling.

In headline after headline this year, American book publishers have appeared to be fighting back against generative AI, from suing Google for copyright infringement to canceling books by authors suspected of using LLMs.
But behind the scenes, at least three of the Big Five US book publishers—HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette—have been quietly incorporating AI tools into their publishing processes without public disclosures or author consent.
According to interviews with more than two dozen workers, all of whom spoke under the condition of anonymity to avoid jeopardizing their employment, publishers are now using LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT to email literary agents, write publicity and back-cover copy, design cover art, and generate marketing materials, often at the direction of their executives.
At the same time, multiple editorial staffers say the widely publicized cases of authors accused of using LLMs to help write their books—like Hachette’s horror novel Shy Girl or Macmillan’s crime thriller Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body—are just the tip of the iceberg. “Every single imprint has a story of someone very esteemed who had a book canceled because of blatant AI use” without ever making the news, one editor says.
At HarperCollins senior leaders purchased Claude licenses from Anthropic months ago “but very quickly realized they didn’t know how to implement them,” according to a current employee. Dozens of junior- and senior-level staff were then “voluntold” to become “AI Champions” and were tasked with discovering use cases in monthly brainstorming sessions with staff across the company.
This spring, when some HarperCollins employees expressed concerns about the legal, ethical, and environmental impacts of AI at one of these brainstorming sessions, a person leading the meeting dismissed their qualms as “the cost of doing business,” according to someone who attended the meeting. Soon after, a statement was added to the new AI section of the HarperCollins online employee portal, noting that “while AI does have an environmental impact, it’s a small part of most individuals’ total digital carbon footprint.”
Some HarperCollins staffers were unnerved by the brainstorming sessions. “It was such a slap in the face,” says one employee. “We’ve been making valid business cases for years to be paid a healthy salary, and instead they spent that money on software that most of us don’t really want.” (The average entry-level salary for New York City publishing employees at the Big Five and Scholastic was $47,583 in 2023.) In addition to Claude, staffers say HarperCollins has also purchased licenses for ChatGPT and Jasper, an agentic platform that promises “to run end-to-end marketing workflows.”
At least one HarperCollins division has been “all in” on AI since gaining software licenses, according to one staffer, including AI-generated marketing videos. But according to workers at HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette, one of the most common use cases for LLMs so far is generating publicity copy.
Readers encounter publicity copy everywhere from Amazon and Goodreads to back covers, and it’s used to pitch books to booksellers, journalists, content creators, and critics. However, “using AI to generate publicity copy is short-sighted,” a Big Five publicist tells me. “Publicists have a duty to engage in good faith with readers and our colleagues in the media, who I’m sure have a low threshold for tolerating AI-generated pitches.”
On the other hand, Meg Reid, publisher of the independent Hub City Press, says LLM-written marketing and publicity unfortunately “feels pretty inevitable” for the Big Five. “That’s one place we’re probably going to see a bigger shift between corporate publishers looking for efficiencies and smaller publishers insisting that the humans involved are the whole point.”
Meanwhile, earlier this year, literary agents began suspecting specific Big Five editors were using AI to write rejection letters. “Among colleagues, we compared emails on different books from the same editors, and they all had the same classic signs of AI writing, like ‘not this, but that’ and the rule of three,” one agent says. Employees at Simon & Schuster, HarperCollins, and Hachette tell WIRED they believe the agents’ suspicions were correct.
A spokesperson for Hachette says the company “support[s] the use of AI tools for operational purposes, when they help our authors’ books reach more readers,” but that it “[does] not support creative uses of AI, including communicating with our authors and partners.”
Wibke Grutjen, global chief marketing and communications officer at Simon & Schuster, says “employees across all functions have access to a limited number of enterprise-level AI tools,” but using them is not mandatory. Grutjen said the company prohibits the use of any AI tool “that has not been vetted and approved” and that “the goal is always to free up more time for our employees to spend on deeper focus and creative work on behalf of and alongside our authors.”
HarperCollins did not respond to requests for comment.
Months ago, workers at Simon & Schuster attended a workshop with representatives from OpenAI. “The person leading the workshop genuinely had no idea what we did,” an attendee says, but one of the AI company’s recommendations for how to use ChatGPT in the book trade was, in fact, composing emails to literary agents. The practice has also grown among editors at HarperCollins and Hachette, employees say.
In May 2024, staffers say Simon & Schuster held a contest among employees to come up with the best use cases for AI, with a $10,000 prize for the winner and $5,000 each for two runners-up. Since then, the company has “rolled back some of the AI-pushing because employees kept complaining about it in town halls,” says one employee. According to several staffers, AI assets are also cropping up in cover art, with some foreign presses distributed by Simon & Schuster openly acknowledging AI use when sharing designs.
All of the agents I spoke with expressed fears that publishers might paste text from their authors’ manuscripts into the LLMs in order to generate things like rejection letters and publicity descriptions. “We’ve added AI clauses to our contracts saying ‘this material can’t be run through an LLM,’” says one agent, who did not want to be named to avoid professional repercussions. “Ostensibly, that was meant to protect authors from tech companies, but it also applies to the company buying and publishing the book. If they're not using a closed-loop model, they could be feeding an LLM with an author’s unpublished writing.” Unlike the LLMs most people use online (Google Gemini, ChatGPT, et al.), a closed-loop model operates on an individual computer or network that’s “air-gapped” so it can’t share data with the AI company’s cloud servers. One source at HarperCollins says multiple editors have asked managers if they could paste a full manuscript into an open-loop LLM and were told not to by the company’s legal team.
Hachette employees are also bracing for the company’s AI policies to “evolve” under new chief information officer Carl Hixson, due to his previous role as chief technology officer at SRMG, a Saudi state-backed company that has publicly embraced agentic AI.
Some staffers across the Big Five say they’re reluctantly experimenting with LLMs only because executives gutted their teams through layoffs and subsequently tripled their workloads.
“It’s skeleton crews everywhere you look,” says one employee. “Large teams have been reduced to just five or six people, give or take, and we’re doing double or triple the number of books. No wonder people are taking shortcuts. I don’t judge them for that. I judge the company for shoving the shortcuts down our throats and saying, ‘Do this or we fall behind.’”
In just the past few weeks, word spread among Simon & Schuster workers that the company was conducting an experimental trial with Skan AI “at the apparent urging of KKR”—the investment firm that purchased Simon & Schuster in 2023. According to its own website, Skan AI “gives leaders the evidence base they need to reduce costs, prioritize automation, and meet board-level transformation mandates.”
In response, Simon & Schuster employees began gathering signatures on an open letter to their CEO, Greg Greeley, expressing their “strong opposition” and “seeking a commitment to not bring Skan AI or other similar software into S&S workflows, either now or in the future.” Beyond the software’s surveillance capabilities, many workers were also concerned with Skan AI’s “automation discovery” tools being used to shadow and replace them.
News of the open letter was published in New York magazine’s Book Gossip newsletter on October 6. On the same day, Greeley sent a memo to Simon & Schuster employees confirming that the company has been exploring Skan AI’s Blueprint product but that “no decision has been made to use Blueprint or any other productivity-monitoring or workflow-analysis tool,” and that he “had not seen the materials relating to this early-stage exploration” before concerns were raised to him the day before. Pangram, which, for better or worse, has become the go-to AI-detection platform, indicates that at least some of Greeley’s memo was written by AI.
Almost two years ago at the UBS Global Media and Communications Conference, HarperCollins CEO Brian Murray said AI presents “more opportunities than risks” for book publishers and that he saw AI playing a role in increasing the number of translated books and audiobooks published by HarperCollins in the future. Since then, multiple editors say they’ve seen LLM-translated manuscripts with AI-use disclosures at the annual Frankfurt and London book fairs, where US publishers buy international publishing and translation rights from foreign literary agencies.
In August, Michael Reynolds, executive publisher at Europa Editions, an independent press in New York best known for publishing Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan Quartet of novels, told a room full of booksellers at the New Voices New Rooms conference in Baltimore he was excited about the possibilities for AI in translation and “seemed baffled by critiques of it,” according to attendees. Europa Editions is already controversial among literary circles for leaving the names of its human (for now) translators off the covers of its books.
“The C-suites at Big Five publishing companies have more in common with the C-suites at other major American companies than they do with the editors and publicists and translators who work for them,” says Dan Sinykin, author of Big Fiction: How Conglomeration Changed the Publishing Industry and American Literature. “They’re always looking for ways to maximize profit, and right now they’re trying to see what they can get away with before there’s a revolt.”
Most of the industry professionals I spoke with just want publishers to provide clear AI usage guidelines and disclosures, at the very least, to help mitigate the current chaos. “We need publishers to be clear about what is being used and when,” says Emma Dries, an agent at Triangle House Literary who previously worked in editorial at HarperCollins and Penguin Random House. A current HarperCollins staffer, meanwhile, says there has been no direction “about what to say to authors or agents about any of this, because I think they know it would start a shitstorm.”
“Short of these tools being banned, which would frankly be my preference,” Dries continues, “everybody should be communicating more.”

Hundreds of thousands lose power as Hurricane Isaias batters Florida, Alabama
Isaias marks the first hurricane of the Atlantic season
Hundreds of thousands of people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle were without power early Saturday after Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous hurricane and left flooded roads and downed trees in its wake as it moved inland.
The storm made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply.
But the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still loomed for parts of the Florida Panhandle, along with heavy rain and potential flooding for much of the region over the weekend and into Monday.
Isaias was about 40 kilometres south-southwest of Montgomery, Ala., and nearly 170 kilometres south of Birmingham, Ala., with maximum sustained winds of 55 km/h, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Saturday.
Forecasters also warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.
The storm's rapid intensification was fuelled by record-warm waters in the Gulf of Mexico. The Gulf has seen substantial warming over the past few decades, and experts say the current marine heatwave was made far more likely due to human-caused climate change.
While the warm waters provided the abundant energy that Isaias needed, its formation was also made possible by favourable atmospheric conditions, including weak upper-level winds that would otherwise have disrupted the burgeoning storm.
But just before landfall, upper-level wind shear increased, causing the storm to weaken slightly, dropping it back to Category 2 and making it more disorganized, expanding the area hit by damaging winds.
Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.
"The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference Friday.
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.
Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.
More than 726,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
A man tries to push a car as waves wash over the road on Friday ahead of the arrival of Hurricane Isaias, in Englewood, Fla. (Facebook/Reuters)
Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, said the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator. Standing water also covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were ripped down, but overall he said the storm wasn’t as bad as he expected.
"As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate," Mowry said.
Mowry said his son, who lives about 15 minutes away, tried to drive to his home after losing power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the roads.
Weakened storm threatens region with floods
Despite weakening, heavy rain is forecast as Isaias moves inland, with 10 to 20 centimetres or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia.
The last hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. was Milton, which tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024.
Isaias also grounded most Friday flights at several airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
In the Pacific, meanwhile, Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it approached Mexico’s coast.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

What is your seafood eating? Investigation traces problems in global feed supply
Fish meal and fish oil used in aquaculture linked to pollution, overfishing and labour abuses
The following story is part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C.
In 2020, a team of government investigators in Goa, India, arrived at a factory named United Marine Products to find out how it was disposing of its toxic wastewater.
For years, local residents had complained that the factory was making their air unbreathable and their drinking water deadly. This factory produces fish meal, a protein-rich powder used to feed farmed fish, which is made by pulverizing and cooking wild-caught fish.
Soon enough, the inspectors discovered that the plant operators had employed a new and illegal way to dispose of the facility's wastewater, drilling bore holes into the ground in a field behind the plant. The authorities later concluded these holes likely contaminated groundwater and sickened villagers and livestock.
The United Marine Products plant in Councolim, Goa, India. In 2020, investigators determined the plant had drilled holes into the ground behind the plant to illegally dispose of wastewater from fish meal processing. (Changing Markets Foundation)
The plant owner denied wrongdoing.
Seafood consumers in Canada might think they have no connection to these sorts of far-away problems.
But this factory in India supplied Skretting, a major feed producer used by dozens of fish farms in Canada — so its product may feed the salmon from British Columbia and New Brunswick or trout from Quebec you see on store shelves.
A five-year investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C., uncovered a variety of similar hidden costs involved in producing this feed, including the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, and violent protests spurred by the horrid stench from fish meal factories.
These social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury types of seafood are eaten.
A worker unloads a crate of anchovies from the holding area of a boat at the port of El Callao, Peru. The world’s largest producer of fishmeal, Peru faces growing concern about overfishing and pollution from its fishmeal industry. (Rodrigo Abd/The Associated Press)
Whether domestically raised or imported, the most popular types of farmed seafood consumed in Canada – salmon, shrimp, trout, sea bass, sea bream – are fed fish meal, which is made from the very kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, say fisheries scientists.
“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of B.C. in Vancouver.
“And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”
Canada’s reliance on global fish meal
Since 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten globally has come from fish farms rather than wild catch, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. Aquaculture is a $444-billion industry and the fastest-growing segment of global food production. Most of these fish farms are powered by fish meal and fish oil, made from wild fish pulled from the ocean.
Unlike growing bivalves such as oysters, clams, and mussels, which do not typically require external feed, the toughest challenge to raising carnivorous seafood, such as salmon and trout, is feeding them.
A worker drives a tractor past mounds of fish meal made from menhaden fish to be used as animal feed supplements in Reedville, Va., in 2015. (Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images)
Canada has more than 200 fish farms, most of which rely on fish meal or fish oil that, when made domestically, comes primarily from Pacific anchoveta, chub mackerel, herring, haddock, pollock, sardines, and frigate tuna.
Canada prohibits boats targeting fish for the sole purpose of making fish meal or fish oil, so domestic fish meal is typically made using skin, bones and other byproducts of processing that would otherwise be thrown away. That’s widely viewed as a more sustainable way to produce feed protein than using whole human-edible fish.
However, at least two-thirds of the fish meal used in Canada, primarily by aquaculture farms – roughly 53,000 tonnes in 2023 – is sourced from abroad, which ties Canadian consumers to these hidden and overseas social costs. Canada also imports more than $4 billion in seafood annually, of which a third is primarily farmed salmon and shrimp, which rely heavily on fish meal and fish oil.
Food for Feed investigation
The Outlaw Ocean Project’s five-year investigation mapped roughly the entire global fish meal industry, including more than 1,400 fish meal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms and seafood retailers.
The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries who visited factories and farms and boarded fish meal ships at sea.
In Gambia and Mauritania, the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are diverted into fish meal factories for export.
Workers sort catch aboard the China-flagged Lu Lao Yuan Yu 010 in Gambian waters in 2019. When Outlaw Ocean reporters boarded vessels, they documented widespread complaints about poor living and working conditions. (Fábio Nascimento/The Outlaw Ocean Project)
In India and Peru, the industry was tied to at least 80 protests, some violent, in the form of labour strikes and demonstrations sparked by the water pollution or the stench from factories cooking thousands of tonnes of decomposing fish. Canada is the largest importer of fish oil from Peru.
In China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labour on fish farms.
The investigation mapped more than 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang and Tibet — two regions subjected to severe state repression — that produce an estimated half-billion dollars’ worth of farmed seafood annually, some of which is exported to the United States and Canada.
A worker tosses fishmeal pellets into pens at a fish farm in Thailand in 2021. Over half of the seafood eaten worldwide comes from fish farms. (Mako Kurokawa)
‘Overexploited’ or worse
The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fish meal production in at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets.
For example, less than 30 per cent of the fleet had publicly available location information and less than 25 per cent had a unique vessel identification number (or ship licence plate). Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.
- A third of global fishing goes unreported, UBC researchers find
- Somalis say foreign ships are stealing their fish, and it's fuelling a piracy resurgence
At least half of the species landed by the assessed fish meal vessels were classified by scientific studies as “overexploited” or worse — including flat and round sardinella in Senegal, oil sardines in India, and anchoveta in Chile.
Most of the vessels in the global fish meal fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish, which can indiscriminately sweep in bycatch and non-target species.
At least 165 of the ships in the fleet were bottom trawlers, a destructive gear type that scrapes the ocean floor with weighted nets.
Fish meal reliance declining, industry says
In response to questions from The Outlaw Ocean Project about the sustainability of fish meal, the IFFO, which is the international fish meal association, emphasized that its “role is not to advise which markets should use fish meal and fish oil.”
Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson from the organization, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system” and is becoming more efficient over time.
Sacks of fish meal stored at a factory in Lima on December 3, 2009. While the aquaculture industry says it has decreased its reliance on fish meal overall, some companies have increased demand as they grow. (Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty Images)
In response to a question about overfishing by the fish meal industry, Jamin said, “Because small pelagics are fast-renewing stocks, their sustainable harvest threshold is much higher than for slow-growing species like cod, tuna, or deep-sea fish.”
The feed and aquaculture industries have emphasized that they are decreasing their reliance on fish meal and fish oil by adding other ingredients to the mix, such as insects, algae, and krill. Between 2000 and 2020, the share of fish meal in global aquaculture feed fell from 23 per cent to eight per cent, according to the IFFO.
Producers of salmon, which typically requires larger amounts of fish meal and oil to thrive, say they have made progress, too. Members of the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance, which includes large producers like Cermaq and Mowi, reduced the proportion of these ingredients in salmon feed to less than 20 per cent, according to a November 2025 press release.
“These results show salmon farming companies have adopted science-based methods that have improved the standard of salmon farm sustainability overall in Canada,” said Timothy Kennedy, president of the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance, in the release.
A salmon farm near Campbell River, B.C., is shown during a routine health inspection in 2018. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)
However, as aquaculture overall grows so too has demand for fish meal.
For example, to meet demand, five of the world’s largest salmon companies increased their absolute use of fish meal or fish oil made from whole wild fish by as much as 39 percent between 2020 and 2024, according to a report from the Farm Animal Investment Risk and Return Initiative.
Two of the salmon companies that increased their absolute use of fish meal have a presence in Canada: Mowi, which announced in June 2025 that it was selling its Canadian farms to Cooke; and Grieg Seafood, whose Canadian farms have since been acquired by Cermaq. (Mowi, Cermaq, Cooke, and Grieg Seafood did not respond to a request for comment.)
Skretting opens investigation
As of 2025, there were at least seven factories processing fish meal and fish oil in Canada, and these plants are not without problems.
Between 2021 and 2024, at least two of the plants were tied to pollution or unsustainable fishing practices, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool created by The Outlaw Ocean Project that tracks the fishing and seafood industries. Neither company responded to the project’s request for comment.
However, the far greater burden of food insecurity, collapsed fish stocks, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fish meal or farmed seafood that Canada imports.
For example, Canada imports over a third of its shrimp from India, where the investigation found explosions, fires, and worker asphyxiations at factories producing fish meal that supplies the country’s shrimp farms.
Freshly caught live shrimp are seen on a shrimp farm in India, April 11, 2025. (Sahiba Chawdhary/Reuters)
As recently as 2022, United Marine Products, the Goan fish meal plant that was found to be illegally dumping wastewater, supplied fish meal to Skretting Canada, which produces feed for many of Canada’s fish farms.
At another factory called Bismi Aquatic Products in 2021, a migrant worker died while he was cleaning a wastewater tank and passed out from the fumes. Major shrimp brands like IFC and AZ Gems, which source much of their shrimp from India, are sold across Canada at major supermarket chains like Metro Canada, Loblaws, and Costco Canada.
Skretting has a “zero-tolerance policy” for breaches of its policies that clearly state business partners abide by all applicable laws and regulations that govern their business activities, said the company’s Sustainability and Communications Director, Jorge Diaz, and has opened an investigation to verify the information found in this reporting.
In response to questions from Outlaw Ocean, Metro spokesperson Stephanie Bonk wrote: “All Metro suppliers are required to respect working conditions across the supply chain as outlined in our Supplier Code of Conduct for responsible procurement.”
IFC, AZ Gems, and Loblaws did not respond to a request for comment.

Relative humidity is a simple concept as weather phenomena go – but it has significant, far-reaching consequences for how we must take care of ourselves on a hot or wet day.
Letting the wind flow freely is the secret to cooling our cities
Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air around us, and there are three ways to track it. The most common of them is absolute humidity: the mass of water vapour in a given volume of the air and water vapour mixture, expressed as kg/m3. The second is specific humidity, equal to the mass of the moisture divided by the mass of air. It is expressed as a dimensionless number (but sometimes also as grams per kilogram, among other similar units.)
The third way is relative humidity: it is important because it factors in the amount of vapour that air can hold at different temperatures. Determining its value is a bit more complicated: it is the vapour density of the air divided by the saturation vapour density at the dry-bulb temperature.
Why does relative humidity matter?
On a hot day, our body uses sweat to cool itself. Sweat is released via our skin to the surface. There, the liquid evaporates. When water changes phase from liquid to vapour, it absorbs heat from the surface on which it lies. So when sweat evaporates, it absorbs heat from the skin, cooling it.
The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more. This means that the sweat on your skin can’t evaporate. At the same time, the body keeps sweating because it is still expecting to cool itself.
As a result, if the relative humidity is high, you can sweat on a hot day even when you are sitting still – while your body also keeps accumulating heat. This can quickly become dangerous.
A relative humidity of 30-60% is generally considered to be comfortable. Environments that have lower levels than this typically use humidifiers to increase the humidity. When the level is higher, a fan will help move the air around you and help sweat evaporate better.
In both cases, drinking water is important.
What does relative humidity imply physically?
Warmer air can hold more moisture than cooler air. So at the same absolute humidity, the relative humidity of warmer air will be lower than that of cooler air. It is like saying two vessels can hold the same amount of water – just that the bigger vessel will be less full than the smaller vessel.
This is why, for example, while Chennai had an absolute humidity of 70% at 2.30 pm on April 23, its relative humidity was lower, around 60%, because it had an ambient temperature of 32 C.
The change in the capacity for moisture as the air warms is also non-linear, meaning it doesn’t increase by the same amount as the air warms. For example, the difference as it warms over 20º C from -20º C to 0º C is small, but there is an enormous improvement in its vapour-carrying capacity as it warms over 20º C from 30º C to 50º C.
How do you measure relative humidity?
There are a few ways to measure relative humidity. One is to conduct a simple experiment with household items; another is to use maths; a third is to use an app or device.
Experiment
For the experiment, you need two mercury thermometers, some cotton, rubber bands, and access to cold water.
First, make sure both thermometers show the same reading, say, under a fan. Next, soak some cotton in cold water and wrap it around the bulb of one of the thermometers with a rubber band. Hold this thermometer under the fan, such that water from the cotton evaporates, and record the thermometer reading after five minutes. Hold up the other thermometer in the air and record its reading after five minutes. You will thus have the wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures, respectively.
Next, subtract the wet-bulb temperature from the dry-bulb temperature to get the temperature difference. Finally, use the relative humidity chart (see below) to get the relative humidity value. For example, if the difference was 6 C and the dry-bulb temperature was 28 C, the relative humidity would have been 59%.
A psychrometer is a device that has two such thermometers plus a chart to get the final reading. Modern, electronic psychrometers can calculate the relative humidity directly.
For a rough sense, the lower the wet-bulb temperature, the drier the air is, and the less relatively humid it is.
Mathematics
There are two mathematical ways (among others) to estimate the relative humidity, one simpler and one a bit more involved.
The first way is to divide the actual vapour pressure by the saturated vapour pressure. The vapour pressure is the amount of moisture that air contains. The ‘saturated’ value is the maximum possible amount. The formula (below) requires the dew point (Td), which you can obtain from a weather website.
RH = (e/es)*100
e = 6.11 x 10((7.5 x Td)/(237.3 + Td))
For es, use the same formula but replace Td with T, the actual temperature.
The second way is to calculate relative humidity starting from the specific humidity, pressure and temperature, using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
App
If you prefer software: Search for “hygrometer” in your phone’s app store to locate some options. (A hygrometer is an instrument that measures humidity.) Note that the app will only work if your phone has a sensor that can sense humidity.
If you like hardware, psychrometers and devices called hygrometers are available in physical as well as online stores.
Why does the wet-bulb temperature matter?
This said, a more direct way to understand the implications of the relative humidity for your wellbeing is in the form of the wet-bulb temperature (a.k.a. the adiabatic saturation temperature). It is the lowest temperature a surface – like your skin – can reach when water evaporates from it. The wet-bulb temperature is equal to the dry-bulb temperature when the relative humidity is 100%.
A wet-bulb temperature in an environment of 32-35º C or higher can be quickly lethal, even if you are not doing any physical activity or are in the shade. (At least one study has shown that even a wet-bulb temperature of more than 29º C can be dangerous.)
The climate crisis is rendering heatwaves more common, more frequent, more spread out, and more potent over the Indian subcontinent. As a study published in May 2022 put it:
“Whether today’s most impactful heatwaves could have occurred in a pre-industrial climate, traditionally a central focus of attribution research, is fast becoming an obsolete question. The next frontier for attribution science is to inform adaptation decision-making in the face of unprecedented future heat.”
One way to adapt is to keep an eye on the relative humidity, drink lots of water, and cool yourself.

For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to an adult. Among the clearest signs of evolution and maturity of this ecosystem is the growing number of startups eyeing a public listing now. For Indian companies, achieving a public listing has for long symbolised operational progression, transparency, and long-term viability. For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation. Currently, a handful of startups, including the likes of Razorpay, PRISM, PhonePe, among others, are in various stages of their IPO journey. Meanwhile, over 70 Indian new-age tech companies have already crossed the milestone and are now listed on the bourses. Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges. While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. Over 60 of the new-age tech companies are currently profitable. In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42's purview are about a decade old. From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra's IPO materialised within four years of its operations. Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal. Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem. The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups. While fintech and ecommerce house 14 names each, 13 enterprise tech startups have listed on the bourses so far. The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of Tonbo Imaging, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts. Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 25 listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru's sixteen and Mumbai's thirteen. While fifteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube. Delhi NCR contributes $93.4 Bn in the cumulative $173 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies. FC Goa (FCG) and Chennaiyin FC (CFC) scored a great goal each as the two teams played out a 1-1 draw in their Indian Super League (ISL) 2026-27 match at the Fatorda Stadium in Goa on Saturday.
The first half failed to inspire chances from either side as both teams lacked the creativity to create clear-cut spaces.
However, CFC was more progressive with the ball, while pressing higher off the ball. It made it tough for the Gaurs to push the ball up, having to opt for long balls over the midfield or trying to work it through the channels.
Both defences had players put their bodies on the line whenever the ball was crossed in. The weather conditions and the cooling break refused to let either team build any sort of momentum as the match swung from one side to another.
CFC’s goalkeeper and captain Mohammad Nawaz made a great save with his foot in the 57th minute to thwart Goa’s Spanish No. 9 Christian ‘Chiki’ Borrego Isabel to keep the game level.
The game was demanding a special moment in the second half.
And Irfan Yadav provided just that — CFC’s right-back Namgyal Bhutia played the ball through to Irfan, who controlled the ball right outside the box and smashed it into the far top corner.
The Gaurs stepped up their intensity immediately after Marina Machans’ striker Ramon Tanque gave up a clumsy foul in his own half. FCG’s left-back, Aakash Sangwan, stepped up to get the ball and put in a peach of a delivery, to which Chiki climbed up the highest to head it into the bottom corner.
FCG’s next challenge will be at the continental level when it hosts Tajik club Regar-TadAZ in the group stage of AFC Challenge League on October 17. Meanwhile, CFC will travel to Bengaluru on the same day for its next ISL fixture.
The result: FC Goa 1 (Chiki 75’) drew with Chennayin FC 1 (Irfan 63’)
