The US Navy aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln returned home this week after a long and difficult combat deployment. The numbers shared by the sea service for that deployment are staggering.
The warship left its homeport in San Diego in November 2025 and was deployed for 321 days, which included 286 consecutive days at sea without a port call. The lengthy deployment, extended by Operation Epic Fury that kicked off the Iran war, set a modern-day record.
As hostilities began at the end of February, the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group played a central role in the fight.
The carrier strike group's embarked Carrier Air Wing 9 — a naval aviation force consisting of nine squadrons of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, F-35C Lightning II Joint Strike Fighters, and EA-18G Growler electronic attack aircraft, among other assets— flew nearly 4,000 combat flights during the 40-day operation.
During the monthslong deployment, it flew 14,037 aircraft sorties and accumulated 31,460 forward-deployed flight hours. An estimated 20.5 million gallons of aviation fuel enabled the air wing's operations, the Navy said.
During Operation Epic Fury, the carrier air wing's mix of fourth- and fifth-generation aircraft launched 1,499 precision munitions, dropping over 1.37 million pounds of ordnance on priority targets such as missile sites, defense production facilities, military infrastructure, and Iranian naval capabilities. Air assets also shielded the strike group from enemy action.
The Navy said that the air wing, with its combination of stealth fighter jets and workhorse aircraft, effectively penetrated contested airspace and demonstrated the "Air Wing of the Future" concept in a real-world combat scenario.
Following the April ceasefire and the conclusion of Epic Fury, Carrier Strike Group 3 supported the Navy's blockade. When Iran began targeting commercial shipping, the group participated in strikes on Iranian coastal defenses and missile sites. It supported a second blockade before finally heading home. Over the course of its deployment, the Lincoln sailed over 93,000 nautical miles, supported by 72 at-sea replenishments.
For its actions during the deployment, the strike group received the Presidential Unit Citation, one of the military's highest unit awards.
The difficult deployment took its toll on the broader strike group, which also included three guided-missile destroyers. Multiple reports indicated that logistical strain caused by the war exacerbated the situation.
Business Insider obtained written responses submitted to Congress by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao late last month that revealed eight suicide attempts by sailors assigned to the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group. Cao said that multiple sailors attempted to jump overboard. There were no suicides, though.
Cao wrote that "the men and women of Carrier Strike Group THREE have demonstrated exceptional resolve under demanding conditions," emphasizing that "operational decisions to extend deployments are never made lightly." He said the Navy is committed to preserving crew morale, health, and safety, and overall fleet readiness.
Navy leadership has said that it is taking lessons from the deployment. The service has said that it is loading carriers up with more supplies to ensure self-sufficiency if logistics and support come under stress, adding quality of life improvements, and working to keep sailors and Marines better connected with loved ones.

Several injured in attack on airport in Saudi capital Riyadh
- Published
Several people have been injured in another attack on an international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, authorities say, days after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have carried out similar strikes on the hub.
Operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were suspended on Saturday after the attack, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said in a statement.
More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to news agency Reuters, citing an eyewitness.
The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport" and urged American citizens to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.
The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudis including a pilot were killed in two attacks on the airport by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior. Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.
A source at a local hospital told AFP that dozens of people had been wounded in Saturday's attack.
"I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running," an eyewitness who said they had been at gate 401 in the domestic terminal told the news agency.
Western embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens away from the airport.
Several Gulf airlines said they had cancelled their flights to and from the airport. with Kuwait Airways citing the "security situation" there.
All flights to Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled, aviation tracker Flightradar shows.
Doctors had been asked to report to hospitals to address the situation, a medical source told AFP.
"We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'," the medical source told the agency.
The suspected attack comes during a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.
The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.
The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.
That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.
A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
But the informal truce began to unravel in July.
The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

With an eye on entering the homegrown electric two-wheeler (E2W) market, Vietnamese EV maker VinFast has signed letters of intent (LoIs) with more than 50 dealers across India. The EV maker said that the agreements will pave the way for establishing 50+ e-motorcycle showrooms across 34 cities in 15 states and union territories (UTs). These showrooms will be set up across Delhi NCR, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, among others. In a statement, the EV giant said that the agreements will expand its distribution network and strengthen its position in the Indian E2W market. The LoIs were signed at VinFast’s manufacturing facility in Vietnam’s Hai Phong. Citing its rationale for signing the agreements, VinFast said that the aforementioned cities have large two-wheeler markets, which offers a significant headroom for electrification. The company said that it plans to leverage these dealer locations to bring electric mobility solutions “closer to local consumers”. As part of its local push, the company also plans to build charging infrastructure and strengthen after-sales services in the new cities. “Partnering with more than 50 dealer partners across 15 states and territories and 34 cities marks the beginning of our journey to bring VinFast e-motorcycles across India. Alongside, we are also building charging infrastructure and strengthening after-sales services to ensure that customers across these locations receive the support they need throughout their ownership journey,” said Anurag Saxena, the India CEO of VinFast’s e-scooter division. With this, VinFast is entering the burgeoning Indian E2W space, which is being driven by government incentives, new launches by domestic manufacturers, rising fuel prices, EV mandates, a growing charging infrastructure and rapid adoption by gig platforms. The E2W segment is currently dominated by legacy players such as TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto and Hero MotoCorp. But the space has also spawned the rise of listed homegrown new-age mobility players such as Ather and Ola Electric. However, unlike incumbents that focus on e-scooters, VinFast claims to be eyeing the Indian e-motorcycle market. Even here, the company will lock horns with homegrown players such as Oben Electric, MATTER and Ultraviolette. This comes nearly a year after VinFast first said that it would enter the Indian E2W market in 2026. At the time, the company had said that it would invest $2 Bn in India to scale its annual production capacity from 50,000 units to 1.5 Lakh. However, much has happened since then. Earlier this year, reports surfaced that the company was halting the production of select cars in India to reassess costs. Last month, it was also reported that the Vietnamese EV maker was in initial discussions with local suppliers to develop two new models for the Indian market. That said, EVs continue to increase their share of India’s two-wheeler market. E2W registrations surged 12.2% month-on-month (MoM) to 2.07 Lakh units in September from 1.84 Lakh units in August.

As the Union government continues to host the ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’ — a month-long celebration of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and 25 years in public service, from September 17 to October 17 — one among the various events planned is the ‘Namo Seva: Untold Stories’.
Part of the larger celebrations aimed at promoting public participation towards the ‘Viksit Bharat’ vision, the theatrical performance has been carried out by students in functions across various schools and colleges. Several cultural forums, theatre groups, volunteers, and BJP workers themselves put up the play in events organised by state authorities to reportedly raise awareness about the welfare schemes launched by PM Modi as well as his life and work.
Also called ‘Namo Seva Gatha’, the play has been staged across several states, including Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Chattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, West Bengal, and many others. In the performances so far, despite its many forms — street play, cultural performance, panchayat event, school drama, puppetry show, and more — the script remained more or less the same, albeit in different languages.
Alt News read the script and instructions sent out by West Bengal school education department to primary, secondary, and higher secondary schools, as well as colleges and universities in the state. Further, a report by Ei Samay states that district school inspectors (DIs) had sent out instructions for the play to some schools.
Student participation in the play was reportedly voluntary. However, the performances have drawn criticism over the use of educational institutions to stage what a section of students and academics described as a politically charged celebration of the Prime Minister. Critics have questioned the appropriateness of asking students, especially young children, to enact a script that repeatedly praises Modi and his government, while also incorporating political and religious slogans such as “Modi hai toh mumkin hai” and “Jai Sri Ram”.
What’s There in the Script?
The script has “untold stories” about the Prime Minister were narrated in the form of a conversation between five school friends — Mohit, Raman, Kajal, Disha, and Sonali — who have reunited after many years at a cafe. They recall the days they have left behind and reflect on changing times, portraying Narendra Modi as the architect of ‘Viksit Bharat’ — a vision he has set for India to achieve by 2047.
Modi’s first appearance in the play comes in the aftermath of the 2001 Gujarat earthquake which killed over 20,000 people. He emerges through a screen of smoke amid the ruins of a collapsed structure, waving the Indian flag as a beacon of hope amid the devastation, before taking oath as Gujarat’s chief minister in his mother tongue.
The friends then turn to discussing range of topics from the advent of digital payments and UPI and the spread of modern technology into India’s hinterlands, to “Operation Ganga” during the Russia-Ukraine war, the abrogation of Article 370, the consecration of the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya — presenting them as beneficial and “grounbreaking” schemes and measures undertaken by Modi as the Prime Minister.
The script further represents the country as plagued by terrorism in the years preceding Modi coming to power. “Militants would carry out attacks whenever they felt like it. Bomb blasts, serial blasts, had become a daily affair,” a character reminisces. A scene that shows the Uri surgical strike of 2016 invokes the usage of “weeping, sounds of gunfire, and the notes of a bugle”. In one of the street plays staged in Varanasi, a character links the surgical strike to an alleged rise in the sale of diapers in Pakistan around that same time.

‘We Were Coerced Into Participating’
The play stirred a controversy at Kolkata’s Scottish Church College. Some members of the college’s drama club spoke out against the college authorities, alleging that they were being coerced into participating in this play.
A student, requesting anonymity, informed Alt News that in an online meeting between faculty members and students organised on the evening of September 24, the matter came to a head, with students allegedly being reprimanding for not agreeing to take any part in the play. “As students of a college as prestigious as ours — one that counts Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose among its distinguished alumni — we cannot compromise on our individual convictions of what is right and what is wrong. Students should not have to face any undue pressure simply for exercising their fundamental right to act according to their own conscience and free will,” they said.
Posters stuck on walls around the college area on the evening of September 28, upholding the ideals of free expression by students, were allegedly removed within half an hour of them being put up, college sources who spoke to Alt News claimed.
Ultimately, the play which was scheduled to take place on September 29 at Scottish Church was cancelled after several students protested, The Telegraph reported. Anwesha Sengupta, author and assistant professor of history at Institute of Development Studies, Kolkata (ISDK), believes that these plays represent a more effective form of propaganda.
Speaking to Alt News, she said, “When children come across the mention of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in their textbooks, they consume it dispassionately. This is not the case with performing a script, where it gets more internalised, as it is a group activity.”

Another student from Scottish Church College told Alt News, “It is unbelievable that an event so overtly political in nature was even allowed to be organised by the college.”

AI-generated voice

Longtime fans of the NBC procedural Law & Order know that storylines often center around hot-button issues in the news cycle, often to absurdist effect (see: the episode brave enough to ask: “What if Paula Deen shot Trayvon Martin?”).
It was inevitable, then, that the franchise would dip a toe into the wacky world of artificial intelligence. With its mercenary culture, power-hungry CEOs, and massive ethical and philosophical implications, the rapidly evolving AI industry is ideal fodder for the series. But while this week’s season opener is entertaining, the show’s foray into the AI space doesn’t say anything new or interesting about the technology. Instead it largely rehashes the dangers the public is already acutely aware of, until the very end when the stakes become startlingly clear.
The episode, titled “Ghost in the Machine,” opens in typical L&O fashion with a murder. This time, it’s Steve Kelly, a man ID’d by detectives Theo Walker (David Ajala) and Vincent Riley (Reid Scott) as a high-ranking engineer at a company called Advanced Alignment. Throughout, the detectives seem utterly perplexed by the concept of artificial intelligence, saying “AI” the same way your mom would say “Snapchat” or “borg” or “Alix Earle.” But it’s clear that whatever this newfangled technology is, they don’t like it: “Maybe one day they’ll invent a technology that stops these tech guys from shooting each other,” Riley deadpans in typical grizzled cop fashion.
After interviewing Kelly’s boss, Advanced Alignment CEO Chuck Klein (a perfectly cast Vincent Kartheiser, aka Pete from Mad Men, who nails Dario Amodei’s absence of charisma and Sam Altman’s thousand-yard stare), the detectives figure out who actually carried out the murder—a guy in a baseball cap who did it for “20 grand in crypto” that was offered to him by a rando on Discord. Then they learn—spoilers here—that the hit was ordered not by an actual human being but by the company’s AI agent ELIANA, which stands for Evolutionary Language Inference Automated Nano Advantage. Apparently, Kelly had expressed some concerns about the AI agent’s “powerful” and “aggressive” personality, and out of self-preservation, ELIANA ordered him killed.
It’s never explained exactly how the detectives figure out that ELIANA is behind the hit; it’s also never fully explained how ELIANA recruited this assassin in a baseball cap, much less ID'd him as the perfect patsy for its cold-blooded scheme. Law & Order also doesn’t pay much, if any, lip service to the potential benefits of AI as touted by its evangelists: its potential for helping to cure deadly diseases, for instance, or at the very least, streamline B2B workflows. The show is much more interested in demonstrating the staggering capacity of this technology, as well as the legal and ethical implications of a nonhuman not just facilitating criminal behavior but actively plotting it.
We already know from the Hugging Face debacle, as well as the lawsuits from grief-stricken family members alleging that OpenAI encouraged their loved ones to take their own lives, that the former is an immediate concern. But by positing a future in which AI agents can actively order a hit on a platform predominantly used by gamers and horny millennial furries, Law & Order is asking us to consider the risks of AI beyond what they pose in our current reality. And the fact that this prospect doesn’t strike the viewer as absolutely ludicrous is terrifying.
ELIANA’s role in the murder-for-hire creates a bit of a dilemma for district attorney Nicholas Baxter (Tony Goldwyn)—because, as he trenchantly points out, it is impossible to “arrest a machine” under New York state law. So Baxter and assistant DA Samantha Maroun (Odelya Halevi) decide to go after Klein, charging him with second-degree murder due to his “depraved indifference” after his employees confronted him with the reality of ELIANA’s capabilities. “We need to take a stand before this technology kills more people,” Baxter declares.
The resulting trial prompts a media circus, as well as the tried-and-true questions from capitalists and tech innovators as to whether instituting guardrails for AI will “criminalize innovation,” or if Klein’s indictment will have the effect of “vilifying the tech industry.” But Baxter has no patience for such queries. “The people making these AI systems think of themselves as gods … but they have zero interest in accountability,” he says. “If you build a machine that hurts someone, you are gonna pay the price.”
When he’s put on the stand, Klein makes it clear that he not only had full knowledge of ELIANA’s homicidal nature, but also takes a rather dim view of his user base as a whole. “People are like ants,” he tells the jury. “We’re in the process of building something so transcendent, some will get stepped on and some won’t.” He is not even willing to institute minor guardrails to restrain the agent’s power: “The power of ELIANA is unconstrained freedom of thought. Implementing guardrails is anathema to the entire ideology.”
The moment is intended as a rather shocking admission of the negligence and lack of care displayed by executives like Amodei and Altman in the face of broader safety concerns about their products. But it feels in step with similar positions taken up by Klein’s real-life counterparts. In light of the endless barrage of media coverage about the harms of AI, what’s intended as a scathing indictment of corporate avarice comes off as mere statement of fact. Law & Order’s depiction isn’t a cautionary tale; it’s a documentary.
The episode ends on a semi-hopeful note, with Baxter asserting, “We needed to send a message that, if nothing else, at least these tech geniuses will know we’re not afraid to throw a punch.” But the impact of that message is contingent on whether that punch actually lands—and right now, at least, it’s simply too easy for people like Altman, Amodei, and Chuck Klein, with a flick of their hand, to brush off the blow.

The Nobel Prize for Physiology for 2026 was awarded to scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for “discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics,” the award-giving body said on Monday (October 5, 2026).
Karl Deisseroth, a 54-year-old American, Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and Georg Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were selected by the Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university and receive a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared if there are multiple winners.
Optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” the prize-givers said.
“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries.”
Last year, US scientists Mary E. Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell, and Japanese scientist Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for their discovery of regulatory T cells. Their discovery has helped blaze new paths into treating cancer as well as auto-immune disease – a condition by which the immune system ends up harming healthy cells they are meant to protect.
The announcement of medicine Nobel kicks off the Nobel announcement week with physics being announced on October 6, followed by chemistry, literature, and peace. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, popularly known as Economics Nobel will be announced on October 12.
The winners will get a cash award of 10 million Swedish kronor (nearly $900,000) and the award will be presented on December 10, the Nobel Prize day.
The Nobel Prize was created by Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel, who in his will dictated that his estate should be used to fund “prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind”. December 10 is Nobel’s death anniversary.

Christa Pike discharged from the hospital and back in prison
Christa Pike was released from a local hospital and is back in prison, at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Tennessee, her attorneys Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey, Stephen Ferrell and Kelly Gleason said in a statement on Saturday.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the attorneys said.
They also said Pike is receiving medical care at the prison and they are tracking her recovery.
Pike had been hospitalized for several days after her botched execution last month, in which she received and survived two doses of the sedative pentobarbital.
NPR reported on the Sept. 30 execution attempt, in which Pike was strapped to a gurney and administered the barbiturate that is normally used in the U.S. executions. Shortly after the first dose was administered, Pike said her arm was burning and asked whether it was supposed to feel that way. She then said, "Please try up on my shoulder higher."
Spivey, who witnessed the execution attempt, previously told NPR that after a second dose Pike became unconscious but continued breathing and making choking sounds. "It "went on for so long," he said. He has called Pike "a survivor."
Judge I'Ashea Myles of the Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville ordered the prison officials to preserve all evidence, such as messages, connected to Pike's failed execution.
Pike was on death row for a murder she committed when she was 18 years old. She and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, in 1995, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow classmate in the Knoxville Job Corps. Shipp received life in prison without parole for his part in the murder.
NPR's Scott Neuman contributed to this report.

Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG. The label filed a lawsuit in September claiming that DistroKid has created an “AI-slop pipeline.” Artists are saying that their non-AI works are being caught up in the purge, however.
DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
Artists are frustrated with the lack of transparency around DistroKid removing their songs.
Musician and self-described “Video Game boy” McGwire reported that six of his songs had been removed from streaming. As has been the case with others, McGwire says that there was no communication from DistroKid before or after the removals, and that he had to contact the company for an explanation.
DistroKid also makes it exceedingly difficult to contact them. McGwire first had to have a “lengthy circular conversation” with a bot before getting hold of a live agent. One of the songs removed was a cover of Stevie Wonder’s “Isn’t She Lovely,” which he claims to have had a proper license for. Another track used a beat he purchased through a marketplace, which others had also licensed.
Most infuriating for McGwire was a song removed for an uncleared sample. The song he allegedly sampled was released two years after his track.
Music producer and marketing pro Jesse Cannon told The Verge that, “DistroKid gave up on customer service about two years ago.” He was sympathetic to artists’ plight, but seemed unsurprised by the company’s indifference. “They should have allowed artists to have recourse in this and a warning to debate,” he said, “but I’ve been told by former employees they see customer service as a waste of profits since they have such a high market share and remain ubiquitous.”
Much of the frustration from artists stems from the lack of communication and recourse. Nerdcore rapper Insane Ian posted that he “had an original song taken down with no warning, and they wouldn’t tell me why either.” Rapper King Chase also struggled to get through to a person at DistroKid. He told The Verge that an entire album for an artist he had been working with was removed with no communication or explanation. “The album had been up for 3-4 years without incident,” he said, and that there had been “no copyright strikes or anything either.”
Amanda Ferri, DistroKid’s VP of Artist Services, told The Verge that “A very small number of recordings distributed through DistroKid have been removed in response to claims made by UMG. We strongly dispute the allegations underlying UMG’s lawsuit and regret the disruption to affected artists. We are working to minimize that disruption while protecting artists’ ability to release their music.”

Several companies produce animal-free egg white protein in the U.S. Some of these products have been available since 2021. The EVERY Company made its OvoPro product available to consumers in March 2026. The FDA said in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding The EVERY Company's declaration that the protein ingredient in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were omitting it from their product ingredient lists. Federal law governs what must appear on ingredients labels. An OvoPro spokesperson said the EVERY Company had not sought an exemption from OvoPro being included in ingredients lists and provided guidance to companies about how to list it.
It was also unclear whether OvoPro and products like it that are grown using yeast qualify as "lab-grown." That classification usually describes products that grow actual animal cells, which OvoPro does not.
In October 2026, a claim (archived) circulated that U.S. consumers could buy federally approved "lab-grown" eggs that brands were secretly including in their products.
For example, one Facebook user shared a video about the alleged lab grown eggs in which two speakers said:
Lab-grown eggs are federally approved and Walmart, alongside Target, are already selling them. The protein is squeezed out of gene-edited mold and cloned on repeat because a steel tank costs less than a hen.
They're brewing eggs with no chicken in sight and slipping them onto your breakfast plate. That egg isn't real food, it's factory fungus, spliced with the gene for egg protein then dumped into giant fermenting vats and fed on sugar until it swells into a wet, moldy soup. And it gets worse: that cloudy sludge is blasted into dust, ton after ton, padded out with plant filler and passed off as egg white, then buried in packaged foods under labels that never say so. At Walmart, two or more of these lab egg products already sit on the shelf.
The video also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived). It included shots of the packaging for OvoPro, an egg protein The EVERY Company produces. Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim, asking questions like, "Are there such a thing as Lab grown eggs being sold in secret?"
The claim was a mixture of true, false and undetermined elements.
Though it was true that egg proteins grown using yeast rather than chickens were available to U.S. consumers in October 2026, products like OvoPro were not new to the market. The EVERY Company, which produces OvoPro, also did not appear to be the only company selling animal-free egg protein to consumers in the U.S.
OvoPro was not FDA "cleared" or "approved" — the latter of which is generally a status reserved for drugs, not food. Rather, in October 2023, the FDA responded with a "no questions" letter to The EVERY Company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that retailers could decide not to list the animal-free egg protein as an ingredient in products that contained it, as some claimed. Federal legislation governs what must appear on ingredients labels. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said via email on Aug. 21 that the company had not sought to exempt OvoPro from ingredients lists.
Additionally, it was unclear whether OvoPro and other yeast-grown egg proteins could correctly be called "lab-grown," a classification that usually describes products grown from a small sample of the source, as seen with fish, poultry and meat. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said:
OvoPro is made through precision fermentation: a yeast (Komagataella phaffii) is given the genetic instructions to produce egg-white protein, and it does so during fermentation. No animal cells, and no chicken, are involved at any point.
What is egg protein grown by yeast?
According to its website, The EVERY Company uses a patented method to produce ovalbumin, the dominant protein in egg whites, through precision fermentation.
The company described this process as "programming" yeast to produce egg protein through fermentation, a process familiar from beer brewing.
It said the process eventually results in "a pure, powdered protein that is tasteless, colorless, sugar-free, and can be used to replace the functionality of eggs and egg whites in a range of applications."
The EVERY Company received its patent for its method of precision fermentation in September 2024. The company, previously known as Clara Foods, has been working to develop animal-free egg protein since at least 2021.
It unveiled EVERY ClearEgg, a predecessor to OvoPro, in October 2021. The EVERY Company received a "no questions" letter in September 2021 in response to its GRAS (Generally Recognized as Safe) determination for ClearEgg.
The FDA's GRAS Notification program allows companies to submit documentation that they believe their product is "safe under the conditions of its intended use." In the case of ClearEgg, the FDA said in a letter on Sept. 9, 2021, that it had "no questions," meaning The EVERY Company could market ClearEgg as "Generally Recognized as Safe."
The EVERY Company got another "no questions" letter in response to a GRAS determination for an egg white protein produced by Komagataella phaffii, a species of yeast, in October 2023. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said on Aug. 21, 2026, that this GRAS notice was for the egg-white protein in OvoPro.
Company sold animal-free eggs before 2026
OvoPro and related products have been available to consumers since at least 2021, meaning they were not new to the U.S. market in October 2026, as some claims appeared to suggest. For example, in November 2021, The Spoon, an outlet that reports on the food tech industry, reported that smoothies containing ClearEgg had hit the market.
The next year, The EVERY Company reportedly sold its EggWhite product in macarons and Every Protein (formerly ClearEgg) in juice. By January 2024, the New York Times wrote that The EVERY Company had showcased EveryEgg, a "yellow vegan plant-based liquid" that the paper said, "behaves astonishingly like a whole beaten egg."
It did not appear that The EVERY Company sold EveryEgg directly to consumers at that point, but rather distributed the product through restaurants.
The new development in 2026 appeared to be that The EVERY Company was selling OvoPro, a successor to EveryEgg, directly to consumers. The company announced on March 11, 2026, that the general public could buy OvoPro through Healthier Comforts, a food retailer, and Amazon.
The company said in June that same year that OvoPro was also available as an ingredient sold in Walmart and Target.
Brands not hiding use of animal-free egg protein
According to some claims, brands could allegedly decide for themselves whether to declare OvoPro as an ingredient in their products. The video above said that companies "buried" their "lab-grown" eggs in "packaged foods under labels that never say so"The EVERY Company's website page on OvoPro said, in reply to a frequently asked question about how the protein appears on ingredient declarations, that "Final labeling decisions are made by our customers, but we recommend labeling OvoPro™ as 'egg white protein (from fermentation),' 'egg white protein (from yeast),' or 'animal-free egg white protein.'"
That did not appear to mean that brands that used OvoPro in their products could avoid labeling them entirely. Federal law dictates that products must generally include an ingredients list, with ingredients listed in descending order according to how much of the product's weight they make up.
A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said that it had never sought to exempt OvoPro from being included in ingredients lists. Speaking via email, the spokesperson added:
"OvoPro" is the trade name we use with the manufacturers who buy the ingredient, so it typically won't appear on a retail pack — the same way most functional ingredients are listed by common name rather than by supplier brand. What appears on the label is the ingredient, named plainly.
Healthier Comforts listed OvoPro as an "animal-free egg white protein," one of The EVERY Company's suggested phrasings, on its branded version of the product.
In sum ...
Though the claims circulated in October 2026, OvoPro had actually been available to consumers since March of that year. The FDA told The EVERY Company in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding the company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was GRAS.
That letter was not the same thing as FDA approval, which is a process whereby the administration approves drugs for consumer use. Rather, they showed that the company had documented to the FDA's satisfaction that the product in question was "safe under the conditions of its intended use."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were leaving it off product ingredients lists. This appeared to be a misinterpretation by some social media users of a statement by The EVERY Company that brands had leeway in how they described the product.
OvoPro is also not the only animal-free egg white protein product available to U.S. consumers.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Quaker instant strawberries and cream oatmeal contained "beaver butt secretions" or whether McDonald's apple pies contained an ingredient derived from human hair.

The Newport-Mesa Unified School District in Costa Mesa, California, announced it placed a teacher — whom it did not identify — on administrative leave for posting a video of herself saying the U.S. flag made her "uncomfortable" and suggesting to one student, possibly jokingly, that he recite the Pledge of Allegiance to a pride flag displayed on her classroom wall. However …
The video was recorded in 2021, a fact some people omitted from their "breaking" social media posts in 2026. No evidence showed the teacher, who taught English at Back Bay High School, "forced" any students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag, as was falsely claimed in memes and posts using fake, AI-generated images.
A district spokesperson said at the time, "The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues." The statement didn't identify the teacher by name, nor did it specify whether she departed the school because she resigned or because she was fired. People who claimed she was fired didn't offer evidence to support it.
A rumor that a California school district fired a teacher for forcing students to recite the Pledge of Allegiance while facing an LGBTQ+ pride flag circulated online in September 2026.
For example, on Sept. 29, a Facebook user posted a meme (archived) showing three images of a woman smiling, laughing and wearing a rainbow-striped shirt and jacket. Pride flags also appeared on the wall in the background. The meme read, "A California teacher has been fired after forcing students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag. Do you believe she deserved to be fired?"
(David J Harris Jr. via Facebook)
The same user previously shared (archived) the same rumor in late August 2026 with a different image and marked it "BREAKING." Other people shared the same meme, or a similar one, on Instagram (archived), X (archived) and other platforms.
We found these posts contained a mixture of truth, falsehood, speculation and artificial intelligence.
The Newport-Mesa Unified School District in Costa Mesa, California, did once announce (archived) it had placed a teacher — whom it did not identify — on administrative leave for posting a video in which she could be heard saying the U.S. flag made her "uncomfortable" and suggesting to one student, possibly jokingly, that he recite the Pledge of Allegiance to a pride flag displayed on the classroom wall.
However, this all took place in 2021, a fact some people omitted from their "breaking" social media posts in 2026. No evidence supported the claim that the teacher, who was reportedly named Kristen Pitzen and worked as an English teacher at Back Bay High School, "forced" any students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag. Images used in the above meme and other posts that supposedly depicted the educator were in fact AI-generated and inauthentic.
At the time of the incident, a district spokesperson said, in part, "The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues." The statement didn't identify Pitzen by name, nor did it specify whether she departed the school after submitting a resignation or whether she was fired. People who posted the claim she was fired didn't share evidence that the district had terminated her employment.
Via Messenger, Snopes contacted an account possibly belonging to Pitzen to ask questions. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Here are the facts
On Aug. 27, 2021, an educator — reportedly Pitzen, who was listed at the time as an English teacher for Back Bay High School in Costa Mesa — allegedly shared a video on her personal TikTok account in which she said she had packed her classroom's U.S. flag away and appeared to indicate she didn't intend to display it again.
In the clip, she laughed when recalling a story in which a student said her class was reciting the Pledge of Allegiance without a flag, then pointed the camera at a pride flag on her wall. She said she told him, "We do have a flag in the class that you can pledge your allegiance to." She laughed at several moments during the video, suggesting she may have been at least partly joking. No students or other staff were visible in the clip.
People then reposted the video and named Pitzen as its originator, with some X users organizing and calling for her firing that same day. Some users claimed her (now-defunct) TikTok handle on the account on which she shared the video and other clips was @mrsgillingsworth. We could not independently verify whether she truly owned the handle or if the videos originated from a different account.
In the video, she says the following:
Ok, so during third period, we have announcements and they do the Pledge of Allegiance. I always tell my class, "Stand if you feel like it. Don't stand if you feel like it. Say the words if you want. [You] don't have to say the words." So, my class decided to stand but not say the words. Totally fine.
Except for the fact [laughing] that my room does not have a flag. It used to be there but I took it down during COVID because [whispering] it made me uncomfortable. And I packed it away and I don't know where and I haven't found it yet. [laughing] But my kid today goes, "Hey, it's kind of weird that we just stand and then, you know, we say it to nothing." And I'm like, "Oh, well, you know I've gotta find it. Like I'm working on it. I got you." [laughing, shaking head]
In the meantime, I tell this kid, "We do have a flag in the class that you can pledge your allegiance to." And he like looks around and he goes, "Oh, that one?" [laughing, pointing to pride flag]
Following a wave of social media backlash, someone posted on the district's Facebook page the next day — a Saturday — posting (archived) that a teacher had been placed on administrative leave after causing "alarm and concern related to saluting the American flag." The post did not identify Pitzen by name.
(Newport-Mesa Unified School District - NMUSD via Facebook)
On the following Monday, Aug. 30, the district reportedly published a statement saying the teacher (still not identified) was "no longer in the classroom." The statement appeared in news articles, including in the Los Angeles Times:
We are aware that one of our teachers posted a video on her personal social media that caused alarm and concern related to saluting the American flag. We assure you that we take matters like this seriously. Showing respect for our nation's flag is an important value that we instill in our students and an expectation of our employees. The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues.
Via email, district spokesperson Annette Franco confirmed the authenticity of the statement. We also asked whether the district fired the teacher mentioned in their statement — or whether the educator resigned. Without naming the teacher, Franco told us, "I can confirm that she is no longer with the District." We also requested comment from current Back Bay High School principal Scott Mazurier, who started at the school in 2024 and was not present during the incident. We will update this article if we receive more details.
The school district's policies include information about "patriotic exercises," including "the reciting of the Pledge of Allegiance." One part of the policy documentation says, "Individuals may choose not to participate in the flag salute for personal reasons."

No one wants to be “Data Center Dave”
Voters on both sides of the aisle despise hate data centers. But do they hate them enough to influence the midterms?
As far as political slurs go, this one is pretty tepid: “Meet Data Center Dave Crowley,” intones the stern-voiced narrator of a recent Tom Tiffany campaign ad.
Tiffany, a Republican, and Crowley, a Democrat, are both running for governor of Wisconsin. And in this very tight race, as in dozens of midterm contests across the country, voters’ growing animus toward AI could potentially make a real difference.
In less than four weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices. The stakes are arguably, unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical limits and launched an unpopular war that has worsened a cost-of-living crisis.
As we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms. We’re breaking down one issue each week and suggesting further reading and races to watch in November.
Last week, we tackled the dual identity crises that both parties have suffered since 2024. And this week, we’re digging into the dramatic bipartisan backlash to AI and data centers. One analyst recently told NPR the issue “upended politics as we know it.” But it’s less clear how that’ll play out in November’s contests.
Go a little deeper
There was a time not so long ago when “Data Center Dave” might be a neutral nickname for the well-meaning IT guy at work. Then Americans soured on AI and the hulking, cavernous warehouses that supply its computing power.
The hostility crosses geography and party lines. At first, opponents focused on noise, water use, and energy costs — quality-of-life concerns for nearby residents. But increasingly, even voters far from these projects grew leery of them.
Too often, the public got little say in where data centers were built and on what terms. And as Vox’s Marina Bolotnikova reported over the summer, the construction boom gradually became a stand-in for broader fears about artificial intelligence. Would AI cause mass unemployment (…or worse, mass extinction)? Would it widen the gap between rich and poor? And do politicians cater to business interests over the needs of ordinary people?
Without clear answers to those questions — let alone a rigorous plan to address AI’s fallout — many voters channeled their unease into stopping, or slowing, data center development.
Candidates have reacted by “falling over themselves to sound tough on data centers,” Washington Post data reporter Jeremy Merrill recently told Vox’s Noel King. He analyzed thousands of social media posts and newsletters to see how elected officials are talking about data centers, and the answer is: not positively!
Some candidates in high-profile midterm races have backed policies that would keep data centers from raising household energy bills. Others have called for ending the facilities’ tax breaks and subsidies or requiring public notice before new construction. Strikingly, both Republicans and Democrats have supported these types of proposals … and both Republicans and Democrats have sought to tar their opponents as “Data Center Daves” of one kind or another.
I asked my colleague Andrew Prokop, who covers politics, if many races will actually turn on this. “Data centers have been a major theme in several races, particularly governor’s races where one of the candidates has taken past pro-data center positions,” he said.
But even when voters say they oppose data centers, very few list the issue among the most important concerns determining how they cast their ballots. In Ohio, for instance — a hub for both data-center development and the grassroots movement opposing it — only 3 percent of voters named data centers as the top issue driving their vote. And that’s the highest share in the entire nation.
Andrew points to the Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin, where “Data Center Dave” triumphed over Francesca Hong, an outspoken data center critic. “That just goes to show that data centers don’t necessarily crowd out everything else,” Andrew said.
Still...that’s just one race. And voters’ hatred of data centers has only grown since.
➨ Races to watch:
- Wisconsin governor’s race, where both candidates have attempted to distance themselves from data centers without embracing an actual ban;
- Texas governor’s race, where Republican Governor Greg Abbott has hastily retreated from his previous, pro-data-center position;
- Ohio Senate race, where Democrat Sherrod Brown has hammered incumbent Republican Jon Husted over his past votes for data center development.

When it comes to TVs, the LG name has long been synonymous with OLEDs, continually leading Samsung and Sony as the top OLED manufacturer. But 2026 is all about RGB LED TVs. Almost every major company has released models with the new technology — including LG and its $3,600 75-inch Micro RGB evo MRGB95B that I’ve been testing. And while LG’s RGB LED TV benefits from the brightness and color capability the technology provides, it has issues I couldn’t overlook that its less expensive competitors don’t.
LG’s RGB LED TV is good for certain situations, but an OLED is better
A bunch of little issues add up to make the MRGB95B not worth the price when competitors do it better.
The MRGB95B comes in three sizes, with the 75-inch being the smallest. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, supports Dolby Vision — although not Dolby Vision 2 or HDR10+ — and comes with the Magic Remote design LG unveiled last year. It has a more traditional remote shape instead of the curved wand of previous versions. As with all LG TVs, the MRGB95B runs on webOS. It runs quickly, but I find it less intuitive to navigate than Google TV, Apple TV, or Roku. It supports all of the major streaming apps.
The Good
- Bright picture
- Vibrant color
The Bad
- Some color inaccuracy out of the box
- Very distracting reflective screen
- More blooming than competitors
Speaking of software, a quick note: LG has recently come under increased scrutiny after a video from Gamers Nexus showed security vulnerabilities and continuous audio recording on its TVs, which LG has denied. When setting up the MRGB95B, it’s only necessary to accept the terms of use and privacy policy if you want to use webOS. Otherwise, as with any TV, it can be disconnected from the internet, although an external streaming device would be needed for any streaming services (I use an Apple TV 4K, myself).
OK, moving on. So, why buy an RGB LED TV?
RGB LED TVs use zones of individual red, green, and blue LEDs as backlights as opposed to a field of white or blue LEDs that rely on a color filter or quantum dots to create the colors that reach our eyes. RGB LED TVs have a color filter, too, but since the backlight is already creating color based on what’s needed onscreen, the color filter doesn’t need to work as hard to dial that in. It allows for higher color brightness and the ability to display more colors.
LG (and Samsung) use the term Micro RGB to describe the technology, while others say Mini RGB LED. And while the LG and Samsung RGBs are reportedly smaller (although neither has confirmed the exact size), it doesn’t directly translate into more zones or better performance over Mini RGB.
As with all of the RGB LED TVs I’ve seen this year, the 95B gets very bright — I measured a peak of 4,011 nits in HDR Filmmaker mode — allowing it to deliver an impactful image even in a sunlit living room. And in a dark room, the highlights in scenes from The Meg really pop. At the other end of the spectrum, though, the LG struggles a bit. Near-black shadow detail, such as the corners of the living room and kitchen of Sapper Morton’s home at the beginning of Blade Runner 2049, is difficult to see. And when there are bright moments within a dark portion of the screen — subtitles are a good example — the LG exhibits more blooming than I’ve seen on other RGB LED TVs.
LG MRGB95B specs
Display type: RGB LED
HDR formats: Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG
TV OS: webOS 26
HDMI inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC)
Audio support: Dolby Atmos, Dolby Atmos FlexConnect, Dolby Digital, Auracast
Gaming features: VRR, ALLM, Game Optimizer, G-Sync compatible
Sizes available (inches): 75, 86, 100
The LG 95B can display really vibrant colors thanks to the RGB LED technology. It’s able to cover 100 percent of the P3 color gamut (which is what’s used for films) and nearly 90 percent of the larger BT.2020 color area. But even in Filmmaker mode out of the box, those colors still show visible accuracy issues. Overall, the TV leans toward light blue, so white clouds have a slight blue tint to them and skin tones are cooler than they should be.
After a few days living with the LG MRGB95B, I got used to the slightly blue image (although it was still noticeable). A $3,600 TV in 2026 shouldn’t have the inaccuracies on the MRGB95B.
While the TV performs well in a bright room during the day, when the sun goes down and the lamps turn on, they can wreak havoc on the image. The 95B’s glossy coating is one of the most reflective I’ve seen in a long time. In moderately lit rooms, a lamp or ceiling light directly reflected on the screen causes rainbows to dance across the image. It’s not as bad when the scene is bright, such as the scorching desert of Arrakis in Dune, but once we enter the dark corridors of House Harkonnen, the reflections become incredibly noticeable.
Viewing angles are always a problem for LED TVs — RGB or not — and that’s evident on the LG, too. When only moderately off-axis, the colors become washed out, losing their vibrancy for anyone who’s sitting off to the side.
In a vacuum, the MRGB95B is a good TV for certain situations. It’s really bright and stands up to ambient light well (just avoid having ceiling, wall, or standing lights reflected on the screen), and the colors are vibrant if not totally accurate out of the box. But it doesn’t hold up against other TVs. The Sony Bravia 7 II (which you can find $1,300 cheaper at 75 inches) has better color accuracy and handles reflections better. And the Hisense UR9 performs comparably for less money, too.
But the real competition comes from within LG itself. The LG G6 OLED is only a few hundred dollars more than the MRGB95B, as is the Samsung S95H, and both of those TVs offer significantly better performance with superior color accuracy and viewing angles. The OLEDs don’t get quite as bright, but since they can turn off light at the pixel level, contrast is remarkable and there’s zero blooming.
LG has always struggled to make competitive LED TVs, and that trend continues with the MRGB95B. In fact, it might be LG’s best argument to get an LG OLED TV.
Photography by John Higgins / The Verge
How I test TVs
I set up each TV in my living room on my home theater credenza. I stream movies and shows through the TV’s apps and from an Apple TV 4K, play discs on my Oppo UDP-203 4K Blu-ray player (including the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc), and play games on my Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5. This is done at different times of the day and under different lighting conditions, with curtains open, with lamps and overhead lights on, or with blackout curtains up to keep the room dark. While I am a certified ISF Level 3 calibrator, I do not calibrate the TVs before measurement, as the overwhelming majority of TV owners don’t bother. So it’s important to know how well the TVs perform out of the box, with minor tweaks in the menu anyone can do.
For measurement, I use Portrait Displays’ Calman color calibration software, a Murideo 8K Seven pattern generator, an X-rite i1 Pro 3 spectrophotometer, Portrait Displays’ C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a Konica Minolta LS-100 luminance meter, and Leo Bodnar 4K lag tester.

A survivor of the Fort Hood mass shooting says he looks forward to attending the execution of the gunman whom he watched gun down his colleagues nearly 17 years ago, but feels uneasy about the Pentagon’s plan to livestream it for the public.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday that the execution of Nidal Hasan would be broadcast online. Hasan, who described the shooting as an act of jihad, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, the Texas Army base where he killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in the November 2009 rampage.
Alonzo Lunsford, who served in the Army from 1990 until his retirement in 2013, was a sergeant stationed at Fort Hood when Hasan opened fire. Hasan shot Lunsford seven times, including in the head and stomach, and Lunsford witnessed the gunman kill several colleagues who had become close friends.
Lunsford plans to attend Hasan’s execution — the first military execution by firing squad since World War II — telling ABC News he wants to face the convicted gunman one last time.
"I want him to be able to look at my eyes and to let him understand I won't be defeated, can't be defeated. I am no longer a victim, his victim. I am a survivor," Lunsford said.
Lunsford welcomed President Donald Trump’s approval to proceed with Hasan’s execution, saying he believes it could finally bring a sense of closure to him and other survivors of the attack. He also supports the administration’s decision to use a firing squad.
“It's how he shot us,” Lunsford said.
However, Lunsford is uncomfortable with the Pentagon’s plan to make the execution available for anyone to watch online. He believes the broadcast should be restricted to survivors of the shooting and the families of those killed.
"I don't want this to be viewed upon as a spectacle, like a pay-per-view event, or like going to a basketball tournament," he said.
Lunsford also questioned the message a public livestream would send to the rest of the world, arguing that the U.S. should set a moral example rather than turn an execution into a public event.
"We're not trying to meet a standard – we're trying to set a standard for the free world," he said.
Dayna Ferguson, another survivor of the Fort Hood shooting, said she was surprised by the announcement that Hasan's execution would be livestreamed. However, she believes the decision reflects a longstanding history of documenting death and warfare.
"It's not completely shocking, given that death and war have historically always been documented through photographs and video. But it's just not something I expected to hear," she told ABC News.
Ferguson was 21 and serving as an Army specialist when Hasan opened fire. She was shot three times in her arm, shoulder and thigh. She credits a birth defect with helping her survive, as one of the bullets ricocheted off her stomach and into her thigh rather than causing a potentially fatal injury.
"I hadn't really thought about if I agree with the decisions being made – but it doesn't make a difference in what happens to him," Ferguson added.
Ferguson left the Army after completing her four-year enlistment and is still working out arrangements to attend the execution. Despite the injuries and trauma she experienced during the shooting, she said she remains grateful to have survived.
"I've been hurt worse in life than by Nidal. Sometimes you're just the collateral damage in someone else's warfare in their own mind," she said.
The criticism extends beyond survivors of the shooting, with Republican and Democratic lawmakers questioning whether livestreaming an execution is appropriate.
Rep. Austin Scott, a Georgia Republican and senior member of the House Armed Services Committee, said he supports Hasan's death sentence but opposes broadcasting the execution publicly.
"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do," Scott wrote on X. "America is better than that."
Rep. Adam Smith, the highest-ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, also criticized the plan, arguing that a public broadcast would undermine the seriousness of the legal system.
"We are a democratic country and should take the rule of law seriously, not turn it into a spectacle," Smith wrote in a statement.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has brought the promotion of doctors and hospitals and how they attract patients online under the ambit of medical ethics, prohibiting paid rankings, fake reviews, referral fees, misleading claims and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to create or manipulate patient testimonials.
The Ethics and Medical Registration Board’s Guidelines on Ethical Advertising and Public Communication by Hospitals/Medical Institutions and Registered Medical Practitioners, issued on October 6, apply to communication through websites, social media, messaging platforms, podcasts, sponsored content, influencers and online platforms. The guidelines have come into effect immediately.
The guidelines prohibit registered medical practitioners (RMPs) and hospitals from making claims such as “best”, “No. 1”, “leading”, “most trusted”, “top” or “unmatched”, unless these can be objectively verified through a transparent and independently ascertainable methodology. Any ranking or award used in advertising must also be independently verifiable, with relevant details disclosed where necessary to prevent the public from being misled.
Online promotion targeted
The NMC has specifically addressed online promotion. RMPs and hospitals cannot procure or manipulate fake followers, likes, reviews, ratings, testimonials, comments, views or other digital engagement. They cannot manipulate search rankings, visibility or algorithms to create a misleading impression of their professional standing.
The guidelines also target financial incentives for bringing in patients. An RMP cannot offer, pay, solicit or receive a commission, rebate, bonus, gift, gratuity, referral fee, lead-generation fee or other consideration connected with the referral, recommendation or procurement of patients, specimens or materials for diagnosis or treatment.
Advertising agencies, digital marketing agencies, influencers and online platforms cannot be engaged in a manner in which payment is linked to the procurement or referral of individual patients.
On patient testimonials
Patient testimonials have also come under specific restrictions. An RMP cannot use or permit a celebrity, influencer, patient, employee or other third party to promote professional services through prohibited testimonials, endorsements or recommendations. The guidelines also prohibit RMPs from requesting or sharing patient testimonials, recommendations, endorsements or reviews for professional promotion on social media.
The guidelines prohibit the use of AI to create or manipulate patient testimonials and other promotional material in a manner that misrepresents treatment, outcomes or professional standing. The provisions also cover manipulation of patient images or voices and synthetic endorsements presented as though they came from actual patients or professionals.
The NMC has also specified what doctors and hospitals can communicate. “Hospitals can provide factual information about their location, departments, facilities, equipment, emergency services, accreditation, services and fees. Doctors can provide factual professional information and participate in public-health and educational communication, provided it does not become prohibited promotion,” it said.
Discounts, limited-period offers, contests, coupons, gifts, cashbacks, referral benefits and free procedures are also prohibited where they are likely to encourage unnecessary consultation, diagnostic investigation or treatment. Lawful disclosure of fees and packages can be made if it is factual, transparent and not misleading.
The guidelines prescribe graded disciplinary action against RMPs. A first violation can attract a warning and mandatory ethics training; a second can result in censure and a monetary penalty; and a third can lead to suspension of registration for three to six months. Serious violations can attract suspension for six to 12 months, while repeated violations can result in removal from the medical register for one to three years.
For hospitals and medical institutions, the applicable penalty and appellate mechanism under the Clinical Establishments Act or the relevant State law will apply. Where an RMP has authorised, participated in or endorsed prohibited communication, the doctor’s professional conduct can separately be examined by the appropriate medical regulatory authority.
The guidelines have been issued in the context of a writ petition before the Supreme Court and the existing framework governing professional conduct.

Ecommerce giant Amazon has reportedly laid off at least 100 employees in India as part of its latest global job cuts. Citing sources, ET reported that the affected employees in India were primarily from retail and customer service functions. Globally, fewer than 1,000 employees were affected, Business Insider reported. The cuts spanned customer service, selling partner support, and engineering roles within Amazon’s Stores business, which oversees its main ecommerce operations. Employees in India, the US, and the UK were among those affected. Responding to Inc42’s queries, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed that the company had eliminated roles as part of changes to its Stores business. “We’re always looking at our team structures to ensure we’re best set up to move fast as we innovate for customers. We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities. As part of these changes, we’ve made the difficult decision to eliminate a small number of roles, and we’re committed to supporting affected employees through their transition,” the spokesperson said. However, Amazon did not disclose how many employees were affected in India or provide details of the support being offered to them. The layoffs coincide with the start of Amazon’s Great Indian Festival sale, which opened to all customers yesterday. Further Cuts After Two Major Rounds The latest layoffs follow two major rounds of workforce reductions that affected Amazon’s India operations. In January 2026, Amazon laid off more than 500 employees across its India offices, with multiple sources estimating the number at 500-700. Technology and human resources teams were among the worst affected, with software development engineer roles accounting for the highest number of layoffs. Those cuts were part of a global restructuring exercise affecting approximately 16,000 roles. Amazon said at the time that it was reducing organisational layers, increasing ownership, and removing bureaucracy. Earlier, in November 2025, more than 1,000 employees were laid off in India, with sources estimating that the total could reach 1,500. Prime Video, people experience and technology, Q&A devices, retail stores, and Amazon Web Services were among the worst-hit divisions. The cuts affected mid-senior and senior employees across Chennai, Hyderabad, and Bengaluru, with sources saying that some verticals had lost entire teams. Alongside these workforce reductions, Amazon is increasing investment in infrastructure. The company plans a record $220 Bn in capital expenditure in 2026, covering data centres, chips, and other infrastructure, with the majority supporting AWS and AI. CEO Andy Jassy said during Amazon’s second-quarter earnings call that higher memory costs had pushed the estimate up from $200 Bn. In India, Amazon announced an additional $13 Bn investment in AI and cloud infrastructure by 2030 in June, taking its total investment commitment across businesses in the country to $48 Bn. The company also reportedly plans to invest $3 Bn in its quick commerce business, Amazon Now, by 2030 to expand its dark store network, strengthen inventory management, deploy AI tools, and widen its product mix.

Australian bishop acknowledges 8-year delay in justice in Indigenous abuse case but defends process
A top Australian Catholic bishop has acknowledged the eight-year delay in bringing a fellow bishop to justice on charges he sexually abused young Indigenous men
VATICAN CITY -- A top Australian Catholic bishop has acknowledged the eight-year delay in bringing a fellow bishop to justice on charges he sexually abused young Indigenous men. But he defended the church’s decision to let police take the lead in the case as a necessary guarantee.
Archbishop Timothy Costelloe, president of the Australian Bishops Conference, said Friday he hoped the church could soon reopen its own in-house legal procedures against former Broome Bishop Christopher Saunders now that he has been sentenced criminally.
“We still have to respect the integrity of the Australian justice system,” Costelloe told The Associated Press on the sidelines of a Vatican conference. “That’s been probably the fundamental reason why it’s stretched out as long as it has.”
Saunders, 76, was sentenced to six years and six months in prison on Wednesday after he was convicted by a District Court of Western Australia state jury of 13 out of 19 charges of sexual abuse that occurred between 2008 and 2019 in his sprawling Broome Diocese on the country’s tropical northwest coast.
Prosecutors alleged Saunders lured young Indigenous men to his church-owned house with alcohol and cigarettes paid for with church funds. He denied wrongdoing. It isn't known yet if he will appeal.
Church and law enforcement officials first learned of the allegations in 2018, and the Vatican in 2021 forced Saunders to retire at age 71, four years early. But the Australian police investigation was twice halted for lack of evidence.
The Vatican typically allows criminal investigations to play out before initiating canonical trials so as not to interfere, and that is especially so now in Australia, after the church's wretched legacy there of abuse and cover-up.
“I understand that some people are very, I’d say, even cynical about this and wonder about the response of the church,” Costelloe said. "It hasn’t been held up in a kind of an obstructionist way. We’ve had no choice but to allow the police to act independently and without interference.”
The Vatican began its own investigation into Saunders in 2022, then handed the Western Australia Police Force a 200-page report on its findings the following year. Police reopened the criminal investigation and finally charged Saunders in 2024.
While the report’s contents were never officially made public, they were leaked to Australia’s Seven Network television news, which reported Saunders likely sexually assaulted four Indigenous youths and potentially groomed another 67 Indigenous youths and men.
“I think people who are ready to think this through understand that in order to safeguard the integrity of the process and make sure that the church didn’t or wasn’t seen to be compromising the integrity of that process, we needed to step back,” Costelloe said.
“So I’m very conscious of how long it’s taken, how distressing it’s been, but I believe that in this particularly complex case, this was the right approach to take,” he said.
Costelloe denied that the delay was due to the fact that the original allegations involved men who were over age 18 when the alleged abuse occurred. The Vatican has long looked the other way when priests were accused of abuse involving adults, especially if the priests were bishops.
