The view from Haylea Rossi's bedroom is constantly changing. Sometimes, she can see snowy mountains. A week later, she could see waves crashing on the shore.
No, Rossi doesn't have a green screen that rotates outside her home. She and her family live in an RV full time, traveling the country year-round.
The mom of two told Business Insider that she loves RV life for lots of reasons, but especially because of the financial freedom it gives her family.
The Rossi family was at a crossroads in 2020.
In 2020, Rossi, 31, didn't get to see her husband, Ryan Rossi, 34, much. Rossi was at home with their two children, Liam and Olivia, who are now 12 and 10, while her husband finished up his military service.
"He deployed almost every single year," Rossi, who is a content creator and social media creator for brands, told Business Insider of her husband's time in the military. "He was constantly away."
When her husband's service was finally done, the Rossis wanted to make up for lost time. When her husband got a remote job as an independent insurance adjuster, which required him to travel to Colorado for six months of training, Rossi was excited that her family could be together.
However, they struggled to find a housing option they could afford as they relocated, particularly because they were trying to pay off debt at the same time.
They decided to try RV life.
The Rossis took the expensive housing in Colorado as a sign to do something different: buy an RV.
Rossi said an RV was more affordable for her family than buying or renting a house, and the six-month span seemed like a good way to test out the lifestyle, which was completely new to them.
"We went into it knowing if it wasn't a good fit, we weren't going to stay in it," she said, adding that she had some trepidation about RV life.
"Once I did some research before we actually did it, I was like, 'There's a whole group of people who do this, and they actually travel, and they experience life,'" she said.
With all that in mind, they decided to give it a go, buying an RV and heading to Colorado.
"We lived there up in the mountains for six months, and then said, 'This is kind of the best thing ever. Let's travel,'" Rossi said.
They've been on the road ever since.
The Rossis have had two RVs in their six years of traveling.
Their first RV was a 2020 Forest River Sabre. They renovated the interior for a more custom, tiny-home feel, as many RVers do.
That RV got totaled, which led the Rossis to buy a newer Forest River Sabre 36DBB in January 2026. It's slightly larger and has separate bedrooms for their kids, unlike their first RV. The Rossis haven't customized their current RV, as the newer design is a good fit for their family.
The new vehicle cost $70,000.
When you enter the RV, you're greeted by the main living space.
The vehicle's main room houses a kitchen and a living area. The kitchen has a stove, oven, microwave, and refrigerator, but it doesn't have a dishwasher. There's also ample built-in storage, including a hidden pantry that sits behind their TV and fireplace.
A large island sits in the center of the room, which Rossi said is a big upgrade for their family.
"It's really spacious compared to a normal little dinette table," she said.
The Rossi kids do most of their schoolwork at the kitchen island.
Rossi homeschools her children on the road, doing many of their lessons from the island and taking them to see the places they're learning about in their travels. They also took one seat out of their couch, so Rossi's husband has a dedicated desk in the living space and does not have to use the same surface as the kids.
Liam Rossi's bedroom is visible from the living area, as it sits in the loft above the space.
They also have a projector screen that pulls out from above the TV, so the family can have movie nights.
The right side of the RV serves as the primary suite.
If you walk to the right when you enter the RV, the primary bathroom and bedroom sit a level above the living area, almost like a private suite.
One wall of the bedroom is made entirely of closets, giving the Rossis built-in storage. Their washer and dryer also sit in one of the closets.
The Rossis' daughter has the second private bedroom.
Although Olivia Rossi's bed takes up much of the space, the bedroom is actually packed with storage for the whole family.
There's a closet for her clothes, a shelf for her and her brother's shoes, and space under her bed for storage.
The mattress also lifts completely to reveal a hidden storage compartment where the family keeps items such as winter clothes, extra toys, and holiday decor.
"You have to live pretty minimally if you live in an RV. You have to be strategic," Rossi said. "It's definitely a challenge at times to cut everything, but we make it work."
There's also a second bathroom attached to the bedroom, which Olivia and her brother use.
The Rossis do most of their travel in the fall and spring.
Ryan Rossi's work can sometimes dictate where the family travels, as he gets sent to different locations after storms. Most of the time, though, they can travel where they want when he's working remotely.
Rossi said her family usually stays in a new place for about two weeks, giving them time to explore. They do most of their traveling in the fall and spring, spending summers in Kansas City with family and winters in Florida.
Many RV families spend time in Florida during the colder months, so they have a community of friends to spend time with in the winter.
Rossi loves the freedom of life on the road.
Rossi said that the quality time she gets with her family because of RV life is the biggest benefit of her lifestyle.
"We had such a big section of our life where we did life away from each other," Rossi said, adding that being able to actually experience everything with their kids is a gift for her and her husband.
She also thinks the experience has changed her family's perspective on material goods for the better.
"When we had a house, my kids had so many toys, and they played with maybe a quarter of those toys," she said. "They would much rather be outside riding their bikes or doing something out there."
Living in the RV isn't always easy, though.
Rossi loves that the RV makes it easy to spend time outdoors, but it can be challenging on days when that isn't an option.
"On days where the weather's bad or it's raining, you can feel like you're closed in a little bit," she said. "Our kids will sometimes argue, just like normal kids, and then it sometimes feels like you can't escape that. I can go to my room, but I can still hear them if they're playing a game and they're arguing. That part really is the hardest for me."
Rossi also said she sometimes struggles with the space feeling cramped.
"It can get very cluttered very quickly," she said. "The upside is it doesn't take long to clean up. It's a small space. But that sometimes drives me a little crazy."
The Rossis will continue living on the road for the foreseeable future, in part because it's the most affordable option for their family.
Rossi said she doesn't think her family will always live in an RV, but it doesn't make financial sense for them to buy a house right now.
"We definitely could buy a house, but then we would feel so much more limited on what we could do financially," she said.
Right now, their monthly household expenses are often under $1,000, Rossi said. The RV payments are around $600 a month, and they're often paying $200 in RV park fees with their Thousand Trails membership, which provides access to a network of campgrounds and resorts.
Between the cost of homes and high interest rates, Rossi said her family wouldn't be able to travel or pay off their debt if they had to pay a pricey mortgage each month.
"We're at the place where we want to pay off our debt," she added. "We want to actually have some experiences while our kids are at home and not feel like we're stuck in the house, just trying to get by."
Still, Rossi said they won't continue living on the road if her kids aren't happy.
Rossi said it's important to her and her husband that their kids are happy with RV life, especially as they get older.
"I know a lot of people have different opinions on this, but I feel like your kids should want to do the lifestyle as well," she said. "We do have frequent check-ins with my kids. We're like, 'Do you feel ready to stop and stay?' But they're both like, 'No, this is the best thing ever. We want to travel.'"
They'll continue checking in with their kids, but Rossi said it's been empowering to know their nontraditional lifestyle makes her children happy.
"Sometimes, it's easy as a parent to feel like you have to make your life look like everyone else's to give your kid the childhood that you think that they should have," she said. "And for us, we have found that our kids are so much happier just having time with us and experiences with us versus things."
At some point, they will likely stop living on the road. For now, though, they're glad to keep the adventure going.
"As long as our kids are happy and we're working toward our goals, we'd rather reach our financial goals first before we think about [moving into a house]," Rossi said.

The death of a laboratory worker in Siberia on October 2, 2026, and the subsequent quarantine of dozens of people have sparked concerns about a pneumonic plague epidemic, with Russia revealing little information publicly. The incident has revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations that the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab.
What happened at the Siberia lab?
The 28-year-old woman, Darya Shipilova, employed at a research institute in Siberia, fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people and dispatch the head of Russia’s health watchdog to the Irkutsk region.
The woman worked at the anti-plague research institute in the city of Irkutsk, where the plague occurs naturally in wild animals. She died at a hospital in nearby Shelekhov that the mayor said had been placed under quarantine. Following the incident, top Russian health officials have travelled to the region.
Russian authorities say the lab worker died of what initially presented as a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection.
Russia dismisses epidemic concerns
Meanwhile, Russia’s health regulator insists there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after the plague institute worker’s death.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on October 7 that it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic.
No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, it said, while adding that 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.
When asked about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution against using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
‘Causative agent behind death not known’
A top official with the World Health Organisation (WHO) said it doesn’t know how the lab worker in Siberia died. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the UN health agency doesn’t know what the “causative agent’ was behind the woman’s October 2 death.
She has urged Russia to provide more information about the incident that prompted global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague. The WHO initially said it estimated the risk of the Russia case to the public as low, but told a press conference on October 7 it could not make a fuller risk assessment due to insufficient information from the Russian authorities.
What is pneumonic plague, symptoms
Reports blamed the woman’s death on pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
Pneumonic plague causes a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time. The severe disease is less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages.
Pneumonic plague and bubonic plague are caused by the same bacteria. The former is spread by respiratory particles while the latter is spread through bites from fleas that have jumped from infected rodents.
Symptoms of pneumonic plague include shortness of breath and coughing-up blood, and they can occur in as little as 24 hours after exposure, according to the WHO. If untreated, the illness can be fatal.
Not linked to a biological weapon
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday (October 8) that the death of the Russian plague laboratory worker did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon.
Mr. Trump said Russia insisted it had the situation under control, but added that not much information was coming out. He, however, said that the United States will help Russia over the incident.
The European Union has also called on Russia to “share timely and transparent reporting” about the death of the plague laboratory technician.

Allahabad HC quashes dowry FIR, warns against criminalising failed marriages
The Allahabad High Court quashed an Agra dowry FIR against a husband and his family. It said criminal law should not routinely be used to settle failed marriages.
The Allahabad High Court has quashed an FIR against a man and his family in a case alleging dowry harassment, physical assault and an attempt to strangulate the wife, while warning against the routine criminalisation of failed marriages. The court said turning every distressed or broken marriage into a criminal case could affect the institution of marriage at its core.
A division bench of Justices Chandra Dhari Singh and Tarun Saxena allowed a writ petition filed by Gaurav Jain and his family members and set aside the FIR registered at Hari Parvat police station in Agra under various provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Dowry Prohibition Act. The court said matrimonial discord cannot automatically be treated as criminality and that criminal proceedings cannot replace adjudication before a matrimonial court.
According to the case record, the marriage took place on November 12, 2024, and the wife left the matrimonial home on February 3, 2025, after about two-and-a-half months of cohabitation. The husband then filed a divorce petition on May 3, 2025, and the FIR was registered on June 30, 2025.
The FIR alleged dowry demands and harassment, denial of food, threats, retention of the wife's stridhan and an attempt to strangulate her. However, the high court noted that no domestic violence complaint, police control room call or contemporaneous police intervention relating to the alleged incidents during the period of cohabitation had been placed on record.
In its judgment dated October 8, the court said that while protecting women from dowry-related violence and cruelty is a statutory and constitutional imperative, the possibility of misuse of criminal law cannot be ignored. It said that if every distressed or failed marriage is routinely converted into an FIR and subjected to the coercive machinery of criminal law, the institution of marriage will inevitably be affected at its core. The court clarified that it had not examined the merits of the pending matrimonial proceedings and said both sides were free to pursue their remedies before the competent matrimonial court, while the complainant could also seek any independent remedy available in law for a distinct cause of action, subject to statutory requirements.

Americans have more trust in science than most of the rest of the world, according to a new survey of people in 140 countries, a finding that may seem difficult to explain in a country deeply divided by issues such as the benefits and harms of vaccines.
According to the newest edition of the Wellcome Global Monitor, 52 percent of Americans report having “a lot” of trust in science. Across the globe, that number is a mere 26 percent.
Americans, in aggregate, are also more eager to get vaccines compared to peer nations; 45 percent of Americans say they would want to get vaccines recommended by a nurse or doctor “right away.” In Germany only 28 percent say the same.
And while the share of people globally who agree that science benefits most people in their society has dropped from 42 percent in 2018 to 37 percent in 2025, the share of Americans who agree with that statement has actually increased from 48 percent to 57 percent.
But the aggregate statistics don’t tell the whole story. STAT’s analysis of the Wellcome data demonstrates that while America may, in general, appreciate and trust science, it is also far more divided than peer nations.
Take the religious divide: According to STAT’s analysis there was, on average, a 5 percentage point gap between the percentage of religious and non-religious people in high-income nations who said science benefits most people in their country. In the United States that gap was 24 percentage points.
A similar divide — 19 percentage points — separates urban and rural Americans on the question of science’s benefits. The divide across other high-income nations is just three points. Education level divides Americans as well — just 47 percent of Americans without four-year degrees reported believing that science benefits most people, compared to 71 percent of college grads.
Wellcome, a British foundation focused on scientific research, funded the survey in 2018, 2020 and 2025. The most recent version was administered as part of the Gallup World Poll through a combination of in-person, telephone and online surveys of more than 140,000 adults. The global findings were weighted “to ensure that global estimates accurately reflect the relative populations of countries in the survey.”
The survey does not offer an explanation for why the United States appears to be outpacing its peers on trust. But at least some of Americans’ seeming polarization may be explained by Americans’ tendency toward extremes.
Americans are “more extreme responders to public opinion surveys,” said Matthew Motta, an associate professor at Boston University School of Public Health who is an expert on public opinion research.
For example, a smaller proportion of Germans than Americans said they would “not get vaccines at all.” Only 8 percent of Germans were completely anti-vaccine, compared to 13 percent of Americans. Instead, the vast majority of Germans said they would “prefer to think about it for some time.”
The survey also showed that Americans who historically have been less trusting are not necessarily souring on science and its benefits. STAT’s analysis finds that the proportion of Americans who identify as religious and who believe science benefits most people increased by four percentage points, from 46 percent in 2018 to 50 percent in 2025. Self-reported religious Americans are also more likely to report an eagerness to be vaccinated when compared to peer countries.
A similar pattern plays out with Americans without four-year degrees. The percentage of non-college grads who say science benefits most people increased by three percentage points over that seven-year period, and they too are more likely than residents of peer nations with similar education to want vaccines right away.
So what is causing America’s growing divide over trust in science? The poll shows it is growing enthusiasm for science among highly educated, secular Americans. Both reported substantial increases in their appreciation of the benefits of science: 13 percentage points for college grads, and 15 percentage points for secular Americans over seven years, the Wellcome survey found.
In short, America is divided not because certain groups are souring on science, but because others are becoming more appreciative of its benefits.
That might seem like good news. But the divide nonetheless underscores that the benefits of science are not reaching a large swath of Americans in ways they can see and feel.
“People are feeling left behind, they are not understanding how this benefits me,” said Brian Castrucci, president and CEO of the de Beaumont Foundation, which focuses on strengthening public health.
Some divisions facing Americans will be difficult to combat in a country as large and diverse as the United States. City dwellers with cancer who can access care at a top-rated university medical center will inevitably see science’s impact on their lives more than people in a rural area who might have to travel a great distance for even the most basic hospital care.
Wellcome found that trust in science is closely associated with confidence in a nation’s health care systems, which presents a problem for the United States as well. Just 40 percent of Americans reported a lot of confidence in U.S. hospitals and health clinics, the same proportion as in Portugal and Uruguay.
Anti-science sentiment coming from America’s top political officials is likely playing a role too, several experts said. Diverging views on science among America’s political parties became apparent during the Tea Party movement of the 2010s and was amplified during Trump’s presidency, said Yotam Ophir, an associate professor of communication at the University at Buffalo.
But experts STAT spoke to underscored that this new data doesn’t just indicate the need for the sorts of systemic changes that can take decades to fulfill. Scientists need to hone their ability to discuss the benefits of science in people’s everyday lives, and to stop expecting the public to blindly trust them, several experts told STAT.
“What we need to do is be better communicators, not better debaters. We are not going to be able to lecture people into trusting us,” Castrucci said.
Mark Henderson, Wellcome’s executive director of corporate affairs and engagement, said scientists who wish to take steps based on the report’s findings should “meet people where they are.”
“Approach people on a level with understanding and engagement and respect, and you’re going to get a better outcome,” Henderson added. “It’s not rocket science, but it often surprises me how hard people in the scientific community find it to do that.”

18 Quirky Gifts That Lego Lovers Will Adore
Featured in this article
Lego isn't going anywhere. Those beloved little bricks won't biodegrade, are machined to incredibly tight tolerances, and—unless your dog chews one up—retain what Lego refers to as their “clutch power” for decades. Their relevance in terms of cultural pastiche isn’t fading on me either. They're as irresistible to me today as they were as a kid.
If you and your loved ones are also obsessed with Lego sets, we have some great gift ideas. For more recommendations, don't forget to check out our other gift guides.
Updated October 2026: I added the Lego Ideas Peanuts: Snoopy's Doghouse, a Lego Batman game, Star Wars Advent Calendar 2026, Star Trek light kit, and Lego Architecture Paris: City of Love.
- Their Favorite Themed Set Lego Speed Champions One of the reasons that Lego sets are so popular is the company's innumerable licensing deals. No matter what you're into, Lego has signed a deal to make a Lego set about it. (And then, in an ouroboros of advertising, the company will then make a movie about the Lego set about the franchise.) Anyway, this is a long and roundabout way of saying that my son and I are obsessed with the Lego Formula 1 sets. I even got to watch the Lego cars hit the track at a Formula 1 race. Ever since then, we've been watching the races and Netflix's Drive to Survive. It's the perfect collaboration because Lego bricks and Formula 1 engineers are on the same page when it comes to precise engineering and tight tolerances. Also, once you're done building, the cars work as toys as well as sets. —Adrienne So
- Smart Bricks Lego Star Wars Smart Play Throne Room Duel and A-Wing If you’re curious about Lego’s new Smart Play system, the Star Wars Throne Room Duel and A-Wing set is a great way to dip your toe in the water. This fun build enables you to reenact the climax of Return of the Jedi, with Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker duking it out as Emperor Palpatine looks on and a space battle rages outside. Smart Bricks add lightsaber noises, lasers, explosions, heavy breathing, and even a rendition of “The Imperial March.” They also light up, but you’ll have to remember to charge them.
- A Lego Centerpiece Lego Botanicals Bouquet of Pink Roses My daughter and my husband love the Lego Botanicals collection. These gorgeous tree and flower sets work well as holiday centerpieces once you're finished building—you can leave them right out on the table, instead of hiding them away in your Lego basement once you're done. My 11-year-old built this lovely rose bouquet, which has articulated heads so you can arrange them in the case. For the winter holidays, we also recommend the Lego poinsettia set ($50), which was our centerpiece last year. —Adrienne So
- A Lego Videogame Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight A superbly loving parody that throws the best of Batman’s movie outings into the blender with a pinch of slapstick comedy and plenty of charm. Gotham is packed with collectibles, puzzles to solve, and an endless supply of thugs to bash. Melee combat is fun, as you counter and dodge to build combos, and there’s plenty of gadgetry to try out. This is the most fun I’ve had with a Lego game in years, and it’s perfect for split-screen couch co-op. If you’re not a Batman fan, there are tons of other great Lego games, based on other worlds, like Star Wars, Ninjago, and Marvel.
- A Fan-Created Set Lego Ideas Peanuts: Snoopy's Doghouse Who doesn’t love Snoopy? This set is an easy build and includes Snoopy, his doghouse, and Woodstock. There’s also a typewriter (fans will recognize the line, “It was a dark and stormy night”) and a campfire, with alternative legs if you want Snoopy to stand, hunch over to type, or lie back on the top of his doghouse. The Ideas range from Lego is based on fan creations that have been shared and voted on to become real sets. This one is lovely, but it’s definitely a display set, not something you’d actively play with.
- A Lego Stocking Stuffer Lego Note Brick If you have a coworker who likes Lego and would like to gift him or her something tiny and thoughtful, I suggest this little notepad. It's very cute, with 224 pieces of paper, and one side looks like a brick. The notes themselves are about 5 inches long, which is big enough for a pretty substantial note! Chronicle Books has a whole line of Lego books, puzzles, and stationery for your Lego-obsessed friend. You could also throw in a pack of these brick erasers ($36) to make a little care package. —Adrienne So
- Lego Playing Cards Lego Brick Playing Cards If you also have an 8- or a 10-year-old, let me recommend a simple life hack—instead of caving to their demands to let them look at your phone while you're out, just always carry a deck of cards in your bag. It's crazy how many times my kids have settled down and waited patiently in a doctor's office or restaurant, as long as they can start a game of Crazy Eights or Go Fish (I do not recommend Speed). These Lego playing cards are beautiful and brightly colored, feel sturdy, and have held up to several rounds of shuffling around a table. The box comes in a pack of two, so your kids can split it. —Adrienne So
- An Advent Calendar Lego Star Wars Advent Calendar 2026 With the holidays approaching, this is a great alternative to regular advent calendars. You get a Star Wars–related minifigure or build behind each door, including irresistibly cute Mando and Grogu figures in Christmas jumpers, critters like a Bantha and Dewback, and tiny ships like an X-wing and the Razor Crest.
- Ornaments for Your Tree Lego Snowman Ornaments I wish we were a family that kept treasured family heirlooms all wrapped up in tissue paper, ready to be marveled over at the next year's tree decorating. Unfortunately, every year finds us with some Christmas tree–related disaster or the other. Our new puppy has chewed the stuffed animals that an uncle has sent us; my son has sent a baseball crashing into the ceramic horse head that I got as a kid. We always need new ornaments, so why not new Lego ones? These are very cute, and my son assembled them in a matter of minutes. —Adrienne So
- A Big Lego Book Page Street Kids The Big Book of Amazing Lego Creations With Bricks You Already Have Have all your sets now become disassembled, and do you need some inspiration while looking at the giant wheelbarrow of Lego bricks on your front porch? This is my kids' favorite book for ideas on what to build. It has been a struggle to not “lose” it from the library. All of the builds are fairly easy, and so far I haven't seen any that require specialized pieces. However, you will probably need more than just 12 red bricks or 14 yellow ones to make many of the builds, so you should make sure your Lego loved one has a substantial collection already. If you want other sources of inspiration, we also like The Art of the Brick ($40), and I would be remiss if I did not include our own Brian Barrett's book, The Art of the Minifigure ($35). —Adrienne So
- A Family Activity Lego Christmas Tree Puzzle If you're having relatives over for the holidays, I suggest having a little puzzle like this to whip out while everyone's waiting for you to put the final touches on dinner. It's not one big puzzle, which can feel overwhelming and makes it hard to get off the dinner table—it's four separate little puzzles. Your kids, or parents, or fun uncle ("funcle") can work on each small puzzle separately and attach them together later. Each of the backs is patterned differently, so you can tell the different puzzles apart when you're putting them away or back together again. —Adrienne So
- A Lego Head Mug Lego Large Ceramic Mug As Lego-branded toys rolled into my house, I do have the caveat that my kids were very confused. ("Why are all these Lego gifts coming in but none of them are Legos?") However, my son was immediately thrilled and delighted with this mug and demands that I wash it every morning for him to drink out of. There are several faces to choose from if your children don't want to match. It's ceramic and can hold about 17 ounces of liquid—so, pretty big for a 7-year-old but nothing their little hands can't handle. It's dishwasher-safe. We've also received these off-brand Lego mugs ($13) as gifts, but again, the clutch power of off-brand Lego bricks is unsatisfactory and the bricks don't stick on very well. —Adrienne So
- A Lighting Kit Light My Bricks Lego Star Trek Enterprise Light Kit You can bring some of your favorite Lego sets to life with third-party light kits. There are various options, but the best brand might be Light My Bricks. This particular light kit is for the Lego Icons Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701-D set, and it’s pretty pricey. That said, the kit is very well-made, with slim components that slot into place neatly; thin, flat cables; and no exposed solder or circuitry. The kits are also globally certified as safe, and the finished effect is awesome. Light My Bricks also makes light kits for a ton of other sets.
- The Best Lego Notebook Lego IQ Stationery Locking Notepad Do you have an artsy little Lego lover? My daughter has been obsessed with this notebook and carries it around everywhere she goes. It's about 6 inches square, so small enough to fit in a backpack or tote bag, with a decent 176 lined sheets. It has a wonderful conceit—the Lego gel pen matches the color of the binding and clicks right into it, so it both locks the notebook shut and ensures you never lose your pen. That's unless you're 10 and leave your pen on the kitchen table, where your puppy finds it and eats it (see next). —Adrienne So

India condemns JD Vance's ‘indentured servants’ remark amid green card curbs
India said the US freeze on permanent labor certification filings by major technology companies undermines shared ambitions.
India on Friday said the US administration’s freeze on green card filings by Indian IT majors such as Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) and Infosys go against shared ambitions of both sides, even as it denounced US vice president JD Vance comparing Indian and other foreign professionals to “indentured servants” as unwarranted and deeply offensive.
The response from the external affairs ministry came hours after the Trump administration froze some Green Card filings by eight IT majors and launched probes into nine elite universities, widening a visa crackdown aimed at curbing fraud and US job losses. The move specifically targeted Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Microsoft, Adobe and Capgemini.
The external affairs ministry noted in a statement that talent mobility adds value to the Indian and US economies, creating opportunities for Indians and equally helping US firms with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation, besides creating shareholder wealth in the US.
Deep Dive
“This is therefore an area of tremendous mutual benefit for the two countries and our expectation is that all stakeholders in this process can appreciate this fact,” the ministry said. “The steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries.”
Also Read | ‘US history shaped by immigrants’: India calls out JD Vance over ‘deeply offensive’ H-1B visa remarks
The Trump administration’s action targeted the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM), a key employer-sponsorship mechanism that has allowed skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency through their employment since 2005. Under PERM, which most employment-based green cards require, employers must show a foreign hire will not hurt US workers’ jobs.
The statement noted that the PERM programme is distinct from the H-1B visa programme, and said the suspension of PERM applications “does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents”. However, the new move can have an impact on the permanent-residency or green card process of “eligible employees of the affected companies”, the statement said.
The Indian side also took exception to comments made by Vance at an event where the new curbs were announced. Vance’s remarks suggested that foreign talents were no more than “indentured servants” whose hiring was resulting in the laying off of American workers.
“We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem,” the statement said.
Also Read | 'Opportunities for Indians but also helps US': India on Vance's remarks amid Green Card curbs
The external affairs ministry pointed out that the history of the US itself has been “shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity”. The statement added, “Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive.”
The developments marked yet another low point in India-US relations during the second term of President Donald Trump. The US administration’s decision last year to hit Indian exports with 50% tariffs sent ties to their lowest point in more than two decades. Though the two sides reached an understanding earlier this year on reducing the tariffs, they have struggled to finalise a bilateral trade deal and recent remarks by Indian and US leaders have suggested an agreement is not imminent.
The twin actions by the Trump administration marked the broadest strike yet against skilled worker immigration programmes, potentially blocking a common path to permanent residency for thousands of foreign tech workers, including Indians.
While announcing the move against the eight tech firms, US labour secretary Keith Sonderling said: “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies.”
Vance added, “I’m sure that everyone here understands the game that is being played. Bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who probably should not be in the United States of America to begin with.”
During his second term, Trump has widened efforts to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and to curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship.
Also Read | ‘Can't replace American workers with foreign servants’: Why Vance's H-1B visa axe fell on Microsoft
The Trump administration has sought to disincentivise US employers from using the H-1B visa programme. In September 2025, Trump announced a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions, though it was subsequently blocked by a US court in June 2026. In August, the Trump administration proposed a fresh $103,265 H-1B visa fee that will apply to all petitions subject to the annual cap of 85,000.
Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, according to Permtrack.app, which compiles US labour department disclosure data.
Nasscom, India’s IT body, said late on Thursday that firms had significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas in recent years while expanding local hiring in the US. Relatively few workers move from H-1B visas to permanent residency through PERM, Nasscom added.
Shares on Indian IT firms rose on Friday. The NIfty IT Index rose 3% while the broader market gained 1.3 per cent.

She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
- Published
When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India.
India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan.
That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.
Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport.
Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats.
Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless.
Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience.
The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana.
In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer.
Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago.
Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world.
Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped.
Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains.
Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on.
Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post.
"I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote.
"Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again.
"Captaincy ends, the journey continues."
Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future.
In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision.
The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket.
Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones.
Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age.
Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai.
The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development.
She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since.
An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills.
Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome.
That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name.
The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history.
Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.
Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals.
India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket.
With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate.

Delhi deploys 2,947 bus marshals, 56 special buses to bolster women's safety
Delhi has expanded its safety network with bus marshals, special buses and live monitoring. The measures aim to speed up emergency response and improve safety for women and children.
The Delhi government has deployed 2,947 bus marshals in Delhi Transport Corporation buses and is running 56 special buses for women as part of its safety measures, Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said on Saturday. She said the government has also linked all buses to a central monitoring system with panic alarms, live CCTV feeds and GPS tracking.
Gupta also outlined steps related to women’s accommodation, child safety, school security and road infrastructure. She said the measures are aimed at ensuring quicker assistance during emergencies, better facilities for working women and safer conditions for children.
Of the 56 special buses for women, 15 run during the evening shift, with armed women police personnel deployed on them after 5 pm, Gupta said in a statement. She said all buses have been connected to the Bus Management System, with panic alarms, live CCTV feeds and GPS monitored round the clock through a control centre.
The Department of Women and Child Development will soon introduce additional accommodation facilities for working women in Vishwas Nagar and Rohini, she said.
“The Delhi government is strengthening systems to ensure that women receive prompt assistance during a crisis, working women have access to essential facilities and every child gets the opportunity to learn, progress and develop their abilities in a safe environment,” Gupta said.
She said Child Welfare Committees and Juvenile Justice Boards are functioning as statutory bodies to protect children’s rights.
Sub-Divisional Magistrates have been designated as Child Marriage Prohibition Officers to prevent child marriages, while around 1.5 lakh CCTV cameras are available in schools to improve children’s safety and confidence.
Self-defence training is being provided in 1,397 schools under the Rani Lakshmibai Self-Defence Training Programme, she added.
Highlighting measures to improve road safety and infrastructure, Gupta said 96,000 streetlights have been installed on roads under the Public Works Department, including 45,000 high-pressure sodium vapour lights and 51,000 LED lights. A total of 2,53,983 CCTV cameras under the department are operational, she said.
Citizens can register complaints through the toll-free number 1908 and the PWD Seva Portal, Gupta added. She also highlighted the multi-layered safety network, which includes the Women’s Helpline 181, DTC services and child protection measures.
Gupta said the government’s safety measures cover public transport, working women’s facilities, child protection, school security and road infrastructure, with monitoring systems, helplines and complaint channels forming part of the broader network.

Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi stayed defiant as he told the Prime Minister to "Arrest all the leaders. Arrest all the young people. Arrest us all," he wrote on X, adding that the Opposition was "not going to back down." The Congress is set to hold its own protest on October 12.
Priyanka Gandhi Vadra accused the government of undermining democratic values, saying, "India is not a democracy anymore. It is a dictatorship being run by Mr. Narendra Modi and Mr. Amit Shah."
Congress National President Mallikarjun Kharge accused the government of transforming the "Mother of Democracy" into a "Muzzled Democracy".
BJP President Nitin Nabin claimed that the Opposition groups are trying to destabilise the country and that their actions were being driven by 'foreign forces'.
Union Minister Sukanta Majumdar also echoed Nabin's sentiments, calling the movement an attempt to "destabilise the country," adding, "Everyone knows where CJP is getting its funding and strength from."
Sambit Patra held a press conference where he claimed "Democracy has triumphed over mob rule. The way democracy has been demonstrated in Delhi today, and the way everything is under control, is commendable. I would like to reiterate one thing: the anarchists have failed."
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said, "I acknowledge that in a democracy, every individual has the right to express dissent. However, one must not forget that spreading anarchy is not anyone's right."
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant himself had to intervene at one point when the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) informed him of advocates being detained by the police. The advocates were released only after the CJI intervened in the matter personally.
The Supreme Court is set to hold a special sitting on Sunday to hear a contempt petition alleging that authorities, including the Union Home Secretary, willfully disobeyed the apex court's order against a complete shutdown of public transport ahead of today’s protest.

The Trump administration plans a public killing
Pete Hegseth’s “barbaric” plan for a livestreamed execution, briefly explained.
Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is planning a public killing.
What’s happening? On Thursday, the Pentagon announced that it would execute Nidal Hasan, a former Army major sentenced to death for a 2009 mass shooting on a military base, publicly and on livestream.
The execution, if it happens, would be unprecedented: The last widely reported public execution in the US was 90 years ago, in Kentucky, but to stream a death live would be something else entirely. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has promoted the announcement with something approaching glee, telling a reporter that “we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.”
What’s the context? According to the Pentagon, Hasan will be executed via firing squad on December 3 — the first such execution by the military in more than 80 years.
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death in 2013 by a military jury following a court-martial for the 2009 shooting, when he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 at Fort Hood in Texas. The execution is set to be carried out at the same Army post.
Will the Pentagon go through with this? It’s unclear, for multiple reasons. The Pentagon’s announcement that Hasan’s death will be livestreamed has generated a great deal of bipartisan pushback, as well as condemnation by religious groups, though that is unlikely to stop the execution itself.
The head of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops decried the decision to livestream the execution as “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death,” and retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) called it the decision “beyond disgusting.”
“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do,” Tillis wrote in a post on X.
On Friday, Vice President JD Vance also said that he was unsure if the livestream would take place.
Hasan’s legal team could also delay the execution substantially — potentially for multiple years — by challenging his detention in federal court, though he has exhausted the military appeals process.

The El Nino that’s upending weather across South America and Asia has intensified to the strongest on record, according to Japan’s national forecaster, threatening widespread economic disruptions that could linger long after the climate pattern dissipates.
The naturally occurring weather pattern warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall.
Sea surface temperatures in a patch of the tropical Pacific Ocean monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency were 4 degrees Celsius above normal as of September, the highest in records going back to 1949, the forecaster said in a bulletin published Friday. The previous record was set in December 1997, when temperatures were 3.7 C above normal, the bureau said.
El Nino has already disrupted weather patterns worldwide. The climate event has led to the weakest Indian monsoon in more than a decade, exacerbated wildfires in Indonesia that have spewed toxic smoke over neighboring Singapore and Malaysia, and threatened sugar and coffee output in Brazil.
The JMA’s outlook comes a day after the World Meteorological Organization said in its latest seasonal forecast that El Nino is set to be the most intense ever. The WMO’s projection is based on the Nino 3.4 region, which overlaps with but lies west of the Nino 3 region tracked by Japan.
The Japanese bureau predicts a 100% chance that El Nino will persist through the Northern Hemisphere winter, in line with the U.S. Climate Prediction Center’s outlook that the weather-roiling phenomenon is certain to last through the January-March period.
Many record-hot years -- including 1998, 2010, 2016, 2023 and 2024 -- followed major El Nino events or developed alongside them.

Amid growing uncertainties over AI’s utilisation and its prospects, union IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said that the government is working on releasing a consultation paper on regulating the nascent tech. Speaking at the release of the World Bank’s latest World Development Report on the subject of ‘The Promise of Artificial Intelligence’, Vaishnaw said the timing is right for India to formalise AI regulation and the upcoming consultation paper will establish the foundational basis for future AI regulation. The regulatory blueprint is also likely to sharpen focus on AI safety and security, navigate the deepfakes risk as well as ensuring adequate skill development necessary to optimise the utilisation of AI. On the deepfake epidemic, Vaishnaw identified AI-morphed content as a “nuisance which can cause huge problems in society” while noting they establish dangerous precedents and narratives that mislead the public. He added that the quality of these is improving continuously. The minister further said that AI and emerging technologies cannot be effectively managed through legislation alone. Hence, the government intends to pursue a techno-legal solution with the active participation of industry stakeholders. “The industry has to take the primary responsibility,” said Vaishnaw, regarding issues such as cybersecurity, safety, user harm, psychological disorders, and deepfake proliferation. Notably, the IT minister had previously emphasised that the IT Act is becoming obsolete and India needs a new legal framework to regulate AI. Reports had also hinted that the Centre was looking at formulating a new framework for AI regulation. As frontier AI models’ capabilities are evolving, the government has increasingly focused on tightening rules to mitigate the harms caused by proliferation of AI-generated content. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) had proposed amending the IT Act to require online platforms to label all deepfakes and AI-generated content as “synthetically generated information.” The news also comes amid a storm over global tech giant Meta’s handling of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on its platforms like Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. A BBC investigation earlier this year alleged that Instagram ads were directing users towards Telegram channels offering CSAM material for sale, resulting in the company facing summons from MeitY and an inquiry by the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR). Following the episode, Meta and Google both ultimately agreed to report content on child abuse to Indian law enforcement authorities.

U.S. death row inmate Christa Pike was released from a US hospital on Saturday and sent back to prison, where she will continue receiving medical care following her botched execution attempt in Tennessee, her attorneys said.
Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years, said attorneys Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, and Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the Tennessee Office of the Post Conviction Defender in a joint release.
Pike, sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, awoke “angry and confused” in the hospital this week, with a long recuperation ahead after surviving the attempted execution on September 30, her lawyers said on Wednesday. They previously believed she could be brain-dead.
Pike, 50, had been taken from the execution chamber to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and with severe arm injuries after two injections failed to kill her at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution.
A Tennessee judge this week ordered State officials to preserve all evidence related to their failed attempt to execute her, a development one of her lawyers called the “first of many steps to preserve and enforce her constitutional rights.”
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year while investigators look into the botched execution of Pike and a similar failure involving Tony Carruthers in May, when prison officials were unable to set up intravenous lines.

Public safety, past lapses: Why Delhi Police denied CJP permission for Jantar Mantar protest
Delhi police said the right to protest is a fundamental right but that granting permission also requires authorities to consider the rights of other citizens.
Delhi Police has denied permission to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar on October 10, citing short notice, alleged violations during earlier demonstrations and concerns over public safety and law and order. The police also defended the restrictions imposed in New Delhi, saying they were necessary to prevent overcrowding and ensure the safety of protesters, residents and commuters.
In a letter dated October 9, addressed to CJP co-convener Saurav Das and joint secretary Balkrishna, the New Delhi district police said the group's communication submitted on October 7 was merely an intimation of the proposed protest and did not constitute a duly submitted application seeking permission.
The police said existing guidelines require applications for programmes at Jantar Mantar to be submitted at least 10 days before the intended date.
Deep Dive
The police said the right to protest is a fundamental right but that granting permission also requires authorities to consider the rights of other citizens and residents.
It cited traffic congestion, safety concerns and the potential disruption of public life as reasons for regulating demonstrations.
Why Delhi Police is citing earlier protests
The police referred to the July protests at Jantar Mantar, saying permission had been granted for a one-day demonstration but that it continued for around a month. In its statement on X, the police said more than 200 personnel were injured during the protests and alleged that the participation of people with criminal antecedents contributed to the violence.
Hindustan Times reported on July 27, citing Delhi Police officials, that police had identified 2,873 people through CCTV footage linked to the July 20 march towards Parliament. Of these, 989 were found to have criminal antecedents, according to the officials.
The cases included murder, robbery, sexual assault and other offences. The police claims about the criminal antecedents of those identified were attributed to officials and should not be read as convictions.
The July 20 march saw clashes at several locations in central Delhi. An FIR accessed by HT alleged that protesters assaulted police personnel, damaged public property and attempted to breach Parliament security. The allegations formed part of the police account of the violence.
In its October 9 letter, Delhi Police said the continuation of an earlier CJP protest beyond the permitted hours had resulted in serious law and order problems and a deterioration in public order.
The police also claimed that women constables had been molested and assaulted by people protesting at Jantar Mantar during the previous week, describing the incidents as deeply troubling.
CJP had estimated 500-600 people for June protest
Documents submitted by CJP to Delhi Police show that the group had estimated a gathering of 500-600 people for its June 20 demonstration at Jantar Mantar.
In an application dated June 17, the group said the protest would be against alleged irregularities and paper leaks in competitive examinations, including NEET-UG and CBSE board examinations, and would demand the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The application specified a protest from 10 am to 5 pm and listed Sonam Wangchuk as a participant. The accompanying undertaking committed the organisers to maintaining order, deploying volunteers, following police directions and keeping the gathering within the permitted limit of 1,000 people.
Delhi Police granted permission for the June 20 demonstration, but the protest continued into June 21.
The eventual turnout of thousands, at the protests which lasted over a month, was also far greater than what CJP had sought permission for.
Police says Jantar Mantar can accommodate 1,000 people
In its statement on X, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar could accommodate around 1,000 people at a time. It argued that authorities needed advance information about the number of expected participants to arrange traffic diversions, emergency access and safe crowd movement.
The police said Delhi's economic activity and daily life could not be brought to a halt every time a protest took place. It said the restrictions were temporary measures intended to regulate the movement of people, prevent overcrowding and protect protesters, residents, shopkeepers and others in the area.
The police also referred to Supreme Court directions issued on July 23, 2018, concerning the regulation of protests, saying the applicable guidelines had to be followed strictly.
Delhi Police and central security agencies have reviewed their handling of the July protests, identifying security lapses and preparing for further demonstrations. The review included concerns about food deliveries allowing people to remain at Jantar Mantar overnight and broken pavement stones and walls that could pose security risks. The report also noted that a Supreme Court-appointed committee was examining allegations of police excesses during the July protests.
Cops denied BSF permission to protest at Jantar Mantar too
Meanwhile, nearly 400 former Border Security Force (BSF) cooks, water carriers and women tradesmen from various states, under the banner of the Alliance of All Ex-Paramilitary Forces, staged a peaceful protest near the BSF headquarters, seeking reinstatement in service. The alliance's general secretary, Ranbir Singh, shared a copy of a Delhi Police letter denying them permission to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar on October 9 and 10. The letter, issued around a month earlier, cited rules against holding a hunger strike continuously for two days at Jantar Mantar and asked the organisers to cooperate with Delhi Police.
“Police denied permission citing different rules for us to protest at Jantar Mantar for two days. So we held protests near the BSF headquarters today. These people were duped by cyber fraudsters who helped them get NSDC skill development certificates, which were later found to be forged. These are people who served in the BSF during Operation Sindoor but lost their jobs after the department learnt their certificates were not accredited by the NSDC. The fact is they also did not know and submitted what they got,” Singh said.
What is CJP protesting against?
CJP has been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The group has continued its campaign through demonstrations and public statements, including a protest in Mumbai on October 2.
The proposed October 10 demonstration at Jantar Mantar was part of the group's effort to press its demands. Delhi Police said the organisers were proceeding without the requisite permission and that the request could not be granted in the larger public interest.
The police said people should be able to raise their concerns peacefully, but organisers must follow the prescribed process so that authorities can ensure the safety of participants and the public.

Two Indian cartoonists, Satish Acharya and Manjul, recently revealed that their Instagram accounts and posts were withheld in India, following orders from the government. While the former’s account was restored on October 6, the latter’s post remains unavailable in India.
On September 23, The Indian Express reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning electoral-roll management and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), including changes to Form 6, voter deletions and restorations, the centralisation of electoral-roll data, and appeals against decisions in West Bengal.
The investigation, based on internal notes and correspondence reviewed by the newspaper, showed that the two commissioners repeatedly said certain decisions had been taken without their knowledge or approval by chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, with Sandhu at one point describing an SIR-related change as “unauthorised and illegal.” Both Acharya and Manjul had posted cartoons satirising this case.
ALSO READ: Instagram takes down content critical of Vizag data centre projects, cites IT Act notices
On September 23, Acharya posted an illustration on Kumar and the SIR controversy. Five days later, on September 28, his account was restricted in India.
However, his profile was still available on Facebook and X, and the said toon was still visible on both platforms.
After his account was banned, on September 28, Acharya posted screenshots of notifications received by Meta, which said that several of his earlier satirical posts were also being banned in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000.
On the same day, he posted the screenshot of his account getting restricted in India, contrasting it with a screenshot of Modi’s comment that “cartoons have healing power and cartoonists are closer to God”.
Speaking to Alt News, Acharya said he found out about his account being restricted while checking news reports on the increasing banning of accounts critical of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government. “I thought of checking my own Instagram account status and found that a list of posts were restricted in India, some of them were posted in 2023-24. By the end of day, I found that my entire profile has been restricted in India,” he said.
“For the last one decade, I have regularly faced restrictions on my cartoons on different social media platforms. (Their) aim was to restrict the reach…mostly during elections or major protests like CAA protests & farmers’ protests. This is the first time that my entire profile was restricted in India. It’s quite shameful that they (the government) are scared that the narratives created by the regime over the last two decades will be demolished by cartoons, journalists, and comedians,” he added.
He said that his reach has been affected after the ban, adding that he written to Meta’s grievance cell.

On September 27, cartoonist Manjul made a post X claiming that Instagram has restricted one of his illustrations in India. He also posted the notice from Instagram, which claimed that this particular post’s access has been restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law enforcement”. (Archive)

I am posting the cartoon again, along with the notice I received from Instagram.

The cartoon, posted on Manjul’s Instagram account on September 24, showed that an electronic voting machine (EVM) with three candidates — the three election commissioners. However, when a person was seen voting for Vivek Joshi, the VVPAT showed that the vote was cast for CEC Gyanesh Kumar.

The satirical cartoon remains visible on both his Facebook and X profiles.
A report by The Indian Express, published on August 18, revealed that between March and July, the government issued a blocking order for online content every 68 seconds on average, which amounted to 1,275 such cases daily and around 2 lakh cases over a period of five months.
According to that report, this government takedowns surged specifically after the Cockroach Janta Party-led students’ protest against the NEET exam irregularities in June and July. Although the government took down social media posts from Facebook, Instagram and YouTube as well, Instagram faced maximum content restrictions given that its user demographic is mostly the Gen-Z. According to the report, out of the total blocking orders, 1,00,000 such orders were for Instagram only while Facebook and YouTube accounted for 80,000 and 15,000 takedown orders, respectively.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
Alt News had earlier reported that in February, the government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. The amendment reduced the time available to social media platforms to remove or disable access to unlawful content from 36 hours to three hours after receiving a valid court order or a “reasoned intimation” from the appropriate government or its authorised agency. This change was notified through a press brief on July 22.
Although the order focused predominantly on countering harms caused by AI generated content and information, critics believe that the amendments have served as a tool to curb anti-establishment content. In our reportage, we found that most of the blocking orders were issued through the Union Home Ministry’s Sahyog portal, a platform created to send such notices, under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000. These orders were issued by various central and state government agencies. Meta has also integrated its Application Programming Interface (API) with the Sahyog portal, enabling content flagged through government directions to be automatically removed from its platforms without being reviewed by a human executive.

Space has plenty of room for more megaconstellations, but only if all operators are willing to share information about where their satellites are and where they’re going, a top executive at SpaceX and its AI subsidiary said this week.
Michael Nicolls, SpaceX’s vice president for Starlink and president of Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, used a presentation Tuesday at the International Astronautical Congress in Turkey as a clarion call for improved data-sharing among satellite operators.
SpaceX’s Starlink constellation now has more than 11,000 satellites, about two-thirds of all active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit. Radars and telescopes routinely track thousands more pieces of space junk.
Starlink is, by far, the largest satellite constellation in operation today. But if you buy the buzz, Starlink is just the tip of the iceberg. SpaceX has revealed plans to launch up to a million satellites for a new constellation, called Starmind, to deploy AI computing capacity in low-Earth orbit. Amazon is in the early stages of launching a network of thousands of satellites to compete with Starlink, and two Chinese megaconstellations are now in full-scale deployment.
Law of large numbers
All of this raises the question of how to mitigate the risk of a collision in orbit, an event that could create thousands more pieces of space junk, potentially triggering a self-perpetuating cycle of debris generation. The risk of a collision on any given day is fantastically low. Space is vast and empty, and low-Earth orbit is a long way from filling up. SpaceX and most other Western operators de-orbit their rockets and satellites at the end of their missions to prevent additional debris in orbit.
“That said, the law of large numbers says that if it can happen, it will happen,” Nicolls said.
There’s still a long way to go to improve tracking, awareness, and coordination in orbit. This is sometimes called space traffic management. No global treaties or regulations require satellites to broadcast their locations and maneuvers or mandate coordination among satellite operators. Without rules of the road, it is up to governments and companies to set norms of behavior.
“Once you can track this debris, and if you can track it well, these are like obstacles on a road. If you can measure them, you can predict where they’re going to be, and you can avoid them,” Nicolls said. “What you can’t avoid is other operators who maneuver without telling you where they’re going to go. We have many examples of this on Starlink, unfortunately.”
Nicolls presented several examples of satellites from other operators closely approaching Starlink satellites as they zip around the Earth at 5 miles per second. The examples did not suggest nefarious intent, such as spying or an attempt at striking a Starlink in orbit. Instead, the other satellites conducted maneuvers and changed their trajectories without their owners informing anyone.
“Either they were not publishing their ephemeris to us, or they were not considering the ephemeris of others when they were maneuvering, and these led to conjunctions of tens of meters to hundreds of meters,” Nicolls said. “Way too close to comfort.”
Michael Nicolls, senior vice president of Starlink at SpaceX and president of xAI, speaks at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, Turkey, on Tuesday, October 6.
Credit:
International Astronautical Federation
Michael Nicolls, senior vice president of Starlink at SpaceX and president of xAI, speaks at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, Turkey, on Tuesday, October 6.
Credit:
International Astronautical Federation
An ephemeris contains information about a satellite’s location and movement. Some operators may not want to share this information, believing secrecy might provide a competitive or strategic advantage. But if spaceflight is to be sustainable, it is vital to err on the side of openness rather than secrecy.
“The minimum standard in low-Earth orbit needs to be that you know where your satellite is, and you know where it’s going. You need to be able to predict where your trajectory is, and that prediction needs to be reliable,” Nicolls said.
SpaceX lauds itself as the benchmark for orbital stewardship. It pretty much has to be, with so many Starlinks in orbit and so much of its business relying on space.
The company has lowered the altitude of the entire active Starlink constellation below 500 kilometers (310 miles), an adjustment that provides three benefits. It moved the network away from other heavily trafficked regions in low-Earth orbit, expedited reentry for any failed Starlink satellites, and improved service for Starlink customers. All of SpaceX’s new-generation Starlink V3 satellites, which began launching on the company’s Starship rocket last month, will fly even lower, at about 350 kilometers (217 miles).
SpaceX also publishes ephemeris data for its Starlink satellites and has asked other operators to share their data, too. Without ephemeris sharing, operators rely on tracking data or their own satellites’ collision avoidance capabilities.
A camera onboard a Starlink satellite captured this view showing a close encounter with another satellite in orbit.
Credit:
SpaceX
A camera onboard a Starlink satellite captured this view showing a close encounter with another satellite in orbit.
Credit:
SpaceX
Starlink satellites, for example, use onboard navigation cameras to detect other objects in orbit. SpaceX calls the system Stargaze, and it now tracks about 90 percent of maneuvering satellites that intersect Starlink orbits, Nicolls said.
That is good, but it would be better if all operators agreed to be more open about what their satellites are doing. It is now a “fairly common occurrence” that Starlink satellites detect an upcoming close encounter and autonomously maneuver out of the way, Nicolls said. If there’s not enough to steer away from a close encounter, Starlink satellites can hunker down at the time of greatest danger. These “ducking maneuvers” involve pointing the satellite to minimize the chance of a collision, Nicolls said.
Starlink satellites perform about 1,000 collision avoidance maneuvers per day to get out of the way of functioning satellites or bits of space debris. In the last few months, Nicolls said Starlink satellites have steered clear of about 650 active satellites from other operators. Only half of those 650 come from operators that participate in ephemeris sharing with SpaceX, he said.
What about China?
“In particular, it’s been very challenging to share data with international operators,” Nicolls said. “There has been good progress here. There have been some good stories here on how we’ve begun to share data. For example, we share data closely with the Chinese space station as well as some other Chinese satellite operators, but there are many that we do not, and we have no information about where those satellites are or where they’re going.”
A chart in Nicolls’ presentation suggested the problem largely lies with Chinese and Russian satellites. But some in the United States, Europe, and Japan also decline to share.
“My fundamental ask here is that we need to make headway here and begin sharing data across all vehicles, from whatever country you are, with us and with others, to promote a safe operating environment,” Nicolls said.
Nearly all Chinese satellite operators decline to publicly share their satellite ephemeris data.
Credit:
SpaceX
Nearly all Chinese satellite operators decline to publicly share their satellite ephemeris data.
Credit:
SpaceX
What do SpaceX’s competitors think? Ars asked the head of Amazon Leo, Rajeev Badyal, about coordinating with Starlink, his chief competitor in the satellite broadband market. Amazon has 396 satellites in orbit today, with hundreds more awaiting launch when their rockets are ready to take them to orbit.
“Space safety is paramount to us as well,” Badyal said. “Every launch we do, we actually coordinate with SpaceX. We coordinate with others who have satellites. We let them know where we’re going to drop them off, how we’re going to orbit raise, etc. So we have regular meetings with companies like SpaceX to exchange data.
“So, for us, sharing ephemeris or sharing the information necessary for space safety is a non-issue,” Badyal said. “We’re big proponents of making sure that all of us operate in this domain in space in a coordinated fashion because [the] consequences of not doing so are significant for everybody, and there’s no reason not to.”
Amazon Leo’s first-generation constellation will consist of 3,232 satellites, and the Federal Communications Commission in February approved Amazon’s request for a 4,504-satellite second-generation network. Amazon has filed for FCC approval for an additional 5,105 satellites for direct-to-device connectivity, but the company is still far from matching the size of the Starlink fleet.
“Obviously, SpaceX is the largest constellation out there,” Badyal said. “We work with them hand in hand. In terms of China and adversaries, that’s something I can’t comment on at the moment. At some point, we will have to coordinate, or it’ll end up being a negative thing for everybody, especially if they get to scale.”
